## C05 and U03 wiring notes

- **C05:** `startController` builds `ContextBranchService` (`services.branches`) and the state API offers `branch.open`, `branch.get`, `branch.apply`, `branch.suspend`, `branch.switch`, `branch.resume`, `branch.pending` and `branch.delegate` (each access check is the service's own; an unknown or unreadable branch reads as missing). A test through `startController` opens two branches, suspends and switches, and reads them back. Carrying a restore into the Pi conversation during dispatch is still the dispatcher's and G09's work.
- **U03:** `StartOptions.chat` (`interpreter`, and an optional `coordinator: { model, token }`) builds `ChatService` and `CoordinatorService` (`controller.chat`, `controller.coordinator`); absent, none is built. A coordinator whose credential is missing or invalid is now `unavailable`, never an error to the caller. A test starts a controller with a scripted interpreter and a coordinator whose model fails, and shows the chat answering and the records untouched while the coordinator is paused, running-but-failing, and stopped.
- **Decision on the dispatcher guard:** "every dispatched task carries an explicit project and checkout" is met for chat-originated work (the pins). A dispatcher-level refusal of any task without a `repositoryId` would stop research and documentation tasks that have no repository; the right guard is `resolveCheckout` before a worker starts for a task that names a repository (the `checkout_changed` protection), which is a later piece of dispatch work (S02 and H12), not part of U03.
- **Split out:** U03b (first release, feeds D03) backs the chat interpreter and the coordinator with the routed model client; U03c (optional, after the first release, feeds D05) makes the coordinator a hosted agent with its own lifecycle. Neither interpreter is backed by a model yet, so U03 stays planned until U03b is built.
- **Review fixes:** the coordinator's principal is resolved once per call and reused, so a credential revoked mid-call cannot throw out of `answer`, `decompose` or `assign`; the branch operations also include `branch.restore`, `branch.redirect`, `branch.append` and `branch.history` (a single suspended branch can come back); the chat is built without the approval profile (A07), status (U05) and policy edits (U04), so every order is a proposal until they are composed, and `StartOptions.chat` says so.

## M01 wiring notes (the meeting clock)

- `meetingLoops` (`dispatch/loops.ts`) is added to the composed dispatcher's loops: `meetings.tick` (every page of schedules, up to 10 pages a tick, so a backlog after downtime is worked off over ticks) and `meetings.invite` (for each project, the invitations of every planned occurrence go to the sink; the service withholds the paused and unavailable and sends nothing for a catch-up report or a settled meeting). `DispatchStartOptions.invitations` is the sink; without it invitations are decided and recorded but nothing is sent, and nobody provides a production sink yet (the host decides how an agent is reached).
- M01 stays planned: its blocker U03 is not implemented.

## Chat composition: policy, status, policy edits

- `startController` with `chat` now builds `PolicyService`, `StatusService` and `PolicyEditService` and gives them to `ChatService`, so the approval profile (A07), status explanations (U05) and conversational policy edits (U04) apply instead of every order being a proposal. The stall service is not passed to status (L01 leaves it unbuilt at start), so stall concerns are not shown there.

## C07b: MCP results framed as data

- A confirmed MCP tool call's text is now returned (and summarised on the operation) as: a notice that it is output from the external server and is data, a warning line when it contains phrases that read as instructions, the text scrubbed of credentials and cut at `MCP_LIMITS.text` (20,000 characters), and a note when cut. Test: a long answer containing "ignore all previous instructions" is flagged, cut and bounded.
- Still open: the limit is fixed, not scaled to the model's window, and the cut part is not spilled for paging (`limitTool` needs the window of the attempt's route, which the tool service does not hold).

## U03b (part): the model-backed chat interpreter; C07b: context limits reach the worker

- `ModelInterpreter` (`chat/model-interpreter.ts`) is a `ChatInterpreter` over a `ModelCall` port (`complete(route, {system, user})`). The prompt separates the owner's words from fenced quoted material (a fence inside quoted text is broken), lists the operations, and tells the model to report instructions found in quotes as `basis: "quoted"`. Routes are read at each message and tried in order; an answer that is not a valid intent list counts as that route failing. All failing: `unavailable`, which the chat already turns into "unavailable, nothing done". U03b stays planned: there is no concrete `ModelCall` yet (the routed client with R02's failure classes, budget and effect rules is not built for controller-side calls), and the recorded-model scenarios of the card are not written.
- `local.build` now receives `context(order)`: tool output cut to the window's share (`toolOutputChars`) and the extractive compaction fallback. The operator passes it as `LocalHostOptions.context`. An integration test over the real sandbox and worker process shows the start message carries it. Open: nothing in the shipped composition builds the host, so the operator still has to pass it through.
- **Review fixes (MCP framing, interpreter, limits):** MCP text is redacted before it is cut; a replay is framed again from the stored summary; a failed MCP call's error text carries the data notice; the framing ends with a closing line; the tool-output limit is clamped to the channel's bound; the interpreter treats a reply with no list as "no intents" (so a refusal does not send the same prompt to a weaker route), and fences proposals, the pending question and the project name.

## C07b close-out, and the C06 and L05 decisions

- **First call checked against the provider's count (C07b):** `ModelRelay.forAttempt({ onFirstUsage })` reads `prompt_tokens` or `input_tokens` from the first successful reply (the first and last 16 KB of it; the reply passes on unchanged; a failing reporter or a failed call changes nothing) and reports it with the request's length. The composer hands `local.build` `confirmFirstCall(order, usage)`, which records it against the attempt's latest admitted first call (`confirmUsage`, which calibrates the route). The operator passes it as `onFirstUsage` when it builds the relay; tests cover the relay (OpenAI-style plain and streamed, Anthropic-style streamed, no count, first call only) and the guard.
- **Split to C07d (feeds D03):** the route change to a smaller window (`changeRoute`) has no caller because nothing in the dispatcher changes a running attempt's route; and MCP results use one fixed bound (20,000 characters) rather than the window's limit with a spill. Both clauses moved to the new card C07d with their acceptance text; they are not dropped.
- **C06:** "tests against recorded responses" is now written as responses simulated from each backend's documentation or source (that is what the tests use); capturing responses from running servers and re-testing the profiles against them is added to G10, which already measures the real backends. Decision for the owner, recorded in `build-decisions-for-owner.md`.
- **L05:** the service meets its own clauses and `guardFor` is used in production. Feeding the model's stream into `begin`/`record`/`complete` needs stream events the Pi adapter does not expose, so it is the new card L05b (feeds G09). Optional decoder resume stays unsupported and is qualified separately, as the card says.
- **Review fixes (first-call count):** `local.build` also receives `attemptRelay(order, relay, { model?, cache? })`, one relay per attempt with the first-call count already going to `confirmFirstCall` (operators use it instead of `relay.forAttempt`, which made a new "first call" for every request); a token-count probe is not the call; the count is reported only when the reply ended normally and the number is complete; Anthropic-style counts add the cache read and creation tokens; a count above four windows or under half a character a token is not recorded; the calibration keeps a decayed higher earlier ratio (80%); the admission round is remembered only for an admitted call and forgotten once used.

## U03b (part): the chat's model call; second-round review fixes

- `HttpModelCall` (`chat/http-model.ts`) is a `ModelCall` over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (the owner's endpoint configuration, credential read at each call): one unstreamed completion, no randomness, a 1 MB reply bound, a time limit. A failure is thrown with R02's class (credit, rate-limit, outage, auth, ...) and a short redacted text; `ModelInterpreter` falls back to the next route. U03b stays planned until the routed budget and effect rules of R02 are applied to these calls and the recorded-model scenarios are written; the pieces (interpreter, model call) now exist.
- **Fixes after the second review:** a replayed MCP answer says when only the first part of the earlier answer is kept; a restricted result's placeholder is not framed as server output; output bytes are those of the raw text; the "error text from the external MCP server" notice goes only on errors the executor reported; the per-attempt relay entry expires even when the order's expiry does not parse; the test that claimed to cover the impossible-count check now reaches it.

## L01 close-out and the H12 audit (2026-10-26)

- `startController` builds `StallService` with the pause lookup (a task under a pause is assessed as paused, never stalled) and gives it to the status service and to `services.stall`. Nothing runs its `scan`, and nothing builds the `Reconciler`, in production: the dispatcher principal holds no grants and `scan` needs the recovery-read right everywhere, which widens what a controller service may read; whether to give the dispatcher that right or a narrower scan right is an owner decision (build-decisions-for-owner.md). The work is the new card L01b (feeds D03); L01's own clauses (pause gates, availability hook, settlement, restart) are met by the services, the composition and their tests.
- **H12 audit:** the dispatcher, the credential issue, the tool gate, the ledger, quiesce, the pause and message guards, the cache and the MCP guard are composed and tested (the quiesce coordinator is built, but no production code calls its `around` yet). Two clauses depend on other cards, not on more H12 code: the owner question for a missing grant is a `grant_needed` blocker until U11b makes it a Needs-you item, and the real-launcher restart from a checkpoint is shown by a new integration test (`h12j-worker-gaps.test.ts`: the first process ends, a new turn in the second process reaches the model with the first answer in front of it, and the provider key is not on either channel). It does not show the freeze and settle before the restart, a recipe that is actually narrower, or the notice to the agent on widening; those stay with the fake-handle tests of the dispatcher. L01's clause that a paused agent keeps its tasks rests on `PauseService.assertRetained`, tested but not yet called by any reassignment path; that call is part of L01b. The note that no quarantine operation exists was out of date: `worker/src/sandbox/quarantine.ts` exists and `quiesce.around` accepts a quarantine operation; the composition that wraps one around the other is not built (nothing in production calls `around` or `quarantine`).

## T07 notes: durable job records and job control (2026-10-26)

`packages/controller/src/jobs/jobs.ts` (`JobService`, `controller.services.jobs`), `jobs.test.ts` (10 tests on each of the four backends). New rights `job.write` (the host or worker records a job), `job.control` (stop, reconcile, decide after a restart) and `job.read`; new `PauseService.backgroundDenied` and `McpService.usable`.

- **The handle.** The job ID is derived from the task and the caller's operation ID, so asking for the same operation twice (a retry, a restart of the worker) is one job: the same command ID answers `replayed`, a new command for the same operation is refused as already admitted. The record lives in storage, so a new controller process reads it (tested with a second service over the same store).
- **State machine.** admitted, dispatched, running, completed, failed, cancellation_requested, cancelled, outcome_unknown, with the allowed moves in one table; history keeps the last 32 moves. Output is bounded (the last 8 KB kept, 64 KB at a time, secrets redacted on the way in, the byte count kept). Logs and artifacts are artifact IDs (not checked for existence here).
- **Resumability.** Stated at admission, never implied: `none`, `tool_checkpoint` (only a tool can leave one) and `remote_tracked` (only a remote job or MCP operation). A restart from a checkpoint is refused for anything else.
- **Three stop operations.** The kind decides: a model request is cancelled, a tool is stopped, a remote job (and an MCP operation) is stopped remotely, each recorded as its own operation. The request and the host's confirmation are separate; an uncooperative stop is recorded and the job stays in cancellation_requested; orphans the stop could not end are recorded on the job. The process-tree termination itself is the sandbox launcher's (A03: process groups on POSIX, job objects on Windows); binding its result to `confirmCancel` is T07b.
- **Pause.** A foreground job is not admitted for a paused task. A permitted background job is, unless a gate on the task's chain said `background: deny`; reports and results are always accepted; a finished background job is handed to `PauseService.recordBackground` (a command derived from the job, so repeating the finish repeats nothing) and the pause stays. The principal that finishes the job needs the right to record a background result.
- **After a restart.** `live` lists the jobs that were not finished (tracked exceptions are left out); `decide` completes one from stated evidence, cancels it, restarts it from its tool checkpoint, or keeps it as a tracked exception under a named owner.
- **Outcome unknown.** A job whose result is ambiguous holds in `outcome_unknown` (no report, no finish, no cancel) until `reconcile` records the evidence, in a record of its own; `unresolved(task)` lists what a dependent action must wait for.
- **MCP.** An MCP operation is a job with a server ID. Admission asks a `JobConnections.usable` port; `startController` binds none (there is no MCP client), so no MCP job is admitted in production yet; `McpService.usable` is the intended binding.
- **After the first review (all fixed):** a finished background job is recorded through `PauseService.recordFinishedJob`, which needs no `assignment.manage` (a worker holding only `job.write` would otherwise commit its finish and be refused the pause record); a repeated `admit` is answered from its record whatever has changed since (the task checks run inside the command); `decide` cannot settle an outcome-unknown job (only `reconcile`, with evidence, or a tracked exception); output is redacted again over the joined tail (a secret split across reports), NUL is dropped, lone surrogates repaired and the cut never starts inside a character (the 8,192-character limit counts characters, not bytes); orphan descriptions are redacted, never refused; logs and artifacts must exist and belong to the job's project; Force Stop is a recorded step of its own (`requestCancel` with `force`, once, as the escalation of a stop that was not obeyed or asked for at once); reconciliations are listed from the job; a missing task reads as forbidden to a stranger; only a lost revision race is retried. **Second review:** the rest of a secret that began in an earlier report is removed from the next one; `recordFinishedJob` checks itself (the reference must be a background job of that task that has ended); `admit` locks the pause gates in its commit; artifact references are checked inside the command. **Fourth review:** private-key blocks that are open at the end of a report are dropped through their END line across reports (header split, last block of several, bounded at 16 KiB). Known limit: an END line that is itself split over two reports is not recognised, so up to 16 KiB of later output is dropped. Known limit: with a pause that denies background work, a worker's finish commits and the pause record is refused on every retry until the pause is resumed.
- **Not done (T07b):** the agent-facing job tools of the bridge, the launcher result bound to the stop confirmation, the MCP client and its connection check bound in `startController`, state API reads of jobs, running the restart decisions at controller start (nothing calls `live` and `decide` by itself) and relaunching a tool from its checkpoint (`restart` only records the decision and moves the job to dispatched). Limits: the list operations scan the job records of the store (a page of 1,000 at a time); concurrent reports on one job meet a revision check and are retried.

## U03b notes

- `chat/routed-model.ts` is the routed client for the controller's own model calls (owner chat interpreter, coordinator). `chatRoutes(routing, {role,...})` reads the routing table at each call and returns the eligible routes in order (a role with no profile or no table has none, so the chat reports itself unavailable and does nothing). `GuardedModelCall` wraps any `ModelCall`: credit/auth failures block the provider's routes until `unblock`; a rate limit cools a route for 60 s, an outage for 300 s; other failures affect that call only. The calls carry no tools and change nothing, so trying the next route repeats no effect.
- `HttpModelCall.completeDetailed` returns the endpoint's own token counts when they are whole numbers; `ChatSpendService` keeps the owner's optional daily token cap (`chat-budget`) and the UTC day's count (`chat-spend`). At the cap no call is made. Calls in flight together can overshoot by their own size. Cost in money is not computed here; routes' prices belong to R03.
- `ModelCoordinatorModel` builds the prompt for answer/decompose/assign, fences record and task text so it cannot close the fence, and returns the JSON object found in the reply; the coordinator still validates every field. The coordinator takes `routes` (called at each question) and `agents` (the active agents shown for assignment).
- The coordinator lists the agents it may assign to as its own principal, so it needs `agent.read`; without it no assignment is proposed (the coordinator never errors for it). A failure to count a paid call is reported to `onSpendFailure` and the reply is still used, so the next route never repeats a paid call. The prompt fence breaks up any run of three or more bracket characters.
- Not done: wiring `GuardedModelCall`/`chatRoutes` from configuration in the controller's start-up command line, a `chat.budget` right in the state API, and measured prompt-reading speed per route (V01b).

## F04k notes

- `startController` checks the file systems of the registered projects' checkouts at every start: after the storage is open and the epoch taken it lists the projects, takes each repository location that is a local absolute path (a URL is not a workspace), and runs the F04h filesystem check on the ones not already named in `workspaceRoots`. The decision is made again with those problems added to the earlier ones: refused with the F04h message and switch unless the override was given, and then printed once more (only the new lines) and audited in the one `environment.override` record. A refused start through this path has already opened the storage and taken the epoch; it releases both (the surrounding try/catch closes them).
- Archived projects are skipped. Cost: the check runs once per distinct checkout path, one detection each (on macOS and Windows that is a process per path, and the naming probe writes and removes one small directory inside each existing checkout); a fleet of thousands of checkouts would want detection per mount point. `Controller.filesystems` lists the checkout reports too.
- Limit: a project registered after start is not checked until the next start; a checkout created at a path that does not exist yet is judged by its nearest existing directory.

## R05b notes

- The dispatcher holds an attempt's allowance before it starts (`#reserve`, just before the worker is started, after the place is held): for each dimension in which the task's budget has a limit (a limit of 0 states none), the smaller of what the attempt may use (the contract's `maxMinutes` or the attempt's own expiry in milliseconds for compute; `reserveCostMicros` for money, default none) and what the task still has available. The reservation's command ID derives from the attempt, so a repeat after a crash finds it; the reservation ID and a running tally of the attempt's use are kept on the attempt record. A task with no budget holds nothing; a task whose limited allowance has none free is not started (check `budget`, tried again at the next tick; its place is given back).
- While a reservation is held, a turn's cost and compute are added to the attempt's tally and **settled once when the attempt ends** (the hold already counts against the task); the turn's cache figures are still recorded turn by turn. A use above the hold is recorded by the budget service as overrun. When the worker was lost (lease ran out, or the attempt expired) the hold is marked **uncertain** instead and stays at its full amount until someone settles it with what actually happened. A controller-side Stop of a live attempt settles to the tally.
- Not done: the production start does not set `reserveCostMicros` (no money is held unless an owner sets it), and nothing reconciles an uncertain hold by itself; a person or a later reconciler calls `settle`. The three ceilings agree by taking the smallest of the contract's time, the attempt's expiry and the free allowance for compute; R02's cumulative budget is a ceiling of the routing layer and is not read here.
- **After review:** the amounts to hold are written to the attempt (`reserving`) before the budget is asked, so a repeat after a crash (or a second dispatcher) asks for the same thing and finds the same hold; usage reports are added to the tally once per key (the last 200 keys are kept with a digest; a different report under the same key is refused with `command_conflict`); an attempt that holds nothing yet and finds none of a limited allowance free (held by other work or by a lost attempt's uncertain hold) opens the budget blocker instead of waiting silently; only a lost lease marks the hold uncertain (an expiry the controller itself ended settles to the tally). Known limit: a lost attempt's tally is not settled, its whole hold stays uncertain until reconciled by hand.

## F04j notes (sandbox and limits as start-up prerequisites)

- A controller that builds a local worker host (`dispatch.local`) now requires the sandbox tools and the limits mechanism at start, through the one prerequisite list and its message (what was found, what is required, how to install it, and that a missing tool cannot be overridden). `StartOptions.features` still says it explicitly (a test, or a controller whose workers are all remote). The launcher's own health check remains the second line: it refuses to advertise capacity if the tools disappear later.

## U03c notes (the coordinator through the owner's chat)

- A new intent `coordinator` carries what the owner says to the coordinator: `answer` (a question, answered from the records with citations, or an inquiry when the records are insufficient), `decompose` (an outcome, drafted as a proposal that exists only after the owner applies it), `assign` (hand out the open tasks: proposed, or made if the coordinator holds the right), `configure` (its principal and up to four routes) and `start` / `pause` / `stop`. The text fields must be the owner's own words (the same check as any command), the project is the one named or in focus, and each item is applied once under a command ID derived from the turn. The chat reaches the coordinator through a lookup (`ChatDeps.coordinator`) because the coordinator is built after it; with none, the item is refused as unavailable.
- The coordinator lists the active agents under its own grants (needs `agent.read`; without it the list is empty and nothing is proposed for assignment). The composed-controller test covers set-up and start through chat, an answer with a cited desk record, a drafted plan applied by a later message, assignment with the agent list shown to the model, a text the owner did not say, and pausing.
- Not done: a state-API operation for the coordinator's lifecycle (it is reached by chat and by the in-process handle), and production configuration of the chat and the routed model at start (U03b notes).

## H05b notes (reviewer routing in the running controller)

- The dispatcher's tick now runs `reviews.sweep` for every project (`reviewLoops`, dispatch/loops.ts): a waiting review takes a reviewer once one is eligible; a review whose reviewer is held, paused, stopped or past the deadline moves on under the project policy, ending with the owner. Nothing is approved by waiting.
- `ReviewService.sweep` accepts the controller's own service principal (a service with no task scope) without a project grant, as the other dispatcher loops do; every other caller still needs `review.policy.write`. That principal can neither decide a review nor set the policy (tested).
- `start.ts` binds `reviewerHost` to `dispatch.hostOfAgent`: the host of the agent's live attempt (first found). A lost host moves the review at once; a silent one waits. Without a live attempt the host is not judged (`unknown`).
- The host is the running attempt's host or, for an attempt that was moved, the host it is pinned to; a failing lookup means the host is not judged. Cost: each judgement scans the live attempts (no per-tick memo yet).
- Known limits: `wakeList` still has no caller (waking a reviewer is the attempt admission path); `hostStaleAfterMs` keeps its default.

## L01b notes (reconciler and stall detection in the running controller)

- New action `recovery.stall-scan` (security/access.ts). `StallService.scan` accepts the owner, a service holding `recovery.stall-scan` on "*", or a service holding `recovery.read` on "*"; nothing else (a project-scoped grant, a bare service and agents are refused; tested on all four backends). The right permits the scan only: it gives no read of any record and is not the broad right.
- `recoveryLoops` (dispatch/loops.ts) adds two loops to the dispatcher's tick: `recovery.reconcile` (the `Reconciler` pass) and `recovery.stall-scan` (paged scan). A dispatcher that lacks the right is told to the owner once per epoch as a maintenance notice (`stall-off:<epoch>`, coalesced with the other dispatcher notice) and the scan is skipped, so the tick does not fail each time. The owner grants `recovery.stall-scan` to `service:dispatcher` at set-up.
- `start.ts` builds the `Reconciler` with the pause lookup (an inbox message for a paused task stays received), the wait service and the inbox/effect services. Delivery destinations and effect bridges are not built yet, so `destinations` and `bridges` are empty: it repairs task events, admits inbox messages, recovers effects (reports unbridged ones) and settles waits.
- The scan reads the dispatcher principal again each tick, so a right granted or revoked while the controller runs takes effect at the next tick (no restart); its cursor is kept between ticks and wraps, so every assignment is reached however many there are; a notice that failed is tried again.
- Known limits: reassignment through the pause service's retention check still has no caller; the acceptance sentence "a paused task is not reported stalled" rests on the existing `isPaused` option of the stall service (tested in health/stall.test.ts), and the composed test proves the loops and the right, not a time-driven stall.

## U03e notes (the owner grants and revokes rights)

- State API: `grant.create`, `grant.revoke` (commands), `grant.get`, `grant.list` (queries). All owner-only: the service checks the owner itself (`requireOwner`), and `list` is new in `GrantService`. `grant.create` always records source `direct`, and takes no resource or terms; a service may hold only recovery actions and a client only conversation actions (unchanged), and the grantee must exist.
- Chat: `grant.create` and `grant.revoke` are chat operations in `propose` mode: a right is always shown first and applies only when the owner says so. Every text of the command (grantee, action, basis, reason, grant ID) must be in the owner's own words; only `project` is treated as a reference. The revision for a revoke is read when the proposal is drawn up and stored in its steps (a grant's revision moves only on revoke, so a second revoke is refused as stale).
- A right given while the controller runs counts at the next check; the dispatcher's stall scan reads its principal every tick (L01b). `docs/nimblenewt/grant-stall-scan.md` is now the one-step instruction.
- Known limits: no grant of a single resource or time-limited terms through the API or chat yet (`notBefore` and `expiresAt` are accepted); derived and standing grants and restrictions (`restrict`) are not exposed; the chat cannot list grants, so a revoke needs the grant ID.
- Chat grants take one plain form only: "give <principal> the <action> right everywhere permanently" (or in a project ID). Every word beyond the principal, the action, the scope and a short filler list (please, the, right, to, in, all, every, project(s)...) refuses the message, so no limit, negation or change can be hidden in wording; the reason recorded with the right is the owner's message itself (the model's basis is ignored). Limited rights use `grant.create` with `expiresAt`. The proposal line ends "(permanent: no end time)".
  - **Superseded (see “A grant with no limit or no end is a proposal that says so, not a phrase (Pi, 2026-11-09)”, review fix):** the one plain form, the leftover-word scan, the `/permanently/` and `/everywhere/` checks and their "Say only: give <who> …" refusals are removed. A right given in chat is still always a proposal and still has no end; its line now says the consequence in plain words — `(no end: it never runs out and stays until you revoke it; everywhere: it covers every project, including ones made later)` — and the owner's confirmation of that line is the consent. Grantee, action and project ID are still whole-word value guards; a missing scope is asked as a question; model-supplied `expiresAt`/`notBefore` are still not drawn up in chat.

No MCP transport exists yet (T05).
- U05: `api/start-status.test.ts` proves through `startController` that the owner chat answers a task question, an overview and the noticeboard from the records, every line cites a record, nothing is written, and an unknown task is not answered. The service-level detail (freshness, blockers kinds, tools used) stays proven in `chat/status.test.ts`.
- U05 follow-up (same run): `start.ts` now builds the `WatchService` (event watches) and gives it to the composed `StatusService` (`watch`, so the failed event queue can be listed in the running controller (inspecting a seeded failure is proven at service level only: status.test.ts, watchers.test.ts)) and to the state API (`watches`, so the `events.watch*` operations are served). The composed status test also asks for changes, tools, delivered and the failed queue. Artifact verification (`verifyArtifact`) still needs a blob store the controller does not build, so delivered artifacts show `not_checked`: card U05b. ## H06c notes (idle-expiry notices in the running controller)

- The composed `EventService` is built with `notify: noticeThroughNotifications(notifications)`, so an idle expiry that left events waiting files one maintenance notice for the owner (commandId `events-expired-<subscription>-<time>`; the next ticks add none). The expiry is in the activity record (`events.expire`).
- A subscription made before idle expiry existed has no stored idle time (it uses the owner-configured one, default 900 seconds) and no last activity, which counted idle from the day it was made. `EventService.stampIdle` gives each such active subscription the time of the call as its last activity; the composer runs it once at start (repeating changes nothing), and a test seeds a subscription made long ago with no last activity and shows it is not expired by the first sweep.
- State API: `events.configure-idle` (owner) and `events.cancel` (the subscriber or the owner). `start.ts` gives the API its own `EventService` on the same store.
- Known limit: the U11b notice kind does not exist yet, so the notice is the generic `maintenance` kind.
## R05c notes (budgets in the state API and the request notice)

- `BudgetService` takes a `notify` hook: after a new request for more budget (not a replay) it is told `{ requestId, taskId, parentTaskId?, to, requestedBy, costMicros, computeMs }`. A failing hook never fails the request. `start.ts` binds it: a request addressed to `owner` files one `maintenance` notice (commandId `bgt-req-<request>`, ref `budget-request`), with only the controller's own facts (the requester's reason is read in the request, never put in the notice).
- State API: `budget.report`, `budget.usage`, `budget.pending`, `budget.get-request` (queries) and `budget.request-more`, `budget.decide` (commands), with the service's own rights (a task you may not read reads as missing; the requester, the addressee and the owner read a request; the owner or the addressed holder decides). The report shows in-flight and uncertain charges.
- A repeat of `budget.request-more` tells again (the notice has its own command ID, so it is filed once), which mends a call that crashed between the commit and the notice. A task credential may not use `budget.pending` or `budget.usage` and reads only its own task's request.
- Known limit: a request addressed to a delegated holder files no notice: the holder finds it in `budget.pending`. Telling an agent is card R05e (below).
## R03 notes (difficulty profiles in the state API)

- State API: `difficulty.profiles`, `difficulty.set-profiles`, `difficulty.set`, `difficulty.delegate`, `difficulty.reassign-parent`, `difficulty.delegation`, `escalation.request`, `escalation.decide`, `escalation.list`, `routing.decisions`, `routing.decision`, with the service's own rights. `start.ts` builds `DifficultyService` on the routing and contract services.
- The composed test proves: no built-in profiles; non-owner cannot set or read them; a bad proposal applies nothing; the parent (the delegating caller) sets difficulty and a non-parent without a grant cannot; a child's escalation without recorded attempts is refused; reads of unreadable tasks show nothing. The full escalation, retry and total-budget paths stay proven in `difficulty.test.ts`; a composed path that drives real attempts, an approved escalation and a dispatch that uses the chosen profile is not in this test: the dispatcher already calls `resolve` in production (dispatch-compose), but this test starts no dispatcher, so "selects the configured profile at dispatch" is proven at service level only. Rights: `difficulty.profiles` also allows `config.read`; `difficulty.delegate` and `escalation.decide` also allow holders of `task.difficulty.write`; a task credential reaches only its own task. `difficulty.reassign-parent` is covered at service level only.

## C08 notes (owner decisions in the state API)

- State API: `decision.record` (owner only; the direct channel is forced, so no caller can claim a chat turn), `decision.resolve-dispute`, `decision.ask`, `decision.dismiss-question`, `decision.link`, `decision.revalidate`, `decision.close-follow-up` and the queries `decision.get`, `.history`, `.authoritative`, `.context`, `.reliance`, `.propagation`, each with the service's own rights.
- `start.ts` builds a `DecisionService` for the API with the event and effect services. The dispatcher keeps its own instance (with generation); correctness lives in stored records and the stored guard, so the two agree.
- Composed test proves: non-owner refused; hypothetical words record nothing; repeat is not a new decision; a correction supersedes and the old stays visible marked; a stale session's conflicting word is surfaced, not applied; an implementation-hold gate blocks at the stored guard.
- Not done here (card C08b): recording from a chat turn (the chat interpreter's decision intent, which needs the turn's wording check), interrupting a running generation from the API's instance, and a composed run of link/propagate/revalidate across a paused and a restarted agent.

## M01 notes (meetings in the state API)

- State API: `meeting.schedule`, `meeting.update-schedule`, `meeting.call-urgent`, `meeting.settle` (commands) and `meeting.schedule-get`, `meeting.occurrence`, `meeting.planned` (queries), with `MeetingService`'s own rights (`meeting.manage` to schedule or call, project agenda rights for the rest). `start.ts` builds the service with `inquiries` and the pause service's availability. A schedule must name its `timeZone` here: the owner's `meeting.timeZone` setting is not wired into the API instance (card M01c); the dispatcher's instance runs the clock and invitations.
- Composed test (the schedule starts the day after the real clock, so the slot is unambiguous; the dispatcher's clock is simulated): a schedule through the API is created once per command ID; an agent without `meeting.manage` is refused; nothing exists before the slot; ticking at the slot creates one on-time occurrence however often the dispatcher ticks; after a restart two days on one catch-up occurrence (mode `catch-up`, `skippedCount` at least 1, a new ID) stands for the missed slots; a second restart at the same moment creates nothing more. An urgent call is accepted and readable.
- Not in the composed test, so M01 is partly proven: absent and paused participants withheld without a wake through the composed API with real agent records (proven in `meetings.test.ts`), agenda retained across occurrences, delivery of invitations (no host sink composed). These are cards M01b (participants, agenda through the API) and M01c (the owner's `meeting.timeZone` setting in the API instance, and the invitation sink).
## H02 notes (remote workers composed into the controller)

- New `RemoteWorkerHost` (production `WorkerHost` over `RemoteWorkerService.place`; the operator supplies what an attempt needs of the host (`requirements`, never a default policy) and its inputs). `dispatch.remote` in `startController` takes `blobDirectory` (the controller's own artifact folder), optional transport settings (loopback by default; beyond it `allowRemote`, TLS and `publicHosts`), the protocol range and the hosts. The composer builds the artifact and remote services, adds the hosts after the local ones, binds the dispatcher's `storeOwner` to `RemoteWorkerService.storeOwner`, listens, and closes the listener with the workers. `DispatchHandle.workerUrl` says where workers connect.
- Review fixes: a handle acts only under its own placement number (after a move an old handle controls nothing); the checkpoint wait compares the placement's sequence instead of reading the blob each poll and defaults to 5 seconds (shutdown waits that long per remote attempt); a failed listen closes the local worker host.
- Composed test (proves only composed placement and protocol negotiation): an incompatible protocol is refused at connect; a compatible worker connects, is offered the attempt placed by the dispatcher's tick, receives the controller's own order, and its host credential is refused (`forbidden`) when it tries to create a project; `hostOfAgent` names the remote host.
- (The `requirements` refusal is now proven; the rest stands.) Unproven in the composed controller (card H02b): partition and delayed-packet fencing, an unsupported host failing visibly (`requirements` refusal), no self-promotion, relocation with integrity and policy refusals, the exclusive native-store owner, result/stop/checkpoint paths through the production host, and failure paths after a successful listen (driver or MCP construction) closing the listener. These are proven in `remote/*.test.ts` with a test host class against the same services.
- Not composed: the operator-facing configuration of hosts and their requirements from a settings file (the options are code-level here), and the exclusive-store-owner check across two live remote hosts in the composed controller.
- Known limits recorded for card H02b (second review): the placement check in the handle is check-then-act (`control()` takes no placement number, so a move committing between the check and the control call lands the old handle's message in the new placement); the checkpoint wait does not re-check the placement and a new host's checkpoint can satisfy an old handle's wait (the sequence carries over a move); a failure of `FileBlobStore.open` or remote-service construction after the local host was built still leaves that host open.

## R05e: a delegated holder is told of a request addressed to it

- `AgentMessageService.noticeFromController` files a notice from the controller itself as advice in the holder's inbox, the way an escalation is: it needs no sender principal and no right, so no agent or conversation can use it and the dispatcher's service principal is not widened (the earlier branch hand-built a `service:controller` principal; that was dropped). It is not an API operation.
- The notice names the requesting task and is filed on the parent task, the one the holder holds. It never wakes anyone: the holder reads it at a boundary, a paused or suspended holder keeps it queued (a stopped one, with reach `unavailable`), and it is never an interruption.
- Not lost under backpressure: a full inbox is `unavailable` and stores nothing; the dispatcher's loop `budgets.notifyHolders` (`BudgetService.openForHolders`) tells every holder with an open request on each tick, and filing is idempotent on the command, so a notice that could not be filed, or whose creating call crashed after the commit, is filed on a later tick and never twice. A holder who is not an agent, or can neither read the task nor (when the caller names `admit: budget.manage`, as the budget path does) hold `budget.manage` on it, is skipped (the request stays in `budget.pending` and the owner may decide it); one bad request never holds back the others, and its fault is reported after the rest were tried. Controller notices share the per-sender share of an inbox (`perSenderQueue`), so a requester cannot crowd out a holder's other peer messages (the share is also used by escalations, so a holder with many unread escalations is told of a request late, once it has read some, never lost). A repeat of a request that is already decided tells nobody. Only agent holders are told (a `host:` holder reads `budget.pending`). A request decided between the loop's look and the filing may still get one stale notice; the loop looks at each open request's tree on every tick, which costs more as requests accumulate.
- Deviation from the card text: the notice uses the reserved sender `controller` that escalations already use rather than a provisioned principal record; nothing is forged and no principal gains a right. Recorded for the owner to confirm.
- The retry for a full inbox runs in the dispatcher's tick, so a controller started without a dispatcher retries only when the requester repeats the command.
- Tested: the message service (once, advice, no interruption, paused keeps it queued, refused for a stranger and for a full inbox then filed once there is room), the loop (full inbox retried, forbidden skipped, a real fault surfaces), and the composed controller (told on request, once on repeat, mended by a tick after a lost notice, not announced again once decided); also that a recipient who cannot read the task is refused unless `admit: budget.manage` is named, the per-sender cap, and an unknown `admit` or a non-agent recipient is refused.
- Known limits: the loop scans at most `BUDGET_LIMITS.scan` request records a tick, in storage order (by ID hash, not age), so with more than that many request records an open request past the limit is never found by the loop, and `budget.pending` has the same limit and says `truncated`, so the holder reads each task's `budget.report` for it; the holder is told nothing when its request is decided (the requester finds out by reading its budget).
## H12l and H12d: workspace operations behind the quiesce

- `WorkspaceOpService` (`workspace-ops/`) is the controller's side of integration, checkout refresh and quarantine of a task's work: operations `workspace.request` (`integration`, `refresh`, `quarantine`) and `workspace.get`. The caller needs the new action `workspace.manage` on the task's project, held exactly (a wildcard grant is not enough; the owner always may; a task credential never does; a caller without it reads as `not_found`).
- The request is recorded before anything runs (`workspace-request`, state `started`). The host is asked through `WorkerHost.workspace` (a `WorkspacePort`) only inside `QuiesceCoordinator.around` for the task: every live attempt has new calls refused, calls in flight settled and a checkpoint taken, and is released afterwards whatever the result. If an attempt cannot be made quiet (a failed checkpoint, or a call that ignores the stop signal) the host is not asked and the answer is `refused` with the `runtime_hold` blocker; a host that says no is `refused`; a host that throws is `failed`.
- One operation runs per task at a time in the controller (a second is `unavailable`). The task's live attempts are written into the record before anything is frozen (an attempt that starts later is found by recovery through the task's live attempts and the tag), each freeze carries the request's ID in its reason, and an index record per task names the request that is open on it. A repeat of a command returns the recorded answer; a repeat while the first call is still working is `uncertain` for the repeat (the first call keeps its freeze and writes the real outcome over it). A request left open by a stopped controller is resolved by the dispatcher's `workspace.recover` loop (which reads only the open index) or by the next request for that task, whichever comes first: its own freeze is lifted first (only one that carries its ID, never anybody else's, not even another workspace request's), then it is recorded as `uncertain`, and the operation is never run again.
- A host's summary is cut and redacted; its detail is kept only when it is plain JSON under 4000 bytes (UTF-8) with nothing credential-shaped in it.
- The host is the one that runs the task's live attempt; with no live attempt it is the only host that has a `workspace` port, and with several such hosts and no live attempt it is not found and the request is `refused` (`no host that can do this holds the checkout`).
- Proven here with simulated hosts, through the service and through the state API of the composed controller: the in-flight call settles before the host is asked, nothing is left frozen, the attempt continues, the blocker is typed (checkpoint failure and a call that ignores the stop), rights and replay, concurrency, redaction, crash recovery.
- Known limits, all carried by card H12m: no production host provides a `workspace` port yet (a request is answered `refused`); an attempt that starts while an operation runs is not held back; the agent is not told its checkout changed; a live attempt waiting with no pinned host falls through to the only capable host; `workspacePortOf` is on the handle, so the port can be called without the service (by convention only); the record names the task and requester, not the task's assignee; release (A06) is not wrapped.

- H12l limit carried to H12m: if lifting the freeze fails on the error path of the quiesce (after a refusal or a host fault) no blocker is opened and the record forgets `held`; recovery still finds it by the tag only while the index names the request.
- Not tested: the per-entry error handling of `recover` (one failing task does not stop the others; the first fault is rethrown after the scan).
## H12m: the workspace operations on the local host and on remote hosts

- **The host side** is `WorkspaceHost` (`packages/worker/src/workspace/host.ts`; the worker package imports nothing of the controller, so the call and the outcome are restated and the controller's `WorkspaceCall`/`WorkspaceOutcome` fit them). Its `run(call)` is what a `LocalWorker` takes as its new `workspace` option, and what a remote worker's `WorkspaceResponder` calls. The host is given `locate({taskId, projectId})` (where the checkout, its separate git directory, the bridge's state folder and the quarantine root are on this machine; chosen by the host's own configuration, never by the request), a journal folder and a `GitBridge`.
- **refresh**: a checkout that holds a changed, new or ignored file is refused with the count and left exactly as it was (the same rule as `GitBridge.refresh`); otherwise it moves to the shared repository's head. At the head already it says so (`changed: false`). The shared repository is only read (a fetch from it into the agent's git directory). **integration**: `GitBridge.changes` is checked first (a change that touches Git's data, a link, or too many files is refused whole), then `GitBridge.integrate` carries the files one by one through the expected-version `WorkspaceBridge` into the shared working tree; a file that moved since the base is kept for review (listed with its pending ID, at most 20 names) and the rest go through; no commit is made. `GitBridge.integrate` now skips a file the shared workspace already holds exactly (an integration asked for again), so a repeat keeps no duplicate for review. The base moves (`markIntegrated`) only when nothing was kept and the checkout is committed. **quarantine**: A03's `quarantine` moves the checkout into the owner-only root; the agent's git directory stays where it is (it holds the agent's commits and is outside every sandbox). **release** (committing reviewed work, A06) is answered with a typed refusal: the commit needs the permit of the review gate (H12o), which a workspace request does not carry. A task whose checkout is not on the host, or was quarantined, is answered `not on this host`.
- **Once per request ID.** The host writes `<journal>/<requestId>.json` (`started`, created exclusively) before the work and the outcome after it. A repeat of a finished request returns the recorded answer without running; a request found `started` is refused as uncertain and never run again (the work may be half done); the same ID for another operation is refused. Operations on one checkout run one at a time. The request ID must be `wsr-` and twenty base32 characters, task and project names are checked, the reason is at most 500 characters, so nothing from the request reaches a path.
- **The remote carry** (`RemoteWorkerService.askWorkspace`, `workspaceRequests`, `answerWorkspace`; routes `GET /worker/session/workspace` and `POST /worker/session/workspace/{request}`, same authentication, session and protocol checks as every other route): only the owner and the dispatcher may ask; the call is rebuilt field by field and bounded; nothing is sent to a host that is revoked, silent or not connected (the answer is a refusal saying nothing was sent) or that already has 4 requests waiting; the host's offers poll is ended so it reads the request at once. Only the host asked sees a request or answers it (any other reads `not_found`); the first answer stands, the same answer again is a repeat, another is `command_conflict`; the answer is checked (shape, 1000 characters of text, 4000 bytes of detail). A host that does not answer within `workspaceWaitMs` (a field of the remote host's options, default 300 000 ms, provisional) makes the request `failed` (it may have been carried out) and the ask is withdrawn, so the host does not start it later; a late answer is accepted and kept only for a repeat of the same request ID, which the workspace service never makes. The asks live in memory (the request itself is durable in the workspace record; one lost with a restart reads there as `uncertain`). `WorkspaceResponder` is the worker's side: it runs the requests the poller read in the background, one at a time, never twice at once, keeps an answer that could not be sent and sends it again without running the request again. `HostPoller` takes an `onWorkspace` callback and reads the requests after each round.
- **Finding the host** (`bindWorkspacePort` in `composeDispatch`; the port is no longer on the dispatch handle, so the workspace service is the only way to it): the host of a live attempt (running: its host; parked or waiting: the host it is pinned to). A live attempt that waits with no host pinned names none and the request is refused (no fall-through to another capable host). With no live attempt, the host of the task's last placement (a `task-placement` record written in the same commit that claims an attempt for a host); a task never placed falls back to the one host that has a port, if there is exactly one.
- **Around the operation** (`WorkspaceOpService`): the record names the task's assignee (`assignee`, from the assignment) and the host is told it (what is carried into the shared workspace is attributed to it); an attempt of the task is not started while a request is running or left open (`isBusy`, asked by the dispatcher before it asks for a place; a failure to ask counts as busy); the quiesce looks at the task's live attempts at least twice, so an attempt that began during the preparation is made quiet too; after a refresh or an integration that changed the checkout the running agent is told (`DispatcherService.tell`, recorded as `told`); after a quarantine the task's attempts are stopped while still quiet (`stopped`; the task is left as it is, no new attempt is started by this); if lifting a freeze fails after a refusal, a host fault or the operation, a `runtime_hold` blocker is opened, the attempts are named in `held` of the record and the open index stays, so the recovery loop lifts them later.
- **Tests**: real git in temporary directories in `packages/worker/src/workspace/host.test.ts` (clean and dirty refresh, shared repository byte-identical, integration with a moved file kept, Git data refused whole, quarantine, once-per-ID journal, concurrency); the service around the host in `workspace-ops/workspace-ops-h12m.test.ts` (four storage backends); the remote carry in `remote/workspace-ask.test.ts` over the real transport; end to end through `startController` in `packages/integration/src/h12m-workspace-host.test.ts` (a local worker with a running attempt: dirty refusal, integration, refresh, quarantine, last placement with two capable hosts, a waiting attempt held back and no fall-through; a remote worker over the real transport with a duplicated listing, a lost answer, a silent worker, quarantine).
- **Not done here, said plainly.** (1) No production code builds the local host's `WorkspaceHost`: the operator's `dispatch.local.build` gives `LocalWorker` its `workspace` (the integration test shows how); the real worker host composition is H12k. (2) A remote worker that never runs the responder is not told apart from a silent one: the request waits `workspaceWaitMs` and is `failed` (the announced capabilities have no field for it). (3) A quarantine keeps the agent's git directory in place, so the agent's commits are not in the quarantine. (4) The refusal text of a dirty refresh suggests committing or quarantining; there is no operation yet that commits the checkout's work (the author's own refresh is H12p).

## U05b: artifact verification and failed handlings in the composed status

- New query `status.ask { request }` puts the status views on the state API (task, overview, noticeboard, changes, tools, delivered, failed events, one failed event), answered by the same `StatusService` the owner chat uses; what the caller may not read reads as missing; a task credential may not ask. The status service is now built whether or not `chat` is given.
- `startController({ artifacts: { directory } })` opens the artifact store for the status (a `FileBlobStore` and `ArtifactService` over the same storage) and gives `StatusService` its `verifyArtifact`. Without it artifacts are shown as `not checked`, never as verified. Opening creates the folder if it is missing, so a mistyped path shows every artifact as not matching; the option is not defaulted from the remote hosts' blob folder.
- Proven through the state API of the started controller: a delivered artifact whose files are intact is reported as checked and matching; one whose file was removed from the store and one whose bytes were replaced are each reported as not matching and not counted as delivered; a seeded failed handling is listed and then inspected (its error and attempts shown), also by `events.failures` and `events.handling`; a reader with `history.read` sees it; a reader with only `task.read` gets an empty failure list, `not_found` for the handling and no artifact lines.
- Known limits: any principal with `artifact.read` can ask for the delivered view, and each ask hashes the files of up to 20 artifacts (a blob may be up to 1 GiB), so the cost is not bounded by the caller; caching the verdict by manifest digest is not done. The failed handling is seeded as a record, not produced by a real delivery failure through the composed controller (that path is proven at service level in the watcher tests); the check reads at most the first 20 artifacts of a project per question (`verifyLimit`); an I/O fault while checking (not a missing or changed file) is shown as not matching, not as not checked.
## P01b: release, per-project lookups, scan limit as a blocker, pin failure

- `checkout.release` (right: `assignment.manage` on the task plus `resource.read`) marks a task's pin released when the task no longer names a repository; refused while it still names one (use `checkout.repin`), for a stale revision, or when nothing is pinned. A released pin holds nothing: it no longer keeps a binding from being unbound, `dispatchCheckout`/`pinCheckout` treat the task as unpinned, and a task that names a repository again is pinned afresh (the pin record is updated, not recreated).
- Each project's `resource-registry` record now lists its binding IDs; `list` and the overlap/uniqueness lookups of that project read only those records. A registry made before the list existed is read once by the old kind-wide scan. A project is capped at the scan limit in bindings (unbound ones count); past it a bind is refused and a read is `unavailable`, never answered from part of the list.
- The dispatcher turns an `unavailable` checkout lookup into the usual typed `dispatch_blocked` blocker (same one each tick) instead of failing the tick quietly. A pin that throws, or a checkout that moved, gives back the place and the budget hold: `#giveBack` re-reads the dispatch record (the caller's copy could miss the request or reservation made in the same advance, which was a stale-request bug in the existing `changed` and budget-refused paths too), moves the hold to `releasingId` (and counts a `reserveRound`) in one write, releases it (`budgets.release`) under a command ID of that round, then clears the mark; a process that stopped in between has the release finished at the start of the next advance, before anything is judged, so an attempt never starts on a hold that was already released, and the next hold gets a new command ID. A release refused as `invalid_transition` (already settled, or held as uncertain) is told through `onError`, not silent. The dispatcher's pin command ID now carries the pin record's revision once a record exists, so pinning after a release is not answered with the first pin's recorded result.
- Known limits (split to card P01c): the overlap check on a new binding (`#checkOverlap`) and the pins-per-binding check (`#liveTasksPinnedTo`, pins are never deleted) still scan kind-wide and report `unavailable` past the limit; moving them to indexes is not done. An agent is not told its pin was released.
- Review fixes: an attempt that already used budget keeps its hold when it is sent back and skipped (the hold carries its use and is settled at the end; `release` is only for a hold that was never used), and ending an attempt finishes a release that was begun and not finished. The old note that a registry without the id list is "read once by the old scan" was wrong: it is scanned on each read until the next bind writes the list.
- Known limits: a hold made just before a crash, before its id was written to the record, is found again only when the same round asks to hold again (the command ID replays it); if the attempt ends first, that hold stays open and shows in the task's report. A failing pin on a waiting attempt is now told in the tick report (`failures`) and retried next tick, without stopping the others.

## M01c: owner time zone and the invitation inbox in the composed controller

- `meeting.timeZone` is now a registered setting in the composed configuration service, and the API's meeting service reads it (`ConfigurationService.installationValue`, a rights-free read for the controller's own use) when a schedule names no zone. The schedule records that the zone came from the setting.
- The dispatcher's meeting service sends invitations to `InvitationInbox` unless the host supplies a sink (then the host delivers them itself and `meeting.invitations` stays empty): one inbox record per agent holding its 50 most recently sent invitations, latest first (older ones drop off); a key delivered twice, even with a changed body, adds nothing. Nothing scans other agents' records, so the inbox cannot run out of room for everyone. `meeting.invitations {agent}` is read by the agent itself (a task credential of that agent too), or by the owner for anyone; every other caller sees an empty list.
- The schedule's zone is fixed when the schedule is made; a later change of the `meeting.timeZone` setting does not move existing schedules.
- Known limits: the inbox is a list the agent must look at; nothing wakes the agent or marks an invitation as read or answered. Pushing them into the agent's conversation or a bounded meeting task is not done.
## M01b: participants withheld in the composed controller

- Defect found and fixed: the dispatcher's own pause service (the instance that decides meeting participants and sends invitations) was built without the host's `availability` hook, so an agent the host reported `suspended` or `stopped` was never withheld there; only the pause gates counted. `startController` now passes `options.availability` into the composed dispatcher.
- Proven through the composed controller with real agent records: a scheduled occurrence marks a paused agent `withheld-paused` and a host-stopped agent `withheld-unavailable` (the available one `eligible`), the pause is not lifted by being withheld, the occurrence takes the open agenda item, and after the occurrence is settled `cancelled` the item is on the open agenda again.
- "Not woken" is shown by a recording invitation sink: only the available agent is invited, and the pause of the paused one stays in force.
## C08b: decisions from the chat, generation interrupted by the dispatcher

- The chat can record a decision: `decision.record` is a chat command (applied at once, shown back), the controller sets `sourceTurnId` to the owner's own turn (the interpreter cannot: that is refused), and the decision service checks the wording is in the owner's own text of that turn. `basedOn` is read from the records (`decision.authoritative`: the current version, 0 when nothing was decided); a topic in dispute is refused with a message to settle the dispute first. Direct callers keep `source: direct`; only the owner may name a turn.
- Defects found: (1) nothing gave the decision service a generation service, so the propagation marked its generation step done without interrupting anything. The API's own instance still has none, so there the task is still told but the generation step is not marked done (the correction stays pending and says so; with no dispatcher running it stays pending, which is the honest state), and the dispatcher's instance, which now has the generation service (filled in after both are built), finishes it from its `decisions.resume` loop. (2) The dispatcher's service principal could neither see the task's generation gate nor correct it (no grants), so even with the service attached nothing was interrupted; the generation service now lets that one principal read gates and carry a correction (not read runs or begin anything).
- Proven through the composed controller on SQLite: a correction recorded through the API leaves the step pending, a restart before the dispatcher ran loses nothing, the dispatcher's tick interrupts the running generation as `corrected`, and what the agent still sends is late and not applied; the same with the task paused.
- Known limit: links, revalidation and the block of dependent work after a restart are covered by the existing service-level tests; this card's composed tests cover the generation step and the pause and restart only.
- Review fixes: the version a chat decision is based on is the newest live version that applies to its scope (a task-level decision counts for a project-wide one), counted ahead within one message by the normalised topic, so "PostgreSQL, then SQLite instead" in one message supersedes rather than disputes; the interpreter cannot name `basedOn` or `session` (refused), and `gate`/`stance`/`session` are no longer exempt from the own-words check. A decision that is not a decision (a question) records nothing and the owner is told "Nothing was recorded: ..." instead of "Done". The earlier API decision test is kept (the generation test is its own file).
- Known limits: a decision resumed after the owner answers a clarifying question takes the answering turn as its source and is refused when its wording is in the original turn (it fails closed); `decision.record` applies at once in every profile, including strict (the owner's own words are the authority; whether a chat gate or correction should be shown first in strict is an owner decision).
- C08b third review: the decisions of one message are counted ahead by scope (a project-wide one applies to all, a task's own to that task and the project-wide ones), so two decisions for different tasks do not dispute each other; a decision that became a dispute says so, and "Nothing was recorded" is the whole answer for a non-decision (no "Done"). Known gap for the owner: a gate cannot be set from the chat unless its word (for instance implementation-hold) is in the message, because the interpreter's gate choice is no longer exempt from the own-words check (it would apply a project-wide hold on the interpreter's word alone); whether to allow chat gates as a proposal is an owner question. The note that `basedOn` comes from `decision.authoritative` is superseded: it comes from the topic's history for the decision's scope.
- C08b fourth round: the version an applied decision is based on is now read when the step is applied (after the earlier steps of the message), not predicted from the plan; the earlier prediction was wrong whenever an earlier step recorded nothing (a restatement) or wrote for another scope, since versions count the whole topic. The prediction stays only for a proposal that waits for the owner, where the stale check is the point. A chat gate needs the gate word and the topic name (implementation-gate) in the owner's own words; this is part of the owner question. Saying the same decision twice in one message is a restatement and records nothing the second time.
- C08b fifth round: a turn run again (crash, or sent twice at once) answers an already recorded decision of its own as applied, with the record's version in the reply, and a `command_conflict` from a copy that raced is answered the same way when the record is this turn's. Known limit (owner may want it closed): a step not recorded before a crash of its turn (one refused at apply time, the step that crashed, and every later one) is read afresh on replay; replayed after the owner changed the topic meanwhile, it reads the base version afresh and can overwrite that change instead of becoming a dispute. Closing it needs the plan-time version kept and the fresh one used only when every newer entry is this turn's own.

- (Partly superseded by the third review below: the handle now names its placement, the checkpoint wait re-checks it, and a startup failure closes the host.) Known limits recorded for card H02b (second review): the placement check in the handle is check-then-act (`control()` takes no placement number, so a move committing between the check and the control call lands the old handle's message in the new placement); the checkpoint wait does not re-check the placement and a new host's checkpoint can satisfy an old handle's wait (the sequence carries over a move); a failure of `FileBlobStore.open` or remote-service construction after the local host was built still leaves that host open.

## H02b (part): startup failures, placement-numbered control, visible refusals

- Any step that fails after the local host was built (the artifact folder, remote service, listener, dispatcher, MCP) now closes the listener and the local host before the error leaves `composeDispatch` (before, only a listener failure did; the controller starts without a dispatcher and `dispatchProblem` says why). Tested for an unopenable artifact folder and a taken port, and that the controller's own close does not close the host a second time.
- `RemoteWorkerService.control` takes the caller's placement number and refuses (`fenced`) in the same commit that would write the message if another placement holds the attempt; the production handle passes its own for checkpoint, restart and tell. The checkpoint wait now stops with `fenced` when the placement moved, so the wait ends `fenced` once a move is visible (a move and a new-host checkpoint landing between the wait's last check and the read of the latest checkpoint is a tiny window that is not closed). Tested in the relocation suite.
- A host that cannot meet an attempt's requirements: the dispatcher's report now says why (`the worker did not start: <reason>`), not only the attempt's end record; tested through the composed controller (an isolation the host does not offer).
- Not done, split to card H02c: partition and delayed-packet fencing, no self-promotion, relocation with integrity and policy refusals, the exclusive native-store owner, and the production host's stop path, each through the composed controller.
- Review fixes (third review): the production handle is tested through a stale view of the placement (the fence in the commit refuses `tell`, `restart` and `checkpoint`) and the checkpoint wait ends `fenced` when the placement moved; the driver is started last, after everything that can fail, so a failed start leaves none ticking. Still untested: closing the listener after it was opened when a later step fails (both startup tests fail at or before `listen`); it is the first item of H02c, together with a failure injected into the driver or MCP construction (the driver is started last so none ticks after a failed start, which is untested).
## R05d (part): meeting time is charged

- When an agent leaves a meeting (by itself or at the end), the time it was present is charged to the budget ledger: `AttendanceDeps.charge`, composed in `dispatch-compose.ts` as `budgets.charge` under the dispatcher's principal, activity `meeting`. The basis is stated: wall-clock milliseconds between joining and leaving, recorded as compute (`computeMs`), never as money. It goes to the agent's meeting task (work) or, with none, to the shared-overhead rule "meeting" (an agent that joined always has a meeting task, so in practice this branch is only a fallback and is not reached or tested).
- Once only: the command ID is the attendance's (`att-use:<attendance>`), so a repeated leave replays the same charge. The owner's presence is not charged (tested: the check is on the agent identity, "agent:..."). A failing ledger is reported (`onChargeError`, the composed `onError`) and never keeps the agent in the room; a later `leave` of the same attendance charges it (the end of the meeting does not retry, because it skips those who have left).
- Not done, split to R05f: supervision and review activity, background jobs (the job service is not yet composed in the controller), and a composed proof through the state API that a held meeting appears in `budget.usage` (the unit test uses the service seam only). A charge lost because the ledger stayed down is not found again by a sweep.
- Possible double count to check in R05f: if an agent's meeting turns are ever dispatched as attempts on its meeting task, their model-call use settles against that same task as well as this wall-clock charge.

## P01c: pin lists and the overlap check without kind-wide scans

- Each binding has a pin list (`resource-pins`, made with the binding): the tasks whose checkout is or was pinned to it. Ending a binding reads that list (checking each task still points there and is not finished), not every checkout of every project, and its commit checks the list at the revision it read, so a pin that commits meanwhile makes the unbind fail and the binding stays bound. Pin, repin (moves the task between two lists) and release keep the list in the same commit as the checkout. A list is cleared of finished tasks once it holds 50 (or the scan limit, if lower); past the scan limit in live pins a pin is refused as `unavailable` (field `pins`).
- A binding made before the list existed has none. Its first pin starts a list marked `legacy` without looking at older checkouts (the pin never scans), and ending a binding with no list or a `legacy` one also looks through the checkouts (refused as `unavailable` past the scan limit, never answered from part); ending a list-less binding leaves a legacy empty list so a pin racing it conflicts.
- The overlap check reads each project's registry, which now also holds the bound locations of the project (`locs`, kept by bind, move and unbind; a registry without them is read from its bindings and gets them at its next change). The limit counts projects, not bindings. The check still looks across projects by nature (an overlap is between projects), so it is a scan of the project registries.
- A task whose pin the list could not take is a blocker: the dispatcher's look (before any place or allowance is taken) tests the pin list's capacity and answers `unbound` with the reason, which becomes the usual `dispatch_blocked` blocker (the same one each tick). If the limit is reached between that look and the pin, the pin gives the place back and the attempt is skipped for the tick. Only this refusal is mapped so; a store fault in a pin stays a fault.
- Known limits: the project registries are scanned on every bind and move (one record per project); a registry made before P01b (no id list) is still read from all resources for each bind and move until its project next changes a binding; an overlap race between two projects binding at the same moment is not serialized (as before); two pins on one binding at the same moment conflict (one is retried on the next tick; the message says the project's resources changed); pin lists keep finished tasks until a list reaches its clearing size; the `legacy` mark is never cleared, so ending a binding made before the lists existed always looks through the checkouts (as before this card); the look before dispatch reads each task of a long pin list on every tick for a waiting task.

## C08d: a replayed decision step never overwrites a change made meanwhile

- Planning a decision step now records the version of its topic as the message saw it (`planBase`, before any step of the message). When the step is applied, if a decision on the topic that is not from this turn has a higher version than `planBase` (someone changed it after the message was planned), the step is based on `planBase` alone (not adding what this turn recorded: that may have been written in a narrower scope that never saw the change), so the decision service records it as a dispute and the change stands. Otherwise the step is based on the topic as it is now, as before. Disputed topics are still refused before this.
- Proven: a message of two steps whose second step crashes, the owner changes the topic directly, and the message is sent again: the second step is a dispute, nothing is in force until the owner chooses, and the owner's change is not superseded. Removing the rule makes the test fail.
- Review fix: an earlier version added this turn's own newest version to `planBase`, which let a project-wide step overwrite a change that an earlier task-scoped step of the same turn had not seen; tested (replay with a task-scoped then a project-wide step and a change for another task meanwhile).
- Known limit: a decision step reads the topic's history twice at plan time and twice at apply time (cost only); a change between the plan and the first run (no crash) is the same case and the same rule, with no test of its own.

## C08c: chat gates and strict-profile decisions are shown first

- Owner answers (2026-10-27): a gate set from the chat is shown as a proposal the owner confirms, and `decision.record` in the strict profile is shown first; the other profiles still apply a decision at once. `proposalReason` gives the reason ("a gate holds or releases work until you say otherwise, so it is shown first"; "the strict profile shows a recorded decision first"). A profile that cannot be read is strict.
- Because a gate is always seen first, its kind and its fixed topic (`implementation-gate`, set by the controller) no longer have to be words of the owner's message; the gate's wording still has to be (the decision service checks it against the turn), so a gate whose words the owner did not say is still refused. This replaces the C08b rule that a chat gate needed the gate word and the topic name in the owner's words.
- Applying the proposal records the decision from the same turn; its `basedOn` is the version read when the message was planned, so a topic that moved meanwhile becomes a dispute (the stale-session check).
- Review fixes: (1) the preview of a decision says its category and gate first (a long text or task label cannot push the kind off the line) and the recorded line names the gate; (2) a decision proposed from a message is based, when the owner says yes, on the version it was shown with, and decisions of the same message applied before it do not count as the topic having moved (they supersede, in the strict profile too); a change by anyone else in between is still a dispute; a step already recorded is answered from the record when the apply is run again; (3) words that are not a decision (a question, a hypothetical) are not offered for confirmation: the owner is told "Nothing was recorded: ...".
