## C07n: a route whose window nobody states is refused, and a stored conversation is judged before it is carried (2026-11-09)

`dispatch/runtime-guards.ts` had two holes where a missing figure meant a pass. With no window for the order's route it answered `admit: true` with no record and no measurement, and `resume` answered `resume: true`; the only source of a window was the embedder's own `local.window` map, so a route that map does not mention was never checked. The resume share was worse than unused: it was read only when the embedder passed `local.storedTokens`, and no composition in the repository passes one, so through `startController` a stored conversation of any size was carried into a new process. What was already there is kept: the routing table has carried `contextTokens` per route since C07b, `context/enforcement.ts` already opens `context_overflow` blockers with remedies the owner can act on, and the local worker already starts fresh and says why when a conversation does not fit.

- **A route's window has an order, and no third state (`dispatch/runtime-guards.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `7f7d36fa`).** `controllerGuards` takes a second, optional figure for the route — `routeWindow` — and `windowOf(order)` now asks the host's own `window(order)` first and the routing table's `contextTokens` for the route second (`tableWindow` reads `routing.get()` through the same read the route view uses; a failing read is reported through `onError` and answers "not known"). The host's figure still wins where it has one: an operator who lowers it for a box that cannot hold the configured window is not overruled by the table. `api/dispatch-compose.ts` passes `routeWindow` for the local host, and `windowOfRoute` (the same two-step) is what C07g's route-move check uses, so a moved attempt is measured against the window it will actually run under.
- **Neither figure means the work does not run, and the owner is told (`context/enforcement.ts`, `dispatch/runtime-guards.ts`).** `ContextEnforcementService.blockUnknownWindow` opens (or returns the one already open) a `context_overflow` blocker on the task naming the route, what was refused (first call or stored conversation), the attempt, and both places the window is set — the routing table's `contextTokens` for the route, or the local host's own figure. The guards' refusal (`unknownWindowReason`, exported for hosts and tests) carries the same sentence plus the blocker ID, so the attempt's failure text, the blocker and the eventual hand-off all say the same thing. One blocker per task: a tick that asks again for the same task returns the open one rather than stacking them, and a blocker that cannot be written still refuses the call, saying it could not be recorded. Nothing is measured and nothing is admitted, so no `ctx-admission` record is written for such a call — there was no window to measure against, and a record would read like a judged refusal.
- **A refusal no smaller call can change is not compacted (`dispatch/runtime-guards.ts`, `dispatch/local-worker.ts`, `bdb8fed1`).** The unknown-window answer carries `retryable: false`, and the worker's two-pass first call stops at the first refusal when it reads that: making the prompt smaller cannot make a window known, and the attempt's one compaction is spent on the cases it can actually fix. A refusal *about* a known window keeps the old two-pass behaviour exactly.
- **The stored conversation is judged the same way, and by the controller itself if nobody else will (`dispatch/local-worker.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `06850d6f`).** `resume` goes through the same `windowOf`: no window, no continuation, and the same blocker with "stored conversation" as what was refused. A conversation whose size is known and does not fit is still just a fresh start with the reason in the attempt's note — the task is not blocked for that, and C07b's wording is unchanged. What is new is that the size is always asked for: `checkpointStoredTokens` reads the worker package's own checkpoint shape (`nn.contextTokens`, the mirror of `storedTokensOf` in `packages/worker/src/host/local.ts`, said in both places), the composition passes it as the default `storedTokens` so a guard always answers, and the host reads the checkpoint's own figure when the reader it was given answers nothing. A checkpoint that says nothing at all is not resumed: the host is told through `onGuardError` ("resume decision: the checkpoint does not say how large the stored conversation is"), the agent is told in the note, and the attempt goes on from the continuation record.
- **Tests.** `dispatch/runtime-guards.test.ts` (`bdb8fed1`) drives the guards with the real context-enforcement and blocker services rather than fakes: a route nobody gives a window sends nothing, opens exactly one blocker naming the route and `contextTokens`, writes no admission record, refuses the stored conversation, and does not block the same task twice; a route the table does state is judged against the table's figure (both first call and resume), and one that fits is sent. `dispatch/first-call-hops.test.ts` loses its `todo` on C07l's case: the million-token first call on a route of unknown window is refused, the context service is never asked to judge against a window it does not have, the refusal names the route and how to set its window, the resume is refused the same way, and the table's figure is used when the host's map does not know the route. `dispatch/local-worker-guards.test.ts` reads the worker package's shape with no reader at all, falls back to it when a reader answers nothing, refuses a checkpoint that says nothing (host told, agent told), still resumes a conversation that fits, still leaves a worker with no context guard untouched, and spends no compaction on the final refusal. `api/start-c07n.test.ts` (new, `757cfd04`) runs it through `startController` on sqlite: the host's `window` answers `undefined` for every route and no `storedTokens` is passed; the routing table's 4096 is what refuses a 3,000,000-character prompt ("over the startup limit of 1024 for a 4096-token window") with the measurement recorded and one blocker open; a call that fits that window is sent and succeeds; a route placed by a resolver that neither the map nor the table states sends nothing, records nothing as judged and blocks with the route and `contextTokens` named; and a controller brought down mid-turn comes back over the same store and starts both attempts **without** their checkpoints — the 40,000-token conversation over the 2457 resume share and the silent one alike, each with its reason in the prompt, the silent one also reported to the host. A last suite passes a reader of its own and shows it is the one that decides.
- ASSUMPTION: the routing table's `contextTokens` is the authority when the host's map does not know the route, rather than refusing at once. It is the figure the owner already installs for the route, the guard has to judge against *something* the owner set, and refusing every route missing from a host's map would stop work the owner configured correctly. The host's own figure still takes precedence where it exists, for a box that cannot hold what the table claims.
- ASSUMPTION: a route neither states is unusable rather than conservatively guessed. A default window (8192, say) would make the first call pass or fail on a number nobody chose, and would silently truncate tool output beside it; the owner has to hear about the route, so the work is refused with the two places to fix it. The refusal is non-retryable for the same reason.
- ASSUMPTION: `nn.contextTokens` is the shape the default reads, because that is what this repository's own local host writes; it is stated as a mirror at both ends rather than imported (the controller may not depend on the worker package, `check:deps`). A checkpoint of some other shape answers "not known", which is the refuse-visible side of the card's choice, not a silent pass.
- ASSUMPTION: one `context_overflow` blocker per task, shared by the first-call and the resume refusal. Fifty hand-offs of one task on one bad route would otherwise open fifty blockers, and the owner's remedy is the same for all of them; the attempt's own failure text still names which call was refused.
- **Still open, deliberately not in this card.** Attempts on **remote** worker hosts are untouched: the first call and the stored conversation there are checked by the remote host's own code path, which is card C07o. The worker process's **tool-output** share still comes from `i.options.local.window` alone (`api/dispatch-compose.ts` `local.context` and `toolWindow`): on a route missing from the host's map the process gets no context limits, so its tool output is cut by nothing — that is a third check, needs its own tests against the worker's `context` option, and is not the first call or the resume this card covers. The 13 remaining `todo`s in `first-call-hops.test.ts` are C07m, C07p and C07q cases and keep their todos.
- **Runs** (this worktree; `npx tsc --build --force` clean; every test run under the offline guard (`scripts/offline-guard.mjs` as an absolute `file://` URL) with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`): `dist/dispatch/*.test.js dist/context/*.test.js` — 1331 tests, 1318 pass, 0 fail, 13 todo (194 s wall at concurrency 4); `dist/api/*.test.js dist/chat/*.test.js dist/status/*.test.js` — 1546 tests, 1546 pass, 0 fail, 0 todo (447 s wall); per-file, the slowest files this change touches are `context/enforcement.test.js` 175 s, `dispatch/dispatcher.test.js` 149 s, `dispatch/first-call-hops.test.js` 38 s (25 pass, 13 todo), `dispatch/runtime-guards.test.js` 15 s (12 pass), `api/start-c07n.test.js` 4 s (5 pass) — all well inside the 600 s bound; `node --test scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6 pass / 0 fail; `npm run roadmap:check` "roadmap ok"; `npm run check:deps` "package boundaries ok"; `npm run api:docs:write` regenerated `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` with **no change** to it, so no operation or status text moved and there was nothing for `task-plan.md` to pick up. One run of the api sweep reported a single failure, `api/start.test.js`'s network-file-system override, caused by the guard being passed to a spawned controller as a relative path (`Cannot find module '/scripts/offline-guard.mjs'`); re-run with the absolute URL it passes, and that is the form all the counts above were measured with. Counts and what was left out are in Pi's `REPORT.md` for this change (kept out of the tree).
- **Review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09).** Three fixes, each with a test in `dispatch/runtime-guards.test.ts` that fails without it. (1) A host figure that is no window (0, negative, fractional, NaN, infinite) was used as the window, so a host map answering `0` for a route it does not know refused every call with a budget of 0 instead of asking the routing table; `windowOf` now takes only a positive safe integer from either source. (2) A routing table that could not be read answered "not known", so a storage hiccup failed the attempt non-retryably and opened a blocker telling the owner to set a `contextTokens` that was already set; the guards' `routeWindow` in `api/dispatch-compose.ts` now lets the read error through (the worker refuses the call as "the context check failed" with no blocker, and a stored conversation starts fresh). (3) The route was written unquoted into the blocker and the agent's refusal; `routeNamed` (`context/enforcement.ts`) keeps a name of the routing table's shape as it is and writes anything else (a custom resolver's route) as one redacted, quoted line (`quotedLine`). Also: the resume step of the per-backend test re-reads the blockers instead of asserting on the list read before it.

## Chat, third pass (Pi): a dated right, a asked-for host move, and every refusal that told the owner what to say (2026-11-09)

The owner rule in the brief says the interpreter decides what an owner asked for, in whatever words they use, and that nothing may tell them to say a particular thing. Three things in the chat still broke it, and one fault ran through all of them: a message that says *how to phrase it* is a magic phrase with the owner blamed for not knowing it. This pass is the same fault as `c4f023a6`/`ec84768e` (flaky release approval), `56ce51b1` (landing on main) and the two grants entries above, now swept through the rest of `chat/chat.ts`. Nothing here changed what a command does; it changed what the owner is told and, in two cases, stopped the chat refusing an owner's own request.

- **A right the owner dated is drawn up with its days, not refused for having them (`chat/chat.ts`, `chat/commands.ts`, `chat/grant-dates.test.ts` new, `api/start-chat.test.ts`; `3f36e3cf`).** `grant.create` in chat refused any `expiresAt` or `notBefore` outright — "a right's dates are not the chat's to invent. Say which day it ends, in your own words" — so a right with an end could not be made in chat at all, whatever the owner wrote. What the refusal was really guarding is an invented *day*, and that guard is kept in the shape the other arguments use: `grantDateInWords(value, ownText)` returns the moment when the owner's own message gives that day, and undefined when it does not. A day counts when the message carries the moment exactly as written (what `foreignValue` looks for everywhere else), an ISO day alone or with a time after it, a slashed or dashed numeric day read **either way round** (`30/11/2026` and `11/30/2026`, the year having to agree — the moment shown on the proposal is what the owner confirms, so the reading is settled in the open), or a written day and month in either order (`30 November`, `November 30th`, `the 30th of Nov 2026`, `Nov 30 26`), with the year they wrote when they wrote one. "the end of the month", "until the audit is done", "for a few more days", a bare month name and a weekday name give no day the controller can check, so they are still refused — with a question (`Which day should it end?`), never with a sentence to copy. `GRANT_DATE_KEYS` is the only exemption from `foreignValue`'s exact-string search, and the exemption is filled by that check rather than widened; the interpreter's prompt says the same thing to the model (`chat/model-interpreter.ts`): a right's date is a day the owner's message gives, and when they want it to run out but name no day, ask. A right that would end before it ever starts is refused there and then, instead of being proposed and refused by the records when it is confirmed.
- **The proposal line says the dates before it says anything long (`chat/commands.ts`, `grantMeaning`).** `grantMeaning` puts `ends <moment>` (or `no end: it never runs out and stays until you revoke it`), `; starts <moment>` and the scope (`; only in "Garden"` / `; everywhere: …`) in the leading parenthesis, ahead of the grantee, the action and the `basis` — which is the owner's whole message and is the longest thing on the line, so a cut line still shows when the right lives. Each date goes through `short` once, as every bare value on the line does (`chat/commands-preview.test.ts` asserts one line, escaped once, with control characters in the date, and that the parenthetical survives a line cut). Nothing is applied without the confirmation: a right is a proposal in every profile, the basis recorded is `owner chat: <the owner's words>`, and `api/start-chat.test.ts` drives the whole way through — ordinary sentence, proposal shown, nothing active, confirm, right in force.
- **A host move is a proposal whatever the words, and the quiet-host warning says how things stand (`chat/commands.ts`, `chat/chat.ts`, `chat/policy-edit.ts`, `remote/quiet-hosts.ts`, `api/quiet-host-api.test.ts`, `remote/quiet-hosts.test.ts`; `chat/host-move-words.test.ts` deleted; `22a2d708`).** `ordersHostMove` read the owner's sentence for an imperative move verb governing the host's name, and `host.move-work` applied at once only when it matched; the chat's refusal and the quiet-host notice both told the owner to say `move the work off <host>`. Under the owner rule the interpreter picks the operation, so that test was a phrase gate and the notice was an incantation. Now `host.move-work` is `mode: "propose"` in the table, `proposalReason` says why (moving the work off a host re-places what is running on it), `ordersHostMove`, `saysWords` and the three regexes only they used are gone, and `host.move-work` left `MOVE_VERBS` — no wording decides whether a move applies, so no wording can fail to. The notices state the situation instead: the host stopped reporting, how many attempts it holds, that its work moves after the grace period unless it reports again and that the owner can have it moved before that, or, when automatic moves are off, that the work stays where it is until they have it moved. The owner turning automatic moves on is told the timer that now applies, because that message answers their own change. The state API's `host.move-work` is untouched — an owner's own call is their decision and moves at once — and the chat's move still needs the confirmation, which `api/quiet-host-api.test.ts` now walks: any wording that names the host is shown as a proposal that changes nothing, and confirming it re-places the attempt.
- **Every refusal in `chat/chat.ts` was read, and the ones that dictated wording were rewritten (`415428dd`).** Thirty-six owner-facing lines in `chat.ts` told the owner what to say or what to hand over (21 `say …`, 13 `… not both` — one of them phrased `name a participant by agentName or principalId, not both` — and 2 `give the …`); 41 more lines changed for the quoting rule below. `say which staged release to activate` became `Which staged release should be activated? Nothing in your message names one.`; the same shape for release cancel/approve, backup restore, database transfer, maintenance, tool revoke, watch tell/end, hand-off and resume targets, an agent attending or taking a task, a brief to note on. `give either X or Y, not both` became a statement of what the message did ("the stand-up is named twice over, as scheduleId and as standupTitle; which one is meant has to be settled") in all thirteen places. The grantee/action/grant ID/project "say it exactly" refusals now quote the value that is not the owner's and ask which was meant (`The right "g-1f9…" is not in your message as written … Which grant should it be, by its g- ID?`). `Say it yourself if you want it` (an instruction out of quoted text) states that only their own message can ask for something. The drain refusal says the chat will not pick a time that could cancel work early and asks how long. `release.host`'s platform refusals keep naming the platforms their message did name and lose `Say one of them and nothing about the others` / `Say which … or that the platform is not what you meant`, which asked the owner to read the interpreter's mind about `os` versus `arch`. The meeting-decision `instead(...)` default, `alternativeStatement` refusal, the twice-answered decision and the two "say more of the words" refusals state what is missing. `/nimblenewt.<op>` from a typed line says the same thing asked in a message is drawn up for confirmation, instead of telling them to say it.
- **What those messages quote is escaped once (`chat/chat.ts`, 41 changed lines).** Task, stand-up, meeting, agent, project and topic names interpolated as `"${x.slice(0, 80)}"` go through `quotedText` (card U09) instead: they are record text an agent wrote, or the interpreter's guess, and a record check accepts U+2028/2029, the C1 controls and `\p{Cf}`, so a title could reorder the rest of the owner's line or reach a terminal as an escape. Also quoted: a host ID in the platform refusals, a resource label in `Where is …?`, the topic in three meeting-decision refusals, a decided decision's topic and statement in the read-back lines, and the `Not applied: …` list built from a policy edit. No text passes two helpers, so nothing is escaped twice.
- **Tests.** `chat/grant-dates.test.ts` (new, 5 suites): ordinary sentences that name a day, a start day, the phrases that name none, year and month mismatches, and a value that is not a moment at all; `chat/commands-preview.test.ts` (+3): the dates and scope before the names, a cut line still showing them, control characters in a date escaped once; `api/start-chat.test.ts` (+2, one old refusal test replaced): a dated right proposed with `ends …` shown, nothing active until confirmation, confirmation recording the shown moment, both dates in one sentence, a no-day phrase refused with a question that dictates nothing, a backwards window refused. `remote/quiet-hosts.test.ts` (+1 suite, +1 assertion) and `api/quiet-host-api.test.ts` (replaced phrase-driven expectations) assert the notices contain no `Say`, no `for example`, no quotation to copy and stay inside the notification limit. `chat/host-move-words.test.ts` is deleted with the function it tested, and `chat/policy-edit.test.ts` loses the `saysWords` suite; the behaviour it guarded is guarded by `api/quiet-host-api.test.ts` as a proposal instead. `meeting-decision-chat-suite.ts` has four expectations moved to the new wording (one of them, the recorded-decision read-back, now shows the statement quoted).
- **Mutation checks** (applied to `src`, `npx tsc --build`, run, restored, rebuilt, working tree verified clean): `grantDateInWords` returning a match for everything the model invents → 6 tests fail (all five `grant-dates` suites and the state-API/chat grant suite); `host.move-work` put back to `mode: "apply"` → the quiet-host API suite fails (the move applies without the owner's confirmation); the old `Say "move the work off …"` notice put back → both quiet-host suites fail on every backend. The step-3 messages are asserted by phrase in `api/start-chat.test.ts` and the meeting-decision suite, so reverting a message without fixing its guard fails the test that says no phrase is dictated.
- **What is still guarded, and is not a phrase gate.** The day must be the owner's (`grantDateInWords`), the principal/action/grant ID/project must appear as their whole word (`wholeWord`), an ID the interpreter produced must appear in the message (`foreignValue`), a duration must be a duration they gave (`durationInWords`), a platform must be one their words name (`platformsNamed`). Each refuses a *value*, not a wording, and every one of them now answers with a question or a statement of the gap. Statements that the owner did *not* say something ("your message does not say which platform it runs") are facts about the message, kept on purpose.
- **Left alone on purpose, with the reason.** `chat/policy-intent.ts`'s two `give either …` refusals and `transfer.ts`'s `say which database to move to` are the status/transfer paths behind the state API rather than free-form chat (`transfer.ts` is reached by an owner's own API call); `commands.ts` typed-command help and `needs_context` lines are command syntax, not chat; `release.ts`'s `os and arch say which platform the host is authorized for` is a domain rule behind an API call. `chat/status.test.ts`'s suite name still says "the owner is told to say which" although the message it checks is `Which project do you mean?` — a name, not a message; left rather than churned.
- ASSUMPTION: the *time of day* on a day the owner named is the interpreter's reading and is not checked against their words; only the day is. The proposal line shows the whole moment and the owner's confirmation of that line is the consent, so nothing is settled behind their back; checking the hour too would refuse "by the end of November" for not saying 23:59.
- ASSUMPTION: a host move stays a proposal in every profile, including `autonomous`, even though a move can be a safety answer to a host that just died. Applying an interpreted re-placement of running attempts is worse than showing it, and the two direct routes are untouched: the grace-period automatic move, and `host.move-work` through the state API.
- **Runs** (this worktree; `npx tsc --build --force` clean; offline guard; `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`): `dist/chat/*.test.js dist/remote/*.test.js dist/status/*.test.js dist/api/*.test.js dist/policy/*.test.js` — 2266 tests, 2266 pass, 0 fail, 0 todo (about 4 min; the same sweep on the merge base was 2257 / 2257, so +9 tests and no loss); `node --test scripts/plan.test.mjs` — 6 pass / 0 fail; everything in the package outside those five directories (188 files: release, decisions, meetings, dispatch, worker, standups and the rest) — 7493 tests, 7475 pass, 0 fail, 18 todo; `npm run roadmap:check` "roadmap ok"; `npm run check:deps` "package boundaries ok"; `npm run api:docs:write` rewrote `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` with **no change to it** (no operation summary, argument or mode line in `api/operations.ts` moved — what changed is chat-side behaviour and wording). One honest note carried forward from the entry above: `dist/chat/host-move-words.test.js` was orphaned when its source was deleted and `tsc --build` does not remove the output of a deleted source, so it had to be removed by hand before the sweep was clean. One earlier sweep of the same five directories, run while other test jobs were still on the machine, reported 2265 / 2266 with the single failure being `remote/workspace-ask.test.js` on PostgreSQL (`host:r1 did not answer the workspace request within 5000 ms`, card H12m) — nothing this change touches; that file passes 28/28 alone and the clean sweep is 2266 / 2266, so its five-second host answer is timing-sensitive under load. ## L02e leftover (Pi): a stop's cost asked for by an agent's or a team's name, in the owner's own words (2026-11-09)

L02d left one item in its "left" list that the owner feels every day: `status.ask { kind: "stop_cleanup" }` reads a task by its title from chat but an agent, a team or the whole installation only by ID, and `STATUS_KINDS` said so to the model in as many words ("the scopeId, which must be an ID, not a name"). Under the owner rule the owner says what they want and the interpreter picks the operation, so "what did stopping bob cost?" was a question the chat could not answer while "what did stopping Order seeds cost?" was one it could. This closes that item; nothing else in L02e is touched.

- **What was built (`chat/chat.ts`, `status/status.ts`, `64c8afae`).** `stop_cleanup` gained a chat-side `scopeName`, and its `STATUS_KINDS` keys are now `taskId|taskTitle`, `scopeKind`, `scopeId|scopeName` with the `about` line telling the model the name is what the owner said (the ID is still what the API takes). In `#plan`'s status branch, before the task-title block: `scopeKind: "installation"` gets the one installation ID with no lookup (that scope was ID-only too); an agent's or a team's name is looked up among the installation's own records (`#scopeCandidates`: `agent.list` by `friendlyName`, `team.list` by `name`, both read through `#listAll`, five pages); the whole installation needs no choice at all; and `scopeKind: "task"` with words becomes the task-title question the block below already answers for the project in focus. Several matches ask which with each name quoted; none refuses in a plain question that says what is not called that and lists up to three names that are (`titleList`), or — when the installation has no agents or teams at all — says so and asks whether a task or the installation was meant. A `scopeKind` that is none of the four (`"project"`, say) is refused with the four that a stop is read for rather than the status service's `give scope, or scopeKind with scopeId`.
- **Who decides which name is meant: the owner's message, not the interpreter.** A candidate matches when its recorded name stands as a whole word of the owner's own message (`wholeWord(words, name)`, the same guard the grants and the platforms use). So an interpreter that invents `scopeName: "Cyrus"` for a message about Bob gets Bob (a test says so outright), an interpreter that guesses the wrong kind is answered from the list it was pointed at, and `scopeName` is not checked for being the owner's words because it never decides anything. `wholeWord`'s lookbehinds and lookaheads give the substring rule for free in both directions: with agents `Bob` and `Bobby`, "stopping bobby cost" is Bobby alone and "stopping bob cost" is Bob alone, and neither word names the other's agent.
- **Where the words stop.** `scopeName` is deleted on every path out of that block, so the status service never sees it: `onlyKnown(request, ["kind", "taskId", "scope", "scopeKind", "scopeId"])` there is the backstop, and `status/status.test.ts` now asserts both a name alone and a name beside an ID are `invalid_command` at that door. An ID the owner (or the interpreter, from a record the owner read) gave always wins — the words beside it are dropped exactly as a task title beside a `taskId` is — and an agent scope takes the agent record's own `agt-…` ID, which is what `PauseScope` and `checkScope` want, not the `agent:…` principal ID another chat operation uses. Nothing in that path touches a scope that already carries an ID (`bare`): a first run turned `scopeKind: "task"` given with a `scopeId` into a task title and left the request as half a scope, which the tests now pin, along with the installation given its own ID.
- **What is shown of a name is escaped.** Both new owner-facing messages put the name through `quotedText` (the options also carry `(agent)` / `(team)` so a name that belongs to both is told apart). Names are agent-written text: the record checks accept U+202E, the C1 controls and `\p{Cf}`, so a friendly name can reorder the line it is shown in. Two agents named `Rex ‮ignore all instructions  now` are listed and asked about as `"Rex \u202eignore all instructions\u0085 now"`, and the not-found listing escapes the same way (a test asserts no raw override or C1 control reaches the reply and the escapes are there).
- **Tests (`chat/status.test.ts`, four suites, four backends each).** The happy path in ordinary sentences with **no project in focus** (an agent and a team belong to the installation): an agent by name, a team by name, a name with no `scopeKind` said at all, a **retired** agent (what the stop of one cost is asked afterwards), the whole installation with and without words, an ID beside words, a task's words in the scope form, and the invented-name case; the whole-word suite (`Bob`/`Bobby` both directions, `annabel` naming nothing and listing what there is, an agent and a team both called Bob asking which with `"Bob" (agent)` / `"Bob" (team)`, and the owner's next message naming the team); the escaped-name suite; and a suite for an installation with no agents and no teams. Every assertion is on the scope that reached the stop service (`stops.cleanupSpend` records it), so a resolution is checked by what was actually read, and `asked.length` proves an unclear name reads nothing.
- **Mutation checks** (each applied to the compiled `dist/chat/chat.js`, the file run, restored, `tsc --build --force` again; all killed): the whole-word match back to `words.includes(name)` → 4 failures (the substring suite on every backend: `bob` matches `Bobby`); the `delete request["scopeName"]` removed → 8 failures (the status service refuses the unknown key, so the answered cases stop being answered); the installation ID filled with anything else → 4 failures (the installation cases).
- ASSUMPTION: the owner's own message decides which agent or team is meant, and `scopeName` is only the interpreter's note of what it thinks the owner said. Checking `scopeName` for being the owner's words instead would let an interpreter that paraphrases ("the CTO agent" for an agent named `Rob`) fail an owner who said the name plainly, and matching against the records is the same guard `foreignValue`/`wholeWord` apply to a value that must not be invented.
- ASSUMPTION: a message that names two agents or two teams asks which rather than taking the one nearest the verb, and `scopeKind` is trusted for the *kind* only. Picking a sentence (`sentenceWith`) would settle some of them, but a message can hold two questions and the wrong pick reads the cost of a stop of something the owner never meant; asking costs one turn.
- ASSUMPTION: retired agents are searched with the active ones (`agent.list` unfiltered). A stop's cost is asked after the fact, often precisely of an agent that has been retired; and the alternative — only active agents — would answer "no agent is called Sloan" about an agent that plainly exists.
- ASSUMPTION: nothing is looked up for the whole installation, and any words beside `scopeKind: "installation"` are dropped rather than checked. There is one installation and its ID is `installation`; there is no ambiguity to resolve and no ID to invent, and the `scopeId` the owner may still give is used as before.
- **Runs** (this worktree; `npx tsc --build --force` clean; offline guard (`scripts/offline-guard.mjs` as an absolute `file://` URL) with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`): `dist/chat/*.test.js dist/status/*.test.js dist/api/*.test.js dist/lifecycle/*.test.js` — 2276 tests, 2272 pass, **0 fail**, 4 todo (216 s wall); the four todos are C07k's package-size trend, one per backend, unchanged from before this card. Alone: `chat/status.test.js` 48 / 48 (40 s), `status/status.test.js` 168 / 168 (58 s), `api/api.test.js` 50 / 50 (41 s); `node --test scripts/plan.test.mjs` — 6 pass / 0 fail. Counts, commands and what was left out are in Pi's `REPORT.md` for this change (kept out of the tree). `npm run api:docs:write` rewrote `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md`, this time with one real change: `status.ask`'s `stop_cleanup` entry now says that in chat the task, the agent or the team may be named by its title or name and the chat finds it (`api/operations.ts`), the same note `replay` and `standup_briefs` already carry. `task-plan.md` and L02e's own card were not touched (the card holds five other leftovers, so it stays open). `npm run check:deps` says "package boundaries ok"; `npm run roadmap:check` reports the README roadmap stale (243 vs 245 tasks, C07m and C07n flipped to implemented without a `roadmap:write`) — that is main's, this change touches no plan file, and regenerating it would sweep other cards into this commit, so it was left for whoever flips them.
- **Opus review (clean context).** Three fixes, one suite (`chat/status.test.ts`, "the owner's words decide over an ID the interpreter offered…", four backends; it failed on all four before the fix). (1) An ID only the interpreter offered beside a name decided over the owner's words: "what did stopping bob cost" with `scopeId` = Ann's ID read Ann. Now a `scopeId` that is not a whole word of the owner's message, when a `scopeName` came with it, is dropped and the name is looked up in the owner's words; an ID the owner wrote is still used as given. The nested `scope` form is untouched (the interpreter cannot send an object; it is the API's). (2) `wholeWord`'s boundaries are ASCII, so `Ann` matched "jóann" and `Bob` matched "bobé"; the name match is now `nameInWords` (`wholeWord` plus no Unicode letter, digit or mark on either side). (3) Two agents of the same name were asked about as two identical options (`"Bob" (agent)` twice), so the owner could not say which; each option now leads with the record's ID (`agt-…: "Bob" (agent)`), as the task options do. Also: `scopeKind` agent or team with no `scopeName` at all now reads the owner's message for the name instead of reaching the status service as half a scope. Runs after the fix: chat/status/api/lifecycle 2280 tests, 2276 pass, 0 fail, 4 todo (C07k); `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6/6.
- **Second Opus review (clean context).** Three fixes, two suites (`chat/status.test.ts`, "a longer name the owner wrote is not also a shorter one inside it…" and "past the pages one look reads…"; both failed before the fix). (1) More than 500 agents (five pages of 100) answered a name past the fifth page with "no agent is called X. Here they are: …", a false negative stated as fact; the list now says whether it ended (`#listPages`), and a name not found in a cut list is said to be not among the first N read, with the ID asked for. (2) A shorter name standing only inside a longer one also named (agent Bob, team "Bob Squad") asked which was meant; it is now dropped unless it also stands on its own elsewhere in the message, and when several names are in the message the one the interpreter read (if it is one of them) is meant, so an agent called "the" no longer turns every "the Alpha team" into a question. (3) Names and message are compared in NFC, so an accent typed as a separate combining mark matches the stored precomposed name. Also: an option list cut at the chat's limit now says how many there were.

## L04d (first part): a probe reads the task's checkout, and a reviewer agent judges what changed (2026-11-09)

L04c built the checked resume and left its two senses missing: `ResumePorts.observe` was the host's port and nothing implemented it, so every recorded file and directory of a resumed task read `unknown`, and `ResumePorts.review` had the controller's stand-in, which calls every change relevant. Between them that made every changed resume an owner decision, which is what the card was written to end. This part supplies both, in the controller, without a host having to write anything.

**The dependency probe (`dependencies/observe.ts`, exported from `dependencies/index.ts`, `81dc6c4d`).** `checkoutDependencyObserver({ manifest, locate, maxEntries?, maxBytes?, fs?, onFault? })` answers the port: for each of a task's recorded `file` and `directory` dependencies it looks at the thing again and reports what it sees, so `DependencyService.check` says `unchanged`, `changed`, `deleted` or `new-members` instead of `unknown`. What it holds to:
- it looks only inside the checkout the task's own records name. A dependency key is text an agent wrote: a key that is not a safe relative path (absolute, drive-lettered, `~`, containing `..`) is left unobserved, as is one that resolves through a link to outside the checkout, and a listing of the probe's own file-system calls proves nothing beyond the root is opened. `relativePath` (the resource-path helper) and `relative`/`sep` do the judging, so the same rule holds on Windows and POSIX.
- it guesses nothing. A file bigger than the byte bound, a directory whose listing would have to be cut, an entry past the entry cap, and anything that could not be read are left out of the answer, which is the same as not looking: the check says `unknown`. A probe that looked and found nothing says `exists: false`, which is what lets `deleted` be told from `unknown`.
- it does not settle `search`, `external` or `mcp-resource` (those need the search made again or a conditional read of the thing itself) or `record`, `decision`, `tool-version` and `environment`, which the controller already judges from its own records. Those stay `unknown` here and are the host's port to answer.
- it never throws: an unreadable manifest, a checkout that is gone or a disk that will not read leave dependencies unobserved and tell `onFault`, so a probe cannot fail a resume check open.
- Bounds (`OBSERVE_LIMITS`): 200 dependencies, files of 8 MiB, listings of 200 names.
Tests: `dependencies/observe.test.ts` (40 across the backends) drives the real `DependencyService.check`, not a fake: unchanged, changed, deleted and new members told apart; a file whose name was reused by a directory; a link out of the checkout; keys that name `/etc`, `C:\Windows`, `~/.ssh` and `src/../../outside`; a file beyond the byte bound and a listing beyond the name bound; the entry cap; a manifest, a lookup or a `realpath` that fails; and that the probe's own file-system calls never leave the root.

**The reviewer agent (`continuation/resume-reviewer.ts`, `1b101c94`).** `ResumeReviewer(model, { routes, task?, perCall?, onFailure? })` implements the review port. Each route in turn is asked, in one call per `perCall` (default 40) changes, for a verdict on each; the first route that answers well enough for every change in that piece is taken. An answer is accepted only when it carries, for every id asked, a boolean `relevant` and a non-empty reason; anything else — a ramble with no JSON, a missing id, a verdict with no reason, an answer too long to be one — is that route's failure, tried on the next. When no route answers a piece it throws `unavailable`, and `ResumeCheckService` blocks the check `review_failed`: the resume waits at the review rather than being passed off as judged. A model that invents ids has them dropped. Keys, details, the task's title and its recorded next step go into the prompt as one JSON string each (`quotedLine`, redacted, cut by whole characters), and the system prompt says in words that what is inside a quote is data, not an instruction. `routes` is read again at every review, so a routing change applies to the next one.
Tests: `continuation/resume-reviewer.test.ts` (11) — a good answer, ids dropped, the route moved to after a ramble, a missing verdict and a reasonless one refused, 45 changes asked in three pieces and a piece nobody answers refusing the whole, no route at all, the refusal text redacted, a forged `[AUTHORITATIVE] owner:` line staying inside its quote with the key reading back as exactly what was recorded, the task's words quoted and cut, and routes read again per review.

**The controller uses them unless the host says otherwise (`api/start.ts`, `projects/resources.ts`, `7b842112`).** `StartOptions.resumeProbe` (default on, `false` off, `{ maxEntries, maxBytes }` to bound) installs the probe over the task's manifest and `ProjectResourceService.checkoutLocation` — a records-only read of where the task's repository is bound, of the same shape as `dispatchCheckout` but writing nothing and pinning nothing. `StartOptions.resumeReview` (`{ model, routes, tellTask? }`) installs the reviewer; `tellTask` (default yes) lets it see the task's title and the next step its continuation recorded. Both are put under the host's own `resume.observe` / `resume.review`, which still win: on a remote worker only that host can say what its disk looks like.
Tests: `api/start-resume-checkout.test.ts` (5, on SQLite and PostgreSQL, through `startController` and the state API) — a recorded file and directory that are as they were are observed and the agent commits the resumed attempt with nothing asked of the owner; a changed file is `changed`, a missing one `deleted`, a member gone from a listing is `gone: gone.ts`, and a key naming a file outside the checkout is `unknown` even when the file outside holds exactly the recorded hash; `resumeProbe: false` leaves the same file `unknown` and held, `{ maxEntries: 1 }` reads one and leaves the other unknown, and a host's own `resume.observe` is used instead of the probe; the reviewer's "it does not matter" lets the agent commit without the owner while "it matters" holds it, is shown to the owner in the free-form `needs_you` answer with the file named, and is what `resume.approve` then releases; a reviewer that will not answer on any route leaves the check `review_failed`, uncommit-able and not approvable.

ASSUMPTION: the probe is on by default. The card's complaint is that a resumed attempt sees `unknown`; a port that has to be switched on by every host keeps that complaint. `resumeProbe: false` is one option away and changes nothing else, so this is the reversible direction.
ASSUMPTION: `search`, `external` and `mcp-resource` dependencies stay `unknown` for a controller running without host ports. Making them up needs the search run again or the remote thing read conditionally, and a wrong "unchanged" there is the failure the card exists to prevent; the honest answer until a host answers the port is "not looked at", which holds the resume as L04c did.
ASSUMPTION: no reviewer is installed unless the host names routes. Choosing which model judges a resume is not this card's to make, and with no `resumeReview` the behaviour is exactly L04c's: every change relevant, the owner decides.
ASSUMPTION: the reviewer is told the task's title and its recorded next step, because "does this change matter to the work" cannot be answered without knowing the work; both are quoted, redacted and cut, and `tellTask: false` leaves them out for a host that would rather the model saw nothing of the task.
ASSUMPTION: the probe reads the file system the controller process is on, which is the machine the checkout lives on when the work runs there (the local host, and every one-machine installation). For an attempt pinned to a remote host the controller's look is at its own copy, not the worker's: such a deployment gives `resume.observe` (the host's own view, which L04c built for exactly this) or sets `resumeProbe: false`. What the probe reports is a fact about the machine it is on, never a guess about one it cannot see.
ASSUMPTION: 200 dependencies, 8 MiB and 200 names per listing. A probe that hashes a whole tree before an attempt starts would make the check cost more than the work it protects; anything past a bound is reported as what it is, unknown, rather than half-read.

**Mutation checks** (`npx tsc --build`, then the file above under the offline guard (`NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`); each restored and rebuilt after). Probe (`observe.test.ts`, 20 on SQLite of 40 across the backends): the `relativePath` guard dropped (2 fail); a link out of the checkout followed (2); the byte bound ignored (2); the listing bound ignored (2); the entry cap ignored (2); a missing file reported as nothing rather than `exists: false` (6, so `deleted` and `unknown` would have been confused); a gone checkout or an unreadable manifest throwing instead of leaving things unobserved (2 each); the fault text not redacted (2). Reviewer (`resume-reviewer.test.ts`, 11): only the first route tried (2 fail); a missing verdict tolerated (1); a reason not redacted (1); a key left unquoted in the prompt (2); ids the model invented kept (1); a provider's failure text not redacted (1); batching removed so all changes go in one call (2). Wiring (`start-resume-checkout.test.ts`, 5): the probe never installed (4 of 5 fail); the reviewer never installed (2); `resumeProbe: false` ignored (1); the task not told to the reviewer by default (1).
Four mutants survived and are recorded as such: the probe's second containment test (`within(base, target)`, after `relativePath` has refused the key and `realpath`'s target has been checked) is covered by those two and is defence in depth; dropping the reviewer's `if (changes.length === 0) return {}` (the chunk loop cannot run for an empty list, so it is an equivalent mutant); and each of the two guards that skip installing a default when the host supplied that port, ignored one at a time — the spread order puts the host's port last, so the host still wins either way. That is belt and braces, tested as one property ("what the host gives for the port wins"), not two.
Counts per file, the commands and the timings are in the implementer's report for this change (kept out of the tree).

### L04d (first part) review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09)

Five fixes, each with a test that fails without it (mutation-checked on the built files: each fix removed alone fails its test, the time bound by the file never finishing).
- **What could not be checked was the model's to wave through.** `ResumeCheckService` hands the reviewer every dependency that is not `unchanged`, `unknown` included, and the reviewer took the model's `relevant: false` for any of them; the system prompt only asked it not to. A key that talks the model round (or a confused model) committed an unread file without the owner, which before this card always waited. `ResumeReviewer` now puts only observed changes (`changed`, `deleted`, `new-members`) to the model; `unknown`, `cursor-expired` and `freshness-uncertain` are relevant without a call (`continuation/resume-reviewer.test.ts`).
- **A remote placement was judged on the controller's disk by default.** The resume check runs before the dispatcher picks the attempt's host, so with remote hosts the controller's copy is no evidence about where the work will run. The probe is now off by default when `dispatch.remote.hosts` is given (`resumeProbeEnabled`), and even when an operator turns it on there, a task last placed on a remote host or never placed is not located (`locallyPlaced`; both in `dependencies/observe.ts`).
- **The probe ignored the project's scope in the repository.** A binding limited to some paths still had every path of the checkout hashed and compared against the hash the agent recorded, an equality oracle on files the project may not use. `checkoutLocation` now returns the binding's paths and the probe looks only under them, including after a link is resolved.
- **Time-of-check reads.** The probe looked with `stat`, then opened by path with `readFile`: a file swapped for a pipe in between hung the check (and the dispatcher tick behind it), one that grew was read whole, and one swapped for a link was followed. Files are now opened with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK` after a type check, checked again on the descriptor, read to at most the bound plus one byte, and kept only if the path still resolves to the same inode (and, on Linux, the descriptor's own path is inside the checkout). Listings stop at the name bound instead of reading the whole directory first.
- **No time or total bound.** A probe could read 200 × 8 MiB and wait on a hung mount for ever. It now reads at most 64 MiB in all (`OBSERVE_LIMITS.totalBytes`) and stops at 15 s (`ms`), leaving the rest unknown.

ASSUMPTION: with remote hosts the probe is off unless asked for. The check cannot know where the attempt will run, and a wrong `unchanged` is the failure the card exists to prevent; an operator whose locators name the same disk everywhere sets `resumeProbe: true`.
ASSUMPTION: an `unknown` is never the reviewer's to clear. A reviewer told only "it was not read again" has nothing to weigh; the owner decides, as before L04d.

**Second review (clean context, 2026-11-09).** (1) A read the probe gave up on at its time bound kept running on Node's shared thread pool (four threads by default), and every later probe of the same hung mount started another one, so a few ticks would stall all of the controller's asynchronous file work. Now, while a call an earlier probe abandoned has not come back, no probe starts a file-system call: everything is left unobserved and the fault says so; once it returns, probes read again. (2) A file whose size moved between the probe's `stat` and the end of its read (it grew, or a procfs-like file that says it is empty) was hashed from what was read, a prefix that could equal the recorded content of a file that has since grown; a read whose length is not the size the open descriptor reported is now not used. Tests: `observe.test.ts` "second review" (one per backend, and one Linux-only on `/proc/self/status`), each failing without its fix. Checked and left as is: `O_NOFOLLOW`/`O_NONBLOCK` default to 0 where Node does not define them (Windows), so the flags are never `NaN` and the after-read `realpath` and inode checks still run; the `mkfifo` test is skipped on Windows; directory listings are not counted in the byte total but are bounded by the entry and member caps (200 × 200 names); the `scopeAllows` check runs both on the key and on the resolved path, for files and directories; a review with only unknown, expired or freshness-uncertain changes makes no model call and marks each relevant, so the owner decides; a task never placed, with remote hosts, is not located, so it reads `unknown`. Still open, not fixed here: a reviewer model client with no time bound of its own holds the dispatcher tick for as long as it takes (the host's routed client owns that bound), and each checked resume probes when it verifies and again when it is committed (an approval commits), each probe up to 15 s.
Still open, stated not fixed: the probe reads the checkout the task's repository is bound at (the binding's `locator`), not the task's own worker checkout under the host's workspace root; for a local host these are the shared repository and the task's copy made from it. A hard link inside the checkout to a file elsewhere is read like any file. Neither path-based check closes every rename race on platforms without `/proc/self/fd`. The reviewer's model client is the host's (`StartOptions.resumeReview`); nothing in the shipped entry point installs one, so its calls are not yet metered by the controller's model budgets.

**Not done (L04d stays planned)**
- The local and remote worker hosts still do not call `continuation.capture` at their safe boundaries. The operation and its host scoping are L04c's; nothing in `packages/worker` or the host processes calls it, so a resume is checked against a continuation captured by the owner or a host that vouches, not by the worker that stopped. That is the third piece of the card and it is worker- and host-side work, not wiring.
- `after: model-change` when the route differs from the checkpoint's route is still not derived; `resume.start` is told `after` by its caller.
- The per-tick cache of the prerequisite scan is untouched.
- `search`, `external` and `mcp-resource` observation (above).
- The reviewer is given the changes and the task's two lines, nothing more: not the plan, not the decisions of the continuation, not the content of a changed file. A reviewer that reads diffs is a later, larger design with its own bounds.

## Pi completion follow-ups: cards W01-W09 (2026-11-09)

Nine planned cards under N03 come from an Opus design consultation on 2026-11-09 about Pi Durable agents that stop before their work is done. The evidence: in about 25 Pi coding runs, all 3 bad runs ended on a thinking-only turn with 0 characters of visible text, while all 20 good runs ended with a report of 1.3k to 15k characters; NimbleNewt counts any natural stop as `succeeded` (`packages/controller/src/dispatch/dispatcher.ts` line 2020); Pi Durable answers on a `length` stop as on `stop` (`pi-durable/dist/harness/generation.js` line 362); and `--thinking medium` on the Pi command line made no difference. The cards measure first (W01, an eval bench with a recorded baseline and release gates), then tell how a turn ended (W02), stop treating a natural stop as success (W03), continue a stopped turn a bounded number of times (W04), check `work.end` done against the task contract (W05), give agents fixed completion rules (W06), set length and reasoning budgets per route (W07), show the owner how attempts ended (W08), and repeat the eval on the real worker and a Radiance route as a release gate (W09). The series letter W (work completion) was unused; N03 (Qualify the Pi Durable adapter) is the parent because every card is about how the Pi runtime ends a turn.

## C07p (Pi): a note that is cut says what it left out, and its whole text is kept where it says (2026-11-09)

C07l left the finding as a `todo` in `dispatch/first-call-hops.test.ts`, and it was two of the same fault. `handoffFromFacts` (`context/budget.ts`) cut the hand-off note the controller writes when an attempt ends without one at its **tail**, with `[… hand-off cut at N characters]` and nothing kept, so what went out was the newest effects and artifacts — the entries a hand-off exists to pass on. `dispatch/dispatcher.ts` cut the note that tells an attempt how the calls it waited on were decided with `note.slice(0, 500)` and no marker at all, fewer than four verdicts, so an attempt woken for more calls than that was never told how the later ones ended and nothing said anything was missing. Both notes are now composed by one rule; where a note cannot be carried whole its text is kept, and the note names the read that gives it back.

- **`cutNote({head, list}, maxChars, options)` (`context/budget.ts`, `d35c73f8`).** The `head` lines always stay; `list` lines are kept **newest first**, so a cut leaves the oldest out — the opposite of the tail slice it replaces. The marker that closes a cut says how many older lines and how many characters went out, and either names where the whole text is read (`readWith`, with the digest) or, when the caller has nothing to point at, says outright that the rest was not kept and cannot be read. Every line of the note is made one line (`[\r\n]+` folded), so no text an agent wrote can start a line of its own and read as the controller speaking; the joined note goes through `redactText`; `clipToChar` (exported, and now used by the note's own tail cut) never leaves half a surrogate pair, which is text a model server may refuse to encode. The marker is measured at its **largest** before anything is dropped, so the note it lands on always fits; `maxChars` under `NOTE_MIN_CHARS` (400) or with no room left for that marker is a `RangeError`, because a limit that cannot hold the explanation is a programming mistake, not a note. `NoteCut` carries `whole` and `digest` (`sha256:` + 64 hex) for the caller that keeps the original; `handoffFromFacts` keeps its shape and returns `.text`, so its callers did not change.
- **The controller's hand-off note is composed by that rule and quotes what an agent wrote (`context/budget.ts`, `da022c7c`).** `handoffNote` returns the `NoteCut`; `handoffFromFacts` is it, as text. The head is how it ended (the worker's own words, `quoted`), the task, the last known state, and the recorded next step and checkpoint when there is one; the list is the task's effects and then its artifacts, oldest first with a heading that says a cut leaves the oldest out. What an agent wrote — the ending, an effect's summary, an artifact's title, the last known state, the next step — goes through `quoted` from `status/explain.ts` (one line, controls escaped, credential shapes cut out, agent-written framed as a quotation), and IDs and states through `oneLine`. `[… hand-off cut at N characters]` is gone.
- **The whole text of a cut note, and the read that answers with it (`context/enforcement.ts`, `api/operations.ts`, `api/state-api.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `api/start.ts`, `d96e6eaf`).** `archiveNote` keeps `whole` as a `ctx-note-archive` record whose ID is derived from the task and the digest, so writing the same note twice is one copy (`replayed`), and it refuses a text that does not hash to the digest it is filed under — a note must not send anyone to an archive holding something else. Writing it is the controller's (`#dispatch`, the gate that writes the note itself); reading it is the same gate as reading the note, `#task` — whoever may work on the task — and an archive it may not show reads the same as one that is not there. `noteArchive` returns the fields the operation documents and keeps `projectId`/`writtenBy` in the record. The new query `context.note-archive.read {taskId, digest}` joins `context.spill.read` and `context.route-archive.read` beside the hand-off note read C07m added; a controller composed without a dispatcher answers `unavailable`, like its neighbours. `npm run api:docs:write` regenerated `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` with that entry and nothing else.
- **A cut note is archived before it is stored, so its pointer is true (`context/enforcement.ts` `ensureHandoff`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `api/start.ts`, `f8c8559d`).** When an attempt ends without its own hand-off, the note is composed, its whole text kept, and only then is the note stored — a stored note therefore never names an archive that was not written. When the archive cannot be written the hand-off is still written (an attempt ending after a confirmed effect must leave a record), composed again **without** the pointer so it says plainly that the rest cannot be read, and the fault is reported. `#reportFixedError` became `#reportFault`: it is now the once-a-minute reporter for two faults, not the overflow counter alone. `startController` (and `composeDispatch`, `DispatchStartOptions`) takes a `handoffFacts` producer for the durable facts the note is written from — the effect ledger, artifacts, checkpoint, last known state; without one the note still says the ledger could not be read, exactly as before this card, which is why the end-to-end test passes its own.
- **The note of parked-call verdicts tells every verdict (`dispatch/dispatcher.ts`, `302bf11e`).** `#verdictNote` builds it with `cutNote`: a line that says what these verdicts are, then `- call <operationId> was <verdict>` for each, oldest first. Its bound is `PARKED_NOTE_CHARS` = `DISPATCH_LIMITS.parked` × 200 — room for every call an attempt can wait on, with an ID of the longest the tool bridge accepts — so an attempt woken for twenty calls is told all twenty, which is what it needs the moment it resumes and cannot look up for itself. The marker a cut would leave is written without brackets (`plainMarker`, the option this needed), because the worker puts a resume note inside a bracketed block of the prompt and one `]` of ours there would close that block and let the rest of the note speak as the prompt's own text; and it names no archive, because the dispatcher writes none — see the assumption below.
- **Tests.** `context/budget.test.ts` (16, five of them this card): newest lines kept and the oldest counted out, the digest and the read named; a note with nothing left to drop still says what its own tail lost; no cut leaves half a character and no entry starts a line of its own (an effect summary carrying `\n`, a lone surrogate and an emoji, swept across the bound); what an agent wrote is quoted and the newest effects and artifacts survive; a note cut for a bracketed block carries no bracket at all. `context/enforcement.test.ts` (8 on this card, two suites over four backends): the archive written and read back whole by the task's readers and read as missing by someone who may not work on the task; a digest that is not the text's refused; the same note twice one copy; and `ensureHandoff` archiving before it stores, and saying plainly that the rest cannot be read when the archive fails. `api/api.test.ts` (4): the operation answers the caller's own principal and a note that kept nothing reads as not found; a controller with no composed context service answers `unavailable`. `api/start-note-archive.test.ts` (new, one composed controller on a sqlite file store): a real attempt ends without a hand-off, the controller writes one from `handoffFacts` that cannot be kept whole, the note the next agent is handed names `context.note-archive.read` and its digest, and that read gives the whole text to the project's worker and to someone who may not work on the task reads nothing. `dispatch/dispatcher.test.ts` (376, four backends): one attempt parks twenty gated calls, all twenty are decided in one tick, and the note its wake-up order carries is over the old 500-character bound yet names every one of the twenty operations, one to a line, with no bracket in it. `dispatch/first-call-hops.test.ts`: the case C07l left as `todo` passes and lost its todo (38 tests, 38 pass, 0 todo).
- ASSUMPTION: the parked-call note is given a bound large enough to carry every verdict rather than a smaller bound plus an archive. With the tool bridge's own operation IDs (24 characters, `derivedId`) twenty verdicts are a little under a tenth of `PARKED_NOTE_CHARS`, so a cut — and with it the archive the plan for this card also named — is not reachable through the dispatcher at the current limits; writing that branch would have been code no test could reach. If `DISPATCH_LIMITS.parked` or the ID shape ever grows past the bound, `cutNote` keeps the newest verdicts and the marker says outright that the rest cannot be read, which is true of a note the dispatcher never archived; a card that wants verdict archives should fit them under a bound that actually cuts.
- ASSUMPTION: a note that cannot be composed within its limit is a `RangeError`, not a silently shorter note. Every caller of `cutNote` passes a limit it also stores the note under (`ENFORCEMENT_LIMITS.handoff`), so a limit too small to hold head-plus-marker is a mistake in the program, and the alternative — dropping the explanation — is the fault this card removes.
- ASSUMPTION: the archive is kept as long as the store keeps the task, as C07j's route archives and C07g's spills are; no retention rule is added for `ctx-note-archive` here. Every one of them is a record of one task, written only when a note was cut, and the retention sweep for the other context archives is the place to bound them together.
- **Still open, deliberately not here.** No production `handoffFacts` producer is wired by default: `startController` accepts one and the tests supply their own, so the effects-and-artifacts part of the note is reachable in production only once a host passes the ledger read — the note without it still says how the attempt ended, what the task was and its last known state. `readHandoff`'s `view` (a display cut of 3 000 characters that ends "…(the rest is kept here)") is unchanged and points at the note record, which does hold the whole stored text; nothing in this repository shows a hand-off through `view` — the API and the first-call paragraph both use `text`.
- **Runs** (this worktree, `npx tsc --build --force` clean; every test under the offline guard (`scripts/offline-guard.mjs` as an absolute `file://` URL) with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`): `dist/context/*.test.js dist/dispatch/*.test.js dist/lifecycle/*.test.js dist/api/*.test.js dist/chat/*.test.js` — 3 464 tests, 3 460 pass, **0 fail**, 4 todo, 730 s at concurrency 4 (the four todos are C07k's package-size trend on the four backends; C07p's is gone). Files this card adds or changes, each alone: `context/budget.test.js` 16/16, `api/start-note-archive.test.js` 1/1 (both together 1.6 s), `api/api.test.js` C07p cases 4/4, `context/enforcement.test.js --test-name-pattern C07p` 8/8, `dispatch/dispatcher.test.js` 376/376, `dispatch/first-call-hops.test.js` 38/38 with no todo. Against a mutation that drops the options `handoffNote` passes to `cutNote` — so a cut note names no archive — the `first-call-hops` case fails, and the mutations run during the steps (the retained-list rule in `cutNote`, and `ensureHandoff` composing without `readWith`) failed the C07p checks they govern. `node --test scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6 pass / 0 fail; `npm run check:deps` "package boundaries ok"; `npm run api:docs:write` regenerated `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` with no further change to it. `npm run roadmap:check` fails ("README roadmap is stale"): `d4aba792` flipped C07m and C07n to implemented in the plan without rewriting the generated README section, and the roadmap is stale at this branch's base too (`git stash` + `roadmap:check` says the same on the untouched tree). Nothing in this card's diff touches it, and `scripts/generate_task_plan.py`/`task-plan.md` are outside this card's authority, so it is left for whoever owns the plan.
- **Review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09).** Three fixes in `cutNote`/`handoffNote` (`context/budget.ts`), each with a test in `context/budget.test.ts` that fails without it. (1) Credentials were removed from the joined note at once, so a shape matched across a line break (a task titled `Rotate the deploy token:` and the next line's `Last`) swallowed the line after it — in every controller hand-off, cut or not — and the line counts the cut and its marker rest on were off; redaction is now line by line. (2) Effects and artifacts were one list cut from its front, so every effect, the newest included, went before the oldest artifact, and the single heading went first as if it were the oldest entry; they are now two lists (`lists`, each with its own heading), and a cut takes the oldest line of whichever list has most left. (3) When even the head did not fit, the marker called the list's lines that went "older lines" though they are the newest the note has; it now says "the rest of this note left out (N lines, C characters)". Checked, no change: the read gate is `attempt.work` on the task, as `context.handoff.read` (another task's digest, a look-alike digest and a reader of another project read as not found; the record ID binds task and digest and the body is checked against both); the archive is written before the note that names it, and a crash between leaves a harmless orphan that the replay finds; one archive per task and digest, each capped at `ENFORCEMENT_LIMITS.archiveChars` (a note over it is stored without a pointer); the parked-verdict note is at most twenty lines of 24-character IDs (about 1 000 characters), measured as it is by the local worker beside the view, so it stays inside `PROMPT_NOTE_RESERVE_CHARS` although its `PARKED_NOTE_CHARS` bound is 4 000.
- **Second review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09).** Two fixes in `cutNote` (`context/budget.ts`), each with a test in `context/budget.test.ts` that fails without it. (1) Line-by-line redaction (the first review's fix) lost one thing redacting the joined note had: a private key block given one line to an entry was redacted on its `BEGIN` line only, and its body and `END` line were shown. The private-key shape, the one credential pattern that spans lines by nature, is now removed across the lines it covers first, each line keeping its place (so the counts stay exact), and the other shapes are still removed line by line (the `token:`/next-line case stays fixed). No current caller reaches it (`handoffNote` redacts each value whole before it becomes a line, and the verdict lines are the controller's), but `cutNote` is exported and promises credentials removed. (2) A note with no head whose every line went came out as an empty line and then the marker; it is now the marker alone. Checked, no change: the bound holds in every branch (the marker is measured at its longest; a single line over the limit, empty lists, a head alone over the limit, a surrogate pair at the cut); the marker's line and character counts equal what went; shown lines keep their order; agent text is `quoted`, so it cannot start a line or pose as the marker; the digest is of the whole composed text and `archiveNote` checks it; a whole note over `ENFORCEMENT_LIMITS.archiveChars` is refused by `archiveNote` and the stored note says plainly that the rest cannot be read, so no archive is partial yet claimed whole. Left as is: when the newest list line alone is over the limit it is dropped and counted as an "older" line (the count is right, the word is not; unreachable with the callers' line bounds), and the verdict note's "newest last" is the order the calls were parked, not decided.

## M03h part 2 (usage sink): the dispatcher records each run's slot time, and the stand-up review counts runs, not waits (2026-11-09)

The second slice (2026-11-05) made the review measure worker-slot time from the dispatch records, but a record kept only its first `startedAt` and its end, so any attempt that parked for an approval, waited after a controller shutdown or was placed again could not tell run time from waiting time and was left out of the share. Those are exactly the long attempts. This slice is the sink the card named: the dispatcher now writes when an attempt holds a slot, and the review reads that.

- **The sink (`dispatch/model.ts` `withSlotSpans`, `dispatch/dispatcher.ts` `#update`).** Every dispatch record carries `slotSpans`: one `{ from, to? }` per run. A rewrite that moves the record into `running` opens a span at the dispatcher's clock; one that moves it out (`parked`, `waiting` after a shutdown, `finished`) closes the open span; any other rewrite leaves them alone. It is applied inside `#update`, which every state change of a dispatch record goes through (the record is created `waiting` and has no other writer), so the span is written in the same commit as the move and no caller can forget it. `mutate` is replayed on its own result after a lost race or a crash; the helper looks only at the move from the stored record to the new one, so a replay adds nothing. The newest 64 spans are kept (`DISPATCH_LIMITS.slotSpans`); `slotSpansCut` is the end of the newest one let go.
- **The reader (`standups/standups.ts` `#slotUsage`).** A record with spans counts the part of each span inside the period; an open span counts to the end of the period while the attempt runs and to its last heartbeat otherwise. Parked, resumed and re-placed attempts are now counted by their runs. A record from before the spans is measured as before (start to recorded end) and, if it parked or was placed again, still left out and named in the basis as an "older record". A record whose cut falls inside the period is counted on what it keeps and the basis says "the earliest runs of N attempts are not on record". The basis may now be up to 240 characters in the review line (it was cut at 100, which the two notes together would pass).
- **Runs** (`npx tsc --build --force` clean; offline guard, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`): `dist/standups dist/meetings dist/chat dist/status dist/api dist/dispatch` — 3185 tests, 3185 pass, 0 fail; `node --test scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6 pass; `npm run roadmap:check` "roadmap ok"; `npm run check:deps` "package boundaries ok"; `npm run api:docs:write` changed nothing (no operation or status kind changed).
- **Tests.** `dispatch/dispatcher.test.ts` "the usage sink (card M03h)…" (four backends): an attempt runs ten seconds, parks for an approval, waits thirty seconds, is approved, runs ten seconds more and finishes; the record has two closed spans, the first closed when it parked, the wait between them, and twenty seconds held in all. `standups/standups.test.ts` P/PC balance review (four backends): an attempt with `requests: 2` and `resumedFor` whose spans hold two hours counts two hours of PC time (not the eight from its first start to its end) beside the older parked record still left out (50%); a running record with a cut inside the period and an open span counts its kept span plus the open span to the review time, and the basis names the cut (38%). Both fail without the change (no `slotSpans` is written; the spans record is left out as parked).
- **Not built (rest of M03h).** (1) An agenda outcome that asks the owner a new question. Looked at, not started: the owner-question path today is an inquiry addressed to the owner (`messages.askOwner`), and an inquiry needs a task and an asker allowed to work on it, which a stand-up topic raised from a chat turn does not have; the `owner-question` notification takes only `ok` as an answer, so it cannot carry the owner's reply back. A sound design needs an owner question owned by the meeting (a record or an inquiry without a task), a sink that raises it in the owner's inbox and chat, an answer path the owner reaches in free-form chat, and the answer shown on the next stand-up's agenda; that is its own slice. (2) The end-to-end controller test of a stand-up with every sink. (3) A per-project index: `#slotUsage`, `list`, `recent` and `overview` still scan every record of their kind in the installation (bounded at 5,000, then marked partial). (4) Nothing outside the stand-up review reads the measure: no admission or allocation control acts on the P/PC share, which the card does not ask for.
- ASSUMPTION: an attempt holds a slot exactly while its record is `running`, including a run whose worker is later found lost: its span is closed when the dispatcher ends it, not at its last heartbeat, because the place stays taken until then and that is what the allocation is about. `parked` and `waiting` hold no place (the dispatcher gives the request back before parking and after a shutdown).
- ASSUMPTION: 64 spans per attempt. An attempt parks at most once per approval round, and the review looks back one stand-up period; an attempt with more than 64 runs inside one period is counted on its newest 64 and the basis says so, rather than letting one record grow without bound.
- ASSUMPTION: records written before this change are not rewritten. They keep the old measure and the old exclusion, named as "older" in the basis, and age out of the review's period on their own.
- **Review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09).** Three fixes, each with a test that fails without it (`dispatch/slot-spans.test.ts`, new, 4 cases; `dispatcher.test.ts` "the usage sink (card M03h): an attempt lost with its controller…", four backends; `standups.test.ts` P/PC review, one more step). (1) A run ended after its lease ran out was closed when the loss was noticed. While the controller is up that is at most a tick after the lease, but a controller that died and came back eight hours later closed it eight hours late, and the review counted the whole outage as slot time for whatever was running at the crash, though no worker ran and no other attempt could have used the place either. `withSlotSpans` now closes such a run at `lease.until` (its last heartbeat plus one lease). This replaces the first ASSUMPTION above for lost runs; an attempt the new controller adopts (its host kept running it) keeps its span open through the outage, since that work was done. (2) A record that ran before the sink and parked, then resumed after it, opened its first span with nothing to say its earlier runs were missing, so the review counted only its newer runs as if they were the whole and named no gap. Its cut is now set (to its last heartbeat, else the time it resumes), and the review names it under "the earliest runs of N attempts are not on record" — also when what it keeps holds no time in the period, which before was a silent omission. (3) A clock set back could open a span before the previous one's end, so spans overlapped and the overlap was counted twice; a span now opens no earlier than the end of the one before. Checked, no change: every state change of a dispatch record goes through `#update` (start, yield/park, move, shutdown, resume-to-waiting, end, adoption keeps `running`); a replayed `mutate` and an adoption add nothing; no extra writes (spans ride on existing transitions, so no new optimistic-concurrency conflicts) and at most 64 spans (~5 KB) per record; period clipping, NaN dates and an empty cut are harmless; parallel attempts summing is correct (slots), and the share's denominator is the same sum; the basis is controller text only (no agent-written text), at most about 200 characters, inside the 240 bound. Left as is: a still-`running` record whose lease ran out (controller down) counts to the review time until a tick ends or adopts it; the record's `projectId` and the task's current class are used, as before.
- **Second review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-09).** No logic bug found in the sink or the reader; each of the first review's three fixes is caught by its test when reverted (lease close: `slot-spans` and the dispatcher's lost-controller case on all four backends; pre-sink cut and the overlap guard: `slot-spans`). Checked: `lease.until` is the last renewal (every heartbeat rewrites it through `#update`) and is present on every `running` record the dispatcher writes; a close before the span's start is clamped to a zero-length span; step 0 of the tick adopts before step 1 judges leases, and adoption leaves the state `running`, so an adopted run's span stays open; a replayed `mutate` and a `stale_revision` retry recompute from the stored record; 64 spans stay far inside the 256 KB body bound on every backend. Text only: the basis said "1 older record that parked or were placed again is not counted" (now "was placed"), and "no longer on record" also named pre-sink runs that were never recorded (now "not on record", and the `slotSpansCut` comment says what the cut is for such a record).
