### T02d finish (Claude agent, 2026-11-13): leftover run records are swept while the controller runs, and on every page

What was left after the close-out: leftover running-call records (a process that stopped, or lost the epoch and could not remove its own) were swept only once at controller start, and only from the first page of records, so a long-running controller with many leftovers kept them (they were never listed past their time, so this cost storage, not honesty).

Done:
- `RunningCallStore.sweep` looks through the same bounded number of pages as the listing (`pages`, default 10 of 500) instead of the first page only; at most 200 removals per run, as before.
- `ToolExecutionService` sweeps by itself: a call that starts triggers one sweep at most every `runRecordSweepMs` (default 600,000 = 10 minutes; `0` turns it off, the start-up sweep remains). It is never waited for and a failure never reaches the call. `StartOptions` needed no change (the default applies).
- No new owner control (nothing here is something the owner sets or decides).
- Tests (every backend): `toolbridge/running-store.test.ts` (4 expired leftovers among 3 live ones with a page size of 2 are all removed, live ones stay), `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (default and `0` do not sweep within a fresh service; a call after the interval sweeps once; and again after the next interval). Mutations (each applied, run, restored; each fails the named tests): sweep reading only the first page; sweep removing live records; the `0` switch ignored; no throttle; the call never triggering the sweep.

What cannot be done offline or remains NOT done (unchanged by this slice):
- **Remote worker hosts.** The remote worker protocol has no tool-execution leg (a remote host cannot run a catalogue script: `tool.invoke` from a remote attempt is refused with "unavailable"), so no catalogue call can be running on a remote host and there is nothing to revoke there. Making a remote host run scripts is a card of its own (a run order, a sandbox on that host, results, abort, fencing and a `revoke` control message beside `stop`, with the choice already on the revocation record and the running-call record pattern to reuse); it was not started here because a revoke message with nothing running on the other end could not be shown to work. Until then "every host" means every host that can run a catalogue tool.
- Clock difference: `until` is the writing process's clock compared with the reader's (processes on one machine share a clock; more than 60 s apart may stop listing a call early).
- A fenced process still cannot remove its own record; a call that ends there stays listed (as in another process) until its time is up. This errs toward asking the owner.
- Latency of the store check (default 2 s) unchanged. Not run on macOS or Windows here: the new tests use fake clocks and short real waits on conditions, no signals, paths or sandbox.

ASSUMPTION (2026-11-13): sweeping is triggered by a starting call (needs no new timer or process hook; an idle controller has no new leftovers to find) rather than by a dedicated interval.
ASSUMPTION (2026-11-13): ten minutes between sweeps; the sweep is bounded and cheap, and a leftover is never listed past its time anyway.
ASSUMPTION (2026-11-13): the remote half is left as a documented gap rather than a protocol message nobody can use; the card's own sentence says remote workers "cannot run catalogue tools yet".

Review of the finish (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-13):
- Fixed: `runRecordSweepMs` set to NaN swept on every call (the comparison with NaN is never "too soon"); NaN, Infinity and negative values now turn the sweep off, as `0` does. A clock set back (time since the last sweep below 0) stopped the sweep until the clock caught up again; it now counts as due and the next interval counts from the new time. Tests in `toolbridge/service.test.ts`.
- Checked, no change: a sweep removes only records whose `until` has passed on the sweeper's clock, revision-guarded (a record replaced or ended meanwhile is left alone), and only while this process holds the epoch; keyset paging is not disturbed by the removals. The revocation reaching another process does not read these records at all: each process asks the store for revocations of the versions it is running itself (`checkRevocations`), so a swept record can never cause a revocation to be missed. The worst outcome of a writer whose clock is more than the 60 s grace behind is that another process stops listing (and may sweep) that call early: the owner's revoke question may then not show it and no choice is recorded for it, so the process running it applies the standing policy; the revocation itself still reaches it. The setting is not wired from configuration (start.ts uses the default), so neither the owner, agents nor chat can change it. The sweep is started without being awaited and wrapped in a catch; a store that fails answers 0.
- Mutations of my own (each applied to built files, run, restored; each fails tests): sweep removing live records; sweep reading only the first page; NaN not treated as off; a clock set back ignored; the store revocation check switched off (integration `t02d-revocation-reach`); `end` removing another writer's record.

## T02d (remote script execution): a catalogue tool runs on the remote worker host, and a revocation reaches it there (Claude agent, 2026-11-14)

Card T02d stays as it is (the owner flips cards). This builds the one part the earlier slices recorded as a gap: a catalogue tool called from an attempt on a remote worker host. Until now the controller refused it ("tools of the catalogue cannot be run for it yet"), so there was no running call on a remote host for a revocation to reach. Now there is, and the revocation reaches it. Everything below is proven offline with a real worker transport, the real client, the real remote service and a fake script sandbox on the host side; what only a real second machine can show is listed at the end.

**Built**
- **Protocol version 2** (`remote/protocol.ts`). `WORKER_PROTOCOL` is `{ min: 1, max: 2 }`. A session negotiates the highest version both sides speak, as before; a worker or controller that speaks only 1 still connects at 1, and for such a session nothing new is ever sent or accepted. New control messages `run` (the run ID and the SHA-256 of the order; never the source or the arguments), `abort` (one run) and `revoke` (the tool name and version and the owner's choice: `finish`, `cancel` or `pause`), beside `stop`; two worker routes, `POST /worker/attempts/{id}/run-fetch` and `.../run-done`. New limits in `REMOTE_LIMITS`: at most 4 scripts running per attempt, source at most 256 KB, standard input at most 64 KB (the bridge's own argument limit), output at most 64 KB (the bridge's own output limit) in a body of at most 512 KB, an error text of at most 500 characters, and a grace of 30 s beyond the script's own time limit.
- **The run order** (`remote/script-orders.ts`, `RemoteWorkerService.runScript`). The tool service checks a call from a remote host exactly as it checks a local one (the exact version, the arguments against the manifest, the access the tool asks for against the task's credential, the host's facts against the manifest, revocation at the start, the approval path of the dispatcher's tool call), builds the same `ScriptLaunch` and hands it to `remoteRuns.run`. The service then requires: the caller is the owner or the dispatcher; the placement is accepted and held by that host; the host's session is the one that accepted it, of THIS primary (the epoch), and negotiated protocol 2; the dispatch contract is confirmed; and the order is within the limits. The run ID is a digest of the attempt, the call ID and the placement, so the same call asked again joins the same run (one order, one wait), and another placement is another run. The order is kept in memory only; the placement keeps the run ID and digest in its bounded control queue.
- **The host-side runner** (`remote/script-runs.ts`, `RemoteScriptRuns`, wired into `RemoteOfferRunner` and `scripts/remote-host.mjs`). The host reads the control message, fetches the order, checks it against the digest and the protocol's bounds (a plain program name, short argument list, sizes, whole-number limits), runs it in ITS OWN sandbox (the worker package's `hostScriptRunner`, the same launcher the host's agents use, a private folder under the host's base) with an EMPTY environment whatever the order says, and reports `done`, `failed` or `aborted`. An `aborted` report is the acknowledgement of a stop, and is sent only after the run's own promise has settled, that is when the sandbox has ended the process. A host with no script runner (no interpreter or no sandbox) answers every order as failed at once ("no script sandbox"), so the controller never waits out a run nobody can start. The interpreters the host offers are announced as its tools (`node@22.19.0`), which is what the manifest check reads.
- **Result and acknowledgement back** (`run-done`). Strictly shaped (known fields, a bounded text, whole-number figures); a missing idempotency key is refused; a report for a run that is not open is answered `kept: false` and dropped; the output is held to the order's own limit; the host's error text is redacted and cut by the host and again by the controller. Nothing of an output or an order is recorded anywhere; the waiting call gets it.
- **Fencing.** `run-fetch` and `run-done` go through the same check as every message about an attempt: another host's attempt is `not_found` (with the security signal), a stale placement or session `fenced`, and a placement that ended or moved ends every run of it for the waiting call (`#wake`); a report from the old holder is then fenced. A run belongs to one placement and one session: a report that names a run of another placement or session settles nothing. A session at protocol 1 is refused by both routes (400) and never ordered a script (the call fails with "speaks worker protocol 1; running catalogue tools on a remote host needs protocol 2: upgrade its worker").
- **`revoke`, carrying the recorded choice.** The tool service keeps, for each running call, an optional hook the remote runner sets. When a revocation is applied (by the listener in the process that took the command, or by the store check in another process: the choice is the one on the revocation record, else the standing policy, as before), every running call is told the choice BEFORE anything is aborted: a remote call sends a `revoke` message with the name, the version and the choice. `cancel` and `pause`: the host stops every run of that version (and refuses an order of it that was already on its way), the call's own signal aborts so the call ends as failed at once, and `pause` pauses the task as before; the abort is not sent a second time. `finish`: the host is told and leaves the run alone, and the call ends on the bytes it started with. A call whose own signal aborts for any other reason sends `abort` for that run.
- **Running-call records.** A remote call is entered as a running call of its version like a local one (`#enter`), so the durable record other controller processes read lists it (`catalog.running`, the chat's revoke question) and the store check reaches it. It is removed when the call ends. Jobs stay on this machine: `job.start` from an attempt on a remote host is refused with that reason.
- **Composition.** `startController` passes `remoteRuns` to the tool service whenever there is a remote worker service; `tools.isLocalHost` still decides which calls are local. A controller started without a remote service still refuses a remote call exactly as before.
- **Tests (all four storage backends: reference store, SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread, PostgreSQL).** `remote/script-runs.test.ts` (14 scenarios per backend and 4 plain): order, fetch, run, result; failures with a redacted reason; the call's abort and the late acknowledgement; the three revoke choices; a revocation that arrives before the order; fencing (another host, a stale placement, a malformed run ID, unknown fields, bad outcomes, an oversize body, no idempotency key, a run settled once); the placement ending; staff only, a host that does not hold the attempt, an unconfirmed contract; a protocol 1 session; limits and joining the same call; a run the host never reports; the control message shapes; the host's repeated and tampered orders and lost reports; the order book alone. `remote/script-tools.test.ts` (9 per backend): the whole path through the real tool bridge (the credential, the call, the order, the host, the answer, the running-call record, no credential or source or arguments in any record), the tool's own checks on a remote host, a service with no remote runner, a protocol 1 host, a revocation taken in this process and in ANOTHER process with each choice (finish, cancel, pause; the recorded choice beats the standing policy). `remote/runner.test.ts` (1 added) and `remote/transport.test.ts` (the protocol range now 1 to 2; an older worker still connects at 1).

**Not done / what only a real second machine can show**
- A real second machine with its own sandbox and clock. Here the host's sandbox is a fake and the two sides share one clock. Not shown: (1) clock skew. The 60 s grace of the running-call record (`RunningCallStore`, `graceMs`) is measured by the controller's clock only and a host's clock is never read (the host is told durations, not times), so skew should not matter; a controller whose clock jumps is the case that was already handled; but it has not been seen with two clocks. (2) Real network loss between the order and its result: a lost `run-done` is tried three times with the same key and then dropped, and the controller then fails the call at the run's own time plus 30 s, telling the host to stop; the loop is exercised with failing fakes, not a dropped connection. (3) A real sandbox that is slow to die or that cannot be killed: the acknowledgement waits for the process, and a run that never ends is failed on the controller after its limit plus the grace, with the owner's log saying the stop was not confirmed; the process is then left to the host's sandbox limits. (4) A host that is upgraded between the order and the result.
- The control queue of a placement holds 20 messages and the host reads it every half second; a flood of orders, aborts and revokes (more than 20 unread) could push an older message out. The per-attempt limit of 4 runs keeps this far from happening; a stop is not protected from it more than it was before.
- A controller that restarts loses its in-memory order book: the wait of a call that was running dies with the process (as a local call's does). Whether the call is run again is the dispatcher's ledger's decision, exactly as for a local call (`dispatch/tools.ts`, `#again`): only a read-only call or one whose approved manifest says `recovery: "restart"` is run again (same run ID under the same placement: a host that still has the old run going does not start a second copy, and one that remembers the outcome reports it again); any other call that was open is settled as uncertain and is NOT run again, so a script that is not safe to repeat is never repeated by a restart. Its process on the host may still finish on its own within its time limit (its report then finds no wait and is dropped, `kept: false`), or is stopped when the host's attempt is fenced by the new primary. The durable record the sweep clears is the running-call record, as before. (Corrected in review: this said such a call is run again.)
- Jobs (`job.start`) on a remote host, the package launcher on a remote host beyond `node` as announced, and tool dependencies (packages) on a remote host are not carried: a manifest that needs a package the host did not announce is refused by the host check, as before.
- Windows and macOS remote hosts: the remote worker program is still Linux only (bubblewrap); the protocol and the host runner contain nothing platform specific, but nothing ran on those systems.

**ASSUMPTION:** the order travels by reference (the control message names a run and a digest, the host fetches the order) rather than inside the control message, so the source and the model's arguments are never written into the placement record, the control queue is not bloated, and a record cannot hold a secret a tool's input carried.
**ASSUMPTION:** a host that negotiated protocol 1 is simply not ordered a script (the call fails with a message that says to upgrade its worker); there is no downgrade path that runs the script on this machine instead, because that would run a task's tool outside the host the owner placed the task on.
**ASSUMPTION:** `finish` is also told to the host (a `revoke` message with the choice), although the host does nothing but note it: the message is the record of the choice at the host, and it means a host that restarts its control reading sees the same instruction every process saw.
**ASSUMPTION:** a run that is not reported within the script's own time limit plus 30 s is failed on the controller and the host is told to stop it; 30 s is the same order of grace the running-call record uses (60 s) and is one option (`scriptGraceMs`).
**ASSUMPTION:** the order book is in memory only (a restart loses the wait, as a local call's wait is lost); making it durable would write the order's arguments to the store, which the first assumption avoids.
**ASSUMPTION:** the new routes need protocol 2 on the session itself (400 for a session at 1), not only a controller that has them, so an old worker cannot be handed a message it would ignore.

**Mutation checks (built files, one at a time, restored; each ran the new test files on the reference store, the first three on all four backends).** Dropping the placement from the run lookup fails the order-book test; dropping the digest check on the host fails 2 (fencing, tampered order); building the script's environment from the order fails the repeated-order test; not telling a running call the choice at a revocation fails 5 (finish, cancel, pause, another process cancel); making `finish` stop the run on the host fails 3; acknowledging a stop before the process is gone fails the abort test; dropping the protocol 2 gate fails 2; not joining the same call fails the limits test; not ending runs when the placement ends fails the placement test on all four backends; telling every call `cancel` whatever the choice fails 3 (the `finish` cases). One mutant survived and is equivalent: not marking a run as revoked (the run is already marked `aborting`, which is what stops the second message).

**Runs** (`npx tsc --build --force` clean, no stale dist tests, `api:docs:write` unchanged, `check:deps` ok; sandbox required; offline guard). Controller: the whole `remote/` and `toolbridge/` folders plus the 40 `api`, `release`, `dispatch`, `status` and `hosts` test files that mention remote workers or the protocol: 1,740 of 1,740 pass on the final run. On the first run 14 failed: 13 were tests that wrote protocol version 1 into a request header by hand (`artifacts`, `workspace-ask`: now the session's own version) or read four placement writes too early on PostgreSQL (my limits test: now waits for all four), all fixed and rerun green; 1 was the existing T02d "revoke taken by another process (pause)" test on PostgreSQL under a machine load of about 80, which passes 20 of 20 alone (its check of the task pause races the call's end by design; known timing, unchanged). `scripts/remote-host.test.mjs` 10 pass, 1 skipped (a new test for the host's script wiring), `scripts/nimblenewt-launcher.test.mjs` pass; integration `k01i-multi-host`, `l05d-remote-sandbox`, `h12m-workspace-host`, `w12-remote-anchor` 7 of 7 with the real remote host program. The whole controller package was not run in shards this time (nothing outside these areas reads the protocol range).

Review of T02d remote execution (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-14; origin/main merged first, clean):
- **Fixed: a remote host was judged by this machine's facts.** The shipped composition (`scripts/local-host.mjs`) passes the local script runner's `facts` as `tools.facts`, which takes no host and answers THIS machine's interpreters; the tool service asked it for every host, so a call from a remote host was checked against the controller's interpreters, not the host's (a host with no Node.js passed the check and then failed on the host). `ToolExecutionService` now asks `facts` only for a host `isLocalHost` accepts; a remote host is judged by its own announcement (`node@22.19.0` from `scripts/remote-host.mjs`) and its declared capacity. The test rig's host now announces its interpreter; a new test (4 backends) shows a host that announced none is refused before anything is ordered although this machine has the interpreter.
- **Fixed: a stopped run could answer a joined call with an empty result.** When a run being stopped (`aborting`) got the host's report, the order book resolved it with `{ text: "" }`; a second caller that had joined the run and was still waiting took that as the tool's answer. It now ends as "the run was stopped before it ended" whatever the host reports (unit test; in the product the dispatcher joins a repeated call itself, so this was reachable only through a direct second `runScript`).
- **Hardened: the 20-message control queue.** A revocation tells every running call of a version, so up to 4 identical `revoke` messages went onto the queue for one attempt. A `revoke` now replaces one queued for the same name and version (as `look` and `kill` do), so they cannot push the owner's `stop` out; another version's is its own message (test: 25 revokes of one version after a stop leave `stop, revoke 1.0.0`, and another version adds one). Otherwise the agent cannot drive the queue: a new run needs a free slot of the 4, and a run ends only after the host read its order (or 31 s or more), so the unread script messages stay at a handful.
- **Added a test** for the primary-epoch check in `runScript` (a controller that took the store over orders nothing of a host whose session was opened with the earlier primary); removing the check survived every existing test before.
- **Corrected the restart note** (above): a controller restart re-runs only a read-only or `recovery: "restart"` call, as for a local call; any other open call is settled as uncertain, never repeated.
- Checked, no change: fencing of `run-fetch`/`run-done` (another host `not_found` with the security signal, stale placement or session `fenced`, protocol 1 refused, a run of another placement or session neither shown nor settled); the digest check on the host; the empty environment on the host (the order's `env` is never read); a task credential reaches neither the order nor any record; the run ID is predictable but is useful only to the host that holds that placement in that session; the control queue is internal (no API or chat path sends `run`, `abort` or `revoke`); revoke before start (refused by `#authorizeStart`), before the order reaches the host (the host's revoked set), during (told, then aborted, no second `abort`), after finish (nothing running, nothing told); another process's revocation reaches the call through the store check; the bounds of every size (source, input, output, body, error text, argument list, limits); host error text redacted on the host and again on the controller (script stderr may name the run's private folder on the host, as a local script's may name this machine's: unchanged from local runs). One mutant remains equivalent: not setting `revoked` in `#revoke` (the run is marked `aborting` at the same time, which alone stops the second message).
- Mutations of my own (built files, one at a time, restored): `facts` asked for every host (new test fails on 4 backends); an `aborting` run resolved again (order-book test fails); revoke messages not replacing one another (fails on 4 backends); host environment taken from the order (repeated-order test fails); the session not compared in the run lookup (order-book test fails); the host check dropped from `runScript` (fails on 4 backends); the epoch check dropped from `runScript` (survived; the new test fails on 4 backends); `revoked` not set (survives, equivalent, above).
