### T02d wiring proof (Claude agent, 2026-11-14): a catalogue tool called in the product's own local host really runs in the sandbox

What was lacking: the clause "the shipped controller runs catalogue tools through the sandbox launcher" was true in the code (`scripts/local-host.mjs` builds `hostScriptRunner` over the real launcher and hands it on as `tools`), but no test ran a catalogue tool through that builder. An auditor swapped `runner: scripts.runner` for a fake `{ run: async () => ({ text: "{}" }) }` and the controller launcher tests, `u14b-local-host` and `h12t-product-host` (25 tests) all still passed.

What is built: `packages/integration/src/t02d-local-host-wiring.test.ts`. It starts the real controller with `launch({ localHost: localHostBuilder(...) })` (owner turns the host on, providers recorded, restart), registers a tool an agent wrote itself (its own accepted desk records), assigns a task, and lets the scripted model make the agent call `nimblenewt__tool-invoke` (it waits for the owner's approval, the owner allows it, the same call id then runs). The tool is a small script that tries to read the controller's data file and a file beside the data directory and to write beside them, and reports what it reached. Through the real worker process and tool bridge the answer comes back into the agent's next model request: the test requires `confined: true` and `reached: []`, that nothing was written, that the run directory is gone, and that the attempt finishes. It also reads what the builder hands the controller (`isLocalHost("host:local")` true, another host false), because one host cannot show the "always true" mistake any other way. A script run outside the sandbox reads both files and writes beside them, so the test can tell.

Why this is not a launch-record check: the builder gives its launcher an empty audit sink on purpose (nothing to read back from the product), so the proof is the script's own report of what it could reach, which is the observable meaning of "confined".

Mutations (applied to `scripts/local-host.mjs`, test run, file restored; each fails the new test): (1) `runner` replaced by the auditor's fake: fails (the agent never gets the script's report); (2) `facts` replaced by one that offers no interpreter: fails (no script report reaches the agent); (3) `isLocalHost` always true: fails (the other-host check); (4) `tools` not passed at all: fails (no script report reaches the agent); (5) the runner given a launcher that spawns the script as a plain process: fails because the report says `confined: false` and lists the two files it read and its write. The unmutated run passes.

Not done / limits: the test needs bubblewrap and a Node.js installed in a folder of its own, exactly as `u14b-local-host` does; where they are missing it skips with the reason, and on Linux with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` it fails instead. Windows and macOS build no local host at all (the product's host is bubblewrap only, noted in `local-host.mjs`), so there the test skips with that reason; no other launcher exists to test. Calls from a remote host were already proven by the remote-execution slice.
- ASSUMPTION: the proof is the script's own report of what it could reach (a refused read and write), not a launcher audit record, because the product's builder deliberately keeps no audit sink.
- ASSUMPTION: a tool the agent wrote waits for the owner's approval; the test approves it as the owner when the agent's model is next asked, which is the real path an owner takes, instead of weakening the policy.
- ASSUMPTION: the probe files are the controller's own database file and a file in the data directory's parent, not system files, so the test does not depend on what a distribution mounts into a sandbox.
- ASSUMPTION: the existing integration tests were left alone; a separate file keeps the card's proof findable by name.

## K02 (second slice): last-known-good record, launcher decision, startup confirmation, protocol compatibility check (2026-11-10)

Card K02 stays planned. This slice adds the machinery after the first slice's staging and journalled switch; no real deployment, launcher process or updater process is started anywhere (all tests use temporary release roots and fixture files).

**Built**
- `release/launcher.ts` (new, exported from `release/index.ts`): the launcher's own record and decision, kept apart from the database because a release that cannot start cannot read it. One file, `launcher-state.json` under the release root, replaced atomically (temporary file, fsync, rename), strictly validated when read (a damaged or foreign-looking file blocks the launch; it is never guessed or repaired). `Launcher.expect()` (the controller announces the release and digest the pointer may name, before the pointer moves), `confirm()` (a started release reports healthy; only the release of the open start attempt; it becomes the last known good), `vouch()` (the owner's confirmation) and `prepare()`, the deterministic decision: the pointer must name an announced release (or the last known good), its files must match its manifest digest, a release whose last start was never confirmed is quarantined, and the launcher then falls back to the last known good only if that still verifies and its declared protocol range still overlaps the workers' (`negotiateProtocol`). With no usable fall-back it blocks and leaves the pointer where it is. Quarantined releases are never run again and never activated again (a rebuilt candidate has another ID).
- `release/activation.ts`: `ActivationBody.lastKnownGood` and `current.confirmedAt`; `confirmStartup()` (called at the end of `startController`; only for the release the process was started from, `releases.runningRelease`, and only when the record names it current with no switch open); `confirm()` for the owner (`release.confirm`: current release only, files verified, revision guarded, not by an agent); `recover()` now also reconciles a fall-back the launcher made while the controller was down (record's current -> the known good, previous cleared, history entry `fell_back`, `failedStarts` in `release.status`); the last known good is spared by removal and pruning; the launcher is told (`expect`) before every pointer write, including `release.activation.resolve`.
- Protocol compatibility before activation and rollback: a release declares the worker protocol range its controller speaks in a digest-bound `compat.json` artifact (`{"protocol":{"min":1,"max":1}}`, strict). Staging reads it into the staged record; activation and rollback check it against the installation's worker range with `negotiateProtocol` (the rollback target against the workers as they are now, so a mixed-version rollback is refused). `startController` sets the requirement by default (`required: true`, workers = this build's `WORKER_PROTOCOL`), so a release without `compat.json` cannot be staged or switched to; `releases.compat` overrides it (a unit-test or lenient installation leaves `compat` out of `ReleaseActivationService` options and nothing is checked).
- A routine release cannot replace the launcher or updater: staging refuses any artifact whose first path part is `launcher` or `updater` (any extension).
- Owner control by chat: `release.confirm` is in the chat command table (a proposal, shown first); the interpreter's operation list is generated from that table, so it names the operation. Ops docs regenerated (`docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md`).
- Tests: `release/k02-launcher.test.ts` (8 scenarios on the reference store and SQLite, symlink and pointer switchers, plus a launcher-only record test: compat strictness, launcher/updater names, protocol refusal incl. rollback with changed workers, confirmation rules and last known good survival, failed start to fall-back to catch-up and quarantine, blocked cases, an incompatible or tampered fall-back, a crash right after the pointer moved, owner confirmation) and `api/start-activation.test.ts` (end to end: no `compat.json` refused, confirmation by a start of the right release only, agent refused, `release.confirm` proposed through chat then applied).

**Not done (follow-up card lines)**
- K02a. The launcher and updater as separate programs: a `launcher` entry point that calls `Launcher.prepare()`, spawns the controller from `releases/<id>` with `releases.runningRelease`, restarts on exit and keeps the launcher itself out of releases; service-manager units for macOS, Linux and Windows; the same on a real macOS and Windows (the Windows pointer file is still only tested on Linux).
- K02b. Signed artifact sets (today digests only; the manifest is unsigned, see the trust model in `activation.ts`) and the trust root for signatures.
- K02c. A grantable release-management permission distinct from `toolbox.manage` (release operations are still the owner's alone); maintenance scope and window enforcement (K07); target-installation binding beyond the platform.
- K02d. Database schema compatibility in the fall-back: the launcher checks the worker protocol range but not whether the failed release already migrated the database past what the known good understands (the controller refuses to start on a newer database, so this blocks the old release rather than corrupting; a pre-upgrade snapshot restore, K01, is the way back). A fall-back that needs a restore should say so.
- K02e. A startup watchdog inside the launcher (a start that is neither confirmed nor exited within a time limit counts as failed); today a start is judged failed by the next launch finding it unconfirmed. (Built as machinery: see the K02e and K02f section; the launcher program that runs it is K02a.)
- K02f. Owner notification (WhatsApp/inbox) when the launcher fell back; today it shows in `release.status` (`history`, `failedStarts`) after the controller is up. (Built: see the K02e and K02f section.)
- K02g. Agent-built NimbleNewt candidate cannot stage or activate itself: still held by the owner-only rule; Pi runtime changes follow G11.

- Runs (`npx tsc --build --force` clean; sandbox required; offline guard): controller in 3 shards 3,937 + 3,231 + 3,975; the only failures were known flakes ('one hundred idle hosts', H12m workspace-ask, dependency-probe 'no probe starts another') and a U11b hung-adapter test that failed once under load and passes alone (88 of 88); `release` tests 180 + `start-activation` pass; integration 128 (118 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed). Mutation check: treating an unconfirmed start as fine fails 16 of the 33 new runs.

**ASSUMPTION:** `compat.json` as an artifact of the release (digest-bound through the candidate manifest, so no manifest-format change and no candidate-ID change) is the smallest way to carry the protocol range; a release whose manifest should carry it itself can move it later.
**ASSUMPTION:** the launcher falls back to the last known good when the pointer names an unannounced release (a hand-moved pointer) rather than only blocking; it is logged (`fell_back`, reason). The record (`release.status`) still reports a hand-moved pointer as `diverged` when the launcher did not act.
**ASSUMPTION:** the default for `startController` is `compat.required: true`: the strict choice, reversible by one option.
**ASSUMPTION:** `release.confirm` is a chat proposal (not applied at once) because it changes where a failed start falls back to; this is the smallest-scope choice and one setting in the command table.
**ASSUMPTION:** one launcher per release root; the launcher file is not a cross-process lock (a service manager starts one launcher).

### K02 second slice: clean-context review (2026-11-11)
- Fixed: the launcher/updater name refusal stripped only the last extension, so `launcher.tar.gz`, `Launcher.d.ts` or `updater..` (Windows drops trailing dots) staged. Everything from the first dot is now ignored. Test: the staging suite's name list.
- Fixed: a last known good whose files did not verify at launch (changed files, or a passing read error) was quarantined. Since only a running controller can vouch for a release, that left nothing to start for good, even after the files were restored. The last known good is now never quarantined: it is blocked while its files are wrong and runs again once they are right.
- Fixed: a crash (or a failed pointer write) between the announcement (`expect`) and the pointer write left the pointer on a release that was no longer announced. With no last known good (for example two activations without a restart), the install could not start. The launcher record keeps the announced release the pointer named at the announcement (`prior`) runnable until the pointer has moved. New test hook `afterAnnounce`.
- Fixed: on a fall-back the pointer was moved before the quarantine was written. A crash in between left the failed release unrecorded, so the controller's record could not catch up (it stayed `diverged`) and the failed release could be activated again. The quarantine is now written first.
- Test added: the last known good, once neither current nor previous, is spared by `remove` and by pruning (removing it from the live set failed no test before).
- Mutation checks (k02-launcher, 4 backend/switcher variants each): reverting each fix fails 4 runs; dropping the rollback compatibility check fails 4; dropping the last known good from the live set fails 4 (0 before the new test).
- Left as notes: the launcher verifies, then K02a spawns from the same directory (same-uid trust boundary, read-only folders); `#startable` treats an unreadable launcher record as no quarantine (the launcher itself blocks on one); a last known good that crashes at every start is restarted without limit (K02d/K02e).

## K02e and K02f: startup watchdog and owner notice for a fall-back or failed start (2026-11-11)

Card K02 stays planned. This closes the follow-up lines K02e (a start is judged failed inside a window, not only by the next launch) and K02f (the owner is told when the launcher falls back or a start fails). Machinery and fixtures only: no launcher process, no deployment.

**Built**
- `Launcher.watchdog()` (`release/launcher.ts`): an open start that is unconfirmed after the startup window is quarantined exactly as a start found unconfirmed at the next launch is (never run or activated again), logged, and a notice written; the caller (the K02a launcher program, which also stops the hung process) then calls `prepare()`, which falls back. Answers `waiting` (with the time left), `failed` (with whether a fall-back exists), `late` or `none`. The last known good is never quarantined: a late start of it is only logged and told once (`late`), as the review of the second slice required. A start already confirmed or already judged changes nothing. `Launcher.watch({pollMs, signal})` polls it until the start is judged or stopped. The window is `startupWindowSeconds` (10 to 86,400, default 300); the launcher cannot read the database, so the controller copies the owner's value into `launcher-state.json` (`setWindow`, at setting time and at every start) and the watchdog reads only the file. A damaged window or notice in the file is a damaged record: the launcher blocks, it does not guess.
- Notices in the launcher's own file (`LauncherNotice`): written in the same atomic write as the decision (fall-back, watchdog failure, a block that leaves nothing to run), so a fall-back made while the database is down is not lost. One notice per kind and release, at most 20 (finished ones make room first), a repeat finding (the same block at every launch) adds nothing, also after the owner acknowledged it. A fall-back folds in a failed-start notice nobody was told yet.
- `Launcher.deliver(sink)` hands each notice over once (`sentAt` after `raise` returned) and tells the sink to close what was acknowledged or confirmed (`settledAt`). A sink that throws leaves the notice pending: nothing is lost when the notification service or channel cannot take it now. The controller calls it (`ReleaseActivationService.deliverStartNotices`) at every start, after the start is confirmed, and on the dispatcher's sweep (`release.start-notices`) as the retry. A launcher program with a channel of its own may call `deliver` with that sink; the controller then does not tell it again.
- `release/start-notices.ts`: the sink over the existing notification service. One `maintenance` item per release (record `release-start:<release id>`), so U11b's open-item cap, the hourly Urgent limit and the per-record gap apply and a repeat only raises the count. Needs you is a queued item (digest); Urgent is `interrupt` (sent at once, also in quiet hours unless the owner set otherwise). The label that may leave the installation holds release IDs only; the launcher's reason stays in the inbox detail. A failed start with no other last known good (nothing was left running) is Urgent whatever the owner chose; a fall-back (an older release is running) is at the owner's `startFailureLevel`, default Needs you.
- Closing: the owner acknowledges (`release.start.acknowledge`, all open notices or one release's; owner only, applies at once because it changes no release and no setting) or a later start that really confirms (`confirm`/`vouch`: a new release reported healthy; the fall-back start of an already good release does not count) closes the notices that were written before it, and the sink settles their inbox items at the next delivery. A notice closed before it was ever told is never told.
- Chat/API: `release.staging.settings.set` takes `startupWindowSeconds` and `startFailureLevel` (null puts the default back; still a proposal in chat, as before); `release.staging.settings.get` and `release.status` report them; `release.status` also lists `startNotices` (kind, release, whether told, open/acknowledged/confirmed). `release.start.acknowledge` is in the chat table. The interpreter's operation list is generated from the table, so it names all of these; no phrase is special. API docs regenerated.
- Tests: `release/k02ef-watchdog.test.ts` (8, launcher alone: window boundary, fall-back after the watchdog keeping its reason, last known good never quarantined, nothing to fall back to, `watch` and abort, a failed send stays pending, dedupe, acknowledge and confirm closing, bounds, damaged file) and `api/start-start-notices.test.ts` (3, real controller on SQLite and real notification service: a fall-back made while the controller was down is told at the next start as Needs you, once over three restarts; the owner's window read by the watchdog from the file; Urgent setting sent through the channel; confirmation closes it at the next start; a refused send is pending then told; chat sets both settings and acknowledges; the interpreter prompt names the arguments).

**Not done**
- K02a is still not built, so nothing runs `watch()` in production and nothing stops a hung controller: the watchdog is the decision and the record, the launcher program that starts the process and acts on `failed` is K02a. Until then the next launch finds an unconfirmed start as before.
- The controller does not run a watchdog on itself: a controller that hangs before it can confirm cannot be trusted to judge itself.
- Only SQLite is exercised end to end; the PostgreSQL path is the same service code and was not run for these tests.
- A launcher-side channel for a fall-back with the controller down for good (WhatsApp from the launcher itself) is the hook `deliver(sink)` only; no such sender is written (credentials stay with the controller).
- The dispatcher-sweep retry (`release.start-notices`) is wired but not exercised by a test; the retry on the next start is.
- K02d (a fall-back that needs a database restore says so) is untouched.

**ASSUMPTION:** the default window is 300 seconds (the owner's setting changes it), long enough for a controller with a slow database migration and short enough that a hang is noticed within minutes.
**ASSUMPTION:** a fall-back is Needs you by default and Urgent when the owner says so; a failed start that leaves nothing to run is always Urgent (like a safety stop it cannot be lowered), because the installation is down.
**ASSUMPTION:** `release.start.acknowledge` applies at once rather than as a proposal: it closes a notice and changes no release, no setting and no authority.
**ASSUMPTION:** the watchdog never quarantines the last known good, only records and tells it, so a last known good that is merely slow is not lost; the repeated-restart loop of a last known good that crashes every start remains the K02d/K02e note from the review (now at least told once).
**ASSUMPTION:** one notice per kind and release, deduped also after acknowledgement; only a confirmation by a later start makes the same finding new again. (Changed by the review below: deduped while open only.)

### K02e and K02f: clean-context review (2026-11-11)
- Fixed: the watchdog quarantined a late start even when there was nowhere to fall back to (no last known good, or one that no longer verifies or no longer speaks the workers' protocol). The launcher then blocked for good, so a first release whose start was merely slow (a long first migration on a slow disk) bricked the installation. The watchdog now quarantines only when `prepare()` could fall back (the same test, shared as `#noFallback`); otherwise the start is `late`: logged, told as Urgent (with the reason), not quarantined, left running. If it later confirms it becomes the last known good and its late notice closes; if it ends unconfirmed the next launch blocks as before.
- Fixed: a confirmation that arrived after the watchdog had set the start aside (the hung controller coming up before the launcher stopped it) took the release out of quarantine and made it the last known good, leaving the "set aside" notice open and the outcome a race. `Launcher.confirm` now refuses a quarantined release (only the owner's `vouch` lifts a quarantine); `confirmStartup` then records nothing.
- Fixed: the watchdog measured the window on the wall clock only, so a clock set forward while a release started (a device without a clock battery syncing its time) failed a healthy start at once, and a clock set back stretched the window. `watch()` now reads the wall clock once (how long ago the start began) and counts on a monotonic clock after that (`LauncherOptions.monotonic`, default `performance.now`; `watchdog(observed)`).
- Fixed: the launcher's watchdog and the controller it started change `launcher-state.json` at the same time (confirmation, window, notice marks, acknowledgement, announcements), and the per-process queue did not cover two processes: a confirmation landing between the watchdog's read and write was overwritten (the healthy release quarantined), or a quarantine was overwritten by the controller's next write. Every change is now a compare-and-swap on the file's text (re-read just before the rename) and is made again from the new content on a conflict (up to 5 times). The remaining window is between that re-read and the rename.
- Fixed: a damaged `window` or notice list in the file blocked the launch (the record counted as damaged), although neither decides what runs and blocking leaves no controller to repair it. A bad window is the default (the controller copies the owner's value again at its next start), and unreadable notices are dropped (at most the newest 20 kept). Release entries stay strict.
- Fixed: an acknowledged notice suppressed the same finding for good, so the last known good blocked again after its files were repaired (or a fall-back repeated after the owner had seen the first) was never told. Only an open notice dedupes now (repeats while nothing runs); the owner can acknowledge only while a controller runs, so a finding after that is new.
- Fixed: at the notice cap an untold notice could be dropped before one already in the owner's inbox. Order now: settled, closed before being told, told, then oldest; never the one being added.
- Tests: `k02ef-watchdog` (now 11: no fall-back gives `late` and a later confirmation closes it, a last known good that no longer verifies, a clock set forward or back under `watch`, a late confirmation of a quarantined release, both directions of the two-process race, garbage window/notices, eviction order, recurrence after acknowledgement) and the new `api/start-start-notices-sweep` (the dispatcher sweep `release.start-notices` retries a notice the start could not tell, once, through the real notification service; the owner's acknowledgement settles it; SQLite and PostgreSQL). Mutation checks: reverting each of the seven fixes fails at least one test; removing the sweep, emptying it, letting the owner's level lower a no-fall-back notice, putting the reason in the label, and dropping the owner check on acknowledge each fail one.
- Runs (`npx tsc --build --force` clean, stale dist removed; sandbox required; offline guard): controller in 3 shards 3,976 + 3,375 + 3,942, all passed, no flake this time; integration 131 (121 passed, 10 skipped, 0 failed).
- Left as notes: `prepare()` still quarantines and blocks a release whose start ended unconfirmed when nothing else can run (K02 second slice; running it again instead is a design choice for K02a/K02d). `release.start.acknowledge` repeated with the same command ID answers `acknowledged: 0` (the effect is idempotent, the count is not replayed). Two notices of one release share one inbox item (same record); acknowledging closes both.

## K02a: the launcher process supervisor and program (2026-11-11)

Card K02 stays planned (service units and the updater remain). This builds the largest self-contained part of K02a: the process that runs the decisions K02 and K02e/K02f already made. Machinery and fixtures only: no service unit, no deployment, no real controller.

**Built**
- `release/supervisor.ts` (`Supervisor`, exported from `release/index.ts`): `Launcher.prepare()` -> start the chosen release's controller as a child (from `releases/<id>`, with `NIMBLENEWT_RUNNING_RELEASE=<id>`, the value of `releases.runningRelease`) -> run `Launcher.watch()` beside it -> on `failed` stop the child (SIGTERM to its process group, SIGKILL after `graceMs`) and loop, so `prepare()` falls back; on `late`, confirmed or nothing to judge leave it running -> when the child exits (any code) loop through `prepare()` again (an unconfirmed start is judged failed there; a child that cannot be spawned counts as an exit). Restart rate: the n-th consecutive run shorter than `stableMs` waits `min(maxMs, initialMs * 2^(n-1))`, a long run resets the count, and `giveUpAfter` short runs in a row end the launcher with exit 4. Stopping the launcher (`signal`) stops the child the same way and exits 0 without a restart. It never reads the database; the wall clock is not used at all (the watchdog's own monotonic handling from K02e is what judges the window).
- Exit codes (`SUPERVISOR_EXIT`): 0 stopped, 2 blocked (`prepare()` found nothing safe to run: unannounced pointer, damaged record, nothing to fall back to), 3 no active release, 4 crash loop. 1 is the program's usage/unexpected error.
- `scripts/nimblenewt-launcher.mjs`: the small CLI (`--root`, `--entry`, `--switcher pointer|symlink`, `--node`, worker range, grace, poll and backoff settings, `--` extra controller arguments; SIGTERM/SIGINT stop it). The child gets the launcher's environment unchanged; the launcher logs release IDs, pids, exit codes, signals and its own reasons only (no environment, no child output).
- Docs: `maintenance-and-updates.md` (the program, its rules and exit codes), `getting-started.md` gap table (service units).
- Tests: `release/supervisor.test.ts` (9, with real fake-controller child processes: confirms and stops cleanly with a secret in the child's environment and output and none in logs, events or the record; a hung start stopped at the window and fallen back with a bystander process untouched; a child ignoring SIGTERM killed with its grandchild; exits at once / cannot be spawned / a first release with nothing to fall back to (blocked, exit 2, no loop); a last known good crash loop with doubling capped delays, never quarantined, exit 4; a stable run resets the delay; wall clock set a day forward does not fail a healthy slow start; no release / unannounced pointer / damaged record start nothing; shutdown during the window) and `scripts/nimblenewt-launcher.test.mjs` (2: end to end through the program, usage errors and exit codes). Mutation checks: removing the SIGKILL fails the stubborn-child test, removing the restart delay fails the crash-loop test.
- Runs (`npx tsc --build --force` clean; sandbox required; offline guard): `release/*` plus start-notices tests 215 of 215; shard 1/3 (root checks, script tests, every other package, controller slice 1) all passed except the known W11 job-wake flake, which passes alone. API docs regenerated: no change (no operation changed).

**Not done**
- Service-manager units (launchd, systemd, Windows service) and the updater program; nothing runs on a real macOS or Windows (the stop uses process groups on POSIX, `child.kill()` elsewhere, untested there).
- A hung last known good is never detected: `prepare()` marks its start confirmed, so the watchdog has nothing to judge; only a crash is handled (restarts with backoff, exit 4). Detecting it needs a liveness signal from the controller (a heartbeat in `launcher-state.json`), which changes the controller.
- The controller side of `NIMBLENEWT_RUNNING_RELEASE`: `startController` takes `releases.runningRelease` as an option; no code yet maps the variable to it (the release's own entry file does, K02a follow-up with the first real release entry).
- After a stop the group is sent SIGKILL a moment after the leader exits (to catch orphaned members); in the tiny window after the leader is reaped a recycled pid could in theory be a group of someone else. A child that exits on its own is never signalled.
- A controller that exits 0 on purpose is restarted like any other exit (no "stay down" request).

**ASSUMPTION:** the child is `node <release>/<entry>` (default `controller.js`) with `NIMBLENEWT_RUNNING_RELEASE` as the way to tell it its release; the smallest choice that needs no change to a release's contents, one function (`child`) to change.
**ASSUMPTION:** defaults: grace 10 s, backoff 1 s doubling to 60 s, stable 60 s, give up after 20 short runs (exit 4 so a crash loop is visible; the service manager's own delay then applies).
**ASSUMPTION:** a blocked launcher exits 2 and is not retried by itself: nothing changes until the owner acts, and retrying would only write the same notice.

### K02a: clean-context review (2026-11-11)
- Fixed: after a stop whose leader obeyed SIGTERM, SIGKILL went to the group number unconditionally, after the leader had been reaped (the pid-reuse window the notes admitted). Signals now go to the group only while it still has a member (a process group ID stays reserved while any member lives, so it is still ours), never to a pid of 1 or less, and the leader only before its exit was seen (seen in the reaping callback). Members that outlive the leader get the rest of the grace, then SIGKILL. Test: `process.kill` recorded: an emptied group gets SIGTERM only, no 0/1/-1.
- Fixed: a controller that crashed left the rest of its process group running (a database it started, say), and the next start collided with it. What is left is now stopped (SIGTERM, grace, SIGKILL) before anything starts again (`leftovers` event).
- Fixed: a controller exit 0 was restarted forever, so the owner could not stop it. Contract (`CONTROLLER_EXIT`): 0 after the start was confirmed is a stop on purpose (launcher exits 0, nothing restarted; a service manager does not restart a clean exit); 0 before confirmation is a failed start as before; 75 asks for a restart (logged, normal rate limit so it cannot spin); anything else is a crash.
- Fixed (could brick an installation): stopping the launcher during the startup window left the start open, so the next launch quarantined the release and, with no last known good (a first install, a slow first migration, a reboot), blocked for good. `Launcher.interrupted()` closes an unconfirmed, unjudged attempt on the launcher's own stop (also when the stop arrives while `prepare()` runs, without spawning). A launcher killed outright or a power loss cannot record it: that start is still judged failed at the next launch (K02d).
- Fixed: a crash loop ended with exit 4 and nothing for the owner. `Launcher.noteCrashLoop()` writes a `failed_start` notice (no fall-back, so Urgent) that the next start able to deliver it tells.
- Fixed: two launchers on one root, or a launcher killed with SIGKILL whose controller (its own process group) ran on as an orphan, let a second launcher start a second controller on the same installation. `lockRoot()`: an abstract socket on Linux, a named pipe on Windows, a socket file elsewhere (a stale one nobody answers on is replaced); the OS frees it when the holder ends. On POSIX the controller inherits the listening socket as fd 3, so an orphaned controller keeps the root locked; the second launcher exits 5 (restartable) until it is gone. A process that escapes the group with setsid and keeps fd 3 also holds it (logged reason; exit 5 is retried, so it does not brick). Not done: macOS and other non-Linux POSIX can race two launchers that start at the same moment on a stale file.
- Fixed: the CLI used `process.once` for SIGTERM/SIGINT, so a second signal (a second Ctrl-C, a service manager repeating SIGTERM) took Node's default and killed the launcher half way through the stop, orphaning the controller. Handlers stay installed (repeats log "already stopping"); SIGHUP stops it too.
- Fixed: a relative `--node` was resolved against the release directory (the child's cwd), so a release-provided file could be run; it is resolved against the launcher's cwd. `--stable-seconds 0` (every run stable: a crash loop never slowed) is refused; values beyond a timer's range are refused and timers are capped (Node fires a longer timer at once: an immediate SIGKILL).
- Windows: the stop uses `taskkill /T /F` on the child's tree while it runs, then `child.kill()`. Untested (no Windows here).
- Checked, no change: release IDs reach the spawn path only through records validated as `rcn-<24 hex>`; `--entry` refuses absolute and `..`; `verifyReleaseDirectory` refuses unmanifested files and non-plain files (symlinks), so the entry must be a verified file; the child's stdio is stdin ignored and stdout/stderr per option, no other launcher fds (Node opens them close-on-exec) except the deliberate lock socket; logs carry no environment or child output (the secret test).
- Known gap kept and documented (module comment, maintenance doc): a hung last known good is never detected.
- Mutation checks: the three requested (no SIGKILL escalation, no group kill, no backoff cap) each fail a test (they did before this review too). New: group-alive check removed, leftovers removed, interrupted removed, exit-0 contract removed, lock removed, lock not inherited, crash-loop notice removed, `process.once` signals: each fails at least one test.
- Tests: supervisor 13 (was 9), launcher CLI 4 (was 2: an orphaned controller keeps the root locked against a second launcher (5) until it is gone; a repeated SIGTERM/SIGINT during the stop still kills a SIGTERM-ignoring controller and exits 0).

## C07q (second part): the process's own compactions join the controller's compaction chain (2026-11-11)

The first part (above, `8caa4bbf`, `b3680886`) bounded the lineage and gave the process's own compaction the owner's decisions. What it left open: nothing recorded a compaction the process made, so in production the controller's chain was empty, `compression` stayed `none` in a continuation capture, and `keptDecisions` / the lineage had no producer. This part builds the missing producer without pretending the controller summarised anything.

**Built**
- **A notice from the process (`contracts/src/worker-channel.ts`, `pi-adapter/src/worker/process.ts`).** The extractive compaction hook (the one the composer gives every process with a known window) sends `{ t: "compacted", messageCount, summaryChars, digest }` after it builds its summary: how many messages it replaced, the length of the summary and its sha-256. The summary text is not sent; it stays in the process's conversation store. A failure to send is swallowed (the compaction stands). The parser bounds the count (0 to 10,000,000), the length (0 to 1e9) and requires 64 hex digits.
- **The host passes it on (`worker/src/host/process.ts`, `local.ts`).** `ProcessHandlers.compacted`, called without waiting; a throw is dropped, so the process is never ended by it. `LocalHostOptions.onCompaction(order, note)`; `OwnerPolicyServices.recordCompaction` is optional and `ownerPolicyOptions(services)` now also returns `onCompaction`, so every host that already spreads it (the controller refuses one that does not) is connected without a change.
- **The controller records it (`context/enforcement.ts` `recordProcessCompaction`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts` `recordCompaction`).** A new compaction record with `process: { messageCount, summaryChars, digest }` and `route: "process"`, continuing the task's latest compaction: generation, bounded lineage (`LINEAGE_KEEP`, older part folded into `earlier`), and the owner's pinned decisions carried on all work as for a controller compaction. Its text is the controller's own note ("compacted N messages into a summary of M characters, sha-256 ..."). No retrieval summary is published (the controller does not hold the text), so `readSummary` answers nothing for it. The key is `pc-` + a hash of the attempt and the digest, so the same compaction reported twice is one record (answered from it). If another compaction finished between the read of the chain head and the write, the call retries against the new head (3 times); one closed as superseded says so. A controller `compact` can follow it (its `parent` is the process record). A failure in the composer goes to `onError` and never reaches the attempt. The continuation recorder (L04d) already builds a capture's lineage from the latest compaction, so captures now carry the real chain.
- **Tests (each fails without its change).** `context/process-compaction.test.ts` (all four backends): a controller compaction pins a decision, then 60 process compactions; every one has the next generation, a lineage of at most 50, listed + folded accounting for every earlier one; the folded part reads back and matches its digest; the pinned decision is still available with its wording whole; the record keeps the note and no summary; a repeat key is replayed; a controller compaction continues the chain (generation 62); a bad digest, negative or fractional count, unknown field, a key that names a controller compaction, and a non-dispatcher principal are refused; three reported at once give distinct generations from 1 (or are closed as superseded). Also: `contracts` channel round trip and bounds; `pi-adapter` `contextPolicyOf` tells count, length and digest and not the text, and a throwing notifier changes nothing; `worker` `host/process.test.ts` (handler reached; a throwing or absent handler changes nothing) and `local.test.ts` (`ownerPolicyOptions`); `api/start-dispatch.test.ts` (the composed service records two compactions in order, a repeat is one, an unknown task is reported not thrown). Mutation checks: no call to `recordProcessCompaction` in the composer, and the host ignoring `compacted`, each fail their tests.

**Not done**
- **Routing the process's compaction through the controller's summariser (`compact` with `registerCompressor`) is still not done.** Unchanged reason from the first part: the conversation lives in the sandbox, so the controller has no records to cite, and `compact` with made-up sources would claim records the summary was not made from. This part records that the compaction happened (and keeps the decisions through it) rather than who wrote it. A real routing needs a request/answer pair on the channel and a way to cite a conversation that is not a controller record.
- **Only the extractive path reports.** Pi's own model summariser runs only when the host gives no `extractive` fallback (a host built without the composer's `context`); its compactions are not reported. Pi gives no other hook point the adapter uses.
- **The summary's text is not recoverable from the controller.** Only the digest and length are kept; the text is in the process's store (and in the checkpoint's conversation).
- **Compactions reported after the process restarted are keyed by attempt and digest.** Two different compactions with an identical summary in one attempt would count once. A summary includes the replaced text, so this needs an identical extract; accepted.
- **No state-API operation or chat question for the chain** (also not for the first part's `earlierLineage`). This is plumbing, not an owner control, so nothing was added to the chat interpreter (ASSUMPTION; the owner's pinned decisions are already reachable by chat). A chat status answer ("how many times has this task been compacted") is a follow-up if Rob wants it.
- **Not run:** a real Pi process compacting through the whole local worker with a decision recorded first; the composed test drives the service the host calls, not a launched process.
- ASSUMPTION: a compaction made by the process is a lineage entry with no retrieval summary rather than a record with invented sources; this keeps `readSummary` honest.
- ASSUMPTION: the notice carries a digest and counts only, so a compromised process can at worst add chain entries to its own task (the same task it can already work on); a chain entry cannot name a record, so it cannot make the controller cite or reveal anything.

**Review (clean-context, 2026-11-11)**
- **Flood.** `compacted` had no bound at the host while `bridge`, `fetch` and `lease.renew` each do: a sandbox process could send notices without limit, each a pair of controller writes (and a record kept even when superseded). Now `PROCESS_LIMITS.compactedInFlight` (2: more are refused and count toward the kill at `refusals`) and `PROCESS_LIMITS.compactions` (1000 per process: more are dropped, the process is not ended for compacting often). Test: `host/process.test.ts` "compaction notices are bounded".
- **Stale attempt.** The composer kept a notice from any attempt of the task. Now only while the attempt is the task's active attempt at the order's generation (assignment `assigned`, `activeAttemptId`, generation, attempt `active`); otherwise nothing is recorded and nothing is reported. Test: `api/start-dispatch.test.ts` (another attempt and an older generation add nothing).
- **Head race.** The retry in `recordProcessCompaction` survived mutation (no test reached it). A deterministic test now lets another compaction finish right after the head is read (`context/process-compaction.test.ts`, all four backends); and a begin that conflicts because another run of the same key began the record uses that record instead of retrying into the same conflict.
- Checked, no change: parser bounds (safe integers only, hex digest), `onlyKnown` on the service, a throwing handler or composer never ends the attempt, the retry loops terminate (3 tries), pinned decisions and generation are carried from the parent, `readSummary` has no production caller (the continuation recorder reads `latestCompaction`), only local hosts spread `ownerPolicyOptions`.
- Not done: a per-attempt bound at the controller (the host bound is per process; a process relaunched for each turn gets a fresh 1000). The notice is sent from the extractive hook before Pi applies the summary, so a compaction Pi then abandons is still recorded.


## U07: responsive web chat over private networking (first slice, 2026-11-10)

Card U07 (N09): "Responsive browser UI, authenticated sessions and private HTTPS deployment guide using Tailscale or equivalent; blocker and cost views". Built: the page, the session layer, the explicit private binding, resume without duplicates, revocation, and the deployment guide ([private-web-chat.md](../private-web-chat.md)).

**Done**
- `packages/controller/src/web/` (new): `binding.ts` (`checkBinding`, `isPrivateAddress`, `isLoopbackAddress`, `remoteAllowed`), `sessions.ts` (`WebSessionStore`), `door.ts` (`WebChatDoor`). Start option `webChat` (needs `chat`) opens it; `controller.webChat` is the handle (`createPairing(ownerToken)`, `revokeAll(ownerId)`, `url`, `port`, `close`). It is a second listener, apart from the conversation transport (U02b), so each keeps its own explicit binding and limits.
- **Explicit private binding.** `host` (an IP literal) and `network` (`loopback` | `private`) are required, no defaults. Loopback accepts 127/8 and ::1, with `behindTlsProxy` when host names are given without TLS. Private accepts RFC 1918, 100.64/10 (Tailscale and other overlay networks), link-local and fc00::/7, and needs `tls` and `publicHosts`. Wildcards, public addresses and host names are refused at start; every request is also checked against the remote address's network (403) and the Host header (421, DNS rebinding). There is no option that exposes it publicly.
- **Sessions.** Sign-in by the owner credential or a one-time pairing code (10 characters of a 32-letter alphabet, 5 minutes, once, made from a signed-in browser or `createPairing`). Cookie `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, plus `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix over TLS or behind a TLS proxy; the store keeps only a SHA-256 of the cookie. Per-session CSRF token header, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site checks, JSON only, 16 KiB bodies, 300 requests a minute per session, 10 failed sign-ins a minute per address. Idle 24 h, absolute 7 d, 20 sessions. Only the owner kind is accepted (any other credential is refused at sign-in, 403, with no cookie or CSRF token, and counts as a failed attempt). **Revocation:** the credential behind the session is authenticated on EVERY request, so rotating or disabling it ends all sessions on the next request; `POST /web/sessions/revoke` (one handle or all others), logout, and `revokeAll` end sessions at once.
- **Resume without duplicate commands.** The browser's outbox keeps each message and approval under its own id until the controller has answered; after a dropped connection, a reload or a lost answer it sends the same id again. `ChatService.submit` already records a turn under the message id and returns the first one (`replayed: true`); the door adds one run for concurrent sends of the same id. An approval carries an `Idempotency-Key` (the chat's `applyProposal` command id). Tested end to end (the controller test sends the same typed pause three ways and checks that the gate did not change on the resend; the UI tests drop the request, drop the answer, close the page mid-send, sign out mid-queue).
- **Views.** Fixed read-only queries, nothing else is reachable: `status` (overview), `needs-you`, `blockers` (needs-you plus attention), `cost` (`budget.usage` plus `budget.pending`), `recovery` (attention, jobs, reconnect), through `api.handle` with the owner's credential. Recovery buttons send the typed `lifecycle-pause` / `lifecycle-resume` lines for the whole installation, so they work with the model down (U06).
- **UI package** (`packages/ui`, was a placeholder): `webChatAssets()` returns page, script, style and manifest; no dependency, no inline script or style (CSP `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'`), text is written with `textContent` only. Phone-first CSS: one column, 44 px targets, 16 px inputs, safe areas, `100dvh`, dark mode, reduced motion. The controller does not import it (package boundaries); the start script passes it as `assets`.
- Tests: controller `web/web.test.ts` 20 after review (binding rules, sessions, door over a real controller: headers, sign-in limits, CSRF/Origin/Host, replay and concurrent replay, typed recovery with the model down, revocation by handle/all/logout/rotation, expiry, pairing, views, approvals, Secure cookie behind a proxy, start refusals); UI `ui.test.ts` 14 (asset rules; the real script run in a VM against a fake controller). Also driven once in headless Chromium at 390x844 with touch (sign-in, chat, offline then online resend, all views, no horizontal overflow, `document.cookie` empty) with a throwaway script, not a committed test.
- The state API did not change (no `npm run api:docs:write` needed); `getting-started.md` and `docs/nimblenewt/README.md` link the guide.

**Not done (follow-up)**
- Live updates: the page asks when you act and when it returns to the front; there is no server push (SSE or WebSocket) or notification, so a reply that arrives later (a held command answered later) is seen on the next action.
- The transcript is only on the phone (local storage, last 100, cleared at sign-out). A second browser starts with an empty chat; there is no server-side history read.
- Sessions are in memory and end at a controller restart (deliberate: nothing credential-like is stored). A persistent, revocable device record (a per-device token instead of holding the owner credential in memory) and a second factor are not built.
- Views show the controller's lines or a plain field list; a designed cost chart, per-project filters and the settings views are U08/U09. A QR code for the pairing code is not drawn.
- No offline app shell (service worker) and no accessibility audit with a screen reader.
- The deployment guide's Tailscale commands were not run on a live tailnet (no deployment is authorized); the private-address TLS path is covered by the binding rules and the Secure-cookie proxy test, not by a real bind to a private address (the test machine has none to spare). `tailscale serve` flags vary by version, so the guide points to `--help`.
- Not run: the real-model chat through the page (the Pi/Radiance benchmark holds the one allowed connection; the interpreter in tests is scripted).
- Windows and macOS were not exercised.

**Review (Claude Sonnet clean-context, 2026-11-10)** fixed: (1) failed sign-ins were counted only after the credential check returned, so attempts sent all at once all passed the per-address check (a burst of N guesses got N tries); the attempt is now counted before anything is awaited and given back on success. (2) Pairing codes outlived the session that made them and "sign out all other browsers": a stolen session could mint a code (5 minutes) and sign back in after being revoked; a code now ends with its creating session and every unused code of the owner ends on revoke-all (`revokeAll` too). (3) An agent credential could sign in and receive a session and CSRF token (refused only on the next call); now refused at sign-in. (4) `checkBinding` took non-canonical IPv4 such as `010.0.0.1` as private 10.0.0.1, while the system resolver reads it as octal 8.0.0.1 (public) at bind time; only plain IP literals (`net.isIP`) or `localhost` are accepted. (5) The cookie's Max-Age was one idle period (24 h) from sign-in and never refreshed, so an active phone was signed out after a day despite the 7-day limit; it now lasts until the absolute end and the idle limit stays server-side. (6) A web chat that failed to open (refused binding, port in use, no chat) left the conversation transport listening after the failed start; it is closed. Each has a test, and the binding, burst and pairing tests were checked to fail with the guard removed.
Accepted as is: behind a loopback TLS proxy every client has the proxy's address, so the per-address sign-in limit is shared by all clients of the proxy (stricter, and a tailnet peer can delay the owner's sign-in by a minute); a request already running when its session is revoked finishes (its commands were authorized when it started); concurrent sends of one message id with different text return the first turn (the chat's own replay rule).

**ASSUMPTION:** a separate listener (not new routes on the conversation transport), because the conversation transport serves bearer-token API clients and the browser needs cookies, CSRF and static files under a different policy.
**ASSUMPTION:** the owner credential is held in the controller's memory for the life of a session (and re-checked on every request), instead of a new device-token record, as the smallest reversible choice that makes rotation revoke everything; the cost is that a restart signs everyone out.
**ASSUMPTION:** idle 24 h, absolute 7 d, pairing 5 minutes, 10 failed sign-ins a minute: provisional, adjustable through `webChat.session` and `webChat.limits`.
**ASSUMPTION:** the recovery buttons pause and resume the whole installation (scope `installation`), the one scope a phone user wants in an emergency; narrower scopes are typed or chatted.

## L02e (part 3): a Stop made after an attempt finished still reaches what its sandbox holds, and a later look can confirm the local worker stopped (2026-11-10)

Two of the L02e leftovers were still open after the wider-scope walk, the charge window, the stop view and chat's name form: (a) a local worker whose close could not end its process was never confirmed stopped (`LocalWorker` had no `release`, so `confirmStopped` answered false for ever and its scratch was kept even after Force Stop killed the process), and (b) a Stop or Force Stop made after such an attempt had finished neither listed nor reached what its sandbox holds, because only live attempts (and ones seen during that Stop) are asked. This slice closes both.

- **Remembered unconfirmed attempts** (`dispatch/dispatcher.ts`). A finished attempt whose worker was not confirmed stopped is added to a bounded list (`dispatch-unconfirmed`, 100, newest kept) in the same commit that finishes it (and in the update that marks a late handle's failed stop); `confirmStopped` takes it off in the same commit that records `workerStopped: true`. `DispatcherService.unconfirmedAttemptsOf(by, { taskId | agentId })` (staff only) lists them, re-reading each record, so an attempt confirmed meanwhile is not listed.
- **The Stop reaches them** (`lifecycle/dispatch-ports.ts`). `resolveScope` now also returns `leftover`: the unconfirmed finished attempts of the agents the scope covers and of its tasks and swarm children. They are not live, so they are not quiesced or stopped; they ARE asked for the processes their sandboxes hold (inventory, so a held process is unresolved), their cleanup cost (charged to the attempt's task like any other), and are killed by a Force Stop (`local.end`), subject to the same `mayControl` filter for swarm children. A dispatcher without the method is unchanged.
- **Local confirmation** (`dispatch/local-worker.ts`). `LocalWorker.release(attemptId)` looks at every sandbox session of the attempt and resolves only if each can say what it holds and none lists a process. It kills nothing (Force Stop's `endLocalWork` does), and refuses when a process is listed, a sandbox cannot say, or this process has no record of the attempt (the controller restarted).
- **Tests.** `dispatch/local-unconfirmed.test.ts` (every backend): attempt listed for its task and agent, not for another task, staff only; not confirmed while a process is listed (and nothing killed); confirmed once it is gone, recorded, and no longer listed; a sandbox that cannot say and an unknown attempt are never confirmed. `lifecycle/dispatch-ports.test.ts` (+1): a Stop of a task and of an agent with nothing live lists the finished attempts' processes (a child's too), charges their cost, a Force Stop kills them, a child the asker may not control is left alone, and a dispatcher without the method asks nothing.
- API: no operation changed, so `api:docs:write` was not needed.

ASSUMPTION: the list is capped at 100 (the oldest are forgotten, which only costs a later Stop its look at them); the add in the late-handle case is a separate update that may be lost on a crash, in which case the scratch is kept as before.
ASSUMPTION: a restarted controller has no record of the local worker's old sandboxes, so `release` refuses (unconfirmed), as it did before; the list still names the attempt, and Force Stop asks the host, which answers nothing for an attempt it forgot.

**Not done (L02e stays open; follow-up).** (1) A per-request cumulative cleanup total (the view shows the budget-window figure and per-attempt totals). (2) A remote worker's own report of its processes (today one unknown item per live placement). (3) Mutation checks were not recorded for this slice.

- **Review (clean-context, 2026-11-11).** Fixed: giving `LocalWorker` a `release` also changed the end of an attempt that has no handle in this process yet (its start had not answered: `#endInner` asks the host to release, and so does the start that finds the attempt over). The look then found the sandbox empty (a start in progress has launched nothing, and a running worker process is the attempt itself and is not listed), so the attempt was recorded `workerStopped: true` while its worker was still coming up; had the later stop of that worker failed, nothing would have listed it again and its scratch could go. `LocalWorker` now counts, per attempt, the workers it is starting or has started whose handle has not been stopped (taken off when a start fails, and once the handle's stop has run, whether or not it ended everything), and `release` refuses while any is counted. Test (`local-unconfirmed.test.ts`, +1): refused during the start and before the stop, confirmed after it; a failed start leaves no count. The stored list is now checked to be emptied by the confirmation, not only hidden when read (that mutation passed before). Mutations: guard removed, list add removed, list removal removed, `mayControl` filter bypassed on the Force Stop kill: each fails a test. Checked, no change: only `#endInner` finishes an attempt, so every unconfirmed finish is listed; the add and the removal are in the attempt's own commit (the list is re-read on each retry); cleanup charges are per attempt (`stop-charge`), so two Stops reaching the same leftover never charge twice; Force Stop kills by sandbox session and the host checks a process's start time before a kill (L02d), so a reused process ID is not killed; a leftover in a swarm child goes through `controllable`; `unconfirmedAttemptsOf` is staff only, as `liveAttemptsOf` is. Left as noted: past 100 the oldest are forgotten, and after a restart a leftover reads as nothing (not unknown), as before this slice.

## U03c: the coordinator as a hosted agent (2026-11-11, first slice)

Code: `chat/coordinator-host.ts` (new: `AgentLifecyclePort`, `agentLifecycle`), `chat/coordinator.ts`, `chat/chat.ts`, `chat/interpreter.ts`, `chat/model-interpreter.ts`, `api/start.ts`, `api/operations.ts`, `api/state-api.ts`. Tests: `api/start-coordinator-host.test.ts` (two tests over the composed controller, real pause gates and stop service), `chat/coordinator-intent.test.ts`. API docs regenerated (`coordinator.get`).

**Done.**
- A coordinator whose principal is an H11 agent record (`agent:agt-...`) is **hosted**: `CoordinatorBody.hosted = { agentId, host: "controller" }`. Nothing new to learn for the owner: "make Ada the coordinator" (chat `configure` with `agentName`, the owner's own words, looked up among active agents like other names; several matches are asked about, none is refused) or `configure` with the agent's principal. A principal that is not an agent record (or a controller built without the lifecycle port) keeps the old controller-held state, unchanged.
- **Lifecycle is the agent's lifecycle.** The coordinator is available only while the agent record is active and no pause gate on the agent's chain (its own, its teams', the installation's) is paused. `lifecycle.pause` / `lifecycle.resume` / `lifecycle.stop` on the agent scope, a team pause or an installation pause therefore reach it at once with no coordinator-specific code; the chat words (start, pause, stop) and `CoordinatorService.setState` use those same gates (`PauseService.pause/resume`, `StopService.request` then `advance`, as the state API's `lifecycle.stop` does). The record keeps the order the owner last gave (revisioned, audited, stale orders refused before they touch a gate); what the coordinator is doing is read from the gates.
- Hosting starts paused: the agent's own scope is paused (before the record exists, so there is no window with a free coordinator) unless a controller-held coordinator that was already running is merely re-pointed at an agent. A repeated set-up is a replay and never re-pauses a started coordinator. Taking it off its agent (configure with another principal) brings it back paused. Starting it lifts only its own gate; the answer says which outer gate (team, installation) still holds it (`stillHeldBy`, and a line in the chat reply), and a refusal reason names the outer gate.
- A pause is reported to the gate (`observe paused`, boundary finished) only when no model call is in flight; a call that had begun ends and is answered, and the report follows when it drains. Stop completes through the stop service (observed `stopped`), shown as `stopped`; a stopped coordinator can only be started, as before.
- **No authority gained.** Hosting creates no grant and no credential (a test checks the agent holds none). Its grants are the agent's: `grant.create` / `grant.list` / `grant.revoke` on its principal, and the coordinator's principal is now read **with the grant records** (`grants.effective`) for every coordinator, so a revoked right such as `assignment.manage` stops counting at once (test: a draft is "by-owner", "by-coordinator" after the grant, "by-owner" after the revoke). It cannot resume or stop itself (no `agent.manage`; test), only the owner uses `CoordinatorService`, and it still changes no record itself.
- **The controller never depends on it**: paused, stopped, retired (reads as "the coordinator's agent is retired", checked before the disabled credential), failing model, or a lifecycle read that fails each give `unavailable`; the chat and the rest carry on (tested).
- New query `coordinator.get` (owner only): principal, routes in order (the fallback list), last order, `hosted`, and for a hosted one `state` (running, paused, stopping, suspended, stopped) with `lifecycle.heldBy` (scope, what was reported, reason, who).
- The chat interpreter prompt now describes the whole `coordinator` intent (it did not before, so the model could not produce it) including setting up by agent name and the pause/stop/start words.

**ASSUMPTION:** "host" is the controller itself (`hosted.host = "controller"`): the coordinator makes only controller-side model calls, so it needs no worker host or sandbox. Running it on a remote host with its own tools is not built.
**ASSUMPTION:** an agent record with the standing `agent.manage` right (a supervisor, a manager) can pause, stop and resume the coordinator like any agent: that is what "the same controls as other agents" means, and it widens nobody's authority.

**Review fixes (clean-context review, 2026-11-11).**
- A pause was reported reached (`observe paused`, boundary finished) while the coordinator could still act: only the model call counted as in flight, so a pause landing between the availability check and the call was reported at once and the call then started, and a pause landing after an assignment round's model call was reported before the round made its assignments under the coordinator's credential. Now the whole operation (`answer`, `decompose`, `assign`, from the availability check to the last write) counts as in flight.
- A hosted coordinator stopped by order and then started again through its agent's own resume (the same controls as any agent) could not be paused by order: the gate was paused first and the record then refused the order as "a stopped coordinator can only be started", a refusal with the side effect already made. For a hosted coordinator that check is made against the gates (before they are touched) and no longer against the order recorded last.
- The coordinator's principal is again `principals.authenticate` alone: it already returns the grant records and restrictions as of the call, so a revoked right stops counting at the next use with no change; the extra `grants.effective` wrapper listed every grant record twice and dropped the principal's `credentialId`. The behaviour of a coordinator that is not hosted is therefore unchanged by U03c.
- Test: `api/start-coordinator-host.test.ts` third test (both cases fail on the code before the fix). Mutations tried: dropping the stale-revision check before the gates, and pausing on every set-up, are each caught by the second test.
- Left as it is: `coordinator.get` shows a hosted coordinator whose agent controls cannot be read as `stopped` (without `lifecycle`); `#usable` gives the precise reason. A pause made through the agent controls directly (not by the coordinator order) is not reported reached by the coordinator; it reads as `paused` all the same.

**ASSUMPTION:** the fallback list stays the coordinator's `routes` (and the routing table through `chatRoutes`); the agent's `defaultProfile` is not read for it yet.

**Not done (follow-up).**
- U03d: `agent.list` / the agents screen do not mark the coordinator or show its lifecycle (only `coordinator.get` and the pause status do); needs a field on the list or a UI card. The agent's own `lifecycle.status` already shows its gate.
- U03e-style: read the agent's `defaultProfile` and permitted overrides for the coordinator's routes, and run the coordinator's model calls under the agent's budget and attribution (today they are charged to the chat's spend, as before).
- The Stop of a hosted coordinator relies on the existing sweep to finish a blocked preparation; a coordinator model call is not cancelled by a Stop (it ends on its own). A stop issued while a call is in flight reports `stopped` only after the stop service's own phases; no new inventory item represents the call.
- Agent-level pause on a coordinator that is hosted is the owner's responsibility to resume; no automatic return (as for any agent).
- Hosting on a remote worker host, and a state-API command to set up the coordinator (it is still set up through the chat or the in-process handle).

## U03d: follow-ups of the hosted coordinator (2026-11-11)

Code: `chat/coordinator.ts`, `chat/coordinator-host.ts`, `chat/routed-model.ts`, `chat/interpreter.ts`, `chat/chat.ts`, `chat/model-interpreter.ts`, `api/operations.ts`, `api/state-api.ts`, `api/start.ts`. Tests: `api/start-coordinator-host-follow.test.ts` (five tests through `startController`), `chat/coordinator-intent.test.ts` (routes optional; the state commands and the model prompt). API docs regenerated (`coordinator.configure`, `coordinator.state`, `agent.list`, `agent.get`, `coordinator.get`).

**Done.**
- **(a) The agent views mark the coordinator.** For the owner (not a task credential), `agent.list` and `agent.get` add `coordinator: { state, heldBy?, routeSource?, profile? }` to the record of the agent that is the hosted coordinator: `state` is what the agent controls say now (running, paused, stopping, suspended, stopped, or `unknown`), `heldBy` the pause gates that hold it with what each reported, reason and who. A holder of `agent.read`, the agent itself and everyone else read the plain record (checked in the operation and, again, by `CoordinatorService.get`, which is owner only). A coordinator that cannot be read marks nothing; the list still works.
- **(b) Routes follow the agent's profile; calls are the agent's usage.** Precedence for a hosted coordinator, the first that gives a route wins: (1) `routes` the owner stated when setting it up (`explicitRoutes`, used as stated, like routes the owner types for any model setting); (2) the routing table's routes for the agent's `defaultProfile` (`chatRoutes` now takes a `profile`; local data and no paid route, as the coordinator role's own routes are; a host may pass `chat.coordinator.profileRoutes`, as the launcher can for cloud); (3) the coordinator role's routes (`chat.coordinator.routes`, as before); (4) the routes stored by a set-up from before U03d (no flag, so they are not an override and the role's routes still beat them, as before). A coordinator that is not hosted is unchanged. `configure` takes routes as optional for an agent record; for any other principal they are still needed. `coordinator.get` says which applies (`routeSource`: owner, profile, role, stored) and the profile. Each successful model call of a hosted coordinator is recorded with the existing `BudgetService.charge` as activity `model-call` against the agent's principal (usage by agent in `budget.usage`, and in the agent totals the aggregate caps use), as shared overhead under the rule `the coordinator's own model calls (hosted agent)`, in the project asked about, with the wall time as compute and no money. It records and never refuses: no new limit, and a failure to record goes to `onInternalError` and changes nothing. The chat's own daily token cap (`GuardedModelCall`) is unchanged and still counts the tokens.
- **(c) State API commands.** `coordinator.configure` (set up; change principal and routes; take it off its agent by naming a principal that is not an agent record, with routes) and `coordinator.state` (running, paused, stopped on a revision), owner only (a manager with `agent.manage`, and the coordinator itself, are refused). They call the very `CoordinatorService` methods the chat uses, so the replay, the stale-revision refusal, the agent gates and `stillHeldBy` are the same. Chat stays the free-form way: the `coordinator` intent is unchanged except that `routes` is optional for `configure`, and the interpreter prompt now says routes are given only when the owner names them, that without them the agent's routing profile decides, and how to take it off its agent. A test checks the operation names and the prompt together.
- **(d) The review's minor items.** `coordinator.get` (and the agent views) say `unknown` when the agent controls cannot be read, with no `lifecycle`, instead of `stopped` (a retired or missing agent still reads `stopped`). A pause made directly through the agent controls (`lifecycle.pause`) is reported reached (`observe paused`, boundary finished) by the coordinator the next time it is read (`coordinator.get`, the agent views) or asked a question while it holds no work; before, the gate stayed unreported for ever. A set-up refused after its pause (a concurrent change took the record, `stale_revision`) lifts the pause it made, and only that pause (`resumeOwnHold` on its request ID); if the lift fails the refusal says the pause is still in place. The pause's command ID now carries the gate's revision, so the owner's repeat of the refused command pauses again instead of replaying into nothing.

**Tests and mutations (each fails with the fix removed).** unknown state (reverted to `stopped`): test 1; the reached report (calls removed): test 2; the undo (disabled): test 3; the profile branch, the owner's stated routes and the usage record (each disabled): test 4. The owner-only marking is guarded twice (the operation and the service), so removing the operation's check alone changes nothing a caller can see; not mutation-checked further.

**ASSUMPTION:** stated routes beat the agent's profile (the owner's own words about this coordinator are the most specific), and a profile that gives no eligible route falls to the role's routes rather than to no model.
**ASSUMPTION:** the coordinator's calls carry no price (the model client reports tokens, not money), so they are recorded as compute time with cost 0; tokens stay with the chat's token cap. A priced record needs a price per route, which does not exist yet.
**ASSUMPTION:** a pause made directly is reported when someone reads the coordinator or asks it something, not by a timer; the report is an `observe` write done inside the read.
**ASSUMPTION:** taking the coordinator off its agent needs no separate command: setting it up again with a principal that is not an agent record does it and returns it paused (already the behaviour of U03c).

- No timer reports a direct pause of an idle coordinator that nobody reads; a maintenance-loop hook needs an in-process principal for the gate write.

**Review fixes (clean-context review, 2026-11-11, merged with main 98b0929c first).**
- A set-up refused after its pause lifted that pause even when the owner's concurrent set-up of the same agent had taken the record: that set-up found the agent already paused and made no pause of its own, so the undo left a hosted coordinator running that nobody had started. The undo now re-reads the record and keeps the pause when the record hosts this agent (this also covers a write that landed before an error); a record that cannot be read keeps the pause and the refusal says so. Test: `review: a set-up refused after its pause keeps that pause ...` (fails before the fix).
- Routes the owner stated for a hosted coordinator were used as stated, past the routing table: a paid route, a cloud route for local data, a disabled or excluded provider or an unknown route was called (and recorded at cost 0). They are now an order of preference among the routes the table lets the coordinator use, judged each alone as dispatch judges a route (`selectRoute` with a one-route profile, local data, unpaid; no table: none); when none is eligible the profile, then the role, decides. Test: `review: the owner's stated routes are used only where the routing table lets ...` (fails before the fix); the U03d routes test now registers its stated route in the table.
