- `meetings/record.test.ts`, five suites (reference store, SQLite, SQLite worker thread, PostgreSQL): an ended meeting is listed; nothing moves before the hour (59 minutes), the outcome goes back at 61 with the item deferred, no question, and a repeat touches nothing (item revision unchanged); a manager-agent is refused and a host without `meeting.manage` is reported in `returnFailed` with nothing moved; an owner who asked first is not asked twice and a lost "returned" write is neither returned nor failed and the next pass finishes it; at most five records per pass (six meetings need two passes); a meeting with no topic motion is not listed and another project's sweep returns nothing; the answer is absent from the summary before it exists, present after, the snapshot agrees, a reader sees it and an outsider sees no meeting.
- `api/start-meeting-record.test.ts`: in the running controller one dispatcher tick returns a tabled motion's outcome (item `deferred`, no owner question) and a second tick changes nothing.
- Mutations killed: the hour check; the five-per-pass cap; listing only meetings with outcomes; leaving the list when done; the summary's "only when there is one"; the dispatcher's `recovering` wiring.

**Not done**
1. The 50-record cap of the list has no test (it needs 51 meetings); a full list leaves further records to the owner, a host or a service returning them by hand.
2. An automatic question for tabled or no-quorum motions is still not built: the lease asks nothing, and the rule for which deferrals deserve the owner's attention is a product choice (see ASSUMPTION).
3. A record that always fails (`returnFailed`) stays on the list and takes one of the five slots each pass until it is fixed; no backoff yet.
4. The hour is not an owner setting, so chat cannot change it.
5. A deferred item already shows on the next occurrence's agenda (M03h); "carried to the next occurrence" needed nothing new. An item never scheduled into a meeting still has no occurrence for its question (M05 item 3).
6. No run against a real model has checked the wording of the interpreter prompt line (card U03b).

- ASSUMPTION: the automatic hand-back waits one hour so the owner can still return a meeting's outcomes with a question first (M05); after that the outcome goes back with no question. `/srv/code/team/DECISIONS.md` says nothing; the smallest reversible choice keeps the owner's attention unspent, and the wish to be asked stays available before the hour.
- ASSUMPTION: the dispatcher hands back at the owner level (`recovering`), as its other sweeps do for work a person already authorized by holding the meeting, rather than receiving a `meeting.manage` grant.

**M03i review (2026-11-11)**
- Fixed: the hand-back walked the list in the same order every pass, so five meetings whose hand-back keeps failing or staying pending took all five places of every pass and the meetings listed after them never went back. Each pass now starts where the last one ran out of room (kept in memory; after a restart it starts at the front). Test: five stuck meetings and a sixth that still goes back on the next pass.
- Fixed: `recordLoops` stopped at the first project whose sweep threw, so one broken project stopped every later project's votes, abandoned-meeting ends and hand-backs. Every project is now swept and the first error raised after. Inside `sweep`, a record whose step fails no longer holds back the other open records, the log check or the hand-back; the first failure is still raised.
- Checked and left: `recovering(by)` is built only inside dispatch-compose from the dispatcher's own principal; an agent, outside app or task credential calling `meeting.record.sweep` is still refused (`isService`). Owner and lease at the same instant: per-item revision guards mean one settles the topic and the other gets `pending` or a `notAsked` note; nothing moves twice, nothing throws for the loop, but the owner's question can be lost to the lease at the hour boundary (the documented one-hour rule). A crash between settling the item and marking the motion returned is repaired on the next pass (the item is no longer scheduled, so it is not moved again). `ownerAnswers` in the summary is the record's own bounded notes, shown to the same readers as the record.
- Limit: a meeting that ends while the list already holds 50 is not listed and goes back only by hand; a meeting whose hand-back always fails stays listed (and tried every pass) until it succeeds. Nothing tells the owner of either.

## A05b notes: an approval is bound to the target's version (2026-11-11)

A03 and A03b are fully built (launcher core, Linux and macOS backends, Windows Sandbox, quarantine, G05 evidence); A04 to A08 are built. This part closes the first limit A05 recorded: "the target is bound by name, not by version". Card status is NOT changed.

**Done**
- **`Operation.target` and `Binding.target` take an optional `version`** (`review/review.ts`): one token of 1 to 200 characters (letters, digits, `. _ : @ + = / -`, starting with a letter or digit), so a commit ID, `sha256:...` digest or revision number fits; spaces, control characters, other types, text that looks like a credential and any other target field are `invalid_command`. The version is part of the stored binding (so the reviewer is shown it in the operation) and of the canonical binding a repeat request is compared with.
- **Admission compares it exactly.** An approval reviewed at version V admits only an operation read at V; another version, or none, is `review_invalid` naming "the target's version"; an approval reviewed with no version admits none (a version the reviewer never saw is a change). A refused try uses nothing up. A repeat request for another version is not cleared against the earlier approval (it gets its own review); the same version still is.
- **The version comes from the controller, never the agent.** `DispatcherDeps.targetVersion(target, taskId)` is a new optional hook; `ToolPath` reads it each time it builds the operation, both when the review is asked for and again immediately before `admit`. The agent's call request still carries only `kind` and `id` (its `version` field is dropped by the existing parser). A hook that throws or answers a malformed version refuses the call (at request time: "could not be asked for"; at admission: the parked call is closed with "the approval no longer admits the call"): fail closed.
- **No capability change.** The grant check still matches the target by kind and ID; a version does not widen or narrow a grant (tested with a resource-scoped grant).
- **Tests.** `review/target-version.test.ts` (5 tests x 4 backends) and `dispatch/target-version.test.ts` (4 x 4). Mutation checks on the built files: dropping the admission comparison fails 8, dropping the parse of `version` fails all 20, skipping the credential check fails 4; in the tool path, swallowing a hook error fails 4 and not putting the version on the operation fails 12.
- API contract: no operation changed, `api-v1.md` regenerates identically.

**Not done**
1. **Nothing supplies `targetVersion` yet.** (Done in "A05b follow-up: the controller supplies each target's version" below.) `startController` does not set the hook, so no live call is version-bound until a card provides a reading per target kind (a branch's head from the Git bridge, a workspace file's `sha256:` from the A04 bridge, a record's revision). Wiring each is small but belongs with the tool that needs it (the first is the git-push/merge tools).
2. The version is read twice (at asking and at admission); a target that changes in the instant between the read and the run is not caught (the effect ledger and the target's own expected-version write, A04, are what close that).
3. The A05 revocation instant (a grant revoked between `admit` reading the grants and committing) is unchanged; so is "no queue/notification/timeout on pending requests" (later cards).
4. No chat or status addition: this is not an owner control; the owner sees the version in the review's operation. If an owner-facing summary of a review should state it in plain words, the review-request notice text is where it goes.

- ASSUMPTION: the version is an opaque token the controller compares for equality; its meaning (commit, digest, revision) is the hook's, and the charset above is deliberately narrow so it cannot carry text that reads as an instruction to a reviewer.
- ASSUMPTION: an approval reviewed without a version admits only an operation without one, rather than admitting any version, because the weaker rule would let a later-added hook silently widen an old approval.

- **A05b review (clean-context, 2026-11-11), merged with main first.** Fixed:
  - **A reading of the version that never answered held the call forever (MED).** `ToolPath` awaited `targetVersion` with no bound, so a hung hook kept the call (and its parked slot) open with no result. The reading now races a timer (`DispatcherDeps.targetVersionMs`, default 10 s); no answer is the same as an error: the call is refused at asking, the parked call is closed at admission, nothing runs and the approval is not used up.
  - **Tests that did not test their title.** The "unreadable when asking refuses the request" half was never asserted, and the agent-version test passed whatever the parser did with the agent's `version` (the hook's malformed answer refused it either way). Added: an unreadable version at asking makes no review and runs nothing; a hung reading at asking and at admission; the agent's `version` is dropped with no reading and replaced with one; six admissions racing for one approval with different versions (only the reviewed one wins, once); a review with no version stores no new field and is cleared and admitted as before.
  - Mutations (each fails tests, then restored): the hook's error swallowed (fail open) fails 16; the version left out of the binding (so out of the clearing key and the admission compare) fails 16; the compare made one-sided (a versioned approval admits an unversioned run) fails 4; the time bound removed fails the hang tests.
  - **Checked, no change.** The comparison is exact on an ASCII-only token (no Unicode, whitespace or case tricks get through the charset; case differences are different versions). The binding stores the operation's target as given, so the version is in what the reviewer sees, in the canonical binding a repeat request is cleared against, and in the request's command payload. Reviews stored before this change have no `version`, compare equal to an unversioned operation and still clear and admit; nothing re-validates stored review bodies. Commit IDs and `sha256:` hex digests match no credential pattern; a hook answer like `token=...` is refused (fail closed). The grant check uses kind and ID only. No reviewer notice shows a target (the review-request label names the tool and project), so nothing shows a wrong version.
  - **Left as is (noted).** A controller from before this change reading a versioned review would compare only kind and ID at admission (a downgrade with live versioned approvals ignores the version; nothing supplies the hook yet). If asking for a review commits but the call's record does not (a store error in between) and the version then changes, asking again under the same `rev:` command ID is `command_conflict` and is thrown, not recorded (fail closed; the same already happens if the policy's reason text changed). Two asks of one call at the same moment join in one process; a replayed `adm:` command ID reports "admitted" again (A05's documented replay), and the effect ledger keeps the effect once.

## A08c notes: per-agent limits on macOS and Windows, first part (2026-11-11)

Card status is NOT changed. The card's acceptance needs fixtures run on real macOS and Windows hardware; this part builds everything that can be built and proven on a Linux host, and leaves the hardware runs and the one Windows mechanism that cannot be built here.

`packages/worker/src/sandbox/resource-watch.ts` (new), `limits.ts` (`limitedPlan` for other systems, `LimitCapabilities.processSampler` and `.diskSampler`, `LimitedPlan.watch`), `launcher.ts` (starts the monitor; `RunResult.limitExceeded` and `.cpuPauses`; `LauncherConfig.usageSampler` and `.sampling`). 23 tests in `resource-watch.test.ts`.

**Done.**
- **A sampling monitor, the mechanism for systems with no kernel group limit a worker may use.** While a run goes, `ps -A -o pid=,ppid=,rss=,time=` (same keywords on macOS and Linux) is read every 250 ms and the run's process tree is summed: resident memory, process count, CPU time. The directories the agent may write (checkout, home, scratch) are walked every 5 s (links are never followed, 500000 entries at most) and the growth since before the process existed is the disk figure. The decision (`judge`) is a pure function: memory, processes and disk end the run past their limit (`RunResult.limitExceeded`: limit, value, observed, numbers only, nothing the agent wrote); CPU is a token bucket refilled at `cpus` core-seconds per second with a 2 second burst, and an empty bucket pauses the whole tree with SIGSTOP and continues it with SIGCONT (50 ms to 2 s per pause, `cpuPauses` counted). `stop()` always continues what is paused, so a run that ends or is killed while paused is reaped.
- **Never claimed unless seen to work.** `detectLimitCapabilities` for a non-Linux system now tries `ps` on itself (macOS only) and a directory walk, and only for the host it actually runs on; a detector asked about another platform says no. Without the capability a limit stays `none` with the reason (as A08b). With it, each limit is reported `partial` (never `full`: sampling is not a kernel guarantee), by "sampling monitor", with what it misses written in the record's detail (a burst between two looks, compressed or swapped memory, threads, exited children's CPU time, deletions offsetting writes). `requireEnforced` therefore still refuses a macOS launch, as the rule says.
- **Windows.** Only the disk limit is held, by the same directory walk over the host paths of the shares (`partial`). CPU, memory and processes stay `none` and the record says why: the Windows Sandbox guest's processes cannot be seen from the host. Even a wrongly set `processSampler` flag is ignored for `win32`.
- The plan itself is never changed for these systems, so the A03/A03b backends are untouched.
- Tests (this Linux host stands in for the process listing): parsers (both `ps` time formats, junk lines, parent cycles); each decision with its boundary; CPU burst, pacing, idle refill and "a drop in the figure is never a refund"; the watcher against a fake sampler and signal (one report, no overlapping looks, a failing look decides nothing, pause then continue, stop continues, disk baseline and interval); the plan and report for darwin and win32 with and without the capabilities; real runs through the launcher in trusted-host mode with platform `darwin`: a 400 MB allocation ended at 200 MB (and a small one not), a fork storm ended at 8 processes, 6 MB written past a 3 MB limit ended while the checkout's existing 8 MB did not count, two busy loops paced under `cpus: 1` with nothing left stopped (skipped, with the reason printed, when the host cannot give the loops 1.4 cores just now), `requireEnforced` refusing. Mutation-checked on the built files: memory, process and disk guards, the disk baseline, link following, the refund rule, `stop()` not continuing, overlapping looks, the Windows process-sampler guard and the detector's host check each fail a test.
- Security: nothing is callable by anyone but the launcher's own code; limits are validated by `checkLimits` and `checkHeadroom` first (A08b); the monitor reads numbers only; it signals only the pids of the run's own tree found in the same look (a process that exits and whose id is reused inside one look interval could be signalled: accepted, the window is a fraction of a second and a stop is followed by a continue); a run that ends is never left stopped. There is no storage in this part, so the four-backend rule does not apply, and no new owner control, so no chat-command or interpreter-prompt change (the limits come from the environment manifest, A08).

**Not done.**
1. The real macOS and Windows hardware runs of the acceptance fixtures (the monitor is proven here against Linux's `ps`; a Mac's `ps` output, `sandbox-exec` interplay with SIGSTOP and the Seatbelt profile's `signal (target self)` rule for the controller side must be run on a Mac: the monitor signals from the launcher, outside the profile, so no rule change is expected). Y02 and H12r own the per-platform runs.
2. A Windows mechanism for CPU, memory and processes. A Job Object on the host side bounds the `wsb` client, not the virtual machine, so it would claim a limit it does not hold. The real options are the guest memory size in the Windows Sandbox configuration (`MemoryInMB`) and a monitor running inside the guest; both need a Windows machine to prove, and the guest monitor needs a reviewed in-guest component. Left as a Windows follow-up (A08c-win).
3. Linux without a user systemd scope still reports the process count as `none`; the same monitor could hold it as `partial` there (a small change to `limitedPlan`'s Linux branch). Not done to leave A08b's recorded behaviour and tests alone.
4. Counting CPU of processes that exited between two looks, and threads; a hard guarantee instead of sampling would need a macOS launchd or Endpoint Security mechanism the project has not chosen.
5. The environment manifest's limits are still not passed into a launch by the dispatcher (A08b's recorded gap, unchanged).

- ASSUMPTION: on macOS a sampled limit is `partial`, so an owner who sets `requireEnforced` cannot run there; the first release accepted that no limit is enforced on these systems (owner decision 2026-10-22), and partial is strictly more than that.
- ASSUMPTION: pausing with SIGSTOP/SIGCONT is the right reaction to CPU overuse (a CPU quota slows work, it does not destroy it); memory, process and disk overuse end the run because they cannot be undone by waiting.
- ASSUMPTION: the disk limit counts growth under the checkout, home and scratch since the launch, not their total size (the card says what the agent may write).

### A08c part 1 review (clean-context Claude reviewer, 2026-11-11)

Merged main e1418825 first (no conflicts). Fixed, each with a test that fails when the fix is removed:
- **Orphans escaped the limits.** The tree was found only by walking parent ids down from the launched process, so a child whose parent exited (`(cmd &)`, handed to init or a subreaper) was no longer counted, paused or ended: a plain bypass of every sampled limit. `ps` now also prints `pgid` and `lstart`; a member is the launched process, every process of its process group (the launcher starts it as a group leader, and a group id is not reused while the group has a member), every process seen before that still has the same start time (one that left the group after a look saw it), and all below them. The run is still watched when the launched process has exited but its group lives. Remaining gap, written in the record: a process that starts its own session and whose parent exits before any look sees it. A real launcher test ends a 400 MB orphan.
- **The directory walk held up the process looks.** The disk walk ran inside the 250 ms look, so a long walk delayed the memory and CPU checks for its whole length, and a pause then stopped process ids sampled before the walk (seconds old: a much wider window for a reused id). The walk now has its own timer and busy flag (`diskTick`); a look signals the ids it has just read.
- **macOS CPU time past 999 minutes** (`1234:56.78`) did not parse, so that process and its whole subtree vanished from the figures.
- **A tree paused when the launcher's process exits** was left stopped for ever. Watches holding a pause are continued from a `process.on("exit")` hook. (A SIGKILL of the launcher cannot be caught; it is the one way left to leave a tree stopped.) The continue timer is armed before the SIGSTOP and a pause never exceeds `MAX_PAUSE_MS`.
- The signal function never sends to pids 0 and 1, the launcher itself or its parent.
- A file with several names (hard links) or a directory reached twice is counted once; `ino` 0 (no inode numbers) is not used for this.
- `detectLimitCapabilities` claimed `diskSampler` on any macOS or Windows host whatever the walk did (`bytes >= 0` cannot fail); it now writes a 4321-byte probe with a second name and claims the walk only when it measures exactly that.
- The default clock is monotonic (`performance.now`), and `ps` is killed with SIGKILL at its timeout (`psSampler(path, timeoutMs)`; a hanging `ps` test).
- Record details now also say: memory shared between processes counts once per process (false kills of a large multi-process build are possible), and disk sizes are lengths (a sparse file counts at full length).

Checked and left: SIGKILL reaches stopped processes, so the time limit and limit ends work while paused; a kill verdict is never taken while paused; `stop()` after a look in flight cannot pause afterwards; `requireEnforced` still refuses on macOS; Windows reports none for CPU, memory and processes.

## K02 follow-up: controller liveness heartbeat for a hung last known good (2026-11-11)

Card K02 stays planned. This closes the largest sound part of the K02a gap: `Launcher.prepare()` pre-marks the start of the last known good as confirmed, so a last known good that hangs (event loop blocked, process still alive) was never found; K02a handles only exits. The K02a supervisor is on the unmerged branch `card10-k02a` (594a5e36), so nothing here imports or copies it: the checker is a standalone module with a thin hook for the merge. No launcher, updater or controller process was started outside tests; nothing deployed.

**Built**
- `release/heartbeat.ts` (new, exported from `release/index.ts`).
  - `HeartbeatWriter` (controller side): an `unref`ed timer, 5 s by default and bounded to 1 to 60 s, bumps a counter in its callback (so the file only moves while the event loop turns) and writes `{v, seq, token, intervalMs}` (about 70 bytes: no path, no time, no credential) to a launcher-owned file. The write is asynchronous, nothing awaits it, and a tick that finds the previous write unfinished only bumps the counter, so a stuck disk never blocks or piles up. Temporary file created exclusively with `O_NOFOLLOW`, mode 0600, then renamed over the target. Never touches the database. A write that fails is told once (code only, no path) and once more when it works again.
  - `HeartbeatMonitor` (launcher side): `begin()` when the controller has confirmed, then `check()` every few seconds. Uses only its own monotonic clock. Verdicts `alive`, `unsupported`, `unknown`, `hung`. Hung means: a beat of this start (right token) was seen, then the counter did not move for the threshold. The threshold is `max(staleAfterMs, 6 x the writer's interval)`; `staleAfterMs` defaults to 120 s and is clamped to 30 s to 1 h, so it cannot be set into false restarts. A missing, unreadable, garbled, oversized, symlinked, other-user, other-start (token) file or a counter that went backwards is `unknown`/`unsupported` and never hung; the time the file was unreadable is not counted (the count restarts at the first good read). A gap between two checks of more than half the threshold, or a clock that went backwards (checker paused, machine slept, clock jump) restarts the count instead of judging.
  - `planLiveness({dir, releaseId, ...})`: the supervisor's single call per child. Creates the launcher-owned directory (0700, refused when it is a link, belongs to another user or is writable by group or others), a random per-start token and file name, and returns `env` (`NIMBLENEWT_HEARTBEAT_FILE`, `_TOKEN`, `_INTERVAL_MS`: nothing else, no secret), `watch({confirmed, signal})` (resolves with a `HungResult` or `undefined` on abort; counts only after `confirmed()` is true; poll a sixth of the threshold, at most 5 s) and `cleanup()`.
- `Launcher.noteHung(releaseId, reason)` (K02f): a `failed_start` notice with `fallback: true` in `launcher-state.json` plus a log entry. It never writes the quarantine list and never changes the last known good. One open notice per kind and release, as for the others.
- `startController` option `heartbeat` (`false` or `{file, token, intervalMs}`); by default on when `env.NIMBLENEWT_HEARTBEAT_FILE` and `_TOKEN` are present (set by the supervisor), off otherwise. Started after the services are up and before the startup confirmation, stopped in `close()`. An unsafe path or token only turns the heartbeat off (told once); it never stops the start.
- Tests: `release/heartbeat.test.ts` (16) and `api/start-heartbeat.test.ts` (1, a real `startController` under the environment variables): bounds; strict parsing; moving/stopped/exactly-at-threshold; GC-like pause below the limit; interval raising the limit; clock jumps forward and back; unreadable/garbled/missing treated as unknown with the blind time not counted; other token and backwards counter; unsupported unless `firstBeatMs`; writer content (no path, mode 0600, bounded rate, stop leaves no temporary); symlink target, symlinked and group-writable directory, planted temporary link not followed; reader refusals; a REAL child that beats and then blocks its event loop is found hung (fake monotonic clock, real file) while a running one is not; `watch` after the confirmation, on abort; `Launcher.noteHung`.

**Supervisor integration (for the K02a merge; about 15 lines in `supervisor.ts`)**
1. Per child: `const live = await planLiveness({ dir: join(root, "run"), releaseId })`, spawn with `env: { ...spec.env, ...live.env }`.
2. `const hung = live.watch({ confirmed: async () => (await launcher.read()).attempt?.confirmedAt !== undefined, signal: controller.signal })`; race it with the exit and the startup watchdog verdict, as `launcher.watch()` is.
3. When `hung` wins: `stop("hung")` (the same SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after `graceMs`, group-wide ladder), count the run as a short run (the existing backoff and `giveUpAfter` then apply to a loop of hangs as to a loop of crashes), `launcher.noteHung(releaseId, hung.reason)`, emit an event, and let the loop restart the same release. Never `quarantine` the last known good for a hang.
4. After the child ended (any reason): `await live.cleanup()`. If the supervisor knows a release writes a heartbeat (for example a field in its `compat.json`), pass `firstBeatMs` to find a last known good that hangs before its first beat.
5. `Launcher.confirm()` of an already pre-marked last known good returns early and closes no notices, so the hang notice survives the restart; a notice for a release that was not pre-marked is closed by its later confirmation as for every other notice.

**Not done**
- (Done in the review below: wired into `supervisor.ts` with supervisor-level tests.)
- A last known good that hangs before its first beat (startup deadlock) is not found unless the supervisor passes `firstBeatMs`; one that awaits forever with a running loop is not "hung" by this measure (the event loop turns); this finds a blocked loop, not a stuck task.
- A release older than this change has no writer: `unsupported`, never restarted.
- Ancestors above the heartbeat directory are not checked for symlinks; ownership checks are skipped on Windows (no `getuid`), and Windows was not exercised.
- A controller that cannot write the file at all (disk full, directory removed) looks like a stalled one after the threshold (and is told once on its own log); see ASSUMPTION below.
- No change to `workers.json`, API docs (no API surface changed; `npm run api:docs:write` produced no diff), or any card status.

**ASSUMPTION:** the default limit is 120 s (minimum 30 s) with the writer at 5 s: long enough for a GC pause or a few seconds of synchronous migration, short enough to matter.
**ASSUMPTION:** no beat ever seen means unsupported, not hung, because the last known good may predate this writer; a false restart of a healthy release is judged worse than a missed hang.
**ASSUMPTION:** a heartbeat that cannot be written counts as a stall: the launcher cannot distinguish it, and a controller that cannot write its own run directory is unhealthy enough to restart (the crash-loop limit bounds the cost).
**ASSUMPTION:** the hang notice reuses the `failed_start` kind with `fallback: true` (Needs you level by default) rather than a new kind, so the notice sink, schema and owner text need no change.
**ASSUMPTION:** the heartbeat directory is `<release root>/run`, created 0700 by the launcher; the file name carries part of a random per-start token so a leftover from an earlier start is never mistaken for the current one.

### K02 heartbeat: clean-context review and supervisor wiring (2026-11-11)
Merged main (K02a supervisor and CLI) into the branch, then wired the heartbeat into `Supervisor` and fixed what the review found.

**Wired**
- `Supervisor` option `heartbeat` (default on; `false` off; `dir` default `<root>/run`, `staleAfterMs`, `intervalMs`, `firstBeatMs`, `pollMs`, `monotonic`). Per child: `planLiveness` before the spawn (a failure only turns it off for that start, logged without a path), the child's environment gets the launcher's three variables, and inherited `NIMBLENEWT_HEARTBEAT_*` are dropped (also when off). `watch()` runs beside `Launcher.watch()` and is raced in both phases (before and after the startup verdict); it counts only once the start of this release is confirmed and not failed. A hang: `hung` event, `stopping` (why `hung`), the same SIGTERM -> SIGKILL ladder, `Launcher.noteHung`, then the loop restarts through `prepare()` and the backoff. A hang always counts as a short run (a controller that always hangs after a while ends in exit 4). `firstBeatMs` is never below the stale limit (and 30 s). The file and any temporary are removed in a `finally` on every path; at start, holding the root lock, leftovers of a killed launcher are swept (`sweepHeartbeats`, only names the module makes).
- CLI: `--heartbeat on|off`, `--heartbeat-stale-seconds` (30 to 3600), `--heartbeat-interval-seconds` (1 to 60), `--heartbeat-first-beat-seconds` (300 to 86,400, at least the stale limit; off by default). Values below the minimums are refused (exit 1), not quietly raised.

**Fixed (each with a test that fails without it)**
- A clean stop was taken for a hang: `close()` stopped the heartbeat first and then waited for backups, workers and the database, so a stop longer than the threshold was killed, recorded as a hang and restarted instead of staying down. The heartbeat now stops last (in a `finally`). Test: `start-heartbeat` delays the database close 2.5 s and the counter keeps moving.
- A hung controller whose SIGTERM handler ran once its loop came back exited 0, which the supervisor reads as a stop on purpose (launcher exits 0, nothing restarted). The hang stop is marked judged. Test: the `hang-once` fake controller exits 0 on SIGTERM; it is restarted.
- The crash-loop notice that ends a run of hangs was swallowed: notices are one per kind and release, and the open hang notice (`failed_start`) had the same key, so the owner never got the Urgent "gave up". The hang notice also told the owner the release "did not start in time and is set aside", which is false. Notices get an optional `cause: "hung"`: its own key and its own label ("stopped responding and the launcher restarted it"). An optional field rather than a new kind, because an older release's controller drops unknown kinds but keeps unknown fields (it would only show the old label). A fall-back no longer folds a hang notice.
- A full disk looked like a hang: the writer only wrote a new temporary and renamed it, which needs new space. Records are now a fixed 128 bytes and, when the new file cannot be made, the existing record is overwritten in place (only a regular file of this user with one link and exactly that size, opened `O_NOFOLLOW`). Test: the directory made read-only (no new file) keeps the counter moving with nothing reported; a hard-linked file is never written through.
- The first-beat wait (`firstBeatMs`) ignored the pause / clock-jump rule, so a launcher paused (or a clock that counts suspend) judged a start at once. Same rule now.
- A counter read backwards (a torn read showing a value ahead) was never taken as the new baseline, so a hang below the old value was never judged. It is now.
- `cleanup()` left `<file>.<pid>.tmp` of a writer killed mid-write (one per kill, forever); removed. The reader opens with `O_NONBLOCK` (a FIFO swapped in after the `lstat` does not block the launcher).

**Checked, no change**
- The counter is bumped in the timer callback, which cannot run while the event loop is blocked (the real-child tests block with a busy loop); the `unref` only stops the timer keeping the process alive. A wedged worker thread or a deadlocked await is not found (documented gap). A saturated libuv pool that never finishes a write stops the file moving: judged hung, which is a controller unable to do file work.
- Startup: the writer starts only after the services are up, so a long synchronous migration before that is "unsupported" (no beat), never hung; after it, a synchronous block of more than 120 s is judged hung by design (killing a migration mid-way rolls back its transaction).
- Sleep and resume: `performance.now` does not advance during suspend on Linux and macOS (both processes paused alike); where it does (Windows), the gap rule restarts the count. The checker paused: same rule.
- File handling: token per start, strict parse, `O_NOFOLLOW`/`O_EXCL` temporary, 0600 file, 0700 directory checked for owner and mode, symlink and other-user refusal, size bound and a read of at most 513 bytes; a hard link or swap inside the 0700 directory needs the same user. The path comes from the launcher (inherited values are dropped); logs carry no path or token.
- `noteHung` never writes `failed` or `known`; `confirm()` of a pre-marked last known good returns early, so the hang notice survives the restart; a hang can only be judged after confirmation, so a hung start is never left unconfirmed for `prepare()` to quarantine.

**Tests**: supervisor 16 (was 13: beat then block -> hung -> stopped -> restarted, notice, no quarantine, exit 0 of the handler not a stop, per-start files removed; beat normally / slowly under load (2.5 s blocks every 3 s) / never beat: never stopped; always hangs and never beats with `firstBeatMs`: exit 4 through the backoff with the crash-loop notice; inherited variables replaced, `heartbeat: false` sets none), heartbeat 19 (was 17; new: full disk, cleanup/sweep; extended: backwards baseline, first-beat pause, hang notice label and crash-loop coexistence), start-heartbeat 1 (close order), launcher CLI (heartbeat flags reach the child; minimums refused). The heartbeat clock in supervisor tests runs 5x real time.
Mutation checks (each fails a test): threshold without the interval factor; token check removed; quarantine on hang; heartbeat stopped first in `close()`; no in-place overwrite; no `cause` in the key; no backwards baseline; no first-beat pause rule; hang stop not judged; hang not counted as short (the crash-loop tests now fail on a bounded wait instead of running forever); no `noteHung`; no cleanup; inherited variables kept.

## K02 follow-up: service units and the updater program (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-11)

Card K02 stays planned. This builds the largest self-contained part of what the K02a notes left open: the service units and the updater. Generation only: nothing is installed, enabled, started or deployed on any machine, and no controller, database, network or model is involved.

**Built**
- `release/service-units.ts` (`generateServiceUnit`, `checkServiceSpec`, `SERVICE_RESTART`, the escaping helpers; exported from `release/index.ts`): a PURE generator for a systemd user unit, a launchd LaunchAgent plist and a Windows Task Scheduler task XML that run `node scripts/nimblenewt-launcher.mjs --root ... --entry ... --switcher ... [-- controller args]`, plus the install steps, uninstall steps and notes as text.
  - Identity: the invoking user only (systemd user manager, LaunchAgent, a task for the logged-on user with `LeastPrivilege`); no `User=`/`UserName`; the printer refuses to run as uid 0.
  - No secrets: environment by reference only (`EnvironmentFile=` on systemd; `node --env-file=FILE` in launchd and Windows, which have no environment-file setting). Controller arguments that look like a credential (names such as token/secret/password/api key, `sk-`/`ghp_`/`AKIA`/JWT shapes, an address with a password) and Node's own `--env-file` are refused; `--token-file=PATH` style names stay allowed.
  - Exit-code contract (`SERVICE_RESTART`, built from `SUPERVISOR_EXIT`): systemd `Restart=on-failure` plus `RestartPreventExitStatus=2 3 4` (0 stays down by itself), `RestartSec=30`, at most 5 starts per 600 s; `KillMode=mixed`, `TimeoutStopSec=90` so the launcher's own ordered stop runs. launchd: `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit=false`, `ThrottleInterval=60`, `ExitTimeOut=90`. Windows: `RestartOnFailure` 3 times 1 minute apart. launchd and Task Scheduler cannot separate exit codes, and the notes in the printed output say so.
  - systemd hardening: `NoNewPrivileges`, `PrivateTmp`, `ProtectSystem=full` (default) or `strict` with explicit read-write paths, `RestrictSUIDSGID`, `RestrictRealtime`, `LockPersonality`, `UMask=0077`.
  - Validation and escaping: every path absolute and normalised in the TARGET platform's spelling (so a Linux machine can print a Windows task), no control characters, line breaks, Unicode separators, lone surrogates or XML-forbidden characters, length and count bounds; a name whitelist; per-format escaping (XML entities; the systemd quoting with `\`, `"` backslash-escaped and `%`/`$` doubled; CommandLineToArgvW quoting for the task's `Arguments`; POSIX single-quote and PowerShell single-quote quoting in the steps). Paths that systemd reads unquoted (environment file, log files, read-write paths, and the root under `strict`) must be plain. Windows paths refuse `< > : " | ? * %`, reserved device names, trailing dots/spaces, UNC and `\\?\`.
- `scripts/nimblenewt-service.mjs`: `print --platform linux|darwin|win32 --root ... [--node] [--launcher] [--entry] [--switcher] [--environment-file] [--log-dir] [--name] [--windows-user] [--protect-system] [--read-write-path] [--unit-only] [-- controller args]`. Prints the unit and the numbered steps (heredoc / here-string for the unit file, a syntax check, the enable/start commands) and writes nothing. The environment-file flag is spelled `--environment-file` because Node itself reads any `--env-file` anywhere on a command line (found when the first draft used that name).
- `release/updater.ts` (`stageRelease`, `announceRelease`, `installRelease`, `UpdaterError`) and `scripts/nimblenewt-updater.mjs stage --root --source --digest [--announce [--switch]]`: described in `maintenance-and-updates.md`. Reuses `verifyReleaseDirectory`, `PROCESS_TOKEN`, `ACTIVATION_LIMITS`, `parseCompat` and `Launcher.expect`; the same file-name rules as `release.stage`; the same `.tmp-<id>-` naming the controller's own sweep recognises.
- Docs: `maintenance-and-updates.md` (service units, the updater, the exit-code sentence now says 0, 2, 3 and 4 stay down), `getting-started.md` gap row. No API operation changed (`npm run api:docs:write` after a forced build: no diff). No owner control was added, so no chat reach.
- Tests: `service-units.test.ts` (13: golden outputs for the three platforms, the strict systemd variant and the install steps under `release/golden-units/`, rewritten with `NN_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1`; identity and no-secret checks; secrets refused; hostile paths on all platforms; hostile arguments escaped per format or refused; spaces and XML specials; names; escaping helpers with an independent CommandLineToArgvW parser; the exit-code alignment test against `SUPERVISOR_EXIT`, `CONTROLLER_EXIT`, the generated systemd directives and the launcher script's header; steps contain the exact unit), `updater.test.ts` (15: layout and modes, announce and switch then `Launcher.prepare` runs it, idempotent repeat, existing release never overwritten (same digest reused, damaged or different refused, empty directory refused), a crash at afterCheck/afterCopy/afterVerify leaves no `releases/<id>` and the leftover is swept when old and kept when fresh, a crash after the rename is completed by the repeat, the release is never visible before the single rename, a source changed or swapped for a link after the check, links of every kind, unmanifested and special files, digest/size/missing, malformed or hostile manifests, damaged `compat.json`, announce re-verification, input checks), `scripts/nimblenewt-service.test.mjs` (4) and `scripts/nimblenewt-updater.test.mjs` (3). Mutation checks on the updater: no `O_NOFOLLOW`, no existing-release refusal, no source verification, no temporary-folder cleanup each fail tests. The Linux unit was also parsed by `systemd-analyze --user verify` (only complaint: the fixture's node path does not exist); the plist and task XML were parsed as well-formed XML with hostile values.

**Not done**
- Nothing was installed or run: no launchd, systemd (beyond `verify` of a scratch copy) or Task Scheduler run, and nothing on a real macOS or Windows machine. The plist and task have not been loaded by launchd or Task Scheduler, only checked as well-formed XML and against their documented schemas.
- launchd and Task Scheduler cannot tell the launcher's exit codes apart, so an exit 2, 3 or 4 is retried (60 s apart on macOS, 3 times on Windows) instead of staying down. An exit-code-aware answer there would need a launcher option such as "exit 0 instead of 2, 3, 4 under a service manager" (a change to the reviewed launcher) or a wrapper script.
- Windows: a scheduled task for the logged-on user, not a Windows service (a real service needs a service wrapper and administrator rights); the launcher's stderr is not kept (no log file); only runs while the user is logged on.
- The environment file is not read, created or permission-checked by the generator (the steps `chmod 600` it); a file with spaces cannot be named for systemd; launchd's `node --env-file` needs Node 20.6 or later (this project needs 22.19); log rotation is left to the owner.
- The updater does not run the maintenance sequence (quiesce, checkpoint, quarantine, verify, revert), does not write the controller's `release-staged` or activation records (a pointer moved with `--switch` is reported `diverged` by `release.status`; a release it installed has no staged record, so `release.activate` of it by the controller is not possible; the controller's own `release.stage` path remains the one for a running controller), and cannot tell where the source came from beyond the digest the caller supplies (no signature or publisher check; the trust store is still undecided).
- No file locking between two updaters of the same ID: the single rename decides, the loser reports `exists`. A hard link into the source from elsewhere is read like any file.
- Windows: `lockTree` is a no-op (modes do not mean this), the file digests are the defence, as for `release.stage`.

**ASSUMPTION:** a launcher exit 4 (crash loop) is not restarted by the service manager (the task said so; the launcher's own header said "may restart on 1, 4 and 5"). The notice is written and the launcher already slowed 20 restarts; the maintenance doc now says 0, 2, 3 and 4 stay down. The launcher script's header comment was first left unchanged; the review below corrected it.
**ASSUMPTION:** exit 3 (no active release) stays down too, like 2: nothing changes until the owner announces and switches a release.
**ASSUMPTION:** a LaunchAgent / user unit / logon task (runs from login, as the user) is the safe default; a system-wide boot-time service would need root or an administrator and is left to the owner.
**ASSUMPTION:** the updater's source directory has the layout `release.stage` produces (`MANIFEST.json` + files) and its trust comes from a digest the caller names; the default is to announce only, and moving the pointer is an explicit `--switch`.
**ASSUMPTION:** `ProtectSystem=full` is the compatible default (the controller's data directory location is unknown here); `strict` is opt-in with the writable directories listed. (Superseded by the review below: no `ProtectSystem` by default.)

**K02 service units review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-11)**
- Fixed (would have broken the controller): the default systemd user unit set `PrivateTmp=true` and `ProtectSystem=full`. In a USER unit any file-system namespacing makes systemd put the service in its own user namespace, and on Ubuntu 23.10 and later (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`, as on this machine) that namespace runs under AppArmor's `unprivileged_userns` profile, which forbids creating another one: bubblewrap failed with "No permissions to create a new namespace" and the worker package's own `bubblewrapBackend().health()` reported unhealthy. Measured with transient `systemd-run --user --wait --pipe` scopes (nothing installed): `NoNewPrivileges`, `RestrictSUIDSGID`, `RestrictRealtime`, `LockPersonality`, `UMask`, `KillMode=mixed` keep the probe healthy; adding `PrivateTmp` or `ProtectSystem=full|strict` alone makes it fail (`NoNewPrivileges` is not the cause). The default unit now has no namespacing option; `--protect-system full|strict` stays an opt-in with a warning note to check the sandbox. A test lists the options that must not appear in the default unit (namespacing, `RestrictNamespaces`, `SystemCallFilter`, `MemoryDenyWriteExecute`, ...).
- Fixed: the Windows task without `--windows-user` had a `LogonTrigger` with no `UserId`, which is "at log on of any user": it fires at every user's logon and registering it needs an administrator, contrary to the "ordinary rights, this user" promise. The user is now required on Windows (named in the trigger and the principal).
- Fixed (contradiction): the launcher's header said a service manager "may restart it on 1, 4 and 5"; it now says not on 0, 2, 3 or 4 and may on 1 and 5, matching `SERVICE_RESTART` and `maintenance-and-updates.md`; the alignment test checks the header sentence and the doc sentence against the table.
- Fixed: the updater program read `--announce=yes` / `--switch=false` as "not given" (silently not announcing); boolean flags with a value are refused there and for the service printer's `--unit-only`. `--switch` now prints a warning on stderr that the controller's record is left `diverged`; the doc now says what that means: the launcher runs the new release normally, `release.rollback` still goes back from the old "current", and a `release.activate` interrupted before its pointer write is left `unresolved` for the owner (its journal's `from` is the record's current, not what the pointer names).
- Tests: a percent sign in the environment file, log directory, read-write paths and root is doubled everywhere (no single `%` left in the unit); the default-unit option list; the Windows user requirement; the CLI refusals and the warning. Mutations killed (each alone on the built file): no `%` doubling in ExecStart (3 failures), no `$` doubling (2), no `RestartPreventExitStatus` (3), `Restart=always` (3), no `%` doubling in `EnvironmentFile` (1, survived before this review), `PrivateTmp` put back (3), Windows user optional (1), old launcher header (1), updater copy hash not compared (1). Two updater mutations survive and are equivalent: the size bound inside the copy loop and the re-verification of the temporary copy (both behind the per-file size and digest check after the copy).
- Checked, no change: `Restart=on-failure` never restarts exit 0 or a clean SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP/SIGPIPE, and `RestartPreventExitStatus=2 3 4` stops those; `StartLimitIntervalSec`/`StartLimitBurst` are in `[Unit]`; `systemd-analyze --user verify` of a unit with a real node path, environment file and log directory reports nothing. `KillMode=mixed`: a normal stop signals the launcher only; whatever is left after the launcher exits (including a controller orphaned by a launcher crash) is killed with SIGKILL, which also frees the root lock for the restart. The abstract-socket root lock lives in the network namespace and is not affected by the unit. The systemd word quoting (`\`, `"`, `%%`, `$$`, lone `;` refused), plain unquoted paths, XML escaping (text only, no attributes take values; control characters, lone surrogates and U+FFFE/FFFF refused; the comments hold no `--`), CommandLineToArgvW quoting with `%` refused (Task Scheduler expands it), the here-document and here-string terminators. Updater: the copy is hashed while read, so a directory swapped for a link after the check can only change where bytes come from, never what is installed; files are written 0444 (no setuid or other mode kept); the temporary folder is in `releases/` (same file system, one rename); an existing release is reused only when it verifies against the same digest.
- Not verified: Task Scheduler on a real Windows machine (whether a `Command` path with spaces such as `C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe` needs quotes there is untested; the generator writes it unquoted, as `New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute` does) and launchd on a real Mac.
## A08d notes: the environment's limits reach each launch (2026-11-11)

Closes the gap A08b and A08c recorded ("the environment manifest's limits are not passed into a launch by the dispatcher"). `controller/src/environments/launch-limits.ts` (new), `dispatch/dispatcher.ts` (`#launchLimits`, `noteLaunch`, `launchLimitsOf`, `DispatcherDeps.launchDefaults`, `.environments` now also needs `resume`), `dispatch/model.ts` (`DispatchBody.launchLimits`), `remote/host.ts`, `worker/src/host/local.ts` (`HostOrder.contract`, `contractLimitsOf`), `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `api/start.ts`, `api/worker-limits-settings.ts`, `environments/environments.ts` (optional `limits.wallTimeMs`), `status/status.ts`.

**Done**
- **One rule.** The effective limits of an attempt are, per figure, the smaller of the pinned environment revision's manifest limit and the installation's limit (the owner's `workers.limits.*` setting over the `dispatch.local.limits` start-up configuration, read afresh at each launch); a figure only one side states is kept; a figure neither states is not limited. An environment (so an agent or a task) can never raise a limit: a figure it asks for above the installation's is cut and listed as `capped` (asked, applied). `effectiveLaunchLimits` is pure; `tightenLimits` is the same rule without sources.
- **Which revision.** The attempt's pin (A08): the dispatcher reads the manifest through `environments.resume(agent, attemptId)`, so a restarted or moved attempt gets the figures it started with even after the owner changed the environment. An agent with no active environment gets the installation's figures only; with neither, nothing changes from before (no limits in the contract, no record).
- **Through the dispatch contract.** `sealContract(order, { limits })` carries the effective figures (`cpus`, `memoryMb`, `diskMb`, `processes`, `wallTimeMs`). The local worker host (`contractLimitsOf`) takes the smaller of them, the workspace's and the owner's per figure into the launcher request; wall time is the launcher's time limit. A remote host's `#carry` used to replace the contract's limits with the owner's; it now takes the smaller of the two per figure and seals again (digest checked). The host's own checks (`checkLimits`, `checkHeadroom`) still run in the launcher.
- **Wall time in the manifest.** `limits.wallTimeMs` is optional (1000 ms to a week). It is left out of a manifest that states none, so such a manifest (every one made before this change) keeps its stored form and its digest, and its wall time is the installation's. The owner makes it; an agent changing it (or dropping it) is refused like any other limit. Unknown keys under `limits` are now refused on entry instead of silently dropped.
- **Validation at every entry.** Manifest limits (whole numbers, bounds, units, NaN, Infinity, strings, fractions, unknown names, a non-object), the installation's figures (the same checker as the owner's setting), the figures in the contract at the host (whole numbers; wall time 1000 ms to a week; unknown name, non-object), and at a remote placement (`checkContract`, unchanged). A launch whose figures cannot be worked out is refused: the dispatcher ends the attempt `failed` with "the limits of this launch could not be worked out (...), so nothing was started" and the usual `dispatch_blocked` blocker for the owner; the host refuses and records `refused` for a bad contract figure. A manifest figure that is valid in a manifest but more than a launch can carry (for example 300 cpus, the launch bound is 256) also refuses, rather than being cut silently.
- **Enforced, partial or none, on the attempt's record.** `DispatchBody.launchLimits` holds the figures given, whose each is (`environment` or `installation`), what the installation cut, the environment revision, and, once the host has launched, `outcome` (started/refused), `bestEffort` and one entry per limit with `enforced: full | partial | none`, the mechanism and the detail (from limits.ts' capability report). The host's `onLaunch` reaches it through `DispatcherService.noteLaunch` (best effort for the caller). The owner's launch record (`workers.limits.enforced`) gains `environment` (revision, sources, capped). Nothing here is a secret.
- **`requireEnforced` honoured.** No new switch: the existing owner setting (`workers.limits.besteffort`, strict by default) is `requireEnforced`. In strict mode a limit the host cannot hold in full (the launcher's own check, now fed with the environment's figures) refuses the launch before anything runs: the attempt fails with the reason and `failed` (which limit, how far) and the owner has a blocker; the record says `refused`. With best effort on, the launch goes ahead and the record names each limit that was partial or not enforced.
- **Wired for real.** `startController` did not pass `environments` to the dispatcher at all (so no live attempt pinned an environment); it does now (`ComposeInput.environments`), and `launchDefaults` reads the owner's effective limits.
- **Status.** The owner's environment view states the wall time (or that the installation's applies) and that each launch uses the figures cut by the limits set for all agents.

**Tests** (mutation-checked: each guard below was removed once and a test failed)
- `environments/launch-limits.test.ts` (6, pure): smaller wins, sources, cut list, never raised, every bad shape on both sides with side/unit/bounds in the message, `tightenLimits`. Mutations: larger wins; checker bypassed.
- `dispatch/launch-limits.test.ts` (6 on each of four backends): figures in the contract and the record; installation cuts and fills (old manifest without wall time); no environment; bad/unreadable installation figure and an over-bound manifest figure refuse with a blocker and start nothing; the host report on the record. Mutations: limits not sealed; larger figure wins; refusal swallowed.
- `environments/environments.test.ts` (+2 on four backends): optional wall time stored as before (digest equal to the digest of the same manifest as it was), pinned, owner-only; entry checks. Mutations: no range check; unknown key kept; wall time dropped.
- `worker/host/local.test.ts` (+1): the contract tightens, never loosens, bad figures refuse and are recorded as refused. Mutations: contract ignored; no value check; no name check.
- `remote/launch-limits.test.ts` (3): smaller of both sides sealed with a matching digest; bad figures offer nothing. Mutation: owner's figures replace the contract's.
- `integration/a08d-launch-limits.test.ts` (1, real bubblewrap, composed by `startController`, a real worker process): strict refuses (disk total) with a blocker and `environment` on the record; with best effort on, a process taking 600 MB under a 256 MB environment limit is ended by the system and one taking 100 MB finishes; an environment asking 4 GB under the owner's 1 GB is cut to 1 GB (recorded as `capped`) and a process taking 1.5 GB is ended, one taking 300 MB finishes. Mutations: contract not sealed; host ignores the contract; environment not merged into the owner's record; host report not noted.

**Not done**
- No way for the owner to set an environment's limits by chat or API: `environment.change` has no operation and no chat command (A08's service is reached only from code and A09's maintenance requests, which cover packages, skills, mounts and settings but not limits). This part needs no new setting (the owner's `workers.limits.*` are the installation maximums and are already chat-controlled and described to the interpreter), so the interpreter prompt and op table are unchanged; an owner control for an environment's own limits is a follow-up (A08e) and must come with its chat command and prompt entry.
- Running attempts keep the limits they started with (as H12k). A restarted or moved attempt keeps its pinned environment revision but reads the installation's figures again at its new launch, so an owner's tighter setting applies to it and a looser one is still cut by the environment.
- The status view shows an environment's limits; the attempt's `launchLimits` is on the dispatcher record and the owner's `workers.limits.enforced`, but no status-ask kind prints "what did attempt X run under" in words yet.
- The check-run sandbox (W05) takes the contract's figures too; a check's time limit is the smaller of its own timeout and the launch's `wallTimeMs` (review correction: the earlier line said the check's own timeout alone applied).
- `wallTimeMs` is enforced per process launch (the launcher's time limit locally, the `wall-time` requirement on a remote worker), not per attempt: a relaunch of the same attempt (recovery, a recipe change, a resume) gets the full figure again. The attempt's own end (`expiresAt`, the dispatcher's attempt time) still bounds the whole attempt.
- Disk stays a per-file cap (`partial`) on Linux, so every manifest (they all state `diskMb`) is refused in strict mode unless best effort is on: that is the launcher's recorded behaviour from A08b made visible, not new; see the ASSUMPTION below.

**ASSUMPTION:** `requireEnforced` is the owner's existing best-effort setting (strict by default), not a new per-agent or per-environment switch: it is already installation-wide, chat-controlled and documented, and a second place to decide the same thing would be a way for the two to disagree.
**ASSUMPTION:** the installation's figures are maximums, not floors: where they are lower than an environment's, they win; where an environment is lower, it wins. This is the reading of "capped by the owner's configured maximums and installation defaults; limits only ever tighten".
**ASSUMPTION:** a manifest made before this change has no `wallTimeMs` and is left exactly as stored (no migration, no new digest); "missing = installation default" is applied at the launch.
**ASSUMPTION:** a figure that is valid in a manifest but outside what one launch can be given is refused at the launch with its unit and bounds rather than clamped, because a clamped figure is a limit nobody asked for.
**ASSUMPTION:** the refusal of a launch whose limits cannot be worked out ends the attempt `failed` without readmission and opens the ordinary `dispatch_blocked` blocker (the owner resolves it by fixing the setting or the environment); no new blocker type.

**A08d review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-11)**
- Checked, no change: min() over every bad shape on both sides (null, undefined, 0, negative, NaN, strings, fractions, Infinity, above the bounds, `__proto__` and other unknown names, a non-object), units (ms, megabytes) consistent between the manifest, the owner's setting, the host and the remote contract (`BOUNDS` equal to `LOCAL_WORKER_LIMIT_BOUNDS`); a stored manifest without `wallTimeMs` keeps its digest and `resume` compares stored digests only (nothing recomputes one), so old revisions verify on every backend; the pin is idempotent per attempt, so a replay reads the same revision; the installation figure is read once before the seal and the host reads the owner's again and takes the smaller, so a change in between can only tighten; a remote host re-seals with the smaller of both and the placement's `checkContract` re-checks the digest; the remote launch record's `requested` is the controller-sealed contract and every worker-reported string is clipped; an agent cannot change or drop `limits` (A08's owner-only rule, tested), and the A09 applier copies the stored limits unchanged; the refusal is the existing host-refusal path (failed, no readmission, one blocker; a test now runs three more passes and sees no new start and the same blocker).
- Fixed in the notes: the check-run wall time line, and that wall time is per launch, not per attempt.
- Mutations of the review (each made alone on the built files, a test then failed, then restored): the pinned manifest not read at the launch; `noteLaunch` replacing the dispatcher's figures with the host's; the host's lower bound for `wallTimeMs` lowered to 1 ms.

## U11f (owner-marked critical path, Needs-you ranking, blocked-critical-path Urgent) (2026-11-11)

The largest part of U11d that was left: the owner-marked critical path, the ranking of the Needs-you items by it, and the Urgent trigger when a decision that waits for the owner holds up a task on the path. Branch `card14-u11f`, on main `7a88cfc5`.

**Done**
- **The marks (`critical/critical-path.ts`, `CriticalPathService`).** One record (`critical-path/installation`) holds up to 100 marks, each `{ kind, id, markedAt }` with `kind` `task` (that task only), `goal` (a task the owner wants delivered: it and everything it waits for through the active dependency records, within its project, bounded to 2000 tasks, not walking through a finished prerequisite) or `project` (every open task of the project). `mark` is owner only (an agent, a host, a service and a task credential are `forbidden`), takes IDs only and never reads a title, needs the task or project to exist when marking (unmarking needs nothing), is replay safe (command ID scoped to the caller, written every time so a repeat answers the first time), refuses unknown fields, kinds and IDs, a project named beside a task that is not the task's own, and the 101st mark. `list` is owner only. Marks are read as the owner wrote them; a damaged record reads as no marks.
- **State API and chat.** `critical.mark` (command) and `critical.list` (query), neither callable from a task credential. Chat: `critical.mark` is in `CHAT_OPS`, always a proposal ("the critical path decides what comes first for you and what pages you, so a change to it is shown first"), the task is named by `taskTitle` and the project by `projectName` as for every operation, `kind` is exempt from the "must be in your words" check like `to` and `level` (an enumeration, not a name), and the interpreter prompt (built from the one operation table plus one added paragraph) describes marking, the three kinds, taking a mark off, the Urgent minutes and the status view. `notifications.configure` takes `criticalBlockedAfterMinutes` (below), also in the prompt's argument text and tested through the chat.
- **Status view.** New status kind `critical_path` (owner only; reached by `status.ask` and so by chat): each mark with the title as the record shows it (quoted, and shown only; nothing is decided by it), whether it is open, finished or gone, and the first 10 waiting decisions that hold the path up, in the Needs-you order.
- **Needs-you ranking (`StatusService.needsYou`).** Critical-path-holding first (the line starts "On the critical path you marked: "), then how many other open tasks wait for the item (the existing rule), then the oldest, then the kind (approval, question, meeting decision, held resume, blocker), then the ID, so the order is the same every time. The result gains `critical` (how many, present when anything is marked). Bounded as before (50 per source, 250 items, limit at most 50); the marks, each task and each project's dependency records are read once per request; with nothing marked, or a failing source, the old order is unchanged.
- **Digest order.** In the digest the items that hold up the path come first (marked " [holds up the critical path]" in the text, which holds IDs and the controller-built label only), then the oldest, then the kind. Bounded to the 1000-item open limit; with nothing marked no extra read is made.
- **Urgent trigger (`UrgentWatch.#criticalCheck`, `NotificationService.raiseCritical/lowerCritical`).** A blocker, review request or owner question that waits for the owner and is about a task on the path is raised to Urgent after `criticalBlockedAfterMinutes` (default 5, whole minutes 1 to 10080, `null` off and puts what it raised back, owner only, with `expectedRevision`, chat-settable). The wait counts from the later of the item's creation and the first sweep that saw it on the path (memory only; a restart delays, never fires early), so marking a task that has long been waiting does not page in the same sweep. Sent at once, also in quiet hours unless `urgentInterruptsQuietHours` is false (then queued and released at their end), inside the hourly Urgent allowance and the gap, counted per PROJECT (`critical|<project>`, the stopped-work lesson of the U11d review): many decisions an agent opens in one project page the owner once per gap, the rest are Urgent in the inbox only, 20 raises per sweep, 100 items examined per sweep from a cursor. The text sent is `URGENT, the critical path is blocked in project <id> by <kind>: <controller-built label>` (IDs and the blocker type only; no title, summary or detail). **Put-back** is silent and has hysteresis: an item that no longer holds the path up (unmarked, task finished, task moved) is put back to Needs you only after it has been seen clear for the same number of minutes, and any sweep that sees it on the path again starts the count over, so a mark taken off and put back, or a flickering blocker, does not page twice. One trigger per decision: an item the stopped-work watch raised is not raised again by this one, one this watch raised is left alone by the stopped-work watch and `lowerStopped`/`lowerCritical` each take off only their own mark. A raised item survives a restart (the state is on the item). Stand-up agendas list it first as "Urgent, holds up the critical path: ...".
- **Agents cannot set, rank, manufacture or suppress.** Only `mark` (owner only) writes marks; criticality and rank are computed from the marks and record IDs and never from a title, summary or detail (tests plant "CRITICAL PATH goal urgent project" as a title). An agent that opens 25 decisions on a task of a marked project causes one message per gap and at most 20 inbox raises a sweep. An agent cannot hide a critical decision (it cannot resolve an owner blocker or answer the owner's question; finishing or cancelling the task is a legitimate end of the wait).
- **Tests (four backends unless noted; fail before, pass after).** `critical/critical-path.test.ts` (28): who may call, kinds and replacement, validation and bounds (the 100 marks), replay and conflict, what is on the path (task, project, goal chain, finished tasks, the walk stopping at a finished prerequisite, foreign project), titles that say "critical", a failing dependency source. `notifications/critical-trigger.test.ts` (40): the full episode with onset delay, once-only message with IDs only, restart, hysteresis and flicker, silent put-back, re-raise inside the gap; kinds of path; the 25-decision burst (20 raises a sweep, one message, no summary); the hourly allowance with three projects; the owner's minutes, `null`, bad numbers and a non-owner; quiet hours both ways; answered / finished / failing source; one trigger per decision; digest order and the failing source. `status/status.test.ts` (+2 suites, 8 cases): ranking with and without marks and with a failing source, the `critical_path` view and who may ask. `chat/critical-path.test.ts` (13): free words, shown first, nothing before agreeing, goal, project, take off, a wrong or unknown name or kind or quoted text marks nothing, an agent with every grant is `forbidden` through the API and the chat, the prompt text. `api/start-critical-path.test.ts` (1, SQLite, through the running controller): mark by the API, Urgent after the minutes, one message with the project and blocker IDs and no title, ranked first, hysteresis, silent put-back, bad number refused. `chat/chat.test.ts`: the minutes are set and turned off in free words.
- **Mutations killed (each made alone on the built files, one test then failed, then restored):** owner guard of `mark`; owner guard of `list`; target must exist; the 100-mark bound; project beside a task must be the task's own; project marks; goal chain; finished tasks not on the path; the walk not passing a finished prerequisite; onset delay; hysteresis; flicker resets the count; put-back; 20 raises a sweep; per-record instead of per-project gap key; release key after quiet hours; `lower` taking only its own mark; digest order; quiet-hours switch; hourly limit and gap; setting validation; Needs-you ranking; its label. Three more mutations SURVIVE and are equivalent, not test gaps: removing the critical watch's skip of stopped items, the stopped-work watch's skip of critical items, and the `criticalAt` clause in the raise guard. Each is a second layer behind the rule that a trigger refuses an item that is already Urgent and the two flags being disjoint, so no behavior differs; they stay as defense in depth.

**Not done**
1. The per-agent half of "nothing else to do" (H12's per-agent view of available work) is still not built; the stopped-work trigger is per project.
2. Answering each Needs-you item in place from the view, the controller-down watchdog, deferred meeting items from M03 in the view, the denial hook from the other refusal points and the remaining security hooks stay in U11d.
3. The inbox listing (`notification.inbox`, used by the stand-up agenda) is not re-sorted by the path; the stand-up agenda lists a raised item first because it is Urgent. A decision that holds the path up for less than the owner's minutes is first in the digest and the Needs-you view but not Urgent.
4. Item-to-task is read from the record each time (blocker subject, question task, review task); a maintenance item or a meeting decision names no task here and is never critical. Meeting decisions and held resumes in the Needs-you view are ranked by their task when they have one.
5. The onset and put-back clocks are in memory; a restart only delays them. Criticality of a goal's chain depends on dependency records agents can write within their project: an agent can put its own task into a marked goal's chain, which costs at most one message per project per gap.
6. No run against a real model has checked that natural wording picks `critical.mark` and its kinds (card U03b); only scripted interpreter turns were tested.

- ASSUMPTION: `task` marks one task, `goal` also marks what it waits for, `project` marks all its tasks. The card says "owner-marked critical tasks" and "the goal-based critical path computed from the task dependency records"; a goal is a task the owner names as the thing to deliver, which needs no new entity. A decision about a prerequisite of a plain marked task is not on the path (the owner marks the goal when they want that); this also keeps agent-written dependency records from widening a plain mark.
- ASSUMPTION: marking and unmarking are always shown first in chat (mode `propose`), because they decide what pages the owner; the owner agrees in their own words.
- ASSUMPTION: the default is 5 minutes (not immediate and not off), the card's "immediate interruption for a blocked critical path" with a short debounce so a blocker opened and resolved in moments is not paged, and the same number is the hysteresis for putting back; `null` turns it off.

- ASSUMPTION: the critical-path message is one event per project per gap (the stopped-work rule), not one per decision, and shares the hourly allowance with every other Urgent trigger.

**U11f review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-11)**
- Fixed: two marks at the same moment on a fresh installation both tried to create the marks record, and the loser was refused as `command_conflict` ("this command ID was used by something else"), so the owner's mark was lost with a misleading error (reference store and both SQLite backends; PostgreSQL happened to serialize).
