**K06d, done.**
- The chat `retention` status kind now answers from the same service as `retention.status` (read-only, owner only: any non-owner, or a refusal from the service, reads as "not offered"). After the values in force it tells: the data disk's free room and share, the reserve (not set, set aside and below or above the free room, in use, or too little room to set aside), each quota class that is set with its limit, warning percent, how many scopes hold how much in all and the three biggest, every scope at or over the warning level (a project cited as the project, an agent by the same reference its quota notice uses) with a line for the ones not shown (10 shown), the backups (count, how many cannot be trusted, the daily and weekly counts, the latest by name and time), the last five deletions (record ID, status, time, how many derived items went with it) and the last five retention runs (by you or automatic, how many records, backups and incidents). Counts and IDs only: the reason an owner typed for a deletion, a note, a record's text and a deletion's backup note are never repeated. Every sentence cites a record (the deletion, the run, the backup, the project, or `retention-settings` for the figures that are no record of their own: the disk and the quota limits).
- The interpreter prompt lists the kind from the one `STATUS_KINDS` table; its text names the questions it answers (how much room is left, which quotas are near their limit, which backups are kept, what retention deleted lately). Tests drive five free-word questions through the chat to the same kind. The `status.ask` operation table says the same. A kind with an argument is refused (it takes none), so a model that invents one gets a refusal, not a guess.
- The quota notice's "See retention.status." now has a chat answer: the owner can ask in words.
- Mutations (each made alone, each failed a test, restored): owner guard removed from the view; deletions list unbounded; stored text not quoted; the dep not wired to the running service; an agent cited by its raw ID; the latest backup taken as the oldest (this one survived the first test, which had a single backup, and the running-controller test now makes a second backup two days later).

**K06d, not done.**
- The disk and quota figures are the controller's own numbers: the disk is the data directory's file system, the quota use is the meter's count of stored record bytes (`quotaUsagePartial` says when the counting was cut). A backup directory on another disk is not reported.
- The acceptance text says "which backups are kept"; the view tells the count and the latest, not a list of every backup (a list of backup names would be unbounded and gives the owner nothing to act on in chat). **ASSUMPTION:** count plus latest satisfies "which backups are kept"; a per-backup list is a small addition if the owner wants one.
- The view reads the whole of `retention.status`, including the per-kind `growth` counts, which are not told in chat (K06d's earlier slice put them in the API only). **ASSUMPTION:** the growth counts stay out of the chat answer; they are not in the card's list.

**K06d acceptance: met** for the card text as written (room, quotas near their limit, backups, recent deletions, owner only, lines citing records, interpreter prompt), within the two assumptions above.

**L02e, done in this slice.**
- *Per-request cumulative cleanup total.* A `wait` on a blocked preparation restarts the request's cleanup budget window (`spent` goes to 0); until now the earlier windows' figure was lost. The request now keeps `spentBefore` (earlier windows, added with `addCapped`, which holds a sum at the largest safe whole number and counts a negative, fractional or NaN figure as nothing) and `cleanupSpend` returns `cumulativeSpent` = earlier windows plus this one. The stop-cleanup chat view adds one line when earlier windows counted something ("Over all its cleanup budget windows (earlier ones counted X) this request has counted Y in total."); with one window, an older record, or an unreadable figure it says nothing extra. The ending's own cost and the per-attempt charges are not part of this total (they are billed per attempt and shown in the attempt lines).
- *The remote worker's own process report.* New protocol route `POST /worker/attempts/{id}/processes` with `{ placement, seq, final, processes: [{ ref, kind: process|child, state: running|uncooperative|unknown }] }`. Fences as for every other message about the attempt: the host's session, the host that holds the placement and its number (an older holder or placement is `fenced`, another host's attempt is `not_found` and counts as a misused credential), the worker session that accepted it (a newer session that has not re-accepted is `fenced`). It is also taken after the attempt completed or ended, since the worker's last word is the point; only a placement that was never accepted, or that moved on, is refused. Shape: exact fields (`onlyKnown`), at most 50 entries, a body of at most 16 KB, a reference of at most 480 characters in, redacted then cut to 120, control and direction characters replaced, a repeat an entry once; `seq` from 1 and rising: the same report again is the same answer, an older one is ignored (`kept: false`), another report under a used number is `payload_changed`, nothing follows a final report. The report is stored on the placement and belongs to the placement number it names; a move or a second placement starts without one.
  - Stop reads it (`RemoteWorkerHost.localWork`): a live placement with no report is one unknown item as before; with a report, the entries as the worker gave them; a placement that is over with a final report shows what that report lists (normally nothing, so a Stop is clean on the worker's word); over with only a non-final report, those entries as unknown (nobody said they are gone); over and never reported, nothing as before.
  - The worker's side (`RemoteOfferRunner`) asks its host (`localWork`) in its control loop and sends a report when the list changed, and once more as final after the sandbox was stopped. A host that cannot look reports nothing; a failed look or send is a trouble the log shows, not the end of the attempt; a fenced answer stops the sandbox. More than 50 processes are cut with a last entry saying how many are not listed.
- Mutations (21 alone, all failed a test, restored): earlier window dropped on wait; the cap removed; the view line always shown; placement fence removed; session fence removed; a move keeping the old report; the host reading another placement's report; an over placement's non-final report read as clean; a sequence allowed to go back; references not redacted; an unknown field allowed; the list unbounded; the body unbounded; the runner never sending final; the runner sending every look. Two survived the first tests (the session fence, the host's own placement check) and now have their own tests.

**L02e, not done (L02e stays open).**
- A remote worker still cannot be made to kill what it holds: Force Stop's `endLocalWork` exists only on the local worker, so a remote worker's uncooperative process is reported but ended only by the worker's own stop. **ASSUMPTION:** adding a Force-Stop control message to the protocol is a separate slice (it changes what a worker is told, not what it reports).
- A live report is as old as the worker's last change: the worker looks every control-loop turn (500 ms), but between looks a process may start. The view says what the worker last reported; it does not say how old. **ASSUMPTION:** that gap is acceptable for now: a Stop read while the attempt is live is the worker's last report, and a look after the worker has stopped the sandbox shows its final one; nothing makes the controller wait for the final report.
- The remote worker reports no cleanup cost (`costs` is still empty in `localWork`), so a remote Stop's charge is not billed from the worker's own figures.
- An attempt moved to another host: the old host's report goes with the old placement; whether the old host cleaned up is not asked.
- The process report is not required to come after the dispatch contract was confirmed (it changes nothing the attempt counts). The deployed `scripts/remote-worker.mjs` was not run against a real controller in this slice (no bubblewrap run here); the runner and the transport are tested, and the program passes the runner the `LocalWorker`.
- Records of a request whose window was restarted before this build keep only their latest window: the earlier figure was never kept, so their cumulative total equals the window.
- The wider walk is still tested against the dispatcher fakes rather than a live swarm (the earlier note on L02e's first slice).

**L02e acceptance: not fully met.** The card text's acceptance (a Stop of an agent ends its tasks' swarm children, 2000 settled entries do not starve the sweep, a task stopped through its agent shows that Stop's cleanup, mutation check recorded) was met by earlier slices; this slice closes two of the three items the last note listed as left (the cumulative total and the remote worker's report), with the limits above. It stays open for the items in "not done".

**Review (clean-context, Claude agent, 2026-11-11).** Merged main eaf0e20e first (notes kept both sides; `api-v1.md` regenerated after the build, unchanged).
- Fixed, the runner reused a report's number after a lost answer: `seq` was raised only when the controller answered, so a report that arrived but whose answer was lost was sent again under the same number with whatever the sandbox listed by then. The controller answered `payload_changed` to that and to every later report, the final one too, so Stop read the attempt's last list as unknown for good. The number is now taken before the report is sent (gaps are allowed; the controller only needs it to rise). The final report is tried three times under one number (same report, same answer) unless it is fenced or refused. Test: `a report whose answer was lost ...` (fails before the fix: 36 refused reports and a lost final).
- Fixed, a restarted worker program could never report again: a re-accept in a newer session keeps the placement and its report, and the new program's runner counts from 1, so its reports read as old (or `payload_changed`) and its final word was lost. A report's sequence now belongs to the session that sent it (`processReport.sessionId`): a newer session that has taken the attempt up again starts its own count, and within one session the number still only rises. The older session stays fenced. Test: `a worker that took the attempt up again in a newer session ...` (four backends).
- Fixed, a report could not fit the body limit: the runner sent up to 50 references of up to 480 characters (so the controller could redact before cutting), but the route takes 16 KB, so 50 ordinary long command lines were refused whole (413), on every look and at the end. The runner now redacts each reference while it is whole, cleans it and cuts it to 120 characters itself (`remote/process-ref.ts`, `cleanProcessRef`, the same function the controller applies again), then shortens the list until the body fits, with a last entry saying how many are not listed. No part of a credential goes over the wire. Test: `a report always fits the controller's body limit ...`.
- Fixed, defensive: a stored reference kept C1 controls, LRM/RLM/ALM, line and paragraph separators and the BOM, and a cut at 120 UTF-16 units could leave half a pair. It now replaces every C0/C1 control, every `\p{Cf}` character, U+2028/2029 and lone surrogates, and cuts on whole characters. The chat already escaped these through `shown`; this is about the stored and API form.
- Decided, a final report taken on the worker's word: kept. The controller cannot look into a remote machine, and before L02e a placement that was over already read as holding nothing without any word at all, so a final report saying "nothing left" gives a hostile worker nothing it did not already have, while a final report that lists something, or a non-final one never confirmed, now shows. A live placement whose report lists nothing reads as nothing, the same as a local sandbox (the running worker process is the attempt itself; Stop ends it through the dispatcher, not through this list). A host the controller has lost contact with cannot report: its session is refused, and a newer session must take the attempt up again first. A new placement (a move, a re-offer) starts without a report.
- Checked, no change: the retention view is owner-only twice (the view refuses any non-owner principal; task credentials are always `kind: "agent"`; `retention.status` refuses too). It shows counts and record IDs only (no deletion reason, no record text). Every list is bounded (10 near-quota scopes, 5 deletions, 5 runs, 3 biggest per class) and every stored string goes through `shown`. A statfs failure reads as "not known". Deletions and runs are newest first by record time with ties broken by ID, and the latest backup is picked by time with ties by name. "Cannot be trusted" means the manifest disagrees with the folder name, which retention never deletes and the nightly rule never counts. `spentBefore`: a replayed or repeated `wait` cannot add twice (the update is guarded on the `blocked` phase and the record revision, and a second choice on a request that is no longer blocked is refused). An older record without the field reads as a total equal to its window. The `processes` route takes no `Idempotency-Key`: the sequence is its idempotency (the same number and figures give the same answer).
- Small, left: "N older deletion(s) are not listed" counts within the 20 the service reads, so past 20 it understates.
- **L02e, what precisely stays open.** The card's deliverable items are all delivered now. Its acceptance clauses (an agent's Stop ends swarm children, 2000 settled entries do not starve the sweep, a task stopped through its agent shows that cleanup) were met by earlier slices. Still open: (1) "mutation check recorded" for part 3's code (the confirmation of a local worker's leftover processes and the reach of a Stop made after the attempt finished). That slice recorded none, and this slice's 21 plus the review's 3 cover only the cumulative total and the remote report. (2) The items under "L02e, not done" above: no remote Force-Stop kill, no remote cleanup cost, no question to an old host after a move, a live report as old as the last control-loop look, and the deployed `scripts/remote-worker.mjs` not run against a real controller.
- Own mutations (each made alone, each failed the named test, then restored): `seq` raised only after an answer (the lost-answer test and the changed flaky assertion); the sequence chain not scoped to the session (the newer-session test, four backends); the runner's body fit removed (the body-limit test).

## CI platform repair: the exhaustive run that was green on Linux and red on macOS and Windows (Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

Exhaustive run 43055560857 (commit 6a530183, `exhaustive.yml`) passed on Linux and failed on macOS (shards 1 and 2) and Windows (shards 1, 2 and 3). The last run green on all three systems was 2cca8b5d; almost every failing test file was added after it (A05b follow-up, K01b, K02a, K02 heartbeat, K02 service units, U14, L05e, Y02, production wiring) and had never run on macOS or Windows. This is a repair without a card. It was done on Linux only: nothing below has run on a real Mac or Windows machine yet, so every "unverified" line waits for the next exhaustive run.

The rule followed: a test that assumed Linux or POSIX was made portable, or skipped on a platform only where the product itself says the feature does not exist there (with the reason in the skip). No assertion was weakened on Linux. Where the logs showed the product doing something wrong on that platform, the product was fixed.

**Product fixes (real bugs on macOS or Windows)**

1. **A05b, macOS: a file version could be read from outside the checkout** (`target-versions.test.ts`, "a directory on the way swapped for a link ..."; failed on both macOS shard-2 jobs). The reading opens only the last name without following a link. On Linux it then asks the kernel where the open file really is (`/proc/self/fd`). Elsewhere it asked for the real path again after the open, but a swap that is undone by then cannot be seen that way: the test's swapper hit that window and the hash of the outside file came back. Fix: on macOS the file is opened with `O_NOFOLLOW_ANY` (macOS 11 and later; value 0x20000000 from `<sys/fcntl.h>`, which Node does not name). With it, the open itself fails if any name on the path is a link at that moment, decided in the same kernel lookup. The real-path check stays as a second layer. Linux is unchanged. Unverified: needs the macOS run. ASSUMPTION: Node 22 and 24 need macOS 11 or later, so the flag is always understood. If an older kernel ignored it, the reading would be exactly as before, no worse.
2. **A05b, all systems: a git that cannot be started gave a plain error, not a `TargetVersionError`** (seen on Windows as `spawn EFTYPE`: `execFile` throws at once instead of calling back). The call was still refused, because the dispatcher refuses on any error, but the module's own contract says every failure is a `TargetVersionError`. Fix: that throw is caught and becomes `unreadable` ("git could not be started"). Test on Linux: a git name with a NUL character, which Node refuses before it starts anything (mutation: without the catch the test fails).
3. **K01b, Windows: `backup encryption-add-passcode` and `encryption-rotate` always failed with "the file system said EPERM"** (`encryption-manage.test.ts`, both CLI tests, Windows shard 2). `syncFile` in `backup/cli.ts` opened the new keyring file read-only and flushed it. On Windows a flush (`FlushFileBuffers`) needs a handle with write access, and the access-denied error reads as EPERM in Node. `encryption-setup` passed because it flushes through the handle it wrote with. Fix: on Windows `syncFile` opens the file for reading and writing (nothing is written through it); elsewhere it stays read-only, so there is no change on POSIX, even for a keyring the owner made read-only. Unverified: the two Windows CLI tests are the regression test, and no Linux test can show it.
4. **K02a, Windows (likely): a controller's confirmation could be lost to the watchdog's read** (`launcher.ts` `writeAtomic`). On Windows a rename over a file that another process has open at that moment fails (EPERM, EACCES, EBUSY). The launcher's watchdog and the controller read and write `launcher-state.json` while both run (the tests poll every 10 ms), and the controller confirms its start once. A lost confirmation means a healthy start is judged failed when the window ends. Fix: `renameReplacing` retries those three errors on Windows only, 10 tries with growing pauses, about 0.45 s in all; any other error, and every error on other systems, fails at once as before. Test (all systems, injected rename): retried and bounded on win32, never retried elsewhere, the real rename still works (mutation: with one try the test fails). This is the best explanation of the node-24 heartbeat failures below, but it is an inference from the logs, not a proven cause.

**Test fixes (the test assumed Linux or POSIX)**

- `scripts/nimblenewt-controller.test.mjs`, Windows, 8 tests. The test installation pinned the `protected-file` secret store, which the product refuses on Windows ("needs POSIX permissions; use the Windows DPAPI store"). The test now chooses the file-backed store this host can use: DPAPI-protected files under `<data>/secrets` on Windows (the store `chooseSecretStore` itself picks there, and its contract tests already run on Windows CI), `protected-file` elsewhere. Two settings tests compared resolved paths with POSIX text ("/r"). `controllerSettings` resolves them, which gives `D:\r` on Windows, so the tests now expect `resolve("/r")`; that is the same text on POSIX. Unverified: the real controller start with the DPAPI store on Windows (it calls PowerShell) has never run in this file.
- Same file, macOS, the A09b environments test. Under `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` it required the local worker host to start, but that host says it is Linux only (`local-host.mjs`, bubblewrap). The requirement now applies on Linux only. Off Linux the test checks that the log gives that reason. Linux is unchanged.
- `scripts/remote-host.test.mjs`, macOS and Windows, 3 tests. They start the remote worker host, which refuses anywhere but Linux (`remote-host.mjs`, bubblewrap), before it uses any stand-in. They are now skipped off Linux with that reason. A new test, run only off Linux, checks the refusal and that nothing was loaded first. Windows, the token-file test: the product deliberately does not judge POSIX permission bits on Windows (every file reads as mode 0o666 there), so the "others can read it" refusal is checked on POSIX only. Simulated with `process.platform` stubbed to darwin and win32: the skips, the new test and the token test behave as intended.
- `scripts/nimblenewt-service.test.mjs`, Windows, 3 tests. A Linux unit was printed with the default node and launcher, which are this machine's: drive paths on Windows, which a Linux unit rightly refuses (and it checks node before root, so the refusal rows saw the wrong error). The Linux-unit cases now name POSIX node and launcher paths. The "defaults are this machine's" check runs as a Windows unit on Windows and as a Linux unit elsewhere (unchanged on Linux). Unverified: the Windows-unit branch has not run.
- `scripts/nimblenewt.test.mjs`, Windows, init: the config file's "owner-only" mode check is POSIX only (no permission bits on Windows).
- `scripts/y02-checkpoint.test.mjs`, Windows, the producer test: it took a folder name with `cwd.split("/")`, and the product's `join` gives backslashes there. It now uses `basename`.
- `supervisor.test.ts`, Windows, 7 tests. Three test the POSIX process-group ladder (a SIGTERM ignored, group members left after the leader, a crashed leader's group). Windows has no process groups and no SIGTERM a process can catch, and the supervisor documents that it ends the tree with `taskkill /T /F` and drains nothing (`leftovers` is POSIX only). These three are skipped on Windows with that reason. The fixtures also start POSIX `sleep`. The lock test's socket-file half listens on a plain file path, which Windows cannot do (`lockRoot` takes a named pipe there whatever `abstract` says). Its holder never answered, the file's event loop emptied, and on node 22 every later test was cancelled with 0 ms. That half now runs off Windows only; the named-pipe half runs everywhere. In the heartbeat hang test, the "the SIGTERM handler exited 0" check is POSIX only, because on Windows taskkill ends the process with code 1, which is still no stop on purpose. The cleanup's `rmSync` now retries (a just-killed child can hold its release folder on Windows for a moment). Unverified: "beats normally / slowly / never" and "always hangs / never beats" (node 24, Windows) timed out with only a `started` event, and every world in them looked like a start that was never confirmed. Product fix 4 is the likely cause. If they still fail, they need a Windows machine.
- `target-versions.test.ts`, Windows, 4 tests. The stand-in git programs are `#!/bin/sh` scripts, which Windows cannot start. The cap test, and the fake-git half of the configuration test, are skipped on Windows (the configuration half and "git missing" still run there). The configuration test wrote a Windows path into `.git/config`, and Git reads its backslashes as escapes, so the whole file failed to parse; the path is now written with forward slashes. "Only relative to the process" cannot be spelled on Windows when the temporary folder is on another drive than the current directory (`relative()` gives the absolute path), so that one assertion runs only when the relative spelling exists; on Linux it always does. Windows has no named pipes in the file system, so the pipe case is POSIX only; the directory, cap, sparse and 8 MiB cases still run there. Unverified: the 50 GiB sparse file on NTFS has not been seen to work on Windows (the test never got that far).

**Not explained / not done**

- The Windows node-22 shard-2 job was not in the list of failing jobs, yet the A05b test fixes above are deterministic on Windows. Its log was not read here, so either it failed too or something there differs. Not investigated.
- Nothing here makes a Mac or Windows machine part of the local check: these fixes are proven only by the next exhaustive run.

## Credential redaction follow-up (U09b / W13 limits): one folded matching view and one cleaning pipeline (Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

Closes the limits written down at U09b ("credential shapes only (a bare hex or base64 key, or one split over two blocks other than a PEM key, is not caught)") and the W13 review's "redact again after stripping".

**Done**

- **One scanner** (`packages/controller/src/security/secret-scan.ts`, `scanSecrets`). `redactText` and `findCredentialShapes` both use it, so what is redacted and what a note or chat message refuses are the same. It matches through a folded view of the text: each code point NFKC-folded (fullwidth `ｇｈｐ＿`, ligatures), every dash a hyphen, and invisible characters left out (`isHidden`: C0/C1 controls except tab and line breaks, zero-width, bidi, soft hyphen, tags, variation selectors, fillers, any `\p{Cf}`, half surrogate pairs). Each unit of the view remembers which original code point it came from, so a match is redacted in the ORIGINAL text (the invisible characters inside it go too) and text with no secret keeps every character it had (a fullwidth word, a bidi mark in Arabic, a decomposed accent).
- What the scan finds: every `CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS` shape. The key prefixes `sk-`, `ghp_`/`gh?_`, `github_pat_`, `AKIA`, `xox`, `npm_` match in any letter case. Prefixed tokens and JWTs are looked for again in a second view where a line break between two token characters is removed, so a key wrapped or split over lines is found. The base64 lines just above a private key's END line with no BEGIN count as the rest of a key split over two blocks (orphan END) and are redacted. The END line itself stays, because it holds no secret and the job output store looks for it to know that a key block begun in an earlier report has ended (the T07b jobs tests found this, on all four backends). The thinking store still hides everything up to an orphan END, as before. A joined match is not used when the part before the line break is already a whole token of that shape and the next line's part is a plain word: `…sk-live-…1234` ending one line must not take the next line's `step` (found by the C07j hand-off cut test). Long high-entropy hex or base64 runs with no prefix are found too (below).
- **Lines are never joined.** A match that covers a line break is replaced line by line (`[redacted]` per line, the break kept), so the line counts `cutNote` relies on stay exact. A whole private key block written as such is still one mark, as before. `redactText` is idempotent (tested).
- **One cleaning pipeline** (`security/clean.ts`, `cleanUntrusted`). It has four ordered steps: redact, normalise, strip invisible characters (keeping line breaks or folding them to one line), redact again. The anchor block's `cleanText`/`datum` (and so `task.recall`, which pages over `cleanText`) and the thinking store's `cleanThinking` now use it instead of their own copies. The thinking store's own copy of the hidden-character list is gone; there is one list (`HIDDEN_RANGES`).
- Other entry points need no copy of their own, because they call `redactText`, which now does the folded matching: status `shown`/`quoted`, chat `refuseCredentials`/`redactForModel`, shared notes (`findCredentialShapes`), and every log, error and stored-text helper that calls `redactText`. `cutNote` now also scans the joined note for the one-token shapes and keys (`JOINABLE`, private key block), so a token split over two entries is redacted in both; `token:` ending one line is still not taken together with the next line (C07p review test).
- **The high-entropy rule** (`highEntropy`), decided from evidence. A survey of every place the product generates hex or base64 (ids.ts, digests, cursors, keys) found that bare unlabelled hex of 24, 32, 40 and 64 characters is shown legitimately all over: artifact blob and manifest digests in error text, git SHAs (40, or 64 in SHA-256 repositories), signing key IDs, release file digests, and the workspace bridge's 32-hex change IDs that agents see. Sealed cursors are `~` plus base64url. Derived IDs are `prefix-` plus 20 base32 characters, and cache keys are `nn-` plus 27. The resulting rules:
  - A run is a maximal stretch of `[A-Za-z0-9+/_-]`, optionally ending in `=`, of 32 or more characters, not right after `~` (a cursor).
  - Pure hex (one case, with a digit and a letter) is redacted unless its length is exactly 32, 40, 64 or 128, the shapes the product shows. So 33-39, 41-63, 65-127 and over 128 are redacted.
  - Anything else must have an upper-case letter, a lower-case letter and a digit, at least 3.7 bits of entropy per character, and at least 25% of neighbouring characters of different classes.
  - Exempt: a digest label (`sha256-`, `sha512-` and the like, as in SRI integrity strings). Exempt: a path or a name made of words (three or more pieces between `/`, `_`, `-`, at least half of them words). Exempt: a code name that is at least 80% pronounceable words (`ThinkingCollectionBodyRevision2UpdatedAt`).
- ASSUMPTION (entropy threshold): 32 characters, 3.7 bits, 0.25 transitions, 0.8 words. These were chosen from measurements, not taken from a standard:
  - Random 24-byte keys (32 characters) never went below 3.90 bits or 0.26 transitions in 20,000 samples.
  - Random keys never reached 0.79 word coverage in 150,000 samples, while real code names had at least 0.81.
  - Across 100,000 random keys per shape, the rule misses about 0.1% of base64url keys and 0.03% of standard base64. On top of that, 0.4% of 32-character keys and 0.07% of 43-character keys are skipped because they lack a character class.
  - No non-test source file in any package and no document holds a run the rule takes (a test checks this).
- ASSUMPTION (output form): matching is always NFKC-folded, but the text itself keeps its characters by default (`form: "none"`). Turning agent-visible text into NFKC changed `e` + combining accent into `é` and broke the anchor's whole-character cuts and recall's page reconstruction (two existing tests), and the owner's view of a model's thinking should show its own characters. The thinking store keeps NFC as before; `form: "NFKC"` is available.
- Tests (`security/secret-scan.test.ts`):
  - A seeded property test (60 seeds by default, `NN_SECRET_PROPERTY_RUNS` to raise it; run at 400 here). It covers 9 secret families (GitHub, sk-, Anthropic, Slack, AWS, fine-grained, JWT, bare base64url key, bare 48-hex key), each disguised at random: zero-width/bidi/tag/soft-hyphen characters inside, fullwidth look-alikes, mixed-case prefix, split over lines. Each disguised key goes through 12 entry points: `redactText`, `findCredentialShapes`, chat `refuseCredentials`, `cleanUntrusted` (both modes), anchor `cleanText` and `datum`, `task.recall` (`composeRecall`), the thinking store, status `shown` and `quoted`, and `cutNote`. Each output is checked for any 12-character piece of the key still readable, and `redactText` additionally for idempotence, line count and the surrounding words.
  - Fixed cases for each disguise.
  - Private keys: a header hidden by a zero-width character or written with fullwidth dashes, a key split over two texts, orphan END through `redactText`, `findCredentialShapes`, the thinking store and `cutNote`.
  - Threshold boundaries, from 31 to 129 hex characters.
  - A no-false-positive test over 200 generated rounds of the product's own shapes: SHA-1/256/512 and MD5 hex, `sha256:`, `v1:sha256:`, `hmac-sha256:`, labelled IDs, UUIDs, ULIDs, derived IDs, `nn-` keys, `~` cursors, SRI digests, dates, paths, URLs, CJK and Arabic text, a decomposed accent. Each goes through `redactText`, `findCredentialShapes`, chat and the anchor.
  - A scan of the repository's own non-test sources and documents.
- Mutation checks (each applied to the build, the new test file and the security, thinking-store, anchor, recall and budget tests run, then restored). Killed: invisible characters kept in the view; no NFKC fold; no line-joined view; 40 hex removed from the shown shapes; prefixes case-sensitive; a span replaced whole across lines; the `~` cursor not exempt; no code-name rule; no orphan-END rule; no entropy rule; `cutNote` redacting entry by entry only; `findCredentialShapes` without the scan. Removing the pipeline's second redaction SURVIVED, and that is expected: because the first redaction already matches through a view with the invisible characters left out, stripping cannot create a match the first pass did not see. The second pass stays as cheap defence in depth.

**Not done**

- A 32-, 40-, 64- or 128-character hex secret with no label is not redacted: it has exactly the shape of the digests and SHAs the product shows. One written as `token: …`, `secret=…` and so on is still caught by the named-assignment shape.
- A key that is encoded (a second layer of base64, URL-encoding, spelled out, reversed) or cut into pieces below 32 characters each, other than the prefixed shapes split over lines, is not caught. Neither is a bare base64 key wrapped over lines into pieces shorter than 32.
- A key wrapped over lines whose first part is already a whole token and whose wrapped tail is a plain lower-case word (`abc`) keeps that tail visible (a few characters of the key).
- A sealed cursor is exempt by its `~`, so an agent could write `~` before a key to slip it past the entropy rule (not past the prefixed shapes). Redaction guards against accidents; it does not stop an agent determined to hide something.
- Code names with many acronyms and digits can fall below 0.8 word coverage and be redacted; the ed25519 public key (60 base64 characters) and signatures (88) are redacted wherever they pass through `redactText`. No place found shows them through it today.
- The anchor's and recall's own delimiters (`NN-ANCHOR`, `NN-RECALL`) are still neutralised only in ASCII; a fullwidth look-alike is left as written (unchanged from before; output stays unnormalised by the decision above).
- Other ad-hoc strippers (`toolbridge` `plainText`, `jobs/runs` `plainLine`, `scratch-cleanup` `safe`, and others) keep their own control-character handling for display; their redaction is the shared `redactText`, so they gain the folded matching, but they were not moved onto `cleanUntrusted`.

## Review leftovers: settings changes in one write (F04m third slice, "left as is (a)") and the meetings notice sink's command conflict (U03c/M03h close-out) (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-11)

### (1) A chat or API setting change is one write; nothing staged goes into force with it

**The problem.** The chat's policy edit of a setting (`chat/policy-edit.ts`) and the database transfer switches (`database.transfer.set`, `api/start.ts`) both staged the change and then applied the layer: two writes. A controller stopped between them left the change STAGED in the layer. No API, chat or MCP operation can discard a staged draft, so it stayed for good; the transfer switch refused every later change while another setting was staged ("apply or discard them first"); and the next chat edit of the same layer applied the WHOLE draft, so the left-over value went into force with the owner's new change without the owner seeing it.

**Fixed at the root (the first of the two ways the review named).**
- `ConfigurationService.change` (`configuration/configuration.ts`): sets and/or removes settings of one layer and puts them into force in ONE write, with the checks of `stage` and `apply` together (value valid, nothing wider than the layers above allow, nothing locked above, the whole combination fits). It never reads, applies, discards or alters the layer's draft. `expectedRevision`: the layer must be at it (0: the layer must not exist yet); left out, the layer as it is when written. A combination that does not fit is `invalid_command` ("the configuration check refused it: ...") and writes nothing, not even a failure record. A repeat of the same command ID is answered from the history entry it wrote (`replayed: true`, its `takesEffect`); the same command ID with other values is `command_conflict`. Rights as for `stage` (installation layer: owner only).
- The chat's setting edit calls it with the revision the owner was shown (0 when the layer did not exist yet); a refusal is still "... Nothing is in force." A resend of the owner's yes after a stop finishes the edit from the record and writes nothing again.
- `database.transfer.set` calls it once. The foreign-draft refusal and the left-over discard are gone: neither is needed, because no draft is ever applied with the switch. Side effect: two of the slice's earlier "Not done" items are closed: an API caller that leaves out `expectedRevision` and resends after a success now gets the replay (it got a stale stage), and a resend is no longer refused because someone staged something in between; and the review's finding (b) (`idempotency_conflict` after a discard) no longer applies, as nothing is discarded.
- `stage`, `apply` and `discard` stay in the service unchanged for embedders and tests; nothing in the composed controller calls them any more.

**Tests.**
- `api/start-config-stop.test.ts` (new; SQLite and an embedded PostgreSQL controller database): a real `startController` with a scripted interpreter. The owner asks in chat to shut the MCP door, is shown it, says yes; a fault beneath the storage guard (`unguarded(c.storage).applyOperation`) lets the first write to the installation settings commit and then fails every later write, as if the process died there. The controller is closed and started again on the same database: nothing is staged, the layer moved by exactly one revision and the setting is in force; the owner's resent yes reports the edit applied and writes no setting again. Then a draft as an older controller would have left (`database.transfer.restart` false, `grants.maxDays` 2) is staged: the next chat edit applies only its own key and the transfer switch is neither blocked nor carries the draft; the draft is still there, out of force. Last, the same stop inside a transfer switch change, then a restart: nothing staged, the switch in force.
- `configuration/configuration.test.ts` (all four backends): `change` in one write; a staged draft kept byte for byte and out of force; 0 for a new layer and stale when it exists; a stale revision writes nothing; a combination refusal writes nothing (no `lastFailure`, draft unchanged); replay from the record after the layer moved, and `command_conflict` for other values under the same ID; remove (only a key set here; not set and removed together); a bad value and a bad revision refused; a config writer refused on the installation layer and refused a task value wider than the installation's; the draft untouched at the end.
- `api/start-transfer.test.ts`: the two tests that asserted the old behaviour (a foreign draft refuses the switch; a left-over switch draft is discarded) now assert the new one (not refused, not applied, draft untouched) and the resend replay.

**Mutation checks** (each applied to the source, built, run, restored): (M1) the chat edit back to stage-then-apply: the composed test fails on both backends (a draft is left after the restart); (M2) the transfer switch back to its old code: the composed test fails on both backends (refused because of the left-over draft); (M3) `change` merging the draft's other keys into force: the composed test fails on both backends and the unit suite on all four.

**Not done.**
- A draft that an OLDER controller left in a layer (a stop between its two writes) stays in the record, out of force, and still no operation discards it. It no longer blocks anything and nothing applies it. ASSUMPTION: no owner "discard staged changes" operation is added, since nothing in the controller stages any more; the smallest change that closes the risk. If an embedder calls `ConfigurationService.apply` on such a layer it would apply that draft (that is what `apply` is for; its caller pins the revision it read).
- An edit that was half way through the old two steps at the moment of an upgrade is retried with `change` at the revision it was planned at, which the old stage moved on, so it ends `stale` and the owner asks again (honest, nothing applied unseen).
- The card's status in the task plan is not changed.

### (2) The meetings notice sink: a notice already filed counts as sent

**The problem (same shape as the stand-up sink fixed in the U03c/M03h close-out review).** `meetingNoticeSink` files the decision notice to an absent agent under the command ID `mtn:<occurrence>:<agent>`, but the text holds the acknowledgement time, which `endMeeting` works out again from the clock each time it runs (and a full requirement record folds entries together, changing tasks and decisions too). A notice filed just before the controller stopped (so `notifiedAt` was not written) was refiled under the same ID with another text: `command_conflict`, which the sink re-raised. The attendance service catches sink failures, so nothing else was blocked here, but the agent was reported "unnotified" although it had been told, stayed in the pending list (capped at 200), and was retried by every sweep; for a folded entry the sweep's text never matches, so it would wait for ever.
- **Fixed:** `command_conflict` from `noticeFromController` counts as sent (only this sink uses the `mtn:` IDs, so a conflict means this notice was filed). Every other failure still reaches the attendance service, which keeps the agent unnotified for the sweep, as before.
- **Tests:** `meetings/attendance.test.ts` (all four backends) with the real `AgentMessageService` and `meetingNoticeSink`: the notice is filed and the process "stops" before recording it; ten minutes later the end is repeated: the agent is reported notified, the inbox holds exactly one notice (the first text), `notifiedAt` is set and the sweep has nothing left. `meetings/notice-sink.test.ts`: conflict resolves; forbidden, unavailable, not_found and stale_revision still reject.
- **Mutation check (M4):** the sink without the conflict rule: the four-backend test fails on all four ("the agent was told; the conflict is not a failure").
- **The other sinks, checked:** `meetingWindowSink` (`mtw:<attendance>:<phase>`) can also meet a conflict (the "ends" warning names the first task returned to, which a retry can change), but `#warn` drops every failure by design and nothing is recorded or retried, so a conflict changes nothing; left as is. The stand-up sinks `improvementOutcomeSink` (key `<item>:<revision>:<agent>`), `agendaOutcomeSink` (`<item>:<revision>`) and `ownerQuestionSink` (the question's ID) key on an immutable item revision or record, so their text cannot change on retry: no shared pattern. `preparationNoticeSink` already had the fix. The wake sink files no notice (the host keys on the request). `reassign-warning.ts` swallows every failure.

**Runs** (worktree off main 39690cef; `npx tsc --build --force` clean, no stale dist tests, API docs regenerated after the build (the `database.transfer.set` summary no longer says it is refused while other changes are staged); `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, load average 60 to 85): `dist/configuration dist/chat dist/meetings dist/standups dist/work-end dist/api` 2,681 of 2,681 pass, 0 fail; after the summary text change `api.test` 58 of 58 and `start-transfer`/`start-config-stop` 20 of 20. Not run here: the rest of the controller (dispatch, domain, storage and the others; `stage`/`apply` are unchanged and only a new method was added to the configuration service), the other packages and integration (none of them calls the changed code).

**Round 2 (exhaustive run 43070175551 on bacc0288: Linux 6 of 6 green, Windows 2 of 6, macOS 0 to 1 of 6)**

- **Round 1's product fix 1 was wrong and is withdrawn: `O_NOFOLLOW_ANY` broke every file reading on macOS.** Every A05b file reading on macOS failed with "the file could not be opened without following a link". That covers the unit tests, `startController`'s hook, the bridge test and the four-backend approval tests. The error code is swallowed there, so the log cannot say whether macOS refused the number (EINVAL) or saw a link in the path (ELOOP). Node's `fs.constants` does not name the flag. It is no longer used.
  - **Replacement (macOS, Windows, any system without Linux's `/proc/self/fd` answer): the walk check.** Before the walk looks inside the checkout root and each directory on the way, it marks each one (lstat: device, inode, modification and change time in nanoseconds). After the read it checks that the file is still the one open and that its real path is the walk's. Then it re-marks the directories, the deepest first and the root last. A rename, a new name or a removed name in a directory moves its times (POSIX requires it for rename), and the root is the controller's own. So if no mark moved, every name on the way named the same directory for the whole time, the open included.
  - A directory whose change time is under 50 ms old is not trusted yet. A file system's clock ticks (Linux's coarse clock moves every few milliseconds), and two changes within one tick leave the times as they were. Any doubt pauses 50 ms and reads again, at most 3 times, then refuses ("a directory on the way changed while the file was being read").
  - Cost: on macOS and Windows a reading of a file in a directory changed in the last 50 ms waits about 50 ms, and a reading while a directory on the way keeps changing is refused (fail closed). Linux keeps the kernel's answer and is unchanged.
  - ASSUMPTION: a refused reading is better than one that might be outside the checkout. A directory that changes continuously under a review is refused, not waited for.
  - Left: a file system whose clock ticks slower than 50 ms (HFS+, one second) and an owner's clock set back. Both are documented in the code.
- **Tests for the walk check, run on Linux too** (option `readCheck: "walk"`, tests only).
  - The free-running swap test runs with both checks. Under the walk check its liveness proof is a reading once the directory is put back, because the swapper changes the root all the time.
  - A new deterministic test uses test-only hooks (`readHooks`). It puts the link in just before the last name is looked at and takes it out just after the open, which is the interleaving that leaked on macOS. Both checks catch it. Mutation: with the walk check's after-read part off, which is the old macOS logic, this test reads the outside file and fails.
  - A new churn test: a directory on the way that changes during every reading is refused; once it is quiet, the file is read.
  - Simulated with `process.platform` stubbed to darwin (so the walk check is the default): all A05b file tests pass. The PostgreSQL group cannot run under the stub, because embedded-postgres then looks for macOS binaries.
  - Unverified: real macOS and Windows timestamps (APFS and NTFS are nanosecond file systems; NTFS updating a directory's times on a rename inside it is assumed).
- **macOS, integration tests that had never run there** (in round 1 the scripts step failed first, and `npm test` runs the workspaces only after it).
  - A09 "an approved package is installed ... by the real local runtime" is skipped off Linux: the runtime says "changing an agent's environment is supported only on Linux so far" (`worker/src/environment/host.ts`).
  - U14b, two tests: the start stand-ins (`facts`, `filesystem`) now also give `features: []`. Before, a start with a local host probed this machine's real bubblewrap, so on macOS the start failed for that reason ("bubblewrap (bwrap): found nothing usable") instead of the reason each test sets up. Linux is unchanged, except that the tests no longer need bwrap installed.
- **Windows.**
  - W13 "no write path": the test turned its own path from dist to src by looking for "/dist/" in a Windows path, which has backslashes, and so read `dist\context\recall.ts`. The swap is now made on the URL.
  - A05b "pipe, directory, too large": NTFS reserves the space of a file extended by truncation (it is not sparse), and 50 GiB was ENOSPC on the runner, so there the huge file is 2 GiB (far above the cap, never read).
  - `meetings/record.test.js` (node 22, shard 2): every subtest passed (the last one 2 s before the end), and the file hit the 600 s per-file limit. Its Linux weight is 96 s and Windows runs about six times slower. The heaviest files (policy-edit 99 s, meetings 92-96 s, chat 87 s) are all near that limit there. The controller's per-file bound is now 900 s (`packages/controller/package.json`). ASSUMPTION: a bound for slow runners, not a hang being hidden (the file was still passing tests when it was stopped).
  - "SQLite on a worker thread: card L05d review: a repeated provider ID ..." (node 24, shard 1): `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'state')`. The run had left "streaming" before the broken-off tool call was recorded. The same test passed on the other three backends in the same job, and stream-feed L05d is on the known-flake list. Judged a timing flake on a slow runner and left unchanged.
- **Linux, found during this round's runs: the K02 heartbeat hang test could catch the writer's temporary file.** The test waited until `<root>/run` held exactly one entry and then compared its name. The heartbeat writer makes each beat as `<file>.<pid>.tmp` and renames it over the record, so that one entry could be the temporary file (it failed once in shard 2 and once alone, under load). The look now counts records only (not `*.tmp`). The assertion is the same: exactly the new start's file. Passed 3 of 3 alone afterwards.

- **Windows node 24 shard 2: a timing assumption in `api/start-stall-relay.test.ts`** (V01c, "a route's declared reading speed ... judges the first call"). The second call was judged at a measured speed (about 1752 tokens a second) instead of the declared 20. A finished call becomes a speed sample when its time to the first output is at least `SPEED_SAMPLE.minReadMs` (1 s) and it read at least `minReadTokens` (200) uncached tokens. ## Test servers left by killed test processes are cleaned up by the next start; the dispatcher tests split by backend (card 19 follow-up, Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

Why: a test process killed from outside (the per-file time-out, SIGKILL) never stops its embedded PostgreSQL server. The server keeps running (re-parented to init) and its `nn-test-pg-*` folder stays in /tmp, which is a RAM disk here. At the start of this work there were 277 such folders and 13 test postgres processes on the machine (4 of them orphaned, parent process 1); /tmp held 27 GB. That memory and CPU add to the load that makes tests flaky.

**Done**
- **Each test server records its owner.** `startEmbeddedServer` (`storage/postgres/testing/server.ts`) writes `owner.json` into its folder right after creating it (atomically: a temporary file renamed into place): the process id, that process's start time (Linux: field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat`; macOS: `ps -o lstart=`), the boot id (Linux), the host name and the time. The start time is what stops a reused process id from being taken for the owner.
- **The next start sweeps first** (`testing/orphans.ts`, `sweepOrphanedServers`, run once per process and folder before the new server's folder is made). It removes a folder only when ALL of these hold:
  - the folder is directly in the system temp directory (or a folder inside it), is named exactly like mkdtemp's folders (`nn-test-pg-` and six letters or digits), is a real directory owned by this user, and is not a symlink (nothing is followed: the owner record and the pid file are opened no-follow and non-blocking, a link inside the folder is unlinked, never followed);
  - its owner record names a process on this host that is provably gone: no such process, a zombie, a process with that id that started at another time, or another boot. An owner that is alive, on another host, or cannot be checked keeps the folder.
  - A folder WITHOUT an owner record (made by the old harness in another worktree, or a start killed in its first moment) is touched only once nothing in it changed for 24 hours (the folder, its data folder, the pid file, `pg_control` and `pg_wal`), and its server only if that server itself started more than 24 hours ago.
  - If a server still runs on the folder it is stopped first, and only after checking that `data/postmaster.pid` names this very data folder and that the process with that id has a command line of `postgres -D <this data folder>`. A pid file naming a process that is gone or is some other program (a reused id) means there is nothing to stop; that other program is never signalled. The stop is fast shutdown (SIGINT), then immediate shutdown (SIGQUIT) after 10 s, then SIGKILL after 5 more, bounded; a server that does not go keeps its folder.
  - Each removal, and each folder kept although its owner is gone, is logged on stderr as `[embedded-postgres] removed orphaned test server folder ...` with the reason and the postgres process id it stopped. A sweep failure never fails the start.
- `NIMBLENEWT_TEST_PG_SWEEP=report` decides and logs without changing anything; `=off` skips the sweep. Windows is skipped (no start times read there; the sweep never runs).
- A report-mode sweep of the real /tmp during this work (it changed nothing) said it would remove 46 folders (no owner record, unchanged for over a day), 2 of them with a running orphaned server. The rest are younger than a day without a record; once the other worktrees run with this harness, new folders carry a record and are removed as soon as their owner is gone.
- **`dispatch/dispatcher.test.ts` split by backend.** It was one file of 388 tests (97 per backend). Measured alone on this machine (load 40 to 50): 268 s; by backend: reference store 88 s, PostgreSQL 82 s, SQLite 48 s, SQLite on a worker thread 49 s; the cost is spread out (median test 0.5 s), only one test stood out ("with twenty asks pending", 12.5 s over the four backends). The tests now live in `dispatch/dispatcher-suite.ts` (`defineDispatcherTests(backend)`, as `lifecycle/stop-suite.ts` does), run by `dispatcher.test.ts` (reference store), `dispatcher.sqlite.test.ts`, `dispatcher.worker.test.ts` and `dispatcher.postgres.test.ts`. Every test and assertion is unchanged. After: the four files together (in parallel, load about 20 to 25) 59 s wall, 388 of 388 pass; one after another: 33 s, 33 s, 73 s and 147 s (load rising from 19 to 51 during that run). Each part has well over half of the 600 s limit to spare even at load 50. `scripts/test-weights.json` has the four new files (the old 75.3 s split by the measured shares) and `orphans.test.js`.
- The "twenty asks pending" test ticked a fixed 12 times; it now stops at the first tick that starts nothing (at most 12). Its assertions (20 calls waiting, the free task ran, no place held) are unchanged: about 3.1 s to 1.3 s per backend at low load.

**Tests** (`storage/postgres/orphans.test.ts`, 5 tests, every folder and process made by the test in a disposable folder of its own under the temp directory; the real leftovers are never looked at):
- removed: owner gone; a reused pid (live process, other start time); a live owner's folder once that owner is killed. Kept and not reported: a live owner, another host, an owner that cannot be checked, young folders without a record or with a malformed one, names not exactly mkdtemp's, a plain file.
- a folder without a record goes only after a day (`now` moved forward), report mode changes nothing, off looks at nothing.
- a symlink with the right name and its target are untouched; an owner record that is a symlink, a folder or a FIFO counts as no record (and reading the FIFO does not block); a link inside an orphan's folder is unlinked and its target survives; a folder outside the temp directory is never swept.
- a pid file naming a live non-postgres process (a reused id): that process keeps running, the folder goes; a pid file naming another data folder keeps the folder; a "server" that ignores SIGINT and SIGQUIT is killed in the end.
- end to end: a child test process starts a real embedded server in the disposable folder and is SIGKILLed; its server is still running (the problem); the sweep stops that server (its process is gone after) and removes the folder; while the child lived the sweep kept it.
- Mutation checks (each alone on the built files, each restored): the command-line check removed (the pid-reuse test fails: the bystander is killed); the start-time comparison removed; `lstat` replaced by `stat`; the temp-directory check removed; the age check removed (3 tests fail); the SIGKILL step removed; O_NOFOLLOW removed; O_NONBLOCK removed (the test file hangs on the FIFO until the time-out); `writeOwnerRecord` not called (the end-to-end test fails). One survived: the `isFile()` check on the owner record, which is now a second guard (a directory or FIFO already fails the read, which is caught).

- Suite runs (`npx tsc --build --force`, no stale dist tests, `api:docs:write` unchanged; `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, and `NIMBLENEWT_TEST_PG_SWEEP=report` so the real leftovers were never touched: the runs logged report-mode decisions only and removed nothing): controller shard 1/3 4,432 of 4,432; shard 2/3 4,516 of 4,518 (the known flakes L05d stream-feed and H07 "one hundred idle hosts"; their files alone 101 of 101 and 73 of 73); shard 3/3 3,468 of 3,469 (the known dependency-probe/observe flake; its file alone 66 of 66); integration 159 (149 pass, 10 skipped, 0 failed); `scripts/*.test.mjs` 139 (138 pass, 1 skipped).
- Noise: every test process's sweep logs one line per folder it would remove or keeps although the owner is gone; in report mode on today's /tmp that is about 46 lines per process. In remove mode these folders are gone after the first sweep, so the lines stop.

**Not done**
- Folders and servers whose owner process is gone but were never given a record (all of today's leftovers) wait 24 hours before the sweep touches them. Nothing already in /tmp was removed or stopped by this work (all its runs used report mode).
- A server whose folder was already deleted (no folder left to find it by) is not looked for.
- Windows: no sweep (process start times are not read there), so a killed test process on Windows still leaves its server and folder.
- The PostgreSQL part of the dispatcher tests is the slowest (every test creates and migrates a schema); a schema template to clone would make it cheaper and is not done.

ASSUMPTION: 24 hours for a folder without an owner record, because no test file may run longer than 600 s and the folders made by the old harness in other worktrees must not be removed while they may still be in use.
ASSUMPTION: the sweep runs in every test process before its first server, not in a separate cleanup command, so nobody has to remember to run it.
ASSUMPTION: splitting the dispatcher file is preferred over cutting test work: the cost was spread over all 97 tests and none waited on long timers.

### Card 19 follow-up, clean-context safety review (Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

Question: can the sweep ever stop or remove a live run's server? Up to 8 agents share `/tmp`. Merged origin/main first (notes: both sides kept). Before the fixes, it could in one setup and on one rule; both are closed now. A report-mode run against the real `/tmp` (296 folders) would have removed 61 folders. All 61 had no record and were more than a day old, and it would have stopped 2 servers, both adopted by init 3 days ago from a deleted agent worktree. No live server was among them.

**Fixed (`storage/postgres/testing/orphans.ts`)**
- **Pid namespaces.** A pid, and the start time `/proc` shows for it, mean something only inside one pid (and time) namespace. A test run in a sandbox with its own pid namespace that shares the temp directory would look "gone" to a sweep outside it, and the reverse. Its server's pid is also invisible from outside, so the server was judged "stale" and the folder was removed from under it. The record now holds `pidNamespace` and `timeNamespace` (`/proc/self/ns/*`); a record from another namespace is never judged. A Linux record without them, as this branch wrote before the fix, counts as no record (the 24 h rule).
- **A server whose parent still runs is never stopped.** A server left by a killed test process has been adopted by init (pid 1). A live run's server is the child of its live node process. Before a stop, the server's parent must be pid 1 or gone, whatever the record says. This also closes the 24 h rule's one danger: a folder from an older harness (main writes no record) with an idle server that has run for over a day.
- **Pid reuse between the command-line check and the stop.** The start time used for the stop was read after the command line was checked. It is now read before and checked again after; a change means "cannot be told" (kept).
- **EPERM and a hidden `/proc`.** A process the signal check reported as existing (EPERM, another user) is "unknown", not "gone", when `/proc` hides it.
- **Output.** At most 10 log lines per sweep plus one summary line. Every test process sweeps once, and in report mode the 61 leftovers were repeated in each.

**Tests (`storage/postgres/orphans.test.ts`, 5 new):** another pid or time namespace, and a Linux record without namespaces; a live parent keeps a recorded and an unrecorded day-old server (never signalled); a pid reused between the two checks; EPERM is never "gone"; the log cap. The real-server test accepts "kept" on a machine where a subreaper, not init, adopts orphans. Own mutations (built files, each restored, each failed exactly one test): namespace compare removed; parent guard removed; recheck removed; name pattern loosened; temp-directory check removed; record without namespaces judged by pid; log cap removed. 7 of 7 killed.

**Checked, not changed**
- Owner record written late or partial: a folder is created and its record written (atomic rename) right after. A concurrent sweep sees a young folder (24 h rule) or a whole record. A corrupt, huge (>4 KiB), linked or FIFO record counts as no record.
- Concurrent sweeps: before each signal the start time is checked again, ESRCH counts as stopped, and `rm` uses `force`. A failed removal is logged as kept and never thrown (`sweepOnce` catches).
- Paths: exact mkdtemp names, directly in a root inside `os.tmpdir()`, own uid, never a symlink, inode checked again before `rm`, links inside are unlinked, not followed. The product sandbox (`--tmpfs /tmp`) cannot share folders.
- Remaining limits: on a machine where a subreaper adopts orphans, servers are kept (a leak, logged), never stopped. `kill()` by pid has a microsecond window between the last start-time check and the signal (Node has no pidfd). A pid would have to be reused within it (pid_max 4194304 here). A first server start can wait up to 20 s per stubborn orphan.
- Dispatcher split: the suite equals the old file apart from the per-backend wrapper and one drain loop that stops at the first tick that starts nothing (the assertions after it still require all 20 calls). The weights cover every new file; the three shards are 719/701/710 s; `dispatcher-suite.js` is not taken for a test file.


## G09 third pass: a provider change through the composed controller (2026-11-11)

Code: `dispatch/relay.ts` (new `forAttempt` option `onEndpointChanged`), `api/dispatch-compose.ts` (the per-attempt relay records it on the task), `dispatch/dispatcher.ts` (step 5a records why an attempt left its configured route). Tests: `packages/integration/src/g09c-provider-change.test.ts` (3, new), `dispatch/relay.test.ts` (1 new), `api/start-route-calls.test.ts` (one assertion added). Details in `g09-evidence.md` (second addendum).

- **Done.** The G09 sentence "continuity is also validated across a provider change", which the first two passes showed only at adapter and service level, is now shown through the real launcher, the worker host it builds from the owner's records (`scripts/local-host.mjs`), the sandboxed worker process running Pi Durable and the controller's relay, with scripted offline model servers. (1) The owner adds a new server and disables the old provider while an attempt is still writing: that attempt finishes on its own route, address and key; the next attempt runs on the new route with only the new key; the attempt-endings view, the routing-controls view and the task's activity say which route each ran on. (2) Four refused changes (stale revision, a key given where its name goes, credentials in the address, an address that is not http/https) change nothing; the running attempt and the next one run on the route in force with its key. (3) The owner changes the address and key name of the provider a running attempt uses: the change applies from that attempt's next call (its whole conversation carried to the new address, the new record's key, never the old one), the next attempt starts there. In every case each call carries exactly its server's key, no key reaches the model's context, an activity step or a view, and no file the installation leaves holds a key.
- **Two gaps found and fixed.** (a) The address change in (3) moved a running attempt to another server silently: nothing on the task said so. The relay now tells its attempt when a call goes to another address than the previous call (host and path only, once per change, before the call is sent), and the controller records it as a `model-selected` step: "Route X: its provider's address was changed while attempt Y ran; its model calls go to H from now on (before: G), with the key the changed record names." (b) When the owner's controls (disable, drain, cutover, health) send a new attempt past its configured route, `routing.decisions` still names the configured route and nothing said why the attempt ran elsewhere. The dispatcher now records one step per attempt and move: "The task's configured route A is closed to new work, so attempt Y goes to the next open route B (A: <the control's reason>)."
- **Mutation checks** (each alone, restored): the dispatcher's new step removed (the route-change test fails); the relay never telling a change (the address-change test fails); the launcher reading one fixed key for every provider (the route-change and address-change tests fail).
- **ASSUMPTION:** a change of the provider record an attempt runs on is applied from the attempt's next call and told, rather than refused or held until the attempt ends: the relay and the launcher already promise "read at each call, so a change applies from the next call" (a rotated key, a corrected address), and the conversation goes on whole. An owner who wants running work moved or stopped explicitly has `routing.cutover`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** `routing.decisions` stays the configuration's choice (the controls are applied after it, as R04c designed); the new activity step is where the owner reads the route actually taken. Changing the decision record would change a stored shape on all four backends for no gain over the step.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the new steps go through the existing activity record path (no new record kind or query), which has its own four-backend tests; the new behaviour is shown on SQLite through the composed controller (the launcher runs on SQLite only).
- **Not done.** Cost views after a change: the launcher-built host records no usage for these local, free routes (`budget.usage` stays empty for every task here), so "cost follows the new route" is not shown; a paid route through the launcher-built host is the place to show it. A change of only the key NAME on the same address is not told (the relay never sees key names; a rotated key under the same name is meant to be silent). Branches keep the model they were made with (first pass); `useModel` still has no audit event or port method; a provider whose secret is missing from the store is accepted by `routing.provider.add` and only fails at the attempt's first call (the relay says "the model endpoint's credentials could not be read"), with no check at change time. No real model (ASSUMPTION as before: the benchmark holds the one allowed connection). The card is not flipped: nothing in production carries a C05 resume or `applyUpdates` result into the adapter conversation (first pass).
- **Clean-context review (2026-11-11).** Two bugs found and fixed. (1) The dispatcher's "configured route is closed" step was written while the attempt was still being checked, before the budget, grant, resume, context, host, place, allowance and model-call checks, any of which can make it wait. An attempt that waited while its route drained and then ran on its configured route was still recorded as having gone elsewhere. The step is now written in the advance just before the start, once the attempt really starts on the other route (`start-route-calls.test.ts`, new test: three ticks waiting with no step, then the configured route with no step, then a placed-past attempt with one step). (2) The relay compared the attempt's addresses as raw text and cut the words before redacting them. Another spelling of the same server (host case, default port, trailing slashes, a query-only change, two spellings of one IPv6 address) was told as a move whose two sides read the same. A key-shaped path segment cut at 200 characters could leave a piece too short for the redactor to see. Addresses are now compared as the URL parser normalises them (scheme, host, path). The scheme is named when only it changed (http to https). The words are redacted before they are cut (`relay.test.ts`, new test). Mutation checks (each alone, restored): the step back inside the checks (the new dispatcher test fails); the step removed (both composed route tests fail); raw-text comparison (the new relay test fails); redaction after the cut (the new relay test fails). Checked and left: the endpoint and its key are read from the records and the secret store at each call (`launcher.ts` `endpointOf`); a disabled provider keeps serving an attempt already on it, as `routing.disable` promises ("running work is left alone"); a removed record refuses the next call ("has no endpoint"). Writes stay bounded: the moved-address step is keyed by attempt and (from, to), so an address flapping between two values is told at most twice per attempt, and each further step needs a new owner write of the record. Not covered: remote hosts (`scripts/remote-host.mjs`) take addresses from their own configuration, not the owner's records, and pass no `onEndpointChanged`.
## L04d wiring: the shipped resume reviewer, on the owner's own route, failing closed (Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

L04d's reviewer agent (`continuation/resume-reviewer.ts`) existed, but only a host that passed `StartOptions.resumeReview` got one, and nothing shipped did. The W10 wiring left the reason open: wiring it into every installation would put a reviewer in front of every checked resume, and a route that was unset or broken could then hold resumes at `review_failed`. This change wires it and settles that: when the reviewer cannot run, the resume behaves exactly as it did before a reviewer existed.

**Done**
- **The shipped reviewer (`api/start.ts`).** When the host gives `reviewerModel` (the launcher always does) and neither `resumeReview` nor `resume.review`, the controller builds a `ResumeReviewer` over the same `BoundedReviewerModel` as W10's second agent (one instance, so the two share its two slots), behind `GuardedModelCall` and the daily cap on the controller's own model calls, told the task's title and recorded next step. Its route is the owner's setting `resume.reviewerRoute`, read at every review and judged by the routing table's own rules (`reviewerRoute(..., purpose: "resume")`). An explicit `resumeReview` or `resume.review` of a host is used exactly as before.
- **Fail closed, as "not run" (`continuation/resume.ts` `ReviewNotRun`).** A review port may now throw `ReviewNotRun(reason)`. The resume check then does not block: it records `review: { state: "not-run", reason, at }`, gives every open change a verdict `relevant: true` with the rationale `not reviewed: <reason>; so the owner decides whether it matters`, and goes to `ready`, so only the owner's `resume.approve` lets the work go on (the rule from before a reviewer). The shipped reviewer throws it when no route is set, the route cannot be used (provider disabled, not in the table), the cap is reached, or no route gave a reasoned verdict (a ramble, a failing model). Any other failure of a port is still `review_failed`, as before. A real review records `review: { state: "ran" }`. The controller's own stand-in for "no reviewer connected" (`resume-ports.ts`) also throws `ReviewNotRun`, so a check with no reviewer says the same thing instead of a fake verdict text.
- **The owner sees it (`status/status.ts`).** A held resume whose review did not run says, in the needs-you list, `… 1 change since it stopped was not reviewed by a second agent (<why>), so it is yours to judge: file src/a.ts (changed)` instead of "judged to matter".
- **The setting discloses what is sent where (`configuration/settings.ts`).** `resume.reviewerRoute` (installation only, owner only) says: what the reviewer does; what happens when it is unset or cannot run; that the task's title, the next step its last checkpoint recorded and, for each changed input, its kind, path or name, status and the controller's short note of what changed (for a folder, names of entries gone or new) go to that route, redacted and quoted as data; never a file's content; inputs that could not be checked are never sent; naming the route allows a cloud or paid route within the daily cap; it is separate from `report.reviewerRoute`.
- **Free-form chat (`chat/model-interpreter.ts`).** The interpreter prompt describes the setting with two example wordings, the `policy_edit` shape, how to remove it, that it differs from `report.reviewerRoute`, and what data a cloud route would get. It is shown first and applied only on the owner's agreement, like every setting.

**Tests**
- `continuation/resume.test.ts` (one more suite, all 4 backends): `ReviewNotRun` gives `ready`, no blocker, `review.state` not-run with the reason, every change relevant, the history note, `held()` names it not reviewed, only the owner's approval commits; any other port failure is still `review_failed`; a later real review records `ran`.
- `api/start-resume-reviewer-wiring.test.ts` (new; SQLite and PostgreSQL through `startController` with `reviewerModel` as an offline fixture and the real `ModelInterpreter` driven by a stand-in that knows only the prompt): no route, nothing asked, not run and held for the owner (the agent cannot commit, the owner can); an unknown-only change with no route also says not run; the owner names a route in free words, nothing is asked until they agree; then only that route is asked (not the table's first safety-supervisor route), "does not matter" lets the agent commit without the owner, 120 tokens counted, the prompt holds the quoted title, next step and path but not the file's content or a secret, and `report.reviewerRoute` stays unset; a ramble, a failing model (secret in its error not recorded), the daily cap (no call) and a disabled provider each give not run and the owner decides; removed in free words, not run again.
- **Mutation checks** (on the built files, each restored): the shipped review not installed (fails); the resume reviewer reading `report.reviewerRoute` (fails); a reviewer failure thrown as a plain error (fails, it becomes `review_failed`); `ReviewNotRun` not handled (3 fail); not-run verdicts made not relevant (3 fail); not-run recorded as ran (2 fail); the status line ignoring not-run (fails); the route pre-read removed (fails: an unknown-only check would say it ran). 9 of 9 killed.

ASSUMPTION: a separate setting (`resume.reviewerRoute`), not `report.reviewerRoute`. The owner who named a route for questioning reports agreed to send report data there, not the paths and notes of a resumed task; reusing it would widen that consent silently. One more chat sentence is the smaller, more reversible choice.
ASSUMPTION: "cannot run" means the owner decides at once (not run), not a `review_failed` hold that retries. A transient model failure therefore asks the owner a question the reviewer might have answered a few minutes later; that is the pre-reviewer rule, so nothing is held or released that would not have been before.
ASSUMPTION: a not-run verdict is reused like any other while the change stays the same, so setting a route later does not re-judge a change already put to the owner. It is the conservative answer (relevant).

**Not done (L04d stays planned)**
- Not tried against a real model (no model calls in this work; the reviewer is an offline fixture).
- The shipped reviewer uses W10's bounds: a user prompt cut at 24,000 characters and a reply over 20,000 characters read as no verdict. A 40-change piece with long rationales could hit the reply bound; it then fails closed (not run, the owner decides) rather than passing. The per-call size is not tuned for this client.
- (Done in the review below: the dispatcher's own notice and wait reason now say "not reviewed" too.)
- Everything on the earlier L04d lists is unchanged: a real Pi process through capture and resume, the compaction lineage in production, pending effects and scratch records in host captures, the per-tick prerequisite cache, `search`/`external`/`mcp-resource` observation, the probe reading the task's own worker checkout, a reviewer that reads diffs, a state-API operation for the daily cap, and the second review's follow-ups (the check using the latest complete continuation rather than the attempt's `resumeFrom`, identity of an incomplete earlier continuation, pruning).

### L04d wiring, clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-11)

Merged origin/main (PostgreSQL hardening) first; no conflicts. Hunted fail-open, disclosure, shared-slot and state-machine faults. No path was found where a missing, failed, garbled, over-long, capped or disabled-route reviewer yields `ran` or lets an agent commit: every such case reaches `ReviewNotRun` (relevant, owner decides). A verdict needs a JSON boolean for the exact id, so prose ("doesn't matter"), two objects, a lookalike token, `__proto__` or a 20,000+ character reply is no verdict. Paths, notes, title and next step are redacted, cut to 200 and quoted as JSON with invisible and bidi characters escaped; no content is sent.

**Fixed**
- **Not reviewed is now per change (`continuation/resume.ts`, `status/status.ts`).** The needs-you line took "not reviewed" from the check's last review, but verdicts carry over when a check starts over. Round 1 not run (change A), round 2 ran (change B): A was said to be "judged to matter". The reverse: A judged, B not run, both said not reviewed. Each not-run verdict now carries `notReviewed: <why>`. `held()` gives `notReviewed` and `notReviewedCount` from the verdicts.
