  - The landing policy (`landingPolicyFrom`) now reads `workspace.landing.protectedPaths` and `workspace.landing.requirePermit` through the task's project. A task the configuration does not know is read at the installation plus the named project's layers (before: the installation alone). The branch is unchanged: the project's own `project.branches.set` landing branch still wins over the installation's.
  - **Never weaker than the installation.** Protected paths add: the installation's paths, the project's, then team, agent and task paths are all in force, and a project's list (even an empty one) cannot take any off. The built-in list (`workspace.landing.protectDefaults`) and the branch (`workspace.landing.branch`) stay installation-only and are refused at the project layer. The permit is a restriction: a project can require it where the installation does not, and cannot switch it off where the installation (or the default) requires it; a task layer cannot switch off what its project requires.
  - **Chat.** The policy-edit `setting` change takes `layer: "project"` with `projectName` (the owner's own words for the name, which must be in the message) or `scopeId` (a project ID), or neither for the project in focus; an unclear name is asked about, an unknown one refused. Like every setting it is shown first. A list that replaces the project's own list names every entry it drops (and the sentence says "of this project"); before, only the installation's list did. The interpreter prompt describes the project layer, the add-only rule and the permit rule, and no longer says there is one landing branch for the whole installation.
  - **Status.** The owner-only `landing` view lists, after the installation's lines, every project that has landing values of its own (a project layer, or its own landing branch): the landing branch and whether it is the project's own or the installation's, the permit and where it comes from (this project's setting, the installation's setting, the default), and the extra protected paths in force with the ones this project adds. Capped at 20 projects with a line saying more exist; a read failure is said in a line. Backed by `ConfigurationService.projectSettings` and `ProtectedBranchService.landings`.
- **Tests.** `configuration/h12u-project-layer.test.ts` (5 per backend: owner-only and revision checks; task reads its own project and team ordering; never weaker (installation-only keys refused, empty list, permit rules, task cannot widen); the landing policy follows the project, a stale task ID, a wrong project, read fresh; the listing); `chat/policy-edit.test.ts` (+1 per backend: chat by name and by focus, shown first, dropped entries named, ghost project, foreign name, installation-only keys, permit off refused at apply); `api/h12s-landing-policy.test.ts` (the status view and policy through `startController` with a real project layer and its own branch); `chat/model-interpreter.test.ts` (prompt and intent). Mutations killed (a bug applied, a test failed, restored): owner-only check removed; a task ignoring its project layer; a task-layer write not checked against the project; the policy ignoring the order's project; an unknown task read at the installation only; a project allowed to widen the permit; dropped entries not named; the project not resolved in chat; the status view without project lines; the listing ignoring the project's own layer.
- ASSUMPTION: a project can only tighten the permit (require it where the installation does not); to relax it for one project the owner switches it off for the installation and requires it for the others. Letting one project loosen a guard the installation requires is the less reversible choice, and the request only fixed the protected list as never weaker.
- ASSUMPTION: the project layer holds any setting that is not installation-only (the layer is generic); only the landing settings were made chat-visible per project, because that is what H12t left open. Other settings in a project layer behave as the combination rules say but nothing else reads them per project yet.
- ASSUMPTION: the status view lists only projects that have something of their own; a project with nothing is covered by one sentence ("every project uses the installation's").
- **Not done.** The built-in protected list and the branch cannot be set per project (installation-only by design); a project's own branch is still the separate branch record (not moved into the layer); a project layer written for a project later deleted stays as a record (no cleanup); the other H12t leftovers (commit/submit in the product composition; macOS and Windows) are unchanged; the web screen does not show the project layer.
- **Review (clean-context Opus, 2026-11-12).** Checked every way to weaken the installation: a project, team, agent or task layer cannot take off a protected path or switch the permit off (the read combines with meet; only the installation replaces the permit), a project value stored while the installation allowed it does not count once the installation requires the permit again, an installation lock wins, path tricks are refused, the order's project always comes from the task record (the mismatch throw is fail closed and no caller can supply another project), and every landing reader (local host, remote host, P10 lease gate) refuses on a read failure. Fixed: (1) chat: a setting with both a project ID and the owner's project name now needs the ID to be a project of that name (before, an ID the model picked, for example from quoted text, silently won over the owner's words); (2) chat: a project name given with an installation or team setting is refused instead of being read as a change for every project; (3) configuration: an agent reading its own scope without a configuration grant can no longer name a project (latent: no route offers it to agents today). Tests: an `H12u review` suite in each of `configuration/h12u-project-layer.test.ts` and `chat/policy-edit.test.ts`. Mutations killed: a project replacing the permit instead of meeting it; the own-scope read with a project; the model's ID overriding the owner's name; a project name with a wider layer; a team layer replacing restrictions.

## T07 meeting-gate follow-ups: host and service credentials and restart decisions are held to the meeting rule (Claude agent, 2026-11-12)

Card status is NOT changed. This closes two of the four T07 follow-ups listed under M04h.

**Done**
- **A host or service credential no longer skips the gate.** The rule "no long-running work during a meeting" used to look only at an agent principal, so the controller's own job host (`service:dispatcher`) could admit a background or long job for a task whose agent was in a meeting. The gate is now `createMeetingGate` (`jobs/meeting-gate.ts`): an agent is asked about itself; a `service` or `host` principal is asked about the agent that OWNS THE TASK (the task's assignment), with the same two checks as before (the agent is in the meeting for this very task; a meeting is near). A task with no agent owner has no meeting and is not held. The owner (a person) is still never held. If the task's owner cannot be read, the work is refused in words that say to try again (fails closed), as a failed meeting check already did. `start.ts` composes it (the old inline gate is removed).
- **A restart decision is held to the same rule.** `JobService.decide` with `restart` starts long work again, so it asks the host's gate for the job's task before it records anything (outside the change, so a refusal leaves the job exactly as it was: same state, same restart count). `complete`, `cancel` and `exception` start nothing and are not asked. A job that has already ended is not asked (the existing "nothing to decide" error stands).
- **Tests.** `jobs/meeting-gate.test.ts` (4: agent, owner, host and service, no owner agent, fails closed, no attendance service, non-controller agent names); `jobs/jobs.test.ts` (new case on all four backends: refused restart changes nothing, an allowed one counts, the gate is asked only for restart); `api/start-safe-long-running.test.ts` (composed `startController` on SQLite, no model: the dispatcher's own credential admitting a background or long job is refused while a meeting is called and admitted before it, short work and the owner are not held; an agent's restart from a checkpoint is refused during the meeting, the owner's is allowed). Mutation checks (each killed, then restored): host and service branch removed (3 tests fail), the owner-read failure returning "no meeting" instead of refusing (1 test), the restart gate removed (the composed test and the four backend cases).

**NOT done**
- Still open from the T07 list: a withheld seat over-refused near a meeting. (The race with a meeting made after the gate read was closed by the review below.)
- W13 `task.recall`: the tool is still offered when the owner's switch is off (the worker's tool list is fixed when it starts and the prompt layout is a prefix-cache contract, so hiding it needs the switch passed to the worker at start and a prompt-layout change; a call is still answered "switched off by the owner" in words), and the MCP door for outside agents still lacks it (an outside agent has no attempt, so there is no task for the credential to be bound to; this needs a design for what task identity an MCP caller may have). Neither was started.
- The composed tests run on SQLite only (the services they touch are tested on all four backends in `jobs.test.ts`).

ASSUMPTION: a host or service credential is held to the meetings of the agent that owns the task, and a task with no agent owner is not held (nobody can be in a meeting for it).
ASSUMPTION: the owner (a person) may still restart or admit long work during a meeting, as before; only agent-side and host-side paths are held.
ASSUMPTION (superseded by the review below): a repeat of a restart command that already succeeded, sent while a meeting is on, was refused by the gate rather than answered from its record.

**Review (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-12)**
- **Bug fixed: a repeated restart command was refused, and the refusal reached callers who may not control the job.** The restart gate ran before the command ID was looked up and before the caller was authorized. A client retrying a restart whose reply was lost got "long-running work is not started" instead of its original success (every other command is answered from its record), and a principal with no control of the job (a reader, a writer, another project's agent, a task credential) was told the owner agent's ID, the meeting's occurrence ID and its end time instead of "forbidden". The gate now runs as `#change`'s `pre` step: after the record lookup (a repeat is answered from its record and the gate is not asked) and after authorization. A restart the change refuses anyway (ended job, no checkpoint, outcome-unknown, being stopped) is refused for that reason, not the meeting.
- **Bug fixed: the gate raced a meeting made after it read.** `JobOptions.longRunningLocks` is read before the gate is asked and committed with the admit or the restart it allowed. The controller binds it to `AttendanceService.meetingLocks()`: a `check` on the global list of waiting meetings (`meeting-open/all`), which every meeting creation and settlement rewrites under a revision check. A meeting made between the read and the commit moves it, the commit fails, and the admit or restart is decided again (and refused). Before the installation's first meeting the list does not exist and a check cannot guard an absent record, so the lock creates it empty; a meeting created meanwhile also creates it, one of the two commits meets the other, and both services already retry that (`MeetingService.#retrying` retries `command_conflict`; the admit's contention answers `stale_revision`).
- **Bug fixed: a failure of the in-meeting check escaped as an internal error.** `meetingOfTask` throwing is now refused in the same "could not be checked ... try again" words as the other checks, without the store's own text.
- **Checked, no change:** every path that starts or restarts long work goes through `admit` or `decide` (API `job.admit`/`job.decide`, the tool bridge's `job.start` (forced `longRunning`), MCP `callToolAsJob` (forced `longRunning`), host and service credentials). `decideAtStart` never restarts (only exception, cancel, unknown; no `relaunch` is composed), and a replayed admit launches nothing (the bridge answers an existing job without `runs.start`, the MCP call returns on `replayed`). The gate reads the CURRENT assignment owner each time, so after a hand-off the new owner's meetings count; the agent principal itself is always held to its own meetings whatever task it acts on. A `client` cannot hold `job.write` (`mayHold`), so its exemption admits nothing; the owner exemption needs the owner credential (the kind comes from the stored principal). M04h: long work on a woken agent's own meeting task is refused (by design, M04e); short jobs are not, so nothing the meeting needs is blocked; no new exemption.
- **Tests:** `jobs.test.ts` (two new cases on all four backends: a repeated successful restart is answered from its record and not asked of the gate, unauthorized callers get `forbidden` with no meeting words and the gate is not asked; a meeting made between the lock read and the commit makes both an admit and a restart be decided again and refused, nothing recorded); `start-safe-long-running.test.ts` (composed: the first long job creates the empty list, a meeting is still called over it, a lock read before a meeting no longer commits, the host's admit is then refused); `meeting-gate.test.ts` (a failed in-meeting check). Mutations (each killed): admit locks dropped, restart locks dropped, restart gate dropped, in-meeting failure uncaught, attendance returns no lock, host principal not held.
- **Not done / remaining:** the lock covers new and ended meetings, not other inputs of the near-meeting check (an occurrence's start moved, the agent's reachability or the lead setting changing in that instant, or the task's assignment moving to another agent): each of those is seen on the next ask. `longRunning` stays the caller's word for a job admitted over the API (the bridge and MCP force it); a job record launches nothing by itself.

ASSUMPTION: a repeat of a restart command that already succeeded is answered from its record during a meeting (as every command is); only a new restart command is held.
ASSUMPTION: a job admit may create the empty global list of waiting meetings before the first meeting exists; it is the same empty state a list returns to when its meetings end.
## U11d (denial counts kept across a restart) (2026-11-12)

Card U11d left "denial counts stay in process memory": a controller restart started every agent's count of refusals again, so an agent that was refused twice before a restart needed three more refusals to reach a threshold of three, and an agent whose run had already paged the owner could page a second time for the same run. This is the smallest complete slice that fixes that. It adds no owner control (the existing `deniedThreshold` / `deniedWindowMinutes` / `deniedAlertsPerHour` settings of `notifications.configure`, which the chat interpreter already describes, govern it).

- **Done.** Each counted refusal now also writes the agent's count to the notification state (the same small store that remembers when "no backup" was first seen), under `deny:<agent>`: the times inside the run (the last 1000 at most), the run's total, whether it already paged, whether that page was held back by the hourly cap, and when the run began. After a restart the first refusal of an agent reads its remembered count, so the count goes on, a run that already paged does not page again (its item's count moves on), and the hourly cap flag is kept. Entries are removed by the controller's sweep when the agent has been quiet for a whole window (a fresh run would start from nothing anyway), when the memory limit of 1000 agents forgets the quietest agent. A remembered count that cannot be read counts as none. Nothing is written when no threshold is set.
- **Tests.** `notifications/urgent.test.ts` "denial counts survive a restart" (all four storage backends): two refusals, restart, the third pages; another agent is counted apart; a second restart does not page the same run twice and the item reads "refused 4 times" with one message sent; after a quiet window the sweep leaves no `deny:` entries; an unreadable remembered count is the same as none. Mutations (applied, test failed, restored): the write of the count removed; the pruning removed.
- **ASSUMPTION:** persisted times are capped at 1000, so with a threshold above 1000 a restart can under-count (it never pages early or falsely). The hourly cap on how many agents page (`deniedAlertsPerHour`) is still in memory: after a restart it starts empty, so at most one extra burst of pages is possible in that hour.
- **ASSUMPTION:** one controller writes these counts at a time (the state record is changed under its revision, so two writers cannot corrupt it, but their counts would race).
- **Not done (stays in U11d):** the controller-down watchdog, answering each Needs-you item in place from the view, the page naming which kind of refusal it was (a grant taken away or never held), the per-agent "nothing else to do" signal, deferred meeting items from M03 in the view, the refusals of the approved-call path, and the remaining security hooks.

### U11d review (clean-context, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 67c20a7e after merging origin/main b48923a4. Real bugs found and fixed (each with a test that failed before the fix, on all four storage backends):

- **The counts lived in the one shared notification-state record.** Every refusal rewrote the record that also holds the digest times, the hourly Urgent window and the sweep cursor. Two harms: (a) size: a record is at most 256 KB, and with a threshold of 20 about 650 agents, or with a threshold of 1000 about 18 agents looping on a refused call, fill it, after which the dispatcher's own writes to that record (next sweep time, the hourly Urgent count) can be refused, so notifications stall; (b) contention: a burst of refusals races those same writes, which give up after 8 attempts. Fixed: one small `notification-denial` record per agent (ID derived from the agent ID with the new `dny` prefix, the agent ID kept in the body and checked on read), written under its revision. `watchMemory`/`remember` are no longer used for counts. The test checks the shared record's revision does not move on refusals.
- **Refusals that arrive together paged several times.** Three parallel refused calls of one agent at the threshold raised three items (three pages); the same right after a restart (each loaded the record separately). Pre-existing since U11c for the in-memory case. Fixed: an agent's refusals (and the sweep's look at its count) run one after the other (a per-agent queue, at most 1000 waiting per agent; beyond that a refusal is not counted, under-count only). The refusal hook is fire-and-forget, so no tool call waits on it.
- **A stop between raising the item and saving the count paged a second time.** The record was saved after the raise; a restart in that gap counted the run again from the old record, closed the item it had just raised and raised (and paged) a new one. Fixed: the decision to raise (with the hourly-cap flag and the project) is written first (`p: 1`), then the earlier run's item is closed and the new one raised with command IDs fixed by the run's start (`urg-deny-reopen:<agent>:<start>`, `urg-deny-raise:<agent>:<start>`), then `p` is cleared. A stop anywhere after the decision is finished by the agent's next refusal, or by the sweep when none comes (so the page is not missed either); a repeat replays the recorded command, and the same ID with other words (`command_conflict`) means it was already done. A stop before the decision loses at most that refusal (under-count).
- **Refusals "in the future" counted.** With the clock put back (or a record written by a controller whose clock was ahead) those refusals stayed inside the window and could page with fewer real refusals, and the record was never pruned until the clock caught up. Fixed: a time later than now is not counted (in memory and when read back); a record of only such times is pruned.
- **A record with values out of range was trusted.** A negative or fractional count, flags other than 0/1, more than 1000 times, a start outside the date range (which made every later update of the item throw), a pending raise not marked raised, or a project ID of the wrong shape now count as none, never page, never throw, and are written over by the next refusal.
- **The sweep could forget a count a refusal had just written** (it read all counts, then deleted them one by one, and also dropped the fresh in-memory state). Now each record is re-read and deleted at its revision in the agent's own turn, at most 100 per sweep from a cursor. With the threshold turned off every count is forgotten (memory and records).
- **The 1000-agent memory limit deleted the forgotten agent's stored count**, so a raised run of an agent pushed out of memory started again and paged again. Now only memory is dropped; the record is read back on the agent's next refusal.

Checked and left: no API, chat or state operation reads or writes the counts (they are not in any operation; the shared record's `watch` stays internal); agent IDs come from the dispatcher, never from an agent, and any text maps to a distinct record ID (hashed), so `:`, `..`, long or unicode IDs cannot collide with another agent or with other state. Retired agents' records go after one quiet window.

- **ASSUMPTION:** one refusal still costs one write (record, audit entry, operation row). Needed to survive a restart; bounded per agent by its refusal rate and per record by 1000 times (14 KB at most).
- **ASSUMPTION:** the hourly cap on agents paging (`deniedAlertsPerHour`) stays in memory: after a restart at most one extra burst in that hour (as the implementer noted). Smallest, reversible.
- **ASSUMPTION:** one controller counts at a time; when a record changed under this controller (another writer) its own count is written over it (last writer wins, never corrupt).
- Mutations (applied, a test failed, restored): no per-agent queue; a raise ID new on every attempt (restart-in-the-middle fault injection); future times counted in memory; the sweep not finishing an interrupted raise; a negative count trusted; turning the threshold off keeping counts; the raise decision not written before the raise. Dropping the loader's own future-time filter is caught by the per-refusal filter (redundant guard, survives on purpose).


## P10 (first slice): one leased integrator per project branch, with an authorised door and a landing that must show the lease (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Card P10, "Land submissions with one leased integrator per project". L03j had built a minimal lease service with no way in and nothing that used it. This slice builds the smallest complete path from "an agent asks for the lease" to "a landing is refused unless it holds it". It is not the whole card (see "Not done").

- **What was built, plainly.** An integrator agent (or the owner on its behalf) can now take, renew, list and give back the lease of a project's landing branch through the state API, and the owner can end one by chat. A landing (`workspace.request` with `operation: landing`) now has to name the lease (`leaseId`, `fence`); the controller checks it when the request is made and again right before the host is asked (a long quiesce can outlast a lease), and refuses a landing under a lease that is not the caller's live hold on the owner's landing branch of the task's project. The host is never asked for a refused landing. The lease used is recorded on the request (`lease`).
- **The four risks L03j left for P10, one by one.**
  1. **A restore can reuse a fence.** A hold now records the controller epoch that granted it, and a hold from another epoch is not live (not renewable, not valid, free for the next `acquire`). A controller start, or a restore followed by a start, is always a new epoch, so a fence handed out before can never pass as a current hold. After a restore the fence counter itself can still repeat (the store went back); that is why `valid` also needs the holder, so a repeated number only ever works for the agent it was handed to. Not fully closed: see ASSUMPTION below.
  2. **`valid` did not check the holder.** It is now `valid(leaseId, fence, holder, taskId?)`; a landing passes the caller's own agent ID (the owner acts for whoever holds it, but still needs the live fence).
  3. **`acquire` did not check the task belongs to the project.** It does now (`forbidden` for another project's task, `not_found` for a missing one); the door takes the project from the task, never from the caller; `handOver` has the same check for the task it moves the hold to.
  4. **The task index is capped at 8.** Unchanged and still deliberate: a ninth live lease for one task is refused with a plain message (nothing is silently dropped). Leases are per branch, so a task needing more than eight branches at once is outside what this slice was asked to solve.
  5. **Nothing renews a lease.** The holder renews through `integrator.lease.renew`; the controller does not renew for it. An integrator that dies stops renewing, so the branch frees itself at expiry on the controller's clock (the one `startController` gives the meetings and the dispatcher, `options.dispatch.clock`).
- **The door (`landing/lease-ops.ts`, `IntegratorLeaseOps`; operations `integrator.lease.acquire`, `.renew`, `.release`, `.list`).** The right is a new action, `integration.lease`, granted per project and checked exactly (a wildcard grant is not enough, like `workspace.manage`); the owner has it, a task credential never does. An agent holds the lease as itself (its agent ID comes from who it authenticated as; naming another agent is `forbidden`); only the owner may take it for a named agent, and must name one. Renewing is the holder's alone. Releasing is the holder's (with its fence) or the owner's (by lease, or by project and branch, no fence needed: it ends whoever holds it). A caller without the right gets `not_found`, as for workspace operations. Command IDs are scoped to the caller.
- **Chat.** `integrator.lease.release` (owner, always shown first: it stops an integrator's landing at once). Taking and renewing are agent actions and have no chat command. Listing is an API query; the chat answers lease questions through the existing status views only. ASSUMPTION: the chat does not take a lease for an agent (it would need agent-name resolution beyond this slice); the owner can do it through the API.
- **Landing gate (`workspace-ops.ts`, `landingLease` dependency).** `startController` composes it from the lease door and the owner's landing policy (`landingPolicyFrom`): the lease must be of the task's project and of exactly the branch the policy names (a project with no landing branch has no valid lease: `forbidden`). `invalid_command` for no lease named, `fenced` for a stale, expired, released or someone else's hold. When no lease service is composed (the unit rigs of the older workspace tests) landings are not gated, and a lease named on any other operation is refused. ASSUMPTION: the gate applies to every caller including the owner, because "never two integrators on one branch" is the card's first criterion and the owner can hold a lease for a named agent through the API; the smallest-scope choice that keeps the rule uniform.
- **Tests.** `landing/lease-p10.test.ts` (four backends: the door's rights, holder and project checks and renew/list/release; foreign-project and missing tasks at `acquire` and `handOver`; `valid` with holder, fence and task, and a lease from another epoch, using a real second epoch; expiry on the injected clock; the landing gate for no, partial, stale, other-agent, wrong-branch, no-branch, foreign-project and expiring-during-quiesce leases, with a count of host calls). `api/start-p10-lease.test.ts` (composed controller: the API, the landing refused before any host, the owner ending a lease by chat on proposal then confirmation). The composed integration tests that land through `workspace.request` (`h12q-landing-quiesce`, `h12s-landing-settings`, `h12t-product-host`) now take the lease first (the owner names a holder; a helper keeps one lease on whatever branch the owner's policy names, taken afresh when the owner moves the branch); where they used to see the host's "no landing branch set" they now see the controller's refusal first (no lease can be shown), and an unreadable landing policy is `unavailable` from the controller. Existing lease and hand-off tests were updated for the new `valid` signature and to use real tasks (the old ones used an invented task ID).
- **Mutation checks (each applied alone, built, run, restored):** `valid` ignoring the holder (9 failures); `acquire` without the project check (4); epoch ignored in liveness (4); landing gate not called (5); second showing before the host skipped (4); the door's right check always true (9); wrong-branch check removed (4); expiry by the machine clock instead of the controller's (20); foreign-project lease check removed (4); the landing gate taking the holder from the lease instead of the caller (5); an agent allowed to take the lease under another agent's name (4). One mutant survived and is equivalent: the door's holder check on `renew` removed (the service itself refuses a renew by a different holder `fenced`, so the guard is defence in depth).
- **Gap recorded (dependency unmet).** H12o (commit through release) does not exist, so nothing here commits, and a landing leaves its files uncommitted in the shared tree as before. P10's queue, reservations and the "integrator writes no content" diff check were not built either, since they sit on that and on P08/P09/Q04.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a controller start (a new epoch) ends every lease. Holders must take the lease again after a restart. This is conservative and cheap (leases are minutes long) and is what closes the restore problem without a durable counter outside the store.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the fence number is not made time-based. After a restore it can repeat for a different holder only; for the same agent and branch a repeated number is the agent's own legitimate new hold. A strictly monotonic fence across restores would need a counter kept outside the restored store (or a time-based fence, which changes every existing fence value); that is a decision for a later slice.
- **Not done.** The oldest-first queue, reservations, base==head check as a lease-holder step, mechanical re-apply, return to author on overlap, refresh-round cap and director escalation, the "integrator writes no content" refusal, a retired author's task reassignment, the Q04 cycle limit, starvation test (all P10 deliverables beyond the lease). Nothing renews a lease for its holder. A chat command to take a lease. Releasing a lease when its task ends (it expires on its own). The remote host still decides the landing branch from its own configuration, so the controller's branch check there is the owner's policy, not the host's. The landing gate is only in `workspace.request`; any other path that writes to the shared tree (none exists today) would need its own.

### P10 first slice: clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 8263f2e0 after merging origin/main 12f36b66 (no conflicts).

- **Checked and sound.** The door takes the project from the task, never from the caller; the right is exact and per project, a wildcard or a task credential is refused, and missing tasks, missing rights and other projects' leases are all `not_found` at the door. Two acquirers: the lease record's revision decides, the loser rebuilds and is refused `unavailable` (PostgreSQL, SQLite and the worker thread alike, the L03j race tests). Renew racing expiry and acquire racing release are fenced by the revision, not the clock. The fence grows on every change of hands, including after an expiry or a release. Every landing reaches the host through `workspace.request` only (state API, MCP and chat all call that operation; no script or other door asks a host to land; a remote host cannot start one). The branch is compared exactly (`main` is not `Main` nor `refs/heads/main`); an unreadable policy is `unavailable`. The hand-off's release/move steps are unchanged and still exactly once; `valid` has its new signature at every call site.
- **Restore and restart, answered.** The epoch lives in the store, so a restore can bring back an epoch number used after the backup; the lease records go back with it, though, so what a stale holder can replay is only its own number on its own agent ID. An *old* holder's (leaseId, fence) can validate again after a restore only if the same agent is given that same number again, which is a new hold of its own. No other holder's stale pair ever passes, because `valid` needs the holder. A restart with a landing in flight is safe: the host was already asked and finishes or refuses on its own side (its landing is one all-or-nothing write under the host's `landing` lock, after a base==head check and a clean shared tree). The controller records the request `uncertain` on recovery and never replays it. A new holder's landing after the restart is refused by the host while the earlier landing's files wait uncommitted. So a lease ending during the host's write cannot make two integrators write at once. The host's write is not itself fenced (the host never sees the lease), which is why this depends on that host lock and clean-tree rule.
- **Fixed: taking the right away did not stop landings.** `checkLanding` checked only that the caller held the lease, so an agent whose `integration.lease` right was removed could go on landing until its hold ran out (up to 24 hours). It now needs the right at each showing (`forbidden`). Test: composed `start-p10-lease` (the grant is removed with `setGrants`, the landing is refused).
- **Fixed: a landing told whether another project holds a lease.** A lease of another project was answered `forbidden` ("not a lease of this task's project") and an unknown one `fenced` ("no lease"); lease IDs are derived from project and branch, so a caller with workspace rights in one project could probe another's. Both now get the same `fenced` answer. Test: `lease-p10` compares the two answers.
- **Fixed: the owner could no longer land through chat.** The gate required `leaseId` and `fence`, and the chat refuses values that are not the owner's own words, so a landing asked in chat could never pass. The owner may now leave both out: the live lease of the landing branch is used (no live holder, nothing lands), and the lease used is recorded. The second showing checks that same hold, so a lease that changes hands during the quiesce stops the landing. Tests: composed (owner landing without a lease, recorded lease), `lease-p10` (no holder refused; a release and re-take by another agent during the quiesce refuses the pinned landing, the host is not asked).
- **Fixed: the owner could name any string as holder.** A typo, the principal form `agent:x` or a disabled agent took the branch for nobody until expiry. The composed door now needs an active agent ID (`invalid_command`). The composed integration tests (`h12q`, `h12s`, `h12t`) now enrol a real integrator agent instead of an invented ID. Test: composed (`agent:ann`, an unknown name and a disabled agent refused).
- **Mutations of this review (each alone, built, run, restored): all killed.** The right not checked again at landing; the second showing not pinned to the first hold; the active-agent check removed; another project's lease answered differently from a missing one; an agent's release without the holder check.
- **Left as they are (noted, not fixed).**
  1. An agent with the right can take leases on any branch name, not only the landing branch. It can therefore fill a task's 8-lease index or hold the real landing branch for up to 24 hours, renewing. That comes with the right; restricting `acquire` to the policy's branch is a choice for the queue slice.
  2. `valid` at landing does not compare the task. One integrator's lease covers landings of every task of the project, which is what an integrator is for.
  3. `integration` (the H12l sharing of uncommitted changes into the shared tree) is not under the lease. It writes the same shared tree through the per-file expected-version bridge and makes no landing. Whether it should need the lease is for P10's next slice.
  4. A remote host lands on its own configured branch (H12t leftover 1). The controller's lease check is against the owner's policy. Overlap with the H12a carry review (branch card20-h12a) was not edited.
  5. An owner-named holder without the right can land through the owner but cannot renew or release its own hold (the door needs the right). A retired or disabled holder's lease stays until it expires; the owner ends it with `integrator.lease.release`.
  6. A forced release by the owner is recorded only as the lease command in the journal, with no activity line. The holder's landing that already passed its second showing still lands.
  7. There is still no chat command to take a lease.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the owner may land without naming the lease, acting for the live holder of the landing branch. That is the same authority the owner already had with the lease's numbers, which it can read with `integrator.lease.list`, and it keeps landing reachable by chat. Reversible: require the numbers again.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a lease of another project is answered `fenced`, like a lease that does not exist (not `forbidden`), so the answer does not depend on what another project holds.

## G09 / L04d / C07 follow-ups: the cost of a route change, resume reviews off the tick, and plain-extract wording (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Three leftovers from the "not done" lists, built together because they touch the same dispatcher steps.

**(a) G09: the cost after a route change is told to the owner.**
- **Done (`dispatch/route-cost.ts`, `dispatch/dispatcher.ts` `#costStep`).** When an attempt starts on a different model route than the task last ran on (the placement record's route), the task's activity gets one more step per attempt and move: "Attempt X moved from route A to route B. Cost: route B is paid / free / not in the routing table ...", what the route it left was ("this change starts a charge", "stops the charge", "too"), and for a paid or unknown route what the task has spent against its limit ("So far the task has spent 1.25 USD of its 5.0 USD limit", "(0.5 USD of it not yet settled)", "it has no money limit", "has no budget record"). It reads the routing table (the provider's `paid` flag) and the budget accounting; a fault in either is reported and the words say the figure is unknown. It never invents a price: there is no price list in the controller, so no rate and no forecast is given.
- **Tests:** `dispatch/route-cost.test.ts` (the words; the dispatcher on all four backends: first attempt says nothing, same route says nothing, free to paid with and without a budget, paid to free, an unknown route is never called free).
- **Not done.** The route the controller's own resolver picks is never paid (it asks with `paidAuthorized: false` and local-only data), so on a real installation the step today mostly says "free, the route it left was free too"; the paid wording is shown through a test resolver. The chat proposals for `routing.*` (cutover, drain, disable, budget) still carry a fixed sentence: they are not given a live "what this would cost" line (that needs a dry-run of where running attempts would move, which does not exist). The launcher-built local host still records no usage for free routes.
- ASSUMPTION: "route change" means the route differs from the task's last placement; the step is written once the worker has started (not when a start is merely considered), like the existing "configured route is closed" step, so an attempt that waits is not said to have moved.
- ASSUMPTION: the step goes in the task's activity (where the other route steps already are), not in a notification: a move between routes is routine and the owner should not be paged for it.

**(b) L04d: the resume check's model calls run apart from the tick.**
- **Done.** Two places ran the reviewer's model call inside the dispatcher's tick: `#resumeCheck` awaited `resumes.start` (which asks the reviewer), and the `resumes.sweep` loop awaited `ResumeCheckService.sweep`, each bounded only by the 60-second loop limit. Now:
  - **`dispatch/dispatcher.ts` `#resumeJob`.** The check's `start` (and its retry) runs as a background job keyed by the check's command key. The tick waits at most `resumeInlineMs` (default 250 ms) for it, so a quick check still proceeds in the same tick; otherwise the attempt waits ("the resume check is being run apart from the tick") and the next ticks take the job's answer when it ends. Jobs run at most `resumeJobsMax` (default 4) at a time; the others wait for a free place, nothing is dropped. A job past `resumeJobMs` (default 5 minutes) is reported once through `onError` and still waited for (the client's own bounds, 45 s slot and 60 s a call, are what end a model call; it cannot be taken back from here). A fault is a wait with its reason, as before; a fault after the inline wait also goes to `onError`. `idle()` and `shutdown()` wait for the jobs (shutdown at most 5 s).
  - **`DispatcherLoop.apart` (`dispatcher.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`, `api/start.ts`).** A loop marked `apart` is waited for only `resumeInlineMs`; it is not started again while it runs, "still running" is not a fault for it, and one past its bound is reported once. `resumes.sweep` is marked.
  - **`continuation/resume.ts` `#reviewing`.** A second advance of a check whose reviewer is being asked in this process now (the sweep while the dispatcher's job waits, an API call) answers where the check stands instead of asking the model again and counting its tokens twice. This also removes the double-call hazard the L04d wiring review had noted.
- **Crash safety.** Nothing lives only in memory: the check is in the store. A process that dies mid-review leaves it in `reviewing`; the next process's job (same command) or the sweep asks again, and the resume is recorded once under the check's own command ID.
- **Tests:** `dispatch/resume-off-loop.test.ts` (all four backends, 7 each: a slow review does not hold the tick; a quick one is used in the same tick; a crash loses nothing and the resume is recorded once; the sweep runs apart and asks once; the cap; the late report; faults inside and after the wait) and `api/start-resume-off-loop.test.ts` (through `startController` on SQLite and PostgreSQL, with the shipped reviewer on the owner's route and an offline model that waits on a gate: another task is dispatched while the review is out, the held one starts when it answers, the model is asked once).
- **Mutation checks** (each alone, each failed a test, restored): the tick waits for the job (2 fail); the cap ignored (2); the late report never said (2); the sweep not marked `apart` in `start.ts` (see below); the loop's `apart` handling off (2); the in-service `#reviewing` guard removed (the composed test fails); the cost step removed (2); the process compaction not degraded (2); the extractive note text removed (2).
- **Not done.** The reviewer's model call itself cannot be cancelled by the dispatcher (the port has no abort); the sweep still advances checks one after another inside its own apart run. The `resumeInlineMs` wait is real time, not the injected clock. `ResumeCheckService.advance` called from the API for a check mid-review answers its current state instead of waiting. The remote hosts' resume path is unchanged.
- ASSUMPTION: a job's answer is kept in memory until the next tick reads it and dropped after ten minutes unread; the check in the store is the truth, and asking again is the same idempotent command.
- ASSUMPTION: the defaults (250 ms, 4 jobs, 5 minutes) are generous for one owner's installation; no owner setting was added.

**(c) C07: the owner is told when a summary is a plain extract.**
- **Done.** A compaction the task's own process reports (`ContextEnforcementService.recordProcessCompaction`) is always the extractive hook's (Pi's model summariser is never used when the host gives the extractive fallback, which the controller's composer always does, and since the remote-anchor change a remote machine with no context of its own does it too). Its record said `degraded: false` and a title that read like any summary. Now its title ends "(N messages, extractive)", `degraded` is `true`, and the stored note begins "[Extractive summary, made without a model: the task's process kept the start and the end of what it replaced, so details from the middle may be missing.]" (`PROCESS_SUMMARY_KIND`; the controller's own extractive summaries already began with the same kind of sentence).
- **The wording the owner reads when deciding about the goal anchor** (`chat/commands.ts` verb of `context.route.change`; `api/operations.ts` `context.route.get` and `context.route.change`) now says the summary that replaces a cut conversation is a plain extract of the start and the end, written without a model, so details from the middle may be missing; and that a remote machine which sets no context of its own writes it that way only while the anchor is on (with the anchor off the model writes it again). The generated `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` follows.
- **Tests:** `context/process-compaction.test.ts` (all four backends: degraded, title, stored note), `api/start-dispatch.test.ts` (through `startController`: the owner reads degraded and the title), `chat/anchor-chat.test.ts` (the proposal wording).
- **Not done.** Old process-compaction records keep the title and `degraded: false` they were written with (no migration). The continuation capture's `compression: { state: "compacted" }` still does not say how the summary was made. The owner's status views do not list compactions at all, so there is no new place to show the label.
- ASSUMPTION: `degraded: true` is the right flag for "not a model's summary" (it already means the fallback summary was used); no new field was added to the stored body.

**Checked, no change:** the effective routing for tasks, the resume reviewer's prompt and the reviewer wiring tests are unchanged and still pass.

### G09 / L04d / C07 follow-ups, clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-12)

**Fixed (with tests):**
- **A stuck review could hold the controller's stop.** `DispatchDriver.stop()` calls `dispatcher.shutdown()` (which gave the off-tick checks 5 s) and then `dispatcher.idle()`, which since this change also waited for every resume job and for the apart `resumes.sweep`, with no bound. A model call that does not end, or a sweep carrying several reviews one after another, kept the controller from stopping for as long as they ran. Now `shutdown` marks the dispatcher shut down after its bounded wait (`resumeShutdownMs`, default 5 s), and `idle()` after that waits only for turns and endings, as before L04d. What the checks leave is in the store; the next controller asks again. Test: `dispatch/resume-off-loop.test.ts` (all four backends: a review and an apart loop that never end; `shutdown` and `idle` both come back).
- **The cost words said more than the controller knows.** "route X is free, so its calls add nothing to this task's budget" was not true: the budget counts whatever cost the worker reports and the compute time on any route, whatever the table's `paid` flag says. It now says "route X is listed as free in the routing table, so its calls are not expected to cost money" ("this change stops paid calls"). A routing table or budget that could not be read was described as "not in the routing table" and "has no budget record"; it is now "the routing table could not be read" and "the task's spending could not be read" (`route-cost.ts` `UNREADABLE`). Tests: `dispatch/route-cost.test.ts` (words; the dispatcher on all four backends with failing reads, where the attempt still starts and the faults are reported).
- **The composed `apart` check could not fail.** Removing `apart: true` from `resumes.sweep` in `start.ts` left `api/start-resume-off-loop.test.ts` passing: there the dispatcher's own job does the review and the `#reviewing` guard sends the sweep straight back. A second composed test now leaves a check mid-review in a stopped controller and pauses the task, so only the next controller's sweep reaches the reviewer. The tick must still come back while the review is out. Removing the mark makes it fail.
- **Mutation checks of this review** (each alone, each failed a test, then restored): `apart` removed from `resumes.sweep` in `start.ts` (the new composed test, 2 failures); the shutdown mark removed (resume-off-loop); an unreadable table said as absent (5); the in-service `#reviewing` guard removed (4 composed); a late apart loop reported every tick (the new once-only test, 4; it survived before that test was added); the job cap ignored (4).

**Checked, no change:**
- The held attempt is not claimed while its review is out (the check runs at admission, before the claim), so there is no lease to lose or take over. The job key carries the attempt, its checkpoint and the model, so an answer is never applied to another attempt or route. A check the owner cancelled or declined meanwhile is read from the store first (the key moves on, or the decline returns), and the commit checks the stored phase. So an unread in-memory answer can never resume a stale check.
- The verdict write is guarded by phase `reviewing`, and the in-process guard keeps a second advance from asking again. Tokens are counted once per model call.
- The shipped reviewer's model calls are bounded by the client. A host-supplied `resumeReview` client brings its own bounds, as before. A hung one holds a slot (reported once as late); the other three slots and the rest of the tick go on.
- C07: only the extractive hook in `pi-adapter/src/worker/process.ts` ever reports a process compaction, so "made without a model" is true for every record it writes. Old records keep their title and `degraded: false`, and nothing reads the title.
- G09: `paid` is a required, validated boolean in the table, so "free" is said only when the owner listed the provider unpaid. A route whose provider is not listed is "not known". The step is written once per attempt and move (the placement record is updated with the route at each start), reads only the task's own accounting, and its faults never fail the start.
- `api/start-resume-off-loop.test.ts` runs on SQLite and PostgreSQL only because `startController` opens no other kind. The in-memory store and SQLite on a worker thread are covered by `dispatch/resume-off-loop.test.ts`.
- Not changed: the "from" route's kind is read from the current table, so an owner who changed a provider's `paid` since the last attempt sees the current listing.

## H12o (product slice): the platform commits a verified done in the task's own checkout (2026-11-12, Claude agent)

**What was wrong.** On the real local worker a verified done stayed as loose files in the task's checkout (the agent cannot commit: its git directory is outside its sandbox), and the landing path only lands committed work ("only committed work lands"), so nothing could land until an operator committed by hand. The test of H12t did exactly that.

**What is built.**
- `GitBridge.release({gitDir, checkout, requestId, taskId, attemptId?})` (`packages/worker/src/workspace/git.ts`): stages the checkout with the existing `stage` (which refuses a Git-named entry, a link or a submodule anywhere, whole), and commits the staged tree with `commit-tree` + `update-ref` on the checkout's own git directory. Nothing else is touched (the shared repository is not read at all).
  - Author and committer are fixed by the platform (`NimbleNewt release <release@nimblenewt.invalid>`); the message and the trailers (`NimbleNewt-Task`, `NimbleNewt-Release: <request>`, `NimbleNewt-Attempt: <attempt>`) are built from the request, the task and the attempt, all checked plain names. Nothing the agent wrote (file content, PLAN.md, a process environment) reaches them.
  - Safe in a checkout the agent can write: argv only (no shell, no alias), the fixed sanitised environment (no inherited `GIT_*`), the repository is the host's own `--git-dir`, `core.hooksPath` points at an empty directory on every command (the `reference-transaction` hook would otherwise run on `update-ref`), `core.fsmonitor` is off, no user or system configuration, and the host writes `info/attributes` (`* -filter -ident -text -working-tree-encoding`), which outranks every `.gitattributes` the agent can write, so a path cannot name a filter or a conversion. The head moves from the staged head to the new commit only (compare-and-swap), and the commit is listed in the host-side release ledger (`nn-release-ledger`) before the head moves.
  - Nothing to commit is an ordinary answer (`committed: false`), so asking twice makes one commit.
- `WorkspaceHost` option `release: true` turns on the `release` operation (`#release`). It reads the owner's landing policy first (an unreadable policy, or a policy that refuses, stops the release before anything is committed, the same fail-closed rule as a landing), commits, and answers with the commit, the parent, the tree, the file count, the attempt, the ignored-file count, the protected paths the commit touches (`protectedHeld`, from the default list plus the owner's `workspace.landing.protectedPaths`) and `permitRequiredToLand`. A host without the option still answers `release` with the old typed refusal. The request ID is journalled like the other operations (carried out once; a repeat answers the record).
- **The permit rule is the landing's, and a release commit never counts as a permit commit.** It is not written to the permit ledger, so `unpermitted` still lists it and a landing under the default policy (`requirePermit` true) refuses it ("do not carry the commit permit"); under `workspace.landing.requirePermit=false` it lands. Protected paths are committed (the commit is in the checkout, not the shared tree) and named in the answer; the landing keeps them for review as before.
- The attempt: `LocalWorkspaces.ensure({..., attemptId})` records the attempt that last worked in the task folder (`<task>/attempt`, beside the checkout, never mounted, written atomically, a name that is not plain is not recorded), `locate` reads it back as `CheckoutLocation.attemptId`. `scripts/local-host.mjs` and `scripts/remote-host.mjs` pass `order.attemptId`. The commit therefore names the attempt that most recently worked in the checkout.
- It is reachable the way the other operations are: `workspace.request` with `operation: "release"` (owner or whoever may ask), which the controller already wraps in the quiesce and records.

**Tests.** `packages/worker/src/workspace/release.test.ts` (10, real git): the commit's identity, message, trailers, parent and ledgers, no second commit, shared tree untouched, forged author in the process environment and forged trailers in PLAN.md ignored; a repeated request ID; hostile hooks path, `reference-transaction` hook, file-system monitor, filter named by `.gitattributes`, alias, `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE` and `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` do not run or apply; nested `.git` and a symlink refuse the whole release; protected paths named and held at landing, permit refusal and `requirePermit=false` landing; an unreadable or refusing policy; a host without the option; the attempt record (forged name, bad file on disk); ignored files counted. `packages/integration/src/h12t-product-host.test.ts` now asks the real product host for `release` through `workspace.request` (instead of the operator's `git commit`) for both projects, checks the platform identity and the attempt trailer, that the checkout is clean afterwards, that the default policy still refuses the landing and that it lands under `requirePermit=false`.

**Mutation checks (each applied alone, a test failed, then restored).** No `info/attributes` (filter test); no `core.hooksPath` flag (hook test); `process.env` passed to git (the `GIT_INDEX_FILE` check); release writing the permit ledger (the ledger and permit assertions); an unreadable policy swallowed; protected patterns ignored; attempt-name pattern loosened to allow white space; identity not set (author falls back to the generic one). Product test: the attempt not passed by the launcher, and `release` not enabled on `LocalWorkspaces`.

**Not done.**
1. **No automatic release after a done.** The commit is made when `release` is asked for (owner, chat, or a later automatic step). Nothing yet asks after a verified done, because the right moment (before or after review) belongs to the review pipeline: the Q01b/P10 submission flow. The old approach of `commitOnce`/`CommitPort` (the review gate's permit, exactly-once recording, `NimbleNewt-Request` trailer) is untouched and not wired: a release commit is *not* a reviewed commit, and nothing here lets it pass a landing that requires the permit. Wiring `commitOnce` to a real `CommitPort` over `GitBridge.commit` (the permit path) is still H12o's main remaining work and needs the submission record.
2. **No submit/stage port in the product composition** (W09); unchanged.
3. **PLAN.md is still committed and landed.** Leaving it out of the commit would leave it as an untracked file, which makes the checkout "dirty" and stops every landing; keeping it out cleanly needs the dirty check, the permit's file list and `markIntegrated` to agree on an exclusion (the open W05/H12o item above). Decision unchanged, now with this reason.
4. **Crash between `commit-tree` and `update-ref`** leaves an unreachable commit and no head change; the next release makes a new commit. The compare-and-swap of the head move has no test of its own (a race cannot be forced without a test seam); it is the same call `GitBridge.commit` already makes.
5. **A release does not refuse ignored files**; it counts them and says a landing will not start (the landing refuses a checkout holding ignored files).
6. The commit names the attempt that last *started* in the checkout. If a later attempt has started but done nothing, a release before it ends would name that later attempt (a release behind the quiesce with a live attempt is possible).
7. The remote host (`scripts/remote-host.mjs`) uses `LocalWorkspaces` too and so also answers `release` now, under its own configuration's landing policy. Its own protected paths come from `carried` only through the landing function; not separately tested there.

**Interplay with P10 (branch `card20-p10`, not on main, not depended on).** P10's integrator lease serialises *landings* per project. A release commit is made inside one task's own git directory and never writes the shared tree, so it needs no lease and does not conflict. After P10 merges, a landing of a release commit holds the lease as any landing does, and `requirePermit` still decides whether the platform commit may land; if P10 introduces its own commit-for-landing step, that step should replace asking `release` rather than stack on it. A lease holder that wants a commit made first can ask `release` (journalled, once per request ID).

- ASSUMPTION: the release commit is made without a review-gate permit and is landable only where the owner set `workspace.landing.requirePermit=false`; the smallest safe choice that keeps the permit rule where it is (the landing) and lets the product land committed work once the owner opts out. Reversible: remove `release: true` in `LocalWorkspaces`.
- ASSUMPTION: protected paths are reported at release and held at landing, not left out of the commit; leaving them out would make the checkout dirty and stop the landing of the rest.
- ASSUMPTION: the platform identity is one fixed name and a reserved `.invalid` address; the agent's name is not used as author because the commit says the platform made it.

### H12o (product slice): clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 697fe96d after merging origin/main b48923a4 (P10 first slice, H12a part 3, H12s, H12t, redaction). One conflict, in these notes (both sides kept). The "Interplay with P10" paragraph above was written before P10 merged; P10 is now on main and nothing in it conflicts (a release writes no shared tree and needs no lease).

- **Fixed: a file swapped for a link during staging could put any host-readable file into the commit.** `git add` looks at a path (`lstat`), sees a plain file and then opens it *by path*, following a link. An agent process still running in its sandbox (a quiesce settles calls, it does not stop the agent's own processes; a background loop survives) can swap a file, or a directory on the way, for a link to a file outside the checkout in that window and put its own file back afterwards; the host's git reads the outside file with the host's rights and stages it as a plain file. Shown against git 2.53 with a swap loop: the outside file's content was staged within 19 tries. It affected `stage`, so both the release and the permit `commit`. Every written file is now read again by `stage` without following any link (each name checked by `resolveSafe`, the file opened `O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK`, must be a plain file) and its Git blob ID must equal the staged one, or the whole stage is refused as tampering (`link_refused`, `tamper`, reported as a security sign). The agent cannot make its own file hash like a file it cannot read. Test: a git wrapper (the bridge's existing `git` option) leaves exactly what the race leaves, deterministically.
- **Changed with it: the neutral attributes file is written by every `stage`**, not only by a release, so the byte-for-byte check also holds for a permit commit in a checkout whose `.gitattributes` asks for `text=auto`, `eol` or `ident` (the content is committed exactly as written; no line-ending conversion). Test: CRLF with `* text=auto eol=lf ident` is committed unchanged.
- **Added: the head's compare-and-swap has a test** (a wrapper moves the head between staging and `commit-tree`; the release fails and the moved head is kept). FIFOs and sockets in the checkout are skipped by `git add` (tested: no hang, not committed).
- **Fixed: one file name that is not valid UTF-8 made every release fail as uncertain.** The Git-name walk read names as text and then could not find the file again (`ENOENT`, an untyped error), so the host left the request `started` and the controller recorded it as uncertain. The walk now reads raw names and refuses a non-UTF-8 name as a typed refusal (and skips a name deleted while it walks). Test: `release.test.ts`.
- **Fixed: the `workspace.request` description still said a host refuses `release`.** It now says what the release does and that it is not a permit commit (API docs regenerated).
- **Checked and sound.** The task's git directory, the release ledger and the attempt record are outside every sandbox mount (`attempt.ts` refuses a plan where the git directory overlaps a mount and protects it), so the agent can write none of them; its whole surface is the checkout's files and names. Every git call is argv only with a fixed environment (no inherited `GIT_*`, `HOME` an empty folder, no system or global configuration), hooks pointed at an empty folder, the monitor off, a 120 s timeout and a 16 MB output bound. A nested `.git` (directory or `gitdir:` file) and every Git-named spelling are refused by the walk; one created after the walk is staged by git as a submodule entry and refused; paths go through `-z` listings and no pathspec is given. Filters, `ident`, `working-tree-encoding` and diff drivers named by `.gitattributes` need configuration the agent cannot write, and the host's `info/attributes` outranks them anyway. Messages and trailers come only from the request ID, task ID and attempt ID, each matched by a plain-name pattern. A repeated request ID answers the journal; a crash after `commit-tree` leaves an unreachable commit (listed in the release ledger only if the crash came after the append), never a moved head without the ledger line.
- **Mutations of this review (each alone, built, release tests run, restored): all killed.** The no-follow re-check removed; the re-check kept but the hash comparison removed (this one first survived because the test's own wrapper left a stray file in the checkout; the test now keeps its copy outside and names the refused path); `update-ref` without the old value; the neutral attributes not written by `stage`; `core.fsmonitor=false` removed; `core.hooksPath` removed; the author taken from the process environment; the release also writing the permit ledger; the Git-name walk skipped.
- **Left as they are (noted).**
  1. An honest agent process still writing files while a release runs (it should not, behind the quiesce) gets the same tamper refusal and security sign as a swap.
  2. A very large or sparse file is staged and re-read in full; only the 120 s git timeout bounds it, and a release does not apply the 8 MB per-file limit a change through the bridge has.
  3. A plain file the agent turns into a FIFO between git's look and its read makes `git add` wait until the 120 s timeout; the release then fails and the request is recorded as uncertain. The re-check opens without blocking.
- ASSUMPTION: a permit commit is now also made with Git's line-ending and `ident` conversions off. A project that relied on `.gitattributes` normalisation gets the bytes the agent wrote; the smallest change that lets the staged content be checked exactly. Reversible: write the attributes file only in `release` and compare permit stages with filters applied.

### H12o (product slice): second clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 256e9398 after merging origin/main be874821 (T07, A09 sixth slice, U11d; no conflicts).

- **Fixed: the first review's re-read could itself be led outside the checkout, so its hash check could agree with what git read there.** `O_NOFOLLOW` covers the last name only. `resolveSafe` looks at each name on the way and the file is then opened by its whole path, so a *directory on the way* swapped for a link between the walk and the open is followed. That is exactly the swap that let git read a host file, and then both reads hit the same outside file and the blob IDs match. The re-read had no check after the open at all, so even a swap left in place passed. The same gap was in `#readChecked` (the older `integrate` path: a host file carried into the shared workspace) and narrowed but racy in `reapply`'s write (its `realpath` look after the open can be fooled by a swap back). New `openedAt(handle, absolute)` (`paths.ts`), applied after every such open, before anything is read or cut: on Linux the kernel's own path of the open file (`/proc/self/fd/N`) must be the checked canonical path, which does not race. Elsewhere the file at the path must be the opened one and its directory must still be real (narrows the window, does not close it). After a tamper refusal, `stage` also resets the index to the head, so the index no longer names the blob read from outside. `#readChecked` now opens without blocking (a file swapped for a FIFO after the walk hung `integrate`).
- **Tests** (deterministic, through a new test seam `GitBridge.create({ hooks: { beforeOpen } })` that runs between the path check and the open): a release whose git staged a host file and whose `src` becomes a link to the host directory after the walk is refused, the head and ledger are unchanged, and the index no longer names the host blob (`release.test.ts`); `integrate` with the same swap leaves the shared workspace untouched; `integrate` with a file swapped for a FIFO is refused, not hung; `reapply` with its directory swapped does not cut or write the host file (`git.test.ts`).
- **Mutations (each alone, built, release and git tests run, restored): all killed.** `openedAt` always true (2 tests); no index reset; `#readChecked` opening with blocking (the file hangs to its timeout); the fallback without the directory check (with the Linux path off: 3 tests); the Linux check comparing the file name only (2 tests); `reapply` with neither check after its open. The fallback alone (Linux path off) passes every test.
- **Checked against a real sandbox** (the product's `bubblewrapBackend` plan from `attemptSandbox`, bubblewrap 0.11.1): the agent runs as the host's own user (uid 1000). A hard link from its home, from a read-only input or from a system directory into `/work` fails with `EXDEV` (each bind mount is its own mount), so an agent cannot hard-link a file it could not already read into the checkout, and a link count above one is not a leak. The task's git directory does not exist inside the sandbox, so writing there fails. The agent *can* make `/work/sub` a link to a host path; it cannot read through it itself, but the host can (shown), which is why every host-side read of the checkout must stay inside it.
- **Checked and sound.**
  - What is committed is the tree from `write-tree`, made from the same index whose blob IDs the re-read is compared with, before the comparison. After the comparison only `git status` reads the checkout, and it prints names and codes, no content. `commit-tree` and `update-ref` read objects, never the working tree. A swap after the comparison therefore changes nothing that is committed.
  - The hash is Git's object ID (`blob <size>\0` + content, SHA-1 or SHA-256 by the ID's length).
  - A file git did not re-read (its stat information matched) keeps its old blob. A file git read from outside differs from the head, so it is in the diff and is re-read.
  - Clean, smudge, `ident`, line-ending and encoding conversions are switched off by the host's `info/attributes` (the legacy `crlf` attribute loses to `-text`), and a filter driver needs configuration the agent cannot write.
  - A gitlink is refused. An ignore rule only hides the agent's own files (they are counted, and a landing refuses a checkout holding ignored files). The executable bit is carried and harmless (the host runs nothing from the checkout).
  - The identity, message, trailers, ledger-before-head order and compare-and-swap are as the first review says.
- **Left as they are (noted).**
  1. On macOS and Windows the check after the open is the second look (no kernel path of an open file in Node there). A swap that is undone within microseconds of the open can still pass. A full fix needs `openat`-style opening (not in Node) or `F_GETPATH`/`GetFinalPathNameByHandle` through a native helper. The Linux worker, the product's sandboxed host, is closed.
  2. `reapply` opens a missing target with `O_CREAT`. Through a directory swapped at that instant, an *empty* file can be created in a host directory before the check refuses the write (nothing is cut or written into an existing file).
  3. In the parent-swap case, git's walk through a swapped directory can stage names from the host directory. The refusal names the first one (at most 80 characters), so one host file name can appear in the refusal reason.
  4. On a case-insensitive disk (macOS), a tracked `README.md` renamed to `readme.md` is committed under both names (the bare git directory does not set `core.ignorecase`). That is a correctness matter for the landing, not a leak.
  5. Size: `git add` reads every file before the 10,000-file limit is applied, and a release has no per-file size limit. Only the 120 s git timeout and the agent's own disk limit bound it (blobs are written to the host-side git directory).
- ASSUMPTION: Linux (`/proc` present) is the platform where the release must be race-free; other hosts keep the narrower second-look check, noted above. Reversible: add a native path-of-handle helper later.

## Secret scanner remaining gaps: look-alike letters and the launcher scripts (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Not a numbered card. It takes the two open items left by the redaction coverage follow-up and its reviews ("Not done": the scripts still strip only `Bearer ...`; "Homoglyphs are not folded").

**Done**

- **Look-alike letters are read as the Latin letter** (`security/secret-scan.ts`, `CONFUSABLES`, applied in `fold`). A Cyrillic or Greek letter that looks like a Latin one (`р` in `ghр_…`, `о` in `tоken=` or `passwоrd:`, `ѕ` in `sk-`, a dotless `ı`, Armenian `օ`, the Latin small capitals) no longer hides a key or a key name. It is a small fixed one-to-one map of about 70 code points, written as numbers so no look-alike letter sits in the source. It changes only the matching VIEW: the text keeps its own characters, a match is redacted at its original offsets, and one-to-one means the view offsets cannot drift. Zero-width and format characters, NFKC, combining marks and line splits were already seen through; they combine with this (test: look-alike plus zero-width plus line break in one key). Config, worker, pi-adapter and contracts get it through the regenerated copies (`node scripts/copy-credential-scan.mjs`; the staleness test and the behaviour test `integration/credential-scan-drift.test.ts`, which now has look-alike cases, pass).
- **The launcher and host scripts print errors through the shared scanner** (`scripts/safe-error.mjs`, `safeMessage(error, max)`). `remote-host.mjs` (`describe`), `remote-worker.mjs`, `local-host.mjs` (four places), `nimblenewt.mjs`, `nimblenewt-controller.mjs`, `-launcher.mjs`, `-service.mjs` and `-updater.mjs` used `Bearer\s+\S+` stripping or raw `error.message`; they now use the built contracts package's `safeText` (the same code as the worker host). Argument-parsing errors, which echo what the person typed (`--bogus-<key> needs a value`), are cleaned too. When the contracts package is not built (a failure before the first build is the likeliest time to print an error) a conservative fallback removes `Bearer` text, named assignments and every run of 20 or more key characters; it removes more than the scanner would, never less than the old rule.
- **A false-positive corpus** (`security/secret-lookalikes.test.ts`): npm integrity hashes (`sha512-…==`, `sha1-…`), git SHAs and `Merge:` lines, ref lines, UUIDs, Docker `@sha256:` and `Image ID:`, go.sum and go.mod hashes, SSH ed25519 and rsa public keys, macOS `/var/folders/…` and `/private/var/folders/…` temporary paths, Windows `C:\Users\runneradmin\AppData\Local\Temp\…`, GitHub blob URLs, query strings, and Russian, Greek and Armenian sentences plus a long all-Cyrillic word: all unchanged and not refused. Corpus values are generated from a seeded generator, so each run tests the same strings.
- **Linear time**: a timing test over look-alike runs, repeated look-alike prefixes and names, one long mixed-script word, zero-width characters between look-alikes, quote and plus joins and a line per key shape. It compares the time for 64 KB with the time for 1 MB (16 times the text; a quadratic matcher would take 256 times as long) with a wide margin, plus a 20 s ceiling, so a loaded machine does not make it flaky. The non-ASCII path costs about 15 microseconds a character (1 MB about 2 to 4 s on this busy machine); the pre-existing ASCII path is about four times faster.
- **Mutation checks** (each alone, tests failed, restored): the confusable lookup removed (three of the look-alike tests fail); `safeMessage` reduced to the old Bearer-only rule (three script tests fail).

**Not done**

- Letters that merely resemble Latin ones in meaning rather than shape (a Greek `ε` for `e`, Cyrillic `з` for `3`, `ь` for `b`) are not in the map; the list is the common exact look-alikes. Extending it is a data change in one place, but each added pair makes a longer chance that ordinary non-Latin text maps to a key shape, which the corpus guards.
- Keys split by plain spaces, written as JSON `\u` escapes or HTML entities, or built through a variable or function call, are still not found (unchanged decision: joining across spaces would blank ordinary text).
- The sandboxed worker's `console` output and a child's stdout other than channel lines are still not redacted at the source (the host redacts what it reports).
- The scripts' own FILE output (for example `y02-checkpoint.mjs` `show(e.message)`, which prints strict-JSON parse errors of repository evidence files, not credentials) and `qa`/`coverage`/`roadmap` tooling messages are unchanged: they are developer tooling about the repository, not the runtime launcher.
- `release/service-units` word test (`secret`, `token`, ... in an argument name) is about names and stays as it was.

**ASSUMPTION:** the confusables are applied to every text, not only to text that already mixes scripts. A pure-Cyrillic key-shaped string is rare, and a mixed-script rule would let a key written entirely in look-alikes (for instance an all-Cyrillic `ѕесrеt`) through.
**ASSUMPTION:** the scripts load the contracts build at start (top-level `await import`) rather than importing the controller, because the launcher scripts already run from the built tree and the controller copy is large.
**ASSUMPTION:** developer tooling scripts (`qa`, `coverage`, `roadmap`, `y02-checkpoint`) are out of scope: they print repository facts, never a credential an agent could have written.

**Review (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-12).** Done with a differential property test: each random text was built from pieces with a plain Latin spelling and a disguised one (look-alikes, fullwidth, math-bold surrogate pairs, ligatures, zero-width, tag and accent characters, line wraps, quote joins), and the pieces a redaction covered had to be the same in both spellings (15,000 cases before the fixes found 27 mismatches; none after, 27,000 cases).

- **Fixed: a key's tail was printed.** The look-alike map was read only after NFKC, and NFKC turns the capital lunate sigma (U+03F9, on the list as `C`) into a plain capital sigma that is not on it, so the key ended there and the rest of it stayed in the text. The map is now read for the character as written first, then after NFKC (a math-bold Greek rho still reaches `p`). The small lunate sigma (U+03F2) is added as `c`. Tests: every entry of the list alone in a key's body, and the property test.
- **Fixed: a wrapped key took the next line's word.** The check that a line-joined match ran on into the next line's word matched the ORIGINAL text with the ASCII pattern, so a token in fullwidth or look-alike letters failed it and the next line's word (`office`) was redacted too. The piece is now folded first.
- **Fixed: `safe-error.mjs` found the build only in a plain path.** It read its folder from the URL's pathname, which keeps percent escapes, so a checkout under `John Smith` or a non-ASCII folder always used the fallback. It uses `fileURLToPath` now (test with both).
- **Fixed: the fallback missed shapes the scanner finds.** It now also removes a password in an address (`postgres://user:password@host`), key prefixes whose shortest key is under 20 characters (`sk-` with 16, `xoxb-` with 10), web tokens, and invisible characters and accents BEFORE NFKC (which would join an accent to its letter and break the run). It still does not read look-alikes. It also drops combining marks from other scripts' text (Hindi, Thai vowel signs) in the rare case it is used.
