- The timing test takes the faster of two runs of the 1 MB text. Measured worst cases (look-alike floods, zero-width floods, `ghp_` lines, quote joins, ligatures, marks, line joins): 1 MB in 0.14 to 0.65 s, ratio to 64 KB 11 to 28, heap under 300 MB.
- Mutations (each alone, tests failed, restored): lookup only after NFKC; lookup only before NFKC; wrapped-key check unfolded; Armenian `n`, the Latin small capitals, a Greek capital, Cyrillic `a` each removed from the list; `safe-error` root from the pathname; the fallback's address rule removed.
- **Left as they are (noted).** 1. A look-alike that is mapped and glued to the front of a short key (Cyrillic `а` + `sk-` and 16 characters) now hides it, as a Latin `a` always did: the mapped letter is a word letter for the patterns' `\b`. A key of 32 or more characters is still found as a high-entropy run. 2. A precomposed accented letter (`ś`) is not read as its base letter (only separate combining marks are left out). 3. Base64 image data (`data:image/png;base64,…`) is redacted as a high-entropy run, which is plain ASCII and older than this slice. 4. `local-host.mjs` prints `scripts.problem()` and `environments.problem`, and `nimblenewt-service.mjs` echoes an unknown command word, without the scanner. These are the host's own sentences or a word the person typed, not an error's text.
- **ASSUMPTION:** U+03F2 is added to the list because it is the lower-case partner of an entry already there and looks exactly like `c`. Reversible: one number.
## P10 (second slice): leases only on the landing branch, retired holders fenced, forced releases told (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Takes three of the follow-ups the first slice's review left open (its "left as they are" list, items 1, 5 and 6).

- **What was built, plainly.**
  1. **No squatting.** `integrator.lease.acquire` now refuses any branch other than the one the owner's policy names as the project's landing branch (`forbidden`, saying which branch it is). A project with no landing branch cannot have a lease taken at all (`forbidden`, "the owner sets the landing branch first"); an unreadable policy is `unavailable`. The branch is read at each ask, so moving the landing branch moves what can be taken. The branch is compared exactly, as at landing. An agent with the right can therefore no longer fill a task's eight-lease index with invented branch names or hold a branch that nothing lands on. The check runs after the holder checks, so a bad holder is still reported first.
  2. **A retired or disabled holder does not keep the branch.** Two parts. (a) A landing under a lease whose holder is not an active agent is refused `fenced`, whether the holder or the owner (acting for it, with or without the numbers) asks; this is checked at both showings, like the right itself. (b) When another agent takes the branch while the old holder is retired and its lease is still live, the old lease is ended on the spot (a release with the note "its holder is no longer an active agent"), then the new hold is granted with the next fence. Nobody waits for the expiry. Nothing runs at the moment of retirement itself: the lease is ended lazily, at the next take, and in the meantime it blocks nothing that matters because it cannot land.
  3. **A forced release is in the task's activity.** When the owner ends a live lease (API or chat `integrator.lease.release`), and when a retired holder's lease is ended by the next taker, a line is put in the activity record of the task the lease was held for ("The owner took the integrator lease of branch main away from ann (fence 2)", or "... was ended because ann is no longer an active agent"). It is recorded as the service `integrator-leases`, once per lease and fence (a repeated release adds no second line), and is best effort: a failing activity record never undoes the release. A holder giving its own lease back is not a forced release and gets no line.
- **Composition.** `IntegratorLeaseOps` takes two new optional options, `landingBranch` and `onForcedRelease`; `startController` wires them (`landingBranch` from the same `landingPolicyFrom` the landing gate uses, `onForcedRelease` into `ActivityService.record`). Without them (unit rigs) nothing changes. No new operation, so the generated API documentation is unchanged.
- **Tests.** `landing/lease-p10b.test.ts` on all four storage backends: exact branch (case, other name, moved branch, no branch, unreadable policy; a refused ask leaves no record), the retired holder at both showings and as the owner with and without numbers, the takeover with its new fence and its single told line, an owner release told once and not again, an own release not told, and a failing hook not undoing a release. The composed `api/start-p10-lease.test.ts` now sets the landing branch first, checks the refusals before and after, and reads the two activity lines through `activity.steps`.
- **Mutation checks (each applied alone, built, run, restored): all killed.** Branch comparison removed (4 + 1 failures); retired-holder takeover removed (4 + 1; the mutant also tripped the type checker, but the compiler still emitted it and the tests ran against it); active-holder check at landing removed (4 + 1); forced-release line not told (4 + 1).
- **Not done.** (b) Binding the lease to one task (`valid` still ignores the task): left as is on purpose, because the first slice's design is that one integrator's lease covers every task of the project and the integrator takes it under whatever task it is working; binding would break that. (e) A chat command for the owner to take a lease for an agent (needs agent-name resolution and a free-form interpreter description; still an API action). (f) The `integration` workspace operation still writes the shared tree without the lease. Releasing leases at the moment of retirement or when a task ends (they are ended at the next take, or expire).
- **ASSUMPTION:** the lease is taken only on the landing branch, and a project with no landing branch cannot have a lease taken (the owner sets the landing branch first, which a landing needed anyway). Reversible: drop the `landingBranch` option.
- **ASSUMPTION:** "fence on retirement" means refuse landing plus release at the next take, not an immediate hook on agent retirement, because no retirement event exists to hook without editing the agent service (another card's code), and the lazy form gives the same visible result (no landing, no wait).
- **ASSUMPTION:** the owner's own `integrator.lease.release` is the only forced release by a person; an expiry is not told (nobody acted).
- **ASSUMPTION:** `valid` stays task-blind (see "Not done"); recorded so a later queue slice can bind per-landing if it wants.

## P10 (second slice) review (Claude agent, Opus, clean context, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 22d0a64d after merging origin/main 93580c97 (no conflicts), then 9d4a1ea9 (notes conflict only, both sides kept).

- **Fixed.**
  1. **A long command ID broke the takeover.** The release that ends a retired holder's lease was named `retired-<the taker's command ID>` and scoped; a valid command ID of 113 to 120 characters became longer than 120, so the scoping threw a plain error (not a refusal) while a retired holder's lease was live, and the agent could not take the branch at all. The release is now named from a fixed-length hash of the taker's command ID (the same length as the acquire's own), and the acquire's own ID is checked before anything is released.
  2. **API documentation.** The summaries of `integrator.lease.acquire` and `integrator.lease.release` now say that only the landing branch can be taken, what an unreadable policy answers, that a retired or disabled holder's hold is ended by the next taker, and that an owner's release is a line in the task's activity (regenerated).
- **Checked and left as they are.** The branch the lease is matched to comes from the same `landingPolicyFrom` as the landing (the project's own branch beats the installation's), compared exactly on both sides, so `refs/heads/main`, case, a trailing slash or `..` can never match one side and not the other. A branch moved after a lease was taken: the old lease stays live but lands nothing (`forbidden` at landing, the branch is read again at each showing). The read and the acquire are not atomic, but nothing depends on it for the same reason. Retirement disables the agent's principal in the same step (`agents.retire`), so the principal state covers retired, disabled and deleted. Two agents taking a retired holder's branch at once: one release wins, the other's is `fenced` and ignored, exactly one acquire wins with the next fence, the other is told `unavailable` (tested on all four backends). The activity line is written after the durable release, for the lease's own task only, once per lease and fence (command ID `lease-force:<lease>:<fence>`).
- **Mutation checks (each applied alone, built, run, restored): all killed.** Old takeover command ID (4 failures; checked again against the final test); an expired hold's release told (4); line told before the release (4); branch compared ignoring case (4). The last three needed two new checks: an owner release with a stale fence tells nothing, and ending an expired hold tells nothing.
- **Left open.** A crash after the owner's release is stored and before its activity line is written loses the line: the repeated ask finds the lease released and returns before telling (best effort, as the slice says). A landing that passed its second showing still writes if the lease changes hands in the moment before the host writes (the first slice's design: the host does not check the fence).
  - **A holder whose right `integration.lease` was taken away still keeps the branch** until its hold expires (up to a day) or the owner ends it, and the owner can still land for it. The review first treated such a holder like a retired one, and the full run showed why that is wrong: the owner deliberately takes leases for an agent with no rights at all as a stand-in (the H12q, H12s and H12t integration tests enroll `integrator` with no grants), so "has no right" does not mean "was removed", and letting the next agent with the right end that lease would override the owner's choice. Withdrawn; telling a revoked right from an owner's stand-in needs a record of who chose the holder.
- **ASSUMPTION:** an owner-named holder needs no right of its own (the first slice's design, which the integration tests rely on), so only a retired or disabled holder is ended at the next take. Reversible: record on the lease whether the owner chose the holder, and end only the self-taken leases of agents whose right was revoked.

## L02e (final slice): a remote worker can be told to kill what it holds, is asked for a fresh look, reports its cleanup cost, an old host's last word is kept, and a child is covered by its swarm parent's agent or team (2026-11-12)

What the card still lacked after the earlier slices (read from the card text, every L02d/L02e section and each "not done" list): the three acceptance clauses were met earlier (an agent's Stop ends swarm children, 2000 settled entries do not starve the sweep, a task stopped through its agent shows that cleanup). What stayed on the "not done" lists: (1) a remote worker could not be made to kill what it holds, (2) a live remote report was as old as the worker's last change, (3) a remote Stop billed no cleanup cost, (4) the old host of a moved attempt was never asked, (5) the deployed `scripts/remote-worker.mjs` was never run against a real controller for this, (6) the wider walk was tested only against dispatcher fakes, (7) no mutation checks for part 3's code. Found while testing (6): the task view of a child did not find a Stop of its swarm PARENT's agent or team, although that Stop ends the child's work. All of it is closed here.

**Built** (`remote/protocol.ts`, `remote/service.ts`, `remote/host.ts`, `remote/runner.ts`, `remote/client.ts`, `remote/server.ts`, `lifecycle/stop.ts`):
- *Remote Force Stop.* Two new control messages, `kill` and `look`. `RemoteWorkerHost.endLocalWork` sends `kill` to a worker that holds a live placement; the worker's runner calls its host's `endLocalWork` (the same one local Force Stop uses), then reports again whether or not anything changed. A worker that does not know the message ignores it (the runner never had a branch for an unknown kind), so no protocol version change. A placement that is already over cannot be told anything (nobody reads its messages): what its worker last listed stays listed; a placement that went over meanwhile is not an error.
- *Fresh look.* A report now carries `canLook: true` when the worker answers `look`. `RemoteWorkerHost.localWork` asks such a worker for a fresh look and reads the report sent in answer; a worker that does not answer within `lookWaitMs` (default 3 s) leaves its last report standing with one unknown item "no fresh report from the worker" beside it, so a stale report never reads as clean. A worker that never said `canLook` is read as before and sent nothing. The runner handles messages before it reports, so a `look` or `kill` in one batch reports what is left after the kill.
- *Cleanup cost.* The report carries `computeMs` (the sandbox wind-down compute so far, a running total, refused above a day or if not a whole non-negative number). `localWork` returns it as the attempt's cost, so the existing per-attempt charge ledger bills a remote Stop once. **ASSUMPTION:** only compute is taken from a worker, not money (`costMicros`): a hostile or buggy worker could otherwise invent a currency charge; compute is capped at a day per placement and the controller already trusts a remote worker's usage figures to that degree.
- *The old host.* When an attempt moves, or is placed again after a worker accepted it, the old placement's last list is kept in `earlier` (at most 5, newest last) instead of being dropped. The old worker's final report is still accepted for the placement it held (only final, only in the session that accepted it; anything else is `fenced` as before). Stop reads it: a final list as given, a non-final one as unknown, an earlier placement that listed nothing adds nothing. **ASSUMPTION:** an old host that listed something and never confirmed stays unknown (so a Stop is not clean) until it confirms; nothing can force it, which is the same position as a live remote placement whose worker went silent.
- *The view of a child.* `cleanupSpend`'s covering lookup now also walks the chain of every swarm ancestor (its agent, a team above that agent, the installation), so a Stop of the parent's agent or team answers for the child, naming that scope. The date a request must follow is the ANCESTOR's assignment (a Stop of the parent's agent made before the parent was given to it did not reach the child). A viewer who may not control that scope is told nothing.

**Tests.** `remote/process-report.test.ts` (+6 suites on all four backends, +2 runner tests: 47 tests in the file): old host (list kept as unknown, final word taken, non-final / wrong placement / other host / newer session refused, compute counted), placed-again path, fresh look (asked, answered, unanswered, never asked of a worker that did not say so, never after a final report), Force Stop message (live, over, another host, exact fields), `computeMs` and `canLook` validation, runner kill/look/cost, a host that cannot end local work and a kill that throws. `lifecycle/stop-suite.ts` (+1 suite, four backends): a child is answered by its parent's agent or team, with the ancestor's assignment date. `api/start-stop-local-work.test.ts` (+1): a REAL controller and dispatcher with a live swarm (parent, child, grandchild, another family): an agent's Stop ends the child's and grandchild's attempts and asks their jobs to stop, leaves the other family alone, the child's cleanup view names the agent, a new attempt of the child is held and let go on resume, and the installation's Force Stop ends the remaining family. `packages/integration/src/l05e-remote-worker.test.ts` (+assertions): the deployed `scripts/remote-worker.mjs`, as a real process with a real bubblewrap sandbox against a real controller, gives a final process report that says it can look and lists nothing.

**Mutation checks** (each made alone, each failed the named tests, restored): runner ignores `kill` (2 fail); host never sends `kill` (4); host never asks for a look (16); a stale report not flagged (4); a move drops the old list (8); an old host's non-final report accepted (8); old host's session not checked (4); the `computeMs` cap removed (4); an old non-final list read as running instead of unknown (12); the runner reports before it handles messages (1); the runner takes another attempt's compute (survived the first test, whose list had our attempt first; the test now puts the other attempt first, then 1 fails); an ancestor's agent not covering a child (1, per backend file run); the child's own assignment date used for the ancestor's agent (1). **Part 3's code, which had no recorded mutation check:** local `release` confirming with a process listed (4); `release` ignoring a worker not yet stopped (1); a Stop not looking at finished-but-unconfirmed attempts (1); the unconfirmed list never added (4); a confirmation leaving the attempt on the list (4)

**Not done.**
- A remote Force Stop reaches only a worker that holds a live placement. A placement already over, or a worker program too old to know `kill`, is not killed: Stop shows what it last listed and Force Stop's own look names what is left. The real deployed program was not driven through a Force Stop of a process that ignores the close (that needs a long-lived sandbox process in the fixture; the runner, protocol and host are tested with stubs and the real service on four backends, and the real program through a whole attempt).
- The remote cleanup compute is the worker's own report; the controller cannot measure it.
- Windows sandboxes still list no processes (unchanged).
**L02e acceptance: met.** The card's three acceptance clauses were met earlier and re-checked here end to end on a real controller; every deliverable item on its list is now delivered, within the limits above. The card is left for the owner to flip.

**Clean-context review of the final slice (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-12).** Merged origin/main a9338dae first (notes conflict only, both sides kept).
- **Fixed: repeated looks pushed a worker's other control messages out of its queue.** Every Stop pass sends a `look` (twice: once for the list, once for the costs) and the queue keeps the last 20 messages. A worker that was unreachable for a few passes came back to find its `stop`, `checkpoint`, `restart` or note gone. Now a `look` or `kill` replaces a queued one of its kind, so they take at most two places (`RemoteWorkerService.control`).
- **Fixed: hosts were asked one after another.** Each remote host can wait up to 3 s for a fresh look, so a Stop over many hosts waited 3 s per host, twice per pass. `DispatcherService.localWorkOf` now asks 16 hosts at a time and reads the answers in host order as before.
- **Fixed: a list nobody confirmed could be silently dropped.** Moves are unbounded and `earlier` keeps 5. The sixth move dropped the oldest entry even when it still listed processes nobody confirmed, so a Stop could read clean. Entries that list nothing (confirmed empty first, then never reported or empty) now go first. An entry that listed something is counted in `earlierLost` (placements, processes, compute). The host that holds the attempt now shows it as one unknown item and still counts its compute. Nothing can confirm it any more. **ASSUMPTION:** this is the same position as an old host that never answers (unknown until Force Stop's own look settles it with the owner).
- **Tests made robust:** the answered-look case waited 400 ms on all four backends. It now waits up to 30 s, which ends as soon as the answer is in, and a separate 300 ms host covers the silent case. The two runner kill/look tests ended the turn after 700/400 ms; they now end it once the scripted messages were handled.
- **Mutation checks (mine, each alone, all killed):** looks not coalesced (4); `earlier` cut oldest-first (4); the kept count not shown (4); hosts asked one at a time (4); `kill` not bound to its placement (1, new stub test); the runner ignoring `look` (1); `canLook` not checked (4).
- **Checked and left:** an old host's final report still needs the host's current session and the session that accepted that placement (`#session` binds the session to the host), and nothing follows a final. `computeMs` is a whole number of at most a day per report and per placement, and the ledger charges a per-attempt running maximum, so a repeated or replayed report never charges twice. A worker's own word stays the only source for a live placement: a worker that omits `canLook` is read as before (as documented). The swarm walk keeps its hop bound and cycle check, and checks the viewer per covering scope. New tests make no POSIX, signal or file-name assumptions, and the deployed-program assertions sit inside the bubblewrap-gated integration test.
## K01i finish: remote hosts' conversation stores, named barrier participants, owner stop of live work, production wiring

What the card still lacked after the earlier slices: (1) the conversation stores kept on other hosts were not in backups or restores; (2) the maintenance barrier had only two participants, so the retention runner, the notification sweeps, the hand-off and resume sweeps and the maintenance loop could write while a restore was staged; (3) a restore was simply refused while agents ran, with no way for the owner to stop them; (4) the local and remote host launchers did not hand their stores to the backup code. All four are built.

- **Remote stores** (`remote/pi-state.ts`). A backup asks every active, fresh host through the existing workspace-ask channel (`pi-state-send`); the host copies its stores with the existing hardened `copyPiState` into a scratch folder and uploads them in 512 KiB base64 chunks (in order, per-file sha256, a repeated chunk is accepted once). The controller verifies index, counts and digests, then writes them with `writePiState` as stores named `rh.<hostslug>.<key>`. Offline, stale or failing hosts are named in the backup's problems; the backup still completes. A restore puts those stores on the controller disk first (the existing staged restore, under `restored-pi-state/<id>`); after the restart a sweep (every 30 s, option `backup.restore.remotePiEveryMs`) delivers each to its host (`pi-state-restore`). The host stages beside the final path, swaps, keeps `.before-restore-<stamp>` asides, rolls back on failure and refuses a store whose attempt is running. Delivered copies move to `restored-pi-state-delivered`. The sweep skips staged copies, asides and anything while the barrier, a pending restore or a restore journal exists (the integration test found the first bug here).
- **Barrier participants** (`NamedWork` in `backup/barrier.ts`): `retention-runner`, `notification-sweeps`, `handoff-and-resume-sweeps`, `maintenance-loop`. A held function does not start; the hold waits for what runs; letting go starts it again. `services.barrierWork` exposes the names for tests.
- **Owner stop** (`backup.restore.apply` with `stopAttempts: true`, chat proposal says so). Before the barrier is raised, the owner's own graceful Stop of the whole installation is requested and driven to its end (`backup/stop-work.ts`), then the dispatcher is ticked until no attempt is recorded as running. Without the flag nothing changes and the old refusal stands. The plan warns how many attempts run.
- **Production wiring.** `scripts/local-host.mjs` and `scripts/remote-host.mjs` give the host the product layout `attempts/<id>/home/pi` (`LocalConversationStores` option `homeFolder`) and the remote host answers the two new asks. The pre-upgrade backup uses local stores only.
- **Tests.** `remote/pi-state.test.ts` (all four storage backends: reference, SQLite, SQLite worker thread, PostgreSQL), `backup/k01i-finish.test.ts`, `integration/k01i-multi-host.test.ts` and `integration/k01i-stop-attempts.test.ts` (SQLite and PostgreSQL through `startController`), `scripts/remote-host.test.mjs`. Mutation checks, each applied alone and restored: removing the held check in `NamedWork` (hangs, killed), skipping the stop call (killed), removing the settle step (killed); earlier in the work: the sweep name filter and the in-flight/busy checks were each killed by their tests.
- **ASSUMPTION:** remote store IDs are `rh.<hostslug>.<key>` (slug = host ID without `host:`), so they can never clash with local attempt IDs.
- **ASSUMPTION:** delivery to hosts happens by the 30 s sweep after the restart, not during the restore; a host that is offline waits and is shown in `backup.restore.status` (`remotePiState`). An agent still running on a host keeps its store (refused, retried).
- **ASSUMPTION:** a backup with an unreachable host is still a complete backup; the host is named in its problems every time until it answers.
- **ASSUMPTION:** `stopAttempts` leaves the work stopped if the restore then fails or is cancelled; the owner resumes it with the normal lifecycle controls. Making that automatic would risk starting work the owner wanted stopped.
- **Cannot be shown offline.** Windows and macOS runs, a real (non-embedded) PostgreSQL server, real remote hardware, and real agent behaviour (a running agent pushing stale state after a delivery). The multi-host acceptance used a stand-in host process, not real sandboxed agents.

### K01i finish: clean-context review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed 39643428 after merging origin/main a9338dae (notes conflict only, both sides kept). Fixes are in `remote/pi-state.ts`, `remote/service.ts`, `backup/staged-restore.ts`, `api/start.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`; tests in `remote/k01i-fin-review.test.ts`.

- **Fixed (an older backup's conversation delivered after a newer restore).** A store an earlier restore left for an offline host stayed in `restored-pi-state/` when a later restore did not contain it, and the 30 s sweep would then put the OLDER conversation on the host, behind the data the controller runs on. When a restore is applied (both at the forward swap and when a crash resumes a finished journal), every `rh.*` store there that this restore did not put there itself is moved to `restored-pi-state-superseded/` (never deleted; running again finds nothing more).
- **Fixed (an attempt resumed on its host before its store came back).** After the restart the dispatcher resumed attempts at once; on a remote host the agent then ran on the conversation from before the restore, and the delivery between two turns replaced it, taking the newest turns away. `RemoteWorkerService.refusals` now passes a host over for an attempt whose restored store waits for it there (`restoreWaits`, a reason that passes: the attempt waits, the owner is not told, H07e); a check that cannot be read holds it too. Deliberately not judged at `place`: a refusal there can end an attempt that has no other host.
- **Fixed (host swap races).** The host asked whether the agent runs only before fetching (minutes for a large store). It now asks again, and judges the store's place again (a `pi` folder or home turned into a link), after staging and right before the first rename; the existence check before moving aside uses `lstat`.
- **Fixed (host disk).** A controller that kept sending chunks without an end could fill the host's disk: a file is never fetched past the size its index line states, the index itself past 128 MiB.
- **Fixed (latent hang).** `RemotePiState.list()` set its release function before it held the lock, so a second listing queued behind the first replaced it and waited forever. Backups are serialised by `BackupService` today, so it could not happen yet.
- **Fixed (owner told).** A restore with `stopAttempts` that fails after the work was stopped (barrier, safety copy, marker) now says the work stays stopped and how to resume it. The `backup.restore.apply` summary no longer says the work stays paused after an APPLIED restore: the stop is recorded after the backup's point in time, so the restored data does not contain it and the work is as the backup recorded it. `backup.restore.cancel` says stopped work stays stopped.
- **Checked and kept.** Owner only: `backup.restore.apply` (and so `stopAttempts`) is `ownerOnly` on the API; a `release.manage` or backup-capable agent cannot stop work. The stop is the owner's graceful installation Stop (bounded by its step limit and deadline), then at most 60 s of dispatcher ticks; every failure says the work stays stopped. The barrier: a participant that throws or never answers is released by `raise` (timeout), tested with a throwing participant after a stop. `NamedWork` callers discard the `undefined` a held function returns; the dispatcher participant settles the driver before the held writers are reached, and a held writer returns at once inside a tick, so no wait cycle. Path safety: store keys and IDs are `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}` (no `/`, `\`, NUL, `..` start or non-ASCII lookalikes), `rh.<slug>` slugs `[a-z0-9-]`, index `rel` paths validated by `parsePiIndex` and checked again against the store folder, files opened with `wx` (an existing link refuses), transfer file names only `index.jsonl` or `f-<n>`, a transfer answers only the host it was opened for, chunks in order, the same chunk counted once, per-file sha256 checked at the last chunk and again against the index, 512 KiB per chunk, 4 GiB and 200 001 files per transfer. A host's stores are only ever delivered back to the same host (the slug in the name), so a compromised host cannot place a store on another. Stores are files only (no links, devices or modes are carried; written 0600/0700).
- **ASSUMPTION (encryption):** remote hosts' stores are sealed in an encrypted backup exactly like local ones (they are staged in the controller's data directory, 0700, and copied into the backup by `copyPiState` with the backup's cipher). On the way to and from a host and in `restored-pi-state*` they are plain, as local conversation stores are on disk; the channel is the authenticated worker channel. No K01b feature was added.
- **Left open.** (1) A host crash between moving a store aside and moving the restored one in leaves the place empty with the aside beside it; the controller got no answer, so it delivers again (and the attempt is held until it does), which puts the store in place. (2) `.before-restore-<stamp>` asides on hosts (inside the agent's own home) and `restored-pi-state-delivered`/`-superseded` on the controller are never pruned; each restore adds one per store. (3) A compromised host can make a backup stage up to 4 GiB per host on the controller's disk. (4) The pre-upgrade backup stays local-only (implementer's choice).
- **Mutation checks** (each applied alone to the compiled code, run, restored): all 10 killed. Busy re-check removed (1 failure); place re-check removed (1); fetch bound removed (1); retirement ignores what this restore put there (1); the restore wait counted as lasting (3); the restore wait never judged (2); the listing lock's release taken before the lock (1, the second listing hung); the stopped-work note dropped (1); the controller's per-file digest check removed (8, a tampered chunk); the host's swap rollback removed (4, all four backends).

## K01i (last slice): bounded leftovers, bounded staging, backups wired into the production entry (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-14)

What the card still lacked after the finishing slice and its review: (1) the production controller entry never gave the controller a backup service at all, so none of the backup and restore work was reachable in a real installation, and a staged restore always told the owner to restart by hand; (2) every restore left more folders behind (`.before-restore-<stamp>` on each host, `restored-pi-state-delivered` and `-superseded` on the controller) that were never removed; (3) a backup could stage as much as 4 GiB per host on the controller's disk, with no total.

- **Production wiring** (`scripts/nimblenewt-controller.mjs`). The entry now passes `backup: { directory, version?, restore: { restart } }`. Backups are ON by default in `<data>/backups`; `--backup-dir DIR` (or `NIMBLENEWT_BACKUP_DIR`) moves them and `--no-backups` (or `NIMBLENEWT_NO_BACKUPS=1`) turns the service off. Under the launcher (`NIMBLENEWT_RUNNING_RELEASE` set) the backup is stamped with the running release and a staged restore restarts the controller by itself: the entry's own restart request closes the controller and exits 75, which the launcher answers by starting it again, and the restore is applied as it starts. Without the launcher the owner gets the plain instruction (stop and start it again). Tests: unit tests of the settings and options, and `a real controller` end to end through `main()` under launcher variables (backup made, restore applied, exit 75, next start has the restored data, the plain case says restart by hand).
- **Bounded leftovers** (`remote/pi-state.ts`: `pruneAsides`). A host keeps the newest two `.before-restore-<stamp>` copies beside each store after a restore (`PiStateHostOptions.keepAsides`); the controller keeps the newest three delivered and superseded copies of each store (`RemotePiRestoreOptions.keepCopies`, `KEEP_RESTORED_COPIES`), pruned after every delivery sweep. Only real folders whose name ends in a compact UTC stamp are considered, only inside the folder being pruned (a link is never followed, a file or unknown name never removed), and a failure to remove one never fails a restore that is done.
- **Bounded staging** (`RemotePiStateOptions.maxBytes`, default 8 GiB). The sizes the hosts' indexes state are added up over one backup; a host whose stores would take the total past it is left out and named in the backup's problems (the backup still completes with the others); the count starts again at zero for the next backup.
- **Tests.** `remote/k01i-limits.test.ts` (asides pruned and tunable on a host across four restores; pruning rules including a link, a file and unknown names; delivered/superseded pruned after a delivery; the staging cap and a cap with room, each on the reference store, SQLite, SQLite worker thread and PostgreSQL), plus the entry tests above. Mutation checks, each applied alone to the compiled code and restored: staging cap removed (4 failures), cap count never reset (4), one aside too many kept (4), pruning also takes files and links (1), controller never prunes (1), host never prunes (2), and in the entry the automatic restart removed (the end-to-end test failed its assertion and left the controller running, so the run had to be killed: detected, but as a hang). Test counts: controller remote, backup, launcher and restore-restart files 1082/1082, K01i integration files 5/5, entry scripts 22/22. Known flakes were not hit.
- **ASSUMPTION: backups are on by default in the production entry.** The card is "production wiring"; an installation without it had no backups at all. The smallest reversible choice is a default folder inside the data directory with a flag and a variable to move or switch it off. Nothing is encrypted or signed by this wiring (no key material exists to choose; K01b's options remain in `startController` and are not exposed by the entry yet).
- **ASSUMPTION:** two asides on a host and three controller copies are enough to undo the last restore or two; the numbers are options, not owner chat controls (they are internal housekeeping, not decisions about the owner's data).
- **ASSUMPTION:** the pre-upgrade backup stays local-only for conversation stores. It runs before the database is open, and so before any host has connected; there is nobody to ask at that moment.

### K01i last slice: review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-14)

Reviewed b193f0ac after merging origin/main c5809816 (clean merge).

- **Fixed: the copy a restore just set aside could be pruned.** Pruning sorted by the stamp in the name, so with a clock set back (or `keepAsides: 0`) the aside a host had just made, the only copy of what the restore replaced, could be the one removed; the same held for the copy the controller had just delivered. `pruneAsides` now always keeps at least one copy per store and takes a `protect` set (the host protects the aside it just made; the controller the copies the sweep just delivered).
- **Fixed: controller pruning could run while a restore was being prepared.** The sweep checked the hold only at its start; a hold that began during a delivery still let the prune run beside the restore (which moves folders into `restored-pi-state-superseded`). The prune now runs only when no hold and no restore marker or journal is present.
- **Fixed: a scheduled backup could fill the disk.** Now that backups are on by default, `BackupService.runScheduled` first asks the disk (`statfs`, injectable `freeBytes`): with less free than the newest backup's size plus 10% and 256 MiB (`SCHEDULED_FREE_MARGIN`) the scheduled copy is not made, the reason is kept in the status, and the usual one-hour wait applies; an owner's own "back up now" is not held back, and a disk that cannot be asked does not stop the backup. A failed backup already removed its partial folder; the data directory's reserve file stays the last line.
- **Fixed: entry settings.** Under the launcher a relative `--backup-dir`/`NIMBLENEWT_BACKUP_DIR` (which would name a folder inside the release directory) is refused like `--data`; `NIMBLENEWT_NO_BACKUPS` is read strictly (1/true/on, 0/false/off, anything else is an error rather than silently "on"); "no backups" together with a backup folder is refused.
- **Fixed: tests that could hang.** The end-to-end entry test now passes its own stop signal (it used to install SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP handlers in the test process) and, whatever fails, stops the controller and waits for it; with the automatic restart removed it now fails in about 30 s instead of hanging. The staging-cap tests stop the hosts' polling loops in `finally` (with the cap removed the file never ended).
- **Checked.** Backups go to `<data>/backups` unless the owner moves them; the backup copies the database, blobs and conversation stores, not the data folder, so it never copies itself; retention (7 daily, 4 weekly) bounds the count. The exit-75 path is an in-process abort followed by the normal close (no signals), the same path the database move already uses on Windows and macOS. No new API operation; backup and restore remain owner-only. Pruning touches only real folders with a stamp-suffixed name inside the folder pruned; an agent can plant folders only in its own home, where it could remove its asides anyway.
- **Mutation checks** (each alone on the built files, run, restored): host protect removed (1 failure); keep-at-least-one removed (1); prune while a restore is held (1); controller protect removed (1); room check removed (1); staging cap removed (the cap test fails, run on SQLite alone, and the file now ends); automatic restart removed in the entry (1, no hang); default backup folder outside the data folder (2).

## K02 (final slice): signed artifact sets, release.manage, plan and target binding, database schema fall-back (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-12)

This slice closes the remaining offline-buildable acceptance text of card K02 (task-plan "K02 — deterministic release staging and activation"). Nothing is deployed, installed or started anywhere; every test uses temporary release roots, disposable databases and in-process keys.

**What the card still lacked before this slice (from the earlier K02 sections' not-done lists)**
- K02b signed artifact sets and a trust root ("signed/verified exact artifact staging"): digests only.
- K02c a release-management permission distinct from `toolbox.manage` ("release-management permission"): owner only.
- Authorization "bound to digest, migration plan and target installations": digest and platform were bound; plan and installation were not.
- K02d database schema compatibility in the fall-back and in a rollback ("rollback is tested against mixed versions", "failed startup preserves compatible known-good path"): only the worker protocol range was checked.
- "A supervisor role alone cannot change protected extensions" and "an agent-built candidate of NimbleNewt itself cannot stage or activate itself": held only by the owner-only rule, with no test of the boundary against agents with broad grants.

**Built**
- `release/trust.ts` (new): the trust root. Ed25519 public keys (base64 DER SPKI, ID = first 16 hex of its sha256), at most 20, registered by the owner only (`release.trust.add/remove/require`, `release.trust.list`). A signature (`release.signature.attach`, value or file) covers `nimblenewt-release-v1\n<candidate id>\n` (the ID is the digest of the manifest naming every artifact digest). Verified when attached (an untrusted or wrong signature is refused and kept nowhere) and again at every use (a forged or damaged record does not count; a removed key withdraws what only it signed). `require` unset follows the root: once a key is trusted, staging, activation and rollback need a valid signature. The chat refuses anything shaped like a key, so a key or signature may be named as a file in `<root>/trust/` (one plain name, regular file, 512 bytes, no links; the owner names no path).
- Updater: `stageRelease({ trust: { keys, signature } })` and `--trusted-keys FILE --signature-file FILE` check a signature over `nimblenewt-release-digest-v1\n<staged manifest digest>\n` before anything is copied (a different text from the controller's, so neither stands for the other).
- `release.manage` (`security/access.ts` ACTIONS, `activation.ts` `mayManage`): only a grant naming exactly that action for all projects counts (not `*`, not `release.*`, not one project, never a task credential); only the owner makes grants (tested). A holder stages, removes staged, verifies, reads status and trust root, attaches signatures, activates and rolls back; it activates only owner-approved candidates even if the owner switched the approval requirement off for the owner. Policy stays the owner's: approve, submit, settings, trust root, confirm, resolve, acknowledge.
- Manifest `migrationPlan` (sha256) and `targets` (installation names), optional, strict, part of the candidate ID only when present (existing IDs unchanged). `release.activate` takes `migrationPlan`: required exactly when the candidate carries one and equal to it; the chat fills it from the candidate's record (the interpreter's value is dropped) and shows plan, targets and signing key in the preview. `releases.installationId` names this installation; a release with `targets` is staged, activated and rolled back to only where it is listed, and is refused where no name is configured.
- Database schema (K02d): `compat.json` may add `schema: {min,max}`. The controller records the highest schema version it opened in `launcher-state.json` (`db`, only raised) as soon as the database is open (`activation.noteDatabase()`, version read from `storage.snapshot()`, so on all four storage backends). The launcher's fall-back (and watchdog) refuses a last known good whose range ends below it, and says a pre-upgrade snapshot restore (K01) is needed; activation and rollback refuse a release the data has outgrown. `release.status` shows `databaseSchema`, the trust summary and each staged release's schema range.
- Tests: `release/k02-finish.test.ts` (9 tests on each of reference store, SQLite, SQLite worker thread and PostgreSQL = 36), a new end-to-end test in `api/start-activation.test.ts` (real controller, API as owner, release manager and worker-only agent, chat proposal for trusting a key from a file, chat activation with the plan, targets and signature shown), updater library and program tests. Mutation checks, each killed: any signature verifies (4 failures), broad grant counts as release.manage (4), rollback skips the signature check (2), activation skips it (2, after adding a test), fall-back ignores the schema (2), activation ignores the schema (2), targets ignored (2), plan not compared (2), a holder activates without approval (2), updater skips the signature check (2).

**What the card still cannot do offline (precisely)**
1. Running the launcher, updater and service units on a real macOS and Windows machine: the pointer, rename and process-group behaviour there were only exercised on Linux (CI repairs exist, off-Linux runs are not available here). The acceptance "an interruption resolves to old or new, never mixed, on macOS, Linux and Windows" is proven on Linux (crash-point tests on both writers) and by reading the platform rules for the others.
2. Maintenance scope and window enforcement, and the Prepare, Quiesce, Checkpoint, quarantined Activate, Verify, Commit-or-revert sequence: that is the text of card K07 (blockers K02, K01, L06, U11, G05), not K02's own mechanics; K02 now offers the hooks K07 needs (separate permission, bound approval, quoted plan, recorded schema).
3. "Pi runtime changes follow G11": G11 (blocked by K07) owns the runtime upgrade path; K02 only supplies the staging and compatibility records it will use.
4. Deployment-specific supply-chain choices that are the owner's to make later: where public keys come from (here: files the owner places), key rotation policy, a hardware-backed signer. The trust root is built; nothing signs anything automatically.

**ASSUMPTION:** Signing covers the candidate ID (the manifest digest) in the controller path and the staged manifest digest in the updater path (the updater cannot recompute a candidate ID, which needs the whole submitted manifest), with distinct text prefixes.
**ASSUMPTION:** With no `require` setting, trusting a key switches signing on and removing the last key switches it off again (digests alone); the owner who wants it to stay on sets `release.trust.require` true (shown first in chat, as are add and remove).
**ASSUMPTION:** A release that states no `schema` range is not checked by the fall-back (the controller itself refuses to start on a newer database, so the harm is a blocked old release, not corruption); the strict reading would block every legacy release.
**ASSUMPTION:** `release.manage` holders are agents only; their activation always needs the owner's approval record; the owner remains the only one who can change approvals, settings or the trust root.
**ASSUMPTION:** The installation's name for `targets` is the `releases.installationId` option (no installation name existed); with no name, a release that lists targets is refused (fail closed). Chat does not carry keys (the credential scanner refuses them), so keys and signatures are named as files in `<root>/trust/`.
**ASSUMPTION:** A signature is required also for a rollback target (a release staged before any key was trusted must be signed before the owner can go back to it) because a rollback runs old code.

### K02 (final slice): clean-context review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed a9518523 (origin/main 6527c352 already merged, no conflicts). Nothing deployed, no release process started; keys generated at run time in tests.

- Fixed (signature strength): a signature covered only the candidate ID, which is the first 96 bits of the manifest's SHA-256. Two manifests made to share an ID (a birthday search of about 2^48 hashes, within reach of one GPU) would have shared a signature. The signed text is now `nimblenewt-release-v1\n<candidate id>\n<full manifest sha256>\n`; `release.submit` returns `manifestDigest` and `release.verify` shows it, so the publisher signs exactly what was submitted. A candidate record that no longer hashes to its ID never counts as signed. Tests: the old ID-only text, another digest, the digest alone and the updater's digest text are refused; a tampered record loses its signature.
- Fixed (race at the commit point): the signature was checked before the switch opened, and trust-root changes do not take the switch lock, so a key withdrawn between the check and the journal's commit let the switch through. `ReleaseTrust.guard()` now decides again inside the operation that opens the journal and pins the trust root's revision and the deciding signature record's revision with `check` changes; a change at that moment refuses the switch (`invalid_transition` when the signature no longer counts, `stale_revision` when the root changed otherwise). Test: a storage wrapper withdraws the key just before the activation's operation reaches the store, on all four backends.
- Fixed (test gaps found by mutation): removing a key dropping the owner's `require` setting (with `true` the last key's removal would have gone back to digests alone) and a rollback skipping the target-installation check both survived; tests added (the owner's `true` and `false` outlive key changes; a rollback to a release made for another installation, or with no installation name, is refused).
- Fixed: `check:deps` failed on the slice (a test string read as SQL); the operation summaries of `release.stage`, `release.activate`, `release.rollback`, `release.status`, `release.stage.remove` and `release.verify` said "Owner only" although a `release.manage` holder may use them.
- Checked and kept: Ed25519 through Node crypto only (no hand-rolled code; OpenSSL rejects a non-canonical S); keys re-exported to canonical DER before the ID is taken; signatures exactly 64 bytes; the two signed texts have distinct prefixes and fixed line structure. `release.manage` exactness: `*`, `release.*`, a one-project grant, a resource-scoped or expired grant, a team or agent restriction and any task credential do not count; only agents can hold it; only the owner grants. Trust root, `require`, approval, submission, settings, confirm, resolve and acknowledge stay owner-only on the service, so on the API, chat and MCP alike. The last known good, current, previous and pointer target cannot be removed by a holder. The launcher record is written atomically (temporary file and rename, conflict check). The updater checks the signature before copying and its errors name no key or signature material.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a missing or unwritable schema record, or a last known good that states no `schema` range, lets the fall-back go ahead (fails open), as the implementer chose: the old controller itself refuses a newer database, so the harm is a blocked start the owner is told of, never corrupted data; failing closed would block every legacy fall-back.
- Left as notes: the separate updater does not know the controller's trust root: run without `--trusted-keys`, it installs (and with `--switch` points the launcher at) an unsigned release even where the controller requires signatures. It is run by someone who can already write the release root, and `release.status` shows the pointer as `diverged`. A first key added at the very moment an unsigned activation commits is not raced against (there is no root record to pin yet). Ed25519 small-order public keys are not rejected; a key is trusted only by the owner's explicit step. Who can write `<root>/trust/` is the same-uid boundary noted for the launcher.

## M03h finish (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5): a per-project index of stand-ups, the end-to-end test on PostgreSQL too, briefs name the agent (2026-11-12)

**What the card still lacked.** Re-reading the card text against the earlier parts: the three acceptance clauses (a stand-up runs end to end with every sink; a stand-up asks the owner a new question; the owner runs and reads a stand-up in chat) were already met by M03h parts 1 to 3, the usage sink, the close-out and M05. **Done.**
- **Per-project index (`standups/standups.ts`).** New record kind `standup-index`, named by the project, body `{ ids }` (sorted schedule IDs, at most 200). `configure` adds the new stand-up to it after the stand-up record is made (a repeat of the same command lists it once; a crash between the two writes is mended by the replay). `list`, `recent` and `overview` read the index and then only that project's stand-ups. A project with no index record (stand-ups from before this change, or none) is scanned once the old way and the index is written from the result, so every later look is cheap; a failed write is not an error of the read. - **Tests (fail without the change).** `standups.test.ts`, three suites on four backends: the index is made by `configure` per project, a repeated command lists once, and `list`/`recent`/`overview` list no `standup-config` kind (a storage spy) and give another project's list none of this one's; a project with a pre-index stand-up is scanned once, the index is written, the next look does not scan, a stand-up made after is added, and a rebuilt index holds a new stand-up exactly once; the 200 limit is refused before a schedule is made (none left behind), other projects are not held back, a caller without the right gets `forbidden`. `chat/standup-commands.test.ts`: the brief read-back carries the agent's name and ID. **Not done, and why.**

A per-project index there means a change to the dispatcher's write path and a backfill of every attempt record, which is the hot path and a different card's code; the review stays correct, only slower on a very large installation. `activeProjects()` also still lists every stand-up record (it is installation-wide by nature, bounded at 2,000).

### M03h finish review (Claude agent, Opus clean-context review, 2026-11-12)

Reviewed c43a2c6a (origin/main 0eccbdab is its base, nothing to merge).
- **Fixed: the index entry is written in the same transaction as the stand-up record.** Before, `configure` wrote the `standup-config` record and then the index in a second command; a crash, a lost connection or exhausted retries between the two left a stand-up whose meetings keep running but that `list`, `recent`, `overview` and every chat lookup by title missed for ever unless the very same command was sent again (nothing could tell the index was stale). The index entry (or the whole index, built from a scan, when the project has none) is now one more change of the `standup.config.create` command, so a stand-up record is never without its entry; a concurrent index writer is a lost race, retried from the fresh index. The separate `#indexAdd` stays only as a no-op guard.

The limit is now checked only before any schedule is made; once made, a stand-up always goes on the index (it may hold a few more than 200 after a race).
- **Fixed: a project with more than 200 stand-ups from before the index lost all but 200** from its lists: the backfill kept the first 200 IDs. It now keeps every one (the limit only refuses new ones).
- **Fixed: a repeat of a set-up whose stand-up was already made was refused at the limit** instead of answered with that stand-up (idempotency). The check now lets a command through whose schedule already exists.
- **Fixed: agent names in the brief read-back reached readers who may not read agents.** A brief is readable by anyone who may read the project's records; agent records need `agent.read`/`agent.manage` (the agent list asks the same). The name is now shown only to such a reader and to the agent itself; others get the ID alone, as before.
- **Fixed (test hygiene):** a controller that fails to start in the composed end-to-end test now still drops its PostgreSQL schema and folder.
- **Checked, no change:** a backfill racing a set-up cannot drop the new stand-up (the backfill only creates the index, never overwrites; the set-up writes it in its own transaction) — now tested; `list`/`recent`/`overview` still ask the meeting-read right first and re-check each schedule's project and the viewer's right per schedule, so the index cannot widen what a caller sees; the limit is told only to a caller with `meeting.manage` in the project; a stand-up never changes project and ended ones stay on the index and are filtered by state as before. The readiness service now knows when this controller started (`startedAt`, given by `startController` on the system clock that the local host setting is recorded by): a choice made before this start with no host joined says "no host has joined since this start; the messages printed when the controller started say why"; a choice made during this run keeps the "joins at the next start" text.
