### M05b (finish) review (Claude agent, 2026-11-13)

Merged origin/main 97a07961 (notes conflict: both sides kept). **Fixed:** every statement in a meeting moves the meeting record on, and the chair's `read`, `readNote` and `attemptChange` guard on it, but the shared command runner does not rebuild a command that lost a race. A chair read made while anyone spoke failed with "meeting-desk-read ... already exists, so this command ID was used by something else" (a false accusation of a reused command ID), and refused attempts sent at the same moment were not counted. The three commands now say a lost race is a `LostRace` (`stale_revision`) and are built again from the current state, at most 8 times (nothing of a lost try is committed, so the read, its inspection and the count each happen exactly once; a revised note is returned at its new revision and the record names it). The API query adds `moreAttempts: true` and the status view a line when there are more refused attempts than shown (before, both dropped the rest silently). New test on all four backends (`desk-reads.test.ts`, "races another writer"): fails on all four without the fix.

**Checked, sound:** the chair check (agent, authenticated, task scope of the meeting's project, open meeting, current chair) runs inside every build, so a former chair or a stranger is refused with no record; a note of another project, a private note or a deleted note (deletion leaves a blank tombstone marked private, so the private check already refuses it; the extra `deleted` check is a second guard no test can separate) is refused; read record and inspection are one storage operation on every backend. Listings carry IDs, revisions, sizes, digests and times, never titles or bodies; inspections stay visible only to the owner and the file's agent. Error texts name IDs only.

**Left open (recorded):** the listing is not owner-only: roster members and the chair of the occurrence see every read record, including the SHA-256 of a private record's title and body, which lets a peer confirm a guess of short private content (the owner decision gave the roster sight of the reads; redacting the digest for peers is a small later change). Attempts are listed by their last repeat, so a cursor over attempts can skip or repeat one that is tried again meanwhile (the API and status view take only the first page). Read times are taken before commit, so with two writers at once a later commit can carry an earlier time than a record already paged past.

**Mutation checks (each alone on the built file, restored):** inspection written in a second commit (4 of 12 fail), chair identity check removed (8 of 12), private note readable (4 of 12), race rebuild off (4 of 12), any agent may list (8 of 12); deleted-note check removed survives (redundant, above).

## H12p (finish): the author refreshes its own checkout with work.refresh (2026-11-13, Claude agent)

**What was lacking.** Part 1 (2026-10-30) built and hardened the worker's three-way re-apply, `GitBridge.reapply`, and nothing called it. The card's remaining acceptance was: the agent's `work.refresh` tool, with no quiesce and recorded in the workspace record; changed and new files survive, conflicts listed and never resolved; refresh rounds counted on the submission; tested on a branch that moved in overlapping and in unrelated files.

**What is built.**
- **Host operation `reapply`** (`WorkspaceHost`, `packages/worker/src/workspace/host.ts`): reads the shared workspace's head, and when the checkout is based on another commit calls `GitBridge.reapply` over the checkout as it stands (changed, new and ignored files, committed or not; no clean-checkout rule, unlike the owner's `refresh`). The shared repository is only read. At the head already it answers `changed: false` and does nothing (the agent's own commits are not reset). The answer's detail is `{ changed, before, base, kept, taken, merged, conflictCount, conflicts: [{ path, kind }], conflictsNotListed? }`; at most 20 conflicts are listed, each path cut to 100 characters, and the whole detail is kept under 3,000 bytes (conflicts are dropped from the end and counted) so the controller's 4,000-byte bound never throws the list away. The summary names the counts and the first five conflicts. The operation is journalled like the others (one request ID, carried out once, a repeat gets the recorded answer) and runs in the checkout's own serial order. **It skips the host's `attemptsQuiet` check on purpose**: the attempt that asks is running by design; every other operation still refuses while an attempt runs.
- **Controller `WorkspaceOpService.reapply(by, { commandId, attemptId })`** (`workspace-ops.ts`): only the agent of a live attempt asks (an owner is `forbidden`; another agent, another task's credential and an unknown attempt are the same `not_found`; an ended or stopped attempt is `invalid_transition`; an attempt that is frozen right now, for an ending or another operation, is `unavailable`). **No quiesce**: nothing is frozen or settled and the agent is not told afterwards (the answer is the telling). One operation runs per task: a refresh while another operation runs or is left open is `unavailable` (never queued); a repeat of the same call returns the recorded answer, a repeat while the first still runs is `uncertain` and never a second host call. The request is recorded before the host is asked (operation `reapply`, `requestedBy` the agent, summary, the host's detail with each key-like path withheld alone) and is readable by the owner through `workspace.get`. The owner's `workspace.request` refuses `reapply` ("the agent asks for it itself"); an owner's refresh of a clean checkout is still `refresh`.
- **Refresh rounds.** A `reapply` that moved the checkout onto a newer head is one round of the task. The count is a record per task (`workspace-rounds`) written **in the same command** as the record that finishes the request (`round` on the record), so one is never without the other. `refreshRounds(taskId)` reads it. `stagedSubmit` now passes it as `refreshRound` on the code submission, and `start()` wires `workspaceOps.refreshRounds` into the submit port. A refresh at the head already, a refusal, a failure and an `uncertain` one are not rounds.
- **The agent tool.** API operation `work.refresh` (agent only; args `attemptId`), bridge operation `work.refresh` (no arguments; the attempt is the one the request came through; refused while the task is paused like every other write; recorded as an effect so a repeated call ID answers as before), and the Pi tool `nimblenewt__work-refresh`. Its description is deliberately short (about 200 characters): every agent's first prompt carries every tool schema, and the longer first draft (about 560 characters) tipped `c07g-route-view`, whose "more questions fit whole on the measured figure" margin is only one question wide; the full rules are in the API operation's summary, which an agent reads when it asks. The refusal text of a submit on a stale base now names `work.refresh`.

**Tests.** `workspace/reapply-host.test.ts` (6, real git: changed and new files survive over a branch that moved in unrelated files, overlapping edits listed with markers and never resolved, a same-file non-overlapping edit merged, delete-versus-change listed, no quiesce, one run per request ID, 30 conflicts with long Han-character paths bounded to the byte limit, a landing-branch link refused as a value); `workspace-ops/workspace-ops-h12p.test.ts` (6 cases times 4 storage backends: own agent only, no quiesce, record and rounds, replay, not-round cases, key-like path withheld alone, owner refused, one operation per task, `uncertain` repeat); `integration/h12p-author-refresh.test.ts` (one case through `startController`, the local worker and the real `LocalWorkspaces` host: the agent's own task credential calls `work.refresh`, markers and merge in a real checkout, shared repository unchanged, the agent not frozen nor told, replay, `workspace.get` record, round 2 after a second branch move, owner and stranger refused, and `work.end { submit }` opens a code submission with `refreshRound` 2); `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (work.refresh names no attempt, forwards the attempt's own credential and command ID, refused while paused). On Windows and macOS the tests use only `\n` text files, Han-character folder names (no Hangul, which a Mac would decompose), no fixed pauses, and the link test is skipped on Windows (symbolic links need a privilege).

**Mutation checks (each applied, tests failed, restored).** Host `attemptsQuiet` applied to `reapply` (test 3 fails); the detail-shrinking loop disabled (test 5); a round counted when the head did not move, the task-credential scope check removed, and the owner allowed to request `reapply` (controller tests 3, 4 and 5 fail on all backends); `work.refresh` removed from the bridge's paused set (the toolbridge pause test). Not applied: the submit port's `refreshRound` (the integration test asserts it).

**Not done, said plainly.**
1. **The per-project cap on refresh rounds (default 3, `integration.refreshRounds`) is not enforced here.** Nothing refuses a refresh past the cap and nothing yet reads the count to reserve a landing slot or escalate to the director: that sits in P10 ("after the refresh-round cap a reservation, then escalation to the director"), which is not on main. The count is now on every code submission (`refreshRound`) and in `refreshRounds(taskId)` for P10 to read.
2. **No end-to-end test against a real model and a real sandboxed agent** calls the tool (no model, no hardware offline); the Pi tool is covered by the bridge test and the controller path by the integration test with a real git checkout.
3. **A crash between the host finishing a refresh and the controller writing its record** leaves the host journal `done` and the controller record `uncertain`: that refresh moved the base but is not counted as a round (an undercount of one, never an overcount). The next refresh finds the checkout at the head or re-applies on top.
4. **A refresh while the agent's other tool calls are writing the checkout** is not prevented (that is what "no quiesce" means). The agent is one turn that calls tools in order, so it does not normally write during its own call; a model that issues parallel writes beside `work.refresh` could race. The host's per-checkout order serialises host operations only. (Superseded by the H12p review below: such a write is now detected and never overwritten.)
5. A file one side deleted and the other changed keeps the agent's side (provisional owner question from part 1, unchanged); the reapply item "a write that fails mid-way (disk fault) leaves the checkout partly updated" is unchanged and retry-safe as noted there.
6. No new owner control: the owner's levers stay the existing ones (`integration.refreshRounds` in chat, `workspace.request` refresh and quarantine, `workspace.get`), so nothing was added to the chat interpreter's command table.

- ASSUMPTION: a "round" is a refresh that moved the base; a refresh at the head, a refusal and a failure are not rounds. Smallest reading of "refresh rounds" that cannot punish an agent for asking when nothing changed. Reversible: change `counts` in `#settle`.
- ASSUMPTION: rounds are counted per task across attempts (a later attempt of the same task continues the count), because the stale-base relation belongs to the task's work. Reversible: key the counter by attempt.
- ASSUMPTION: `work.refresh` is refused while the task is paused or the attempt is frozen (it rewrites files), unlike `work.end`, which stays possible. Reversible: remove it from `WRITES`.
- ASSUMPTION: the shared workspace's head is the landing branch's head for this operation, as for the owner's `refresh` (the landing itself checks the branch). 

## H12p review (2026-11-13, Claude agent, Opus): live-checkout safety, round forgery, pause at the controller

Reviewed 25446501 after merging main (855e902b; only the notes conflicted). Problems found and fixed, each with tests:
- **A write the agent made during a refresh could be lost silently** (notes item 4 above understated it: Pi may run tool calls in parallel and a job started with `job.start` writes the checkout on its own). `GitBridge.reapply` read the agent's work once, then wrote the landing version (or the merge) over each file the landing branch changed: a write to such a file in between was overwritten with no sign, and a file the agent created at a path the landing branch adds was overwritten too. Now every file the refresh may write or delete is looked at (identity, size, nanosecond times) BEFORE the agent's work is read, again before the first write (a change: nothing is written, `stale`), and on the opened file just before it is cut (a change: not written, the refresh stops, `stale`); a file that was absent is created exclusively. The host answers `stale` as a refusal (not a round). A stop in the middle leaves the files before it with the landing version and the base unchanged; asking again finishes the refresh (an already-taken file equals the landing one and is passed over, a file with this commit's markers is not merged again), tested. Files the landing branch did not change are never touched, so writes to them cannot race. Left: the window between the last look at the opened file and its truncation (microseconds), and a same-size rewrite within one timestamp tick on a filesystem with coarse times (FAT, some network shares).
- **A merged file whose new content failed part-way (full disk, read error) was left cut short**, losing the agent's version of it (it was only in memory). Now the agent's version is written back and the answer says so (or says plainly that it could not be). A host crash (process killed) between the cut and the end of the write can still leave that one file short: not fixed (an atomic rename into place would need a temporary file inside the checkout); recorded.
- **`refreshRound` could be stated by the agent itself** through the API operation `submission.record` (any number 0..1000, recorded as given). `SubmissionService` now takes the controller's count (`refreshRounds`, wired in `startController` to `WorkspaceOpService.refreshRounds`) and records THAT on every code submission; a different number given is refused (`invalid_command`). `work.end submit` already took it from the records.
- **Pause was checked only at the tool bridge.** A client calling the API's `work.refresh` directly with the attempt's credential was not refused while the task was paused. `WorkspaceOpService.reapply` now refuses a paused task (`unavailable`) before anything is recorded.
- **The caller's `attemptId` was shown back raw in error texts** (up to 200 characters of the caller's text): now redacted and cut to 80.
- `git merge-file` ran without the fixed settings (it found a repository from its working directory by searching upwards); it now runs with the same `-c` settings and the checkout's own git directory as every other command.

Checked and found right: only the live attempt's own agent may refresh (another agent with a full or a task credential, another task's credential, the owner, a non-agent client, an unknown, ended, stopped, held or paused attempt: each tested and refused before the host is asked); the attempt names the task, the caller cannot (an extra `taskId` is refused); the bridge operation takes no arguments; the round count is written in the same command as the finished record, a repeat returns the recorded answer, and a controller that stopped after the host moved the checkout counts that refresh as no round (tested with a second controller over the same storage: at most one too few, never too many; per task across attempts); the shared repository is only read (`fetch` into the checkout's own git directory); conflict paths that look like keys are withheld one by one and the summary passes the scanner; case and Unicode collisions are refused before any write (`resolveSafe`).

**Mutation checks (each applied to the built file, tests run, restored):** agent's changed file replaced by the landing version (10 fail), live-write check off (1), owner allowed to call `reapply` (4), owner's `workspace.request` allowed `reapply` (fails cleanly now, an assertion was added where it only hung before), replay off so a repeated request ID counts twice (12), round counted at the head already (4), controller count ignored on `submission.record` (4), pause not checked at the controller (4), key-like attempt ID shown back (4). The check before the first write has no seam of its own (the check on the opened file and the exclusive create are tested).

## P06 (finish; Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13): retirement and archiving of agents and projects, owner-confirmed and ledgered

**What was there before.** Only three bare pieces: `agent.retire` (flips the agent to `retired` and disables its identity; refused only while active agents report to it; tasks, leases and grants stayed untouched), `project.update state=archived|active` (a state flip with no checks) and `responsibility.update state=retired` (final, releases its resource claims). Nothing released leases or worker holds, nothing revoked grants or credentials, nothing refused retirement while live work remained, nothing was ledgered, and a retired agent's records were not named in any retention hold.

**What is built now** (`packages/controller/src/retirement/`, no other card's code changed except the three small hooks named below):
- **A plan, read now (`planAgent`, `planProject`, `gather.ts`).** For an agent: blockers are *live assignments* (an assignment in state `assigned` whose task is not done or cancelled, matched on the agent ID or its `agent:` principal ID), active responsibilities it answers for, and active agents that report to it. It lists what retirement would release: held maintenance leases, held integrator leases, active grant records where it is the grantee, and whether it has a credential. For a project: blockers are live assignments of tasks in the project; it lists active/paused responsibilities, held leases of both kinds, bound resource bindings and active grants whose `project` is this project (a grant for `*` is not the project's to revoke). Every list is read in full, capped at 200 per list (more is a blocker, never a silent cut), and the scan fails closed (`unreadable` blocker) if more than 50,000 records of a kind exist. A `digest` covers the record's state, every blocker and every released ID.
- **`RetirementService` (`service.ts`).** `preview` (changes nothing), `retireAgent`, `archiveProject`, `restoreProject`, `list` (the ledger). All owner only. A retirement needs `confirm` = the digest of a preview of the subject as it is now (so what is done is what was shown); a wrong or stale digest is `invalid_command`, a blocked plan is `invalid_transition` naming what to release or transfer first. Steps, each idempotent and each re-read from the live record: release maintenance leases (forced, with a recorded reason), release integrator leases, (project) retire responsibilities, unbind resources, revoke grants, (agent) revoke the credential, then last the subject itself (`agents.retire` disables the identity, or `projects.updateProject state=archived`), so a stopped retirement never leaves a retired agent that still holds something. Just before the last step the blockers are read again; a task assigned in the meantime stops it there (this last look is built but has no test of its own: a race of that kind needs a hook between the steps).
- **Ledger record (kind `retirement`, ID prefix `rtm`).** Written first as `started` (who, why, what digest was confirmed, exactly what will be released) and finished as `done` with the time. A retirement that stopped halfway shows as `started`; the same command sent again carries on (release steps use fixed-length command IDs derived from the record, so nothing is done twice) and finishes the same record. A repeat of a finished command answers `replayed`; the same ID with other words is `command_conflict`. The restore of a project is ledgered the same way and its note says what archiving released and that it stays released.
- **Plain `agent.retire` now also refuses while the agent holds a live assignment** (one hook in `agents.ts` using the same scan), so the old path cannot strand a task on a retired agent. It still releases nothing else; `retirement.agent` is the full path. The summary in the API says so.
- **Retention.** `RetainedMaterial.why` now holds kind `retirement` and kind `agent` for good (`retention.check` shows `retained`), so no retention rule can ever remove the ledger or a retired agent's record. Nothing else in K06 changed: the archive does not touch desk records, replay material, summaries or checkpoints; an unfinished task in an archived project is still resumable, so its material is still held by the resumable-task rule, and replay holds are unchanged.
- **API.** `retirement.preview`, `retirement.list` (queries), `retirement.agent`, `retirement.project`, `retirement.project.restore` (commands), all owner only, wired in `start.ts` and `StateApi`; `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` regenerated.
- **Chat, free words.** The three commands are chat commands, always shown first (`propose`). The owner names the agent (`agentName`) or the project (`projectName`, or the one in focus) in their own words; the chat looks the agent up among active agents (one exact or loose match, else it refuses and says which), makes a preview just now and fills in `confirm` itself (a digest the model wrote is dropped, as for `retention.run`), fills the reason with "requested by the owner in chat" when none is given, and puts the preview's account in the proposal. A blocked plan is not proposed: the refusal says what to release or transfer first. The interpreter prompt has a paragraph with example words ("let Ann go", "we are done with the garden project, archive it", "bring the garden project back") and says retiring is not stopping or pausing.
- **Searchable under the same access rules.** Nothing is moved or hidden: archived projects and retired agents keep their records, `task.get`, `task.list`, `project.get`, `agent.list state=retired` still answer, an outsider is refused exactly as before, and a project grant that was revoked by the archive is revoked (access follows the grants, not the archive).
- **A retired agent's ID is never reused.** IDs come from the creating command and the record is never removed; a test creates another agent with the same name and sees a different ID, and repeats a creation command to see it names the same record.

**Tests (all four backends where storage is touched).** `retirement/retirement.test.ts` (17 tests): the full agent retirement (refused with a live assignment, plain `agent.retire` refused too, a finished task does not block, owner only, wrong digest, credential-shaped reason, release of both leases, both grants revoked, credential and identity gone, ledger, replay, conflict, already-retired refused, retired agent still listed, new agent gets a new ID); a retirement that fails midway (`started`, then the same command finishes it, one ledger record, the done grant not revoked again); a project archived and restored (blocked by an open assignment, a cancelled assigned task not blocking, duties retired, binding unbound, leases freed, only the project's own grants revoked, the agent untouched, reading as before for owner, reader and outsider, no new task while archived, restore, ledger of both, note); API and chat end to end (owner only, blocked refusal in chat, proposal with a model-written digest replaced, apply once, replay, project archive and restore by name); and the retention hold plus the interpreter prompt.

**Mutation checks (each applied alone to the built file, run, restored; all killed).** Finished tasks counted as live (4 failures); the digest check removed (6); the agent's grants not revoked (9); the plain-command guard removed (6); the retention hold removed (1); a `*` grant revoked with the project (4); the subject record step left out (16).

**ASSUMPTION:** a *live assignment* is an `assigned` assignment whose task is not done or cancelled. An open task that nobody holds is not a blocker (nothing works on it and the dispatcher skips archived projects), and it stays as it is on archive.
**ASSUMPTION:** an agent that answers for an *active responsibility* also blocks its retirement through `retirement.agent` (a responsibility is an assignment of duty), but the plain `agent.retire` does not check this (coverage already reports a retired holder as a gap), so no existing caller changes behaviour beyond the live-assignment refusal.
**ASSUMPTION:** archiving retires every active or paused responsibility of the project. Retired is final in P04, so restoring the project does not bring them back; the owner makes new ones. Resource bindings stay unbound and grants stay revoked on restore, and the ledger note says so. The alternative (suspend and resume them) needs a pause state across P04 and was not worth the risk.
**ASSUMPTION:** "worker slots" and "active resources" are released by the live-assignment refusal plus the lease and binding release: a slot or an attempt exists only while a task is assigned, and nothing can be assigned-and-unfinished at retirement. Task credentials exist only for a live attempt, so none can remain.
**ASSUMPTION:** one retirement handles at most 200 records of each kind (past that it is a blocker, not a partial retirement); the owner releases some first.
**ASSUMPTION:** restoring a project is a `propose` chat command and needs no digest (it releases nothing), but it is owner only and ledgered.

**NOT done / cannot be met offline.**
- No end-to-end test on the running controller with a real worker process holding a live slot, and none against a real remote host: the unit and four-backend tests use the real services and stores but no worker. A real remote host's attempt would also be covered by the live-assignment refusal; that is argued, not demonstrated.
- The ledger is a database record (in backups), not also an out-of-database ledger file like the K06 deletion ledger: a restore of an older backup brings the database's older view back, including an agent that had since been retired. Re-applying retirements over a restore (as the deletion ledger does) is a possible later slice.
- No chat status kind for reading the retirement ledger (`retirement.list` is an API query; retired agents show through the `agents` status kind with `state retired`). Not added to avoid touching the status card's tables.
- A project's unassigned open tasks are not cancelled on archive; the owner cancels or finishes them. A paused, not retired, responsibility state for archived projects is not built (see the third ASSUMPTION).
- An agent's desk records, scratch notes and history are left to the K06 rules as before; retirement does not archive them (the K06 task archive covers finished tasks, not agents).

### P06 (finish) review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-13)

Plain words first. The slice was sound in shape (owner only, a fresh digest, releases before the subject, a ledger record, resumable), but five things could hurt the owner's records or work, and they are fixed here with tests.

**Fixed.**
- **A lease could be freed from the wrong agent.** Each release step re-read the lease and released it if it was `held`, by anyone. A retirement that stopped and was sent again (or ran late) would force-free a lease that had since passed to another agent, under that agent's work. An agent's retirement now releases only a lease the agent itself still holds.
- **Archiving revoked read-only grants, and restore never gave them back.** Every active grant record of the project was revoked, `task.read` included, so a reader lost access to the archived project for good. The card asks for *execution* grants to be revoked and for records to stay searchable under the same access rules. Archive now revokes only grants whose action is not a single `.read` action; the test of the slice that said "the reader reads nothing now" was changed to show the reader still reads.
- **Two retirements of the same agent (or project) at once both ran and wrote two ledger records.** Nothing tied them together (the record ID came from the command). A claim record per subject (kind `retirement-claim`, prefix `rtc`) is now taken in the same write as the `started` record; a second command that meets one under way carries that one on (one ledger record, same ID in both answers), a different action under way is refused, and the finish frees the claim in the same write as `done`. A repeat of the command that carried another on is answered from what it did.
- **Work could still be given to a retired agent, or assigned inside an archived project,** and the plain `project.update state=archived` still archived with live work. `task.assign` and `task.transfer` now refuse a retired agent (by agent or principal ID); `task.assign` refuses a task of an archived project (release and transfer stay allowed, so the owner can still hand work off); the plain archive refuses while a task of the project is assigned and unfinished (the same check `agent.retire` gained). This also puts the live-assignment check inside the archive's own write, as it already was for `agent.retire`.
- **A lease in use by an agent working elsewhere was freed by an archive.** An agent working an assigned task in project B can hold a maintenance lease on a resource of project A. Archiving A now lists such a lease as a `lease` blocker (and the run checks again just before releasing).
- Also: a retirement carried on now releases what was taken or given since it started (a look made at that moment, recorded in `released` at the finish); the last look before the subject step also stops on anything still held (`held` blocker: the same command again releases it).

**Checked and found right.** A task in any unfinished state (proposed, ready, in progress, blocked; pause and wait are separate records and do not change the assignment) blocks. A stale digest (a grant given or a task assigned after the preview) is refused before anything is written. Releasing an assignment or transferring it ends its attempt in the same write, so no running attempt outlives its live assignment. A failed credential revoke stops before the agent record changes and the credential still works; `revokeCredential` is idempotent. `*` grants and other projects' grants are untouched. The ledger and the claim are ordinary records in the `aggregates` table, so every backup copy has them (tested through `storage.snapshot()`), and retention holds both for good (no retention rule deletes either kind: the deletion paths act only on desk records and what was made from them). Agents with every grant, an agent's own token and a task credential are all refused by every `retirement.*` operation; chat refuses an agent; a chat proposal whose plan changed before the owner's yes is not applied (the digest it carries is stale). Nine credential shapes in the reason (Anthropic, GitHub, AWS, Slack, PEM, a bearer JWT, `password=`, OpenAI project, GitLab; built at run time) are all refused.

**Review tests** (`retirement/retirement-review.test.ts`, six tests on each of the four backends): unfinished states and stale digests; the last look (a duty given to the agent while its grants are being revoked stops the retirement before the agent record changes; a task assigned while a project's bindings are unbound stops the archive; the same command finishes once cleared); two retirements at once (one held halfway while a second runs from a fresh preview, and three truly at once); a lease that changed hands, a busy lease blocking an archive, a failed credential revoke; read-only grants kept, restore re-grants and re-binds nothing, assignment guards; backup copy, retention, owner-only API for agents and task credentials, a stale chat proposal, credential-shaped reasons.

**Mutations (each applied alone to the built code, both retirement test files run on four backends, restored; all killed).** Subject record changed before the releases (16 failures); the carry-on removed so a second retirement makes a second ledger record (4); the final blocker look removed (4); a lease freed whoever holds it (4); read-only grants revoked on archive (8); a retired agent can be assigned (4); the plain archive ignores live work (4); a busy lease not a blocker (8).

**ASSUMPTION:** an *execution grant* of a project is any grant record whose action is not a single `.read` action (`task.read`, `desk.read`, ...); a wildcard (`task.*`, `*`) counts as execution and is revoked.
**ASSUMPTION:** a second retirement command for a subject that has one under way carries that one on rather than being refused, so the owner in chat (whose commands get new IDs) can finish a stopped retirement by asking again.
**ASSUMPTION:** in an archived project a task can still be released or transferred (to clean up), but not newly assigned.

**Left open (recorded, not fixed here).**
- A write at the very same moment on PostgreSQL: a task assigned in the instant between the live-assignment check inside `agent.retire` (or the archive's `project.update`) and its commit is not seen (the two writes touch different records). The window is one command's commit; closing it needs the assignment write to check a record the retirement changes, which would make every assignment conflict with unrelated agent updates.
- The scans fail closed above 50,000 records of a kind; an installation that has ever had more than 50,000 assigned tasks cannot retire or archive at all ("unreadable"). Each live assignment also reads its task. An indexed look-up by owner and by project is needed before installations get that large.
- (Closed by the identity-grants follow-up below.) Grants written directly on an agent's identity record were not revoked by an archive and could still write in an archived project.
### P06 follow-up (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13): grants on a principal's own record no longer write in an archived project

**What was lacking.** An independent audit showed that archiving a project revoked only grant records. A grant written on a principal's own record (`principals.enroll`, `setGrants`) was not listed in the preview or the ledger and still worked: an agent enrolled with `task.update` on the project changed a task title after the archive.

**What is built.** The access snapshot (`effectiveOf`, used by authentication and every service that builds a principal) now leaves out any grant that is for ONE archived project and is more than a read (`security/grants.ts`, `fenceArchived`). Nothing is deleted or rewritten. Read-only grants (`task.read` and the like), grants for every project (`*`) and the owner are untouched, and grants for other projects are untouched. It applies to grant records as well, so a record revoked later or not at all makes no difference. The preview and the ledger now list these grants as `release.fencedGrants` (`<principal>|<action>`), the digest covers them (so a grant added or removed after the preview makes the digest stale and the archive is refused with the same message as any stale digest, and the digest of a project with none is exactly as before), the one-line account says how many stop working, and the restore note names them as "only suspended and work again now". Restoring the project makes them work again with no further step, because they were never removed.

**ASSUMPTION:** the smaller and more reversible of the two options is to refuse non-read access to an archived project at the access snapshot instead of deleting grants from principals' records: nothing is lost, restore needs no re-grant, and no principal record changes during an archive. The cost is that the grants stay visible on the principal's record while they do not work; the preview and ledger say so.
**ASSUMPTION:** "more than a read" uses the same rule as the grant-record case (an action that is not a single `.read` action; wildcards count as execution).
**ASSUMPTION:** `fencedGrants` is a new optional field of the ledger's released lists; earlier ledger records lack it and read as none.

**Tests.** `retirement/retirement-identity.test.ts`, one scenario on each of the four storage backends: writer, reader, all-project and other-project principals enrolled with identity grants; the writer updates before the archive; the preview lists exactly the one grant and the digest differs once another principal gets such a grant (a stale digest is refused, and returns to the old value once that grant is removed); after the archive the writer's `task.update` is refused and the title is unchanged, the writer and a reader still read, the all-project and other-project grants and the owner still write; the ledger lists the suspended grant; restore names it and the writer can update again. Mutations of my own (each alone, restored, all killed with 4 failures): fence removed; read-only grants fenced too; `*` grants fenced too; fenced list left out of the preview.

**Left open from the earlier review (checked again).** Still open and unchanged: the same-moment write race on PostgreSQL (needs a record both writes touch), and the 50,000-record scan limit (needs an indexed look-up). Neither is cheap or safe to fix here. The "last look" has no test of its own because a race needs a hook between steps. Added limit: the fence reads each distinct project a principal holds a non-read grant for once per access snapshot (one small read per such project); a principal with grants for very many projects pays that on each authentication.

### P06 identity-grants follow-up: review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-13)

Plain words first. The fence itself was right for grants on a principal's own record. The review found and fixed two real problems and one cost problem, and recorded the remaining write paths that do not rest on grants.

**Fixed.**
- *What counts as "read-only".* It was a name pattern (`<word>.read`). Tool names may contain one dot (`dispatch/model.ts`), so a tool named `files.read` gave the action `tool.files.read`, which counted as read-only: its grant kept working in an archived project, and a grant record for it was not revoked at archive, though a tool can do anything. `readOnlyGrant` now accepts only the controller's own `.read` actions from the `ACTIONS` table. Tools, wildcards (`task.*`, `*`) and any action the table does not name (a new one included) count as more than a read and are fenced. Read-like actions with other names (`conversation.receive`) are fenced: the safe side. Every grant action ending in `.read` that the source uses is in the table; the other `*.read` strings are API operation names.
- *Task credentials.* A task credential narrows a grant for every project (`*`) to its task's project after the fence had run, so a credential for a task in an archived project (an owner-issued one has no attempt and no default end) kept every `*` write right there. `effectiveOf` now fences again after the narrowing (one read of that project, task credentials only).
- *Cost.* Measured per authentication with 1,000 projects granted through grant records (write grants against read-only grants, which read no project): reference store 136 against 82 ms, SQLite 69 against 54, SQLite on a worker thread 110 against 64, PostgreSQL 228 against 56; with 200 identity grants PostgreSQL 84 against 44. The base is already high because every snapshot pages through all grant and restriction records. `archivedAmong` now reads the project list a page (500) at a time when 50 or more projects are wanted, capped at one page per 50 wanted (so an installation with far more projects than the principal holds never reads the whole list: the rest are read one by one). Every snapshot still reads fresh: no cache, so an archive or restore made by another controller counts at the next request. After: reference 61 against 52, SQLite 42 against 37, worker 57 against 50, PostgreSQL 51 against 47 ms.

**Checked and right.** Restore: the fence is a function of the project's state alone, so restore (by the ledger or by a plain project change) brings every grant back at once, twice is harmless, and a failed restore leaves the project archived with the grants still fenced; nothing is half-suspended. A later agent retirement disables the identity, so its grants stop regardless. Digest: a project with no such grants has no `fencedGrants` key, so its digest is made from exactly the same lists as before; earlier ledger records lack it and read as none.

**Left open (they do not rest on grants, older than this slice; recorded, not fixed here).**
- Deliverables: a role in a project counts from any grant there, a read-only one included, and a director is anyone with a live grant naming the project, so drafting, revising, submitting and deciding deliverables of an archived project still work with only `task.read` (`agents/agents.ts` `rolesOfPrincipalIn`, `submissions/acceptance.ts`).
- Meeting records: statements, motions, votes and rulings are allowed by roster or chair, not by grants; schedules of an archived project keep making occurrences (`meetings/record.ts`, `meetings/meetings.ts`, `dispatch/loops.ts`). What a meeting decides is still carried out under fenced grants.
- Hosts and services act by their kind (budgets, the job host, context services, event handling, the review sweep) and do not check project state; ordinary write services (task update and transition, transfer, attempt admission, artifacts, desk, history, reviews, waits) do not refuse an archived project by state either, and rely on grants. A grant for every project (`*`) still writes in an archived project by design.

**Tests.** `security/archived-fence.test.ts` (one unit test and three per backend, all four backends): the read-only rule; paged, capped and one-by-one reads agree with reading each project for many page sizes and subsets, right after an archive and a restore, with a missing project; a principal holding only read and `*` grants reads no project; with the default sizes an agent with grants for 55 projects (and a `tool.files.read` grant) loses the write in the archived one at once and has it back after the restore; a task credential's narrowed `*` grant is fenced and comes back. `retirement-identity.test.ts` also checks that a project with only read grants has no fenced list in its preview, ledger or restore note. Deliberate breakages on the built files, each alone: fence removed; old name rule; no second fence on task credentials; page cap removed; end-of-list stop removed; unseen projects not read; fenced list left out of the preview; restore note text; read-only grants fenced too (cost only, caught by the no-read test); final filter dropping read grants; an empty fenced list always written. All 11 caught.

### P06 follow-up (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-14): the meeting schedules of an archived project are on hold

**What was lacking.** The last P06 review left open that "schedules of an archived project keep making occurrences". The meeting clock (`meetings.tick`) made a meeting for every active schedule whatever its project's state, and `dispatchInvitations` (the `meetings.invite` loop) invited the roster of a planned meeting in an archived project.

**What is built.** `MeetingService` reads the schedule's project fresh each time (`#archived`, no cache, so an archive or restore by another controller counts at the next tick).
- `tick` (`#advance`): a schedule whose project is archived makes no occurrence and is not touched at all: same revision, cursor, state and counts. It is not reported as skipped slots either, because nothing was dropped. After the restore the next tick carries on as after any downtime: one meeting for the latest due slot (a catch-up report if its time is already over) with the earlier slots counted as skipped, exactly as the existing rule for a controller that was down.
- `dispatchInvitations`: for an occurrence of an archived project it returns nothing invited and nothing withheld, sends nothing and marks nothing as invited, so the invitations go out after the restore if the meeting has not ended by then.
- Where schedules are shown: the chat's `standups` status answer puts one plain line first when the project is archived and at least one listed stand-up is not ended: "This project is archived, so its stand-ups are on hold: no meetings are made and no invitations are sent. Nothing is lost; they carry on when the project is restored." Nothing is said for an active project, after the restore, or when only ended stand-ups are listed. No new API field, so `api-v1.md` is unchanged.
- No data is changed by the archive or the restore: a paused schedule stays paused after a restore (tested).

**Tests (all four storage backends).** `meetings/meetings.test.ts` (two scenarios per backend): archive, a due slot passes, another project's schedule still makes its meeting, nothing for the archived one and the schedule is byte-for-byte as it was (revision, cursor, state, count), days pass, restore, one catch-up meeting, then a meeting already planned gets no invitation and no `invitedAt` while archived and its invitations go out after the restore; a paused schedule stays paused through archive and restore. `status/status.test.ts` (one per backend): the note appears once, first, citing the project, not for an ended stand-up, and goes after the restore. Time is moved by the injected clock; nothing sleeps. The test uses a Berlin-time schedule and the clock change day of 25 October 2026 on purpose (09:00 Berlin is 08:00 UTC that day); the zone rules come from Node's own time zone data, so it is the same on every system.

**Mutations (each applied alone to the built file, run, restored).** Tick check removed; invitation check removed; tick check inverted; "archived" compared against another state; status note removed; status note also shown for ended stand-ups. (The results were not recorded with this slice; the review below repeats the check.)

**Other standing activity of the same kind (listed, only the small part fenced).** The dispatcher runs these loops per project from `projectIds`, which lists archived projects too: `meetings.invite` (now fenced inside `dispatchInvitations`), `standups.prepare` (a meeting planned before the archive is still prepared, briefs only: its advance notices are held since the review) and `standups.deliverOutcomes` (outcomes already decided), `reviews.sweep`, `decisions.resume`, `records.sweep` (meeting record settling), `improvements.deliverOutcomes` and `improvements.untold`, `responsibility` check generation, incident escalation and archive, `lease expiry` notices and the responsibility runner (archiving retires the responsibilities of a project, so the last four mostly find nothing). Also `meetings.tick`'s own sweep of unheld occurrences (it settles an archived project's unheld meeting as missed: a record clean-up, not a new action). Not fenced here: filtering `projectIds` would change all of them at once, and some (reviews that are already waiting, a record settling, outcomes already decided) are clean-up that the owner would want to finish; each needs its own look.

**ASSUMPTION:** archived means "on hold", not "ended": the schedule keeps its state `active` and its cursor, so the restore needs no step of its own. The alternative (pausing schedules on archive and resuming on restore) would change records and could not tell a schedule the owner paused from one the archive paused.
**ASSUMPTION:** after a restore the existing downtime rule is used (one meeting for the latest due slot, the rest counted as skipped), not a new "skipped because archived" report, because the schedule's slots while archived are not failures and the owner is told in the standups answer that the stand-ups were on hold.
**ASSUMPTION:** a meeting planned before the archive gets no invitations and no advance notices while archived (both fenced); its briefs are still made, since they are records only.
**ASSUMPTION (changed in review):** an urgent meeting (`meeting.urgent`) in an archived project is refused in plain words ("project ... is archived; restore it to call a meeting"), even for the owner: its invitations would be held by the fence above, so it would otherwise be reported as started and reach nobody. A direct invitation by the owner (`meeting.invite.direct`) only marks the participant; the invitation itself goes out through `dispatchInvitations`, so it waits for the restore like the others.
**Left open.** A schedule that is mid-way through making an occurrence at the very moment of the archive can still finish that one occurrence: the project is looked at when the tick looks at the schedule and again inside the write (review), but the write does not lock the project record, so two controllers can still cross in that moment; the same moment-sized window as the other P06 fences. The look inside the write is not tested (it needs a hook between the two looks). `reviews.sweep` can still give a waiting review of an archived project to a reviewer (new work for an agent); it needs its own look.

**Review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-14).** Found and fixed, with tests on all four backends:
- Cost: the tick read the project of every active schedule on every tick, due or not. It now reads it only for a schedule with a slot due (and again inside the write, which happens only when an occurrence is made). `dispatchInvitations` reads it once per planned meeting per pass, bounded by the open-meeting cap.
- An urgent meeting called by the owner in an archived project was made and reported as started, but its invitations were held by the new fence, so nobody was told. It is now refused with a plain reason (`meetings.test.ts`, the urgent-meeting test).
- `standups.prepare` still sent the advance notice ("Stand-up at ... reach a safe boundary and save your position") for a meeting planned before the archive. It now sends none while the project is archived and records nobody as told, so the notices go out after a restore if the meeting has not ended; the briefs (records only) are still made (`standups/standups.test.ts`).
- The notes promised mutation results "below" that were not there.

### P06 follow-up (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-14): an archived project is not given new agent work or sent notices by the other dispatcher loops

**What was lacking.** The meeting-schedule follow-up left open that `reviews.sweep` could still give a waiting review of an archived project to a reviewer (new work for an agent), and listed the other per-project dispatcher loops without a look at each.

**What is built.** `liveProjectIds` (`dispatch/loops.ts`) lists the projects that are not archived. It reads the project list from storage on every call, no cache, the same rule as the meeting clock, so an archive or restore by another controller counts at the next tick. `dispatch-compose.ts` now gives it to every loop that starts new work for an agent or sends something to people. Nothing is changed or deleted for the archived project: the waiting review, correction or outcome stays in its own record, and the first pass after the restore finds and does it. Read for each loop:
- Fenced (skip an archived project): `reviews.sweep` (hands a review to a reviewer); `decisions.resume` (passes a correction on as notices to the agents of the affected tasks); `improvements.outcomes` (messages the proposing agents); `improvements.untold` (tells the owner); `standups.deliverOutcomes` (sends decided outcomes back to conversations and agents; `standupLoops` has a new optional fourth argument for this list, default as before); `responsibilities.checks` (records due checks, escalates incidents, notifies people); `responsibilities.run` (starts check work); `responsibilities.lease-expiry` (tells the owner).
- Not fenced, on purpose: `meeting-records.sweep` (closes votes that are over, ends records nobody finished, writes the log and summary; it settles records that already exist and gives nothing new to an agent); `standups.prepare` and `meetings.invite` (already fenced inside the meeting and stand-up services); `meetings.tick` (fenced since the schedule follow-up); `archiveLoops` is not wired.

**Tests.** `dispatch/archived-fence.test.ts` (two per backend, all four): the eight loops with a waiting item in each of two projects; active serves both; archived leaves the archived project's item waiting in every loop and serves the other project; the record loop still reaches the archived project; restore serves it at the next pass; archive, restore again: nothing served while archived, served exactly once after. A paging test for the list. `api/start-dispatch.test.ts` (one, SQLite): the real controller tick, with the real services watched at their class; the exact set of (loop, project) calls for active, archived and restored. That test is the one that checks the wiring in `dispatch-compose.ts`. Nothing waits on the clock.

**Mutations (each applied alone to the built files, run, restored; every one failed a test).** Review loop given the full project list; decisions loop given the full list; improvement outcome loop; improvement untold loop; stand-up outcome list put back to the full list; responsibility checks; responsibility run; lease expiry; the record loop wrongly fenced (test fails: it must keep settling); `liveProjectIds` not filtering; `liveProjectIds` inverted; the stand-up outcome argument ignored.

**ASSUMPTION:** "starts new work for an agent or sends something to people" decides what is held. A correction that reaches agents as notices (`decisions.resume`) and outcomes sent back to agents (`standups.deliverOutcomes`) count as sending, so they are held; the held records keep their pending state and nothing is lost.
**ASSUMPTION:** `meeting-records.sweep` stays running for an archived project: it only settles existing records (closing a vote that is over, ending an unfinished record), so holding it would leave records open for ever and gives the owner nothing. Its hand-back of outcomes (`#sweepReturns`) is a settlement of an ended meeting and is left with it; if the owner wants it held too, it needs its own change inside the record service.
**ASSUMPTION:** one list read per tick per loop is enough (a loop works through the projects it was handed; one archived in the middle of a long pass can still be served in that pass).

**Left open.** The same moment-sized window as the other P06 fences: an archive made during a pass can let that pass finish one more project item, because the check is on the list and not inside each write. Hosts and services acting by their own kind (see the earlier P06 notes) are unchanged.

**Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-14).** Plain words first: the fence is wired where the notes say, and the record sweep exception is safe; one test gap was found and closed.
- *Fixed (tests).* The "paging test" made four projects, so it never read a second page (a page is 100). Three deliberate breakages of the page loop in `liveProjectIds` passed every test: moving the cursor only past live projects (a full page of archived projects then starts again from the front for ever), stopping when fewer than 100 live projects were found (a partial list: every project after the first page served by nobody), and dropping the last page. Added in `dispatch/archived-fence.test.ts`: a unit test over 0 to 350 projects with archived projects at the page ends, a whole archived first page and all archived, checking the exact list and the number of reads; and a test per backend (all four) with 101 projects where the 100th and 101st are archived. All three breakages now fail.
- *Checked and right.* A failed read of the project list throws, so the loop fails that tick and is tried again: the list is never silently empty. A project body without a state counts as live (the safe side for work). Cost per tick is unchanged: each fenced loop read the full list before (`projectIds`) and reads it once now, and skips the archived projects' service calls. Two controllers: every read is fresh, so an archive or restore by either counts at the next tick of both. A restore mid-pass serves the project at the next tick; held items keep their own records and the services' own once-only rules (command IDs, marked-told records), so nothing is done twice. The record sweep: its hand-back (`#sweepReturns`, `returnOutcomes`) only marks agenda items as having an outcome; the sending is `standups.deliverOutcomes`, which is fenced, so nothing reaches agents or conversations while archived. It still writes the summary of an ended meeting once (one model call if a narrator is set) and lets owner holds run out as declines (silence widens nothing).
- *Other loops in `dispatch-compose.ts` and `start.ts`.* The ones that take a project list are all fenced or listed as deliberate. The rest act by kind (messages, budget notices, stall escalation, handoffs, resumes, event sources, coverage, grant lapse): new assignments in an archived project are already refused (`domain/assignments.ts`) and an archive needs no live assignments, so they mostly find nothing there; unchanged and already recorded in the earlier P06 notes.
- *Left open.* Time-based rules keep counting while a project is archived: a review whose reviewer deadline passed during the archive is moved to another reviewer or the owner at the first tick after the restore, an incident whose escalation time passed is escalated then, and untold improvement decisions older than the set days are shown then. Nothing is lost, but they arrive together after a restore. `liveProjectIds` repeats `activeProjectIds` (`api/default-sources.ts`); they could share one function.
- *Mutations of the reviewer's own (each alone on the built files, restored).* The three page-loop breakages above (now caught), the live list cached after its first read, the responsibility checks given the full list in `dispatch-compose.ts`, the record sweep fenced too, the stand-up outcome loop reading the full list: all caught.

## P02b (first slice, Claude agent): optional work-in-progress branch backup, everything that can be built and proven offline (2026-11-13)

Nothing of P02b existed before this slice (P02 itself has no slice recorded either; this builds on the workspace code the H12 cards left: the worker's `GitBridge`, `CheckoutLocation` and the host pattern). All tests use disposable bare repositories in temp folders: no real remote, no GitHub, no network.

**What it does, in plain words.** It is OFF. The owner turns it on for one project by chatting in any words ("keep a copy of my agents' unfinished garden work on /backups/garden.git every 20 minutes"); the chat shows the proposal first and applies it only when accepted. That records ONE standing approval for exactly that remote and that project's own branches under `refs/heads/nn-wip/<project>/`, with the owner's wording, and the owner can revoke it at any time ("stop backing up the unfinished work" applies at once). A scheduled sweep then, every N minutes (default 15, 5 to 1440), asks the host that holds each task's checkout to back it up. A push to any other remote or branch is not covered by the approval, is never made by this service and takes the normal approval path (`authorize` says so in words).

**What was built.**
- Worker, `GitBridge.backupWip` (`packages/worker/src/workspace/git.ts`) and `WipBackupHost` (`wip-host.ts`). The files go into a TEMPORARY index (`nn-wip-index-*` in the checkout's own git directory, started from the head so a tracked file an ignore rule matches is kept); the agent's index, HEAD, base, branches and configuration are untouched (tested byte for byte). The commit is made with `commit-tree`, platform as author and committer, trailers `Developer`, `Executor`, `NimbleNewt-Task`, `NimbleNewt-Project`, `NimbleNewt-Base` and `NimbleNewt-WIP: unreviewed`, never `Reviewed-by` or `Reviewed-via`. Every file is read again without following a link (the same check the review gate's staging uses) and handed to a scan; a file the scan names, a link or submodule entry, a file over 8 MiB and a file that changed while it was read are LEFT OUT and returned in `blocked`. A missing scan refuses the whole backup (no scan, no push); a scan that throws leaves that file out. The push names one ref under the namespace (`wipRef` refuses `main`, any other branch, a tag, `..`, `.lock`, a plus sign and anything not exactly `refs/heads/nn-wip/<name>/<name>`), never forces, and the remote's answer is read back (`ls-remote`) and must be the commit; only then does the local `refs/nn/wip-last/*` ref move, so a failed push is never counted and the next commit builds on the last counted one (successive pushes are fast-forwards; an unchanged workspace is confirmed without a new commit). A remote that starts with `-`, has a space or line break or `::`, or is an `ext:` address is refused before git runs.
- `GitBridge.restoreWip` puts a branch back into an EMPTY checkout with a new git directory: the files are the branch's tree, the base and head are the commit the work was based on (the `NimbleNewt-Base` trailer), so `status` shows exactly the backed-up work as changes. It refuses a branch that is not a `NimbleNewt-WIP: unreviewed` commit. Test: the restore equals the last successful push, not the later state of the checkout.
- Controller, `WipBackupService` (`packages/controller/src/wip-backup/`): per-project setting (`wip-backup-setting`, no record means off), per-task state (`wip-backup-state`: last confirmed success, last failure, consecutive failures, left-out files), `get`, `set` (owner only, remote must be one address or folder with no password or key in it, https, ssh or a local folder only), `authorize`, and `sweep` (one at a time; skips before the interval; a task with an odd name is skipped; a branch the owner protects under the A07f rule is refused; the owner is told once when a task starts failing and once per change in the set of left-out files). The failure never changes the last success (and is dropped only when the remote changed).
- The controller's own scan for the host: `createWipScanner` (`wip-backup/scan.ts`) is the existing `scanSecrets` (credential shapes, key prefixes, private key blocks, split tokens, high-entropy runs) plus the F09 secret values in use, looked for as bytes (text or binary). The reason names the kind or the secret's NAME, never a value.
- Reach: state API `wip.backup.get` and `wip.backup.set` (owner only; `api-v1.md` regenerated), chat command `wip.backup.set` (proposal for turning on or changing the remote; turning off applies at once, like forbidding best effort), the status kind `wip_backup`, the interpreter prompt paragraph (free words, remote copied exactly from the owner's message, no password in it), `StartOptions.wipBackup { port, tasks }` and the dispatcher loop `wip.backup` (runs apart from the tick, off unless the option is given).

**Tests.** `worker/src/workspace/wip-backup.test.ts` (8, real git), `controller/src/wip-backup/wip-backup.test.ts` (9 on each of the four storage backends), `scan.test.ts` (4), `end-to-end.test.ts` (turn on, sweep, secrets left out, forced-push refusal, failed push not counted, restore matches, off stops it; on all four backends, real git), `api/start-wip-backup.test.ts` (API, chat in free words, status view, loop). Mutation checks (bug applied, a test fails, restored): refspec forced with a plus; scan skipped; success counted before the push; a `Reviewed-by` trailer added; a failure moving the last success; the remote check removed from `authorize`; the namespace check weakened; the secret-value search removed. Two mutations survived because another layer says the same thing (not a gap): removing the sweep's own "revoked" skip (`authorize` refuses the same push) and removing the password-in-address regex (`redactText` refuses the same address).

**Not done (P02b stays open, no flip).**
1. **No real remote has been pushed to.** A push to https or ssh needs the host's credentials (an SSH key, a credential helper). The worker's git runs with an empty home and no user configuration on purpose, so a real remote needs the host to give a `pushEnv` (for example the address of a credential agent); that was not exercised and cannot be offline. First real-remote proof: a trial against a scratch repository the owner names.
2. **No production host builds `WipBackupHost` or the `tasks` source.** As with H12m, `startController` takes `wipBackup { port, tasks }` and the dispatcher loop exists, but nothing in the product yet builds the local host's `WipBackupHost` from the operator's checkouts, nor says which tasks have work in progress (`tasks`), nor gives the scan its secret values from the real secret store. A remote worker host does not carry the call over the worker protocol yet (the scan is a function, which does not cross the wire; a remote host would run its own configured scan).
3. **No owner command to restore.** `GitBridge.restoreWip` exists and is tested; nothing in chat or the API asks a host to restore a task from its branch.
4. **Owner-facing deletion of old backup branches** is not built (turning it off leaves what is on the remote; the status view says so). Branches of finished tasks are not pruned.
5. **The standing approval is a record of this service, not an A07 grant.** It is the owner's own, scoped, revocable and audited, and no existing grant or approval rule is widened. It is not shown among the A07 standing-rule proposals or `grant.list`.
6. The scan is conservative: a long random-looking string (a lock file's integrity hashes, a minified bundle) may be left out and reported rather than sent.
7. A backup does not pause the agent: files are read one by one, so the branch is a consistent set of files but the agent may be mid-edit (a file changed while read is left out).

**ASSUMPTION:** the "one standing owner approval (A07)" is recorded as the project's backup setting itself (owner-made, with the owner's words, exact scope, revocable, audited through the command log) rather than as a `GrantService` grant: a grant needs a grantee principal and an action from the closed list, and the controller's own scheduled push has neither; making one would widen the grant model. Nothing else is given the right.
**ASSUMPTION:** the namespace is `refs/heads/nn-wip/<project>/<task>`, two plain names deep, one branch per task, so a restore needs no search and two tasks never share a branch.
**ASSUMPTION:** ignored files (build output, `node_modules`) are not backed up; a tracked file an ignore rule matches is. The count of ignored entries is returned.
**ASSUMPTION:** a remote may be an https or ssh address or a local folder; `http://`, `git://` and others are refused, and an address with a password or key in it is refused (credentials belong in the host's credential helper).
**ASSUMPTION:** turning the backup off, and turning it on for the same remote again, are plain edits; turning it on, or moving it to another remote, is shown first in chat because it authorizes pushes to an outside place.
**ASSUMPTION:** an unchanged workspace is confirmed (the remote is asked) but makes no new commit, so an idle task adds nothing to the remote.

**P02b first slice, review (Claude agent, 2026-11-13).** Merged main e3c8ee45 (start.ts and dispatch-compose.ts long lines combined by hand). Found and fixed:
- **Project history went to the backup remote.** The work-in-progress commit's parent was the checkout's head, so the first push carried the project's whole committed history with it, including a committed file the scan names (it was left out of the work-in-progress tree but was still in the parent's). Now the first backup of a branch has NO parent and later ones build on the last counted one: the branch holds only scanned snapshots (each one is the whole tree, every file scanned). `restoreWip` takes `baseFrom` (the project's shared workspace) to fetch the base commit; without it the snapshot itself is the base (`baseFound: false`: every file is back, the changes just do not show against the old base). Test: a committed secret file never reaches the remote, the remote holds one commit, and a restore without the base still brings every file back.
- **A restore wrote whatever tree the branch held.** A branch someone else wrote could hold a link or submodule entry, which `read-tree -u` would have made in the checkout; a branch with one is now refused before anything is written (a backup never makes one).
- **The scan missed a secret value stored in another encoding.** `createWipScanner` now also looks for each secret value in use as UTF-16 (both byte orders), hexadecimal (either case) and base64 (standard and URL-safe, at every byte alignment), in text and binary files.
- **A remote `user:password@host:path` (the scp-like form) was accepted** and would have kept the password in the setting record; refused now.
- **A controller test imported the worker package**, which the controller may not do and which broke a clean build (the controller builds before the worker). The end-to-end test moved to `packages/integration/src/p02b-wip-backup.test.ts`.
- Added tests: turning the backup off (or moving it to another remote) while a sweep is under way stops the pushes still queued in that sweep; in chat, moving an active backup to another remote is only proposed. Wider polling bound in the start test for slow machines.
Mutation checks, each caught by a failing test: history parent restored; the scan's verdict ignored for one file; the scan skipped; a plus on the refspec; the agent's own index used; the branch check removed (push to main); the restore link check removed; the owner check removed from `set`; the sweep using the setting it began with instead of re-reading it; the encoded-value search removed; chat applying a remote change directly. The two surviving mutants of the slice are judged safe: without the sweep's own "revoked" skip, `authorize` still refuses (the cost is a recorded failure and one notice, no push); without the password regex, `redactText` refuses the same https/ssh forms.
Left as it was (not unsafe): the sweep's single-flight is per process; with two controllers on one store the older one is fenced by the epoch and a push is never forced, so an overlap can at most make one push fail as not a fast-forward. If the host's counted ref is lost (its git directory rebuilt) while the remote branch exists, the next push is not a fast-forward and fails (reported every streak) until the owner deletes that branch. A checkout with more than 10,000 files (all of them, not only the changed ones) cannot be backed up. A call already queued in the host when the owner turns the backup off still runs (the controller re-reads the setting before each call, not inside the host).

## P02b finishing slice (Claude agent, 2026-11-13): the backup runs in the product, the approval is a real standing grant, the push credential has a seam, and the owner can ask for a restore

An independent audit found four things lacking in the first slice and its review. This slice closes them; nothing of the earlier 60 tests was reworked. The card is NOT flipped here (a separate audit does that).

**1. The backup now runs in the product.**
- `scripts/local-host.mjs` (the worker host on this computer) builds the backup host over the SAME checkouts the agents work in (`LocalWorkspaces.wipHost`: the same `locate` as every other workspace request, so a backup reads exactly the folder the agent used), with the scan fed by the real secret store, and hands the controller `start.wipBackup = { port, localHostId: "host:local" }`.
- The scan: `createWipScanner` (credential shapes, key prefixes, private keys, high-entropy runs) plus every secret VALUE the installation uses, read through the new `LocalHostContext.secretValues()` at each scan. The values come from the names the configuration and the owner's records give (model provider keys, the database address, transfer targets, the owner's own credential, and the push credentials owners named); the store is never listed, a missing secret is left out. Tested end to end: a file holding the value of the provider key is left out and reported as "holds the value of the secret primary-key", the value is in no record.
- Which tasks have work in progress: when `tasks` is not given, the controller offers every task of the project that is ready, in progress or blocked and that some host has taken an attempt of (the dispatcher's own placement record); the owning agent (or the creator) is the developer, the host that last took it is the executor (`wipTasksSource`).
- Remote worker hosts: the call cannot cross the worker protocol (the file scan is a function, and a host's credentials are its own). `wipBackupRouter` sends a backup and a restore only to this computer's host; a task that works on another host is REFUSED with the plain reason "the task works on host:X, a remote worker host, and the worker protocol cannot carry a work-in-progress backup or restore to a remote host yet; only tasks on this computer's worker host are backed up". It is recorded as a failed backup and reported once, like any failure. Nothing is pretended. NOT built: carrying the call to a remote host (a protocol change plus a per-host scan configuration).

**2. Push credentials (seam only; no real credential was read, created, printed or stored).**
- The owner names a SECRET, never types one: `credential` on `wip.backup.set` (chat: "sign in with the secret named garden-token") is the NAME of a secret in the host's secret store. Only the name is kept in the project's setting. A name that looks like a credential, holds a space, or is given for a folder or ssh remote is refused. The owner puts the value there by hand (`node scripts/nimblenewt.mjs secret set NAME`); the chat is told to tell them so if they paste one.
- At the moment of a push or restore the host resolves the value (`LocalHostContext.secret`, which refuses the owner's own credential name) and `wipPushEnv` builds the environment of that ONE git process: an https remote gets a Basic `Authorization` header through `GIT_CONFIG_*` scoped to the remote's own origin (`http.<origin>/.extraHeader`; a token alone is sent as user `git`, `user:password` as given); an ssh remote gets the host's ssh agent (`SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `ssh -o BatchMode=yes`) and refuses a named secret; a folder gets nothing. The value is never logged, never returned to the controller, never in a file, and `redactEnv` removes the header, its decoded pair and the secret itself from every message the host sends back. A missing secret fails the call naming the secret, not its value. The controller's scan also treats the named push secret's value as a secret in use, so a file holding it never leaves.
- Tested with fake secrets made at run time: the header is exactly the Basic pair, scoped to the origin, git really sends it (a loopback fake server sees it on every request; nothing is sent without a credential), the failure says nothing of it, and a failed push is not counted.
- **REAL-ENVIRONMENT LIMIT (owner).** No push or restore has been made against a real https or ssh remote. The https leg was proved over plain http on loopback (the same environment keys, no certificate); the TLS leg, the ssh agent leg (host key trust: the host's `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, an agent that holds the key), a provider's rules for token user names and a provider's size limits are untried. First trial: the owner names a scratch repository, sets the secret by hand, turns the backup on for one project and checks that the first confirmed backup appears on the remote.

**3. The standing approval is now a real A07 grant.** A07's grant model CAN express it: a standing grant (`source: standing`) held by the controller's own service principal `service:dispatcher` (the one that does the scheduled push; a service may hold only `recovery.*` actions, so the action is `recovery.wip-backup`), for one project, narrowed to ONE resource (`wip-backup` on `refs/heads/nn-wip/<project>/`, so no ordinary push is covered by it) with the remote and the branch scope in its conditions, and the owner's words as its basis. Turning the backup on makes it; it is listed with the other standing rules (`grant.list`, `grant.get`) and the owner revokes it the same way (`grant.revoke`), or by turning the backup off (which revokes it FIRST, so no push is covered whatever happens to the record). A push is covered only while that grant is active, names this remote and project and the setting refers to it; `authorize` says in words when it is not. Revoked elsewhere: the sweep pushes nothing and says nothing (the owner ended it), `wip.backup.get` shows `enabled: false`, `approvalHeld: false`, and turning it on again records a new approval. A setting recorded before the grant existed covers nothing until turned on again. A change that is refused after its grant was made revokes that grant at once.

**ASSUMPTION:** the grant has no idle window and no end date (the owner revokes it); a standing grant that lapses from non-use would stop a backup silently while the task is merely quiet.
**ASSUMPTION:** a remote address is now at most 250 characters (the grant's condition text is limited to 300).

**4. Restore, API and chat.** `wip.backup.restore {project, taskId}` (owner only) and the chat command of the same name (proposed first, applied only when accepted; free words, no magic phrase; described in the interpreter prompt). It restores EXACTLY the last backup the remote confirmed to the controller: the host refuses a branch that is any other commit (someone else changed it, or a later push was not confirmed), one that is not an unreviewed work-in-progress commit, or one holding a link or submodule. The host never writes over a live checkout: a task whose folder is GONE gets its workspace back as its own checkout (built privately and renamed into place with the `complete` mark, so the task goes on in it); a task whose folder is still there gets a NEW folder `<host root>/restored/<project>/<task>-<random>` that nothing uses, and the answer says where. A failed restore removes what it made. After a restore the restored commit is the last counted one, so the next backup is a fast-forward of it (found by test; `restoreWip` now records it). It works whether or not the backup is still on (reading back the owner's own remote needs no push approval). One record per command ID: asking again returns the same answer and never restores twice. Files a backup left out because they looked like secrets are not in it. Only tasks on this computer's worker host can be restored.
