## A09 seventh slice: the reviewer reads the install scripts before approving (2026-11-13)

Closes the leftover "a reviewer view of install behaviour beyond the `installScripts` flag" (third to sixth slices). Before this, the reviewer was told that scripts run only after approval; now, for a package or extension that waits for a person, they also see what the artifact itself declares.

**Built (done)**

- **`LocalEnvironmentRuntime.inspect(artifact)`** (worker, `environment/runtime.ts`): fetches the named source through the host's own artifact source, compares the bytes with the digest the requester named BEFORE reading them, unpacks them in memory with the same limits and checks as an install (an archive an install would refuse, such as one with a link, is shown as refused), checks the artifact names itself the requested package and version, and returns the declared install scripts (phase, file, size, sha256, first 4000 bytes of text). Nothing is written to disk or the store and no script runs (a test compares the whole directory before and after and counts script-port calls). A digest or identity mismatch returns a reason and none of the content.
- **`MaintenanceOptions.inspector`** (controller): called once, in the background after the maintenance ID is returned, for each package or extension request that waits for a person. The answer is cleaned (redact, strip invisible and direction-changing characters), bounded (6 scripts, 2000 characters each, the rest counted as `omittedScripts`) and stored beside the request in its own record `maintenance-inspection` bound to the request's spec digest. A host that cannot read, throws or takes longer than 30 s (`inspectTimeoutMs`) is stored as "could not be read" with a cleaned reason. A request decided while the host was reading is not written to. The request itself is not changed by the reading (no new revision, so a decider's `expectedRevision` is unaffected), and a replayed request does not ask the host again.
- **The review summary** (`maintenance.get` and `maintenance.list`, so the owner's views too, read by the same people as before) carries `review.inspection` (what was read, the script texts marked untrusted, or why nothing could be read) and `review.inspectionWarning` when the artifact differs from the claim (declares scripts though the requester said none, or the reverse).
- **Wiring**: `startController` hands `maintenance.environmentRuntime.inspect` to the service when the runtime has one (the local environment host does). The `EnvironmentRuntime` port has an optional `inspect`.
- No new owner control: reading is automatic and the existing views show it, so no chat command or interpreter prompt entry was needed.

**Tests.** `worker/src/environment/inspect.test.ts` (5, Linux/macOS; skipped on Windows like the rest of the runtime). `maintenance/maintenance-review.test.ts` (+4 tests on each of the four backends: readers and non-readers, exact artifact asked, record unchanged, listing carries it, replay; warnings, cleaning and bounds; no answer, throw, slow, no inspector, rule-approved request and mount never read; decided while reading). Mutations of my own (each alone, restored): no cleaning of the host's text; the 6-script bound removed; the pending recheck after the host answers removed; the timeout removed; the warning removed; the worker's digest check removed; the worker's identity check removed (each killed: 4 failures, one per backend, or 1 for the worker); the binding of a reading to the request's spec digest removed is NOT killed, because a request's spec never changes after it is made, so the guard is defence in depth only and cannot be tested through the service.

**NOT done**

- Showing is not gating: an approval does not require that the reading exists or matches (a host outage must not stop a decision; an install still refuses a mismatching or script-declaring artifact on its own).
- A remote host has no environment runtime, so nothing is read there; macOS/Windows have no environment runtime at all.
- The text of a script is shown, not analysed: no judgement of what it does.
- Mount and network application (sandbox enforcement) is still not built, so those approved requests wait. Mounts still lack a resource store to mount from. Network: since H12i (on main) the controlled route exists (recipe `route`, worker proxy, controller relay with per-connection checks, revoke and log), but an approved A09 `network` request is per agent and per site, while H12i grants are per task and per exact host and port; nothing connects the two yet (see the review below).
- An administrator role for host policy and the base.

ASSUMPTION: the owner is the only administrator. The product has one owner principal (`maintenance` tests already prove a supervisor cannot decide the protected kinds); a second human role would be a new kind of principal and a permission model decision that is larger than this card, so "owner or administrator" is met by the owner alone.
ASSUMPTION: the reading is made at request time, once, not when a person opens the request, so opening a request never makes the controller fetch anything, and what the reviewer sees is what was read when the request was made.
ASSUMPTION: a request that the owner's rules approve is not read (nobody reviews it; the install verifies the digest itself).

### A09 seventh slice review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-13)

Merged origin/main 6d2271d1 (H12i, H12p, flip audits; only this notes file conflicted, both sides kept). Checked: the digest is compared before any parsing; the in-memory unpack uses the install limits (32 MiB fetched, gzip output capped while it is read, 10000 entries, 128 MiB of files, path depth and length, no links, no special files, no set-ID bits, no long-name or pax headers, duplicate and file-versus-directory names refused ignoring letter case, a checksum on every header, nothing after the end marker); a nested archive is only a file's bytes and is never opened; nothing is written or run. The fetch goes only through the host's own source (the https source has a required host list, follows no redirect and caps the size; the local host uses its offline mirror), so a request reaches no host it could not already name for its install; what changes is that the fetch now happens before a decision. The stored text is cleaned (redacted, invisible and direction characters removed, redacted again) and is cleaned again when shown. Agents never see it: the tool bridge's maintenance-status shows only status fields, and the chat's decide preview shows only the spec. Read access is the request's own (owner, requester, its supervisor).

**Fixed.**
- Readings had no limit on how many ran at once. Each runs inside the controller process and may hold the archive, its unpacked tar and a copy of every file (several hundred MiB at the install limits), and every package or extension request started one at once (up to 20 waiting per agent). Readings now run one at a time in a queue. Past 50 waiting, a new one is recorded as "could not be read" with that reason, so nothing queues without end.
- The 30 s limit stopped waiting but left the host's fetch going (the https source has its own 60 s limit). The inspector is now given an abort signal: at the limit the fetch is aborted, and a reading stopped after its fetch is not unpacked (`LocalEnvironmentRuntime.inspect(artifact, signal)`, `EnvironmentRuntime.inspect` and `startController` pass it through).
- Tests: `maintenance-review.test.ts` adds "readings run one at a time, a reading given up at the limit is told to stop, and past the queue bound a request is recorded as not read" on the four backends; `inspect.test.ts` adds the signal reaching the source and an aborted reading not being unpacked.

**Breakages tried (each alone on the built files, restored).** Caught: the queue bypassed; the abort removed; the digest check before unpacking removed; the abort check after the fetch removed; the name and version check removed; the decided-meanwhile recheck removed. Survived: (1) the spec-digest binding in `reviewSummary` (the implementer's survivor). A request's `specDigest` is set when it is created and no command changes it, so a reading can never belong to another spec under the same ID. The check is defence for a hand-edited record, and leaving it untested is acceptable. (2) The "a replay does not ask again" guard. The "already read" record check in `#inspect` covers it, and with the queue the replay's reading always runs after the first has written. This is redundant, not wrong.

**Left as it was (noted).**
- A controller that stops while a reading waits or runs loses it. Nothing reads that request again, and its review shows no `inspection` at all, the same as "not read yet". A follow-up could have `resume()` queue pending package and extension requests with no inspection record. The command ID `inspect:<id>` already makes a second controller's write harmless.
- The unpack is synchronous, so one reading may block the controller's event loop for up to about a second at the install limits. Installs already do the same, after approval.

**H12i and network application.** A follow-up slice that applies an approved A09 `network` request needs to:
- (a) decide how an agent-level, per-site approval becomes reach. The fitting form is for `admit` to also accept a destination that the agent's active environment revision lists, with A09's site deny rules winning, rather than minting per-task H12i grants;
- (b) add the route to the attempt's recipe when the pinned environment revision has network entries (Linux bubblewrap only; other backends refuse a route, as H12i tests);
- (c) when the A09 change is revoked, close open connections through H12i's revoke push and timer recheck;
- (d) log those connections in H12i's `net-conn` records with the A09 request ID as the grant.

Mount application still needs a resource store first.

## H12i (finish): tasks get controlled network routes through the worker relay (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13)

**Read first.** Before this slice the card had nothing built: a sandboxed worker had no network and no way to ask for one (`network: "none"` was the only recipe value), there were no grants, no connection log and no web tool. `internalHost`/`resolvePublic` (the rebinding guard used by the MCP connector, T03) and the policy class `open-network` (A07) existed and are reused. This slice builds the whole route and proves it on Linux with a real bubblewrap sandbox; the parts that need macOS, Windows or the real internet are listed under "Not done".

**How it works, in plain words.**
- The sandbox still has no network interface. With a *route* in its recipe, the worker process serves an ordinary HTTP proxy on the sandbox's own loopback (port 3128 by default). Every connection a program in the sandbox makes through that proxy is sent over the existing worker channel (new `net.*` messages) to the host, and from the host to the controller's *network relay*, which connects to the real destination only if the task holds a live grant for exactly that host and port. Nothing else leaves the sandbox. The recipe's environment is given `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` (and the lower-case forms) so `curl`, `git`, `npm`, `pip` and most browsers use it; a recipe that sets any proxy variable itself is refused.
- **Grants** (`controller/src/network/grants.ts`, `NetworkGrantService`, aggregate kind `net-grant`). A grant names the task, ONE destination (host and port written exactly: no wildcards, ranges, schemes, paths, credentials, or number-spelled addresses such as `2130706433`, `0x7f.1`, `127.1`) and who approved it and how. The default is none. The owner grants directly. An agent's own credential can only *ask*: the approval policy judges the request as tool `open-network` (class access change); it is allowed without the owner only through a standing approval grant that names it (never merely a permissive profile), and never when the grant allows a private address. Otherwise the request waits as `requested` and the owner approves or denies it (`network.decide`). A grant ends with its task, or when the owner revokes it (`network.revoke`, by ID, by task+host+port, or all of a task's grants).
- **The check on every connection** (`admit.ts`): the destination is read as a plain host and port; the attempt's log is not full; the task holds a live grant; the name is looked up ONCE and every address it gives is checked (resolver answers must be IP literals; a mixed answer with one private address is refused; a name that gives a different answer the second time is never asked again, because the connection goes to the pinned address, not the name); private, loopback and local addresses are refused unless the grant says `allowPrivate` (owner only); addresses nobody can reach (0.0.0.0/8, 169.254/16 including the cloud metadata address, multicast, reserved, `::`, `fe80::/10`, `ff00::/8`, and their IPv4-mapped forms) are refused even with `allowPrivate`. A log that cannot be written refuses the connection (fail closed). A refusal's reason goes back to the task but never names the internal address that caused it.
- **The relay** (`relay.ts`, `NetworkRelay.forAttempt`): moves bytes one piece in flight each way (acknowledged pieces, so a slow reader slows the sender instead of filling memory), counts bytes, closes a connection when its grant is revoked (pushed at once in the same process, and found by a timer recheck every second otherwise, so a revoke or the end of the task made by another controller process also ends open connections), has an idle limit, a connect timeout and a limit on open connections per attempt.
- **The log** (`net-conn-<task>` records): every attempt, allowed or refused, with task, attempt, destination, resolved address, grant, who made it (relay or web tool), outcome, how it ended (client, target, revoked, ended, idle, error, attempt), bytes each way. The log per attempt is bounded (1000 records), so a hostile worker cannot fill the store with refused attempts. Text in it goes through the secret redaction.
- **The web tool** (`web-tool.ts`, catalogue name `nimblenewt.web-fetch`, class `inspect` in the policy table): the controller itself fetches an `http`/`https` page (GET or HEAD, no redirects followed, body bounded, text cleaned as untrusted data and flagged for instruction-like sentences). It needs the ordinary `tool.nimblenewt.web-fetch` grant PLUS a network grant. It connects to the checked address with the right TLS server name. A grant may state a credential: a header name and the NAME of a secret (never the secret); only the web tool adds it, the relay never adds any credential. The tool is built into the tool bridge (`ToolExecutionService` `builtins`), so it is listed, described, schema-checked and run like any catalogue tool and recorded as a durable call.
- **Owner controls.** State API operations `network.grant`, `network.decide`, `network.revoke`, `network.grants` (query), `network.connections` (query). All are in the chat (`network.grant` and `network.decide` are shown to the owner first in every profile; `network.revoke` applies at once because it only narrows). The chat interpreter's prompt is built from the same operation table, so "let the research task read docs.example.com" or "stop task X reaching the internet" reach these operations in free-form words; no magic phrase.

**Found while testing (and fixed).** (1) The web tool first passed `agent: false` to Node's HTTP client together with a `createConnection`; Node then ignores `createConnection` and looks the NAME up again, which silently defeats the pinned address. Found by the test with a name that does not resolve offline; the same mistake was in the proxy forwarder. Both now pass no agent, and a mutation putting it back fails the web tool test. (2) A refused tunnel destroyed its stream with the reason as an error and, with nobody listening yet, would have crashed the worker process; the forwarder now holds a listener. (3) A key pasted where the NAME of a secret goes is refused.

**Tests (all the storage-touching ones run on the four backends).**
- `network/grants.test.ts` (grants: default none, owner grant, request/decide, policy only through a standing grant, never private, hostile destination list of 30 forms, credential rules, ends with the task, revoke by three routes, replay and conflict, log, bounds).
- `network/relay.test.ts` (bytes both ways to the one checked address, a rebinding resolver asked once, mixed/private/metadata answers refused, private grant, revoke ends an open connection with no restart, task end ends it, failed connection, closeAll, caps). Loopback servers only; the "public" address is a documentation-range address that the test remaps to a loopback server.
- `network/web-tool.test.ts` (plain http on loopback: cleaning, flags, redirects not followed, bounds, hostile URLs, credential from a secret by name and kept out of the log).
- `pi-adapter/worker/proxy.test.ts` and `process.test.ts` (the forwarder: CONNECT, plain http, 403 with the host's reason, bad targets, bounds, one acknowledged piece in flight, close; the process serves it only with a route and fails the start when the port is taken).
- `worker/host/process.test.ts` (host side of `net.*`: refusals, bounded connections, pieces acknowledged, close on end), `sandbox/recipe.test.ts`, `launcher.test.ts`, `windows.test.ts` (the route is part of the revision, absent changes nothing; proxy variables only from the route; refused on a backend without a private network), `contracts/worker-channel.test.ts` (messages and bounds), `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (built-in tool).
- `integration/h12i-network-route.test.ts`: a REAL bubblewrap sandbox. The program inside is the real forwarder; the host side is the real worker-process host and relay. Inside the sandbox a direct connection to an outside address cannot be made; the granted page is served through the proxy; another host, another port, a loopback address and the metadata address are refused with 403; an open tunnel ends when the owner revokes the grant while it is open, and the next connection is refused; the log shows every attempt with its outcome and byte counts. Skipped where bubblewrap is absent (a failure when `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` on Linux).
- **Mutations** (each applied alone to the built file, test failed, restored): the never-reachable filter removed; a revoked grant reported live; the revoke push removed (open connection never ends); the pinned-address mistake put back in the web tool; the route left out of the recipe revision; the launcher's refusal of a route on a shared-network backend removed; the host's wait for the process's acknowledgement removed; the forwarder's wait for the host's acknowledgement removed (found weak at first: the test only counted pieces; it now checks that never more than one is unacknowledged).

**Not done, and why.**
- **macOS and Windows.** The proxy, grant checks and relay are plain Node code with no operating-system part and their tests run on every platform. But a route needs the sandbox to have its OWN loopback; the macOS Seatbelt and Windows backends share the host's (or a VM's) network, so a loopback proxy would be open to other processes on the machine. Those backends therefore REFUSE a recipe with a route (`invalid_recipe`, tested), and the Windows proof stays with H12r/A03b, as the card's own text says ("Windows proven on the A03b launcher"). Not provable offline here.
- **A real browser or real internet.** A browser in the sandbox was not run (none is installed in the offline sandbox mounts); the proxy speaks the standard HTTP-proxy protocol, tested with Node's HTTP client and the shell's environment variables. The `https` path of the web tool (TLS to the checked address with the name as server name) is written but not exercised: it needs a TLS server and a trusted certificate, and the offline guard allows none.
- **Non-HTTP protocols** (ssh, raw TCP not through CONNECT) are not offered: only what an HTTP proxy carries. A client that ignores the proxy variables has no network at all. (That is the point of the design, noted so nobody expects otherwise.)
- **A grant list screen.** The grants and connections are on the state API and chat; there is no web screen.
- **Known limits.** A connection record whose controller crashed stays `open` (there is no sweep); the list of grants for a task scans the task's `net-grant` records (bounded to 50 per task).
- **Wiring of real name resolution.** `start.ts` composes the grant service, the operations and the web tool; the dispatch option `network: { resolve }` is what a deployment passes (a real resolver is a deployment input). With the option absent nothing is routed and the web tool is not offered: the default is no network. No deployment was changed.

**ASSUMPTION:** one grant is one exact host and port (no wildcards or ranges). A wildcard grant would let a task reach every name an attacker can register under it; the owner can grant several exact ones.
**ASSUMPTION:** the owner's own grant is not sent through the approval policy (the owner is the authority the policy asks); only an agent's request is. A grant naming a private address is the owner's alone.
**ASSUMPTION:** a redirect from the web tool is reported, never followed, because the target is a different destination that needs its own grant.
**ASSUMPTION:** a route is accepted only by a backend that gives the sandbox a private network (`privateNetwork`): bubblewrap today. The safer reading of "behave the same on every platform" is the same checks everywhere and a refusal where the sandbox cannot isolate the proxy, rather than a proxy another process could use.
**ASSUMPTION:** a client that half-closes (sends its end) keeps the tunnel open until the destination closes it or the idle limit (five minutes) does, as for any TCP half-close.
**ASSUMPTION:** the card is not flipped; its status stays as it is until the macOS and Windows proof exist.

### H12i (finish) review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-13)

In plain words first: the allow list holds. A grant is stored under the task, the exact host and the exact port together, so a grant for one task or one port never serves another. Every spelling of a host is reduced to one form, or refused. A name is looked up once and the connection goes to the address that was checked. Revoking a grant closes open connections. Six things were not right, or were left loose, and are fixed here.

**Fixed.**
- **A metadata address written inside other IPv6 forms passed a grant that allows private addresses.** The never-reachable check decoded only the `::ffff:` mapped form. It now also decodes the SIIT (`::ffff:0:a.b.c.d`), compatible (`::a.b.c.d`, not `::1`), NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`, `64:ff9b:1::/48`) and 6to4 (`2002::/16`) forms. A translating gateway would otherwise carry `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` to 169.254.169.254. The grant itself and the relay's address check both refuse these forms (`ipv6Bytes` in `mcp.ts` is now exported for this).
- **The relay's cap on open connections could be passed by opens made at the same moment.** The count was read before the wait for admission, so every open that started together passed. Connections still being admitted now count against the cap. The host's own cap (16 for each process) was hiding this at the default setting.
- **A connection still being admitted when the attempt's connections were all closed would open after the close.** `closeAll` (the process ended or was stopped) now starts a new generation. An open from an older generation is refused after admission and after the connect, and its log record is completed (`attempt`, `failed`). It is a generation and not a latch because a runtime restart launches a new process in the same sandbox with the same opener. That process opens connections as before.
- **A process could send many `net.data` pieces without waiting for `net.ack`.** The host would then start one socket write for each piece, with no bound on the memory they held. A second piece that arrives while one is still being written now closes that connection, and the process is told why.
- **Records a stopped controller left `open` stayed open.** `NetworkGrantService.sweepOpen(before)` now runs when the relay is built. It closes every `open` record that began before that moment as `failed`, ended by `error`, with a reason that says the controller stopped. A record that began after the cut-off is never touched. It looks only at tasks that ever held a grant, because a connection opens only under a grant.
- **The secret name field accepted text that is plainly a token.** Before, only a few known key prefixes were refused. `keyLikeName` also refuses what the shared secret scanner finds, and a run of 20 or more characters that mixes letters and digits with no separator.

**Changed by decision.**
- **ASSUMPTION:** `network.grants` and `network.connections` are for the owner only, as the review brief states. Before, the task's own worker and project readers could also list them. An agent learns its standing from the answer to each connection: the refusal text says whether there is no grant, the request is waiting, it was refused or revoked, or the task ended. This is the narrower rule, and it is easy to widen later.

**Checked and found right.** Host case, a trailing dot, Unicode names (refused; give the ASCII `xn--` form), brackets, IPv6 spellings (one canonical form), IPv4 in decimal, octal and hex, and `127.1` (all refused as names whose last label is a number). In the web tool, URL userinfo is refused, string ports are refused, and default ports become 80 or 443. A name with one private answer among several is refused. A name is looked up once and the dial uses the checked address (relay and web tool alike, with no HTTP agent). Revoking in this process closes connections at once, and the 1 s recheck covers task end and a revoke from another process. The log holds no header values: the grant keeps only the header name and the secret's name, and reasons are redacted. Only the owner can grant, decide or revoke, and only the owner can state a credential. An agent's request goes through the policy only with a standing approval grant, and never for `allowPrivate`. In chat, grant and decide are `propose`, and revoke is `apply`. The interpreter prompt lists every chat op, so the three are included. The web tool does not follow redirects, bounds the body, has a 30 s overall timeout, cleans the text and flags it as untrusted. Error texts name only the host and port the task asked for, never a resolved private address. A recipe without a route has the same revision as before. A route is refused on backends without a private network (Seatbelt, Windows). The bubblewrap integration test skips when bubblewrap is absent, and fails only when `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` on Linux.

**Review tests.** `network/review.test.ts` covers the embedded IPv4 forms, the secret-name check, the sweep on the four backends (with an embedded-metadata grant refused and a token-shaped name refused), the relay cap under opens made together, and a close during admission followed by a later open that works. `worker/host/process.test.ts` covers a flood of unacknowledged pieces. The listing test in `grants.test.ts` now expects owner only.

**Mutations.** Each was applied alone to the built code. The four network test files ran on the four backends, then the file was restored. All ten were caught (the number of failing tests is in brackets): a grant for another port accepted (16); revoke not closing open connections, with both the listener and the recheck removed (1); a private address allowed without the owner's flag (8); the owner check removed from grant (8); the credential header written to the log (4); a NAT64-embedded metadata address reachable (5); the relay cap ignoring connections being admitted (5); `closeAll` not stopping a connection being admitted (1); the sweep closing records opened after its cut-off (4); and a non-owner allowed to list grants and the log (4).

**Left open (recorded).** Counting a task's grants, and counting an attempt's log records, scans a list every time. That is bounded, but slow for a store with very many grants. A credential header is sent over plain `http://` if the owner grants an http destination with one. That is the owner's choice and is not refused.

Added tests: the chat wording with the automatic removal off, stores not reached, a cut-short count and a damaged block (status tests), and a project reader, a chat client, a host and the service refused (four backends). ## U13 finish (2): deferred commands follow the shared command words (2026-11-13)

Code: `api/command-state.ts` (`deferredCommandState`), `domain/assignments.ts` (`AssignmentService.deferredCommand`, `currentCommand`), `security/secured.ts` (`deferredCommand`), `api/operations.ts` (`command.state`), `status/status.ts` (`command_state` view), `chat/chat.ts`. Tests: `domain/assignments-command.test.ts` (all four storage backends), `api/start-u13-finish.test.ts`, `status/status.test.ts` (all four). The API document is regenerated.

**What was lacking.** An independent audit of U13 found one unmet clause: "long-running commands report accepted, queued, running, completed, blocked, failed or outcome-unknown". Jobs and stops carried `commandState`, but the only commands the operation table marks as deferred (`task.assign`, `task.transfer`) said `accepted` in the envelope and the reads they pointed to (`assignment.get`, `activity.get`) returned the task's own states, not those words. There was no way to ask "what became of command X".

**What is built.**
- **`command.state` (a query; argument `command` is the command ID you sent).** Answers `{ item: { commandId, op, taskId, generation, state, reason, recordedAt, assignment?, attempt?, taskState?, deliveryState?, partial? } }`. The state is worked out from stored records only: the audit entry of the command (which generation it made), the assignment now, the owner's attempts of that generation, the outbox message that tells the owner's worker (`pending`/`claimed` or `delivered`) and the task's state. `reason` is a fixed sentence (no stored free text, nothing secret). The envelope's `awaits` text of both deferred commands now names `command.state`; the API document says so.
- **Mapping (`deferredCommandState`).** Active attempt: `running`. Succeeded: `completed`. Failed: `failed`. No attempt yet: the task `blocked` is `blocked`; the task done or cancelled is `failed`; the message in the worker's inbox is `queued`; otherwise `accepted`. A generation replaced or released before any attempt began is `failed` (it never took effect).
- **Replay safe.** A read; the same command ID read again (also after the command itself was repeated and answered `replayed: true`) gives the same answer and writes nothing. A refused command was never recorded, so its ID is not found.
- **Access.** Command IDs are kept per sender (as for the command itself), so you follow your own commands: another principal naming the ID finds nothing. The caller also still needs `assignment.read` on the command's task (a withdrawn right ends the answer), and a task credential reaches only its own task. A refusal reads the same as a missing record (the same `#hide` rule as `assignment.get`).
- **Bounded.** Attempt records have no per-task index, so a generation that is no longer current is looked up by reading attempt records in pages of 200, at most 2000 (`ATTEMPT_SCAN`). If the end was not reached and nothing certain was found the answer says `partial: true` and the state is `outcome_unknown` (never a guess of success; see the review below). A current generation with an active attempt is found directly.
- **Chat.** New `status.ask` kind `command_state` (`taskId|taskTitle`): "what became of the latest assignment or transfer of this task", from the task's current generation (so the owner needs no command ID). It is in `STATUS_KINDS`, so the interpreter prompt describes it for free-form questions; the chat resolves a task named by its title. Because it starts from the generation record, not a command, it cannot see the outbox message and never says `queued`: a generation with no attempt yet reads `accepted`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** an attempt the owner `abandoned` (it left without a reported outcome), and one that a later transfer or release `superseded` or `released` while it was active, are `outcome_unknown` (its work may have been done in part and nothing says it was not). Reversible in `api/command-state.ts`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a command whose ID is not a `task.assign`/`task.transfer` (a command that was completed when accepted, a job, a stop) is not found by `command.state`; jobs and stops keep their own `commandState` on `job.get` and `lifecycle.get`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** `command.state` takes the ID in `command` because `commandId` in the arguments is reserved by the API for the command's own ID.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a paused task (as against a `blocked` task) is not read as `blocked` here: the pause is the owner's own hold and the task state does not change. Reversible by consulting the pause service.

**Mutation checks** (each made alone on the built files, each made tests fail, each restored): a delivered message is not `queued` (5 tests); a superseded attempt is `completed`; an abandoned attempt is `failed`; a replaced generation is not `failed` (5 each); the attempt lookup ignores the generation; the task right is not checked (the API test); the command ID is not scoped to the sender (the API test); a blocked task is not `blocked`; the chat view reads a task the caller may not read (4 of 4 backends).

**NOT done / cannot be met offline.** Other commands are completed when accepted, so they report `completed` in the envelope and have no deferred progress to follow. A pending effect with an unknown outcome is not consulted (an attempt that ends in a recorded unknown reads `outcome_unknown` through its attempt state only). The chat view does not show whether the worker was told. A paused task is not `blocked`. No live worker was run (none allowed offline); the "worker admits an attempt" step is driven by the service calls the dispatcher makes.

### U13 finish (2): review (2026-11-13, clean-context Claude review of 132fac69)

Based on current origin/main (6d2271d1); nothing to merge.

**Problems found and fixed.**
- **A cut-short scan could report an earlier attempt as the answer (truthfulness).** When the 2000-record scan stopped before the end but had found some attempt of the command's generation, `partial` was not set and the latest attempt found was used. Attempt IDs are not in claim order, so a later attempt of the same generation could lie beyond the cut: attempt 1 `succeeded`, attempt 2 `failed`, and only attempt 1 read gave `completed`. Now a cut scan counts a found attempt only when its number is the task's last attempt of all (numbers rise over all generations, so nothing later of its generation exists); otherwise `partial: true` and `outcome_unknown`. `deferredCommandState` checks `partial` before the attempt.
- **The scan ran before the rights check (cost).** `SecureApi.deferredCommand` looked the command up in full (up to 2000 attempt records) and only then checked `assignment.read`, so a caller whose right was withdrawn still caused the whole read. The service now takes an `authorize` callback, called with the command's task right after the command's own record is read; a refusal reads no attempt record (tested by counting list calls).
- **Needless scans.** A task that never had an attempt (`attempts` 0 on the assignment, counted over all generations) is no longer scanned: a replaced generation of such a task reads `failed` at once instead of depending on the scan.
- **The scan limit is a service option** (`attemptScan`, default `ATTEMPT_SCAN`), so the cut-off path is tested with a limit of 1 on all four backends.
- **Small.** `commandStateLines` had been inserted between the W08 doc comment and `attemptEndingLines`, so that comment described the wrong method; moved.
- **Timing test made load-proof.** `secret-coverage` "hex runs on one long line stay linear" measured one wall-clock run per size. On an oversubscribed machine a 50 ms run can finish inside one scheduler slice while a 600 ms run is preempted, so the 10x ratio failed (5 of 64 concurrent copies on 32 cores failed, ratios 12 to 20; unloaded, each unit is cleanly linear). It now measures the process's own processor time (`process.cpuUsage()`), fastest of three, with the absolute ceiling raised to 3000 ms (the ratio is the real check: quadratic is about 16x for 4x the text). 128 of 128 concurrent copies passed; an injected quadratic look-back is still caught.

**Checked, no change.** Every mapping combination was walked against the code: transfer and release end an active attempt in the same write (`superseded`/`released`), so an old generation is never `running`; a transfer to the same owner is a new generation (old command `outcome_unknown` if an attempt was active, else `failed`); a task with no assignment record cannot have a recorded assign. `completed` comes only from a `succeeded` attempt of the command's own generation, never from the task state (tested: failed attempt then task moved to done reads `failed`). A failed attempt followed by a new attempt in the same generation goes back to `running` (pessimistic in between, never optimistic). A `proposed` task reads `accepted` (no attempt can be admitted until it is ready). Access: IDs are scoped per sender, so another sender's ID finds nothing; a found command with no `assignment.read` and a missing ID give the identical error (owner `not_found`, others `forbidden`, by the existing `#hide`), with nothing naming the task or project; a task credential carries its agent's ID but `allows` refuses another task; a client may hold only conversation rights, so there is no reading client. `reason` is a fixed sentence (the one variable part is the task state from the closed list), never stored free text. Chat: the interpreter prompt is built from `STATUS_KINDS`; the title is resolved only in the focus project (two tasks of one title are asked about; another project's title is not found and not named).

**Assessed, not changed.** An index for attempts is feasible cheaply without a new record: `admitAttempt` could keep `lastAttemptId` on the assignment and a transfer or reassignment could copy the ending generation's last attempt ID into the new generation's record; old records would keep the scan. It changes the assignment model's stored bodies, so it is left as a recommendation. The dispatcher's per-task attempt list (`dispatch-task-attempts`) is another source, but the assignment layer should not read dispatcher records. A store with exactly a multiple of the page size up to the limit can say `partial` when it read everything (errs toward unknown, as the stale-artifact scan does).

**Tests added.** `domain/assignments-command.test.ts`: "completed means the attempt succeeded, not that the task finished ..." and "the attempt scan: rights are checked before it, a scan cut short says partial ..." (both on all four backends). `api/start-u13-finish.test.ts`: a sender with `assignment.manage` but not `assignment.read`, a reading agent that sent nothing, the owner and another sender's ID; and the chat by title through the model interpreter (prompt, answer equal to the state API, ambiguous title, another project's title).

**Breakages** (each alone on the built files, each restored; failing tests in brackets): a failed attempt read `completed` (13); another sender's command visible (2); rights not checked (2); rights checked after the scan (6); a cut scan trusting an earlier attempt (4); a superseded attempt `completed` (9); a replaced generation not `failed` (9); the chat not resolving a title for `command_state` (1); the status view not checking rights (4, one per backend); a quadratic look-back in `redactText` (1, the timing test).

## U13 (2026-11-17): versioned deliverables whose contract changed are stale artifacts in the overview

**Read first.** Every U13 acceptance clause was already built and proven (see the clause list above, and the flip audit `c0c73371`). The card stays `planned` only because its blocker Q01 is `planned` in the plan (Q01's own blockers P02 and P03 are planned), and the plan test refuses a card marked done while a blocker is not. That is a planning matter, not missing U13 code. The ASSUMPTION above that "Q01 is not built" is out of date: Q01's versioned deliverables (`AcceptanceService`, `deliverable.record.get/list/events`) are on main. This slice joins the two: the overview's stale artifacts now include Q01 deliverables.

- **Done.** `status.attention` kind `stale_artifact` has a third reason, `contract_changed`: a versioned deliverable whose newest version is submitted, under review or accepted, and was checked against a task contract version whose work fields have changed since. Each item cites the deliverable (`deliverable`, ID, revision), names the responsible agent (the agent filter matches it), `at` is when the work first changed after the version it was checked against (the time filters use it), and `detail` has `deliverableId`, the quoted title, `version`, `state`, `checkedAgainst`, `contractVersion` and `fields` (field NAMES only; the contract's own text is never shown). The chat's `attention` view tells it in one cited line ("Deliverable "Install guide" (version 1, accepted) on Write the guide was checked against contract version 1; the task's contract has since changed its acceptance criteria (now version 3), so it may no longer be what the task asks for."). Order inside a task: stale artifacts, then stale deliverables by ID; the cursor (rank 4) pages through them.
- **Where.** `AcceptanceService.contractStale(by, taskId)` (`submissions/acceptance.ts`) decides, under the deliverable's own read rule (the one `deliverable.record.list` uses: owner; task readers for `task` scope; only the responsible agent or creator for `owner` scope). `StatusDeps.deliverables` (optional; absent means no deliverable is ever listed as stale) is composed in `api/start.ts`. Reads are bounded: at most 100 deliverables per task (Q01's own cap) and the newest version of each; each contract version is read at most once per call (deliverables checked against one version share one walk of at most 20 later versions); a task with no deliverable costs one read and its contract is not read. They are counted against the attention scan budget.
- **ASSUMPTION:** only the contract's work fields make a delivered result stale: `expectedResult`, `acceptanceCriteria`, `requiredEvidence`, `checks` (`CONTRACT_WORK_FIELDS`). A new priority, budget, difficulty, P/PC class, permission list or recovery need changes how the work is run, not what it must deliver, so it does not. Reversible: add a field to the list.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a draft, rejected or superseded version is never stale (it is not standing as the delivered result); a new version submitted against the contract in force clears it. Nothing is written: the deliverable is not voided or reopened, it is only shown for a person to decide (Q01's own rule that a later contract change does not void a version stays as it is).
- **ASSUMPTION:** `at` is the time of the FIRST contract version after the one it was checked against whose work fields differ from it; after more than 20 later versions the current version's time is used, and the item says so (`detail.at` is `current_version` instead of `first_change`, and the line adds that the work changed earlier). A field changed and later changed back still counts as the first change when another work field differs now (the time is when the work first moved away from what was checked, not when the present difference began). When the version record it was checked against is missing, the deliverable is not called stale (nothing is guessed).
- **Tests.** `status/status.test.ts` "attention: a deliverable submitted or accepted against a contract whose work changed since ..." on all four backends (no item while unchanged; priority and budget changes leave it; a criteria change lists the submitted, accepted and owner-scoped ones but not a draft or another task's; the detail, `at`, agent, cite; a later change keeps the first time and names both fields; since/until/agent/task/state filters; paging one a page; rights: a task reader does not see the owner-scoped one, the responsible agent does, another project's agent sees none; no port, no item; a new version as draft and then submitted against the current contract clears it; the chat line quotes the title with its bidi character escaped and shows no contract text). `api/start-attention.test.ts` (composed controller, SQLite, through the state API and `status.ask`).
- **Mutation checks (each alone, restored).** Counting priority and budget as work fields: the four-backend suite fails on every backend. Dropping the deliverable read check: fails on every backend. Never finding the first change time: fails on every backend. Removing the port from `api/start.ts`: the composed test fails.
- **First review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-17).** Merged origin/main (T6b, G10, U08d, H12n, M00; no conflicts, start.ts keeps both sides). Access, contract-text and title handling, the work-field list, read-only behaviour and the composed wiring found sound. Changed: (1) `contractStale` read each contract version once per deliverable (a task with 100 deliverables on one version read the same 22 records 100 times) and read the contract even when the task had no deliverable; it now reads each version once per call and skips the contract when there is nothing delivered. (2) The `status.attention` argument texts for `agentId` and `since` now name the artifact maker / deliverable's responsible agent and the contract change time. New four-backend suite `status.test` "attention: contract_changed edge cases ...": a contract changed back is not stale; a changed check counts; a deliverable submitted before any contract (version 0) is not made stale by priority, budget, difficulty, class, permissions or recovery but is by an expected result; a credential limited to one task sees that task's and not another task's (through the overview and the service directly); a host reads none; an old version record without `contractVersion` and a missing checked-against contract version are not stale; a history longer than the walk uses the current version's time, within it the first change; reads counted exactly (contract versions once per call; one read for a task with nothing delivered); a title that reads like an instruction is one quotation with its quotes escaped and the credential removed; asking changes no revision; a second service instance on the same storage gives the same answer. Mutation checks of this review are listed in the commit message.
- **Second review (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-17).** Merged origin/main 0f42d7b7 (Q01b; no conflicts, operations.ts, api-v1.md and the notes keep both sides, checked by script). Checked: the read rule per principal (owner; a credential limited to one task, through the API's own-task rule and the service's task check; task readers; the responsible agent for owner-scoped ones; another project's agent; hosts, clients and services read none), no contract text, the title quoted with controls and bidi characters escaped, the cursor (rank 4 after the artifacts) under changing data, the filters, the work-field list, read only, a second service on the same storage. Changed: past the 20-version walk the `at` given is the current version's time, which is later than the first change, and nothing said so; the item now carries `detail.at` (`first_change` or `current_version`) and the line says the work changed earlier (the operation text names it too). New tests in the edge-case suite (four backends): the walk's edge (a first change exactly 20 versions on is found, 21 on is not), paging one a page while deliverables stop being stale between pages (none repeated or skipped), and host, client and service principals with the task read right seeing no stale deliverable through the overview. Mutation checks (each alone on the built files, restored): walk bound 21 (fails on 4 of 4 backends), the deliverable cursor repeating the last item (4 of 4), the title shown unquoted (8 of 8), a contract changed and changed back still called stale (4 of 4), any principal leaving the project out (5 tests), hosts allowed to read deliverables (4 of 4).
- **NOT done.** Plain artifacts (not deliverables) still use the earlier superseded/aged rule only; nothing marks a deliverable stale when the artifacts it names are later superseded by a newer artifact of the same name (`deliverable.check` covers changed bytes). Q01 itself (and its blockers P02, P03) must be audited and flipped before U13 can be marked done; this slice does not change any card's status.

## M04h (host proof): a woken stopped agent attends one meeting on the real local worker host (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13)

**Read first.** An independent audit found one unmet clause of the card's acceptance: "The owner's wake of a stopped agent works against a real host: the agent attends one meeting and is back as it was." `api/start-wake-attend.test.ts` hands the woken agent's attempt to a fixture host that only connects and sends heartbeats, so the agent never did anything in the meeting, and at the end the attempt was only frozen ("not finished"). Nothing used the real local worker host for a wake. The product code was NOT lacking: the proof was. No product change was needed; the new test found none.

**Built.** `integration/src/m04h-wake-local-host.test.ts` (one test) on the composed controller with the REAL local worker (bubblewrap sandbox, the worker process running Pi, the tool bridge, the real checkout layout) and a scripted OpenAI-style model on a loopback port (no real model, no network; the offline guard stays on). It does, in one run:
1. Stops an agent (`lifecycle.stop`), gives it other work (held by the stop), records its stop status and grants.
2. Calls a meeting, opens its room, and the owner wakes the agent (`meeting.attend.wake`).
3. The controller's own wake loop brings it into the room and the dispatcher starts the meeting attempt on the real local host (`host:w1`). The scripted model is given the bounded meeting task, the agent makes a note on it through the real tool bridge, and is then in a second model call (held open: it is still working).
4. The agent speaks in the meeting record with its own credential (`meeting.record.join`, `meeting.record.append`, a statement is recorded) while it reports `available`.
5. The meeting ends. The agent reports `stopped` at once; the dispatcher's graceful stop reaches the real worker, the worker answers the checkpoint, and the attempt's stop FINISHES (state `finished`, outcome `abandoned`, no live attempt of the task, not merely frozen).
6. Back as it was: same stop status, same grants, its other work still held and never started, the meeting task held again, the seat left, the wake no longer listed.
`w03-rig-support.ts` got a `bare` option (controller, real local host, owner and project only; the test makes its own agent, meeting and tasks) and returns the owner's token; existing callers are unchanged.

**Mutation checks (each applied alone, test failed, restored):** the attempt's stop never sent (the stop times out unfinished), the agent reported `available` for ever after a wake, the join never done (the agent is never brought in), the attempt never admitted (nothing runs), and the bounded meeting permission removed (the meeting task stays held). Two survived and are covered elsewhere: removing `endWake` (ending the room already makes every seat leave, so only a wake the owner stops while the room is open shows it: `api/start-wake-attend.test.ts`) and keeping the spent lease record (not observable from the owner's list; `meetings/wake-host.test.ts` covers it).

**NOT done.** Real hardware and a real model: the scripted model only calls the tool bridge, it never reads an agenda or composes a statement of its own; the agent's statement in the meeting record is written by the test with the agent's credential, because the controller has no tool that lets a running attempt write a meeting turn (no product path was changed to add one). The remote worker program (`scripts/remote-worker.mjs`) was not used: the local worker host is the one the owner's controller runs on, and the remote protocol carries no idle signal and is covered by the fixture host. A real host on macOS or Windows (no bubblewrap) is not exercised: the test skips where the sandbox is unavailable, as the other composed tests do (with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` on Linux a missing sandbox fails).

ASSUMPTION: "speaks in the meeting" is shown through the meeting-record path with the agent's own credential while the attempt runs, since no tool of a running attempt writes a meeting turn; adding such a tool is a product scope change.
ASSUMPTION: "the stop finishes" means the dispatcher reports the attempt `finished` (outcome `abandoned`) with no live attempt, the same end the owner's other graceful stops reach.
ASSUMPTION: the meeting is an urgent one the owner calls (`meeting.call-urgent`), so the test needs no moved clock and the real worker's timing stays real.

**Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-13).** In plain words: the test is a real proof that the owner's wake brings a stopped agent into one meeting on the real local worker host and puts it back exactly as it was. It is a weaker proof of "attends" in the sense of "takes part": the statement in the meeting record is written by the test with the agent's credential, not by the agent's model. What is proven: the wake makes the agent present (seat attending, `available`), its bounded meeting task runs on `host:w1` and the model's own tool call goes through the real bridge, the meeting record accepts the agent's turn, and afterwards the stop, grants, held work, meeting-task hold and seat are as before and the attempt has finished. What is not proven: that the agent itself delivers a meeting turn. No tool of a running attempt writes a meeting turn, and adding one now would go around the floor rules of M05 (an agent speaks only when it holds the floor, and the controller writes its turn down with `speaker`); that is M05's work, not a small addition. A control was added: a second stopped roster member who is not woken is refused by the same record ("may not take part in that meeting"), so the accepted turn is shown to come from the wake.
- **Found, not changed (ordering).** The meeting record copies its list of absent members once, when it opens (`withheld`, used for quorum). An agent woken after the record opened stays absent in the record: it sits in the room and its seat says attending, but `meeting.record.join` and `append` refuse it. The test passes because it opens the record after the wake. Fixing this changes who counts for quorum mid-meeting (M06: quorum cannot change mid-vote), so it is left for M05/M06; until then the wake must come before the record opens.
- **Breakages applied to the built product, one at a time (test failed for each, at the stated check):** the stop never sent to the worker (stop never finishes); the agent left available after the room ends, two variants (not back to stopped); the stop's hold lifted from all the agent's tasks during the wake (other work not held); a grant added by the wake (grants changed); the pause exemption left active after leaving (meeting task not held again); the agent never joined (never attends). The implementer's two survivors were checked: removing `endWake` fails 5 tests of `api/start-wake-attend.test.ts`, and keeping a spent lease fails the lease-removal tests of `meetings/wake-host.test.ts`. The new test passed 5 of 5 alone (about 3 s each); every other test file using the rig passed.

## X09b finish (Claude agent): the owner submits by chat, a host program that starts from a file, and a told timeout (2026-11-14)

In plain words: the three parts that were still missing from "a release job runs on a registered host end to end and the owner can drive it in chat" are built. Earlier slices (the job protocol, the host runner library, chat words for host, start, cancel, approve, interrupt and the release view) were not redone.

**What was lacking.** (1) The owner could not submit a candidate by chat (`release.submit` was API-only), so a release could not start from chat. (2) The host side was only a library: nothing started it on a test machine, nothing kept its session with the controller alive, and no real suite adapter existed (only fakes in tests). (3) A test whose host went silent was already ended as `timed_out` by the controller's own clock (the `release.expire` loop, which earlier notes still call "nothing interrupts an overdue attempt"; it exists and is wired), but nobody was told and no test drove the loop through the composed controller. (4) The interpreter prompt had no paragraph on release testing.

**Built.**
- **Chat `release.submit`** (`chat/commands.ts`, `chat/chat.ts`). Always shown first (a platform left out would never be tested, so approval would not need it). The proposal line shows every platform first (`must pass on linux x64 and win32 x64; commit ..., suite ..., N artifact hash(es), N lock hash(es)`), so a cut line cannot hide one. Every text in the manifest (commit, suite revision, names and hashes) must be in the owner's own words, and each platform's `os` and `arch` must be named by the owner in any spelling (linux-x64, my mac, windows, aarch64): `os` and `arch` are fixed choices the words check lets through, so the chat checks them itself and refuses one the owner never named, asking which platforms they meant. The same manifest is the same candidate (immutable, idempotent). The owner learns the candidate ID from the `release` status view, as for the other release words.
- **Interpreter prompt** (`chat/model-interpreter.ts`): a paragraph describing the whole release flow in free words (submit, host, start, cancel and interrupt, approve, the release view, the timeout).
- **The operator's suite as a program** (`remote/release-command-suite.ts`, `commandReleaseSuite`). The host's configuration names one executable and arguments; the payload never chooses a command. No shell. The program gets the job on standard input and in `NIMBLENEWT_RELEASE_*` variables (attempt, candidate, commit, suite revision, time limit, memory) and writes one JSON file named by `NIMBLENEWT_RELEASE_RESULT` (what it tested, counts, summary, optional OS version). Only a small environment is passed on (PATH, HOME, temp folders, locale); the host's credential and everything else of the host's environment is not, and variables starting `NIMBLENEWT_` cannot be overridden by the operator's own settings. Everything printed is digested as the log (only the digest leaves the machine); more than the output limit (default 64 MiB) ends it. A non-zero exit, no result, an unreadable or wrongly shaped result, a program that cannot start, or an abort is a failed test (the adapter throws, the runner reports `fail`, never a pass). An abort ends the program and what it started (its process group on POSIX, `taskkill /T` on Windows).
- **The host program** (`remote/release-host.ts`, `remote/release-host-main.ts`): `node dist/remote/release-host-main.js <config.json>`. The configuration is strict JSON (unknown settings refused, relative paths are relative to the file) and never holds the credential: it is read from `tokenFile` or the environment variable `tokenEnv` (default `NIMBLENEWT_HOST_TOKEN`, removed from the process environment before any test program starts); a `token` written in the file is refused. `runReleaseHost` connects, sends heartbeats (default every 15 s), connects again when the controller no longer knows the session (a restarted controller), tells a controller that is down instead of dying, keeps looking, and on SIGINT/SIGTERM stops running suites and waits. Exported from `remote/index.ts`.
- **A told timeout** (`release/release.ts` `expire` now returns the attempts it ended; `api/dispatch-compose.ts` loop `release.expire`): once per attempt (the command ID is the attempt's) the owner gets a notice that the test sent no result in time, is not counted as passed, and can be started again. `ReleaseService` in `startController` now reads the dispatcher's clock like the other services (it was the system clock), so the loop can be driven with a fixed clock.

**Tests** (`api/x09b-release-finish.test.ts`, 9; `chat/release-submit-words.test.ts`, 4 backends): the command suite (job in, only the written answer read, digest, environment not leaked, adapter variables win; seven ways to fail; abort ends the program, checked by its process being gone); the configuration (credential from file or variable, never in the config, strictness); the session loop (heartbeat, reconnect after a forgotten session, a down controller told; stop ends a suite and reports nothing); the whole flow by chat on a real controller and the real worker transport with a real child process as the suite (submit, authorize host, start, runs, the result reaches the gate, the release view, approve); the host program as a real process from a configuration file (passes a job, stops; a bad configuration exits 2 and prints no credential); a silent host ends as timed out by the controller's clock through the dispatcher's loop, the owner told once, the platform free for a retry. Chat test on SQLite, a worker thread, the reference store and PostgreSQL: proposal first with all platforms, recorded only on agreement, a platform or hash or commit the owner did not say refused, a single-platform matrix shown as it is, the same words are the same candidate.
- **Breakages applied to the built product, one at a time (a test failed each time, then restored):** platform check removed from the chat; summary hiding a platform; exit code ignored; the whole host environment passed to the suite; abort not ending the program; ended attempts not reported to the notice loop; session never forgotten; a credential allowed in the configuration file.

**Not done / cannot be met offline.**
- A real suite for the repository's own test run on Windows, macOS and Linux, and applying `memoryMb` (it is passed to the program as `NIMBLENEWT_RELEASE_MEMORY_MB`; the program must apply it). The operator writes that program; a real run on three operating systems and a reboot test need real machines.
- The outer test supervisor for reboot and partition tests with an external effect sink is X10's.
- Logs and artifact bytes from the host (digest only), a boss above the direct supervisor, and chat words for `release.stage`/`release.activate` beyond the existing table.
- No service unit file (systemd, launchd, Windows service) is written: the operator starts the program however the machine starts services.
- ASSUMPTION: a host that is silent is ended only by the job's own limit plus ten minutes of grace, not earlier: a reboot test legitimately silences a host, and the existing host-silent Urgent notice (U11c) already tells the owner earlier. The owner can cancel or interrupt sooner by chat.
- ASSUMPTION: `release.submit` is always shown first, in every profile (it changes what approval requires, though it runs nothing).
- ASSUMPTION: the suite's answer is a result file rather than the last output line, so a test program's own output can never be mistaken for the answer.
- ASSUMPTION: the notice for a timed-out test is a `notice`-level maintenance item, not Needs-you: nothing is waiting on the owner, they can retry when they like.

**Independent review (Claude agent, 2026-11-14).** Found and fixed, each with a test that fails without the fix:
- The failure line of a program that exited badly carried the last 200 characters of its output, and the runner sends that line to the controller as the attempt's summary, so some of the log left the machine (the slice says only the digest does). The line now names only the exit code.
- What the program started outlived the test when the program exited by itself (a background helper kept running after a pass or a failure), and a helper that kept the program's output open held the host until the job's time limit. On POSIX the program's process group is now ended as soon as the program exits; output still open `CLOSE_GRACE_MS` (5 s) after the exit fails the test ("left a process running that kept its output open") instead of waiting.
- The result file was read whole whatever its size; it is now refused above `RESULT_MAX_BYTES` (1 MiB) without being read whole.
- With a custom `tokenEnv`, the credential's variable stayed in the host program's environment (only the default name was removed). The configuration now reports which variable the credential came from and the program removes it too. (The suite never saw it: its environment is built from a short list.)
- The proposal line for `release.submit` left out `targets` and `migrationPlan`, which bind what may later be staged; both are now on the line when the candidate names them.
- Comment corrected: the timed-out notice is not offered again; a failed notice (or a stop between the end and the notice) leaves only the release view, which shows the attempt as timed out.

Known limits, not changed: on Windows, what the program left running after exiting by itself is not found (Windows keeps no process tree for an exited parent; a job object would be needed), and on an abort `taskkill /T` ends the tree. On every system, a host program that is killed outright (SIGKILL, a crash) cannot end a running suite, which runs in its own process group on POSIX: the attempt ends by the controller's timeout, and a restarted host reports the job as failed without running it again.

## K06b (finish): the "bulk logs" tier, and what the card still lacks (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-14)

**What was lacking.** Checked against the card text, the earlier slices (K06b first slice, K06 finish for scratch and transcripts, K06c, K06d/e/f/g) cover: off by default; audit and decisions never touched; anything a resumable task or a replay cites is held and shown as retained; a preview before every expiry and an audit record after (`retention.expire`, IDs and ages only); tier changes owner-only and recorded with old and new value; archive then restore of the original (scratch tier and `retention.archive`/`retention.restore`); derived copies following their source (a deletion removes summaries, compactions and archives that stand on a record); transcripts, scratch, thinking, notes, incidents. The one tier named in the card that had no rule was **bulk logs**: the record of every message sent to the owner (`notification-delivery`) holds the full text of the message and grew for ever (each owner message, each digest, each escalation).

**What is built.**
- New setting `deliveryLogDays` (7..3650, `null` = keep, default OFF), owner-only, in `retention.settings.set` (so free-form chat reaches it: the interpreter prompt is generated from the operation table, whose summary now names it), shown in `retention.settings.get`, and `retention.status.growth["notification-delivery"]` counts the records.
- Runner rule: a `notification-delivery` record whose state is `delivered` and whose last change (the delivery) is older than the window is a candidate. Preview first, digest to confirm, one revision-guarded delete per record with a tombstone, audit `retention.expire` with rule `delivery-log-days` (ID and age, never the message text), counted in the run record and in the automatic pass when `autoRun` is on.
- Never removed: a delivery still waiting (`pending`) or `failed` (the notification index lists them and the owner may need them), the notices themselves (`notification-item`, so the inbox is unchanged), and audit records. A delivered record is in none of the index's lists, so nothing points at it.
- Tests: `retention/delivery-log-retention.test.ts` (all four storage backends, real `NotificationService` delivering through a loopback channel: preview removes nothing, off by default, only delivered and old records go, pending/failed/young/notices/inbox stay, audit carries no text, second pass finds nothing) and `api/start-retention-delivery.test.ts` (running controller: bounds, old and new value in the answer, status growth, owner-only, preview and confirmed run).
- Mutation checks (each alone on the built file, a test failed every time, then restored): delivered-state check off, age check off, rule off, wrong audit rule name, growth count off, `enabled` flag not counting the setting.

**NOT done, and why.**
- Other bulk-log kinds still without a rule: tool-operation records and the replay's own steps (a replay cites them, so they need a replay-aware rule), `agent-message` and `inbox-message` records (the receiving agent's own history), dispatch records. Each is a separate small rule of the same shape; none is needed to meet the card's wording.
- An index so a run need not read every record of a kind (every rule here scans up to 100000 records per kind and says `partial` beyond that).
- Archive-before-expiry exists for scratch and desk records; delivery logs and the other kinds are removed, not archived (a sent message is a copy, the notice stays).
- Backups made earlier still hold the removed text until they expire (stated since K06).

**ASSUMPTION:** only delivered records count as a log; a failed delivery is kept until it is dealt with, because the owner may still be told about it.
**ASSUMPTION:** day minimum 7 and default OFF (the standing K06 rule).
**ASSUMPTION:** age is the record's last change, which is the moment of delivery (a delivered record is never written again).
**ASSUMPTION:** no backup deletion ledger entry (system bookkeeping with no owner-written text beyond the notice, which stays), as with K06d/e.

### K06b (finish): review (clean-context Claude review of a0c118f2, 2026-11-14)

- **Checked and sound.** Access: `retention.settings.set` and `retention.run` refuse anything but the owner (generic `kind !== "owner"` check; the API test now also shows a wildcard-granted agent refused for both and the setting unchanged). ## L04d (finish): one dependency scan per tick, and a resume says when its checkpoint is not the one it was checked against (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-14)

What was still open on L04d after the earlier parts (real dependency observation, the reviewer agent, host captures and `after: model-change` are done and tested on main): the per-tick cache of the prerequisite scan, and the second-review follow-up that the check can name a different checkpoint than the attempt restores. Both are done here as far as they can be offline.

**Built**
- **One scan of dependency records per tick (`planning/contracts.ts` `prerequisitesOf(taskId, scan?)`, `dispatch/dispatcher.ts`, `api/dispatch-compose.ts`).** Before this, every task the dispatcher looked at in a tick read every dependency record of its project (pages of 500) to find its own few edges, so a tick over N tasks of one project cost N full scans. The dispatcher now makes one `Map` per tick and hands it to the `prerequisites` port; `prerequisitesOf` keeps the project's edge list in it (as a promise, so tasks asked at the same moment share the one read) and filters per task. The prerequisite tasks' states are never cached: they are read fresh on every call. A read that fails is dropped from the scan, so the next task asks again. Without a scan (every other caller) nothing changes. The map is dropped when the tick ends.
- **The record says which checkpoint was checked (`dispatch/dispatcher.ts` `#checkpointStep`, `continuation/resume.ts` `latestCheckpoint`).** The checked resume uses the task's latest complete continuation. If the attempt restores a later checkpoint that did not read back (so it was captured incomplete), the check and the resume record name the earlier complete capture. The task's activity now gets one step (a stable command ID, so repeated ticks add nothing) saying which checkpoint the attempt resumes from, that it has no complete capture, and which complete capture the check was made against. Nothing is blocked: Pi still verifies the checkpoint it restores on the host, as before.
- Tests: `dispatch/resume-checkpoint-scan.test.ts` (3 tests, 4 storage backends = 12): one shared scan per tick and a new one for the next; `prerequisitesOf` with a scan reads edges once (an edge added after the scan is not seen through it, is seen without it), refuses a bad ID; the activity step appears once for a differing checkpoint and not at all for the same one.

**Mutation checks** (built, run, restored): the dispatcher not passing the scan (4 fail); the edge list never stored in the scan (4); the scan ignored when reading (4); the step always said (4); the step never said (4); the comparison skipped (4). Survivors: dropping the scan at the end of the tick is an equivalent mutant (a new map is made at the start of each tick); not discarding a failed read from the scan is untested (a failed scan would fail every later task of that tick closed, which is the safe direction).

ASSUMPTION (superseded by the review below: a change is now seen within the tick): edges added after a tick's first read are seen from the next tick. A task started in that window would also have been started in the old code by the same race between read and start; the dispatcher's later checks (the generation and the attempt record) are unchanged. The smallest, most reversible choice: states are still read fresh and the cache lives for one tick.
ASSUMPTION: a checkpoint mismatch is told, not blocked. Holding the attempt would wedge it on a checkpoint Pi can verify itself, and the owner can act on the step in the activity; making the check follow the attempt's own checkpoint needs the continuation service to look a capture up by checkpoint, a change to the capture model left for a separate card.

**Not done / cannot be met offline**
- A real Pi process through capture and resume, and a remote host's own view of search, external and MCP-resource dependencies, need a real worker or network and are not exercised here. Without them those dependency kinds stay `unknown` (held for the owner), as the first part decided.
- A reviewer that reads diffs, the probe reading the task's own worker checkout, compaction lineage in production (C07q has no production caller), pending effects in host captures, pruning of continuation records, and identity of an earlier incomplete continuation are unchanged from the earlier lists.
- The card stays planned (not flipped).

### L04d (finish), clean-context review (Claude agent, 2026-11-14)

**Fixed**
- **A dependency added while a tick ran did not hold a task asked about later in that tick.** The scan kept a project's dependency records for the whole tick. A tick advances waiting attempts and starts workers one after another, and a claimed attempt is checked again in its advance in the same tick, so the window in which a new edge went unseen grew from the moment between one task's read and its start to the whole tick, and the second check at the advance no longer read the records again. `prerequisitesOf` now keeps the scan under the project's dependency registry revision (`dep-registry`, which every add and remove updates in the same write) and reads that one record on every call: an unchanged project reuses the scan, a changed one is read again. The registry is read before the records, so a kept scan is never older than its revision. This holds across two controllers too (the registry is in the shared store). A failed read is dropped only if it is still the entry kept. Tests (`dispatch/resume-checkpoint-scan.test.ts`): `prerequisitesOf` reuses the same scan entry when nothing changed, sees an edge added and one removed after the scan was made, and reads a prerequisite cancelled after the scan as cancelled (the old test only checked that a state was present); a new dispatcher test adds a dependency between the first task's check and the second's in one tick and the second task waits on `dependency` (4 backends each).
