## L04e (L04d follow-up): a remote host looks at a task's files itself, a remote turn's checkpoint is captured, and a real Pi process is resumed through the check (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-16)

What was lacking (from the L04d "what is left" lists): for a task on a remote host the resume check never looked at its recorded files (they always read `unknown`, so every such resume waited for the owner); a remote turn's result carried no checkpoint, so no turn of a remote attempt was ever captured as a continuation; the local probe read the repository's folder rather than the checkout the agent really worked in; and nothing had run a real Pi process through capture and resume.

**Built**
- **The remote host looks at the files on its own disk (`remote/observe.ts` `observeOnHost`, `remote/service.ts` `askObserve`, `remote/responder.ts`, `scripts/remote-host.mjs`).** A new workspace request, `observe`, goes over the existing authenticated worker channel to the host the task was last placed on. It names the task's recorded `file` and `directory` dependencies (at most 20 per request, keys of 1 to 300 characters, no NUL, distinct IDs) and the project's paths. The host reads them in the task's checkout on its disk with exactly the same rules as the controller's probe (`observeEntries`, which is `checkoutDependencyObserver`: nothing outside the checkout or beyond the project's paths, links out of it not followed, size and time limits) and answers only `exists`, a file's sha-256 or a directory's member names. Content and host paths never travel. An answer that does not fit names the rest in `later` and only those are asked again (at most 12 requests per check). Anything the host could not read, refused, or did not answer within 8 s (`resumeProbe.remoteWaitMs`) stays out of the answer, which the check reads as `unknown`, never `unchanged`. The controller keeps only well-formed fields (`observationOf`). Only the owner and the dispatcher may ask. A host started without an observer refuses, saying so.
- **Which disk is read (`continuation/resume-observer.ts` `resumeObserver`, `api/start.ts`).** A task last placed on a remote host: that host is asked and this machine's disk is never read for it. A task placed here (or any task on a one-machine installation): the checkout this machine's worker keeps for it (`StartOptions.resumeCheckout`, set by `scripts/local-host.mjs` from `LocalWorkspaces.locate`), else the folder its repository is bound at. A task never placed, with remote hosts: nothing (it may be about to go to a remote host). The probe is now on by default with remote hosts too (`resumeProbeEnabled`); `resumeProbe: false` still turns it off.
- **A remote turn's checkpoint is captured (`remote/service.ts` `resultCheckpoint`, `remote/host.ts` `RemoteWorkerHandle.run`).** The checkpoint a worker sends with a completed result is kept on the placement as `resultCheckpoint`, and the dispatcher's handle returns it with the result, as a local host does. So the dispatcher captures the turn as a continuation with the worker's own read-back check (`nn.durable`) in it: complete when the check passed, incomplete when it failed or the worker said nothing. A result with no checkpoint captures nothing: an older checkpoint of the placement (a control checkpoint) is never taken for the turn's.
- **Tests.** `remote/resume-observe.test.ts` (4 tests x 4 storage backends; real worker transport and dispatcher placement): unchanged, changed, deleted and new-member results from the host's disk; keys outside the checkout and a link out of it stay `unknown`; only the host holding the task is asked; a host with no checkout, a silent host and a host without an observer leave everything unknown; malformed and oversized requests and a host principal asking are refused; split answers are completed and an entry too big for any answer stays unknown. `remote/remote-capture.test.ts` (1 x 4 backends): passed, failed and missing read-back checks over the product `RemoteWorkerHost`, and a result without a checkpoint. `continuation/resume-observer.test.ts` (3): worker checkout before the bound folder, under the project's paths; remote and never-placed tasks never read here; a failing lookup is told and never throws. `scripts/remote-host.test.mjs`: the host passes its observer to the responder and looks in the checkout it made. Two real-process tests, offline (a scripted local HTTP model, no Radiance, bubblewrap sandbox): `integration/l04e-real-pi-resume.test.ts` (the real local host: a real Pi turn captured complete with its own read-back, the next run checked against that capture with the files observed in the worker's checkout, approval, and the same conversation continuing) and `integration/l04e-remote-resume.test.ts` (the real `scripts/remote-worker.mjs` program with a real Pi process: the same, with the files looked at by the remote host on its own disk, a key outside the checkout left unknown, no file content, host path or secret reaching the controller or the program's output).

**Mutation checks** (built files, each restored): the remote handle not attaching the result's checkpoint (remote-capture fails on all 4 backends); the observer never asking a remote host (8 runs of resume-observe and resume-observer fail); the host never naming entries that did not fit (the split-answer test fails on all 4 backends).

ASSUMPTION: a task whose repository has no bound folder on the controller carries no project paths to the host, so the host reads the whole task checkout (as the local probe does with a worker checkout and no binding). Only hashes and names leave the host, and only for keys the task itself recorded.
ASSUMPTION: the look is not held back by the host's busy check: it changes nothing and runs before the resumed attempt starts.
- Seen in the PostgreSQL run: a host can carry one `observe` request out twice when a poll already on its way returns it again just after the answer was sent. This is the responder's behaviour for every workspace request (the controller drops the second answer); for a look it only costs a second read. The tests count at least one look; changing the responder to remember answered requests is left alone here because every other operation shares it.
ASSUMPTION: 8 s per request and 12 requests per check bound how long a silent host can delay a resume; what is not answered by then is `unknown` and the owner decides, as before.

**Not done**
- `search`, `external` and `mcp-resource` dependencies are still not observed on either path (they need the search re-run or the remote thing read, which needs network or tools a check does not have); they stay `unknown` and hold the resume for the owner.
- Not tried against a real model (the real-process tests use a scripted offline model by design). A reviewer that reads diffs, compaction lineage in production (C07q), pending effects and scratch records in host captures, and the reviewer's call not being cancellable by the dispatcher are unchanged from the L04d lists.
- Windows/macOS: the real-process tests need bubblewrap (Linux); the link case of the remote test is skipped where links cannot be made.

### L04e second review (clean-context, Claude agent, 2026-11-16)

Merged origin/main (clean), rebuilt, API docs and package rules unchanged. Checked: only the owner and the dispatcher may ask a host to look (`#staff`); the host's error text stays in its own log; the request bounds (20 entries, 50 paths, keys of 1 to 300 characters, 12 requests, 8 s) and the host's 6 s look; one shared count of abandoned reads on the host; the remote turn's checkpoint taken only from the placement that reported; the four storage backends in the remote tests.

Found and fixed:
- **A missing file was followed through links.** A recorded file whose path ended in a link with a missing target, or ran through a folder link to outside the checkout, was reported `deleted`: `realpath` followed the link to say so, which also told the check (and so the resumed agent) whether something exists at a place outside its checkout. Now a missing path is `deleted` only when the nearest part of it that still exists is that same path inside the checkout with no link in it (`ProbeFileSystem.present`, an `lstat`); otherwise it stays unobserved (`unknown`). A file system without `present` (a test's fake, a host's own view) keeps the earlier rule. Applies to the local probe and to a remote host's look alike.
- **Tests that could not fail.** No test checked that the controller drops what a host adds to its answer (any field beside `exists`, `hash`, `members`; a hash in the wrong form; members that are not names; an answer for an entry it did not ask about), or that a host that keeps putting entries off is asked a bounded number of times: `remote/responder-observe.test.ts` now does, with a stand-in host. The product local host's `resumeCheckout` wiring is asserted in `integration/a09b-local-environment.test.ts`.

Mutations (built files, each restored and compared): host answers taken whole (fails the new answer test), the owner/dispatcher check removed (4 backends fail), the host's error text sent to the controller (fails), the no-progress guard removed (fails), an older checkpoint taken for a turn without one (4 backends fail), the project's paths not sent (4 backends fail), the link rule turned off (the new link test fails), a new count of abandoned reads per request (fails).

## L04d (searches): a recorded search is made again by the controller at a resume (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)

Where L04d stood on main (f5c72556), clause by clause. *A resumed attempt on a new host has its file dependencies observed*: met (the local probe reads the agent's own checkout, a remote host looks on its own disk, L04e). *A change the reviewer agent judges not to matter is committed without the owner*: met with an offline fixture model (L04d wiring); never tried with a real model. *A host captures a complete continuation at a turn boundary and a resume uses it*: met, including a real Pi process offline (L04e). *Mutation check recorded*: yes. What the deliverable still asked for and nothing did: the observer reads each recorded **search** and **external** dependency again. Both always read `unknown`, so every resume that relied on one waited for the owner. This change does the search part, which needs nothing outside the controller.

**Built**
- **A search is the controller's to judge (`dependencies/dependencies.ts` `SearchJudge`, `#searchAgain`, `#verifySearch`).** A `search` dependency names the controller's own word search (`search`: desk records and histories of a project), so no worker can see better than the controller whether it still finds the same. With the new `searches` port, for a search of the task's own project, the controller makes the search again at every dependency check and compares: `unchanged` or `changed` ("the results differ"), or `cursor-expired` when retention has cut the project's events after the search was made (the rule C03 already had). A worker's observation for such a search is ignored: the controller's own records win. It runs with the rights the recorder has **now** (`PrincipalService.current`: grants and restrictions as of now, nothing for a principal that is gone or disabled), so the owner or the dispatcher running the check gets the agent's view, not their own, and a record the agent may not read never counts. At most 10 different searches are made again per check (`DEPENDENCY_LIMITS.searches`; the same reader and query once); the rest, and any search that fails or whose recorder is gone, stay `unknown`. It never throws.
- **Recording a search is checked like recording a record.** The controller makes the search again with the recorder's rights; a hash that is not what it finds now is refused ("a dependency is recorded as it was read"), and so is a position past the project's event stream. The stored entry then names its recorder in `reader`, set by the controller only (a caller sending `reader` is refused). A search of another project, and searches recorded before this change (no `reader`), are judged as before: from a worker's observation, else `unknown`.
- **The digest (`context/retrieval.ts` `searchDigest`).** The first 50 hits of the search with no cursor, each as its link and a sha-256 of the title and text it matched in, plus whether more lay beyond them. A hit added, gone, reordered or edited changes it. No text leaves in it.
- **The operation (`api/operations.ts`, `api/start.ts`): `resume.dependencies.search {projectId, query, key?}`** answers the `search` dependency to record for the caller's own search now (`kind`, `key` = the query on one line, `scope`, `cursor` = the project's next event position, `hash`), ready for `resume.dependencies.record`. Anyone may ask; what they may not read is not in their digest, and recording still needs the right to work the task. `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` regenerated.

**Tests**
- `dependencies/search-again.test.ts` (5 tests × 4 storage backends = 20): unchanged without any worker observation, a worker's contrary claim ignored both ways, a new matching record and an edited hit are `changed`, the check without the port as before; the recorder's rights (the owner checking still gets the agent's view, another agent's private draft that matches changes nothing, a disabled recorder is `unknown`); recording refuses a wrong hash, a position not reached and a caller-set `reader`, the owner's own search is recorded under the owner, bad query and key refused, `unavailable` without the port; `cursor-expired` after retention, a failing search `unknown`, an entry from before this change `unknown`; another project's search judged from the worker's observation; 11 searches plus a repeat give exactly 10 searches made and the rest `unknown`.
- `api/start-resume-search.test.ts` (2 tests × SQLite and PostgreSQL, through `startController` and the state API): the agent asks `resume.dependencies.search`, records it, the owner's `resume.start` finds it unchanged and the agent commits the resumed attempt without the owner; a new matching record makes the next check say `search soil lime (changed)` in the owner's needs-you list and the agent cannot commit; a stale hash is refused; a host's own `resume.observe` does not take the search away from the controller; an agent with no rights in the project gets a different (empty) digest and cannot record it.

**Mutation checks** (built files, each restored): 9 of 9 caught: the search never made again (16 of 20 fail); the position check at recording removed (4); the hash check at recording removed (4); `reader` not stored (20); the 10-search bound ignored (4); the same search not shared (4); the digest ignoring a hit's text (4); a disabled principal still acted for (4); the operation not wired in `startController` (4 of 4 in the API test).

ASSUMPTION: the search is made again with the rights its recorder has at the time of the check, not a snapshot of the rights it had. A narrowed right then reads as `changed` (the owner decides) rather than letting a check see what its recorder no longer may.
ASSUMPTION: 10 searches per check. Each is a scan of up to 2,000 records; ten keeps a check's cost near the file probe's. The rest are `unknown`, which holds the resume for the owner exactly as before.
ASSUMPTION: only searches of the task's own project are judged. Another project's search stays as it was (a worker's observation or `unknown`); widening it would let one task's check read another project in its recorder's name.
ASSUMPTION: the dependency's position is the project event stream's next sequence number at the time of the search, so `cursor-expired` means an event after the search has been cut by retention.

**Not done (L04d stays planned)**
- `external` and `mcp-resource` dependencies are still not read again: that needs a network request to the resource (a conditional read with its ETag or a query to its server), which a resume check made offline cannot test and which is outside what this change may do (no network, no credentials). They stay `unknown` and hold the resume for the owner.
- A Pi agent working through the worker cannot record dependencies itself: the bridge offers it no `resume.dependencies.*` tool and it has no file tools of its own, so in a real run dependencies are recorded only by the owner or a client of the state API. Giving agents that tool (and deciding what they record automatically) is a separate card.
- Not tried against a real model; the earlier L04d lists (a reviewer that reads diffs, compaction lineage in production, pending effects in host captures, the reviewer's call not cancellable) are unchanged.

**First review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)**
- **`resume.dependencies.search` told anyone a project's event position.** "Anyone may ask" let an agent with no rights in a project (or a task credential of another project) learn that project's event count, and whether it exists, from `cursor`; the event stream itself is readable only with `history.read`. It now answers only the owner (inside a task credential's project) and those who may work a task of the project (a project-wide or one-task right) or read its desk records or histories; everyone else gets `forbidden`, the same for a project that does not exist.
- **A superseded hit read as unchanged.** The digest hashed a hit's title and text only. A record superseded by one that does not match the words still matched word for word, so the search read `unchanged` although the note the agent relied on was no longer current (the `record` dependency already counts superseding as a change). A desk record's status is now part of each hit's hash.
- **Tests added** (`search-again.test.ts`, one more case on 4 backends): who may ask (no rights, a project that does not exist, a task credential of another project, a one-task right inside and outside its project, the owner); a task credential's search recorded under its agent and found unchanged; the recorder's read right taken away reads `changed`; a superseded hit reads `changed`; retention cut exactly at the search's position is not `cursor-expired`, one further is. The API test now expects `forbidden` for a caller outside the project. The same words searched by the agent and by the owner are two searches, each found unchanged for its own recorder (a shared result would read one of them `changed`).
- **Mutation checks of this review** (built files, `timeout 150` each, restored): the door removed (6 fail), a hit's status not hashed (4), one result shared by two recorders of the same words (caught after the test above was added; it survived the first try), another project's search judged by the controller (4), a search at the stream's exact head refused at recording (24), a failing search throwing out of the check (4), the recorder loaded without its grants and restrictions (8). The "more beyond the first 50" flag left out of the digest survived: with 50 hits it is always set, so it only differs when a project crosses the 2,000-item scan bound with fewer than 50 hits, which no test builds.
- Checked and left as they are: the fingerprint is ordered (record ID order, then histories) and covers each hit's link and text, so a hit removed and another added never cancel out; a hit beyond the first 50, or beyond the 2,000 items one search looks at, is not in it, exactly as it was not in the page the agent read. A checker that may read less than the recorder still learns only "changed" or "unchanged" from the recorder's view, never which note. A task credential's search is made again with its agent's rights (no task scope): inside the task's own project the two read the same records.

ASSUMPTION: asking for a search dependency needs a right in that project (work a task there, or read its desk records or histories), because the answer carries the project's event position.

**Second review (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-17)**
- **A one-task right over every project reached every project.** The owner may grant `attempt.work` with project `*` narrowed to one task. `resume.dependencies.search` counted that right in any project (the check matched the grant's own task in whatever project was asked), so its holder learned any project's event position and, from a project ID that does not exist (position 1), which IDs exist. A one-task right now counts only when its task is in the project asked about.
- **A project that does not exist answered differently from one without rights** for a caller holding a right over every project (`desk.read` on `*`): it got a search dependency at position 1. Every caller but the owner now gets the same `forbidden`, word for word, for a project that does not exist.
- **Hardening:** each hit's hash now takes the title and the text as separate fields instead of joined by a line break (titles are single-line today, so no collision was reachable; it no longer depends on that).
- **Tests added** (`search-again.test.ts`, one more case on 4 backends): the refusal for a missing project is identical to the one for a project without rights, also for a right over every project; a one-task right over `*` answers in its task's project only; the owner through a credential limited to one task is refused in another project and in a missing one; two identical private drafts (same title, text and status) of two agents give different digests (a hit's link counts); a hit's title alone, then its status alone, revised reads `changed`.
- **Mutation checks of this review** (built files, `timeout 150` each, restored and compared by sha-256): project existence not checked (4 fail), a one-task right counted in any project (4), the title left out of a hit's hash (4), a hit's link left out of the hash (survived; caught after the drafts test was added), the 10-search bound off by one (4), retention boundary moved by one (20), searches made again with the owner's rights instead of the recorder's (8), a missing project answered `not_found` (8), the owner's one-task limit ignored (4).
- Checked and left as they are: the fingerprint is JSON of (link, hash of [status, title, text]) per hit in record ID order then history order, plus the "more" flag, so field boundaries cannot shift; a hit beyond the first 50 (or beyond the 2,000 items one search looks at) is not compared, which matches what one search page shows, and an agent that paged further than 50 hits is not covered (said in the operation summary: "the first 50 hits"). The 10 searches made again are the first 10 distinct (recorder, query) pairs in manifest order (entry ID order), so the same ones every time. The check reads nothing in memory, so a restart or a second controller on PostgreSQL makes the same searches. Doors: the tool bridge does not offer `resume.dependencies.*`; MCP and chat reach it through the state API with the caller's own principal; services and clients cannot hold a desk or work right and are refused; a host is judged by its grants like an agent. Errors, the API answer and the needs-you line carry the query (the caller's own words) and never a note's title or text. The new tests use no pauses, signals or paths.

## T3 (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5): P04 leftovers - the Suspend note for teams and tasks, provider outages narrowed to the routes an agent uses (2026-11-15)

Built from the P04h "not done" list. Nothing here calls a model, touches the local AI server or a credential.

**Done**
- **The Suspend note also covers stopping a team or a task.** `noteSuspendedResponsibilities` takes an optional third argument of ports. A **team** stop (`teamAgents`, wired in `api/start.ts`) notes every responsibility answered by an active agent in that team or any team below it (the same chain a team gate holds); the note says the agent "was suspended/stopped with its team". A **task** stop (`taskResponsibilities`, `ResponsibilityChecks.responsibilitiesOfTask`, a controller-only scan of check records whose run names the task, whether the task was opened for the check or the check rides on it) notes the responsibilities whose check that task carried; its wording is different, because the agent itself keeps working: the check stays owed until a check entry is recorded, the service keeps running, and Suspend and Release names a new monitor. One note per affected responsibility; one reached twice in a request (an agent listed twice, two teams) is noted once; the command id is `stop-note-<request>-<responsibility>`, so a repeat of the same request writes nothing. A retired responsibility, one with no answering agent and an unfinished stop (`recovery-required`) are not noted. A scope with no port (the earlier call shape) is not noted, as before. The agent and installation scopes are unchanged. The notes are still written under `service:stop-notes`.
- **A provider outage is narrowed to the routes the answering agent uses.** The gap key carries what failed (`provider:model:<route>`, `provider:account:<name>`, `provider:endpoint:<name>`). `routeUseOf` turns an agent's routing profile into the route, account and endpoint names it can reach (an alias counts as the route it resolves to). `gapAppliesTo` lists a provider outage for a responsibility only when the agent can reach that name; the kind of name is compared with the right list. `CoverageGapService.withEpoch` takes an optional `routesOf(ownerId)`; `covering` calls it only when a provider outage is among the gaps and the caller brought no routes, and `api/start.ts` wires it from the agent record, the routing table and the route topology. `responsibility.observed` therefore shows an outage of a provider the agent does not use no longer.
- **Safe direction when unsure:** the routes are "unknown", and every outage stays listed, when the agent has no `defaultProfile`, the table lacks that profile, the agent has any `permittedOverrides`, the owner id is not an agent record, routing or the topology is not ready, the lookup fails, the key cannot be read, or the key was cut at its 160-character limit. A responsibility with no answering agent is still not affected (unchanged).
- **`responsibility.observed` summary unchanged.** Its text already says gaps are narrowed to what a responsibility depends on, so the summary, `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` and the op table were left alone (`npm run api:docs:write` changed nothing). `responsibility.gaps` (the project's whole list) is unchanged.
- **Tests.** `projects/t3-p04.test.ts` (4 cases x 4 backends: team note, task note, outage narrowing with a failing and an absent route reader, `routeUseOf` and `gapAppliesTo` rules) and `api/start-t3-p04.test.ts` through `startController` (a cloud outage hidden from an agent that uses only the local endpoint, listed for a broad profile and for an agent with no profile, the local outage listed; a team stop reaching an agent in a sub-team and not agents outside). Eleven mutations were run on the built files, each failing a test and then restored: outage always listed, name kinds swapped, overrides ignored, unknown routes hidden, a failed route read hiding the outage, team not noted, retired responsibility noted, an extra note written, any task matching, sub-teams not reached, route reader not wired.

**Not done**
- The Suspend and Release mode inside the stop service stays with L03 (the hand-off).
- A task stop notes only responsibilities whose check task it was; a task that was merely assigned to an agent that answers for a responsibility says nothing (the agent was not stopped).
- "Scans fail closed above 50,000 records" (`answeredBy`, the index, the new task scan) stays as listed; a fixed bound is the design of every P04 scan and changing it for one of them would make them differ.
- An agent with no `defaultProfile` is "unknown", so its outages stay listed (kept as the smallest change; its check tasks' routes are known from the execution profiles, see the review below, so this could be narrowed later).
- The earlier not-done items about outages the model router never saw and kind-only event source names are unchanged.

**ASSUMPTION:** an agent's routes are known only from a `defaultProfile` with no `permittedOverrides`; anything else is unknown and keeps the outage listed. ASSUMPTION: a team stop notes the agents in the team and its sub-teams as they are when the stop settles (every agent record under the team, whatever its state: the same list the team gate holds; corrected in the second review, which found the earlier wording said "active" but nothing filters by state). ASSUMPTION: a task stop is about the responsibilities whose check records name that task in their run, not every responsibility of the task's assignee. ASSUMPTION: the `responsibility.observed` summary stays as is because it makes no claim narrower than what is now done. ASSUMPTION: the 50,000-record bound was left as listed (not trivial to change without making the P04 scans inconsistent).

**Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-15).** Base 16ef7406 was still current (no merge). Found and fixed:
- **Narrowing hid real outages (dangerous direction).** The routes were taken from the agent's `defaultProfile` only, but a responsibility's check runs as a dispatched task, and the dispatcher picks every attempt's route from the task's difficulty (execution) profile (`DifficultyService.resolve` in `api/dispatch-compose.ts`: the profile's own `provider/model`, then its routing profile's routes), never from the agent; `defaultProfile` is read only for the hosted coordinator's chat. So an agent with a local-only `defaultProfile` whose check tasks run on a cloud route had that cloud endpoint's outage hidden. Now `dispatchRoutesOf` (every execution profile, mapped or not, since a task's difficulty can change) is added to the agent's reachable routes; no execution profiles configured, or a custom dispatch route resolver (`options.dispatch.route`), makes the routes unknown (listed).
- **Past outages judged against today's table.** A gap on an endpoint, account or model since renamed or re-mapped would not match the current topology and was hidden. `RouteUse.known` now holds every name the current routing table reaches; an outage of any other name stays listed. Remaining limit: an outage of a name that still exists but that the agent's tasks no longer use (the owner changed the execution profiles after the outage) is judged by today's profiles.
- **A task-stop note claimed an answered check was unfinished.** `responsibilitiesOfTask` returned every check record naming the task; it now keeps only checks still owed (slot after the responsibility's last check, the rule `pending` uses), so stopping a task after its agent recorded the check writes nothing.
- **One unreadable agent cost a whole team its notes.** A failing `answeredBy` (or `get` for a task) is now caught per agent / per responsibility; the first failure is raised after the rest were written.
- **A stop settled by another controller to a different end.** `StopService.#settle` told `onSettled` its own computed outcome even when its write was refused because the request had already moved (for example to `recovery-required` by a second controller), so a "was stopped" note could follow an unfinished stop. It now reports only when the record's phase is the one being settled, with the recorded outcome. (The second review added the test for it, below.)
- The team walk in `api/start.ts` now reuses `agentsUnder` (the same walk the team gate uses: sub-teams, 50-hop bound, so cycles end) instead of an inline copy.
Checked and left as is: aliases resolve through `targetOf`, the same function the health records use, so names match exactly (topology names are plain identifiers; no case or trailing-slash forms exist); model-level health is a rate-limit cooldown that never opens a gap; overlapping teams cannot double-note (one map per request, command id per responsibility); `recovery-required` is not noted. Tests added to `projects/t3-p04.test.ts` and `api/start-t3-p04.test.ts` (a local-only agent whose task may run on the cloud route sees the cloud outage; a renamed endpoint's outage stays listed; no execution profiles keeps it listed; answered check not noted; per-agent failure isolation). Breakages on built files, each failing a test and restored: known-name check removed, dispatched routes ignored, dispatched routes not wired in start, owed filter removed, per-agent catch removed, team dedupe removed, team port unwired, cloud outages hidden, retired responsibility noted.

**Second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-16).** Re-checked the first review's conclusions from the code. Confirmed: a dispatched task's route comes only from its difficulty profile (`DifficultyService.resolve`, the task's own `provider/model` then its routing profile), and the fallback service is asked with that one route (`routeCallsOf`), so no other route is reachable from a check task; health records and gap keys name the route's `targetOf` canonical, account and endpoint, the same names `routeUseOf` compares. Found and fixed:
- **A note that could not be written cost a stopped task its lifecycle entry.** In `api/start.ts` the stop's `onSettled` wrote the Suspend note first and the task's activity entry ("Stop stopped.") after it; before T3 the note did nothing for a task, but now a task stop reads check records and writes notes, and a failure there (a storage error, the 50,000-record scan bound) was raised before the entry was written (and `#settle` swallows it, so nothing retried). Now the entry is written either way and the note's failure is raised after it.
- **The `#settle` change had no test.** Added to the stop suite (four backends, `lifecycle/stop*.test.ts`): the suite's services now record what `onSettled` is told. An ordinary stop is reported once; a stop that a resumed scope moved to `recovery-required` while this pass's ending ran is not reported; a stop that another caller's Force Stop settled while this pass's graceful ending ran is reported with the recorded forced outcome (`graceful: false`), not this pass's own.
- **The task stop had no test through the running controller.** Added to `api/start-t3-p04.test.ts`: a task that carries a responsibility's check is stopped, the note has the task wording and is written by `service:stop-notes`, another task's responsibility is not noted; then, with the history write failing, a task suspend still ends and still gets its lifecycle entry.
- Notes: the team-stop ASSUMPTION said "active" agents; `agentsUnder` does not filter by state (corrected above).
Breakages on built files, each failing a test and restored byte for byte: `#settle` reporting regardless of the recorded phase; `#settle` reporting its own outcome instead of the recorded one; the note failure no longer caught in `onSettled` (lifecycle entry lost); the task port not wired in start.

ASSUMPTION: when the note fails, the lifecycle entry is written first and the note's error is still raised to `#settle` (which keeps it best effort), so the behaviour seen by the stop is unchanged.

**Third check (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-16).** Re-checked the second review's commit. The order is right: the note and the entry each have a fixed command id per request, so a second report of the same request (the Force Stop race reports it from both passes) writes neither twice, and nothing retries `onSettled`. Found and fixed: a note that could not be written left no trace anywhere (`#settle` swallows the error and the lifecycle entry does not mention it). `onSettled` now also prints one line to the controller's log naming the request and the error ("... its note on the affected responsibilities could not all be written ..."); the stop is unchanged. Test: the failing-history case in `api/start-t3-p04.test.ts` checks the line, and that nothing is printed when the note is written. Breakages on built files, each failing a test and restored byte for byte: note first again (error raised before the entry), note failure not caught, phase check dropped in `#settle`, own outcome reported, task port unwired, log line removed. Remaining limit: the owner is not told in chat; a lost note shows only in the log.

## Test repair "browserclean": the real-browser test closes the browser before it removes the browser's profile (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-16)

**Problem.** `packages/controller/src/web/browser.test.ts` ("the real page in a real browser") starts a real Chromium with a throw-away profile in the OS temp folder (`nn-browser-*`). Under machine load it failed now and then with `ENOTEMPTY` while removing that folder (for example `profile/Default`): the test killed the main browser process outright (SIGKILL) and removed the folder at once, while a helper process the browser had started was still writing `Network Persistent State` into it. The removal retried 10 times 100 ms apart, which was not always enough.

**What is done (test code only; no product code changed).**
- The browser is now asked to close through its DevTools connection (`Browser.close`), so it shuts its own helper processes down and finishes its writes. The test then waits for the process's exit event (bounded at 15 s, not a fixed sleep). Only if it is still running does it call `child.kill()` (the platform default: SIGTERM on Linux and macOS, termination on Windows) and wait again, and only then a forced kill. The profile is removed only after the browser has been seen to exit.
- The folder removal retries only on `ENOTEMPTY`, `EBUSY` and `EPERM` (a helper still finishing a write, or a Windows file lock), with a growing wait (100 ms doubling to 2 s), about 30 s in all. Any other error is not retried.
- A cleanup problem never hides the test's own failure: if the test body failed, the cleanup problem is only reported (test diagnostic and stderr). If the body passed: a browser that would not exit fails the test; a folder that could not be removed fails the test only when it is outside the OS temp folder (it never is today), otherwise it is reported with the folder name and the error.
- A second small test in the same file checks the helpers without a browser (so it runs on every machine and on CI): the exit wait gives up after its bound for a running process and is true once the process ended, a process with no DevTools connection is ended by `kill()` and its exit is seen, a missing folder counts as removed, and the temp-folder check.
- The edits are confined to the imports, new helpers above the test, one `passed` flag and the `finally` block, so they merge cleanly after `card20-encflake` (which changes the launch flags and start-up messages of the same file).

**Checks.**
- An earlier, interrupted attempt reported 15 passes out of 15 runs under load, no `ENOTEMPTY` (its scratch files are gone, so which version of the file it ran cannot be confirmed). The failure is real (two reviews and one implementer saw it) but rare; it was not reproduced on this machine.
- With the change, a probe run showed the browser exits after `Browser.close` (no kill needed) and the profile is removed on the first try.
- Mutation checks, each restored byte for byte (`cmp`): (1) dropping the exit wait after `Browser.close` (removal runs while the browser is shutting down): the real-browser test still passed, but afterwards its `nn-browser-*` folder was found again in the temp folder with a `profile` inside: the browser, still shutting down, wrote into the profile after it had been removed. That is the reported race, seen once at normal load; it is NOT caught by a test (the test cannot see a write that lands after it finished), and stress loops are no longer allowed on this shared machine to measure how often. (2) making the exit wait answer "ended" at once: the new helper test fails (and the real-browser test leaves its browser running, so the run never ends until that browser is stopped by hand).

**Not done.**
- The failure rate before and after under heavy load was not measured: Rob asked (2026-11-16) for no CPU burners or stress loops on the shared machine, and one test run at a time. The fix is judged by reasoning plus the probe and the helper test above.
- Leftover helper processes of the browser are not hunted down by process group (that would need POSIX-only calls); the retrying removal covers the short time they need to finish.

ASSUMPTION: a profile folder that cannot be removed within about 30 s does not fail a test whose body passed when the folder is inside the OS temp folder: it is a leftover the operating system clears, and failing on it would turn a cleanup race into a false test failure; it is still reported by name. Outside the temp folder it fails, so a leak elsewhere is not hidden.
ASSUMPTION: a browser still running after `Browser.close`, `kill()` and a forced kill fails a test whose body passed, because a process that cannot be ended is a real problem, not a cleanup race.
ASSUMPTION: the last-resort forced kill uses `kill("SIGKILL")`; Node supports that name on Windows too (it terminates the process), so it is not POSIX-only.

**First review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5).**
- Without a DevTools connection (the browser failed before it was connected) the close no longer waits 15 s for an exit that nothing asked for: it goes straight to `kill()`.
- A failing controller close no longer skips the folder removal or replaces the body's own failure: it is thrown only when the body passed, otherwise reported. A controller that fails to start removes the temporary folder before the error is passed on.
- The step wait and the removal budget are parameters (defaults 15 s and 30 s), and removal takes an optional remove function, so the helper test now also covers: a child that ignores SIGTERM is ended by the forced kill (signal checked on Linux and macOS); ENOTEMPTY, EBUSY and EPERM are each retried until removal works; another error (EACCES) is returned after one try; repeated ENOTEMPTY stops at the bound.

**Second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-16).** Merged origin/main 5d330ef5 (encflake): `browser.test.ts` merged without a conflict (encflake's launch flags, D-Bus variables, 90 s start wait and last-stderr-line messages sit in the body; this card's helpers and `finally` block are untouched by it); the notes conflict kept both sections. Found and fixed:
- **The rule "a cleanup problem fails the test only when the body passed" had no test.** It was written inline in the `finally` block, so changing it (never failing, or replacing the body's failure) passed every test. It is now one function, `cleanupOutcome(passed, dir, closing, stuck, left)`, used by the `finally` block and checked by the helper test: a failed body throws nothing and each problem is reported; with a passed body a controller that did not close, a browser that did not exit and a folder left outside the temp folder each fail; a folder left in the temp folder is reported by name but does not fail. With a passed body the first problem is thrown and the rest are now reported (before, a failing controller close was thrown and a stuck browser at the same time was not mentioned).
- **Nothing checked that the polite `kill()` comes before the forced kill.** Removing it passed the helper test. The test now checks, on Linux and macOS, that an ordinary child ends by SIGTERM.
Breakages on the built file, one at a time, each run bounded by `timeout 150`, each restored and compared with `cmp`; every one fails the helper test: forced kill removed; EBUSY not retried; retry bound removed (the test fails at its 60 s limit); the temp folder itself counted as inside it; the exit wait answering "ended" on timeout; `kill()` step removed; a cleanup problem replacing a failed body's error; cleanup problems never failing a passed test; a folder outside the temp folder only reported.
Checked: after the real-browser test passes, no Chromium process with an `nn-browser-` profile is left and the run's TMPDIR is empty. Portability: no fixed sleeps in the new code, `inTempFolder` uses `path.relative` (case-insensitive on Windows, and the folder comes from `mkdtempSync(tmpdir())`, so a macOS `/var` to `/private/var` link does not matter), signal names are checked only off Windows. Remaining limit (as before): the browser's helper processes are not ended by process group; on POSIX that would need a detached process group, which would also leave the browser running if the test runner itself were killed.

## Test repair: K01b command-line test and the real-browser launch (card20-encflake)

- Why the K01b command-line test was slow: the real backup command line makes Argon2id wrappers (pure JavaScript, 64 MiB, 3 passes), and the test ran about 20 derivations (setup, add-passcode, rotate and their proofs); the file's other tests that call `runBackupCli` for setup or rotate did the same. On a loaded machine (load average over 90) one test took 80 to 120 s. There were no fixed sleeps.
- ASSUMPTION: the smallest seam is an optional fourth parameter of `runBackupCli(argv, print, lockEnv?, newKdf?)` that is passed to `createKeyring`, `addPasscode` and `rotateKeyring` (which already took these options). `cli-main.ts` never passes it, so the real command uses the default Argon2id. The tests pass the existing quick scrypt settings (N 2^16, the stored floor), so the product's floors and defaults are unchanged. A new test checks that without the seam the command line still writes Argon2id with m at least 65536 and t at least 3; the K01b test checks that the quick settings reached setup, add-passcode and rotate. Mutation checked: rotate ignoring the seam fails the K01b test.
- Real-browser test: the launch now sets `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` and `DBUS_SYSTEM_BUS_ADDRESS` to `disabled:` for the browser process only, adds `--disable-dev-shm-usage` and `--disable-features=MediaRouter,OptimizationHints`, waits 90 s (was 30 s) for the DevTools line, and the timeout and exit failure messages now start with the browser's last stderr line, then the tail; a launch error (the browser could not be started at all) gives the launch error's own message. ASSUMPTION: the CI failure was a slow start with dbus noise; the dbus message is only noise, so the cause cannot be proven from the log, and the longer wait is the part that matters. Checked with a fake browser that exits after printing a bus error: the message shows the last line.

- **Review (Opus):** the seam was checked for reach: `runBackupCli` has one caller outside tests (`cli-main.ts`, which passes three arguments), and nothing in the API, chat or configuration calls it. The floors are checked when a wrapper is made, not only when it is read: passing scrypt N 2^10 or 2^15, or Argon2id m 1024 or t 1, through the seam makes `encryption-setup` refuse (exit 1) and write no keyring. The quick settings are exactly the stored scrypt floor (N 2^16, r 8). Defect fixed: the new "real settings" test called `runBackupCli` in the same process, so it would still pass if `cli-main.ts` passed quick settings; a mutation of the built `cli-main.js` that does so passed it. The test now also runs the real entry point (`node dist/backup/cli-main.js encryption-setup ...`) in a child process and checks its keyring; the same mutation, and a mutation of the default argument, now fail it.
- ASSUMPTION: the CI log line ("Could not parse server address: Unknown address type") is the same line this Chromium prints locally with the D-Bus variables set to `disabled:` and with them unset, and it prints the DevTools line within about 1 s either way. So the D-Bus setting does not remove the message and is not shown to be the fix; in CI the browser printed that one line and then nothing for 30 s. The likely cause is a slow first start on a loaded runner (shard 1 runs PostgreSQL servers alongside); the 90 s wait is what addresses it, and that is unproven until the next exhaustive run. A browser that never starts still fails, after 90 s, with its last stderr line (checked with a fake browser that hangs and one that exits).
- **Second review (Opus):** confirmed against the built command in a scratch folder: `encryption-setup`, `encryption-add-passcode` and `encryption-rotate` write Argon2id (m 65536, t 3) wrappers, and every option that might carry key settings (`--kdf`, `--scrypt-n`, `--argon2-m`, ...) is refused as an unexpected argument (exit 2); environment variables have no effect. Through the seam, scrypt N 2^10, 2^15 or r 1, and Argon2id m 1024 or t 1, are refused with no keyring or recovery file left. Mutations of the built files (cli-main passing quick settings; the default made scrypt; setup, add-passcode or rotate ignoring the seam) each fail a test, and each file was restored and compared byte for byte. The new test makes four Argon2id derivations (setup and its proof, in process and in the child); it took 27 s at load average 55, well inside its 300 s limit. Not changed here: in 1 of 10 local runs of the real-browser test (and 0 of 5 with main's launch flags) the test's final temp-folder removal failed with ENOTEMPTY on `profile/Default`, because a browser helper process wrote `Network Persistent State` after the main browser process was killed. The cleanup code is unchanged by this card, so this looks like an existing race of the kill-then-remove cleanup, not something this change causes; it is unproven either way.

## G10: native caching measured on the owner's Radiance server (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-16)

Full results, tables and the capability matrix: `g10-evidence.md`; raw figures: `evidence/g10-radiance-run1.json`. Radiance came back into scope on 2026-11-16 evening (Rob: "It can go back now").

- **What ran.** `packages/integration/src/g10-radiance-bench.ts` against Radiance 2.1.0 on localhost:8002 (`qwen3.8-flash-next-iq4r`, hybrid, two R9700 cards), 46 requests one at a time over 7 minutes, nothing loaded, unloaded, switched or reset. Part A goes through the production `CacheAdapter` with the Radiance profile: cold, repeat, fork (a second conversation on the same head), switch back, no session label, changed head, and a repeat after 90 s idle, three repeats with a new 13,470-token head each. Part B runs C06b's two-agent conversation (moved into `c06b-scenario.ts`, now shared by the C06b simulator test and the bench) with the NimbleNewt and the naive Pi layout, at the simulator's size and four times larger.
- **Numbers.** Cold: 0 cached, 2.8 to 12.3 s to the first token (the machine was busy). Every reuse (repeat, fork, switch back, no label, after idle): 12,288 of about 13,470 tokens cached, 0.4 to 1.3 s to the first token, 5 to 30 times faster than the cold step of the same repeat (6 to 7 times in repeats 1 and 3; repeat 2's cold step was slowed by load). Changed head: 0 cached, judged a miss, full time. 21 of 21 answers right (the code word or team hidden in the head), cached or not. Part B: NimbleNewt 3,971 against naive 10,605 tokens computed at scale 1 (72% against 0% from cache), 8,437 against 8,717 at scale 4 (71% against 65%); the second agent read the shared head on its first request only with the NimbleNewt layout.
- **Findings that change the design.** (1) On this hybrid model reuse comes in steps of 2,048 tokens (the linear-state snapshot interval): up to 2,047 tokens are recomputed every turn, and a prompt under 2,048 tokens is never reused. A shared head only pays off once it passes 2,048 tokens; C06b's stable-first order still matters, but the gain is in whole steps. (2) The snapshots, not the KV, limit memory: about 119 MB per 2,048 tokens (four times the KV of those tokens); the store's size was not recorded, so whether a 200,000-token transcript can stay fully resumable with the current server setting is not known (41 snapshots were evicted for retention during the run, none because the store was full: `store_full` stayed 0); that is the owner's server configuration, recorded, not changed. (3) `session_id` is a label only (reuse was the same without it), so Radiance shares by opening tokens across every client: isolation `none` is confirmed. (4) The hybrid caveat (a hit that still re-runs the linear layers) did not occur: prompt time fell in proportion to the hit every time.
- **Code changed.** Radiance profile: `fork` is `qualified` (the only qualified capability; the profile test now enforces exactly that), `minPrefixTokens` is 2,048 for a hybrid model (option still overrides), basis, caveats and the `--checkpoint-slots` tuning note record the measurement. ## G10 hosted OpenAI route measured through Hermes (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-25)

Authorised by the owner on 2026-11-25 ("you can use my chatGPT token inside of hermes"); Claude was NOT measured and no Claude credential was used. Fixtures: `packages/integration/test-fixtures/g10-hermes-openai-codex/` (README there); code: `packages/integration/src/g10-hermes-route.ts` (tested converters and `HermesTransport`) and `g10-hermes-bench.ts` (manual runner, never run by CI); tests `g10-hermes-route.test.ts` (5).

- **Route.** The `hermes` command's one-shot mode (`-z`, `--provider openai-codex -m gpt-6.1-sol --reasoning low --ignore-rules`, an empty working folder) with `--usage-file`, which reports uncached input tokens, `cache_read_tokens`, output tokens and the number of provider calls from the provider's own usage fields. Hermes's configuration, credential files and the local model were not touched, read or switched; Radiance was not used. The production `CacheAdapter` and the production `openai` profile judge each call; the only new part is a `Transport` that flattens the messages into one prompt and turns the usage report into the OpenAI chat shape (`prompt_tokens` = uncached input plus cache read, `cached_tokens` = cache read).
- **Live calls: 12 Hermes runs, 23 provider calls** (one run is two provider calls, the answer and Hermes's own short title call; the resumed run made one): 1 first probe, 9 bench runs (2 repeats of cold, repeat, fork, changed head, plus one 330 s idle repeat), 2 resumed-session runs. Synthetic prompts only.
- **What the usage fields show.** Hermes sends about 20,000 tokens of its own system text and tool declarations before the prompt, so every call's prompt is about 24,300 tokens and the 4,300-token synthetic head is at the end. New session, same prompt again: cached 3,968 against 3,968 cold (repeat 1) and 3,712 against 3,712 (repeat 2): the synthetic head was never served from cache; a different question on the same head, a changed head and the idle repeat were the same kind. Separately, some calls (repeat 1 changed head, repeat 2 fork) were served 19,840 tokens, which is no more than Hermes's own prefix, with no relation to what the test changed: not reuse of the head (why only those calls got it, for example which provider machine served them, is not visible to us; that is an inference, not a measurement). A resumed session (the same Hermes session with a growing prefix) was served 24,192 of 24,358 tokens (99.3%; 166 computed). Every one of the 11 answers contained the fact placed early in the prompt (11 of 11), cached or not.
- **Findings.** (1) Hosted OpenAI cache reads are measurable through Hermes: `cache_read_tokens` is present on every call, so the route supplies the field C06's `openai` profile reads. (2) A fresh Hermes process did not reuse the repeated synthetic head in any of the 9 bench calls; only Hermes's own prefix was reused across processes, in 2 of the 9. Reuse of the whole prompt was seen only within one resumed session. That the cache scope is the Hermes session is an inference (the request's cache key is not visible to us, and the 2 cross-process prefix hits show the scope is not strictly per session), so cross-process sharing of a NimbleNewt head on this route is not shown. (3) Time to first token is not reported by one-shot mode; wall time per run (about 5.7 to 7.4 s, includes process start and the title call) was recorded in the raw results only and shows no cold-against-cached difference worth stating. (4) Cache-miss fallback: the answer is complete and correct whatever was cached (every call carries its full prompt); the adapter judged repeats "partial" when more reuse had been expected and "hit" when it came. (5) This route cannot carry `prompt_cache_key`: the production profile put one in every request body, and `HermesTransport` hands Hermes only the flattened prompt, so it records the key in `droppedCacheFields` on every call. That list is our transport's own bookkeeping, not something Hermes reported; whether Hermes sets a cache key of its own on its provider request is not visible here. The profile's key and any retention field were therefore not on the wire.
- **Still unqualified.** Claude (cache breakpoints, 512-token minimums, 5-minute and 1-hour lives, string against array user content): not measured, no key. OpenAI `prompt_cache_key` and `prompt_cache_retention` (not carried by this route, so the retained-marker run is not possible here); the 1,024-token minimum and 128-token steps (not isolated: the head sat behind a 20,000-token prefix whose cached part varied between calls); retention beyond one 330 s idle probe (inconclusive because that call showed only the small prefix); concurrency; the public API key route; Strata, vLLM and llama.cpp (RunPod rental awaits the owner). No capability in the `openai` profile is marked `qualified`: nothing measured here proves one on its own wire.
- **Card status.** Not flipped. Against the acceptance text: the hosted OpenAI-compatible cache is measured through its usage fields, fixtures are captured and the profile re-tested; Claude, the other engines and the retained-marker and concurrency runs on hosted and Radiance remain. G10 is therefore not complete.
- ASSUMPTION: the model is `gpt-6.1-sol` (the senior programmer's model, known to work with the existing openai-codex login), reasoning low, to keep the calls small; another model is a new measurement.
- ASSUMPTION: the profile used is `openai` (the ChatGPT backend is OpenAI's), with no `promptCacheKey` or retention options, since this route cannot carry them.
- ASSUMPTION: the bench was run once, by hand; its raw results stay outside the repository and only usage figures and the short answers are kept as fixtures.
- **Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-25).** No live Hermes or model call was made; `~/.hermes` was not opened. Secrets and privacy: the diff, fixtures and notes hold no token, bearer string, address, account, organisation, user, session, request or device id, cost field, home path or host name; the fixtures keep only the fields `readHermesUsage` allows. The bench starts `hermes` with `execFile` (no shell), reads only the usage file it named, prints usage figures only, and is not a `*.test.js` file, so neither the package runner nor CI starts it; the tests replay fixtures and spawn nothing. Recomputed every figure from the fixtures (prompt totals 24,340 to 24,358; 3,968/3,968 and 3,712/3,712; 19,840 on exactly r1 changed head and r2 fork; 24,192 of 24,358 = 99.3%; 11 of 11 answers; 21 provider calls in the kept runs, 23 with the unkept first probe). Corrected: (1) "Hermes drops `prompt_cache_key`" was read as something Hermes reported; `droppedCacheFields` is our transport's own record, now said so. (2) The 19,840-token hits were explained as routing between machines without saying that is an inference; now labelled. (3) Finding (2) said cross-process prefix sharing was not shown, though Hermes's own prefix was reused across processes in 2 of 9 bench calls; reworded, and the session-scope inference qualified. Added a test pinning the notes' figures to the fixtures, fixture paths built with `path.join`, and the bench refuses a prompt starting with `-` (it would be read as an option). Six deliberate breakages (cache read dropped, total miscounted, dropped-field record removed, type check removed, the production `openai` profile's read disabled, cached off by one) each failed the tests and were restored byte-identical (sha256).

## H12o (approved-submission slice): the release commits an approved submission, exactly once (2026-11-17, Claude agent)

**What was missing.** H12n now opens a real code submission from `work.end { submit: true }` (base, tree and patch ID read by the host), and a reviewer can approve it with a `review` submission (Q01b). But nothing tied the commit to that submission: the release (H12o product slice) committed whatever the checkout held, and the old `commitOnce`/`CommitPort` path (A06 permit) was never wired. This slice ties them together through the existing `release` operation.

**Built.**
- **Approval is read from one record** (`submissions.ts`). Every `review` submission is added, in the same write, to a per-subject list (`submission-verdicts`, keyed by the reviewed submission; at most 50 reviews, the 51st refused). `SubmissionService.approvalOf(submissionId)` (no caller; for the controller's own code) answers: approved when the NEWEST review says `approve` (a later `changes` or `reject` takes it back), or when the code submission recorded `review_disabled_single_agent`; otherwise not, with the reason.
- **The request** (`workspace-ops.ts`, `workspace.request`): `release` takes an optional `submissionId`. Before anything is recorded or frozen: only `release` may name one; the submission must be a code submission of this very task (`not_found` otherwise) and approved (`review_invalid` otherwise). The approved base, tree and approver go on the request's record (`submission`). Right before the host is asked (after the quiesce), the approval is read again; taken back or changed, nothing is asked of the host and the request is `refused`. The host is told `{ id, base, tree }`.
- **The host** (`git.ts` `GitBridge.release`, `host.ts`): with a submission, a commit this checkout already made for it is answered again (`detail.recovered: true`, no second commit). It must be listed in the host-side release ledger against the submission (a fourth field, written before the head moves), still in the history of the head, with exactly the approved parent and tree and the `NimbleNewt-Submission:` trailer. Otherwise the checkout is staged and must make exactly the approved tree on exactly the approved base, or the release is refused ("a new submission and a new approval are needed") and nothing is committed. The commit is the platform's (same identity, hooks, attributes and compare-and-swap as the product slice) with the extra trailer. A malformed submission, or one on another operation, is refused before anything is done.
- **Exactly once at the controller.** A `submission-commit` record (one per submission) is written in the same write as the release's outcome, only when the host answered for this very submission with a commit of the approved parent and tree. A later release of the same submission is answered from that record (`detail.alreadyRecorded`) without asking any host or making anything quiet. A host answer lost after the commit (`failed`), or a controller that stopped while the host worked (`uncertain` after recovery), leaves no record; the next request finds the commit on the host and records it (`recovered: true`). `WorkspaceOpService.submissionCommit(id)` reads the record (no caller; not an API operation).
- **Remote hosts** do not carry this yet: `RemoteWorkerHost` refuses such a release without sending anything, and the request check refuses a `submission` field, so a remote host can never make a plain release in its place.
- **Wording fixed:** an agent told after a release now hears that its checkout "was committed by the platform in the task's own history", not "integrated into the shared workspace"; the chat's description of `workspace.request` no longer says release is refused and names `submissionId`. API docs regenerated.

**Tests (all four backends where storage is involved).** `controller/workspace-ops/workspace-ops-h12o.test.ts` (5 cases x 4 backends): every refusal before anything is recorded; the host told the approved base and tree, the record written once and a repeat not asking the host; a host answer that is not this submission's approved commit never recorded as it; an approval taken back (or a tree changed) during the quiesce; a lost answer, then a controller restart with the request left open, then the commit recorded once as recovered and a late first answer changing nothing. `controller/submissions/submissions-h12o.test.ts` (1 x 4 backends; moved there from `submissions.test.ts` in the first review): approval by newest verdict, repeat kept once, single-agent rule, the 50-review bound. `controller/remote/workspace-ask.test.ts` (+1 x 4): remote refusal. `worker/workspace/release.test.ts` (+4, real git): exact commit, trailer and ledger line, repeats (also with new work on top) find it; changed files and a moved head refused; a forged ledger line naming a commit without the trailer is not taken; a listed but unreached commit (crash between ledger and head move) counts for nothing; malformed submissions. `integration/h12o-submission-commit.test.ts` (through `startController`, SQLite, the local worker over real git): work.end submit, refused before review, reviewer approves, committed, repeat answered from the record, stray file refused, lost answer then retry with one commit.

**Not done (said plainly).**
1. A submission commit is **not a review-gate permit commit**: it is not written to the permit ledger, so a landing under the default `workspace.landing.requirePermit=true` still refuses it, as it refuses a plain release. Making an approved submission count as permitted changes who can open the human gate (A06 is owner-only by default; a reviewer here is an agent), so it is left for P09/P10 or an owner decision.
2. Nothing asks for the release automatically after an approval; the owner (or whoever holds `workspace.manage`, such as an integrator) asks with `submissionId`.
3. The old `commitOnce`/`CommitPort`/`CommitGateService` path is still not wired (the gate service is not composed in `startController`); this slice does not use it.
4. Remote hosts refuse it (no protocol field yet).
5. Q01b's `attemptId` on code submissions is now on main (merged into this branch in the second review); the approval does not check which attempt made the tree (the host checks the tree and base themselves).
6. Reviews recorded before this slice have no verdict list, so a submission reviewed only before it reads as not approved (the safe side).
7. A deliverable accepted through `AcceptanceService` (Q01) is not read as an approval; only review submissions are.

- ASSUMPTION: "approved" means the newest review submission of it says `approve`; a later `changes` or `reject` takes it back. Reversible in `approvalOf`.
- ASSUMPTION: a code submission that recorded `review_disabled_single_agent` (no other agent could review) counts as approved, named as such in the record, so a one-agent project is not stuck; the commit stays in the task's own checkout and landing keeps its own rules.
- ASSUMPTION: the submission commit is not counted as a permit commit (see Not done 1); the smallest choice that leaves the human gate where it is.
- ASSUMPTION: the commit is the platform's (`NimbleNewt release`), as in the product slice; the approver is on the controller's record, not in a trailer.
- Mutations (each alone on built files, the relevant tests run, the file restored; all killed): the host's trailer check on a ledger commit removed; the "still reached by the head" check removed; the exact base/tree comparison removed; the controller recording a commit the host gave for another submission; the "already recorded" answer removed; the approval re-check after the quiesce dropped; the oldest review deciding instead of the newest; the remote host's refusal removed.

## Test repair "flake-scratch": the scratch-cleanup crash test closes its hung run before the storage (card20-flake-scratch, Claude agent, 2026-11-17)

- The failure (GitHub CI run 44017611587, job "typical tier (ubuntu / node 22)", commit d1cba8a0): all tests of `work-end/scratch-cleanup.test.ts` passed, then both variants (reference store, SQLite) of "a crash between the order and its answer ..." reported "generated asynchronous activity after the test ended ... the storage is closed" and the whole file failed after 140 s.
- Root cause (test only): the test starts a second `ScratchCleanupService` whose host never answers and dropped its run with `void`. That run waits on the order's real time limit (`orderMs`, two minutes). The test then closed the storage but never closed that service, so two minutes later the timer fired, the run tried to record "the host did not answer" on the closed storage, and its rejection had nobody waiting for it. The ref'd timer also kept the test process alive, so the file always lasted at least two minutes and failed whenever the runner waited for it (here it failed on every run of the file alone: 54 passed, file failed, 142 s).
- Not a product leak: the controller's shutdown (`api/start.ts` `close`) already calls `scratchCleanup.close()` before `storage.close()`, and `close()` cancels every call to the host in flight and waits for the runs. The test now does the same: it keeps the run's promise, calls `hanging.close()` in the test (and again in `finally`, before `store.close()`), and checks that `close()` returns well before the order's time limit and that the hung run ends without an error and leaves the sweep's "removed" as it was.
- Evidence: the file alone, 22 runs in sequence through the test slot, all passed (about 30 s each, was 142 s); mutation: with `close()` no longer cancelling (`this.#down.abort()` removed) the new check fails; the unchanged test is itself the old behaviour and fails every time as above.
- Not done: nothing else in this file or elsewhere constructs a `ScratchCleanupService` that is left open (checked); other test files were not searched for the same pattern with other services.
- **Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17).** Merged origin/main 7a83661f (notes: both sides kept). Diagnosis confirmed from the code: `run()` is tracked by the service, the order waits in `#bounded` on a ref'd `orderMs` (120 s) timer, and `close()` aborts `#down` (every host call in flight answers "aborted" at once, the lease is given up) and then waits for the tracked runs. Production needs no change: `api/start.ts` `close` calls `scratchCleanup.close()` before `storage.close()`, and the other uses of the service are tests. Reproduced the failure with the old test on the built file in the typical tier (`NIMBLENEWT_TIER=typical`, reference store and SQLite, as CI runs): 54 pass, the file fails with the two "generated asynchronous activity after the test ended ... the storage is closed" errors, 142 s. With all four backends the old test passes locally but the file lasts 185 s (the last timer keeps the process alive), so the failure shows only when a timer fires while the runner is still collecting results. Defect fixed in the test: it did not check that `close()` waits for the run (with the wait loop removed from the built `close()`, the test, and the whole file including A4, still passed); the test now closes the storage right after `close()` returns, as the shutdown does, and then requires the run to have ended cleanly, so that mutation fails on all four backends with "the storage is closed". The time-limit message was reworded (it described the opposite of the failure). Mutations of the built files, each restored and compared: the old test (no `close()`, run dropped) fails as in CI; `close()` without `#down.abort()` fails "close() cancels the hung order at once" (both typical backends, after 120 s each); `close()` not waiting fails as above. The bound (`orderMs / 4`, 30 s, against a close that took well under a second) is not a timing risk on slow runners; no fixed pause was added and nothing is platform-specific. Runs of the file alone with the strengthened test (through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, sandbox required, offline guard, `timeout 300`): all four backends 5 of 5 pass (108 tests, 71 to 92 s at load average 20 to 36), typical tier 3 of 3 (54 tests, 39 to 73 s); each process ended within 0.1 s of its last test.

Diagnosis confirmed independently: the hung run waits in `#bounded` on the ref'd `orderMs` timer, `run()` and `recover()` are tracked, and `close()` aborts `#down` and waits for every tracked promise. Production: the only service is built in `api/start.ts` and its `close` stops maintenance and the dispatcher, then calls `scratchCleanup.close()`, then `storage.close()`; nothing else in the code creates one.
