### w01iso second review (Claude agent, Opus, clean context, 2026-11-17)

Reviewed `card20-w01iso` at `5aeac3e5` (origin/main still `ba0b2b06`, no merge needed). No request to Radiance and no model call: the stand-in model server, the fake agents and the real Pi program against the stand-in only.

**Where this machine keeps credentials** (listed by name, no value read out; then checked from inside the real sandbox with a probe agent started by `runOne`): the owner's home (`~/.ssh`, `~/.pi/agent/models.json` with the Radiance key, `~/.config/gh-token`, `~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, `~/.docker`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.paperclip` with Paperclip's secrets and key file, `~/.hermes`, `~/.modal.toml`, `~/secrets`, keyrings, browser profiles, shell history); `/srv/ai`; `/srv/code/team/secrets` and `private`; `/srv/code/test-postgres/credentials` and `secrets`; the owner-only `/srv/code/qa-vm-aii2166` (a QA virtual machine's disk and sources) and `review-reports/aii-2293-*`; the per-user sockets in `/run/user/1000` (ssh-agent, gpg-agent, keyring, D-Bus); `/run/docker.sock`, `/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock` (mode 0666), `/run/dbus/system_bus_socket`, `/run/ssh-unix-local/socket`; and over the network: **the team's Paperclip database on 127.0.0.1:54329 and its socket `/tmp/.s.PGSQL.54329`, whose login is the Paperclip package's built-in one** (so its password is no protection), Hermes on 127.0.0.1:8642, the model server on :8002. Also: `/dev/shm` holds the database servers' shared memory (Paperclip's included), readable by the same user. Nothing was found in `/etc`, `/opt`, `/var` or `/tmp` holding a key (a pattern search for key formats and a count of the real Radiance key: 0 outside the home). No worktree under `/srv/code` holds a `.env` today (only `.env.example`). Two machine findings outside the bench, reported to the owner and not changed: `/opt/Synergy/synergy-service` is mode 0777 (writable by every user, run by a root service) and `/etc/Synergy/loginInfo` is owned by the owner and read by Synergy's root login launcher.

**What was wrong, in plain words.**
- **The network was a way to the team's data.** With the network shared, an agent could log in to Paperclip's database (127.0.0.1:54329, built-in login) and read or change every assignment, reach Hermes, the tailnet and the internet, and the host's abstract sockets. Now the agent runs in a network namespace of its own with only a loopback device; the model route is the one way out: `lib/net-bridge.mjs` listens on a loopback port inside the namespace and forwards to the key proxy's unix socket in the run's folder (checked from inside: 54329, 3100, 8642, 8002, 22 all refused; curl, python, nc, the real git with `-c protocol.allow=always`, a commit hook calling it and `submodule add` all fail; the loopback listener sees no connection).
- **The agent could write outside its folders.** The file system was shared writable except `/srv/code`: `/tmp/nn-slot.sh` (the script every test run here goes through, outside any sandbox) could be rewritten, and so could `/opt/Synergy/synergy-service` and `/etc/Synergy/loginInfo` (both used by a root service). Now the whole file system is read-only but the run's checkout, temporary folder and artifacts.
- **`/tmp`, `/run` and `/dev/shm` were shared.** Other programs' scratch files, the database servers' sockets and shared memory, the X server's socket, tailscale's and the system bus's sockets were reachable. Now `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/run` and `/dev/shm` are private (empty, its own), `/dev` minimal; supplementary groups such as `docker` are gone inside the namespace anyway.
- **The hidden list knew only fixed paths.** Now `credentialPaths()` also hides, in what stays readable, files named like keys or logins (`.env`, `*.pem`, `id_*`, `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.npmrc`, `credentials.json`, `*-token`, ...), folders named `.ssh`, `secrets` and the like, and owner-only (0700) folders, five levels deep (about 0.3 s over `/srv/code` here, 305 paths: mostly `.npmrc`, plus `qa-vm-aii2166` and the two review folders; one worktree named `secrets` is hidden too, harmlessly).
- **A contaminated run counted as a verified finish in the report and the gates.** `stats.mjs` ignored `contaminated`. Now a contaminated run is left out of the table and the gates (a variant with only contaminated runs is "not measured", so it fails), the report names them and their kinds, and `compare.mjs` shows them as `C`, never a finish.
- **The proxy**: no body cap (now 413 over 64 MB, refused before the body when declared), no connection cap (now 32), a server that echoes request headers in an answer would have handed the key to the agent (the key is now cut out of answer headers and bodies, also across chunk boundaries; only a chunk end that could start the key is held back, so streams are not delayed), and a stream cut short mid-answer got the 502 text appended (now the connection just ends). Hop-by-hop headers (`upgrade`, `te`, `trailer`) are dropped; upstream connections are not reused (a fresh one per request) and the proxy keeps client connections longer than any client's idle limit.

**Checked and found right.** The token compare (`timingSafeEqual` after a length check: only the length could leak, and it is fixed); absolute-form request lines, `?x`, `//`, `%2e%2e`, a trailing `/`, HEAD and OPTIONS all answer 404 and reach nothing (tested); the Host header is replaced; Node's parser refuses a request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding; nothing is logged; streams end cleanly. Runs may overlap (`--concurrency` up to 3 without the Radiance gate): each has its own token, socket, port and namespace. SIGINT/SIGTERM of the bench removes the per-run folders (proxy socket included); a killed sandbox launcher takes its agent with it (`--die-with-parent`, the process namespace); only a SIGKILL of the bench leaves a per-run folder (git settings and Pi configuration, never the key).

**The rare real-Pi failure.** Run 15 times alone (all pass) and in every full run since. Two causes were tried: two runs of the test sharing a run ID (second resolution) and so an artifacts folder (forced with a fixed stamp: the two sub-runs still pass; the earlier visible-home run cannot share by timing, being over a second earlier); a kept-alive upstream connection closed by the server as the next request goes out (3,000 timed tries with the old proxy: not reproduced). Not proven; the proxy no longer reuses upstream connections, and the test's messages carry the record, Pi's stderr and the requests, so a repeat will say why. A baseline copy run from the scratch folder failed every time for an unrelated reason: the offline guard named in `NODE_OPTIONS` lay in a folder hidden from the agent (stated in the README).

**What the agent can still do** (README "The agent's isolation" says the same): read what the user can read outside the hidden places (`/srv/code` with other worktrees and the reference checkout, `/etc`, Node's and Pi's installs); a credential under an unknown name or deeper than five levels; send model requests through the proxy; run the real git by its full path (no network); push into a repository inside its own folders.

- ASSUMPTION: the agent gets no network but the model route. No current task needs the network (dependencies are copied in; NimbleNewt's tests use loopback, which exists inside the namespace).
- ASSUMPTION: `.npmrc` files of other worktrees are hidden with the other login-file names: they can hold registry tokens, and hiding another worktree's copy costs nothing.
- ASSUMPTION: the Synergy permissions are the owner's machine settings and are reported, not changed (changing system files is not this card's).
- **Breakages of my own** (each alone on the source, restored and checksum-compared, the relevant tests run): no network namespace; the root bound writable; `/tmp` shared; the host's `/dev` bound in; the redaction without holding back a split key; the declared body cap removed (first passed: the streamed count also refuses; a test that the refusal comes before the body was added, then it failed); contaminated runs counted in the stats; owner-only folders not hidden; the bridge losing the agent's signal; the 502 text appended to a cut stream; upstream connections kept alive; `compare.mjs` counting a contaminated finish; a header holding the key passed back; the bridge not started. Each fails a test (the writable root and the host `/dev` only through the argument check: no host-writable folder outside the run is shown to the test agent).

## CI repair "winflake": two Windows-only failures of exhaustive run 44069322935 (card20-winflake, Claude agent, 2026-11-17)

The exhaustive CI run 44069322935 (on 71264d30) passed 16 of its 18 cells. The two failures were both on windows-latest with Node 24.21.0, one test each. The earlier exhaustive run 44041210187 passed the same two cells (windows-latest / node 24.21.0, shards 2 and 3), so neither test had failed before: both are intermittent, not tied to Node 24.

- **(A) `start-security-detect.test` (U11d): "one credential's burst is ONE more item (got 3)". Cause: the test's clock, not the controller.** The security detectors bound one credential's burst per *clock hour* (`perSubjectPerHour` 3, then one item for the rest of that hour). The test ran its steps with the real clock, and in this run it ran across 11:00:00 UTC (the file's results were printed at 11:00:11, the test took 5.7 s on a slow runner). In the new hour the credential had its share again, so the closing burst raised three more items. That is the designed behaviour (the bound is per hour), so nothing in the detector changed.
  - **Test fixed:** the test now gives the controller a notifications clock that runs with real time but starts ten minutes into an hour, so the test can no longer meet the end of an hour by chance. It then moves that clock on by a whole hour on purpose and checks the credential gets its share again (three named pairs and one item for the rest).
  - **Small production change:** the detectors used the system clock even when the controller was given a notifications clock (`options.notifications.clock`), while the Urgent watch they report to uses that clock. They now use the same clock, so the two never disagree about which hour a burst is in. A clock that throws or gives no readable time falls back to the system clock (a detector must never throw). Without a notifications clock (every real installation) nothing changes.
- **(B) `k01h-review2.test`: `EPERM: operation not permitted, rename '.nn-data.lock.<nonce>.new' -> '.nn-data.lock'` from `setStaleMinutes`. Cause: a real (small) defect on Windows.** The lock holder rewrites its lock file (to record the owner's `dataLockStaleMinutes`) by writing a new file and renaming it over the old one. On Windows that rename fails while any other reader has the lock file open at that moment. In the test the reader was the holder's own refresh, which reads the file every 20 ms there. In a real controller the reader is the refresh (every 1 to 60 s), the keeper's check or another start reading the holder. The controller swallowed the error (`start.ts` calls it with `.catch(() => undefined)`), so on Windows the owner's setting could silently fail to reach the lock file.
  - **Production fixed:** `setStaleMinutes` now uses the existing `renameReplacing` from `release/launcher.ts`, the one the launcher and the trust mirror already use. On Windows it retries EPERM, EACCES and EBUSY up to ten times, about half a second in all. Elsewhere, and for any other error, it fails at once. If the rename still fails, the old record stays in place (same nonce, the lock stays this holder's) and the rewritten `.new` file is removed. The lock rules themselves are unchanged (exactly one winner, the owner file unchanged). `LockEnv` gained injectable `rename`, `platform` and `pause` for tests.
  - **Test added** (in `k01h-review2.test`, portable, no Windows needed): a rename injected to fail twice with EPERM, EACCES or EBUSY on "win32" goes through on the third try with pauses 10 and 20 ms. The new staleMinutes is in the file, the nonce is the same, the lock is still held and no `.new` file is left. A rename that never stops failing gives up after exactly ten tries with the rename's own error, leaves the old record (staleMinutes 15) and no `.new` file, and the lock stays held. On linux (EPERM) and darwin (EBUSY), and on win32 for ENOENT and EXDEV, there is exactly one try.
- **Breakages of my own** (built files, each run in `timeout 150`, restored, compared with `cmp`):
  - (A) the notifications clock not passed to the detectors (`start.js`): the new-hour check fails.
  - (A) the detectors' hour read from `Date.now()` and not from `now` (`security-detect.js`): the new-hour check fails.
  - (A) the passed clock wrongly scaled (`t / 1000`): the new-hour check fails.
  - (B) the retry judged as "linux" always (no retry): fails with `EPERM: rename`.
  - (B) the `.new` file not removed after a failed rename: the leftovers check fails.
  - (B) EBUSY dropped from the launcher's retried errors: fails with `EBUSY: rename`.
- **Storage backends:** neither change touches storage. The data lock is a plain file in the data directory, and the detectors keep their counts in memory. So the four backends do not apply. The controller test runs on SQLite, as before.
- ASSUMPTION: (A) is a test timing assumption, not a defect. A burst that straddles a clock hour may raise up to twice its hourly share, which is how the per-hour bound is documented ("in an hour"). I did not change it to a rolling window.
- ASSUMPTION: reusing the launcher's retry (ten tries, 10 ms more each time, about 450 ms) is right for the lock file too. The readers hold the file for a single read, so half a second is plenty, and a longer wait would only delay the owner's settings change. It is bounded, so it cannot loop for ever.
- **Not proven without Windows:** that the retry is enough on a real Windows runner (only a failing rename injected on Linux was tested), and that nothing else in the lock races the same way on Windows. One case seen while reading the code and not changed: a takeover's `rm` of a stale lock while another start is reading it may leave a name that is "pending delete" for a moment, and Windows can refuse a new link to that name with EPERM. Today that falls back to an exclusive create and would fail that start with an error, not take the lock twice. Whether (A) can still flake on Windows for another reason is also not proven; the next exhaustive CI run will show both.

### First review of "winflake" (Claude agent, 2026-11-17)

I read the code before these notes. origin/main had not moved past ba0b2b06, so there was nothing to merge.

- **(A) The detectors' clock: correct.** The detectors read time in one place only (`#hour()`: the subject's hour, giving a share back, the overflow key and the `many:` key). They have no other `Date.now`, no expiry and no stored timestamps. The Urgent watch counts its hourly allowance as a sliding window on the same notifications clock. Real installations set no notifications clock, so their behaviour is unchanged. The fallback (a clock that throws or gives an unreadable time means the system clock) cannot loop. It could only mix two clocks in a test that passes a broken clock.
- **(A) A weakness of the design, not changed.** The burst bound counts per fixed clock hour, not over a rolling hour. One credential can raise its 3 named items plus 1 "many" item at 10:59, and the same again at 11:00: 8 items in two minutes, at most twice the hourly share. The Urgent watch's own `securityReportsPerHour` cap is a rolling window and still bounds the total. This matches the documented "in an hour" and is not a clear defect.
- **(B) `renameReplacing` is a plain rename, tried again.** It does not copy and then replace. The lock file is never missing, so no other start can take the lock in between, and "exactly one winner" is unchanged. The pauses are `setTimeout` (async, 10+20+…+90 ms = 450 ms) and never block the event loop. There are at most 10 tries. The `.new` name holds this lock's own random nonce, so the cleanup cannot remove another holder's file.
- **Fixed: the holder's own refresh still collided with the rename, and a release could be undone.** In the CI failure the reader was the holder's own 20 ms refresh. The retry only made that collision less likely. A release asked while a rewrite was between two tries removed the file, and the pending rename then put it back. That leaves a lock file with a live pid that this process no longer counts as held, so other starts on the same host would see it as busy until the process exits. Two rewrites at once also shared one `.new` name. Now the refresh, `isHeld` (which the keeper asks), the rewrite and the release take turns on one chain inside the lock. A refresh that is already waiting is not queued again, so the chain cannot grow. Other processes' reads are still covered by the retry.
- **Fixed: a failed rewrite left the holder refreshing more slowly than its record said.** `setStaleMinutes` re-armed the refresh at the new period before writing. When the write failed, the file still announced the old (perhaps shorter) refresh period, which other starts use to judge staleness, while the holder had moved to the new one. A failure (of the write or the rename) now goes back to the old stale time and period. The write of the `.new` file is inside the cleanup too.
- **Fixed: the failure was silent.** `start.ts` swallowed it with `.catch(() => undefined)`. Both calls (at start and on the owner's change of `dataLockStaleMinutes`) now print one line, the same way the retention reserve failure is printed. The text names the error, which is a file path and a code, never a secret. A failure to read the settings is still ignored at start, as before.
- **Tests added.** In `k01h-review2.test`: a release asked while the rewrite waits between tries does not settle (watched for half a second), and the file is gone afterwards; no refresh (every 5 ms) touches the file during a 60 ms rename, and refreshes resume afterwards; a failed rewrite keeps the old record (staleMinutes 1, refreshMs 15000) and the 15 s refresh period, seen through a wrapped `setInterval`, and a later rewrite that succeeds moves both to 2 and 30000. In `start-backup-restore.test`: a controller whose lock rename is refused prints the line at start and again on `retention.settings.set`, and a later change that can be written reaches the file. In the existing retry test: the next try waits for its pause.
- **Breakages of my own** (built files, each in `timeout 150`, restored, sha256 compared). Every one made a test fail:
  - retry on any error code;
  - eleven tries;
  - pause not awaited;
  - platform check inverted;
  - release not on the chain;
  - refresh not on the chain;
  - failed rewrite keeps the new period;
  - start's failure line dropped;
  - the detectors' hour frozen at the first reading of the clock (the new-hour step then does nothing);
  - `.new` left behind on a failed rename.
- **Left as it is.**
  - Between `owns()` and the rename, another start could take over a lock it judged stale (only possible when this holder has not refreshed for at least 2 refresh periods plus 30 s). The rename would then write over the new owner's record. This existed before. The retry widens the window by at most 0.45 s, and it needs a holder that is already stale.
  - Other places that replace an existing file with `rename` and no Windows retry, in packages' sources:
    - Same risk (another process reads the file regularly): `release/heartbeat.ts` (the launcher reads it), `notifications/watchdog.ts` (the Urgent watch reads it) and `release/activation.ts` (`current`, `current.json`).
    - Lower risk (one-shot, or no concurrent reader): `backup/staged-restore.ts` (journal and pending marker, written during the offline swap), `backup/cli.ts` keyring, `migration/guard.ts`, `transfer/transfer.ts`, `config` `protected-file.ts` and `windows-dpapi.ts`, and the worker's `workspace/host.ts`, `bridge.ts`, `local-host.ts` attempt file and `git.ts` attributes.
    - Different (directory renames): `remote/pi-state.ts`, `backup/targets.ts`, the worker's environment stores and `workspace/local-host.ts`.
    - Already retried: `pi-adapter/thinking-purge.ts`.
    - None of these is in `data-lock.ts`, so none was changed here.

### Second review of "winflake" (Claude agent, 2026-11-17)

I read the code before the notes above. origin/main had not moved past ba0b2b06, so there was nothing to merge.

- **The single chain: no deadlock found.** A link that fails does not stop later ones (`chain.then(f, f)` and the chain keeps `r.catch`). Nothing inside a link waits for the chain: the rewrite calls `owns()` and `arm()` directly, never `isHeld`; the keeper's `isHeld` waits on the lock's chain from the keeper's own chain, and the lock never calls the keeper, so a rewrite that is retrying only delays the keeper's check by at most about half a second. A release waits for a rewrite that is still trying (at most ten tries, 450 ms of pauses, plus the write), so `close()` is bounded by that. The controller's `close()` runs the shared shutdown (`stopAll`) first and releases the keeper afterwards; the keeper and the lock both clear their timers before they wait on their chains, and a rewrite that fails after a release does not re-arm (`if (!released)`). A refresh never rejects (its errors are caught), so the timer's `void serial(beat).finally(...)` leaves no unhandled rejection. A refresh whose file read hangs would hold up the release, but a release did that read before this change too.
- **Fixed: a release let another start in the same process take the lock while the rewrite could still put the record back.** The release took the nonce out of this process's held set at once and only then waited for the rewrite. During that wait another start in this process (same pid, so the record counts as leaked by a failed start) took the lock over, and the pending rename then wrote this holder's record over the new owner's; the release then removed it, leaving the new owner without a file until its keeper noticed. The nonce now leaves the set only once the release has removed the file (in a `finally`). Test: a second start during that wait is refused as busy, and takes the lock once the release is done.
- **Untested before, test added: "at most one refresh waits".** Queuing a refresh on every tick made no test fail. A new test counts the refreshes that run after a 150 ms rename with a 5 ms refresh: at most three, not one per tick.
- **Fixed (follow-up of the first review's list): the controller-down watchdog's record.** `notifications/watchdog.ts` replaced its record with a plain `rename`, while the controller reads that file on every look of the Urgent watch. On Windows a refused rename after a successful tell lost the new `tells` count, so the next look told the same outage again. It now uses `renameReplacing` (same rule: Windows only, EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY, ten tries). To keep the watchdog's small process from loading the launcher (and through it the activation code), `renameReplacing` moved to a module of its own, `release/rename-replacing.ts`, with no imports but `fs`; `release/launcher.ts` re-exports it, so nothing else changes. `writeWatchdogRecord` takes optional test options. Test in `watchdog.test`: two refusals then success with pauses 10 and 20 ms, ten tries then the error, one try on linux, darwin and for ENOENT, the old record kept and no temporary file left.
- **Left as they are (follow-up card suggestion):** `release/heartbeat.ts` already falls back to overwriting its record in place when the rename fails (same size, opened for writing, which Windows allows while a reader has the file open), so a refused rename costs nothing there. `release/activation.ts` (`current`, `current.json`) is written once per activation and read by the launcher at its start, not regularly. A card "Windows rename retry for the remaining replaced files" could cover activation and the lower-risk list above if a Windows run ever shows them.
- **Lock rules: unchanged.** The holder's nonce and pid never change (the rewrite writes the same record with the new times); exactly one start wins a takeover (the guard and the hard link, untouched); the stale rule (2 refresh periods plus 30 s) is untouched, and a failed rewrite goes back to the old period (both halves of the restore are covered by a test). On linux and macOS the rename is tried once, as before. The window the first review left (another start that judged this holder stale takes over between `owns()` and the rename) needs a holder that has not refreshed for over two periods plus 30 s; it heals itself (the new owner's refresh finds the file not its own, its keeper retakes or waits), and the retry widens it by at most 0.45 s, only on Windows. I agree it is no worse.
- **The printed line:** one line, only at start and when the owner changes the setting (never on a refresh tick), through the same `print` as the retention reserve line. The text holds the error's message (a code and the lock file's paths and this holder's nonce, which the lock file itself shows to anyone who can read it), no secret. I changed its wording: a setting that could not be written also reaches the file when the keeper takes the lock anew, not only on a restart.
- **(A):** the detectors read time only in `#hour()`, and with this change that is the notifications clock when one is given. The "3 named plus 1 many per fixed hour" (up to 8 items in two minutes across an hour's end) is within the documented "in an hour", and the Urgent watch's rolling `securityReportsPerHour` bounds the total. The fallback for a clock that throws or says no time has no test (it only matters for a broken injected clock; no installation passes one).
- **Breakages of my own** (built files, one at a time, each test file in `timeout 150`, restored and sha256 compared); each made a test fail unless said:
  - the nonce taken out of the held set before the release waits (my new test fails);
  - the watchdog's write back to a plain rename (my new test fails);
  - a link without a rejection handler and the chain kept rejected (later rewrites never run: 2 tests fail);
  - the release put on the chain but not awaited (5 tests fail);
  - a refresh queued on every tick (only my new test fails; nothing caught it before);
  - a failed rewrite restoring only the period, and separately only the stale time (each fails the first review's period test);
  - the failure line dropped on `retention.settings.set` only (fails);
  - the platform check as `includes("win")` (darwin then retries: 2 tests fail);
  - EBUSY retried only on the first try (2 tests fail);
  - the rewrite run beside the chain instead of on it (3 tests fail);
  - `isHeld` beside the chain (my new test fails);
  - the detectors' clock read once when the controller starts (U11d fails);
  - the bad-clock fallback returning 0 instead of the system time: no test fails, as noted above.
- **Tests on Windows:** the new tests use injected renames and pauses, bounded polls (10 s) and no fixed waits other than the 150 ms inside the injected rename; paths are joined with `join`; no signals; the injected rename, platform and pause are options of one lock or one call, so they cannot reach another test.

All nine benchmark tasks' scored tests pass at their solutions inside the sandbox.

### w01iso final look (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-17)

Read `0c60e835..494b43b6` (the third check). origin/main still 78c0158c, so no merge; the merge 6100e919 checked with `python3 -I`: every notes line either side added is present (81 ours, 122 theirs; the only extra lines are 14 blank separators), `packages/` equals origin/main's and `scripts/` equals the branch's, the notes the only file with a combined diff.

- **Group-only rule: correct.** An entry is hidden when another user owns it, its group is one of the process's supplementary groups (the primary group left out: it is the owner's own) and the group bits grant read or enter that the "other" bits do not (`(mode >> 3) & 5 & ~(mode & 5)`); a group-only folder is hidden whole and not entered. ## L04g: external and MCP resources are read again at a resume where the owner allowed it, a Pi agent records its own dependencies, and the reviewer sees the change itself (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)

The three limits the L04d audit left, each with what was built, how it is bounded and what it is tested by. Branch `card-l04g-impl`. The card stays planned until an audit.

**1. External and MCP resources are observed (changed, unchanged or deleted), not left unknown** (`dependencies/resource-read.ts` `resourceReader`, `network/web-tool.ts` `WebFetch.conditionalRead`, `mcp/mcp.ts` `McpService.resumeReadable`, `mcp/http-client.ts` `RemoteMcpClient.readResource`, `api/start.ts`).
- Nothing is fetched without the owner's allowance, given twice: the installation setting `resume.externalReads` (owner only, **off by default**; read at every check), and then per resource the allowance the owner already gives for that thing: for an `external` address a live network grant of the task for exactly that host and port (`admit`, the web tool's admission: the one checked address, a private or loopback address only when the grant names it, the name looked up once); for an `mcp-resource` an approved, not revoked, remote server whose audience holds the task's project, whose `allowed.resources` lists the URI, and which is still pinned to the protocol revision the read was made at. A local (stdio) MCP server is not started by a check.
- One request per resource per observation, of one shape per kind: for `external` a GET, conditional (`If-None-Match`) when an ETag was recorded; for `mcp-resource` one `resources/read` over the MCP connector's checked public connection (one session, initialize at the pinned revision, the read, the end). Bounds (`RESOURCE_READ_LIMITS`): 10 resources per observation (the rest unknown, said so), 1 MiB per answer (a longer one is not hashed), 10 s for all the reads of one observation together (a timer of its own, so even a read that holds nothing open is given up). A redirect is not followed (unknown, "a redirect is not followed"). Resources recorded with `freshness: none` are not read (they stay `freshness-uncertain`, as before).
- What is compared: 304 to the conditional read is unchanged; a 200 is compared by ETag when both sides have one, else by the sha-256 of the body; 404/410 is `deleted`; anything else (another status, too big, no answer, a refusal, a server without an ETag when only an ETag was recorded) is `unknown` with the reason. For MCP the digest is the sha-256 of the canonical JSON of the `contents` list.
- The reason is in the check: `Observation.unread` (new) is shown as `unknown` with "it was not read again: <reason>" (one line, redacted, 200 characters). The reasons the owner can meet: not allowed by the setting, no grant for that destination, a private address the grant does not name, no network route or no remote MCP server here, the MCP server not registered / revoked / local / outside the audience / the resource not allowed / pinned to another revision, redirect, HTTP status, too big, did not answer in time, more than 10.
- Credentials: the only credential sent is the grant's own header (the secret read by its name at each use, the kept-secret rule applied) or the MCP transport's server header; refusal and error texts are redacted before they reach the check, the connection log or the fault log. Every external read is written to the task's connection log with `via: "resume-check"` (a new value of `ConnectionBody.via`) and its bytes, and the log's per-attempt bound applies (`maxLogged`, default 1,000 records under the pseudo-attempt `resume-check`).
- `WebFetch.run` and the new `conditionalRead` now share one private request path (`#fetch`); `run`'s behaviour is unchanged (its tests pass as they were).
- Wiring: `startController` always installs one `observe` port, which is the files part (this machine's probe, a remote host's look, or the host's own `resume.observe`, which still wins for the entries it reports) plus the resource read. The read reaches the web tool's reader through the dispatch handle (`DispatchHandle.network.web`, new) and the MCP connector through `dispatch.mcp` with a client bounded to 1 MiB and 10 s; without `dispatch.network` / `dispatch.mcp` those resources stay unknown with the reason.

**2. A Pi agent records its own dependencies, checked by the controller** (`pi-adapter` `bridge.ts` tool `nimblenewt__dependency-record`; `toolbridge/service.ts` op `dependency.record`; state API `resume.dependencies.note`; `dependencies/agent-notes.ts` `DependencyNotes`; `continuation/resume-observer.ts` `entriesLook`).
- The agent names only the kind and the key (up to 20 per call): `file`, `directory`, `search`, `record`, `decision`, `external`, `mcp-resource`. The tool takes no task: the bridge sends the attempt's own task with the worker's own credential, keyed by the call ID; a `taskId` argument is refused; a pause refuses it (it is a write).
- The controller checks the caller's right first (`DependencyService.mayRecord`, the same right `record` checks) and only then looks: a file or folder in the task's checkout with exactly the resume probe's rules and placement (the worker's checkout here, or the remote host that holds it, under the project's paths); a search made again (`searchDependency`); a desk record hashed when the agent may read it; an external or MCP resource read once under the same allowance as at a resume (unconditional, `note` mode). A hash, ETag or member list the agent gives must equal what the controller finds, else the whole note is refused and nothing of it is recorded. What the controller cannot look at (outside the checkout, a host that does not answer, a read the owner has not allowed) is recorded only when the agent gives what it saw, and the answer says `checkedBy: "recorder"` with why; without it that item is refused.
- An older controller without the operation is answered in words to the model ("not available on this controller; nothing was recorded"), as for `task.recall`.
- The tool's declaration is kept small (kind, key, and optionally hash and server; one short description), because every bridge tool's schema is part of every prompt's head: a first, fuller declaration (all fields described) put the C07g real-process test over its 32,768-token route's startup budget (8,518 tokens needed of 8,192). The controller's operation still takes every field (`query`, `etag`, `members`, `freshness`, `protocol`) for other clients. `integration/c07g-route-view.test.ts`'s fixture questions are now 300 characters instead of 500: with the larger tool head the measured and the assumed view both kept 4 whole 500-character questions, so its "more questions fit on the measured figure" check could no longer tell them apart; the test's claim is unchanged and passes.

**3. The reviewer is given the change itself** (`dependencies/change-view.ts` `boundedDiff`, `changeViews`, `RecentTexts`; `dependencies/dependencies.ts` text kept beside an entry; `continuation/resume-reviewer.ts` option `change`).
- When the controller reads a text when an entry is recorded (a file through a note, an external or MCP resource), it keeps that text beside the entry (`dependency-text` records, one per task and entry, only for the hash the entry holds; redacted; at most 64 KiB; only valid UTF-8 without NUL), written in the same command as the manifest. When a check reads a text again (this machine's probe hashing a file, a resource read), the text is kept in memory for the reviewer (500 texts, 30 minutes, per task and entry, with its hash). Text a remote host looked at never travels: L04e's rule that only hashes and names leave the host is unchanged.
- For each change put to the reviewer (only observed changes; an unknown is still never put to the model), its CHANGE line ends with `change="..."`: a unified-style line diff of the kept text and the text read now (`@@ line N @@`, two lines of context, a line longer than 400 characters cut and said so, at most 3,000 characters with what was left out counted; a `deleted` change shows the old text as removed), quoted as data, redacted again by the reviewer, and cut further until its quoted form fits a third of a call. Or `change=(not shown: <why>)`: the earlier text was not kept, the text now was not read here, the kind has no text (a folder: its note already names entries gone and new), or the visible text is the same (what differs was redacted). The system prompt says what `change=` is and that it is data.
- The installation setting `resume.reviewerSeesChanges` (owner only, **on by default**) turns the view off; then the reviewer is told only the note, as before. The `resume.reviewerRoute` description and the chat interpreter's text now say that a short redacted diff goes to the reviewer's route, and how both new settings are set in free-form chat.

**Tests** (each fails without its change; breakages below)
- `dependencies/resource-read.test.ts` (2 x 4 backends, and one plain): external resources through the real `WebFetch` and `NetworkGrantService` to a stand-in HTTP server on loopback (a public-looking name dialled to loopback): switch off and no grant fetch nothing; with the grant, 304 unchanged, a body hash unchanged, 410 deleted, 302 not followed, 5,000 bytes over a 1,000-byte bound, HTTP 500, a name resolving to a private address under a grant that does not name one; exactly one request per readable resource, the conditional one with its ETag, the grant's header sent, only the checked address dialled, the connection log `resume-check` and no secret in it, the check or the faults; changed content changed; a hanging server given up within the bound; the 10-read cap. MCP through the real `McpService`, `RemoteMcpConnector` and `RemoteMcpClient` to a stand-in TLS MCP server: unchanged, changed, outside the audience, resource not allowed, server not registered, protocol moved, only the allowed resource read once, revoked server read no more. A read that never answers and a port that throws (plain test).
- `dependencies/agent-notes.test.ts` (1 x 4 backends): a caller without the right is refused before anything is looked at or read; file, folder, desk record, search and external filled in by the controller, one external taken on the recorder's word with the reason; the kept texts (a secret in the file not kept), replaced when the file is recorded again; wrong hash, wrong record hash, wrong members, missing file and wrong external hash refuse the note and record nothing; outside the checkout without a hash refused, with one taken as the recorder's word, no text kept; bounds and shapes.
- `dependencies/change-view.test.ts` (2): the diff's form, context, alignment, cuts and bound; the view against kept and recent texts, each reason, age and hash checks, a failing store.
- `continuation/resume-reviewer.test.ts` (one more): the view quoted after key and detail, a secret in it redacted, a quote-breaking view staying inside its quote, the reasons, a long-quoting view cut to fit, no view asked for an unknown, nothing added without the port.
- `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (one more, and the pause test): `dependency.record` reaches `resume.dependencies.note` with the worker's credential, the attempt's task and a bridge command ID; a named task refused; the activity step; refused while paused. `pi-adapter` `bridge.test.ts` (one more and the tool list): the tool sends what the model wrote, takes no task, renders an older controller's refusal in words.
- `api/start-resume-external.test.ts` (2 x SQLite and PostgreSQL, through `startController`, the state API and a stand-in server): the owner's setting, then the grant (with a credential header), then one conditional request per check (304 unchanged, a new ETag changed), the log, redirect, 404, a private address; the agent's `resume.dependencies.note` filled in by the controller for a file and an external page, a wrong hash refused, the secret in the file absent from the manifest and from the reviewer's prompt, both diffs in the reviewer's prompt; `resume.reviewerSeesChanges: false` leaves them out.
- `integration/l04g-real-pi-dependency.test.ts` (real Pi worker process, bubblewrap, offline scripted model, no Radiance): the model calls `nimblenewt__dependency-record` naming only `src/a.ts`; the controller records the hash of the worker's checkout and says `checkedBy: controller` to the model; the file changes, the next run is held with `src/a.ts changed`; approval lets it finish.

**Breakages** (built, run, restored; tier typical on the unit files): owner switch ignored (fails); `If-None-Match` not sent (fails); a redirect taken as an answer (fails); the reason not shown in the check (fails); MCP allowed resources not checked (fails); MCP audience not checked (fails); the 10-read cap ignored (fails); the observation's own deadline ignored (the hanging-port test does not pass; for external reads the signal handed to the read gives the same bound, so that part is equivalent); the agent's hash not checked (fails); the look made before the rights check (fails); texts not kept (fails); kept text not redacted (fails); the reviewer's view not redacted (fails); the view not given to the model (fails); the bridge sending another op (fails); the composed controller not observing resources (fails), not reading the owner's switch (fails), not giving the reviewer the view (fails), ignoring `resume.reviewerSeesChanges` (fails), the probe keeping no text (fails).

ASSUMPTION: the owner's allowance for re-reading is the setting `resume.externalReads` (off by default) together with the allowance the owner already gives per destination: a live network grant of the task for that host and port, or an approved remote MCP server that lists the resource. Off by default is the reversible direction: nothing is fetched until the owner says so, and then only what the owner had already let the task reach.
ASSUMPTION: only the task's own grants count, not the sites its agent's environment holds through maintenance requests (A09): a check acts for the task, not for the agent's environment.
ASSUMPTION: an external resource's hash is the sha-256 of the response body's bytes as received (no decoding, no cleaning); an MCP resource's is the sha-256 of the canonical JSON of `{ contents }` from `resources/read`. An agent that records through `resume.dependencies.note` gets these from the controller; one that records with `resume.dependencies.record` must use the same rule.
ASSUMPTION: "one request per resource" is per observation. A check observes when it verifies and again when it is committed (as for files since L04d), so a committed check reads each allowed resource twice; each read is logged.
ASSUMPTION: an MCP resource is allowed when its URI is listed, as written, among the server's `allowed.resources` (capability names may be URIs); a deployment that names resources otherwise leaves them unknown, the safe direction.
ASSUMPTION: the reviewer is shown a diff by default (`resume.reviewerSeesChanges` true): the card asks for it, the text is redacted, cut to 3,000 characters and quoted as data, and only text the controller itself read is used. An owner who named a cloud reviewer route sees the setting's description and the chat's text say so, and can turn it off.
ASSUMPTION: the earlier text is kept only when the controller itself read it while recording (a note through `resume.dependencies.note`); entries recorded with `resume.dependencies.record`, earlier entries, binary or larger texts and files looked at by a remote host have no diff, and the reviewer is told why.
ASSUMPTION: the Pi tool offers the kinds an agent can name from its own work (file, directory, search, record, decision, external, mcp-resource); tool versions, environments and negative lookups stay with `resume.dependencies.record`.
ASSUMPTION (first review): dependency texts are kept after a task ends, as its manifest is. A cleanup when a task ends would need a new end-of-task hook in the retention service, and a task that is reopened would lose the earlier text its reviewer needs; it is not a small, clear fix, so it stays a stated limit.

- **Runs** (this worktree, `npx tsc --build`, offline guard, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, through `nn-slot.sh`): controller `dist/api/*.test.js` 672 of 672; controller `dist/{chat,configuration,continuation,dependencies,mcp,network,toolbridge,remote,domain,dispatch,status,setup,work-end,security,context}/*.test.js` 6,495 tests, 6,494 pass, 1 fail: `security/secret-scan.test.ts` "no false positives over the product's own text" flagged the B round-1 grant-proposals run folder name in the W01 section of these notes (commit `c6f5be29`, not this change's; main has since reworded it, merged here); pi-adapter 253 of 253; integration 219 tests, 208 pass, 10 skipped, 1 fail (C07g, fixed as above and passing on rerun, with `l04g-real-pi-dependency` passing after the tool was made smaller); `check:deps` package boundaries ok; `roadmap:check` ok; `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6 of 6; `api:docs:write` added `resume.dependencies.note`.

**Limits**
- Redaction is the controller's pattern-based `redactText`: a secret that matches no known shape could be kept in a dependency text or reach the reviewer in a diff, as with other text the controller keeps.
- Dependency texts are not pruned when a task ends (at most one per task and entry, 64 KiB each, 500 entries per task).
- A remote host's files have no diff (content does not travel). A directory's change is shown by its note (up to five names each way), not as a full list.
- No MCP call record is written for a check's `resources/read` (those records are for an agent's calls); the read is told to the fault log only when it fails.
- Not tried against a real model, a real web server or a real MCP server (offline stand-ins only, by design; no request was made to Radiance).

### W01 night batch: why the server refused the history (offline finding, Claude agent, 2026-11-17)

Card W01 stays planned. Branch `card-w01-badargs` off origin/main `02182c0e`. Offline only: no request of any kind to Radiance; the request was rebuilt from the run's `agent.jsonl` and the installed Pi code (`~/.local/pi-cli`, `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `pi-agent-core` and `pi-ai` 1.5.0), which was read, not changed.

- **Which message.** Pi's OpenAI-style request is one entry per session message here: the system prompt is `messages[0]`, every assistant message and every tool result one entry each (`pi-ai/dist/api/openai-completions.js` lines 890 to 1080; no images, no user message after a tool result, no empty assistant message in this run). So `messages[74]` is the run's assistant message 74 (of 77 `message_end` events, counting the system message as 0): its only tool call, `edit` `call_121c7719...`, the call that succeeded ("Successfully replaced 2 block(s)"), not the one before it that Pi refused (message 72).
- **What the model sent.** Both `edit` calls (72 and 74) carried `edits` as a JSON string instead of an array (6,119 characters for 74's arguments). 72's string is not valid JSON (an escape the model got wrong), so it stayed a string, Pi's schema check refused the call ("edits.0: expected object, got string") and the history kept valid JSON. 74's string is valid JSON.
- **What Pi did with it (root cause).** `pi-coding-agent/dist/core/tools/edit.js` lines 41 to 59, `prepareEditArguments`: "Some models ... send edits as a JSON string instead of an array", so it runs `JSON.parse(args.edits)` and assigns the result **into the same object** (`args.edits = parsed`, line 52). `pi-agent-core/dist/agent-loop.js` lines 474 to 486 pass `toolCall.arguments` itself, so the tool call stored in the conversation is changed after the event log wrote it (the log shows the string; the history now holds the array). Parsing the string decoded the model's escapes: 74's `newText` (a regular expression of characters that must not reach a line) now held a real NUL, control characters, bidi controls and two **lone surrogates** (U+D800 and U+DFFF from the model's `\ud800-\udfff`). On the next request `openai-completions.js` line 1029 sends `arguments: JSON.stringify(tc.arguments)`, which writes them as `\ud800` and `\udfff`; unlike every text field (system, user, assistant text, thinking, tool results: `sanitizeSurrogates`, `utils/sanitize-unicode.js`), tool-call arguments are not cleaned of lone surrogates. A JSON string with an unpaired surrogate escape is refused by strict parsers (it is not valid Unicode text), so the server said "arguments is not JSON". The 400 came on the first request after the call. It was not truncation (the reply ended `toolUse`), not double encoding by Pi, and not text Pi stored raw: the model's text was valid JSON; Pi's in-place repair made it invalid Unicode.
- **Evidence it is that and nothing else.** Re-serialising every stored tool call of the run as Pi does: only 74, after the in-place parse, has surrogate escapes outside a pair (`.../[\u0000-\u001f...\ud800-\udfff]/...` in the re-sent text; 5,803 characters). NUL and the other control characters are written as valid `\u00XX` escapes, so they are not the cause. Not shown: the server's own parser (its code was not read and nothing was sent).
- **Same failure in earlier runs?** No. Over all 39 run folders (the 30-run baseline of 2026-11-10/11, the 2026-11-17 runs and this one) `edits` came as a string in 3 calls besides 72 and 74 (landing-proposal A round 2 message 105, phrase-hints A round 2 messages 83 and 89): none was valid JSON, so Pi never parsed one in place, none put a lone surrogate in the history, and every run went on. No stored tool call in any run holds a lone surrogate. So the server's check has never been tested by an earlier run: whether server 2.1.0 is stricter than the version of 2026-11-10/11 (not recorded in those records) cannot be told from the runs, and it does not matter: the request is malformed whatever the server.
- **Side effect on the work.** The same in-place decoding is what the edit wrote to `commands.ts`: the model had escaped one level too little, so the file got raw control characters and a `\u${` that no longer compiles (`hidden-setup.log`: TS1125 at `commands.ts(517,50)`). Even without the 400, that edit was broken.

**Done here (bench side).** `scripts/pi-eval/lib/classify.mjs`: a new ending `server-rejected-history` (`REJECTED_HISTORY`): the last reply ended in `error` with an HTTP 400 whose text names `messages[N]` within its first 200 characters (narrowed in review, below). It is a non-finish (in the verified-finish denominator, not in the false-done gate, not unclassified), named apart so a batch driver need not read it as a server or bench fault; the reason keeps the field path and the server's own words. `compare.mjs` letter `R`; README's ending list. Tests: `classify.test.mjs` (the exact 400 from the run; a 400 naming no message, a 500 or 401 that names one, an aborted reply and a late index stay `error`; a timeout still wins), `stats.test.mjs` (counted as itself in the table and gates). The classifier applied offline to the run's own log gives `server-rejected-history` (the stored record was not rescored: `eval-results` is read-only here; `rescore.mjs` would change only that one record).

- Runs: `npx tsc --build --force` clean; `node --test scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs` through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`: 94 of 94 passed.
- Also fixed: main's night-batch section above quoted the run's folder name, which `security/secret-scan.test` ("no false positives over the product's own text") flags; it now names the run in words. That test: 12 of 12 after the change (11 of 12 before).
- ASSUMPTION: a new ending is better than `error` with a sub-kind, because the night batch's stop rule reads `error` as "the server or the bench failed", and this is the agent stack failing a task. A driver may still choose to stop on it.
- ASSUMPTION: no repair is coded here. The repair belongs between Pi's tool preparation and the request, which the bench reaches only through a Pi extension (`pi -e <file>` with a `before_provider_request` handler, `pi-coding-agent/dist/core/extensions/runner.js` line 1069, or a replacement `edit` tool); that changes the agent under test, so it is a card, not a bench fix.

**Not proven.** The server's exact rule (only inferred from the error text and JSON's Unicode rule; no request was sent); whether NimbleNewt's production adapter (Pi Durable, its own tools, no Pi `edit` tool) can hit the same path: it shares no `prepareEditArguments`, but if it serialises tool-call arguments as `pi-ai` 1.5.0 does, a model call whose own arguments decode to a lone surrogate would be re-sent the same way.

**Recommended card (added in review as W01b, below).** "W01b: tool-call arguments in Pi's history are always valid Unicode JSON. Pi 1.5.0's `edit` tool parses a string `edits` argument in place, so the stored call is changed after logging and, when the decoded text holds a lone surrogate, the next request is refused (`messages[N].tool_calls[0].function.arguments is not JSON`; W01 night batch run 1). Do one of: (a) in the bench, a Pi extension loaded by `pi-agent.mjs` that, in `before_provider_request`, replaces lone surrogates in every `tool_calls[].function.arguments` with their `\uXXXX` text (or U+FFFD) and records how many it changed in the run record; (b) report upstream to Pi: `prepareEditArguments` should return a new object instead of assigning into the model's arguments, and `openai-completions` should clean tool-call arguments as it cleans every text field; (c) check the production pi-adapter's serialiser for the same gap with a test: a tool call whose arguments decode to a lone surrogate must reach the server as valid JSON. Acceptance: a replay of this run's 74 messages through the chosen path builds a request whose every `arguments` string parses with a strict Unicode JSON parser; an offline test of it; the bench record says when a repair was applied."

**Review (Claude agent, Opus, 2026-11-17; offline, no request to Radiance).**

- **Root cause re-checked.** From the run's `agent.jsonl` (77 `message_end` events: system, user, 34 assistant, 41 tool results; the system message as index 0): `messages[74]` is the `edit` call whose `edits` string is valid JSON; `messages[72]`'s is not. Applying Pi's `prepareEditArguments` step (read in `edit.js` lines 41 to 59: `args.edits = parsed`, in place; `agent-loop.js` `prepareToolCallArguments` keeps the same object when the tool returns it) and then `JSON.stringify` as `openai-completions.js` line 1029 does, only that call (of all tool calls in all 39 run folders) holds lone surrogates, U+D800 and U+DFFF, 5,803 characters re-sent; the logged arguments themselves hold none. String `edits` across all runs: 5 calls, of which only 74 is valid JSON (the notes said 4 besides 72 and 74; it is 3, corrected). Also confirmed: `sanitizeSurrogates` is applied to every text field in that file but not to `function.arguments`. Could not verify: the server's own rule (nothing was sent, its code not read) and that the request's message list is one entry per logged message (read from the code, not from a captured request; the index falling on the only call with lone surrogates supports it).
- **Classifier narrowed.** As written, any 400 naming `messages[N]` within 200 characters became `server-rejected-history`, including a content-type refusal (which the branch's own test asserted), an unknown role or a context-length refusal that names a message: those are limits or a server incompatibility, which a batch should still stop on as `error`. Now (`rejectedHistory()` in `lib/classify.mjs`) it also needs the entry said not to be valid JSON or Unicode (or a field path ending in `arguments`), and no word of a size or context limit in the first 400 characters. Tests for each, plus: the same refusal after the hidden tests passed is still not a finish; a contaminated refused run is still left out; `compare.mjs` shows `R` and counts it among the other non-finishes, and its legend names `R` (it did not). Over all 39 run logs only this run classifies as `server-rejected-history`, and no other ended in `error`.
- **Breakages tried, one at a time and restored:** the condition widened back to any 400 naming a message, refused runs left out of the denominator, letter `R` dropped from `compare.mjs`, the rule moved after the generic error rule (and, separately, the timeout rule moved after it): each failed exactly one test. Before the review the `R` letter and the narrow condition had no test.
- **Card W01b added** (the draft said W01c, which is already the name of a bench worktree, `worktrees-pi/w01c`; W01b is used nowhere): planned under N03, needs W01, and is added to D05's dependencies (the plan has one leaf). ASSUMPTION: D05 rather than W09, since the real worker does not use Pi's `edit` tool and the bench failure was 1 of 39 runs; W09's own runs would show it if it mattered there.

**Second review (Claude agent, clean context, 2026-11-17; offline, no request to Radiance).**

- **Root cause re-checked independently.** Pi 1.5.0 under `~/.local/pi-cli`: `prepareEditArguments` assigns the parsed `edits` into the model's own arguments object, `prepareToolCallArguments` keeps it, and `openai-completions.js` sends `JSON.stringify(tc.arguments)` without `sanitizeSurrogates`. The run's log starts with the system message, so `messages[74]` is log message 74. Replaying that step over every tool call of all 39 run folders: only that call holds a lone surrogate after Pi's parse (none holds one as logged), and only this run ended in `error`. The production adapter's pinned `pi-ai` 1.3.0 also sends `JSON.stringify(tc.arguments)` unsanitised, so W01b's adapter check has something to look at.
- **Classifier fixed.** The size words matched the bare word "token", so a parser's own wording of the same refusal ("arguments is not JSON: Unexpected token ...") fell back to `error`. Now only a token count ("40000 tokens") or `max_tokens` counts as a size limit; tests for both sides. Checked as `error`: a prompt-too-long 400 without an index, an invalid role, an unknown tool name, `messages[3].content` of the wrong type. The real run still classifies as `server-rejected-history`.
- README: the batch loop stops on no outcome; the wording now says a driver can tell this ending apart, and may still choose to stop on it.
- Breakages (one at a time, restored, checksum compared): bare "token" word back, the rule switched off, the `arguments` path ignored, the ending removed from `OUTCOMES`: each failed at least one test.

## W01b: tool-call arguments kept valid Unicode JSON on the bench, and the production serialiser checked (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)

Card W01b stays planned (not flipped here). Branch `card-w01b-impl` off origin/main `1eb54c6f`. Offline only: no request of any kind to Radiance, no model call; Pi 1.5.0 under `~/.local/pi-cli` was read and run against a loopback stand-in server, not changed.

**(a) The bench's Pi extension.** `scripts/pi-eval/arg-clean-extension.mjs`, loaded by `pi-agent.mjs` with `pi -e`. Its `before_provider_request` handler (Pi's runner hands it the whole request body, `extensions/runner.js` line 1066) runs `lib/arg-clean.mjs`:
- In each tool call's `arguments` JSON text (`messages[].tool_calls[].function.arguments`, and OpenAI responses `input[]` items of type `function_call`), a `\uD800`-style escape that is not half of an escaped pair becomes the escape `\ufffd`, and a raw lone surrogate becomes U+FFFD. The text is scanned escape by escape (`\\` is skipped as one escape, so a written-out `\\ud800` is left alone). Note what JSON.stringify does: it writes a lone surrogate as the six-character escape, so the arguments text itself is ASCII and well-formed; only decoding it gives the lone surrogate. A raw-character check (`isWellFormed`) on the text would therefore miss the night batch's case; the escapes have to be read.
- In every other string of the request a raw lone surrogate becomes U+FFFD (pi-ai already cleans its text fields; this is a net for anything it does not). Escape-like text outside arguments is the author's and stays.
- Valid pairs (escaped or raw) and every other byte stay. The body is copied only along changed paths; a request that needs nothing gets no return value, so Pi sends its own body unchanged. The handler never throws (its own try/catch, besides the runner's).
- Counts only, never content: `arg-clean.json` beside the log (`PI_EVAL_ARG_CLEAN_FILE`, set by `pi-agent.mjs` to the run's artifacts folder, which the sandbox already makes writable) holds requests, requests changed, strings changed, arguments changed and errors, written at load and after every request. `lib/runner.mjs` `readArgClean` copies the numbers into the run record as `argClean`, with `applied` true when any request was repaired. README section "Tool-call arguments kept valid Unicode JSON".
- Isolation: the extension sits beside `pi-agent.mjs`, whose folder the sandbox already binds readable for the agent script (and `/srv/code` is a read-only tree anyway); it imports only `lib/arg-clean.mjs` from the same folder and writes only into the artifacts folder. It adds no path, network or permission.

**(b) The production adapter.** The gap is real in NimbleNewt's pinned pi-ai 1.3.0, and not only through Pi's edit tool: any model tool call whose arguments decode to a lone surrogate is re-sent invalid. `openai-completions.js` line 1041 and `openai-responses-shared.js` line 242 send `JSON.stringify(arguments)`; `anthropic-messages.js` line 1176 sends the object as `input`, which the SDK stringifies the same way. A test (`packages/pi-adapter/src/argument-clean.test.ts`) shows it for all three APIs: the real adapter, a scripted provider whose first reply is a tool call with lone surrogates in its arguments, and the body pi-ai builds for the next request (`testing/wire.ts`, stopped before sending); built without the adapter's repair a strict reading refuses it. The adapter owns a simple hook point: every model call already goes through `shapeModels` (`cache-shaping.ts`), which hands pi-ai an `onPayload`. It now always does: the cache shaping (when any), then the caller's own `onPayload`, then `argument-clean.ts`'s `cleanPayload` (the same rules as the bench's, in TypeScript), also for compaction calls (`completeSimple`). With it the next request is valid Unicode JSON on all three APIs, the valid pair kept, and the tool itself still got the model's arguments as they were (the repair is only on the wire). A body that needs nothing is built byte-for-byte as pi-ai builds it alone (tested on all three APIs).

**(c) Offline proof.**
- `scripts/pi-eval/arg-clean.test.mjs`: the cleaner's cases (lone high, lone low, broken pair, escaped and raw pairs, `\\` before an escape, a high escape before a pair, mixed case, a short escape); the real failure shape (a string `edits` with `\ud800-\udfff` escapes, decoded by Pi's step and re-stringified: refused; cleaned: accepted by a UTF-8 decode with `fatal: true`, `JSON.parse` and `isWellFormed` on every string, the broken pair U+FFFD, the pair 𐏿 and all else kept); no-change returns the same object; responses API; never throws (a throwing proxy, a cycle, a deep nest, non-plain objects); the extension through a fake runner with Pi's chaining rule; `readArgClean`; `pi-agent.mjs` passes `-e` with the extension beside it and the record file beside the log (a fake Pi binary).
- The card's acceptance replay: the night run's 77 logged messages, reduced to `scripts/pi-eval/fixtures/w01b-night-run-messages.jsonl` (48 KB: every text replaced by its length, the tool calls' arguments exactly as the model sent them), with Pi's own edit step applied (Pi 1.5.0's `createEditToolDefinition(...).prepareArguments` when installed, else the same step written out), built into a request by pi-ai's OpenAI chat builder (Pi 1.5.0's when installed, and the pinned 1.3.0 always), stopped at `onPayload`. Without the extension exactly `messages[74]` fails the strict check, the index Radiance named; through the extension every arguments text passes, one argument is counted, and only that text changed, by the two escapes. The same messages as logged (before Pi's step) need nothing: the handler returns nothing and counts zero changes.
- The real Pi (`isolation.test.mjs`, last Pi test): Pi 1.5.0 in the bench's sandbox via `runOne`, against the loopback stand-in, which now records bodies and, when told to, refuses a request whose tool-call arguments are not well-formed Unicode JSON with Radiance's 400 text. The stand-in's first reply is `edit` with `edits` as a JSON string holding `\ud800-\udfff` and the escaped pair `𐏿`. Pi decodes it in place and edits the file; the second request reaches the stand-in well-formed (`newText` ends `U+FFFD-U+FFFD 𐏿`), the run ends `stop`, and the record says `argClean: { applied: true, requests: 2, requestsChanged: 1, stringsChanged: 1, argumentsChanged: 1, errors: 0 }`; the record file holds no request text. With the `-e` removed the same test fails (the stand-in refuses the history, as Radiance did).

**Runs.** `npx tsc --build --force` clean. Through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, the offline guard, none skipped: `scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs` with `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 113 of 113; pi-adapter whole suite 258 of 258; controller `security/*` (secret scan included) with integration `c06b-cache-stability` (the other user of `shapeModels`' `onPayload`) 268 of 268 before this section, secret-scan again after it; `npm run check:deps`, `npm run roadmap:check`.

**Breakages tried, one at a time, each restored and its checksum compared:** the cleaner off (7 tests failed, the real Pi test among them); escaped pairs no longer kept (1, the cleaner's cases); the count not written after a request (2: fake runner, real Pi record); the extension not loaded by `pi-agent.mjs` (2: the launcher test, the real Pi test); the handler's try/catch removed (1: fake runner); the adapter's repair removed from `withCleanArguments` (3: one per API).

- ASSUMPTION: U+FFFD rather than the escaped text of the surrogate (`\\ud800` as written-out text). The card allows either; U+FFFD is what `toWellFormed` and a replacing UTF-8 decoder give, cannot be mistaken for the model's own text, and keeps the arguments' length in escapes. The model's file edit itself is not repaired: Pi wrote what it decoded (the night run's edit was broken anyway).
- ASSUMPTION: the replay fixture is the night run reduced, not the run's whole 4.8 MB log, and is committed so the acceptance replay runs anywhere (CI too, with pi-ai 1.3.0); the 1.5.0 replay and the real Pi test skip where Pi is not installed.
- ASSUMPTION: the cleaner is written twice (bench JavaScript, adapter TypeScript) instead of the bench importing the adapter's build: the bench scripts need no build, and the two copies are tested against the same cases.
- ASSUMPTION: the adapter's repair records no count. Its worker has no run record; a count would go through the audit, a wider change than this card. The bench's record is the one the card asks for.
- ASSUMPTION: the repair is always on, with no switch: it changes nothing in a request that needs nothing (tested), and a switch would let a batch run without it unnoticed.

**Not proven / limits.** Not tried on Radiance (no request was allowed): that the server accepts `\ufffd` in place of the escapes is inferred from JSON's rule, not seen. Only the OpenAI chat and responses shapes are read as arguments text; another provider shape that carries arguments as text elsewhere would get the raw-surrogate net only. Reporting the in-place parse and the missing cleaning upstream to Pi remains the owner's option.

### W01b first review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)

Reviewed and fixed on the branch; card not flipped, nothing pushed, no request to Radiance.
- **Fixed: a pair written half escaped, half raw was broken.** `"\ud800` followed by a raw U+DFFF (or a raw U+D800 followed by `\udfff`) decodes to the valid pair, but the cleaner replaced both halves. Both copies (`lib/arg-clean.mjs`, `argument-clean.ts`) now keep a pair however its halves are written. pi-ai's `JSON.stringify` never writes such a mix, so the night batch was not affected.
- **Fixed: arguments text that is not valid JSON was read as escapes.** Such text is now treated like any other string (only raw lone surrogates replaced): the escape reading runs only where it found something, and is kept only when the text parses.
- **Fixed: object keys were not cleaned.** An Anthropic `input` object (or any object of the request) with a lone surrogate in a key was sent as it was; the key is now replaced the same way, the key order and values kept (a `__proto__` key stays an own key).
- **Tests added:** the cases above, idempotence, a megabyte each of arguments, backslashes and raw lone surrogates (linear, a generous time bound), and a `shapeModels` unit test: the repair runs last on both `streamSimple` and the compaction call `completeSimple`, the caller's `onPayload` sees the body before the repair, a caller's replacement is what gets cleaned, a body that needs nothing comes back as the same object, a caller's own error still reaches pi-ai.
- Docs: the escape written is `\ufffd` (two places showed the character instead).
- Checked, no change needed: the extension is read inside the sandbox from the folder already bound for `pi-agent.mjs` and writes only `arg-clean.json` beside the log; the record copies only the five counts; the fixture holds no credential (every text replaced by its length, the tool calls' arguments as the model sent them: commands and edits of this repository); the 1.5.0 replay and the real-Pi test skip with a stated reason when Pi is absent; the real-Pi test uses the bench's existing stand-in server on an ephemeral loopback port and the bench's own timeouts; the worker does not compose the adapter.

- Runs (once, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, the offline guard): `scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs` with `scripts/*.test.mjs` 332 of 333 (one skipped: a non-Linux-only check); pi-adapter whole suite 261 of 261; controller `security/*` 262 of 262; the integration tests that compose the adapter (`c06b-cache-stability`, `h12e-pi-cache` and 13 more) 46 of 46; `npx tsc --build --force` clean; `check:deps`, `roadmap:check` ok.

### W01b second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-17)

Reviewed with a clean context and fixed on the branch; card not flipped, nothing pushed, no request to Radiance, no model call.
- **Fixed: a pair written half escaped, half raw still left a lone surrogate on the wire.** The first review kept such a pair as it was, because JSON decodes it to the pair. But the arguments text is itself a string of the request body: its raw half, alone in that string, is written by `JSON.stringify` as a lone `\udfff`-style escape in the body, which a strict server refuses before it reads the arguments. Both copies now write the raw half as its escape (`\ud800` + raw U+DFFF becomes `\ud800\udfff`): the same pair once decoded, and the text well-formed. pi-ai never writes such a mix (only a payload built by other code could hold one), so the night batch was not affected. The test helper `strictJson` now also requires the text itself to be well-formed, the stricter reading that would have caught it.

- **Added: a seeded property test** (`arg-clean.test.mjs`) comparing the bench copy with the adapter's build on 20 000 generated inputs (escapes, raw halves, pairs in every form, backslashes, broken JSON, keys): both agree on text, counts and payload; the result is well-formed and strict; cleaning again changes nothing; already strict input and a payload needing nothing come back unchanged. Before the two fixes it found both. Exact cases for both fixes in both suites.
- Checked, no change needed: escapes inside a string that is itself JSON (a `\\ud800` written out) are left alone; key order, number formatting and duplicate keys inside arguments text are untouched (the text is only edited at a replaced escape); the caller's `onPayload` sees the body before the repair, which is intended (anything it adds is cleaned too) and no production caller passes one; the repair runs on `streamSimple` and on `completeSimple`, the only two model calls pi-durable makes; prompt-cache keys and the prefix tracker are computed from the context, not the body, so a body that needs nothing is byte-for-byte as before; tool executions get the arguments as the model sent them. Five megabyte inputs take at most about a second in either copy (linear).
- Limits kept: only the OpenAI chat and responses shapes are read as arguments text (Mistral's and Google's carry them elsewhere and get only the raw-surrogate rule); containers deeper than 64 levels are not walked. That Radiance accepts `�` in place of the escapes is still inferred from JSON's rule, not seen.
