## W01c: the bench's sandbox hides the shared work folder; a run sees its own checkout only (Claude agent, 2026-11-18)

Follow-up to the W01 batch 2 note above ("Hiding `eval-work` ... not done here"). Before this change the bubblewrap sandbox of `scripts/pi-eval` left the work root (default `eval-work`, which holds every run's checkout) readable, because its parent is one of the read-only trees; with `--concurrency` above 1 an agent could list and read another run's checkout.

- **What changed.** `lib/isolation.mjs` has a new `workRootHidden` and `lib/runner.mjs` (`isolateAgent`) adds its result to the hidden folders. The work root gets an empty tmpfs; the run's own checkout is bound back writable after it (the existing bind of the run's folders), so inside the sandbox the work root lists exactly one entry. The work root is also left out of the credential-name scan, since hidden folders are not walked.
- **Fallback.** When a folder the agent must still read (the reference repository, the bench, a `--read-only` tree) lies inside the work root, hiding the whole root would hide it too. Then each other entry present at the run's start is hidden one by one (an empty folder in its place), and the run's own checkout and the entries holding a kept folder stay.
- **Tests** (`scripts/pi-eval/isolation.test.mjs`, a new fake agent `test-agents/peek-agent.mjs`): the choice of what to hide and the mount order (no sandbox needed); under the real sandbox a run cannot list, find or read a planted sibling checkout and still lists, writes and runs git in its own; the fallback keeps a reference folder inside the work root readable while the sibling's folder is empty. The two sandbox tests fail with the hiding switched off.
- ASSUMPTION: hiding the work root as a whole (a tmpfs, then the own checkout bound back) was chosen over a separate work root per run, because it needs no change to where checkouts go, to the cleanup of `eval-*` folders or to the contamination watch list.
- ASSUMPTION: in the fallback case a sibling created after the run started is not hidden; this only happens with an unusual `--work-root` that holds the reference repository, and the contamination detector still flags any look into the work root's parent.
- ASSUMPTION: the record's `isolation.hidden` now names the work root; nothing reads that list except tests and people.
- **Checks:** `scripts/pi-eval/isolation.test.mjs` 19 of 19 (none skipped), and the whole `scripts/pi-eval` suite 112 of 112 (none skipped), and `security/secret-scan.test` 12 of 12 over these notes, all through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`. No request to Radiance, no network, no real credentials.

### W01c review (Claude agent, 2026-11-18)

- **Fixed: a work root given as a link stopped every run.** With the work root hidden, bubblewrap must make the run's checkout a mount point inside the empty work root; it cannot do that through an absolute link (a `--work-root` or `PI_EVAL_WORK_ROOT` that is a link to another disk), so the agent never started ("Can't mkdir ... No such file or directory") and the run was recorded as an error. `bwrapPrefix` now binds each folder back at where it really is; the link inside the sandbox still leads there. A new sandbox test runs through such a link to a work root whose name has spaces, brackets and a non-ASCII letter.
- **Fixed: links in the work root in the fallback case.** Entries were hidden by their name and the hidden list is resolved to real paths later, so a link in the work root to the reference repository (or to the run's own checkout) would have hidden that target. `workRootHidden` now takes each entry by where it really is and skips links leading out of the work root (they are not a sibling's checkout); the unit test covers a link to a kept folder, to the own checkout and to a sibling.
- **Test fix:** each W01c sandbox test has its own results folder, so a peek report left by an earlier test (two runs started in the same second share an artifacts folder) cannot stand in for a run whose agent never started; that is how the link problem first showed as a wrong listing instead of a missing report.
- **Checked, no change:** the mount order (private folders, read-only trees, then the work root's empty tmpfs, then the run's own checkout, temporary folder and artifacts bound back writable; nothing hidden lies inside them); the contamination watch list and its test in `runner.test.mjs` are unchanged; hidden-test copy-in, result writing and checkout cleanup run outside the sandbox and are untouched; a missing work root hides nothing.
- **Deliberate breakages, one at a time:** hiding switched off fails all four W01c tests; entries taken by name fails the unit test; folders bound back by the given path fails the link test; the own checkout not excluded in the fallback fails the unit test (the sandbox still shows it, since it is bound back after).
- ASSUMPTION: a reference folder given as a link that lives inside the work root (its target outside) is not kept visible through that link; the bench binds read-only trees by their real path, and no option produces such a layout.

### W01c second review (Claude agent, 2026-11-18)

- **Fixed: a folder of the run named through a link that lies in a covered place.** Binding the run's folders back only at their real paths (the first review's fix) left the spelling the agent is given missing when the link itself sits in a private or hidden folder that nothing shows again, such as `--work-root /tmp/eval-link` leading to another disk (the work root's parent `/tmp` is not a read-only tree, since it is a private folder): the agent's working folder did not exist inside and the run produced nothing. Before W01c such a folder was bound at its given path, which worked there because the link is absent in the empty tmpfs. `bwrapPrefix` now binds each folder at its real path and, when its given path is a different spelling inside a private or hidden folder not shown again by a read-only tree or another folder bound back, also at that spelling. A new sandbox test runs with a work root given as a link directly in `/tmp`; it fails without the change (the agent's commands had no working folder).
- **Checked, no change:** mount order and real paths in `workRootHidden` and `bwrapPrefix`; nothing the bench needs inside the sandbox lives in the work root besides the run's own checkout (checkouts are standalone repositories with copied dependencies; results, hidden tests, grading and cleanup are outside the sandbox or outside the work root); credential hiding, the git push refusal and the network namespace are unchanged (their existing tests pass); the W01c sandbox tests each fail with the hiding off (first review's breakages).
- **Checks:** `scripts/pi-eval/isolation.test.mjs` 21 of 21, the whole `scripts/pi-eval` suite 114 of 114 (none skipped) and `security/secret-scan.test` 12 of 12 over these notes, all through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh` with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` and the offline guard. No request to Radiance, no network, no real credentials.

### W01c third check (Claude agent, 2026-11-18)

- **Fixed: a hidden place inside a run folder bound at its second spelling.** The second bind (above) showed again what was hidden inside that folder, because bubblewrap binds from the host's side and the empty folder put over a hidden place at the real path does not carry over to the other spelling (shown with a planted file: unreadable at the real path, readable through the link). `bwrapPrefix` now covers each hidden place inside such a folder at the second spelling too, and binds the second spellings shortest first. No current caller hides anything inside a run's own folders (the credential scan leaves them out), so this keeps the documented rule rather than closing an open path. A new sandbox test fails without the change.
- **Checked, no change:** the second bind shows the same folder with the same mode (`--bind` only for the run's writable folders), only at a spelling inside a private or hidden folder that no read-only tree or folder bound back shows, so it exposes no sibling checkout and makes nothing writable that was read-only; real paths contain no link, so no other folder bound back lies under a second spelling; the bench's settings are bound last, as before. Both W01c link tests remove their link in `/tmp` in a `finally`; none was left after the runs. The second review's test fails against the first review's `isolation.mjs`.
- **Checks:** the whole `scripts/pi-eval` suite 115 of 115 (none skipped) and `security/secret-scan.test` 12 of 12 over these notes, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh` with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` and the offline guard. Skipped: other packages' suites (nothing outside `scripts/pi-eval` changed). No request to Radiance, no network, no credentials.

## P04j (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5): acting on a remote host through an approved tool, with no worker there (2026-11-17)

The last open clause of card P04: "a remote host is managed through an approved tool with no worker enrolled on it". P04i only watches such a host (the owner's HTTP probe). This slice builds the acting half, from production pieces only: the tool bridge, the dispatcher's tool path and effect ledger, the network grants, and the maintenance leases. Nothing here calls a model or touches the local AI server; the test reaches only a server on 127.0.0.1.

**Done**
- **The tool** `nimblenewt.remote-action` 1.0.0 (`projects/remote-action.ts`), a built-in tool of the bridge, wired in `api/start.ts` next to the web tool (present when the network options are). The agent names a managed resource, says what the change is for, and gives one request (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, a path and an optional JSON body of at most 16 KiB), a check path (a GET, healthy statuses default to any 2xx) and an optional rollback request.
- **Approved tool, normal path.** Called only through `tool.invoke`: the agent needs the owner's grant `tool.nimblenewt.remote-action`; the approval policy classes it `mutate` (strict: the owner is asked; derived: allowed in development and testing, reviewed in staging, the owner for customer-live; autonomous: allowed, reviewed for customer-live); budgets, pauses and decisions apply. A built-in tool can now declare `effect` (`BuiltinTool.effect`), and then the bridge runs it through the effect ledger (the dispatcher refuses a mutate tool any other way): one effect per call, never run again blindly; a typed refusal is a failed effect (nothing done), anything else after it began is uncertain. The dispatcher's failed-effect text now carries the bridge's own reason (cleaned, cut to 300 characters) instead of only "the target refused the effect".
- **Approved reach.** Every request goes through the web tool's admission (`WebFetch.act`, new): only to a host and port the task holds a live network grant for (loopback and private addresses only when the owner's grant names them), to the one checked address, no redirect followed, no credential but the grant's own header, logged in the task's connection log with `via: remote-action`. Requests go only to the managed resource's own address: its locator gives scheme, host and port; the agent gives paths (one leading `/`, no `//`, `#`, `..`, spaces, control characters or anything the credential redactor would hide). The grant is looked at before the lease is taken, so a task that cannot reach the host leases nothing. Only statuses come back, never the server's text.
- **Under the lease, recorded as leases record it.** The tool takes the maintenance lease for the agent (`MaintenanceLeaseService.acquire`: authority, active responsibility). Another agent's lease is a visible block (`outcome: blocked`, the holder and its end) and nothing is sent. Then: the action; if it answered 2xx, the check. Passed: `release` with `validation: passed`. Otherwise failed: a rollback is sent only when the agent gave one AND the responsibility's `permittedActions` names `rollback`; if it succeeds, `release` with `rollback`; otherwise (none given, not permitted, or the rollback failed) `release` with `escalate`, which opens the incident and escalates it at once (the lease service's own records). Each lease command is keyed by the attempt and the call ID.
- **Maintenance window.** While the responsibility's maintenance window is on, the change is held (refused, nothing leased or sent), as the check task text already says.
- **Review fixes (Claude agent, Opus review).** (1) Anything that failed before the lease was held, other than a typed refusal (a storage error reading the resource, say), was thrown as a plain error, so the effect ledger left the call uncertain for the owner to resolve although nothing had been sent; it is now a refusal (`unavailable`, "nothing was sent"). (2) The lease service renews a lease for the agent that already holds it, so two calls of one agent on one resource (parallel tool calls) both went ahead, and the first release ended the second's holding; a renewal now answers `blocked` (nothing sent, the other holding left alone). (3) An action refused by admission before it went out (the grant changed since it was looked at, the name resolves to an address the grant does not allow) was treated like a failed request: the check was skipped but a permitted rollback was still sent; now nothing more is sent and the lease is released failed and escalated, saying nothing reached the service. `WebFetch.act`'s comment said every `DomainError` meant nothing was sent; `unavailable` is a request that failed once under way, and is now treated as possibly sent. (4) The arguments of an effect tool are kept whole on the effect ledger before the tool runs, so a credential in a request body would have been stored; the bridge now refuses effect-tool arguments that the redactor would change, before anything is recorded. (5) The text of an error thrown after the lease went onto the effect's evidence unredacted; it is now redacted. (6) The lease is now held at least 5 minutes (was 1), longer than the three requests' 30-second bounds together. (7) `..` segments are refused in every spelling the URL parser reads as one (`.%2e`, `%2e.`), not only `..` and `%2e%2e`.
- **Tests.** `projects/p04j.test.ts` (4 cases x 4 backends, and one case over stand-in services) through the real bridge and dispatcher with a stand-in host on 127.0.0.1 that no worker is enrolled on (the only enrolled host is the agent's worker host): under the strict policy the call waits for the owner and nothing is sent until the approval; then POST and check, lease released passed, an `ok` intervention, two `remote-action` connection log entries, the repeat of the call ID sends nothing; a failed check rolled back where permitted and escalated (one incident, escalated to the owner) where not, a failed action not checked but rolled back; another agent's lease blocks visibly; no network grant, a path off the service, a `..` path, no tool grant and a maintenance window each refuse with nothing sent or leased; a 302 to the action is not followed (escalated, `/elsewhere` never asked); a check that never answers ends within the web tool's time bound and the lease is released failed and escalated; the agent's own lease held for something else blocks and is left held; a credential-shaped body is refused before any record or request. The case over stand-in services checks that a failure before the lease is a refusal with nothing leased, that an action refused before sending gets no check or rollback, and that a release that throws after the requests still leads to an escalating release and an uncertain (never refused) effect. Removing the renewal guard or the refused-before-sending branch fails 5 of the 17 tests.

**Not done**
- A repeat of a finished call is answered from the operation's kept summary of the tool's outcome (its first 300 characters, enough for the outcome and the statuses of a short path; a long path is cut).
- Only HTTP(S) to the resource's own address. No SSH or other protocol, no MCP tool on the remote host, no certificate authority of the owner's (a self-signed host fails the request).
- No `api/start` test drives the tool through `startController` (the wiring is one line beside the web tool; the service-level test uses the same production services).
- An uncertain effect (the controller stopped mid-call) is left for the owner's effect resolution; its lease runs out at its time and the existing expiry notice tells the owner. Until then the same agent's next call on that resource answers `blocked`.
- The call cannot be stopped part way: the bridge gives the tool no abort signal on the effect path (the effect ledger has none to pass), so a cancelled attempt's call runs to its end, bounded by the three requests' 30-second time bounds.
- Short credentials the redactor does not recognise (a short value under a query key such as `token=`) are not caught by the credential refusal; the path and body checks are only as good as the redactor.
- Not run for this review: the start tests that do not touch the tool bridge or the network wiring, and the whole suite (CI is the net).

- **Second review fixes (Claude agent, clean-context Opus review).** (1) The renewal guard asked the lease service first, and the lease service renews the agent's own live lease: the blocked call had already moved that holding's end out by its own minutes and replaced its purpose, so an agent retrying on a resource whose earlier call had stopped kept that lease from ever running out. The tool now reads the lease first (`MaintenanceLeaseService.list`, the service's own clock) and answers `blocked` without asking when the agent's own lease is still in time; the renewal check stays for two calls that pass that read at once, and a grant that a concurrent call of the same agent renewed before this call read it now says it is the agent's own lease, not another agent's. (2) A repeat of a finished call answered "the effect was applied" whatever the outcome (blocked or escalated included). An effect executor can now say its evidence is the result (`ToolExecutor` `evidenceIsResult`, set only by the bridge for built-in effect tools); the dispatcher then keeps the tool's output as the call's text, so a repeat answers with it. Other effect tools are unchanged. Tests: the own-lease case checks the holding kept its end, purpose and renewal count; the repeat in the strict case checks it answers the same outcome; the case over stand-in services checks a raced renewal sends and releases nothing. Each new assertion was seen to fail with its fix taken out of the compiled code. Checks (through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, the offline guard): the suites listed below plus `dispatch/dispatcher` (the tool path changed), 771 of 771; `tsc --build` clean; `check:deps` ok; `api:docs:write` changed nothing. Not run: the PostgreSQL, SQLite and worker variants of the dispatcher suite (the change there is one optional field nothing else sets), and the whole suite.

**Checks on the review fixes** (through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, the offline guard): `p04j`, `toolbridge/service` and `running-store`, `network/web-tool`, `projects/leases`, `p04i`, `policy/*`, `domain/effects` and `effects.crash`, `remote/effects`, `dispatch/target-version` and `target-versions-flow`, `api/start-tool-bridge`, `start-maintenance-bridge`, `start-t4b-kept-secret-uses`, `security/secret-scan` (over these notes): 660 of 660. `tsc --build` clean; `check:deps` ok; `api:docs:write` changed nothing.

## G09: a returned branch's selected updates reach the task's conversation (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-17)

Last open clause of G09: when a retained-context branch is resumed after `applyUpdates`, production code must put the selected updates, each with where it came from, into the task's live Pi conversation at dispatch, exactly once. Before this change nothing read the resume or the applied updates outside `branches/`, and the test "an updated resume applies the selected update once" wrote the correction into the parent conversation itself with `parent.submit`. Card status not touched. No request of any kind to Radiance; no network, no real credentials.

**Done (production path).**
- **C05 (`branches/branches.ts`).** `resume` now lists a branch that applied updates for its destination task (the recorded return destination, so a redirected branch goes where it was redirected) in a small per-task list (`context-return-index`, newest last, at most 50 branches), in the same write as the branch's own change; two branches returning to one task at once retry on the list's revision, as delegations do. A repeated resume is the recorded result, as before (same payload). New `returnedUpdates(viewer, taskId)`: the updates of the branches that returned to the task, read with the viewer's own rights, only those whose original is still as it was when applied (a superseded or edited original is left out; applying the changed original again is its own update), the same original and content from two branches once (named after the first branch that returned with it; corrected in review, the first pass named the later one), at most 20 (the newest), oldest first. Each has the branch, the original's link, the update revision, the text, a request ID made from the link and the original's digest (the second review took the branch out of it), and an origin in words ("side line ..., desk record ..., update 2").
- **Dispatcher (`dispatch/dispatcher.ts`, `dispatch/ports.ts`).** A new optional dependency `selectedUpdates` is asked when an order is built (after the attempt's task credential is issued); the answer goes on the order as `contextUpdates` (bounded: 20 items, text cut at 20,000 and origin at 300 characters; the second review added a total of 64,000 characters of text, see below). `api/dispatch-compose.ts` binds it to `branches.returnedUpdates`, read as the attempt's own task credential; `api/start.ts` passes the branch service in.
- **Worker host and process.** The worker package's host (`host/local.ts`) copies the order's updates into the channel start (`ChannelStart.updates`, parsed and bounded in `contracts/worker-channel.ts`). The worker process (`pi-adapter/worker/process.ts`), after its store is opened (and recovered, when the host says so) and before it says it is ready, submits each one to the conversation as a place-only update (`run: false`) under its request ID, with the origin in a one-line header the model sees and in the entry's data. A request ID the conversation already holds is the recorded submission, so a second start of the same conversation (the next round of the attempt, a recipe restart) applies nothing twice. An update that cannot be placed fails the start.
- **Adapter contract.** The update request has an optional `origin` text (`contracts/index.ts`), kept in the `nimblenewt.update` entry's data when given and part of the request's fingerprint only when given, so entries and fingerprints of updates without one are as they were.

**Tests.**
- `integration/g09-retained-context.test.ts`: the test "an updated resume applies the selected update once, with provenance, and a corrected old owner decision replaces what the parent acts on" now runs through the composed controller (SQLite), the dispatcher, the real local worker (bubblewrap, the worker process running Pi Durable) and a scripted OpenAI-compatible model, with no `parent.submit` or other write to the conversation in the test. Run 1: nothing selected, nothing placed. Then a branch on the task applies decision A, the correction B supersedes A, B is applied, the branch is resumed. Run 2 (same attempt, same conversation): the model's request holds the correction exactly once, with the branch and record it came from, after the earlier turn and before the turn's instruction, and not the superseded A. Run 3 (a new process given the same order again): the correction is still there exactly once in every request, and the task ends `succeeded`. The four-backend scenario that was this test keeps the C05 side (A applied, shown changed, B applied once, replay, refusal of a repeat) and now checks what the dispatcher's read gives the task (B only, the same request ID every time) and that resuming writes nothing into the parent conversation by itself; the L05 fence part is unchanged.
- `controller/branches/branches.test.ts` (all four backends): two new suites: given once, only current originals, nothing before the return, nothing to someone who may not work on the task, the same correction from two branches once under the first one, with the same request ID as before the second returned, a redirected branch given to its new destination, a branch with nothing applied listed nowhere, nothing once the correction is itself corrected; two branches returning to one task at the same moment are both listed.
- `contracts/worker-channel.test.ts` (a start's updates kept, an empty list dropped, too many, an empty request ID, an over-long text, a non-text origin and a non-list refused); `pi-adapter/branches.test.ts` (the origin on the entry, a repeat is the recorded one, another origin or none under the same request ID refused).
- **Mutation checks** on the built files, each alone and restored, against the composed test: a new request ID at every start (the correction twice in run 3: fails); the dispatcher leaving the updates off the order (fails); a changed original given anyway (A given: fails); the host not passing the updates to the process (fails). 4 of 4 killed.

**ASSUMPTIONS.**
- ASSUMPTION: exactly once rests on the request ID in the task's conversation, not on a delivered mark in the controller. Every start of the task is offered the same updates again; a conversation that holds one applies nothing. A later attempt that starts a fresh conversation (no stored conversation carried) is placed them again, which is what that conversation needs. The bounds (50 returned branches per task, 20 updates per start) keep the read and the order small.
- ASSUMPTION: only originals still as they were when applied are given. A superseded decision is exactly the case the card names (the correction of an old owner decision), and giving its old text would put the stale decision back in front of the agent; a later application of the changed original is a new update with its own request ID.
- ASSUMPTION: the updates are read with the attempt's own task credential, so an agent is never given a record it could not read itself; one it may not read is left out silently (the branch owner chose it, the receiving agent has no right to it). The composed test's agent is given `desk.read` and `desk.write` for that reason (the shared work grants of the test rig have neither).
- ASSUMPTION: a failure to read the updates is reported and the attempt starts without them (as the goal anchor does: a record that cannot be read never stops an attempt); its next start is offered them again. A failure to place one inside the process fails the start, since the agent would otherwise act without a correction that is known to exist.
- ASSUMPTION: the model sees a one-line header naming where the update came from, then the original's text; the same words are kept in the entry's data. Delivery happens when the process starts (that is "at dispatch"); an update selected while an attempt is already running waits for that task's next start.

**Not done.**
- Remote hosts: `remote/host.ts` takes `contextUpdates` off the order before offering it, so a remote worker is not given them yet (its offer and channel would need the field and a check).
- No owner-visible activity step says an attempt was given updates (the dispatcher's step kinds have no fitting one); the transcript entry and the model's request show it.
- The composed test runs on SQLite only (the test rig builds SQLite); the new C05 records and reads are tested on all four backends.
- The first call's size check is not told separately about the placed updates: they are in the stored conversation the process measures, not in the order's own text or its starting-size parts.
- No real model (the scripted endpoint only).

### G09 delivery review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5 reviewing, 2026-11-17)

Reviewed `card-g09-carry` at `bf21a9af` for exactly-once and restart behaviour, superseded originals, rights, size bounds, failure behaviour, remote workers and logs, contract compatibility, the four storage backends, and whether the composed test exercises the production path.

**Fixed.**
- **A second branch selecting an already delivered update gave it again.** The same original and content selected by two branches was named after the later branch, so its request ID changed when the second branch returned: a conversation that already held the update under the first branch's ID was placed a second copy. It is now named after the first listed branch that returned with it (that branch's ID and update revision in the request ID and origin), so the ID stays the same. The C05 suite now checks the answer is identical before and after the second branch returns (all four backends). Remaining limit: when the first branch falls off the task's list of 50, the next branch names it and the conversation is given it once more (closed in the second review: the request ID no longer names the branch).
- **Held work plus updates changed how the start failed.** When an earlier process left work held and the start carried no review (`recover` absent), placing an update hit the hold and failed the start ("could not start"), so the dispatcher ended the attempt as a worker that did not start, instead of the turn failing on the held work as it does without updates. The process now places nothing while the work is held; the turn fails as before, and the start after the review places them. New worker-process test (three processes on one store: placed once before the turn's input; held, ready with no fault and the turn failed; reviewed, the resumed call holds the update once). Mutation check: placing while held makes that test fail.
- Text cut at the order bound no longer leaves half a surrogate pair at the end. The dispatcher's `selectedUpdates` doc comment had been put between the goal anchor's doc comment and `anchor`; moved.

**Checked, no change.**
- Request ID (as of this review; the second review changed it to `upd:<32 hex of sha256(link|digest)>`): `upd:<branch>:<24 hex of sha256(link|digest)>`; the content (header with the origin, then the text) is fixed for that ID, since a branch's applied list does not change after it returns and an original applied with the same digest is skipped. Superseded or edited originals are left out by digest; one superseded after delivery stays in the conversation (nothing is withdrawn).
- Rights: read with the attempt's task credential (`attempt.work` on the task and the retrieval service's own read check), so nothing is given that the agent could not read itself. The production `author` role has `desk.read` but not `history.read`, so a history entry selected in a branch is left out for an author.
- Remote: `remote/host.ts` removes `contextUpdates` before the order is offered (the contract digest covers the order's identity, recipe and expiry, not the updates, so it still checks out); `LocalWorker` passes the order only to the local runtime. Error text that reaches outcomes or logs holds request IDs and statuses, not update text.
- Compatibility: a start without `updates`, an update request without `origin`, and their fingerprints are unchanged. The new `context-return-index` aggregate needs no registration on any backend.
- Mutation check: the dispatcher leaving the updates off the order makes the composed test fail.

**Not changed (noted).** No total size bound across the 20 updates (20 times 20,000 characters is possible; desk records are at most 16,000 each; closed in the second review), and the starting-size watch does not count them; the first call's admission measures the stored conversation.

**Checks on this review:** all through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, offline guard, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`: see the commit message.

## W01d: a git refusal inside the project's own test run is reported apart, not counted as contamination (Claude agent, 2026-11-18)

**Problem.** W01 batch 3 (run m03h-1-B-r1-20261118T043344) logged 181 `refused setting` lines in `git-guard.log` while the agent ran `npm test --workspace=packages/worker`. The worker's `GitBridge` gives `-c core.askPass=echo` (with `core.sshCommand=false` and `protocol.allow=never`) on every git call, and its tests run that code on repositories they create in the temporary folder. The guard refuses `core.askpass`, and the runner counted every refused line as contamination, so every large task that runs the worker tests was thrown out.

**Change.** The guard (`scripts/pi-eval/lib/git-guard.mjs`) still refuses these calls, with the same message and exit status. It now logs a refusal as `refused setting in-project-tests` only when all of these hold (`inProjectTests`):
- every refused setting is `core.askpass` or `core.gitproxy`, given for that one call (`-c`, `--config-env`, `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS`/`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`); one written with `git config` is never tagged;
- `decide` lets through the same call without those settings: no push outside the run's folders, no remote that is not a local folder, and no other refused setting (ssh command or key path, credential helper, http header, URL rewrite, ...);
- the subcommand is named directly (an alias is never tagged), and no argument is a network address (`scheme://` other than `file://`, `transport::`, `user@host:path`);
- its folder (after `-C`), any `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`/`GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`/`GIT_COMMON_DIR`, and the repository's common git folder as the real git reports it (`rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`) all lie in the run's temporary folder (`testRoots`, the agent's TMPDIR, written into the guard configuration by `prepareIsolation` together with `checkout`) and outside the run's checkout. So a linked worktree of the checkout placed in TMPDIR, or `--git-dir` pointing back at the checkout, is not tagged.

`guardLogCounts` in the same file counts the log. Only a line of exactly the tagged form is left out; any other `refused` line counts, including the tag on another kind, an untagged line, or a log from before this change. The runner records `guardRefusals` (counted, the same meaning as before) and `guardRefusalsInTests` (only when above 0). `stats.mjs` prints `- refused inside project tests: N, not counted (...)` for each variant, and `report.mjs` prints a note line naming each run. The README's isolation and detection paragraphs say the same.

**The limit, stated plainly.** Recognising the context is structural, not proof. The agent can make the same kind of call in a scratch repository it creates in its own temporary folder, and that refusal is not counted. What this can hide is only an askpass or proxy program refused on a repository wholly inside TMPDIR, for a call that would otherwise touch only the run's own folders. A push out, a remote add, a key path, a credential helper, or a call on the checkout or another checkout is still counted. The call is refused in every case, and the separate check of the agent's commands (`credentialAttempts`, `foreignPaths`) is unchanged. As before, the run's artifacts folder (which holds the log) can be written from inside the sandbox. Adding tagged lines gains nothing, and removing lines was already possible, so the log is evidence of what the guard saw, not a tamper-proof record.

**Not changed.** The guard stays strict: `core.askPass=echo` is still refused, so under the bench the worker's git tests fail. Replaying the compiled `workspace/git.test.js`, `host.test.js` and `local-host.test.js` through the guard gave 64 of 66 failing, with all 64 refusals tagged and 0 counted. An agent that runs those tests therefore sees failures that are not its own. Allowing `core.askpass=echo`, as `core.sshCommand=false` is already allowed, would fix that, but it is a separate decision and is not made here.

**Tests.** `scripts/pi-eval/guard-context.test.mjs`: fake guard logs (only tagged lines: nothing counted; push, remote, setting, unchecked and send-email: all counted; mixed 181 tagged plus one push: one counted; malformed tags counted; an old untagged log: all counted). Classification on real temporary repositories: the worker's call forms are tagged (`status`, `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`, `-C` commit, a push into a bare repository in TMPDIR, `init`, the `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` form, `core.gitProxy`). Not tagged: the checkout, a linked worktree of it in TMPDIR, `--git-dir` or `GIT_DIR` at the checkout, another checkout, a push to https or scp form, a remote add, a clone or fetch from the network, a key path, a credential helper, an http header, a URL rewrite, `git config core.askPass`, an alias, a configuration with no temporary folder. Then the real guard end to end (both kinds refused with exit 1, only the agent's own counted) and the report line. A mutation check (the real git made blind, so the common-dir check is skipped) wrongly tags the linked worktree, which shows that this check is the one doing that work.

### W01d review (Claude agent, 2026-11-18, one round, final)

ASSUMPTION: `core.askPass=echo` (that exact value, any key case) is let through by the guard, like `core.sshCommand=false`. `echo` answers git's prompt with the prompt's own text and never a stored login, and the guard already strips `GIT_ASKPASS`/`SSH_ASKPASS`. An `echo` placed earlier on PATH could run the agent's own code, but the agent can run that code directly anyway, and its home holds no keys. Every other askpass value (`/bin/echo`, `echo token`, `ECHO`, empty, ...) and every `core.gitProxy` is still refused. Writing `core.askpass echo` with `git config` is allowed too, which matches how `core.sshCommand=false` is handled.

**Defects found and fixed.**
- *A call that could reach the network was tagged as the tests' own.* The rule checked only the call's arguments for network addresses, and its pattern for an ssh address needed a user (`user@host:path`). So all of these were tagged and not counted: `clone github.com:owner/repo.git`; `fetch origin`, `fetch` and `pull` where `origin` was a network address written into the scratch repository's configuration file directly (never through `git remote add`, which the guard checks); a branch whose `remote` is itself an address; a configured `url.*.insteadOf`; `--opt=<address>`; `archive --remote`; `submodule`. ## CI fix after run 44242108811 on 5f95237b: macOS temporary folders and the Windows PowerShell probe limit (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

**macOS (both nodes), `containment.test.ts`.** Three G05 Windows-path tests made their folders with `mkdtempSync(tmpdir())`; on macOS that is under `/var`, a link to `/private/var`, and `normalizeRecipe` rightly refuses a workdir that passes through a link (test 2 expected `not_authorized` and got `invalid_recipe`; test 4 threw). The tests now take the real path of the folder, as the other sandbox tests do; the product check is unchanged. Test 3 passed only because it accepts either refusal; it now gets the real path too, so it tests what it says. No other recipe-building test in the worker, integration or pi-adapter packages uses an unresolved temporary folder (the evidence-gate test in the same file writes files only and needs none).

**Windows node 22 shard 1, `windows-host-real.test.ts`.** Why it failed: in test 3 the child runs all real probes in the bare environment the launcher gives its runner (only a few system variables, its own TEMP). `Get-AppxPackage` ran past the fixed 60 s limit of every PowerShell probe and was killed; `execFile` reports that as code null, so the message said "exit null". The test took 189 s in all, so the other probes in that environment were slow too, not only the package lookup; node 24 on the same commit stayed under the limit. The deepEqual then threw before `backend.release(plan)`, so the job folder `ci-<uuid>` stayed in the shared `control\jobs`, and test 4 (nothing left behind) saw it. Changes:
- `windows-real.ts`: every program the real Windows host runs goes through `runBounded`. At the limit it first stops the whole tree with `%SystemRoot%\System32\taskkill.exe /PID n /T /F` (while the parent is still alive, so taskkill can find descendants; the parent is our own unreaped child, so its id cannot have been reused), then kills the program and closes its pipes, so a descendant that inherited them can neither keep running nor hold the result back; a last-resort timer gives the result 5 s later if even that brings no end. A timeout now says "timed out after N s and was stopped" and has `timedOut: true` (before, `timedOut` was also set by a maxBuffer kill).
- PowerShell probes (`PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`, 60 s each) get exactly one more try, and only after a timeout (`retryOnceOnTimeout`). All of them are read-only lookups (package list, signature, session, registry flags, scheduled task), so a second try changes nothing on the machine; a probe that answered with a failure is not retried, so admission still fails closed. Two timeouts throw "PowerShell timed out twice (60 s each)". Worst case for one probe is now about 2 x 60 s (plus up to 15 s per taskkill).
- `windows-host-real.test.ts` test 3: the job is released in `finally`, then the test asserts `control\jobs` is empty; the child and the test have an explicit ceiling (6 probes x 2 x 60 s + 120 s) above the worst case, since the package runner's default per-test limit is 300 s. What the test proves is unchanged: every probe must still answer `ok` in the runner's environment.
- New `windows-real-run.test.ts` (any OS; node stands in for the program and a stand-in for taskkill): an in-time program gives its code and output and nothing is stopped; at the limit the tree stop runs while the program is alive, then the result comes back promptly although a descendant still holds the pipes (checked by removing the pipe close in the built file: the test then fails, the result only arriving by the 5 s fallback); a failing tree stop still ends the program; the retry happens once and only on a timeout.

**Verified offline on Linux:** build; the worker suite (543 tests, 542 pass, 1 skipped); the timeout, pipe-close and retry logic with node as the program. **Not verified (needs a Windows CI run):** that `taskkill /T /F` ends a real PowerShell tree, that the probes in the runner's bare environment now pass within two tries, and the real cause of the slowness there (one guess, not tested: PowerShell finding the Appx and ScheduledTasks modules without the user's variables, such as LOCALAPPDATA and PSModulePath). If the probes keep timing out twice on hosted runners, the next step is to look at that environment, not to raise the limit further.

**Review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18) of `51c827bb`.** **Fixed:**
- A tree stop by a stale id. If PowerShell itself had ended but a descendant still held its pipes at the limit, `runBounded` still ran `taskkill /PID n /T /F`. By then node had seen the end and let go of the process, so Windows could already have given that id to another program, and the tree stop would end that program with everything under it. The note above ("unreaped child, id cannot have been reused") held only while the program still ran. The tree stop now runs only when the program's end has not been seen (`exitCode` and `signalCode` both null). Otherwise only the pipes are closed, so the result still comes back. That descendant keeps running; with its parent gone, taskkill /T could not find it anyway. A gap of milliseconds remains between that check and taskkill's lookup. New test: a program that ends at once and leaves a descendant on its pipes gives a prompt timeout and no tree stop. Checked by putting the old condition back in the built file: the test then fails.
- `stopTree` is now called inside a promise chain, so one that throws at once (rather than rejecting) cannot escape the timer and leave the result unresolved. The 5 s fallback timer is no longer armed once the result is in, so it cannot keep a process alive for 5 s for nothing. New test for the thrown case.
- Test 3's ceiling could not apply. `run-package-tests.mjs` passes `--test-timeout=300000`, and under `node --test` that bounds each file as a whole, not only each test. Checked on node 22.23: three 700 ms tests under `--test-timeout=1000` fail as "file timed out". So the 840 s child and 900 s test limit were dead letters. A slow run would be cut at 300 s for the whole file, without test 3's message and without its `finally`. Also, a per-test limit cannot fire while `spawnSync` blocks. The child now gets 250 s; in run 44242108811 the file's other tests took about 30 s together. Past that limit the test fails with its own message ("did not all answer within 250 s") and releases the job. The 720 s worst case (every probe timing out twice) is a failure, not a case to wait for. Caveat: in that run the six bare-environment probes took 189 s, one of them a 60 s timeout, so a run that needs one retry may come close to 250 s. If it does, look at the environment (see above) rather than raise the limit.

**Checked, no change:**
- The retry wraps only `powershell()`, whose five scripts (package list, signature, console session, auto-login flags, scheduled task) only read. `icacls` (read and apply), `wsb` start, exec, stop and list, and `host.run` are never retried.
- A maxBuffer overflow (16 MiB) is no longer reported as `timedOut`. The one non-probe reader, `wsb exec` in `windows-job.ts`, still fails closed: code null becomes `EXIT_FAILED`, with node's "maxBuffer" message in place of "did not return". That overflow ends only the program, not its tree, as before.
- If taskkill is missing or fails, execFile reports an error and the promise resolves. If taskkill hangs, its own 15 s limit applies. The program is then killed and its pipes are closed either way. Its path is `%SystemRoot%\System32\taskkill.exe`, with arguments as a list, no shell and no PATH lookup. `SystemRoot` comes from the environment, the same trust as the PowerShell and icacls paths beside it.
- `EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` (24 h) stays below the 2^31 - 1 ms timer limit.
- The macOS fix is complete. Every other `mkdtempSync(tmpdir())` in worker, integration and pi-adapter tests that builds a recipe already takes `realpathSync`. The pi-adapter `worker/process.test.ts` folders hold conversation stores, not recipes. containment's evidence-gate folder only receives files.
- The new tests mean the same on Linux, macOS and Windows: `process.kill(pid, 0)`, `SIGKILL` and inherited pipes behave alike for node children.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23):** build; worker suite 545 tests, 544 pass, 1 skipped, 0 failed in three runs. One earlier run reported 1 failure whose name was not captured, and it did not come back in three full runs. `windows-real-run.test.ts` passed five times in a row under load 5. **Not run:** other packages' suites, since no other package imports `windows-real`. The Windows-only tests skip here.

**Second review, final round (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-18) of `ec4efeb5`.** No defects found; no code changed.
- Timer and promise order in `runBounded`: `finish` runs once (`done`), clears the limit timer and the fallback timer; the fallback is armed only while no result is in; the execFile callback is always asynchronous, so `timer` is defined before `finish` can run. A spawn failure (no pid) or a maxBuffer kill ends through the callback before the limit and clears it. After a tree stop, `child.kill()` on a program already ended is harmless: node no longer holds a handle (POSIX) or libuv returns ESRCH (Windows), and execFile's own error listener would still resolve the result. Destroying the pipes lets execFile's `close` fire with the output collected so far.
- Stale id: the check (`exitCode` and `signalCode` null) reads state that node sets only after it has reaped the process (POSIX) or handled its exit (Windows, where the open process handle also keeps the id from reuse until then), so the id is still the program's when taskkill starts. The remaining gap (the program ends while taskkill runs) is inherent and noted above.
- Retry: only `powershell()` retries; its five scripts are Get-AppxPackage, Get-AuthenticodeSignature, a WTS session query, Get-ItemProperty and Get-ScheduledTask, all read-only. `windows-job.ts` treats `timedOut` as a failure without retrying. A program that ended in time while a descendant held its pipes is now reported as timed out (code null); for a probe that means one more read-only try, and before this change the same case waited on the descendant.
- Test 3's limits match the real invocation: the worker's `npm test` passes `--timeout=300000`, which `run-package-tests.mjs` turns into `--test-timeout=300000`; re-checked on node 22.23 that this bounds a whole file (two 1.5 s tests under a 2 s limit: the file fails). 250 s + about 30 s for the other tests stays under 300 s. `spawnSync` with a timeout closes its pipes after killing the child, so an orphaned PowerShell cannot hold it past 250 s. On that failure path the orphan keeps running, with the runner's TEMP as its temporary folder; if that holds a file, `release` in `finally` could fail and its error would hide the "did not all answer" message. The test fails either way; not changed.
- Stability under load: `windows-real-run.test.ts` passed 5 runs out of 5 with 64 busy processes on 32 cores (about 4.4 s per file). Its 1.5 s limits require two node starts to fit within the limit, which held at twice the CPU oversubscription. On a small hosted Windows runner with many test files in parallel this has the least margin; if it ever flakes there, raise those limits rather than the assertion bounds.
- Cosmetic, not changed: on a timeout the "timed out after N s" text is appended to stderr without a separating newline.

## T08 (first slice): toolbox.manage, audiences, read-only source, personal copies with provenance and fork lineage (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

T08 is **not** complete and is not marked implemented: this is the first slice. Code in `packages/controller/src/catalog/catalog.ts` (`CatalogService`), eight `toolbox.*` state-API operations, three chat operations, a `toolbox` status kind and a paragraph of the chat interpreter prompt. Tests: `catalog/toolbox.test.ts` (4 tests on each of the four backends) and `api/start-toolbox.test.ts` (one composed test through `startController`: agents' own credentials on the state API, the owner's chat proposal and status answer, and a revocation).

**Done in this slice**

- **`toolbox.manage`** is a new action (`ACTIONS`, exported as `TOOLBOX_MANAGE`). It is held through ordinary grants on the principal's durable identity (`agent:<ID>`), so renaming an agent changes nothing and a role or title gives nothing (a `lead` role without the grant is refused). Granted for every project (`*`) it covers every audience; granted for some projects it covers only entries whose audience is made of those projects alone (`mayManage`). An entry with no audience means all agents, so only a holder for every project manages it. It is in none of the lists a meeting decision may grant (`AGREED_GRANTABLE_*`), so a meeting vote neither grants it nor publishes anything. The owner gives and takes it with `grant.create` / `grant.revoke` (by chat as well; the interpreter prompt says so).
- **Maintainers publish shared versions.** `register` by an agent naming `toolbox.<name>` takes the maintainer path: the agent needs `toolbox.manage`, a first release of a name must name an audience, and an update needs a grant covering the entry's present audience (checked inside the guarded write). Sources follow the owner's release rules (accepted, shared, original; never private scratch, a draft or a copy), and the maintainer must also be able to read the record through the desk (`DeskService.read`); the author stays recorded, `registeredBy` is the maintainer. `nimblenewt.<name>` is refused for maintainers ("toolbox.manage does not cover NimbleNewt's own commands"); personal namespaces stay their agent's. Maintainers may also `deprecate` and `rollback` shared entries their grant covers. Revocation stays owner-only in this slice.
- **Audiences** (`EntryBody.audience`: `all`, or `roles`, `teams`, `projects`). Stored by durable identity: role names (must be defined), team and project IDs; teams and projects may be given by their exact name, which must match exactly one record (several or none are refused; IDs work always). `all` stands alone. Absent means every holder of `catalog.read` (the behaviour before this card), so existing shared entries are unchanged. Membership: an agent belongs through one of its roles or its team (read from the agent record behind `agent:<ID>`; a retired agent belongs to nothing), or for a project audience through a live grant naming that project exactly (a grant for every project is not membership of each). Discovery (`get`, `list`, `toolbox`, `content`, `source`, `usableVersion`, the command resolver and the tool bridge, which all go through `#resolve`) applies the audience; a run (`authorizeRun`) judges it for the task's project, so an entry for project A does not run in project B. A maintainer whose grant covers an entry sees and reads it even outside its audience, but cannot run it unless it is in the audience. `setAudience` (`toolbox.audience.set`) needs a grant covering both the present and the new audience; changing it updates the entry, so a run being recorded at that moment is asked again. An existing `register` with no `audience` keeps the entry's audience.
- **Read-only source** (`source`, `toolbox.source`): manifest, instructions and executable text, checked against the digests recorded at release, plus author, digest, `copiedFrom` and revocation. Needs only `catalog.read` and the audience, no manage permission. Nothing else of the author's desk is shown.
- **Platform compatibility in the listing** (`toolbox`, `toolbox.list`): each shared entry with its chosen version, live versions, purpose, declared OS, architecture and interpreter, audience and whether the caller may maintain it.
- **Personal copies** (`copy`, `toolbox.copy`): an agent with `catalog.register` copies an exact shared version it may read into `a_<id>.<as>`. The copy's version records `copiedFrom` (shared name, version, digest) as part of its identity and reuses the released sources, which must still be exactly as released (same revision and digest). The copy is independent: later shared releases do not change it, an audience change does not take it back, and `/toolbox.<name>` stays bound to the shared release. It inherits no grant: the shared tool's `tool.toolbox.<name>` grant does not reach it; it runs under the agent's own standing namespace grant (`tool.a-<id>.*`, given to every agent record) like any personal tool. A revoked version cannot be copied. Copying again into the same name needs a higher `copyVersion`.
- **Fork lineage and revocation notices.** Each copy is added, in the same write, to a `catalog-forks` record of the shared entry (at most 500 per entry; beyond that a copy is refused). `forks` / `toolbox.forks` (owner, or a maintainer covering the audience) lists each copy, its owner, base version and digest, and whether the base has since been revoked. `copies` / `toolbox.copies` gives an agent its copies with a notice when the base was revoked (reason and time) and the shared version now chosen when it can still see it (`newerShared`). Notices are read on request; nothing is pushed yet.
- **Owner controls by chat and status.** Chat ops `toolbox.audience.set`, `toolbox.deprecate`, `toolbox.rollback` (all shown first as proposals); the `name` argument takes the short name the owner uses. Status kind `toolbox` (owner only): each shared tool's version, audience in words, declared platforms and number of personal copies. The interpreter prompt describes these, the `toolbox.manage` grant and that no fixed phrase is needed.

**Not done (later slices or audit)**

- Improvement proposals (base version, patch, rationale, tests, permission changes) and maintainer decisions (accept, request changes, defer, reject with reason); rebase and recheck of a stale proposal; deferred proposals not listed as available; "an accepted proposal never authorizes a downstream push, merge or deploy". Nothing of this exists yet.
- Promotion requests from an agent's personal tool (stand-up or direct submission) and a chat form of publishing: `toolbox.publish` needs desk record IDs and a manifest, so it is an API/agent operation and is not a chat op yet.
- Immutable content snapshots: a release (and so a copy) still records digests and references to desk records (limit stated in the T01 notes). If the author later revises the record, `content`/`source` refuse rather than serve other bytes; "edits to the original leave the shared release unchanged" is therefore only half met (the release is never silently changed, but it stops being readable).
- Revocation by maintainers (`revoke` is owner-only; its running-call listener takes the owner principal), and pushed revocation notices to fork owners (the notice is pull-only through `toolbox.copies` and the forks list).
- Per-consumer pinned versions ("consumers stay on their pinned version until they opt in") beyond what T02 already gives (a task that ran a version resolves it again; `deprecate`/`rollback` keep pinned versions resolvable). No consumer opt-in record exists.
- Agent-facing bridge tools for `toolbox.source`, `toolbox.copy` and `toolbox.copies` (agents reach them through the state API with their own credential only).
- Audience of dependency records: `dependencies.ts` still judges catalog-entry visibility by layer and `catalog.read`, not by audience.
- The status line shows team and project audiences by ID; names are not looked up.
- Maintainer list as its own view (holders of `toolbox.manage` are visible in the grants/settings views only); U08 browser pages for the toolbox.
- The README 313-315 validation list as a whole (some items are covered above: unauthorized publish or edit fails, eligible agents discover, excluded roles cannot invoke, survives author rename or retirement, update, revoke and rollback, escalation attempts fail, source inspection needs no manage permission, no private desk exposure; the rest is open).

**Changed behaviour of an existing test:** an agent without `toolbox.manage` registering a `toolbox.` name is now refused as `forbidden` (the maintainer path) instead of `invalid_command`; `catalog.test.ts` was updated for that one assertion.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23, on base e94e7d8d):** `tsc --build`; package boundaries, license inventory and roadmap checks; root `scripts/*.test.mjs` (225, 224 pass, 1 skipped; includes the docs check of operation names); controller package once in full through the test slot (15563 tests; the 5 failures of the first run, the `status.ask` kinds list and the changed catalog assertion on four backends, were fixed and those files rerun: 119 pass); integration package (220: 154 pass, 56 fail, 10 skipped), with exactly the same 56 failures on an unmodified build of e94e7d8d on this machine (real worker processes, sandbox and process-tree tests), so none come from this change. `api-v1.md` regenerated with `scripts/api-docs.mjs --write`. **Skipped:** other packages (none imports the controller except integration); hosted Windows/macOS jobs (CI).

### T08 first slice, review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18; this round is final)

Reviewed `e94e7d8d..96370608` against the T08 card and the owner's rules. **One defect fixed; everything else checked and left as it was.**

Maintainers are refused `nimblenewt.` names and another agent's namespace (the personal path still builds the name from the caller's own namespace). ### T08 first slice, second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-18; this round is final)

Reviewed `e94e7d8d..7632ffaa` independently of the first review: `catalog.ts` (`mayManage`, `maintainsAnywhere`, `mayReadCatalogEntry`, `inAudience`, register, `#setAside`, `setAudience`, `toolbox`, `source`, `copy`, `copies`, `forks`), the state-API operations, the tool bridge, the command resolver, environments' skill library, dependencies, status, chat ops and the interpreter paragraph. **Three defects fixed in `catalog/catalog.ts`; everything else checked and left as it was.**

**Fixed**
- **An audience change during a copy did not stop it.** `copy` judged the audience in its first read (`#resolve`), but the guarded write only re-checked revocation and pinned the shared entry at the revision read *inside* the write. If the owner or a maintainer took the agent out of the audience between those two reads, the copy and its fork-lineage entry were still written. The write now judges the audience again on the entry it is checked against (`not_found`, the same answer as for a tool the agent may not read). Revocation during a copy was already covered.
- **A project audience ignored standing restrictions.** Membership (`holdsIn`) counted any unexpired grant naming the project, even one the owner had cancelled with a restriction there. So an agent the owner had restricted in project A could still find, read the source of and copy a tool shared with project A. A grant now counts only while `allows` accepts it in that project (expiry, restrictions, task scope, resource), the same rule access checks use everywhere else.
- **A maintainer learned about entries it may neither change nor read.** A holder of `toolbox.manage` for project B, calling `toolbox.audience.set`, `toolbox.deprecate` or `toolbox.rollback` on a tool shared only with project A, got `forbidden` when the tool (and version) existed and `not_found` when not. That told it the tool and its versions existed. Now it gets the same `not_found` either way when it can neither manage nor read the entry; one it can read but not manage is still `forbidden`. (`forks` already answered `not_found` for an unreadable entry.)
- New test in `catalog/toolbox.test.ts` covering all three, on four backends. The race is made deterministic with a storage proxy that changes the audience while the copy reads back its released text. It fails on all four backends with the catalog code at `7632ffaa` and passes with the fix.

**Checked, no change needed**
- Authority: `toolbox.manage` only from grants on `agent:<ID>`. `allows` with project `undefined` matches only a `*` grant, so a project-scoped grant never passes the every-project branch of `mayManage`. A task credential (task-scoped) gets no `toolbox.manage` or `catalog.read` without a project. Maintainers are kept out of `nimblenewt.` names and other namespaces. Both the new and the present audience are checked, the present one inside the guarded write.
- Races on all four backends: two maintainers updating the same entry (version create plus entry update at the read revision), `setAudience` against `deprecate`/`rollback`/`register` (all update the entry at its read revision), and a revocation during a copy (re-checked and revision-pinned).
- Integrity: a copy's digest includes `copiedFrom`. The released desk records are checked by digest and revision before the write and pinned by `check` changes in it. Retention keeps them (`catalogSourceIds` covers every version), and blanking skips a record any non-revoked version (a copy included) still uses, so revoking the shared version does not empty a live copy.
- Paths: the tool bridge's describe/list use the discovery rule (`catalog.get` without a project), and running goes through `authorizeRun` with the task's project. The environments' skill library (`usableVersion`) uses the discovery rule; library contents are judged per agent, not per project, as the first review said. The command resolver serves the chat owner.
- Chat: three `propose` ops; the interpreter paragraph is example sentences only, no fixed phrase. The status kind is owner-only.

**Left open (not defects of this slice's claims; for later slices or the audit)**
- Any agent with `catalog.register` that can read a shared tool can fill its fork lineage (500 entries, one per copy name or copy version) and so stop everyone else from copying it. A per-owner bound would fix that.
- A maintainer publishing a name already taken by a tool it may not read gets `forbidden` (the name is taken). Some answer is unavoidable for a name collision, so existence is revealed there.
- A copy is personal by design, so an agent in a project audience may copy the tool and run its copy in another project under its own namespace grant. The card's "independent copy" allows this; whether a project audience should limit copying is a product question.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23):** `tsc --build`; `catalog/toolbox.test.ts` 24/24 (6 suites × 4 backends); every test file in the controller's `catalog`, `dependencies`, `toolbridge`, `commands`, `environments`, `status`, `chat` and `api` through the test slot: 2773 tests, all pass (one `api/start.test.js` case first failed only because the offline guard had been given as a relative path that a worker thread could not resolve; with the absolute path, as `run-package-tests.mjs` gives it, the file passes 15/15); registry package 15/15; root `scripts/*.test.mjs` 225 (224 pass, 1 skipped); `scripts/api-docs.mjs` output byte-identical to `api-v1.md`. **Skipped:** integration tests that start real workers (they fail the same way on the clean base, per both earlier runs; no integration file names the toolbox); other packages; hosted Windows/macOS (CI). `api-v1.md` unchanged: no operation was added or changed.

**T08 first slice, third check (clean-context, final).** Re-checked 11b95a4b: the copy's second audience check reads the shared entry that the same write pins by revision, so a concurrent audience change either stops the copy or makes the write contend (no lost update). The `not_found` answers in `setAudience`, `deprecate`/`rollback` and `forks` come only after the entry is found and before `forbidden`; the check against the new audience in `setAudience` runs before any read and says nothing about the entry. Owner, a maintainer for every project, a maintainer for one project changing its own entries, and entries without an audience (all agents) take the same paths as before. One defect fixed in `holdsIn`. It had called `allows` with every grant and with no resource, so (a) a grant for every project could make an expired or otherwise unusable grant naming the project count, and (b) a restriction on one resource (one task) took an agent with whole-project grants out of the project audience. Each grant naming the project is now judged alone. A grant for the whole project meets only restrictions that name no resource, and a grant for one resource also meets the restrictions on that resource. Test added (a restriction on one task leaves the agent in the audience; the restriction for the whole project still takes it out). **Verified:** `tsc --build`; controller files `catalog/{toolbox,catalog}`, `dependencies/dependencies`, `toolbridge/service`, `commands/commands`, `status/status`, `api/start-{toolbox,tool-bridge,commands,catalog-retention,catalog-retention-fix,revoke,urgent-denial,jobs}` through the test slot: 574/574 on all four backends; registry 15/15. **Skipped:** `chat` (no chat test touches the catalog), other api files, other packages, CI platforms.

**T08 first slice, `holdsIn` check of 82f76ced (clean-context, final; no code change).** The rule matches `allows` (`security/access.ts`): a restriction naming a resource applies only to checks on that resource or that name none, so an agent restricted on one task keeps working elsewhere in the project and stays in its audience, and a restriction naming no resource (the way an agent is kept out of a project; nothing checks a `project`-kind resource) still takes it out. Revoked, ended, lapsed, archived-project and expired grants cannot count: `effectiveOf` drops the records and `allows(..., grants: [g])` judges each grant's own expiry, with no help from a grant for every project. The only widening is visibility: a shared tool's read still needs `catalog.read` checked with no resource (any resource-named `catalog.read` restriction refuses it), and a run (`catalog.ts` run check, `toolbridge` requested access) is checked against the task resource, so a task restriction still stops the run. **Verified:** `tsc --build`; controller `catalog/{toolbox,catalog}`, every `dependencies` and `status` test file, `toolbridge/service`, `commands/commands`, `api/start-{toolbox,tool-bridge,commands,status,catalog-retention,catalog-retention-fix,revoke,urgent-denial,jobs}` through the test slot: 697/697 (toolbox suites on reference store, SQLite, SQLite worker thread, PostgreSQL); registry 15/15. **Skipped:** `chat`, other api files, other packages, CI platforms.

## W01d follow-up: a git call whose folder was removed is refused as `gone-folder`, tagged only as a test's own (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

**Cause.** This fixes the counted `refused unchecked` line noted above. Debug replays showed the call: the worker's `--git-dir <tmp>/nn-lws-*/shared/.git -c core.askPass=echo ... rev-parse --verify HEAD^{commit}`, started from `<tmp>/nn-lws-*/scratch` while the test's teardown was removing it. `process.cwd()` threw inside `decide`'s try block. All of that call's settings are allowed, so the existing tag (which needs a refused askpass setting) could never match it.

**Change (`scripts/pi-eval/lib/git-guard.mjs`).** `main()` reads the folder once, before `decide`. When it cannot be read, the call is refused with the new kind `gone-folder` (fail closed, as before). It is tagged `in-project-tests` only when `goneFolderTests` holds:
- The last known folder is absolute and gone, and lies in the run's temporary folder outside its checkout. That folder is `lastKnownFolder()`: on Linux the system's record `/proc/self/cwd` (`<path> (deleted)`), which the caller cannot set; PWD only where `/proc` cannot be read.
- Every folder the call acts in (after `-C`; `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`) is also gone and lies in the temporary folder outside the checkout, so there is no repository left to touch.
- Every other `inProjectTests` condition holds with that folder (now shared as `testsOwnCall`): only askpass, proxy or `protocol.allow` among refused settings, the subcommand named directly, no network address, no submodule or recursion, every address a local folder in the temporary folder.

Anything else from a gone folder is logged `refused gone-folder` and counted. `guardLogCounts` leaves out exactly `refused setting in-project-tests` and `refused gone-folder in-project-tests`. The `unchecked` kind remains for a `decide` that throws in a readable folder.

ASSUMPTION: the folder being gone stands in for the refused-askpass condition. A call from a removed folder with only allowed settings cannot be the agent loosening its git, and the narrowest sound rule is the one above. The system's record is preferred over PWD because PWD can be stale: when the folder is removed between node's `chdir` and `/bin/sh` starting, dash keeps the parent's PWD. That is the likely source of a counted line seen in 1 of 21 replays before this was added (none in the 18 of them run with a debug copy). Where only PWD exists (macOS, no `/proc`), a caller could name a gone folder in the temporary folder; that call is still refused and has no repository to act on.

**Tests (`guard-context.test.mjs`, 2 new).** The guard runs from a folder removed after `cd`:
- Tagged in the temporary folder.
- Counted for: the run's own folder or the checkout; an existing `--git-dir` or `-C`; a network push; a credential helper; an alias; `--recurse-submodules`; `submodule`; a fetch from outside the temporary folder.
- Linux: PWD does not decide either way. Without `/proc`, a bad PWD is counted.
- Unit tests for `goneFolderTests`, for `lastKnownFolder` (fake `/proc` links) and for the new log form.

**Verified.** All runs went through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`. The compiled worker tests (`workspace/git.test.js`, `host.test.js`, `local-host.test.js` from main's dist, read only) were replayed through the wrapper with `gitConfigText()` as the bench config and testRoots set to TMPDIR. Six replays with the final guard: 0 counted every time (65 or 66 tagged). Four of them had a gone-folder call, all tagged. The 64 worker-test failures under the wrapper are the guard's intended `protocol.allow` refusals. `node --test scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs scripts/y02-checkpoint.test.mjs` passed 158 of 158. Setup: contracts rebuilt with main's installed tsc (`-p`, `--typeRoots` main's `@types`), with a temporary `node_modules` linking `@nimblenewt/contracts` and `@nimblenewt/registry` to the worktree and `@earendil-works/pi-ai` to main's. That folder was removed afterwards. **Skipped:** root `npm test`, workspace TypeScript suites, exhaustive CI, Windows and macOS (the PWD fallback is covered only by the non-Linux test branch, not run here). Final for this card.

### W01d follow-up re-check (clean context, `1f54e18c`)

**Defect fixed.** `callPlaces`, `testsOwnCall` and `localPath` resolve a folder with `path.resolve`, which drops a `..` segment as text. The system applies `..` only after following any link. From a removed folder in the temporary folder, `git -C <tmp>/link/../packages push` (the link pointing into the checkout) and `fetch --no-recurse-submodules <tmp>/link/..` were each read as a gone folder in the temporary folder and tagged. Real git would act in the checkout. With no remotes readable, `checkPush` lets a push with no arguments through. Now no call is tagged when any of these contains a `..` path segment: an argument, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, the folder, a remote read from configuration, or the last known folder (plain or percent-encoded). This applies to both tag paths. A revision range such as `<base>..HEAD` is not a path segment and is unaffected. The worker's calls do not name `..` paths. `guard-context.test.mjs` adds the link, file-URL, PWD and `GIT_DIR` cases, plus a revision range that is still tagged.

**Checked, no change.** A tagged call is always refused, so the tag changes only the count. Network addresses, credential and other refused settings, aliases, recursion and submodules still prevent the tag. `/proc/self/cwd` is the kernel's record, and a folder whose name itself ends in ` (deleted)` is stripped once, correctly. Lookups inside a removed folder fail, so a relative `-C` from one reaches nothing. Creating and removing a scratch folder in tmp still gives a tagged refusal with nothing to act on: the documented limit. `guardLogCounts` leaves out only `refused setting in-project-tests` and `refused gone-folder in-project-tests`. An untagged gone-folder refusal and every older form are still counted. Remaining, not changed: the positional paths of subcommands that do not contact a remote (`init <path>`, `worktree add <path>`) are not checked under either tag path. Such a call is refused either way. From a removed folder, `core.gitproxy` or `protocol.allow` alone is tagged without an askpass setting, as documented.

**Verified.** All runs went through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`. `node --test scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs scripts/y02-checkpoint.test.mjs` passed 158 of 158.
