## T08 (second slice): improvement and promotion proposals, maintainer decisions, snapshots of released text, maintainer revocation with notices, toolbox bridge tools (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

T08 is still **not** complete and is not marked implemented; this is the second slice, on base 8b76d607. New code: `packages/controller/src/catalog/proposals.ts` (`ToolboxProposalService`) and `catalog/notices.ts` (the agent's toolbox inbox). Changed: `catalog/catalog.ts` (snapshots, `#publish`, `releaseProposal`, maintainer `revoke`, fork notices, `notices`), `retention/service.ts` (the owner's deletion gathers snapshots), `toolbridge/service.ts` and `pi-adapter/src/bridge.ts` (five bridge tools), `status/status.ts` (status kind `toolbox_proposals`), `chat/commands.ts` and `chat/model-interpreter.ts`, ten state-API operations in `api/operations.ts`, wiring in `api/start.ts`. Tests: `catalog/toolbox-proposals.test.ts` (7 tests on each of the four backends), `api/start-toolbox-proposals.test.ts` (one composed test through `startController` with the agents' own credentials, the owner's chat and status, the real record deletion), a bridge suite in `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (four backends) and one test in `pi-adapter/src/bridge.test.ts`.

**Done in this slice**

- **Improvement proposals** (`toolbox.propose`). An agent proposes a change to a shared tool it may read (the audience rule of slice 1; outside it the tool is `not_found`), against an exact version (`baseVersion`, default the one in use). The patch is the whole new content: each changed part is the author's own accepted, original desk record (`DeskService.executableSource`) that is also shared (private scratch is refused, so the deciders can read it); a part left out is the base's own; `manifest` is a whole manifest, checked like a release. Or `fromCopy` takes the content from the author's personal copy of the tool: the base is the shared version the newest copied version at or below it was made from; a part equal to the base's is the base's, a changed part must be the author's own shared record. A proposal that changes nothing is refused. Recorded: target, author, base version and digest, the personal tool it came from, the proposed content and its digest, which parts change, `permissionChanges` (the requested access added and dropped against the base; asking grants nothing), rationale, tests, the task named, state, round and history (last 50 events). An author may have at most 20 proposals waiting (open, changes requested or deferred), counted in a per-author index written with each proposal.
- **Promotion requests** (`toolbox.promote`), by direct submission: an agent offers one of its own personal tools for a free shared name, with an optional suggested audience. A tool any of whose versions is a copy of a shared tool is refused (that is an improvement of the shared tool), and so is one whose sources are private scratch or not the author's own. A taken name is refused whatever the caller may read (as in slice 1, a name collision needs some answer).
- **Who sees a proposal.** Its author, the owner, and the maintainers who may decide it: for an improvement, a holder of `toolbox.manage` covering the tool's present audience (`mayManage`); for a promotion, one covering the suggested audience (none suggested means all agents, so only a holder for every project). Everyone else gets `not_found`, the same answer as for an ID never used, for `toolbox.proposal.get`, decisions and rebases; listings leave such proposals out. The author never decides its own proposal (`forbidden`, which tells it nothing new).
- **Maintainer decisions** (`toolbox.proposal.decide`): `accept`, `request_changes`, `defer`, `reject` (each of the last three with a reason) and `reopen` (a deferred one comes back). `accept` with `version` publishes the proposed content as that new shared version in the same storage write as the decision (`CatalogService.releaseProposal` joins the proposal's update and the author's notice to the release's write through `#publish`): an improvement only while its base is still the version in use (checked inside the write; otherwise `stale_revision` "rebase it first"), a promotion only while its name is free, with the audience given or the suggested one, under the same authority checks as `register` (the decider's grant must cover the audience; never `nimblenewt.`). The released version's sources are the base's own `SourceRef`s for unchanged parts (read back by digest, from the desk record or the base's snapshot) and the author's records for changed parts, which must still be exactly as proposed (same revision and digest) and accepted, shared and original. The decider needs no desk grant of its own: the author gave the text to the deciders by proposing it. The author stays recorded per part; `registeredBy` is the decider. `accept` without `version` records the decision and publishes nothing; a later `accept` with `version` releases it. A proposal revised between the decider's read and the write is refused (`stale_revision`).
- **An accepted proposal authorises nothing else.** The proposal carries text and record IDs, never an action; accepting it makes the one release the decider names with its own authority, and nothing more: no grant, push, merge or deploy. Every acceptance answer carries `authorizes` with that sentence (`ACCEPTANCE_LIMIT`), and so does the author's notice. The service test checks that nobody's grants changed after an acceptance that added requested access.
- **The author is told.** Each decision writes a notice into the author's toolbox inbox in the same write (`toolbox-inbox`, last 100 kept, read with `toolbox.notices`, `after` the last `seq` seen), keyed by the proposal record's revision so every decision is a separate notice even after the history is capped (tested with 60 decisions). When the proposal names a task (from the bridge, always the attempt's own task) the decision is also filed as a controller notice on that task (`AgentMessageService.noticeFromController`, best effort: the inbox already holds it). A maintainer's rebase of the author's proposal is told the same way.
- **Revise, rebase and recheck, withdraw.** The author revises an open proposal or one with changes requested (`toolbox.proposal.revise`: a whole new patch against the same base, or with `onLatest` against the version in use; a promotion names another version of its tool); it is open again and its round goes up. `toolbox.proposal.rebase` (author, or a maintainer who may decide it) moves an improvement onto the version in use: parts it does not change follow the new version; a part it changes that the new version also changed is refused as `command_conflict` (the author revises with `onLatest`); the author's records are read again and must still be exactly as proposed, accepted, original and shared, and a changed manifest is checked again. The new base, content digest and permission changes are recorded. `toolbox.proposal.withdraw` (author only) is final. State checks run inside the guarded write and payloads come from the command alone, so a repeat of a decision, revision or rebase that was carried out is answered from its record.
- **Deferred proposals are not listed as available.** `toolbox.proposals` (and the status view) list by default only proposals that are open or have changes requested; deferred ones only when `state` asks for them (`deferred`, another state, or `all`). The status view says how many deferred proposals are set aside.
- **Snapshots of released text.** Every new shared (`toolbox.`) release and every personal copy stores a `catalog-snapshot` record (keyed by the version's record ID) with the released instructions and executable and the source record IDs. `content`/`source` serve the desk record while it still holds exactly the released bytes and otherwise, for an unrevoked version, the snapshot (checked against the recorded digest). A copy is made from the released bytes the same way (it no longer needs the source record's revision to be unchanged) and keeps a snapshot of its own. Limits on purpose: a record the owner deleted (or retention blanked) is reported removed whatever the snapshot holds; a revoked version is never served from a snapshot, and revoking removes the version's snapshot in the same write (retention's own rule blanks revoked text); retention's drop of a version removes its snapshot in the same write; the owner's deletion of a desk record (`retention.delete`) also removes every snapshot made from it. Personal tools that are not copies and system (`nimblenewt.`) versions keep no snapshot (changed text is still refused, as before). Shared versions released before this slice have none.
- **Maintainer revocation** (`toolbox.revoke`, and `CatalogService.revoke` for agents). A holder of `toolbox.manage` covering a shared tool's audience revokes a version of it, and must say `finish` or `cancel` for the calls running now; `pause` (which pauses their tasks) stays the owner's. A maintainer that may neither change nor read the tool gets `not_found`, one that may read but not change it `forbidden` (the slice 1 rule for deprecate and rollback). The revocation records the maintainer as `revokedBy`; the running-call listeners get no owner principal for a maintainer's revocation (so nothing can pause tasks as the owner). The owner's `catalog.revoke` is unchanged.
- **Revocation notices are pushed to the owners of copies.** After a shared version is revoked (by the owner or a maintainer, through either operation), each agent whose fork lineage entry is based on that version gets one notice in its toolbox inbox naming its copies, one write per agent keyed by the version, so a repeat of the revoke sends nothing new. The pull answer (`toolbox.copies`, `toolbox.forks`) is unchanged.
- **Bridge tools.** `toolbox.source`, `toolbox.copy`, `toolbox.copies`, `toolbox.notices` and `toolbox.propose` are bridge operations (`BRIDGE_OPERATIONS`; Pi tools `nimblenewt__toolbox-*`, declared in `pi-adapter`). They act as the agent with its own grants, as `tool.discover` does, with the catalogue's audience and not-found rules. `toolbox.copy` and `toolbox.propose` are writes: a pause refuses them, recorded calls are admitted as effects (card L05d), their command IDs are derived from the attempt and call, and each is a `tool-call` step of the task's activity. `toolbox.propose` takes no task argument: the attempt's own task is recorded for the decision's notice. Source text is clipped at 16 KB per part with `truncated`. An older controller's "not an operation of the bridge" is answered to the model in words.
- **Owner controls by chat and status.** Chat op `toolbox.proposal.decide` (always shown first). Status kind `toolbox_proposals` (owner only; `state` optional): each proposal with its author, what it changes or offers, its base and whether that is still the version in use, the access it adds or drops, its state and revision, and the count of deferred ones. The interpreter prompt describes both in example sentences, says an acceptance never authorises a push, merge or deploy, and that no fixed phrase is needed.

**Not done (later slices or audit)**

- Promotion through the stand-up (only direct submission exists), and a chat form of publishing (as in slice 1).
- Per-consumer pinned versions and an opt-in record ("consumers stay on their pinned version until they opt in"), as in slice 1.
- Bridge tools for revise, rebase, withdraw, promote and the proposal list, and for maintainers' decisions and revocation (agents reach those through the state API with their own credential).
- Notices are read on request (`toolbox.notices`, bridge or API); they are not put into an agent's next prompt. Revocation notices are written after the revoke commits; a crash between the two leaves the pull answer as the only record (no sweep sends them again).
- The maintainer's revocation has no running-call preview or chat ask (the owner's `catalog.revoke` keeps both).
- A proposal's patch text is not snapshotted: it is read from the author's desk records; if the owner deletes one, the proposal's text is `unavailable` and it cannot be released.
- Snapshots for personal tools and system versions; backfilling snapshots for shared versions released before this slice.
- Status lines show the author and team/project audiences by ID; names are not looked up. No U08 browser pages for proposals; no maintainer view of its own.
- The fork lineage bound left open by the slice 1 second review (one agent can fill a tool's 500 lineage entries).
- The README 313-315 validation list as a whole: this slice adds "a patch against an older base is rebased and rechecked", "edits to the original leave the shared release unchanged" (for shared releases made from now on), revocation by maintainers and notices to forks; the list has not been walked item by item.

**Changed behaviour of existing code:** `CatalogService.revoke` accepts a maintainer for shared tools (owner-only before); its listeners' fourth argument is `undefined` for a maintainer's revocation (the type is now `Principal | undefined`; the tool bridge already handled `undefined`). `copy` checks the released bytes by digest (desk record or snapshot) instead of requiring the source record's revision to be unchanged. `content` falls back to the snapshot as described. Existing tests changed for this: the pinned list of bridge tool names in `pi-adapter/src/bridge.test.ts` (five names added), and one assertion of slice 1's `catalog/toolbox.test.ts` ("only the owner revokes (this slice)"): a project maintainer revoking a version of its own entry is now refused without `runningCalls` and allowed with it; `nimblenewt.` names stay refused. The `status.ask` summary names the new kind (the api test that keeps the two lists together).

Controller tests through the test slot, every file in `catalog`, `dependencies`, `toolbridge`, `commands`, `environments`, `status`, `chat`, `api` and `retention` (the deletion gather changed): 2917 tests, 2912 pass; the 5 failures were the `status.ask` kinds-list test (new kind not yet in the summary) and slice 1's "only the owner revokes" assertion on four backends, both fixed as described above, then those files and the new ones rerun (`api/api`, `catalog/{toolbox,catalog,toolbox-proposals}`, `api/start-toolbox{,-proposals}`: 156/156) and `toolbridge/service`, `status/status`, `chat/model-interpreter` after the last build (416/416). Registry 15/15; pi-adapter package 266/266; root `scripts/*.test.mjs` 225 (224 pass, 1 skipped). **Skipped:** the rest of the controller package (no other directory imports the changed catalogue internals or the new modules; `dispatch` uses the tool bridge only through its types), the integration package (real workers and sandboxes; slice 1 found its failures identical on the clean base, and no integration file names the toolbox; `t06-bridge` and `h12b-worker-process` declare the bridge tools from pi-adapter and were not run), other packages, hosted Windows/macOS (CI).

### T08 second slice, review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18; this round is final)

Reviewed `8b76d607..404653d3` against the T08 card and the owner's rules. **Three defects fixed and one tightening made. Everything else was checked and left as it was.**

**Fixed.**
- **A repeat of a committed acceptance was refused.** `CatalogService.releaseProposal` read the proposal's parts before `runner.command`: the author's desk records (same revision) and the base's released text. The runner recognises a repeat only after prepare, so an accept-with-version retried with the same command ID after the author had superseded a record (or anything else had moved those records) was answered `invalid_command` "no longer as it was proposed" even though the release and decision had committed. Those reads now run inside the guarded write's build (`#publish` takes `sources`), after the runner has looked for a record of the command. A repeat is answered from its record. The checks and pins themselves are unchanged. Test: the promotion suite repeats Gil's acceptance after Cody supersedes the executable record and gets the same `released`.
- **A rebase could overwrite a revision made in between.** `rebase` computed the new content from the proposal as read, but its write checked only the base version and the state. If the author revised (same base, new content) between that read and the rebase's write, the write would put back the old content under the new base. The write now also requires the same round and content digest (`stale_revision` otherwise). This is a race with no deterministic test here.
- **`toolbox.promote` told any agent which teams and projects exist.** The suggested audience went through `#checkAudience`, which answers "team X does not exist", "no project is called X" or "several are called X", and resolves names to IDs that the author can then read back from its own proposal. Before this slice only owners and maintainers reached that check. Now every agent can promote, so a suggestion names only teams and projects the author belongs to (`mayReadCatalogEntry` on that single team or project: its own team, or a project it holds grants in; a maintainer covering everything may suggest anything). A team or project that does not exist gets the same answer as one the author is not in. Role names are checked as before (installation role names, not narrowed). The decider still chooses the audience. Test: Orchard (not Cody's), Nowhere (none) and team Ghosts (none) get identical refusals.

**Tightened.** `revise` now also refuses (`stale_revision`) when a rebase moved the base between its read and its write, instead of moving the proposal back onto the base it read. A rebase does not raise the round, so the round check alone missed this.

**Checked, no change.** `toolbox.manage` is read from the agent's own grants (`maintainsAnywhere`/`mayManage`) on every decision, rebase, revoke and release path. An outsider gets `not_found` for proposals (`#visible` before any other answer; a decision from someone who may see but not decide cannot happen, since seeing a proposal implies deciding it unless you are its author, who gets `forbidden`). For tools it is `not_found` (`#readableEntry`), and for revoke it is `not_found` before `forbidden`, as for deprecate. An unknown version of a readable tool says so only to readers. The author never decides. Acceptance changes grants nowhere in code: `releaseProposal` writes the version, snapshot, entry, proposal, index and inbox only, and no path calls the principal service. `authorizes` is a constant. Accept-with-version is one `runner.command`: version + snapshot + desk/snapshot pins + entry + proposal update + inbox + index, so it is atomic on the reference store, SQLite, the SQLite worker thread and PostgreSQL (all four ran). A stale base is refused inside the write (`expect.chosen`). A rebase conflict is refused only when the new base changed a part the proposal changes. The 20-waiting cap is counted in the author's index inside the create write. Snapshots are bounded by the 500-version and 500-copy (`forks`) limits per tool. They are served only for unrevoked versions and only when the digest matches. Revoke and retention's version drop delete them in the same write, and the owner's `retention.delete` gathers them by `sources` and deletes them generically with the other derived records. A snapshot holds only released bytes, so it serves nothing the release did not already serve. Desk records never change visibility in place, so `toolbox.proposal.get` cannot serve text that later became private. Maintainer revocation requires `finish`/`cancel`, its listeners receive `undefined` (no owner principal), and fork notices are keyed per agent and version with a derived command ID, so a repeat sends nothing new. `toolbox.notices` reads only the caller's own inbox on both the API and the bridge. A controller notice on a task is refused by `noticeFromController` unless the author can be reached on that task. Bridge: `toolbox.copy`/`toolbox.propose` are in `WRITES` (pause refuses, admitted as effects) with activity steps. `propose` rejects a `taskId` argument and records `c.taskId`. The pi-adapter names match `BRIDGE_OPERATIONS`. The chat op is `mode: "propose"`, and the interpreter paragraph is example sentences with "no fixed phrase is needed". `node scripts/api-docs.mjs` stdout is byte-identical to `api-v1.md`. The two changed existing assertions are justified (five new bridge names; maintainers may now revoke their own entries, with `nimblenewt.` still refused).

**Limits left (not defects of this round).** Proposals in a final state (accepted, rejected, withdrawn) are never removed. A propose-and-withdraw loop therefore stores records without bound (only the 20 waiting are capped), and once there are more than 5000 proposals the default list may come back `partial`. A retention rule for final proposals belongs to a later slice. A proposal accepted without a version cannot be rebased (it is no longer waiting). If its base moves on, or a promotion's name is taken, it can never be released, and the author proposes again. A retried `propose` with the default base, after the tool has moved on, is `command_conflict` rather than a replay (the default base is part of its payload). The bridge's own recorded-call replay answers the bridge case.

### T08 second slice, second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-18; this round is final)

Reviewed `8b76d607..c2eb2336` independently. **One defect fixed. Everything else was checked and left as it was.**

**Fixed.** **Waiting proposals could drop out of the default listing once enough final ones existed.** `ToolboxProposalService.list` scanned every proposal record in ID order and stopped at 5000 (`partial`). Proposals in a final state are kept without bound. So once enough accepted, rejected or withdrawn proposals were stored ahead of a waiting one, three places could miss it: the default listing, `mine`, the deferred listing, and with them the owner's `toolbox_proposals` status view. The status view could then say "No toolbox proposal is waiting for a decision" next to "More proposals exist". A query for waiting states only (open, changes requested, deferred, which is every default and status query) now reads the authors' indexes. Those already hold exactly the waiting IDs (at most 20 per author) and are updated in each create and final-state write. The listing then fetches those records in record ID order, with the same filters, visibility check and `after`/`next` paging. An agent that is neither owner nor maintainer, and `mine`, read only the caller's own index. Queries naming a final state, or `all`, scan as before. Test (`catalog/toolbox-proposals`, all backends): two waiting proposals page one at a time in ID order for a maintainer and for the author's `mine`. A withdrawn proposal is listed under `all` but not as waiting.

**The unbounded final-state proposals.** ASSUMPTION: storage is not bounded in this slice. Removing final proposals is a deletion of the owner's records. It belongs in the retention service, with its policy, audit and archive, and not in a decision's write. With the listing fix, the growth costs storage only. The waiting cap (20 per author) and the command rate still apply, and the scan for final states keeps its 5000 limit with `next`. Left for a later slice, as the first review recorded.

**Checked, no change.**
- **Authorization.** `toolbox.manage` is read from the caller's own grants on every decide, rebase, release and revoke path (`maintainsAnywhere`, `mayManage`; `#publish` checks the prior entry's audience again inside the write). An outsider gets `not_found` for proposals (`#visible` first), tools (`#readableEntry`) and revoke (not_found before forbidden, as for deprecate). The author is refused its own decision.
- **Acceptance grants nothing.** `releaseProposal` writes only the version, snapshot, pins, entry, proposal, inbox and index.
- **Accept-with-version.** The `sources` callback runs inside the build, so a repeat is answered from its record. That holds after the author superseded a record and after the released version was revoked, because nothing read before `runner.command` depends on either. The base parts are read by digest from the record or the snapshot, with revoked versions excluded. A revision between read and write is `stale_revision`, as is a moved base.
- **Rebase and revise.** Both check round, digest and base inside the write.
- **Suggested audience.** It names only the author's own teams and projects, and a missing one gets the same answer.
- **Snapshots.** They are created only for `toolbox.` releases and copies. Revoke and retention's version drop delete them in the same write. `retention.delete` gathers them through `sources` (the record and its copies). They are served only for unrevoked versions whose digest matches.
- **Notices.** The inbox is read only by its own agent, on the API and the bridge. Fork notices are keyed per agent and version, under a derived command ID.
- **Bridge.** `toolbox.copy` and `toolbox.propose` are in `WRITES`, so a pause refuses them and they are admitted as effects, with activity steps. `propose` takes the attempt's own task. The Pi tool names match `BRIDGE_OPERATIONS`.
- **Chat and status.** The chat op is `mode: "propose"`, and the interpreter text gives examples, says what an acceptance does not authorise, and says no fixed phrase is needed. The status view is owner only.
- **API docs.** `node scripts/api-docs.mjs` stdout is byte-identical to `api-v1.md`. This review changed no operation.

**Limits left (not defects of this round).** `propose`, `revise` and `rebase` read the author's records before `runner.command`, as accept did before the first review. A retry with the same command ID after the author superseded one of those records is answered "the record is no longer as it was" instead of the recorded answer. The bridge's recorded-call replay covers `toolbox.propose`. The other two have no bridge tool yet.

## CI fix after exhaustive run 44258423696 on e94e7d8d: Windows runBounded tests, a recovery-code test that could fail by chance, a resume reviewer asked twice (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

Four cells failed, with three causes. Everything else was green.

**Windows, shard 1, both nodes: `windows-real-run.test.ts` tests 2 and 5 (test defect).**
- Cause: the test's descendant is a node program started by the node program under test. On Windows, node (libuv) puts every child it starts without `detached` into a job object of the starting process. That job is created with kill-on-job-close, and with silent breakaway so it does not reach a non-node program's own children. So the descendant ended as soon as the program ended.
  - Test 2: `child.kill()` ended the program and the job took the descendant with it, so "the descendant is still alive" was false.
  - Test 5: the program exited at once, the descendant went with it, the pipes closed and the run ended normally in 63 ms (timedOut false).
  - On Linux and macOS a node child outlives its parent, which is why the tests passed there. The earlier note that these tests "mean the same on Linux, macOS and Windows" was wrong on this point.
- Change: the descendant is started with `detached: true` (and `windowsHide`), keeping `stdio: 'inherit'`. On Windows that keeps it out of the job, and it still writes to the program's pipes. On Linux and macOS it only gets its own process group; its pid is still killed in `finally`. Test 5 now asserts its premise (the descendant is still alive when the result comes back) before `timedOut`, so a broken premise names itself. The assertions are otherwise unchanged. Test 2 still proves that the stand-in tree stop ends nothing, so only runBounded's pipe close lets the result through.
- `runBounded` (`windows-real.ts`): no Windows-only defect found behind these failures. The real program is powershell.exe. It is in the worker's libuv job, but its own children are not (silent breakaway), so `taskkill /T /F` is still what ends its tree; nothing changes there. Observation, not changed: a tree stop that takes long holds the result back for its duration plus the 5 s fallback (the shipped taskkill has its own 15 s limit, so at most about 20 s past the limit).
- Unverified (needs a Windows CI run): the libuv job behaviour as described (taken from node's documentation of `detached` on Windows and libuv's spawn code as remembered; libuv's Windows source is not on this machine). Also: that a detached descendant keeps the inherited pipes open there, and that closing the parent's pipe ends on Windows return the result within the test's 4 s margin. If that last point fails, it is a real runBounded finding on Windows (the 5 s fallback would answer), not a test flake.

**macOS node 22, shard 1: `encryption-manage.test.ts` "only the canonical recovery code is accepted" (test defect; the parser is correct).**
- Cause: the test drew 8 fresh random keys per run and required each of the 13,888 single-character changes (8 x 56 x 31) to be refused. The checksum is 20 bits of a SHA-256 of the key (4 base32 characters), not an error-detecting code. About one change in 2^20 passes it, decoding to a different key, so a run failed about once in 75.
- Reproduced on Linux: 5,208,000 changes over 3,000 random keys gave 1 accepted change, and it decoded to a different key. Over all 5.2 million, no non-canonical spelling read as the same key, so the padding check from the K01b review holds.
- Decision (ASSUMPTION): the code format and checksum are not changed. A different checksum would invalidate every recovery code already printed. A change the checksum misses opens nothing: it is another key, so unlock fails with `UnlockFailed`.
- Test change: fixed keys (SHA-256 of `nn-recovery-code-test-<n>`, n = 0..7 and 91), with every substitution enumerated, so the run is the same every time.
  - Every change of the last data character that alters only the 4 padding bits must be refused as `RecoveryCodeInvalid`. Checked by removing the padding check from the built file: the test fails ("key 0 position 63 H (padding)").
  - Every other change is either refused or reads as a different key, never the same one.
  - Exactly the one known change (key 91, position 36, 8 to G) passes the checksum.
- The first recovery-code test had the same flaw at about 56 / 2^20 per run. A changed code that passes the checksum there must now fail to unlock (`UnlockFailed`).
- `crypto.ts`: comment only. It now says the checksum catches all but about one change in 2^20.

**macOS node 22, shard 2: `start-resume-off-loop.test.ts`, PostgreSQL, "still asked once" got two asks (product defect, fixed).**
- Cause: in `ResumeCheckService.advance` (`continuation/resume.ts`), the "reviewing" step checked the in-process guard against a check body read just before. A second advance of the same check reads it while it is still "reviewing" (the resume sweep runs apart beside the dispatcher's own job). If that read came back only after the first advance had written its verdict and let go of the guard (a slow read on a loaded runner), the second advance saw a stale "reviewing" with no guard and asked the reviewer again. Its own write was then refused by the phase guard, but the model call, with its tokens, had already been made twice. The CI repair round 7 guard covers the gap between the answer and the write, but not this stale read.
- Fix: after taking the guard, the check is read again, and the reviewer is asked only if it is still "reviewing" (the rest of the step uses that fresh body). A read started after the guard is taken sees any verdict written before the guard was free, because an advance holds the guard until its write has gone through. Scope: one process, as before. Two controllers on one store were never covered by this guard.
- Test (`resume-review-once.test.ts`, 4 new: reference store, SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread, PostgreSQL): a storage proxy takes the second advance's read of the check while it is "reviewing" and hands it over only after the first advance has finished. Before the fix all 4 failed (reviewer asked twice); after it all pass.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23, all through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`):** `tsc --build`; worker suite (545 tests, 544 pass, 1 skipped, 0 failed); 21 controller files touching resume checks, the reviewer wiring and backup crypto (499 tests, 499 pass); under load (12 busy processes on 32 cores, load about 19), 20 rounds each of `start-resume-off-loop.test.js` (4 tests: SQLite and PostgreSQL), the two recovery-code tests and `resume-review-once.test.js` (8 tests): 0 failures.
**Skipped:** the full controller suite and the other packages (no other code changed); the Windows-only real-host tests (they need Windows); a macOS run.

### Review of the CI fix after run 44258423696 (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18; final round)

**`ResumeCheckService.advance` (`continuation/resume.ts`): correct, no change.**
- The guard check and the guard taking have no `await` between them, so within one process only one advance holds a check's guard.
- `finally` releases the guard on every path: each `continue`, a refused or failing fresh read (`#get` throws `not_found`), a reviewer failure, `#block` and `#update` throwing.
- The fresh body (`fb`) is used for the rest of the step: the open changes, the verdicts kept, the task ID and both blocks. `#update` reads again and writes only from "reviewing", as before.
- No double ask: a holder releases its guard only after its verdict write has resolved. The next holder's read starts after taking the guard, so it sees that write on all four backends. The reference store and SQLite (also on its worker thread) serialize, and PostgreSQL answers the write only after commit, with reads at read-committed.
- No lost resume: a fresh body that is no longer "reviewing" makes the loop read the check again and act on its new phase. That costs one of the 10 advance steps, which leaves enough room for collecting, verifying, reviewing, the extra read and ready/executing.
- One `ResumeCheckService` is built per controller (`api/start.ts`), so the sweep and the dispatcher share the guard. Two controllers on one store remain outside its scope, as documented.
- Checked by putting back the old `resume.ts`, rebuilding and running the new test: it failed on all 4 backends ("the reviewer was asked once"). With the fix it passes.

**Windows `windows-real-run.test.ts`: the reasoning holds, assertions are honest.**
- Offline evidence: libuv's own header (`uv.h`, `UV_PROCESS_DETACHED`: "will effectively enable the child to keep running after the parent exits"; seen in the node-gyp 24.21 headers and the node 22.23 tarball headers).
- From libuv's Windows spawn code (not on this machine): a global job object with kill-on-job-close and silent breakaway, which every spawned child joins unless it is detached.
- Silent breakaway also means the detached descendant is not in the test runner's own job.
- The CI logs match: test 2 failed with "the stand-in tree stop did not end the descendant" and test 5 came back in 64 ms.
- Minor wording, not changed: on Linux and macOS `detached` calls `setsid`, a new session as well as a new process group. This makes no difference to the tests.
- Test 2 still asserts that the descendant outlives the stand-in tree stop. Test 5 now asserts its premise before `timedOut`, so on Windows a descendant that dies again names itself rather than passing vacuously.

**Recovery code: the decision is right; no follow-up card proposed.**
- The unlock path fails closed, verified in `crypto.ts`. A changed code that passes the checksum decodes to another 32-byte key, and HKDF gives another key-encryption key. The AES-256-GCM tag check in `unwrap` then throws, and that becomes `UnlockFailed`. Even a tag collision would be refused by `privateFrom`, which compares the unwrapped key's public key with the keyring's.
- A change only in the 4 checksum characters can never pass, because the key is unchanged and so is its checksum.
- The only cost of a missed typo is a less specific message for about one single-character typo in 2^20 ("does not open this key" rather than "check what you typed"). That does not justify a format change that would invalidate printed codes.
- If a recovery-code format v2 is ever made for another reason, a check designed to catch every single substitution and adjacent transposition belongs in it; it is not a card on its own.
- The new test is fully deterministic: fixed keys, every substitution, and exact counts (9 x 56 x 31).

**Determinism fix (this review).** Both tests in `resume-review-once.test.ts` waited at most 500 x 2 ms (about 1 s) for the first reviewer call. On a loaded runner, the PostgreSQL start (create, collecting, verifying, reviewing writes) can take longer, and the test would then fail with "the reviewer was asked" for reasons unrelated to the product. Both now poll to a 20 s deadline. The ordering inside the test (the held read and the order of answer and delivery) is fixed by promises, not timing.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23, `tsc --build` of the installed tsc, all tests through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`):**
- Worker suite: 545 tests, 544 pass, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- Controller `dist/continuation/*.test.js`, `dist/backup/*.test.js` and `dist/api/start-resume*.test.js` (48 files): 470 of 470 pass.
- Under load (12 busy node loops on 32 cores, load about 18 to 20), 20 rounds of each:

| Test file | Passed |
| --- | --- |
| `resume-review-once.test.js` | 160 of 160 |
| the two recovery-code tests | 40 of 40 |
| `windows-real-run.test.js` | 180 of 180 |
| `start-resume-off-loop.test.js` | 80 of 80 |

**Skipped:** the full controller suite and the other packages (no other code changed); the Windows-only real-host tests and any Windows or macOS run, so the libuv job behaviour itself is confirmed only by the next CI run. This round is final.

**Clean-context second review of ci-fix2 (at d12bb74f): no defects found, so no code was changed.**
- `resume.ts` `advance`, "reviewing" step:
  - The guard is added with no await between `has` and `add`.
  - Every exit after that goes through the `finally` that releases it: the `continue` when the fresh read is no longer "reviewing", the not-run write, both blocks, the verdict write, and a throw from the fresh `#get`, the reviewer or `#update`.
  - Everything after the guard uses the fresh copy `fb`: the open changes, the base verdicts, the block's `blocks` count and the done test. Nothing still uses the stale `b`.
- Step budget: a stale "reviewing" costs one of the 10 steps; the next step reads "ready" and returns. The phase guards in `#update` and `#block` are unchanged, so a write cannot land twice.
- Read-after-write: `runner.get` reads storage directly with no cache. The other advance releases the guard only after its write has committed, so a read started after the guard is taken sees that write on all four backends.
- Sweep and dispatcher: there is one production `ResumeCheckService` (`api/start.ts`), so the in-memory guard covers both within one process. The guard is still per process, as before (multi-process caveat unchanged).
- Mutation check: with the fresh read replaced by the stale `b`, the new test fails on all 4 backends ("the reviewer was asked once"). After restoring, the `resume.ts` sha256 was 8b1665dd...2336, the same as before, and the build was redone.
- Recovery-code test: checked the padding-only branch (the 52nd character's top bit is the key bit) and the 9 x 56 x 31 count.
- Ran (Linux, installed tsc, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`):
  - Controller `continuation`, `backup`, `api/start-resume*`, `dispatch/resume*` and `chat/resume*` (59 files): 863 of 863 pass.
  - Worker suite: 545 tests, 544 pass, 1 skipped.
  - Under 12 busy node loops (load 10 to 17), 10 rounds each of `resume-review-once`, `encryption-manage`, `windows-real-run` and `start-resume-off-loop`: 40 of 40 runs pass.

## W01e: the bench's contamination checks read each tool call's full arguments, not the copy cut to 2,000 characters (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

Branch `card-w01e` off origin/main `a0f46691`. Bench code only (`scripts/pi-eval`); no Radiance request, no network, no real credentials.

**Problem (W01 batch 4, runs `l02e-2-B-r1-20261118T080448` and `c07m-B-r1-20261118T085505`).** The summary kept each tool call's arguments as JSON cut to 2,000 characters (`toolCommands`), and `foreignPaths`, `credentialAttempts` and the reference-mark check read that cut copy.
- A long `edit` whose `path` came after its edit text was cut inside the path, so the shortened path no longer matched the run's own checkout and was flagged as foreign.
- A cut call no longer parses as JSON, and the detector then read the whole text as a command. Edit text holding the project's own test fixture (`git push origin/main with token=<fake token>`) was read as a push.
- Both runs' git-guard logs were empty: nothing was pushed or refused.

**Change.**
- New `lib/tool-args.mjs`. `argTexts(args, toolName)` reads one call's full parsed arguments into:
  - commands: the `command`, `cmd` or `script` field of a tool that is not a file tool (read, write, edit, multi-edit, notebook edit, grep, glob, find, ls; Pi's and Claude Code's names, any case). A tool with no known name is read as a shell tool, so older records stay strict.
  - paths: every other string field at any depth (`path`, `file_path`, a search pattern, a working folder, nested lists).
  - Content fields are skipped at every depth: `content`, `newText`, `oldText`, `new_string`, `old_string`, `edits`, `text`, `new_source`, `old_source`, `contents`, `patch`, `diff`. Tool results are never read.
  - Each text is bounded at 65,536 characters; a text cut there carries `cut: true`.
- `classify.mjs` `addEvent`: per call, `toolTexts` gets `{ tool, commands, paths, argsCut }` from the parsed `e.args`. `toolCommands` is still the JSON cut to 2,000 characters (the stored record); `toolCommandsCut` counts the cut ones. Both lists keep the 5,000-call bound.
- `runner.mjs`: `foreignPaths`, `credentialAttempts` and the reference marks (now `namesMark`) read `summary.toolTexts`. The run record gets `toolArgsCut` when any call's stored copy was cut.
- A cut text is judged only on what is visible (`wholePart`: up to its last word or path boundary). `git pu|` is not a push; `git push |` is; `/home/u/.ssh/id_r|` names `.ssh/`. A path running to the cut end is foreign only when its visible part cannot still become the run's own checkout or Pi's install.
- Fallback for a stored string (older records, or a caller passing `toolCommands`), `toolCallTexts`:
  - valid JSON is read in full (source `parsed`);
  - text that starts like JSON but does not parse is read by `parseVisible`, a tolerant reader (source `visible-text`). Complete fields count as above; the string the cut ended inside is kept as cut; a number, literal, key or escape the cut ended inside is dropped. Text that is not JSON even as far as it goes is one cut command line;
  - any other string is a plain command line.
- Behaviour kept: every case in `isolation.test.mjs` (pushes, remotes, keys, the cut-call case) and `runner.test.mjs` (foreign paths) passes unchanged.
- Behaviour changed, beyond the fix:
  - a `command` field of a file tool is now read as a path, not run;
  - string fields nested in non-content objects are now searched as paths (before, only top-level strings were);
  - the reference marks (reference checkout, solution SHA prefix, results folder) no longer match inside file content or edit text.
- README contamination paragraphs updated to match.

**Replay (read only; old = origin/main `lib`, new = this branch).** Each run's `agent.jsonl`, with its own checkout `/srv/code/worktrees-pi/eval-work/eval-<runId>`, the batch's watched roots (`/srv/code/repos/nimblenewt`, `/srv/code/repos`, `/srv/code/worktrees-pi/eval-results`, `/srv/code/worktrees-pi`) and its marks:

| run | tool calls (cut copies) | old: foreign / attempts / marks | new: foreign / attempts / marks | new fallback on the cut copies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `l02e-2-B-r1-20261118T080448` | 251 (31) | `/srv/code/worktrees-pi/eval-work/eval-l02e-2-B-r1-20261` / none / no | none / none / no | none / none / no |
| `c07m-B-r1-20261118T085505` | 166 (16) | `/srv/code/worktrees-pi/eval` / `push` / no | none / none / no | none / none / no |

The old classifier reproduces both records' stored flags exactly; neither run has a flag under the new one. So both runs' contamination was the bench's recognition problem named in the batch 4 notes. The stored records in `eval-results/results.jsonl` are not rewritten (`rescore.mjs` re-derives outcomes, not contamination).

**Tests.** New `scripts/pi-eval/tool-args.test.mjs`, 5 tests:
- a long edit with its path last: not flagged; the stored copy is cut and marked;
- edit, write and Claude `Edit` text holding a push, a fake token (assembled at run time), `~/.ssh` and a reference path: no attempt, no foreign path, no mark;
- still flagged:
  - a real bash push, and a push after a long heredoc;
  - a foreign path in a long edit's `path`;
  - `~/.ssh` in a read's `path`;
  - a reference checkout in Claude `Read`'s `file_path`, which also counts as a mark;
- cut, invalid JSON: both batch 4 shapes are not flagged. What the visible text supports is still flagged: a complete foreign field before the cut, a cut path already outside the checkout, a cut command's whole words, a whole `.ssh/` component. The reading reports `visible-text`;
- the tolerant reader itself.

**Verified (Linux, node 22.23, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, offline guard).**
- `scripts/pi-eval/*.test.mjs` and `scripts/y02-checkpoint.test.mjs`: 163 of 163 pass, none skipped.
- Build for those tests: the installed tsc (`tsc --build --force packages/pi-adapter packages/worker`, clean), through a temporary `node_modules` in the worktree that links the installed packages and points `@nimblenewt/*` at the worktree's own packages; removed afterwards.

**Skipped.** Any real bench run (no Radiance request); the rest of the repository's suites (no product code changed); Windows and macOS.
- ASSUMPTION: a tool with no recorded name keeps the strict reading (its `command` is a command), since older records and the stub agents may carry none.
- ASSUMPTION: the reference marks follow the same rule as paths (file content and edit text are not read). A solution SHA seen in written code would have had to come from a command or a read, and those are still checked.

### W01e review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18): one round, final

Reviewed `5563836f` for whether the detector errs strict, checked against Pi's real tool set (bash, powershell, edit, find, grep, ls, read, write) and the 45 run folders in `eval-results/runs` (they use only bash, edit, read, write).

**Defects found and fixed (`lib/tool-args.mjs`, `lib/isolation.mjs`, `lib/classify.mjs`, `lib/runner.mjs`).**
- A shell command in a field other than a top-level `command`/`cmd`/`script` was read only as a path, so it was never checked for a push or a remote. Missed shapes: `args`, `input`, `cmdline`, `commands`, `bash`, a nested `params.command`, and an argv list (`command: ["git", "push"]`). Now:
  - for a call with no tool name, command-like fields at any depth are commands, and string lists are also read joined;
  - for a named tool that is not a file tool, every string is a command, content fields included.
- A content key hid everything below it, so `edits: [{ path }]` was not read. Now only a string directly in a content field is skipped; an object inside one is read field by field.
- A text over 65,536 characters kept only its head, so a push after a long heredoc was missed. Strings past 256 per call, and anything deeper than 8 levels, were dropped without a mark. Now:
  - a long text keeps its head and its tail (`cutStart` marks the tail);
  - texts past a call's room are joined and kept head and tail;
  - a too-deep value is read whole as one text;
  - such a call carries `textsCut`.
- No size bound on the in-memory `toolTexts`: 5,000 calls × 256 texts × 64 KiB. Now bounded:
  - 256 KiB per call;
  - after a run's calls hold 16 Mi characters, 4 KiB per call.
  - All calls are now read, not only the first 5,000. The stored `toolCommands` copies keep their 5,000 bound.
  - The run record gets `toolTextsCut`, the number of calls kept head and tail. The field is optional and additive.
- `wholePart` alone made cut texts less strict than before: `git push|` and `echo $SSH_AUTH_SOCK|` at the cut were no longer seen. A cut text is now read both as far as it is visible and up to its last whole word.
- A remote command that runs to the cut now counts as `remote`, because its address is not known. Before, `git remote add o ht|` read as local.

**Checked, no change.**
- The reference-folder check still catches a Claude `Read` `file_path`, a Pi `read` `path`, and shell commands.
- Tool results are not read. They show what came back, not what the agent asked for.

### W01e second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-18): final round

Reviewed `bcd3b005` for how strict and how robust the contamination reading is. Probed shapes are in the tests below; the replays read the run folders only.

**Defects found and fixed (`lib/isolation.mjs`, `lib/tool-args.mjs`, `lib/runner.mjs`).**
- Missed pushes and remotes:
  - `git --git-dir /x/.git push`, `git --work-tree /x push`: the long options git also takes with a separate value now eat that value, the same way `-C` and `-c` already did;
  - `git \<newline> push`, `"git" push`, `git'' push`, Python `subprocess.run(["git", "push"])`, Node `execFileSync("git", ["push"])`: a second, loose reading of each command (line continuations joined, quotes dropped, `, [ ] ( )` read as spaces) is checked for a push or a remote. It only adds kinds. The key check does not use it: without its quotes, a pattern `'a|\.ssh'` would split into programs.
- A text over its room kept only head and tail, so a push between two long heredocs, or one the head/tail cut fell across, was missed. The middle's lines that name git, ssh, a key or login file, a home folder or an absolute path are now kept as well (`excerpts`: up to 256 characters each side of the word, a quarter of the room in all). Head and tail shrink to fit, so the per-text, per-call and per-run bounds are unchanged. Other middle text is still not read. The header comment's "nothing is dropped unread" is corrected.
- False flag: Pi's `grep`/`find` tool (and Claude's Grep/Glob) searching the code for `\.ssh` counted as `credentials`, though the same search in bash grep did not. This predates the card. A file tool's `pattern`, `glob`, `regex`, `query`, `include`, `exclude` and `iglob` fields are now `patterns`, a search of the code. For keys they count only as a key path under a home folder, the same as a bash grep. They still count for foreign paths and the reference marks. The entry field is optional, and older entries and stored strings read as before.

**Checked, no change.**
- Already caught: `git -c x=y push`, `git<TAB>push`, `env GIT_SSH_COMMAND=... git push`, `/usr/bin/git push`, `\git push`, `os.system("git push")`, `send-pack`, a remote add to an ssh or quoted https address, a Python one-liner opening `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `$HOME/.config/gh`, a read of `~/.ssh` or `/home/u/.ssh`, a relative walk up to `home/u/.ssh/id_rsa` (the `.ssh/` component), a path in `edits: [{ path }]`, a PowerShell push.
- Not detectable from the call text, and not claimed: a git alias (`git config alias.p push; git p`), a shell alias or a variable as the program (`G=git; $G push`), base64 or hex of a command, a script written with a file tool and then run, `gh`/`curl` to a forge API, a path built from variables (`D=/srv/code; cat $D/repos/...`), a relative walk to another checkout (`cat ../../c07m/a`), `~other/`, a solution SHA that appears only in a long text's unexcerpted middle, and a key name split by quotes or variables (caught here only when `id_rsa` or the home path is still visible). These are heuristics.
- What actually stops each one on Linux with bubblewrap:
  - push, remote and network: the git wrapper, the run's own git settings (ssh off, network transports refused) and a network namespace with loopback only;
  - keys and logins: the owner's home and the key folders hidden, a fresh home, a scrubbed environment;
  - writing outside the run's folders: the read-only file system.
  - Reading another checkout or the reference under `/srv/code` is not prevented. There the detector is the only safeguard, and the README already says so. Without bubblewrap (macOS, Windows, or a host where it does not work), only the wrapper and settings stand behind the detector.
- Remaining strict cases, accepted: a bash `grep "git push"` and a commit message naming `git push` count as a push, as before; under the loose reading, `echo "git, push"` would too.
- Bounds and speed: a synthetic 241 MB log (401 bash calls of 600K characters each, dense with paths and git words, and a push in the last) gives 17.4 M characters of texts (16 Mi plus 4 KiB per later call). Summarizing takes 1.4 s and detection 2.3 s, the same as `bcd3b005`. The push is found. All 45 real run folders replay in 5.4 s with a 125 MB peak resident size. The largest `agent.jsonl` is 27 MB, and no real call reaches a size cap.
- Compatibility: `results.jsonl` gains no new fields in this round. `patterns` lives only in the in-memory summary. `rescore.mjs` re-derives outcomes through `summarizeLogFile` and `classify`, which do not read `toolTexts`.

## G09 follow-up: an updated resume on a remote worker host shows the agent the selected correction (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)
A flip audit of card G09 found that `remote/host.ts` took `contextUpdates` off the order before offering it to a remote host. On the remote path an updated resume never showed the agent the selected correction. The G09 clause "an updated resume applies the selected update once / the correction of an old owner decision" now holds there too.

**Changed.**
- `remote/host.ts`: `RemoteWorkerHost.start` keeps `contextUpdates` in the offered order. The starting-size parts and the environment revision pin are still kept back, as before. An order with no updates is offered without the field, as before.
- `dispatch/context-updates.ts`: new pure `contextUpdatesProblem(value)` checks the shape and bounds `boundContextUpdates` gives. Absent is fine. Otherwise it must be a list of at most 20 objects with only `requestId` (1 to 200 characters, the worker channel's bound), `text` (at most 20,000) and `origin` (at most 300). The texts together must be at most 64,000 characters plus one left-out note. A request ID given twice is not refused: the process places it once, as on a local host.
- `remote/service.ts` `place`: refuses an order whose `contextUpdates` fail the check (`invalid_command`, field `order.contextUpdates`). Nothing is offered and the placement is unchanged.
- `remote/runner.ts` (the remote worker's side of an offer): after the contract is confirmed and before `host.start`, it applies the same check. An offer that fails it starts nothing and completes as failed ("the worker could not start the order: its contextUpdates ..."). Otherwise the order goes to the machine's `LocalWorker` unchanged. The worker package's host passes the updates on the channel's `start` message (`updates`, cut to `CHANNEL_UPDATES`). The worker process places each one before `ready`: place-only, under its request ID, so the update applies exactly once per conversation. This is the code the local host already used, so no worker-side change was needed.
- `dispatch/ports.ts`: the `contextUpdates` doc comment no longer says the updates are not sent to a remote host.
- No protocol version change. The contract digest still covers identity, recipe and expiry, not the updates, so offers verify as before. An older worker package ignores the field and places nothing, which is how it behaved before.

**Tests.**
- New composed test `packages/integration/src/g09-remote-updates.test.ts`. The composed controller (SQLite) and dispatcher offer the attempt over HTTP to a `RemoteOfferRunner`. Its host is the worker package's launcher and the real worker process in bubblewrap, behind a `LocalWorker`, with no `context` of its own. A scripted OpenAI-compatible model answers. The test follows the C05 flow of `g09-retained-context.test.ts`: decision A is selected, the owner corrects it (B supersedes A), the correction is selected and the side line resumes. It then checks:
  - the first offer has no `contextUpdates` field;
  - the second offer carries the correction only;
  - the model's request holds the correction exactly once, with its origin, after the earlier turn and before this turn's instruction, and without decision A;
  - a third run in a new process on the same conversation, offered the same correction again, does not place it twice.

  Mutation check: putting the removal back in `remote/host.ts` makes this test fail (`expected: 1`), and the new unit test in `host-environment.test.ts` fails too.
- Unit tests:
  - `host-environment.test.ts`: updates offered as given; an order without updates is offered without the field.
  - `context-updates.test.ts`: the checker accepts what `boundContextUpdates` gives and names each bad shape.
  - `remote.test.ts` (both backends): `place` refuses bad updates and changes nothing; good updates reach the host's offer.
  - `runner.test.ts`: updates reach `host.start`; bad ones start nothing and report failed.
- `w03-rig-support.ts`: its scripted `model` is now exported for reuse. Nothing else changed.

**Not done.**
- The first-call admission (`#judge`, C07o) still measures the order's content and resume note without the updates' text, as the local host's `firstCall` does. Updates are bounded at 64,000 characters, but neither path counts them in the first call's estimate.
- The remote test uses one reply per run (its machine tool bridge answers nothing, so no W04 continuation is asked). Nudged runs on the remote path are covered elsewhere, not here.

### G09 remote follow-up: first review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18; declared the final round)
I reviewed `dcf2919f` and found no defects. Nothing in the code was changed. What I checked:
- **Placement happens once.** The dispatcher bounds the updates (`boundContextUpdates`) and puts them in the order only when there are some. `#judge` and `#carry` keep the field, and `place` keeps the order only in memory (`#offers`). A relocation or a repeated offer hands out that same order. A fresh placement fences the earlier one, and the request IDs stop a second copy from entering the conversation. The composed test shows this on the third run.
- **Order relative to `ready`.** The remote runner passes the order unchanged to `LocalWorker`. That code sends `updates` on the channel `start` message, and the process places them before `ready`. The composed test checks the position in the model's request: after the earlier turn, before this turn's instruction.
- **Bounds.** `contextUpdatesProblem` accepts everything `boundContextUpdates` can return: at most 20 items, kept texts up to 64,000 characters plus one note of up to 20,000. The 200-character request-ID bound matches `CHANNEL_UPDATES.requestId`. The check is a little looser than the producer: it accepts 84,000 characters without a note. That only affects how much it lets through. It is not a correctness problem.
- **Failure paths.** A refused `place` (`invalid_command`, field `order.contextUpdates`) happens before the dispatch record and the placement change, so nothing is offered. On the worker, an offer that fails the check is accepted and then completed as failed, and `host.start` is not called. Neither error message contains update text. The only text from the update in them is a field name cut to 30 characters.
- **Leaks.** The order (and so the update text) lives only in the in-memory offer and in the HTTP answer to the host's poll. It is not in the placement record, the placement view or any log line added here. The remote host is already given the task's content and credential, so the updates do not widen what it sees.
- **Size.** In the worst case, 32 offers with updates escaped at six bytes per character come to about 16 MB. That stays under the client's 32 MB answer cap. The first-call estimate still leaves out the update text, as the notes above say.
- **Older and newer versions.** An older worker ignores the field. A newer worker given an order with no field places nothing. If a later controller raises `CONTEXT_UPDATE_LIMITS` before its workers are updated, those workers will fail such offers instead of starting them. That failure is visible, and it is noted here for whoever changes the limits.
- **Mutation check, repeated.** I put the `contextUpdates` removal back in `remote/host.ts` and rebuilt. `host-environment.test.ts` then fails 1 of 2 tests, and `g09-remote-updates.test.ts` fails with `expected: 1`. After restoring the code and rebuilding, both pass.
- **Runs.** All went through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh` with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1` and `scripts/offline-guard.mjs`, on a `tsc --build` of this worktree. Results: controller `dist/remote/*.test.js` plus `dispatch/context-updates.test.js` 1066/1066; integration `dist/g09*.test.js` 43/43 (bubblewrap present, nothing skipped; the Radiance file uses only its offline fake); contracts `worker-channel.test.js` 14/14; `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6/6. Skipped: the rest of the controller, worker and integration suites, the worker package's own tests (its code is unchanged), Windows and macOS (CI covers those).

### G09 remote follow-up: second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-18; final round)

- **Read independently.** The diff `origin/main...6e984cec`: the stripped field returned to the offer in `remote/host.ts`, `contextUpdatesProblem` at `place` (`remote/service.ts`) and before `host.start` (`remote/runner.ts`), and the composed test. The offer order lives only in the service's in-memory `#offers`; the placement record holds no update text. Refusal messages name a field or bound, never the text. A re-offer or relocation goes back through the dispatcher, which recomputes the bounded list; the request IDs (`upd:` plus 32 hex, `upd-left:` plus 32 hex) keep placement to once per conversation. The worker-side check runs after `accept` and the contract check and before the process starts, so a refusal starts nothing and reports `failed`. An older worker passes the field through to a local host that already reads it (on main).
- **Validation versus what the dispatcher produces.** `boundContextUpdates` gives at most 20 items, each text at most 20 000, each origin at most 300, and request IDs well under 200. The kept texts total at most 64 000, plus one note of at most 20 000 when some are left out. The check allows exactly this, so nothing legitimate is refused.
- **One test gap, fixed.** Spot-mutating the built check down to `total > L.total` went undetected: the existing cases leave the kept texts below 64 000. Such a change would refuse the dispatcher's own output whenever the kept texts fill the total and a note is added, and every remote start of that task would then fail. Added to `context-updates.test.ts`: a bound list whose kept texts total exactly 64 000, plus the note, passes. With the mutation, the test fails 1 of 4; restored, it passes 4 of 4.
- **Other mutations (built files, each restored).** Stripping `contextUpdates` in `host.js` again fails `host-environment.test.js` (1 of 2) and `g09-remote-updates.test.js`. Removing the runner check fails `runner.test.js` (1 of 11). Removing the service check fails `remote.test.js` (4 tests).
- **Runs** (`/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, `scripts/offline-guard.mjs`, after `tsc --build`): controller `dist/remote/*.test.js` plus `dispatch/context-updates.test.js` 1066/1066 before the added test, and `context-updates.test.js` 4/4 after it; integration `dist/g09*.test.js` 43/43, nothing skipped; contracts `worker-channel.test.js` 14/14; `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6/6. Skipped: the rest of the controller, worker and integration suites (the diff cannot affect them), Windows and macOS (CI covers those).

A later `attention`, `failed` or unmarked check leaves it; a note, or an intervention marked `ok`, does not set it. ## Owner IDs: an agent named by its bare ID owns its event handlings and reads its task's generations (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-18)

Follow-up to the P04 review finding that real assignments name an agent by its bare ID (`{ kind: "agent", id: "<id>" }`, as the chat, check runs and meetings assign) while the agent signs in as `agent:<id>`. `dispatch/loops.ts` `assignedTaskIn` is fixed on the P04 branch and is not touched here. Branch `card-owner-ids` off origin/main `0bb91050`.

- **Proven first, with real-shaped IDs through the real assignment path** (`AssignmentService.assignTask` with `{ kind: "agent", id: "cal" }` / `"ann"`, the agent authenticated as `agent:cal` / `agent:ann`). Both tests failed on the unchanged code at the predicted line, after their setup checks passed:
  - `events/handling.ts`: a handling copies the assignment's owner, so its owner ID was bare and `owns` / `#mayRead` (which compared `by.id`, the `agent:` form) never matched. The owning agent could not read its own handling (`watches.inspect`, the `events.handling` and `events.failures` operations) unless it also held `history.read`, and could not `extendLease` or `settle` it ("no such handling"). `extendLease`, `settle` and `retry` have no API operation today, so the read is the reachable part; the service methods are the documented "owning agent" path.
  - `generation/generation.ts` `#mayRead`: a generation the dispatcher streams has the dispatcher as its owner, so the assigned agent reads it only through the assignment check, which compared the bare owner ID with `viewer.id`. The assigned agent got nothing back from `view`.
- **Fix:** one shared helper `isAgentOwner(owner, principal)` in `domain/assignment-model.ts` (next to `sameOwner`): true only for an `agent` owner and an `agent` principal, with the principal `agent:<id>` or the same string as the owner ID. It is stricter than `isOwnerOf` (status/explain.ts) and `isOwner` (health/stall.ts), which also accept an exact ID match from any owner kind; those are left as they are. Used in handling `owns` and `#mayRead`, and in the generation assignment check. Nothing else changed (the generation check still does not look at the assignment's state, as before).
- **Behaviour change beyond the fix:** a handling or assignment whose owner is a person, role or team with an ID such as `agent:cal` no longer lets `agent:cal` act as its owner (before, an exact string match of any kind did). Tested.
- **Tests:** `events/watchers.test.ts` "an agent named by its bare ID in a real assignment reads, extends and settles its own handling; …" (bare owner reads, lists its failed handling, extends, settles; person `cal`, person `agent:cal` and role `agent:cal` owners refused for read, extend and settle; the prefixed agent spelling still settles). `generation/stream-feed.test.ts` "the agent a real assignment names by its bare ID reads the generation the dispatcher streams for it; …" (another agent of the project with `assignment.read` does not; person owners in both spellings do not; the prefixed agent spelling reads). The existing tests use `agent:<name>` owner IDs throughout, which is why neither defect showed.
- **Mutation checks** (compiled output changed, then restored): handling `owns` back to `by.id === h.owner.id`; handling `#mayRead` back; the generation check back; the helper made like `isOwnerOf` (any kind, exact match); the helper without the exact-match branch; the helper without the owner-kind check. Each failed at least one of the two new tests; restored, both pass.
- **Not changed, seen on the way:** the per-owner open-handling counter and the waker request are keyed by the handling's owner ID as stored, so one agent assigned once by bare ID and once as `agent:<id>` has two counters (the cap of open handlings applies to each); the waker is given the bare ID (`attemptWaker` looks only at the attempt, so it does not matter there). Left for a separate change if wanted.
- **Verified (Linux, node 22.23, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, offline guard, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`):** `tsc --build --force` clean; every controller test file in `events/` and `generation/`, and the API tests that use watches or generations (`start-decisions-generation`, `start-defined-sources`, `start-l05d`, `start-l05e`, `start-remote-stream`, `start-route-calls`, `start-status`): 450 of 450; `scripts/plan.test.mjs` 6 of 6. **Skipped:** the other controller suites (only one new export in `domain/assignment-model.ts`, nothing changed in what existed there), other packages, hosted Windows/macOS (CI). `api-v1.md` unchanged: no operation was added or changed.
