## G04 follow-up: a kill inside a protected tool call no longer leaves a write open, unreported or reported as not done (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19)

Branch `card-g04fix-s1`, built on the G04 tool slice (`card-g04-s1`) merged with main `c31be6da`. The details and the per-boundary table are in `g04-evidence.md`, section "A kill inside a protected tool the model calls".

- **The problem.** The G04 tool slice killed the controller and Pi together while the model's `push` ran through the tool bridge route (card L05d), and it found three gaps. (1) A write that was admitted but never started stayed open for good. (2) A write that had started was never resolved, and nobody was told, because the production reconciler has no bridges and only counts such writes. (3) When the push had happened, the model was told it "did not finish", so a real model retrying would push twice.
- **Done.**
  - **Presented again, not repeated.** All bridge tools now tell Pi they are safe to present again (`BRIDGE_REPLAY = "safe"`, `pi-adapter/src/bridge.ts`). After a crash Pi runs the interrupted call again with the same call ID, and the controller answers it from the effect ledger. A finished write gives back its recorded result, a never-started one runs once, and a started one is checked with the target and never run blindly. The model is therefore told "pushed" when the push happened. The worker keeps the call's old ID (the first review of `card-g04-s1` pointed out that declaring the tools replay-safe alone would send the call under a new number): `AdapterConversation.openToolCalls()` lists the calls with no result, matched by position because a provider may reuse one call ID across replies, and `seedFromConversation` (`bridge.seed(ids, open)`) gives each its old number. The worker does this before it releases the hold, because the release presents the calls at once. This is proven end to end in `restore.test.ts`: a child process runs the real bridge tools in a real Pi conversation and is killed by SIGKILL during its second `desk.write`, which used the provider ID `call_0` a second time. After the restart, Pi presents that write again under the same `d:` ID the controller saw before the crash, and the model's next `call_0` gets a new number. The first version of `openToolCalls` matched results by ID only, and this test caught it: the reused ID was treated as answered.
  - **No "busy" right after a restart.** An effect claim now records the primary epoch. A claim from an older epoch (a controller that died or was replaced) is given up at once instead of after the 5-minute lease. Recovery still treats it as a vanished executor.
  - **Nothing left open, nobody left uninformed.** In `EffectService.closeUnbridged`, the reconciler handles effects of kind `bridge` (tool bridge calls). While their attempt still holds the task, it leaves them alone. Once the attempt has lost the task: a never-started write is closed as `failed`, and a started write whose executor vanished is marked `uncertain`, which opens an `effect_uncertain` blocker for the owner. Nothing is run.
  - **Tests.** The G04 tool tests now assert guarantees, not gaps, on SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread and PostgreSQL. First, with the production setting, all 16 kill points end like the uncrashed run. Second, with a call that is not presented again, every kill point ends with nothing open: closed as failed, or uncertain with a blocker. Every run is checked for no open effect, every uncertain effect reported, and no failed effect that started. Unit tests were added for the epoch rule and `closeUnbridged` (four backends, `domain/effects.test.ts`), for the bridge keeping an interrupted call's ID (`bridge.test.ts`), and for `openToolCalls` after a real kill (`restore.test.ts`). The old bridge test that asserted "no replay flag" now asserts `"safe"`. There are four mutation checks; each was caught (listed in `g04-evidence.md`).
  - No state API operation changed, and `api-v1.md` was regenerated unchanged. No new bridge tools were added.
- **ASSUMPTION: an attempt may finish as succeeded while one of its admitted writes is still `intended`.** `finishAttempt` neither refuses nor closes it. Refusing would strand an attempt on a write it can no longer present. The reconciler's next pass after the finish closes the write instead: a never-started write as `failed`, and a started one as `uncertain` with a blocker. This is the smallest reversible choice.
- **Honest limit of the kill test.** In production, the generation is begun, recorded and completed from the model stream before the tool runs. In the test those steps sit inside the tool, so 7 of the 16 boundaries stand for a kill while the stream is recorded, not inside the bridge.
- **ASSUMPTION: presenting every bridge call again is safe.** With `admitCall` on (the default), writes are answered from the ledger. Every other operation's command ID is derived from the attempt and the call ID, so the same call ID is the same command. A catalogue tool's own restart policy is still decided by the controller from its manifest. Alternatives rejected: replay only some tools (every write already goes through the same ledger, so a list would only add a way to get it wrong); have the controller replay interrupted calls itself (the model's conversation is Pi's, and only Pi can put the real result in place of "interrupted"); add a new bridge tool to ask "did my call happen" (the tool budget is nearly used, and the model would have to choose to ask).
- **ASSUMPTION: an uncertain result is better than a guess.** A started bridge write whose attempt is gone becomes `uncertain`, even when nothing was pushed, because no reconciler bridge can ask the bridge operation's own service. The owner checks and settles it with `effect.resolve`. The reconciler only closes `bridge`-kind effects. Other kinds are still settled by the dispatcher's own bridges, so they are not raced.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a call is presented again by the same attempt, after a local worker restart with `start.recover`. If the task goes to a new attempt, the reconciler path above closes or reports the old attempt's writes.
- **NOT done.**
  - A real out-of-process worker killed together with the controller and then presented again end to end. The G04 tool test uses the adapter in the killed process, with a tool that takes the production replay setting. The worker's seeding order and `openToolCalls` are covered by unit tests only.
  - A started bridge write that answered "not finished yet" (an idempotent `tool.invoke` or `job.start` whose claim was given back) is still only counted after its attempt ends; it is not marked uncertain. Doing so would raise false alarms for long jobs that outlive their attempt.
  - Effects with no fence that never started stay open, because no owner exists to judge them.
  - With `admitCall` switched off by the owner, a presented call relies on each operation's command ID alone, not on the ledger.
  - macOS and Windows were not run (Linux only).
- **Verified** (Linux, Node 22, through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, with the offline guard and `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, after `tsc --build --force`):
  - G04 tool files on SQLite, the SQLite worker thread (with `NIMBLENEWT_G04_HEAVY=1`) and PostgreSQL: 6 of 6.
  - The whole pi-adapter suite: 269 of 269.
  - `domain/effects`, `reconcile` and `effects.crash`: 122 of 122.
  - Controller domain, toolbridge, generation, slice, `start-l05d`, `start-replay-finish` and `start-remote-stream`: 887 of 891 before the follow-up's own test slip was fixed. The 4 failures came from an edit that touched the wrong test; that file was rerun above.
  - Controller dispatch and remote: 2655 of 2655.
  - The other G04 files and `l05d-remote-sandbox`: 26 passed, 10 heavy skipped.
  - `api-v1.md` was regenerated with no change.

First review of the follow-up (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19):
- **Fixed: a call presented again under a different number could be run twice.** The worker's bridge counts its uses of a provider call ID only when it runs a tool, but `seed` counts every use in the stored conversation. A use that Pi answered itself without running the tool (arguments that do not validate, a tool that is not available, a call aborted before it started) is counted after a restart and was not before, so with a provider that reuses `call_0` the interrupted call can come back under a higher `d:` number. The controller still finds the same recorded call (a repeated ID stands for the newest call with that base) and the ledger answers it, but `tool.invoke` and `job.start` are run again by the ledger with the same key when they started and did not settle, and their key (the dispatcher's operation record, the job ID) is the bridge call ID: under a new number that is a second run. Now `GenerationService.admitCall` reports `otherCall` when the call was admitted under another command ID, and the bridge then hands the ledger a non-idempotent bridge: a started effect is never run again under the new number (it is answered from the ledger, or becomes `uncertain` with a blocker); one that never started runs once. Tests: `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (the ledger is given an idempotent bridge only under the admitting call ID) and `api/start-l05d.test.ts` (`otherCall` from the real generation service); both caught their mutation on the built files.
- **Added:** a worker-process test (`worker/process.test.ts`, G04 follow-up review): a process that reuses `call_0` is ended while its second bridge call is with the controller; the restarted process with `start.recover` presents that call under the same `d:` ID and numbers the model's next `call_0` on. Removing the seed from the built `process.js` fails it.
- **Checked and kept:** every bridge operation that writes is admitted (the ledger) or keyed by `bridge:{attempt}:{call}`; the others read. The epoch rule only shortens the wait: an older-epoch claim is still recovered as a vanished executor (`trustNotApplied` false), so a target that may still receive the old request is never run again without its key. `closeUnbridged` never closes a started effect as failed (it goes through `#recover` with a bridge that cannot be asked or retried, so `uncertain`), races with the bridge's own run through the revision-guarded claim and the fence guard on the claim, and touches only kind `bridge`. Production generation runs carry a fence (`stream-feed.ts`).
- **Leftovers (not fixed):**
  - The order "seed, then release the hold" is in place, but no test can catch the reverse order: Pi presents the call asynchronously after the release, so a seed placed after it still usually wins the race.
  - The bridge numbering itself is still only exact when Pi ran every earlier use of a reused provider ID; making `seed` count only the uses that reached the bridge would need a marker Pi does not store. The fix above keeps it safe, not exact (an affected started call becomes `uncertain` instead of being answered).
  - A call presented again while the controller (same epoch, worker-only crash) is still running the first request is answered `effect_busy`; a model may then make a new call. Waiting for the running one would be better. (Fixed by the second review below.)
  - With `admitCall` off, `tool.invoke` and `job.start` presented again under a different number are new calls (no ledger).
  - The tests ran on Linux only.
- **Merged** `card-g04-s1` 36035bf5 (its second review: the child reports the boundary it dies at, and the model told "pushed" needs a confirmed effect); `g04-evidence.md` keeps both the fix's replay setting and the label check.
- **Verified** (Linux, Node 22, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, after the merge and a build): G04 tool files on SQLite, the SQLite worker thread (`NIMBLENEWT_G04_HEAVY=1`) and PostgreSQL 6 of 6, every kill on its numbered boundary under both flipped tests; the pi-adapter suite 270 of 270; controller `generation` 222 of 222; `toolbridge/service` and `api/start-l05d` 200 of 200. Not rerun: effects, reconcile and the dispatch shards (no change of this review touches them).

Second review of the follow-up (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19):
- **Fixed: a call presented again while its first request was still running was answered "busy".** After a worker-only crash the controller keeps running the first request, and Pi presents the call again at once; the ledger then refuses it as `effect_busy`, and a model told that may make the call again under a new call ID, which is a new effect and a second write (`message.send`, `job.start`, `tool.invoke` and the other admitted writes). `ToolExecutionService#admitted` now waits for the running request (steps of 200 ms, at most 30 s) and then answers from the ledger like any repeat; nothing is run by the wait. Any other refusal is not waited on. If the wait runs out, the model is told the call is still being run, is not run again, and must not be made again under a new call ID. Test: `toolbridge/service.test.ts` (busy twice, then answered from the ledger, the operation never run; a `fenced` refusal asked once); it caught the mutation on the built file.
- **Fixed: the kill sweep did not exercise the epoch rule.** The slice harness gives effect claims a lease of 1 ms, and the restart advances the clock 10 minutes, so the killed process's claim had always expired; removing the epoch rule from the built `effects.js` passed the whole sweep. The G04 tool scenario now uses a lease of one hour (`TOOL_EFFECT_LEASE_MS`, new optional `SliceWorld.effectLeaseMs`; other slices keep 1 ms). With the rule removed, both SQLite tests now fail at "after effect.claim" (left open).
- **Added:** a reconciler test (`domain/reconcile.test.ts`, four backends): while the attempt holds the task nothing is closed; after it loses the task a never-started `bridge` effect is closed as failed and a started one with a vanished executor becomes uncertain with exactly one blocker, nothing is run, and effects of another kind with no bridge stay `intended` (the started one only counted). Before, switching the closing to every kind passed all controller tests. It caught that mutation and the removal of the blocker on closing.
- **Checked and kept:**
  - The 16 kill points are real SIGKILLs of the child at the numbered boundary (the child writes the label to stderr first and the parent compares it); all 16 end like the uncrashed run on SQLite, the SQLite worker thread and PostgreSQL with the long lease.
  - Epoch failover with an old executor still running: the store refuses the old controller's writes (`stale_epoch`), and the new primary treats its claim as a vanished executor: a target that cannot be asked and has no key becomes uncertain (never run again); `tool.invoke` and `job.start` run again only with the same key (their dispatcher record or job), and an `otherCall` turns that off. The claim epoch lives in the effect's JSON body, so there is no schema change and no migration; old claims without an epoch keep the lease rule; SQLite and PostgreSQL both return the epoch as a number.
  - Parallel calls in one reply: each is its own effect; the calls with a result stay answered, the open ones keep their numbers. A provider reusing IDs across replies and missing or non-string IDs: non-string IDs are skipped by `openToolCalls` and the transcript alike, so the numbering stays consistent; an inexact number is safe through `otherCall`, or ends in a refused call, never a second run.
  - Mutations caught on the built files (each restored byte-identical): the `kept` numbering ignored (bridge, restore and process tests, 3 fail); `closeUnbridged` closing an effect whose claim was given back, or while the attempt holds the task (`effects.test`).
- **Leftovers (not fixed):**

The result is a false alarm for the owner, never a second run.
  - When the 30 s wait runs out, the model still does not learn the outcome of the first request.
  - An open personal-tool call with a reused provider ID leaves a kept number that the model's next bridge call with that ID takes; that call is found as the newest call and answered correctly, so only the numbering shifts.
  - The tests ran on Linux only.

Not rerun: the whole pi-adapter suite (no change there; its bridge, restore and process files ran in the mutation check) and the dispatch shards.

## Q03 (first slice): documentation obligations verified against tested code; a behaviour change or a release flags them and opens assigned update tasks (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19)

Card status is NOT changed. Blockers: C02 is implemented; Q02 (QA evidence) has its first slice on main, which is what this slice builds on (the QA gate of a code submission). This slice builds the obligation records, their verification and the impact and release checks; the rest of Q03 is listed below as not done.

- **What is built.** `DocObligationService` (`submissions/doc-obligations.ts`), wired in `api/start.ts`, reached through six state API operations (`doc.obligation.record`, `doc.obligation.verify`, `doc.impact.check`, `doc.release.check`, `doc.obligation.list`, `doc.obligation.get`; `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` regenerated). No agent bridge tool was added (the tool-schema budget is nearly used): a docs agent reaches the operations through the state API like the Q02 and Q04 ones.
  - **An obligation** (`doc-obligation`, `dob-` ID, index `doc-obligation-index` per project, at most 500 per project) records: the document's title and where it lives, who it is for (`user`, `developer`, `support` or `promotional`), its owner (the agent answerable for keeping it current, which must be an active agent), the version it applies to, the implementing tasks whose behaviour it describes (1 to 20, all of the project), any capabilities it claims (each naming one of those tasks), its validation state (`unverified`, `verified`, `stale`) and why, what it was last verified against, and its update tasks. Replacing it (`obligationId` + `expectedRevision`) with other tasks, claims or version makes it `unverified` again; a new title, place or owner keeps its state.
  - **No unsupported claims.** A claim that names no implementing task of the document is refused when recorded. Verification needs, for every implementing task, a code submission of that task whose QA gate (Q02 `qa.evidence.gate`) passes now; if one does not pass, nothing is verified and the refusal names the claims that would be unsupported.
  - **Linked to the tested artifact.** `verify` binds the docs role's `document` submission (card Q01b: only the docs role submits that kind; its artifact digest is kept) to, per task, the code submission and tree that passed. Only the owner or the document's own owner verifies. Verifying settles the document's open update tasks (marked settled on the record; the tasks themselves are ordinary tasks the agent finishes).
  - **Impact check.** `doc.impact.check` takes a task and its new tested code (the named code submission, or the newest one with independent QA evidence). Every document of the project describing the task becomes `stale` when it was verified against another tree of the task (`behavior_changed`) or its evidence for the task no longer passes QA (`evidence_lost`); each such document and each unverified one gets an update task: created, made ready and assigned to the document's owner, its text naming the tested code submission and tree, the claims, and how to finish (submit the document change, then verify). The task IDs are derived from the document and the reason, so asking again (or a crash between the record and the task) repeats nothing and opens any task not yet opened. An assignment that cannot be made (a retired owner) leaves the task ready and unassigned; the result says `assigned: false` and the view says "not assigned".
  - **Release.** `doc.release.check` with a version flags every document of the project that applies to another version (user and developer documentation, support guidance and promotional assets alike; counted per audience in the result), each with an assigned update task; a verification must then name that version.
  - **Who.** Reading: the owner or an agent that may read the project's tasks. Recording, impact and release: the owner, or such an agent holding the docs or director role in the project (the role alone opens nothing). Task credentials may read and verify, not record or run the checks.
  - **Owner chat.** Status kind `docs` (the project in focus) lists every document, flagged ones (stale, then unverified) first, with what it was verified against, why it is flagged, its claims and its open update tasks (assigned or not). Chat operations `doc.obligation.record`, `doc.obligation.verify`, `doc.impact.check` (task by title) and `doc.release.check`, all shown first (each hands work to an agent or names records the interpreter picked); a replacement or verification is pinned to the obligation's revision. Titles, places, versions and claims must be the owner's own words; record IDs, the agent, the tasks and the audience come from the views (`DOC_EXEMPT`). The interpreter prompt describes all of it in free words.
- **Tests.** Affected suites run here: chat, status and submissions in full plus the api, chat-gaps, start-commands, start-defects, start-qa-evidence, start-acceptance, start-docs, guide-commands, web, desk-reads and retirement files (97 files, 1907 tests; the one failure was the status.ask summary missing `docs`, fixed and re-run: api.test 58 of 58), `scripts` d02-docs, roadmap and plan tests 41 of 41, `roadmap:check` and `check:deps` ok. New: `submissions/doc-obligations.test.ts` on all four storage backends (reference, SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread, PostgreSQL); `api/start-docs.test.ts` through the running controller, a real docs-role document submission, real QA evidence and the owner's chat (impact and release proposed and applied, the `docs` view, a record by chat refused when the version is not the owner's word). Mutation checks: verifying without the QA gate check, and an impact check that ignores a changed tree, each failed the tests; restored.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the impact and release checks run when someone asks (the owner by chat, or a docs or director agent), like Q02's `qa.evidence.check`; nothing calls them on a new code submission or a release candidate yet. Reversible: a later slice can call `impact` when QA evidence is recorded and `release` from `release.submit`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** "the version a document applies to" is the project's own version text (for example `1.0`); a release flags every document whose version text differs, exact match. Reversible: a version scheme can be added later.
- **ASSUMPTION:** an update task is an ordinary task of the project, created by the caller of the check and assigned to the document's owner; an assignment that cannot be made leaves it unassigned and visible rather than failing the check.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a document submission of any task of the same project may carry the change (the docs agent often works in its update task); the verifier is the owner or the document's own owner.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a repeated impact or release check with the same command ID answers `replayed: true` with nothing flagged (changed by the second review; with other arguments it is `command_conflict`); the update tasks still open are opened if they were not.
- **NOT done (rest of Q03):** automatic impact on every behaviour change (a code submission, a landing or QA evidence) and automatic release flags from the release service; support guidance and promotional assets as their own record kinds (here they are obligations with an audience); a check of the document's actual text against its claims (the claims are what the recorder lists; nothing reads the document); unverified or stale documents gating a release or a task's `done`; the owner told by a notice when documents go stale (the view and the assigned tasks show it); the docs view per task, and the X03/D01 user guide linking to it (D01's "not done" list waits for this); taking an obligation away (retiring a document); bridge tools for the docs agent (the tool-schema budget, see above).

Review (first Opus 5.5 reviewer, 2026-11-19), fixed with tests (`submissions/doc-obligations.test.ts` on all four backends; mutation checks on the built file, each alone and restored byte-identical: the owner's read right, the verify gate, the newest-tree binding, untested code flagging, settled reasons counted as known, the one-open-task-per-subject rule, the keeper role, the verifier, the read right and the document submission's project each failed the test):
- **A document could be verified against the old code it was flagged away from.** After `doc.impact.check` flagged a document for a task's new tested code, `verify` accepted any passing code of the task, so the older submission it had been checked against cleared the flag without the change being looked at. A document flagged for a task now verifies only against the tree of the newest flag of that task (`reasons` are kept on unverified documents too for this, and the `docs` view shows them).
- **Going back to earlier code did not flag a document.** Reasons were de-duplicated against every update the document ever had, settled ones included, so code the document was flagged for in an earlier, settled round (a revert) flagged nothing. Now only reasons noted since the last verification or record, and open update tasks, count; update task IDs come from a per-document count (`seq`, `updateCount`) instead of the reason, so the new round gets a new task.
- **Untested code flagged documents.** A named code submission whose QA gate fails made documents stale with an update task saying "its tested code is now" that submission. Such code now flags nothing as changed (a document's own lost evidence is still found); the result says `verdict`.
- **Duplicate update tasks.** Every further change of a task (or a second release) gave the same document another open update task for the same keeper, and once 20 updates had ever been made the whole check was refused for every document of the project. Now one update task is open per subject (an implementing task, or the release); a further reason is noted on the record (and binds the verification, above). Settled updates beyond 20 are dropped oldest first; the check never refuses on the limit.
- **A keeper outside the project.** The owner of a document could be any active agent, so an agent of another project would be assigned this project's update tasks. The owner must now be an agent that may read the project's tasks (its effective grants at recording).
- Tests added: a document submission of another project refused; two release checks at once (PostgreSQL included) make one update task per document.
- Leftovers (not fixed): the QA gates `verify` reads are not bound into its write (only the document submission's revision is), so QA evidence invalidated between the read and the write is not caught; a repeated impact or release check with the same command ID but other arguments is not refused when nothing new is found (no command is written); a task credential may verify a document of its project naming code of other tasks, as far as the QA gate lets it read them; the update task's title and text carry the document's title and place unredacted (the claims are redacted).

Second review (clean-context Opus 5.5 reviewer, 2026-11-19), fixed with tests (a second test in `submissions/doc-obligations.test.ts` on all four backends, with a moving clock; `api/start-docs.test.ts` now submits the updated document before verifying a flagged one; mutation checks on the built file, each alone and restored byte-identical: the flag-time rule, keeping reasons and the release flag on a replacement, the title and the location redaction, finishing a half-opened update task and the command-ID check with nothing to write each failed the new test):
- **Re-recording a flagged document cleared its flags.** A replacement with other tasks, claims or version dropped `reasons` and `releaseVersion`, so a docs agent could re-record the document and then verify it against the old code and the old version. A replacement now keeps the reasons on tasks it still describes, the release flag and the flag time.
- **A document change made before the flag answered it.** `verify` accepted any document submission of the project, also the one the document was verified with before it went out of date. A flag now records `flaggedAt`; a flagged document is verified only with a document submission made no earlier (the stored record's creation time).
- **Same command ID, other arguments.** `doc.impact.check` and `doc.release.check` went through the command runner only when something was new, so a reused command ID with other arguments was answered as nothing new; and a repeat of a written check answered `replayed: false`. The runner is now always asked: a reused ID with other arguments is `command_conflict`, the same command is `replayed: true`, and "nothing new" (also a concurrent check that wrote first) finishes the open update tasks instead of answering `stale_revision`.
- **A half-opened update task stayed half-opened.** The repeat only opened update tasks that did not exist; one created but not made ready, or ready without an assignment (a failure between the steps), was never finished. It is now.
- **Title and place unredacted.** The document's title and location are now redacted when recorded (as the claims and the Q04 deliverable titles are), so the update task's text, the `docs` view and every read carry no secret-shaped text.
- Leftovers (judged, not fixed): the QA gate reads in `verify` are still not bound into its write (binding needs the gate to name the records it read; a QA change between the read and the write is caught by the next impact check); a task credential of the document's owner may verify naming other tasks' code (the same agent may do so with its own credential; the QA gate's read rule still applies); within one open flag round, going back to the tree the document was verified against does not lift the newest-flag rule, so it must be verified against the newest flagged tree while that still passes; an unflagged document may be verified against older passing code while newer tested code exists, until an impact check flags it; two concurrent checks touching the same document can still answer one caller `stale_revision` (ask again); a replacement that changes the keeper leaves the open update tasks assigned to the old one; owner chat cannot yet verify a document in practice, because no chat view lists document submissions (the docs agent verifies through the state API; a later slice can list a flagged document's newer document submissions in the `docs` view).

Re-check of the second review's late commits (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19, exactly `b6e83159..66783f09`):
- Checked and right: the flag time and a submission's creation time come from the same runner clock in the same fixed `…T..:..:..mmmZ` form (the storage rejects any other), so comparing the text compares the times; a tie counts as made since the flag. Re-recording never moves `flaggedAt`, and only a check that notes a new reason moves it, so a flagged document can always be verified by submitting the document again (no endless loop), and a document change made before the flag is refused. Authority and project checks are unchanged (they run before the command). The command runner now always sees the check, so a reused command ID with other arguments is `command_conflict` and the exact repeat is `replayed: true` on all four backends.
- Test added: the half-opened update task that was made ready but never assigned (the assignment step stops) is finished by the exact repeat of the release check, which is a replay. Mutation checks on the built file, each alone and restored byte-identical: removing the title or the location redaction, keeping reasons, keeping the release flag, keeping the flag time on a replacement, the flag-time check, setting the flag time, "nothing new" answered `stale_revision`, skipping the runner when nothing is new, finishing a proposed task and finishing a ready task with no assignment each failed `submissions/doc-obligations.test.ts` (the flag-time check and setting it also failed `api/start-docs.test.ts`). Before this test, finishing a ready task with no assignment was not covered.
- Leftover (not fixed): a replacement that changes only the claims of a verified (not flagged) document makes it `unverified`, and the document change it was verified with still verifies it (there is no flag time); the claims are what the recorder lists, so this matches the "nothing reads the document" limit above.
- **Follow-up card line (proposed, not yet in the plan): "Q03b: the owner's chat can verify a document".** The `docs` view lists, for each flagged document, the newest document submissions of its project made since the flag (IDs shown as other views show them, only those the viewer may read), and the interpreter prompt passes `documentSubmissionId` to `doc.obligation.verify` only when it was shown. Not done here: submissions have no index by project or time (they sit in one table in hash order), so finding the newest needs a bounded scan of every submission or a new index, which is more than a few lines; until then the docs agent verifies through the state API.

Re-check of 503d961f (the busy wait's settings; clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19):
- **Checked:** with no `busyWait` the wait is as before (200 ms steps, refused once 30 s are reached); no construction passes it (`startController`'s `tools` option is a `Pick` without it). The wait runs nothing and waits only on `effect_busy` before anything ran.
- **Fixed (bounded for every setting):** a limit of `Infinity` waited for ever; a step under 1 ms (a timer waits at least 1 ms, so the counted time fell far behind the real one) could wait for hours or for ever; a step of `Infinity` or over 2147483647 reached `setTimeout`, which waits 1 ms and warns. Such settings now end the wait at once; the service test covers all three (one ask each, refused as busy).

## Q03b: the owner's chat can verify a document (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19)

Follow-up of Q03's first slice (its re-check left this over: no chat view listed document submissions, so the interpreter had nothing to pass to `doc.obligation.verify`). Card status is NOT changed.

- **What is built.**
  - **An index of each project's newest document changes.** Submissions sit in one table in hash order, so "the newest document changes of a project" could not be read without scanning everything. Each `document` submission is now added, in the same write, to its project's index (record kind `document-submission-index`, keyed by the project, IDs and tasks only, newest last, at most 100 kept; older ones drop off the front, the records themselves stay). Two document changes of one project at the same moment: the one that loses the index write is built again from the index as it now is (the same retry a review's verdict list uses).
  - **A read path: `submission.documents`** (state API query; `SubmissionService.documents`): the newest document changes of a project, newest first, with each record's `createdAt` (the time `doc.obligation.verify` compares with a flag), `since` (only those recorded no earlier), `limit` 1 to 50 and a sealed `after` cursor bound to the caller and the project. Each item is filtered exactly as `submission.get` is (owner: all; an agent: those of tasks it may read, with a task credential only that task, that it made or was asked to review); a project the caller may not read at all is `not_found`. No bridge tool was added.
  - **The `docs` view** ends each flagged document's line with "To verify:": the newest document changes of the project made since the flag (at most 3, saying how many when more), each with its task, who made it, when and its digest, only those the viewer may read; or that there is none yet and the keeper must submit the updated document first; then per task the code to check against (the newest code it was flagged for, else the code it was last verified with unless that lost its QA gate; otherwise "see the qa view"), and the release version when a release flagged it.
  - **Free-form chat:** "verify the user guide" is `doc.obligation.verify` with only the obligation (the interpreter picks it from the docs view by title or place). The chat fills the rest from the same records and shows it first: exactly one document change since the flag is filled in (the preview says which and why); several: the owner is asked which (the newest 3 as choices; the answer carries the proposal on); none: the owner is told the keeper must submit the updated document first, and nothing is proposed. A document change the interpreter names must be one the view lists or one the owner wrote out; otherwise it is refused before anything is shown. Evidence left out is filled from the record (as above) or the owner is asked which tested code; the release version is filled from the release flag. An already verified, unflagged document is answered "nothing to verify". The interpreter prompt, the chat command's description, the status kind's description and the `doc.obligation.verify` summary say all this; `docs/nimblenewt/api-v1.md` regenerated.
- **Tests.** New `submissions/submissions-documents.test.ts` on all four storage backends (reference, SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread, PostgreSQL) with a moving clock: newest first, another project left out, `since` (a tie counts), paging and the cursor bound to caller and project, the read rule (own changes, an assigned reviewer, no right = not found, task credentials), a repeated command indexed once, the bound (oldest drops off), two changes at the same moment both indexed; plus the pure code-suggestion rule. New `api/start-docs-verify.test.ts` through the running controller and the owner's chat: verified (nothing to verify), flagged by chat, none since the flag (view and chat say so; an unlisted ID refused), one (proposed, preview shows the change and code, applied, verified), a release and two changes (the chat asks, the owner's answer carries it on with version 2.0 filled in, applied), and `submission.documents` through the state API. Mutation checks on the built files, each alone and restored: not writing the index, dropping the read rule, dropping `since`, dropping the race retry (fails on SQLite, the worker and PostgreSQL), picking the first of several instead of asking, accepting an unlisted ID, and the view not passing the flag time each failed a new test.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a per-project index written with each document submission, not a bounded scan of every submission: a scan in hash order cannot say which are newest without reading the whole table, and document changes are few, so one small record per project written with them is cheap. Reversible: the index is an ordinary record.
- **ASSUMPTION:** document submissions made before this change are not in the index (there is no back-fill); the docs agent submits the document again, which a flagged document needs anyway (only a change made since the flag verifies it). Nothing is launched yet, so no real data is affected.
- **ASSUMPTION:** for a document never flagged (unverified since it was recorded) every listed document change is offered, not only those made since it was recorded, because the service accepts any; with several, the owner is asked.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the code filled in for the evidence comes from the document's own record (flagged code, else last verified code); the QA gate is still checked when the verification is applied, and the owner can name other tested code (from the qa view) in their words.
- **NOT done:** document changes older than the newest 100 of a project are not listed (the records stay and the state API's `submission.get` reads them); the chat does not resolve a document by title in code (the interpreter picks the obligation from the docs view, as for Q03's other commands); evidence the interpreter names is checked by the service (QA gate, task), not against what the view showed; everything Q03's own "NOT done" list names.

Review (first Opus 5.5 reviewer, 2026-11-19), on `58b7675d`:
- Checked and right: the index entry is a change of the same `submission.record` command (one `commitOperation`, as the H12o verdict list), so on every backend the submission and its index entry are written together or not at all; a lost index write is rebuilt from the index as it now is (the `VerdictRace` retry, at most 5 tries, then `unavailable`); a repeated command is answered from the stored operation and touches no index; the index is trimmed from the front (oldest), keeps write order (a loser of the index write is rebuilt with a later record time, so write order and record time agree), and is at most 100 small entries. Every listed item is read back and filtered at read time with `get`'s rule (owner; an agent: tasks it may read, a task credential only its task, own or assigned for review); a project the caller may not read is `not_found`; old data without an index lists nothing (the documented assumption). The cursor is sealed with the caller and `project:<id>` (task cursors carry a task ID, so the two cannot be mixed), and `limit` is checked in the operation and the service.
- Fixed: the `docs` view read the project's document changes once per flagged document (up to 30, each read may go through the whole index of 100); a release flags many documents at the same flag time, so the view now reads once per flag time and reuses it.
- Tests added: `api/start-docs-verify.test.ts` covers a verified document re-checked with a named document change (an ID the view does not list is refused unless the owner wrote it out; written out, it is proposed with the code filled in); `submissions/submissions-documents.test.ts` now writes three document changes at the same moment past the bound and checks the newest three plus the one before them are kept in order.
- Mutation checks on the built files, each alone and restored byte-identical (scratch `q03b-review`): no index write, keeping the oldest instead of the newest, dropping the project read check, dropping `since`, dropping the document race retry (each failed `submissions-documents.test` on all four backends), and refusing an ID the owner wrote out (failed `start-docs-verify.test`).
- Run here (sandbox required): chat, status and submissions suites in full plus `api.test`, `start-docs`, `start-docs-verify` (1826 of 1826); `check:deps`, `roadmap:check` ok; `api:docs:write` leaves `api-v1.md` unchanged.
- Leftovers (not fixed): a cursor whose entry has since dropped off the index answers an empty page, not a refusal; `next` is offered while index entries remain even when none of them is readable by the caller; a choice the chat offered that drops out of the newest three before the owner answers is refused (ask again); a crash between the submission and its index entry cannot happen by construction (one write), so no test simulates one.

Second review (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19), on `c061de2f`:
- Checked and right: the read rule of `submission.documents` is `get`'s, applied per item at read time (owner all; agent: readable task, task credential only its task, own or assigned for review, reviewer role still held); a project that does not exist and one the caller may not read give the same `not_found`; the cursor is sealed with caller and `project:<id>` and is checked before anything is read; items carry no title or location of anything unreadable. A repeated `submission.record` is answered from the stored operation before the index is read; a duplicate sent at the same moment meets its own submission (`command_conflict`, then answered from the record). The index's write order agrees with record time (each winner reads the index after the previous winner committed, so its clock is later). `since` compares fixed-form ISO times from the controller's one clock, as `flaggedAt` is; checked on PostgreSQL too. Old submissions without an index entry: the docs agent's path (`doc.obligation.verify` with an ID through the state API) does not use the index, and the docs view and chat tell the owner the keeper must submit the document first, so neither dead-ends.
- Fixed (real regression): the index made every document change of a project write one shared record, so changes of DIFFERENT tasks at the same moment now met, and the lost ones were rebuilt only 5 times with no wait: 20 at once failed 11 to 15 of 20 with `unavailable` on every backend (before the index all would succeed). A lost index write (`DocIndexRace`) is now rebuilt up to 40 times after a short random wait (up to 50 ms); review races keep their 5. 20 at once all succeed on all four backends (repeated five times).
- Fixed (first review's leftovers): a cursor whose place dropped out of the index is refused (`invalid_command`, "the listing moved on ... list again without after") instead of an empty page; `next` is offered only when another item the caller may read (and recorded since `since`) follows, found by reading one past the page. The operation's summary says both; `api-v1.md` regenerated.
- Tests added: `submissions-documents.test` (no `next` when the rest is unreadable or older than `since`; a cursor pushed out of the index refused; a burst of 20 document changes all recorded and the newest kept); `start-docs-verify.test` (an answer naming a document change that was not offered is refused and proposes nothing).
- Mutation checks on the built files, each alone and restored byte-identical (scratch `q03b-second-review`): the old 5 tries for a document race (failed on two backends), the old empty page for a dropped cursor, the old `next` whenever index entries remain (each failed `submissions-documents.test`); the chat taking the first of several, the docs view not passing the flag time, the chat accepting an ID only the interpreter named (each failed `start-docs-verify.test`). Removing the random wait alone did not fail a test (40 immediate rebuilds also clear 20 at once); the wait is kept to spread retries under load.
- Run here (sandbox required): chat, status and submissions suites in full plus `api.test`, `start-docs`, `start-docs-verify` (1826 of 1826); `check:deps`, `roadmap:check` ok; `api:docs:write` leaves `api-v1.md` unchanged after the regeneration committed here.
- Leftovers (not fixed): the index is still one record per project, so a very large burst (well beyond 40 simultaneous document changes of one project) could still answer `unavailable` (send again; idempotent); sharding the index would need a merge by time at read and is not worth it at current scale. A choice offered by the chat that drops out of the newest three before the owner answers is refused (ask again), as the first review noted.

## CI fix 4: a Windows landing-check test, two flakes (compaction race order, macOS link replacement) and the Windows probe's time limit (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19)

Branch `card-ci-fix4` off origin/main `43e92085`. Four problems found by a read-only diagnosis of the latest CI runs.

Done:
- **Windows landing-check test (failed every time on the hosted Windows runner).** `worker/workspace/landing-checks.test.ts` compared the sandbox work folder with `realpathSync(base)`, which on Windows keeps the short 8.3 name of the temporary folder (`RUNNER~1`), while the program (`landing-checks.ts`) uses `fs/promises` `realpath`, which expands it. The test now uses `realpathSync.native(base)`, as `windows-host-real.test.ts` does. The program was already right: the check folder is named by its full, long path, which is what the Windows sandbox launcher accepts (it refuses short names), so no code change.
- **Flake: "a compaction that loses the race for the chain is closed as superseded"** (`controller/context/enforcement.test.ts`). The test released whichever summariser had reached its gate first and assumed that was compaction a. The gates are now kept by route, the test waits until both are present, then releases a first and b second, so the order no longer depends on timing. Checked by starting b before a in the built test: it still passes. The other tests with a list of gates (dispatcher restarts, tool bridge T02d, reviewer model) release one gate at a time or all at once and do not depend on which call arrived first, so they were left as they are.
- **Flake with a small code fix: a link read while another writer replaces it** (`worker/environment/agent-environments.ts`, `active()`). A new `active`/`previous` link is made beside the old one and renamed over it. On macOS a `readlink` that met that replacement once answered EINVAL ("not a link"). `active()` now asks again up to five more times (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ms apart) on EINVAL only; a path that is still not a link after that is reported as `corrupt` ("the active link of ... is not a link") instead of a raw EINVAL. Other errors pass through at once, and a missing link still means "none activated". The link reader can be injected through the existing `FileIo` option (`readlink`, optional; the real one by default). Tests (`environment/runtime.test.ts`): three refused reads then the answer (four reads); refused forever gives `corrupt` after six reads; a real plain file where the link should be gives `corrupt`; EACCES is not retried; no link answers undefined. Mutation checks on the built file, each restored byte-identical: no retries (test fails); a raw error after the retries instead of `corrupt` (test fails).
- **Windows probe time limit** (`.github/workflows/own-hardware.yml`). The probe job (one run of the whole suite on each own machine) had 60 minutes; the Windows runner needs about twice the Mac's 21 minutes and one run was cancelled at 60. It now has 150. The `sandbox-windows` job keeps its 420. `scripts/evidence-workflows.test.mjs` pins both values; the file parses with PyYAML.
- **ASSUMPTION:** the probe job is one matrix job for both machines, so the Mac also gets 150 minutes; it finishes in about 21, so the larger limit only matters if it hangs. A per-machine limit by expression was not used, to keep the workflow simple and checkable without running it.
- **ASSUMPTION:** ENOENT is not retried: `rename` replaces the link in one step, so a missing link is a real state (never activated, or removed by `restore`), not a passing one.
- Run here (sandbox required, after a forced build): worker `environment/*` and `workspace/landing-checks` (69 of 69), controller `context/enforcement` on all four backends including PostgreSQL (172 of 172), `scripts/*.test.mjs` (237 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed).

Not done:
- The Windows-only test and the macOS flake could not be run on those systems here (Linux only); they are checked by the next CI round.

## Windows probe 44479324035: the meeting record tests split by backend, and the crash-loop supervisor test keeps its own error (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **`meetings/record.test.ts` split by backend.** On the own-hardware Windows probe the file (65 tests on each of the four backends and 4 tests of the appliers, 264 in all) was cancelled at the 900 s per-file limit with 898 s of finished work (about 200 s reference store, 250 s SQLite, 285 s the worker thread, PostgreSQL 36 of 65 done in 166 s). The suites are now `meetings/record-suite.ts` (`defineRecordTests(backendName)`, the same pattern as `dispatcher-suite.ts`, `history-suite.ts` and `stop-suite.ts`; the body is moved unchanged, not re-indented) and four files: `record.test.ts` (reference store and the four applier tests), `record.sqlite.test.ts`, `record.worker.test.ts`, `record.postgres.test.ts`. Each part is about a quarter of the old file, so about 300 s at most on that machine. The global timeout is unchanged. The test names were compared before and after (the old file built from origin/main and run beside the new ones): the same 264 names, all passing. `scripts/test-weights.json` gives the four files the old file's 96 s divided by their measured shares.
- **`release/supervisor.test.ts` crash-loop case.** It failed after 120.4 s with EBUSY from `rmSync` in `world()`'s cleanup. Node 22's `rmSync` does not retry a folder whose first removal fails with EBUSY (its JavaScript rimraf throws that at once, whatever `maxRetries` says; Node 24's native `rmSync` may differ), so a release folder still held by a child killed a moment earlier ended the test with that error. That error took the place of the real one, most likely the 120 s wait for the crash-loop exit. `world()` now keeps the body's error: it waits (bounded, 15 s) for the supervisors it started to end, kills what is left, and removes the folder with its own retries on EBUSY, EPERM, EACCES and ENOTEMPTY (a growing pause, about 15 s in all). A cleanup that still fails is thrown only when the body passed; after a failed body it is printed and the body's error is the one reported. Only `.pids` and `.gpids` files are read for processes to kill, and a failure to read them after a failed body is printed too. Second review: these two points added; a recorded PID that has already exited may in principle have been reused by another process by the time it is killed (as before this change), which this test does not guard against.
- **ASSUMPTION:** why the case ran more than 120 s on Windows (about 12 s on macOS and Linux, and the similar single-hang test took 7.8 s on the same Windows run) is not known: the error that would have shown the events was lost. One possible cause is a lost confirmation (the fake controller ignored a failing `launcher.confirm`, and the startup watchdog runs on the test's fake clock, so an unconfirmed start would wait forever). That is not shown, so nothing in the supervisor was changed. The two crash-loop waits get 240 s on win32 only (120 s elsewhere), the fake controller writes a failed confirmation to `<id>.confirm-errors`, and a `waitFor` timeout now names the wait, the events, the supervisor's last 40 log lines and any failed confirmations. The next Windows run shows which one it is.
- Run here (Linux, sandbox required, after `npx tsc --build --force`): the four record files (264 of 264, 71 s together), the old record file from origin/main (264 of 264, 232 s alone), `release/supervisor.test.ts` (16 of 16).

Not done:
- Neither change could be run on Windows here; the next own-hardware probe checks both.

## Own-hardware run 44501483353: a Windows progress-count flake, a missing not-applicable reason, and the Windows Sandbox access-denied start explained (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **`controller/dispatch/relay.test.ts` (V01b, the monitor's progress reports).** The fixed bound "1 to 3 reports" failed on Windows with 4: timers there are about 15.6 ms, so the 15 ms gaps between chunks became 20 ms or more and every chunk earned a report. The bound now comes from the measured stream time: each report needs a full interval since the first bytes or the previous report, all inside the span the test measures with the same clock, so at most `floor(span / interval)` can be told (exact with integer `Date.now()` values). The stream is eight chunks plus the counts at a 40 ms interval, so an unthrottled relay (eight reports in about 135 ms, bound 3) still fails, and at least one report must arrive.
- **`scripts/y02-scenarios.json`.** The win32 not-applicable list of `sandbox-resource-limits` lacked "needs a shell and ps" (`worker/sandbox/resource-watch.test.ts`, the real ps sampler test), so that Windows-only skip failed the scenario three times. Added. The map digest is computed from the file at run time (no pinned value to refresh). `y02-checkpoint.test.mjs` now reads every `process.platform === "win32" ... t.skip("...")` reason in `resource-watch.test.ts` and requires each to be named for win32, so the next such skip is caught on Linux.
- **Windows Sandbox start refused with E_ACCESSDENIED.** The confinement probe's `wsb start` answered exit 2147942405 "Access is denied. (0x80070005 (E_ACCESSDENIED))" while the console user was the configured owner: the runner was not in that user's interactive session (a runner installed as a service runs in session 0). The session probe (`windows-real.ts`) now also records two facts about the process asking (its PowerShell child shares its session and account): `processInConsoleSession` (its session id equals `WTSGetActiveConsoleSessionId`) and `processIsConsoleUser` (its SID equals the console user's, by `NTAccount.Translate`; when that cannot resolve, only the exact full name, case aside, counts). Parsing is the pure `sessionFromProbe`; a fact it cannot determine is left out. `verifySession` (both modes, after the existing owner check, which is unchanged) refuses when either fact is false or unknown, with "start the runner interactively with run.cmd as the console user (not as a service)" (`INTERACTIVE_RUNNER_HINT`), so health and every job start refuse before anything is started. A `wsb start` that still answers access denied (exit 2147942405, its signed form -2147024891, or 0x80070005 / E_ACCESSDENIED in its text) is reported with the same sentence (`isWsbAccessDenied`); the 0x8000401A explanation is unchanged and checked first. The real-sandbox summary's facts gain "runner in the active console session" and "runner is the console user". `own-hardware-runners.md` says the Windows Sandbox job needs the runner started interactively with `run.cmd` by the console user, not as a service or over remote desktop.
- **ASSUMPTION:** a runner in a remote desktop session (not the console session) is refused too, as the task asked for the active console session; whether Windows Sandbox itself would start from there was not tested.

### First review of own-hardware run 44501483353 fixes (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **The session facts no longer refuse.** `verifySession` refused health and every job start unless this process was in the active console session as the console user. That contradicts `windows-unattended-findings.md`: Windows Sandbox started from SYSTEM in session 0 while the owner was signed in (minimal and mapped-folder configurations), and 0x80070005 came there from a mapped output folder's permissions, not from the session. The design keeps a background supervisor while an owner session exists, and the auto-login and lock mode is meant for one, so the refusal would have turned away a set-up that worked. The facts are now explanation only: an access-denied `wsb start` is reported with them, read again at that moment (`describeWsbAccessDenied`): unless both are yes, the run.cmd hint and then the shared-folder cause; when both are yes, the shared-folder cause alone. The probe, `sessionFromProbe`, the summary facts and the existing owner, nobody-signed-in and lock checks are unchanged. The run's diagnosis (a runner installed as a service) is described as likely, not established, in `own-hardware-runners.md`.
- **ASSUMPTION:** explanation rather than refusal is the smaller, reversible choice; if a Windows run shows that a service start always fails with 0x80070005 even with usable shared folders, a refusal can be added then, with that evidence.
- Checked without change: the relay bound (the relay compares integer `Date.now()` values with `>=`, so k reports need k full intervals after the first bytes, all inside the span measured with the same clock; eight chunks each at least 15 ms apart guarantee one report at 40 ms; an unthrottled relay gives eight against a bound of three here, and even with 31 ms Windows timer gaps eight against seven); the y02-checkpoint parsing (reads the real test file, every current single-line Windows skip, including "needs ps and two cores", is found; dropping a reason from the map fails it).


### Second review of own-hardware run 44501483353 fixes (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **What the run's artifacts show about the access denied.** The runner ran under the owner's own account (the checkout step used the owner's profile as home), the share account and the owner were both the console user (nothing configured), the base folder was a fresh `C:\ProgramData\nn-wsb-real-*` made by that account, and every per-job `icacls /save`, `/grant` and `/deny` before `wsb start` succeeded. Nothing there shows a grant to the wrong account or a folder outside what the sandbox could read: the research's fix (an explicit Modify grant for the signed-in owner on each mapped folder under ProgramData) is what the code already does. The detail could not settle it: it kept only the last 12 host calls, which cut off the first grants, and named each call by its first two arguments, so neither the account a grant named nor the `.wsb` configuration was recorded. The earlier entries' "a runner installed as a service" is therefore not supported; `own-hardware-runners.md` and the code comments now say the cause was not established.
- **Differences from the research that remain open (not tested, no change made):** the configuration sets `<ProtectedClient>Enable</ProtectedClient>`, which Microsoft describes as running Windows Sandbox inside AppContainer isolation, while the mapped folders are granted only to the share account (whether the research configuration used it is not recorded); the protected `.git` is mapped again, read-only, inside the writable checkout with a deny entry for the share account, which the research configuration did not have; and the runner here was the owner's account, not SYSTEM as in the research. Protected-client mode and the `.git` deny stay as they are (removing either would loosen confinement without evidence).
- **Change: the next failure carries what decides it.** After an access-denied `wsb start`, `windows-job.ts` (`sharedFolderReadback`) reads back each mapped folder's access list with `icacls` while the job's grants are still in place and adds one line per folder after the reason (`shared <guest> <- <host> (read-only|writable, why): <entries>`, each list cut to 600 characters). The health probe's reason is that first line, now whole (it was cut at 300 characters, which dropped the shared-folder sentence of the access-denied text); the read-back stays out of the summary. `windows-real.test.ts` keeps the last 40 host calls in the redacted detail, each with its arguments (cut to 1,800 characters; the redaction withholds anything with a name in it), so the exact configuration and the account each grant names are recorded.

### Re-check of the second review (9ca65d3e): the new diagnostics and the public record (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **Found: accounts of an unknown domain passed the redaction.** The read-back joined a folder's entries on one line (`...: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F); CORP\alice:(RX); ...`). `windows-redact.ts` names the account of an access list line by line, once per line, so with realistic samples `CORP\alice.smith`, `FAMILY\kidaccount` and an icacls argument `OTHERDOM\carol:(OI)(CI)(W,DC)` came out unchanged (the machine's own accounts, the console user, SIDs, home folders and e-mail forms were already replaced); the line rule also turned the folder's whole head (guest and host path) into `<user>`. The real-sandbox detail's arguments were joined the same way and cut at 1,800 characters BEFORE redaction, which can leave half a name the redaction no longer recognises (the redactor's own rule is to cut after).
- **Fixed:** the read-back now writes the folder's head line (`shared <guest> <- <host> (read-only|writable, why):`) and then one indented line per entry, as icacls does, and cuts whole entries at 600 characters per folder (`… n more entries`); a thrown, failing or timed-out icacls marks only that folder and the start's reason stays first. The redaction gained an inline rule: the account after a single `DOMAIN\` followed by `:(rights` goes unless well known (the domain stays, as in the escaped rule), so entries a summary flattens onto one line (`containment.ts` `short` does) are covered too. Its domain and account runs are bounded (64 and 104 characters) and a look ahead to the single `\` comes first: a first version with an unbounded look back made the 3 MB one-line timing test run for 84 minutes. The real-sandbox detail keeps the arguments as their own field, one indented line each, redacted and then cut to 1,800 characters (`scrub` limit), so they neither crowd out the call's output nor are cut before redaction. Text cut before any redaction (the probe reason at 600, the wsb start text at 300) is cut between words (`cutWhole`).
- Tests: `windows-redact.test.ts` runs a realistic read-back (profile path, console user, `PC\account`, unknown domains, SIDs, Azure AD and Microsoft accounts), the flattened and argument forms, the length interplay at 400, 1,800 and 2,048 characters (redaction lengthens, the cut stays within the limit and the field is not withheld), and `cutWhole`; `windows.test.ts` checks the line layout, a throwing and a timed-out icacls, and the whole-entry cut.

### `wsb list` diagnostics and bounded retry (Claude agent, 2026-11-19)

- **Why:** in own-hardware run 44607130723 (runner elevated and interactive) the client trust checks pass, then `wsb.exe list --raw` fails inside the job (a gRPC timeout to localhost, then Cancelled, exit 2148734208). The cause is not known, so this change records evidence and gives a cold server start more time. It does not guess a fix.
- **Change:** `windows-list.ts` (`listSandboxes`) is the one place that calls `wsb list --raw` (health check, `sandboxRunning`, the stop check in `releaseJob`). First call limit 120 s, then at most two retries of 60 s with a 2 s pause (at most 3 calls, about 244 s in all). The detail line records each call's outcome and duration, the Sandbox server processes (id and start time) before and after, and whether each of HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA, LOCALAPPDATA, TEMP, TMP, SESSIONNAME and any GRPC_* variable is present or absent (names only, never values). The line passes through `redactAndCut`.
- **Host interface:** two optional members, `envNames()` and `serverProcesses()` (PowerShell `Get-Process WindowsSandboxServer`, id and start time only). A host without them records "not available".
- **Fail closed (unchanged):** when no call gives a list, health says the sandboxes could not be listed, with the detail in the reason; no probe or job sandbox starts. A list that works but shows a sandbox this program did not start still refuses. The detail is also in `auditDetails().wsbListDiagnostics` after a health check.
- **Tests (`windows.test.ts`, simulated host):** slow first call then success, the 120/60/60 s limits and the cap of two retries, all calls failing (three calls, nothing started), environment names without values (proxy credentials, profile paths and a GRPC value do not appear).
- **Run:** `windows.test.js` and `windows-redact.test.js` through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh` with `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`. Nothing ran on Windows; the next own-hardware run's detail line should show which call hangs and whether the server process changes.
- **First review (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19).** Fail closed checked in every caller: health refuses on a failed list (no probe start), `sandboxRunning` gives `unknown` (never `none`), and `releaseJob` keeps the sandbox record and lock when a stop failed and the list did not answer. The detail is built only from fixed words, numbers, ISO times and the fixed list of variable names (GRPC_* names filtered by pattern), then redacted. Fixed: (1) the server-process probe used the general PowerShell probe (60 s, retried once on timeout), so a silent server could add up to 4 minutes of diagnostics around one list; it is now one try of 30 s (`SERVER_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS`), so one list is bounded by about 244 s + 2 x 30 s, about 5 minutes. (2) `releaseJob` and `sandboxRunning` take the list options too (the backend passes its own), so tests of the release path need no real 2 s pauses. (3) The cleanup step of `own-hardware.yml` had 15 minutes; with a silent list, one leftover (stop 120 s, list about 5 min) plus the final check could exceed it, so it is now 30 (step sum 380, job limit 420, the workflow test's sum + 30 still holds). (4) New test: a failed stop with a list that never answers keeps the record, the next health check refuses and starts nothing, and `sandboxRunning` reports `unknown` (and `running` when a retry answers).
- **Second review (clean-context Opus 5.5, 2026-11-19).** Fail closed confirmed again in all three callers (health, `sandboxRunning`, `releaseJob`), no other `wsb list` in the product code (the real test's own `wsbList` helper keeps its single 60 s call), sandbox start unchanged, the controller API untouched (`api:docs:write` not needed; `sandboxRunning` and `releaseJob` gained only an optional last parameter). Fixed: (1) the server-process script read `$_` after a `try`/`catch` around the start time; inside a catch `$_` is the error record, so the process is now kept in `$p` first. (2) The server line copied whatever the host returned as the start time: it now copies only a whole process id and an ISO time (else `unknown`) and at most 8 processes, so even a host that returned a path cannot put it in the public line (new test, with a failing probe giving `not readable` and no message text). (3) The time bound was understated: a timed-out program can take up to 20 s more to stop (`taskkill` 15 s, then 5 s), so one silent list is bounded by about 404 s (50 + 140 + 2 + 80 + 2 + 80 + 50), about 7 minutes; the workflow comment says so. The cleanup step stays at 30 minutes (one leftover whose stop failed plus the final check fit unless the client probes are also slow; the step continues on error and keeps every record). (4) `own-hardware-runners.md` describes the new diagnostics line. Not changed, noted: with `wsb list` silent, every real-test health check takes up to about 7 minutes instead of about 1, so the A03b step (90 min) and the Y02 step (150 min, whose test timeout is 10 minutes per test) have less room; they fail either way in that case.

### `wsb list` failure context and a diagnostic call (Claude agent, 2026-11-20)

- **Why:** on the owner's Windows runner (elevated, interactive) every `wsb list --raw` in the Sandbox job still fails after about 30 s (a gRPC timeout to localhost:80, then Cancelled), while `wsb list` run by hand in a window answers. The existing detail line did not say how the job's process differs from that window. This change records more facts on failure; it does not change behaviour.
- **Change (failure detail only):** when every normal call failed, `listSandboxes` adds `context: ...` and `diagnostic call through cmdExe with a minimal environment (recorded only, the list stays failed): <outcome> after N ms (limit M ms)`. A list that answers records neither and makes no extra call.
  - Context (`contextText`): this process's token elevated yes/no/unknown and integrity level (low, medium, high, system; other RIDs "other"); this process's session id and the console session id ("none" when no console session); for each WindowsSandboxServer process (at most 8) its session id, elevation and integrity; the chain of this process and its parents (at most 8, this process first), each name recognised only if it is one of node, pwsh, powershell, cmd, Runner.Worker, bash (case aside, `.exe` dropped) and then shown as its label (nodeExe, pwshExe, powershellExe, cmdExe, RunnerWorkerExe, bashExe; see the next section), else "other". Only fixed words and whole numbers are copied from the probe; any text it returned is not. A list wrapped as `{"value":[...]}` (Windows PowerShell 5.1) or a single object is read as a list.
  - Diagnostic call: once, after the normal calls and the server probe, `wsb list --raw` through `%SystemRoot%\System32\cmd.exe /d /v:off /s /c ""<wsb>" list --raw"` (verbatim command line), working folder the client's folder, environment replaced by SystemRoot, windir, USERPROFILE, LOCALAPPDATA, APPDATA, TEMP, TMP and PATH (those set in this process). Limit 60 s (`DIAGNOSTIC_TIMEOUT_MS`, `diagnosticTimeoutMs` in the list options). A program path or argument holding a quote, percent sign, line break or NUL, or an argument that is not a plain word, is refused (recorded as "could not run"). Its result never sets `ok` or `attempts`.
- **Host interface:** two optional members, `listContext()` (one PowerShell probe, one try, 45 s: `OpenProcess`/`OpenProcessToken`/`GetTokenInformation` for elevation and integrity of this node process, passed as NN_PID, and of each server process; `Get-Process` session ids; `WTSGetActiveConsoleSessionId`; the parent chain from `Win32_Process`, not following a "parent" created after its child) and `runMinimalEnv()`. A host without them records "not available"; a probe that throws records "not readable" with no message text.
- **Time bound:** a list that does not answer now takes up to about 9 minutes (the earlier about 404 s plus 45 s + 20 s for the context probe and 60 s + 20 s for the diagnostic call). The cleanup step's 30 minutes still covers one leftover whose stop failed plus the final check; the workflow comment says so.

Public line: only fixed words, whole numbers and the fixed chain names; probe and diagnostic errors are swallowed without message text. PowerShell read through: the process handle is opened before its `try` and closed in `finally`, the token likewise, the buffer freed; `TokenElevation` (20, 4 bytes) and `TokenIntegrityLevel` (25, label SID pointer first, last sub-authority read) are right; the console id is cast to int64 so "no console session" (0xFFFFFFFF) arrives intact; the parent walk stops at a "parent" created after its child and at 8. cmd.exe line: with `/s` cmd strips only the outer quotes and runs `"<wsb>" list --raw`; inside the quotes & | < > ^ are literal, `%` is refused and `!` is inert under `/v:off`; `/d` skips AutoRun; the refusal throws synchronously and is recorded as "could not run". - **Symptom.** In own-hardware run 44823422754 the Mac probe (runner account `nimblenewt-runner`) failed two tests of `windows.test.ts`, suite "wsb list: diagnostics and a bounded retry": "when every call fails, the reason adds the context ..." and "the context copies only fixed words and numbers, whatever the probe returned". The chain read `node < cmd < <user>.Worker < other ...` where the tests expected `Runner.Worker`.
- **Cause.** `windows-redact.ts` searches for the machine's account name (USERNAME, USER and the process's account) and for each part of it of four or more characters (split at blanks, dots, underscores and dashes), plus the joined form, as whole words: case aside, between characters that are not ASCII letters or digits. `nimblenewt-runner` gives the part `runner`, which matches the `Runner` of `Runner.Worker`. The tests depended on the machine's account name, and the same would happen on a Windows runner account such as `runner` or `node`: the public detail would lose its diagnostic value (nothing leaked; the redaction erred toward removing text). The line is redacted in `listSandboxes` and again when a record is written (`containment-windows-evidence.ts` scrubs the reason), so redacting less in one place would not help: the labels themselves have to survive the search.

The diagnostic call is named `cmdExe` in the line (`diagnostic call through cmdExe with a minimal environment`). A label is replaced only when an account is named exactly that (or its parts joined give exactly that), which is not expected; then the redaction still wins and only that label is lost.
