## Windows redaction follow-up: over-long SID runs and e-mail addresses in any script (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-21)

Not a numbered card. It takes open items the Windows-findings redaction left (A03b second review "leftovers": a SID longer than 15 sub-authorities; the redaction-time re-check: "Non-ASCII local parts and IDN domains written in Unicode are not recognised as addresses"). Only `packages/worker/src/sandbox/windows-redact.ts` and its test changed; no storage, API or chat surface is touched (so no four-backend run applies).

ASSUMPTION: of the open redaction items, the two picked are the smallest and safest: each only makes the public-record redaction hide MORE, in one file, behind its own tests. Left open on purpose: the per-name searches of a line full of addresses whose local parts also appear on their own (a speed limit, not a leak; making it linear means changing the order of the name searches, which the current tests pin); a key quote-joined with a following word (`"ghp_…" "next"`, text lost, nothing leaks; a fix would let a lower-case tail of a real split key through, as the line-joined rule already does, so it lowers redaction); SHA-384/224 hex and `xxd -p` lines still blanked (showing them also lowers redaction). Nothing here waits on Rob.

**Done**

- **A run of more than 15 sub-authorities goes whole.** Windows allows at most 15, so such a run is not a SID; it was matched in parts and the numbers after the fifteenth stayed as plain text in the record. The text pattern (`SID_IN_TEXT`) now takes the whole run of numbers, and `redactSid` already writes `<sid>` for anything that is not SID-shaped, so the whole run becomes `<sid>` (the icacls asterisk kept: `*<sid>`). A real SID (1 to 15 sub-authorities) is redacted by class exactly as before. In an access-list line the account is a placeholder either way (`<user>`). The last gate (`scrub`) treats a raw over-long run as personal and withholds the field, so it fails closed if the text rule is ever bypassed.
- **E-mail addresses in any script.** The address pattern took only ASCII, so `jürgen.müller@beispiel.de`, `пример@почта.рф`, `用户@例子.中国` and math-alphabet local parts passed through, and their names were not searched for elsewhere. The local part and the domain labels are now letters, digits and combining marks of every script (plus `._%+-` in the local part as before); the last label is letters with their marks, or an ASCII-encoded one (`xn--p1ai`, tried first so `b.xn--p1ai` is not cut after `xn`). The linear search (`replaceEmails`) keeps its rule (one try per run of local-part characters, then the rest of the run is skipped) with the same character set as the pattern, and never starts inside a surrogate pair. The last gate finds these addresses too (it uses the same search).
- **Names from such addresses are found in any letter case.** The one-pass search for which address names occur (`occurring`) folded only A to Z, while the searches it feeds fold case like any `i` regular expression; so `JÜRGEN` after `jürgen@…` was not searched for and stayed. It now compares letters exactly as those searches do (`canon`: the one-unit upper-case form, never turning a non-ASCII letter into an ASCII one, so `ſ` and the Kelvin sign stay apart from `S` and `K`), so the result is again the same as searching for every name.
- **In-word joiners, wide at signs, ideographic dots** (first review). Internationalised names use characters inside a word that are not letters: zero-width non-joiner and joiner (Persian `علی‌رضا`, Devanagari conjuncts), the Catalan middle dot (`marcel·la`), the katakana middle dot (`ジョン・スミス`), Hebrew geresh and gershayim, the Tibetan tsheg. They are local-part and label characters now; before, the address was cut there and the word before it stayed in the record. The full-width and small at signs (`＠`, `﹫`) are at signs, and the ideographic, full-width and half-width full stops (`。`, `．`, `｡`) are label dots, as internationalised domain names read them.
- **A name's other spellings** (first review). The case-insensitive searches compare UTF-16 code units one to one, so after `jürgen@…` a decomposed `JU\u0308RGEN`, after `ismail@…` the Turkish `İSMAİL`, after `ılgın@…` `ILGIN`, after `straße@…` `STRASSE` or `STRAẞE`, and after `ŉame@…` `ʼNAME` all stayed. A name's search pattern (`namePattern`) now takes each letter with a canonical decomposition composed or decomposed, in any mix within the name; each Turkish i (`i`, `I`, `İ`, `ı`, with or without a combining dot above) for any of them; the sharp s as `ß`, `ẞ` or `ss`. A name's full upper- and lower-case forms are searched too (`nameForms`), once per distinct pattern (usually one). Which address names occur at all is now judged by a loose fold (`looseFold`: case-mapped both ways, decomposed, marks dropped), which everything those patterns match folds to as the name does (checked for every code point by a test), so a name that could be found is never dropped by the one-pass check. Known names given by the caller get the same pattern (more is hidden, nothing less).
- **Tests** (`windows-redact.test.ts`, 2 new, 1 tightened): exactly 15 kept by class and 16 or more `<sid>` in text, with the asterisk, before `-<`, in an access-list line, twice redacted, through the gate; a seeded random test (2,000 runs of 16 to 60 numbers under four authorities, nine wrappings and lower case): no number survives `redact` or `scrub`; a 3 MB run is linear. Addresses in Latin with accents, Cyrillic, Chinese, Greek, Devanagari, Turkish, math-bold letters and punycode; their names elsewhere in upper case and after a machine name; non-addresses unchanged (versions, scoped packages, no domain end, prose in other scripts); the gate withholds an address seen only after placeholders are removed; the address-name search compared with giving those names as known users (ü/Ü, long s, Kelvin sign, Æ/Å, the title-case digraph ǅ); 3 MB of `ä`, CJK, astral letters, emoji, `ä@` and dotted labels each under 1.5 s; 40,000 Unicode addresses on one line.
- **First review tests** (2 new): the other spellings above, composed and decomposed in both directions and mixed within one name, through `redact` and `scrub`; joiners, middle dots, wide at signs and ideographic dots inside an address in both; 1 MB of joined letters, of wide at signs between letters and of ideographic dots after an at sign each under 1.5 s; the loose fold checked against every code point (case forms, Turkish case forms, NFC, NFD, and what the case-insensitive search equates).
- **First review breakages** (each alone on the built file, restored byte-identical; each fails a test): no decomposed alternative in a name's pattern; no sharp-s alternative; no Turkish-i class; no full case forms; the occurrence check exact instead of loose; an ASCII-only at sign; no in-word joiners. The first full worker run failed the 3 MB wide-at-sign timing (1.58 s against 1.5 s under the suite's parallel load; 0.6 to 0.8 s alone), so those three linear checks use 1 MB.
- **First review runs** (Linux, after `npx tsc --build --force`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`): worker suite 633 tests, 631 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped (macOS-only); `scripts/evidence-workflows.test.mjs` 8 passed; `check:deps` passes; `api:docs:write` changed nothing.
- **Breakages of my own** (each alone on the built file, the redaction tests run, restored byte-identical): the SID run capped at 15 again (2 tests fail); an ASCII-only local part (fails); an ASCII-only domain (fails); the address-name search folding only A to Z (fails); the punycode last label removed (fails); the run skip replaced by a step of one (the file stops finishing: quadratic); non-ASCII never starting an address (2 fail). Survived: stepping one unit into a surrogate pair after a non-letter (equivalent: a letter's pair is always entered at its first unit, and a low surrogate alone never starts an address).

- **Runs** (Linux, after `npx tsc --build --force`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard): the whole worker suite through `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`: 631 tests, 629 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped (macOS-only). `scripts/evidence-workflows.test.mjs` (uses `scripts/redact-log.mjs`): 8 passed. `check:deps`, `licenses:check`, `roadmap:check` pass; `api:docs:write` changed nothing.

- **Second review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-21; origin/main 3585b62e merged). Finding: a letter with two or more marks written partly composed or with its marks in another canonical order stayed (`việt@…` then `VIÊ\u0323T`, as text converted from Windows code page 1258 writes Vietnamese tone marks; `한국@…` then `하\u11AB국`): the loose check found the name, but its pattern took only the fully composed and fully decomposed forms. `namePattern` now takes every canonically equivalent spelling of such a letter (`spellings`: each order of the later parts, with any of them composed onto the first, kept where its decomposition is the letter's own). Tests: the Vietnamese and Hangul cases, and every letter of three or more code points (every 61st Hangul syllable, 488 spellings) composed pairwise and with its later parts reversed. The 3 MB linear checks of the any-script test are 1 MB (3 MB of CJK took 325 ms of the 1.5 s limit on an idle machine). Breakages (each alone on the built file, restored byte-identical; each fails a test): no partial spellings; SID run capped at 15; ASCII-only local part; ASCII-only at sign; ASCII-only dot; exact instead of loose occurrence check; no Turkish-i class; in-word set cut to the middle dot; no full case forms. Measured (idle Linux): 3 MB hostile lines of marked letters, repeated names, Turkish i with dots and `s` runs against a sharp-s name 0.2 to 0.4 s; 3,000 addresses whose names stand alone 0.6 to 0.75 s whether ASCII, umlaut or Vietnamese. Worker suite 633 tests, 631 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped; `evidence-workflows` 8 passed; `check:deps` passes; `api:docs:write` changed nothing.

- **Re-check of the second-review fix** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-21). Finding: the spellings were made per code point, so a letter with no composed form of its own stayed in its other spellings (Yoruba `ọ́` = `ọ` + acute, written `ó` + dot below or with the marks in the other order), and so did a name whose address wrote its marks out of canonical order even when written the same way again (`q` + acute, dot below, horn). `namePattern` now takes a letter together with the marks after it (`spellings` of the unit; Turkish i and sharp s units as before). Bounds: at most three later parts are reordered (the most any composed character has; 9 alternatives is the most any one takes), a longer run of marks takes only its given, decomposed and first-decomposed spellings, and the cache is cleared at 10,000 units (it was keyed by any text from an address). Not covered: singleton equivalents that NFC never produces (`ά` U+1F71 for `ά`, the Angstrom sign), and an address written out of canonical order with more than three marks on one letter. Tests: Yoruba spellings; `ú` + diaeresis is not `ǘ` (the equivalence filter could be removed with every test passing); a letter with 30 marks found composed and decomposed. The 40,000-address timing check is 20,000 (0.55 to 0.65 s of its 1.5 s limit on this loaded machine; a per-name search without the occurrence filter takes 2.7 s at 20,000). Breakages (each alone on the built file, restored byte-identical; each fails a test): no reordering; no equivalence filter; per code point instead of per letter-with-marks. Measured (Linux, load 36 on 32 cores): 1 MB hostile inputs (9-way Greek letters, Vietnamese and Yoruba near-misses, Hangul, 3-mark letters, 2,000 to 3,000 addresses, a 200-mark letter) 0.1 to 0.31 s each, as before the change.

- **Final re-check** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-21; last round for this slice). Randomized comparison of the old pattern (a416bf34) with the new over names in Latin, Vietnamese, polytonic Greek, Cyrillic, Hangul, Turkish, German, Devanagari, Arabic and Hebrew, with random marks, case and the old pattern's own per-code-point spellings (8 seeds, 800,000 strings the old pattern accepts). Finding: a letter of two or more parts followed by marks that made more than three later parts in all (`ữ` + two marks, a Hangul syllable with a final + two marks) lost its partly composed spellings, which the old pattern took (`Ư` + tilde + the marks). `spellings` now also takes, for such a unit, the first code point's own spellings followed by the marks as written (at most 12 alternatives then; 27 still the bound). After the fix: 0 of 800,000 missed; every alternative of 200,000 random units is canonically equivalent to its unit; at most 12 alternatives seen; 50,000 distinct units leave the cache under 10,000 (its values depend only on the key, so text cannot poison it). Test: both cases. Breakages (each alone on the built file, restored byte-identical; each fails a test): no first-code-point spellings for a long mark run; no reordering; no equivalence filter. Measured (Linux, load 17 to 25 on 32 cores; three runs each, first run cold): a 512 K-mark run after an address 0.05 to 0.08 s; 64 x U+1F82 name against 1 MB of near-miss spellings 0.1 s; a 200-mark letter against 1 MB 0.05 s; 3,000 marked names that all occur 0.27 to 1.0 s; 20,000 distinct Hangul and Vietnamese addresses 0.12 s; 1 MB of 3-mark Yoruba near-misses 0.15 s; 64 long-mark names all present in 1 MB 0.2 to 0.6 s. The 20,000-address test check takes 0.21 to 0.27 s cold in its own process against 1.5 s. Not covered (beyond the list above): partly composed spellings with marks in another order when the letter has more than three later parts in all; the cache clear has no test of its own. `windows-redact` 28 passed and `evidence-workflows` 8 passed.

**Not done**

- A language written without spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) glued to an address now loses the joined words with it (`連絡はjim@example.comまで` is one `<email>`), and that joined local part (up to 64 characters) is searched for elsewhere. Text is lost, nothing leaks.
- Emoji and other symbols are not local-part characters (`🙂name@ex.com` is `🙂<email>`: the symbol stays, the name goes).
- Spellings that are not the same letters: a name written with compatibility characters (the ligature `ﬁ` for `fi`, half-width katakana), or without its accents (`MARIA` for `maría`). Pieces of a local part are split at `._%+-` only, so `スミス` alone after `ジョン・スミス@…` stays (it is also under four characters).
- The per-name searches are still one regular expression per name over the whole text (the open speed item in the assumption above); a pattern with a decomposed alternative is slower than a plain one (5,000 addresses with umlauts whose names also stand alone: about 2 to 5 s on this machine, about twice the ASCII figure).
- `windows-plan.ts` `IDENTITY` still accepts at most 14 sub-authorities for a configured identity: a validation that refuses a 15-sub-authority SID (fails closed), not a redaction; unchanged.
- The open items named in the assumption above.

## The Sandbox job's process context before its first `wsb` call (card wsb-console, Claude agent, 2026-11-21)

Plain words first. On Rob's Windows runner every `wsb` call made by the Sandbox job takes about 30 s, logs a gRPC timeout to localhost:80 and ends with "Cancelled", while the same call made by node from Rob's administrator PowerShell window answers (also with `windowsHide`, `detached` and piped output). Elevation, session and the environment were already ruled out by run 44823422754. This card does not try a fix: it records, once, before the first `wsb` call, the facts about the job's own process that could still differ from Rob's window, so the next own-hardware run shows them side by side with Rob's own test of the runner started by hand. The cause is not assumed.

- **What is done.**
  - New `scripts/wsb-job-context.mjs` (always exits 0; off Windows one "not Windows" line and the environment names). On Windows it records: the kind of account (by SID: a local or domain account, local system, local service, network service, a virtual service account; the name and SID are never printed) and whether it is the console user, whether it runs in the console session, whether someone is signed in and whether the console is locked (the backend's own `session()` probe); the integrity level and how Administrators is held (enabled, deny only, absent) from `whoami /groups /fo csv`, read by SID so a translated Windows reads the same; this process's and the console's session ids; whether this process has a console (a helper PowerShell leaves its own console and calls `AttachConsole(<node pid>)`: success is yes, error 6 is no) and whether the helper itself got a console window; whether this process is in a job object (`IsProcessInJob`) and the job's limit and UI-restriction flags in hex (read by the helper, which is in the same job unless it broke away); the parent chain as fixed letter-only labels (node, bash, sh, cmd, powershell, pwsh, Runner.Worker, Runner.Listener, RunnerService, services, svchost, explorer, conhost, OpenConsole, WindowsTerminal, wininit, winlogon, userinit; anything else "other"), each marked "(service)" when it is a Windows service's process, and "under a Windows service yes/no"; the window station and desktop names (the helper's, inherited from node; any name outside `[A-Za-z0-9_$-]` is "other"); the environment variable NAMES only (sorted, twelve per line so a withheld line does not hide the rest; names outside a strict pattern are only counted); and one `wsb list` (as Rob ran it: `wsb list` from PATH, with `windowsHide` and piped output like the backend) with a 45 s limit: outcome (answered, failed with the exit code in hex, no answer within the limit, not found on PATH), duration in ms, number of output lines, fixed markers (grpc, localhost:80, deadline, cancelled, access denied, timed out) and its first error line through the shared credential scanner, cut to 160 characters.
  - Every line goes through the shared credential scanner (`safe-error.mjs`, the contracts `safeText`) in the script, and the workflow pipes the output through `redact-log.mjs` (account, machine and home names, SIDs, addresses; a line still looking personal is withheld whole).
  - `own-hardware.yml`, Sandbox job only: new step "Record the job's process context before wsb" (`id: wsbctx`) after the build and before the real Sandbox tests (the first step that calls `wsb`), `continue-on-error`, 5 minutes, not read by the outcome step. It writes the redacted output to `$RUNNER_TEMP/wsb-job-context.txt`, prints it and adds it to the job summary in a code block. Step limits plus 30 now total 415 of the job's 420 minutes. No other job changed.
  - `own-hardware-runners.md` (setup step 6) names the step and what it records.
- **Tests.** `scripts/wsb-job-context.test.mjs` (14 tests after the review, Linux-runnable): whoami CSV parsing (quotes, translated names, unreadable output), account kinds, environment names (values never printed, odd names counted, case duplicates once), the helper's answer in fixed words and with missing or odd values (never copied), every `wsb list` outcome with markers, a key in the error line removed and a long line cut, rendered lines unchanged by the shared scanner when they hold no key (this caught "token: integrity", which the scanner reads as a credential; the line now says "integrity level"), the helper script's fixed text (no interpolation, writes only to NN_OUT, reads only NN_PID and NN_OUT, leaves its console before attaching), and a real run off Windows passed through `redact-log.mjs` unchanged. `scripts/evidence-workflows.test.mjs`: the new step's place, settings, pipeline, that the outcome does not read it, that no other job runs it, and the job limit.
- **Not done.** Untested on the real machine until the next own-hardware run. The helper's C# and PowerShell have not been compiled or run anywhere (no Windows or PowerShell here); if it fails, the lines say "unknown" and "helper: no answer" and the other facts still print. The previous attempt at this card (a fresh console window for every `wsb` call) was discarded unmerged as a speculative fix; its diff is kept only in the session scratch folder.
- **Review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, first review, 2026-11-21). Findings fixed: (1) every program ran under `spawnSync` with a `timeout`, which ends only the program itself and then still waits for its pipes to close, so a descendant holding them (csc.exe under `Add-Type`, or anything `wsb` starts) could keep the step waiting until its 5-minute limit cut off the record and the summary. whoami, the helper and `wsb list` now run through the backend's own bounded runner (`windowsRealHost().run`, `runBounded`: `taskkill /T /F` at the limit, then the pipes closed), and the runner's own "timed out ... and was stopped" text is taken off before the markers are read (it would have shown as the marker "timed out"). (2) Nothing bounded the whole run (the session probe alone can take 2 x 60 s): there is now an overall limit of 240 s that prints what was recorded by then and a line saying the rest was not; the console-user probe starts first, in parallel, and `wsb list` waits for it at most 30 s; the slowest path otherwise (each limit reached and 20 s to stop each tree) is 215 s. (3) Output was written and the process ended with `process.exit` straight after; it now ends in the write's callback. (4) A console session id of 0xFFFFFFFF (none attached) reads "none attached"; an empty parent chain no longer reads "under a Windows service no"; the `{"value": [...], "Count": n}` form Windows PowerShell 5.1 can give an array is read. (5) The job's comment still said 380 minutes of step limits; it is 385. Checked and kept: the helper's C# is C# 5 (no newer syntax), the P/Invoke signatures and the job structure offsets (`LimitFlags` at 16; 64 bytes on 64-bit, 48 on 32-bit; class 4 is the UI restrictions), the hashtable keys are all `[uint32]` (PowerShell keys are typed), the here-string closes at column 0, and `-Command` with a multi-line script holding double quotes is how the backend's own probes already reach Windows PowerShell 5.1. PowerShell and the C# compiler are not installed here, so the helper is still unrun. Tests: `windowsLines` now takes the host, and a fake host checks the order, the helper's NN_PID and NN_OUT, the limits, `wsb list` last and nothing personal in the lines; the runner's results map to each outcome; the time arithmetic. Eight deliberate breakages (runner text kept as a marker, the 5.1 array form, the console none, `--raw` added, NN_PID dropped, the scanner off, the overall limit shortened, the job limit lowered) each failed a test and were restored.
- ASSUMPTION: `wsb list` (not `wsb.exe list --raw` by the resolved package path, as the backend calls it) with `windowsHide`, so the line compares with Rob's hand test (his was node's `spawnSync`; here node's `execFile` through the backend's bounded runner, the same process start); the Sandbox tests right after it still make the backend's own calls with their diagnostics.
- ASSUMPTION: 45 s limit for the one call: the failure seen ends at about 30 s, so the limit shows how it ends while keeping the step within 5 minutes.
- ASSUMPTION: the window station, desktop and job flags are read in the helper, which inherits them from node (node's spawn sets no desktop and no job breakaway); that is said in the line.
- Nothing here waits on Rob: the next own-hardware dispatch carries the evidence, together with the result of his hand-started runner test.
- **Second review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, 2026-11-21). Checked and kept: the step cannot fail the job (`continue-on-error`, the script always exits 0, `redact-log.mjs` always exits 0) and cannot pass its 5 minutes (every program through `runBounded`, the overall 240 s limit, slowest path 215 s); nothing personal is printed (account kind by SID, fixed labels, names only for the environment, the one error line through the scanner and the log redaction); the C# is C# 5 and its P/Invoke declarations, `JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION` offsets and buffer sizes are right; the PowerShell keys its hashtables by `[uint32]` throughout and `+=` adds each ordered dictionary as one element; `-Command` with the multi-line script reaches Windows PowerShell 5.1 the same way as the backend's `SESSION_SCRIPT`, which has run on the owner's machine (no backslash or `%` in the script, so node's argument quoting changes nothing). Finding fixed: the parents line said "under a Windows service yes" whenever any parent was a service's process, which a runner started by a Task Scheduler task at logon also has (the Schedule service's svchost), so the configuration that works would have read like the one that fails. The line now says whether the runner's own service (RunnerServiceExe) is among the parents; the "(service)" marks in the chain stay. Tests: the Task Scheduler chain, and at most 16 parents shown. Nine deliberate breakages (the runner's stop text kept as a marker, a "yes" string read as a service, odd environment names printed, local system unmapped, `--raw` added, the 16-parent cap removed, deny only unread, a negative session printed, `continue-on-error` removed from the step) each failed a test and were restored; the cap had no test before. Left as is: if the overall limit is ever reached, a program still running then (at most one `wsb list` or helper) is not stopped when node exits; the slowest path stays 25 s under that limit.
- CORRECTION (2026-11-21, supersedes the earlier ASSUMPTION result line): the claim that the Sandbox job passes when the runner is started by hand was wrong. On run 44947256972 (runner started with `run.cmd`, elevated) `wsb list` still failed (exit 2148734208 after about 30 s, three attempts) and the Sandbox tests, G05 and Y02 failed; the step markers had shown success because those steps are continue-on-error. Running as a service is therefore not shown to be the cause. The next own-hardware run prints the job's process context (this card's step); compare it with the owner's administrator PowerShell, where `wsb list` works.

## G04 slice 5: the kill harness stops a child that hangs and checks where every kill landed (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-21)

Branch `card-g04-s5`, on main `6db9c5ad`. Test code only; no production file changed.

- **ASSUMPTION (which leftovers, nothing waits on Rob).** The G04 notes leave seven open items: (1) a child that hangs instead of reaching its boundary is ended only by the file's 300 s time limit and is not killed by the parent; (2) the older kill files (`g04-kill`, `g04-wait`) do not check the label the child reports it died at; (3) a kill inside the model stream before the tool runs (Pi's side) is not measured; (4) no test can catch "release the hold, then seed" in the worker; (5) the bridge numbering is exact only when Pi ran every earlier use of a reused provider ID; (6) with `admitCall` switched off, `tool.invoke` and `job.start` presented again under another number are new calls; (7) when the 30 s busy wait runs out the model does not learn the outcome. This slice does (1) and (2): both are in the shared kill harness, are test-only, and make every other G04 result more trustworthy (a kill that landed somewhere else, or a child stuck forever, now fails with its reason). (3) to (7) change production behaviour or need a new measuring rig and stay open.
- **Done.**
  - **A hung child is killed by the parent.** `runChild` (`packages/integration/src/g04-fixture.ts`) now has a deadline, `CHILD_DEADLINE_MS` = 120 s (a child normally dies within about 1 s on Linux and 7 to 10 s on the hosted Windows runner), under the package's 300 s per-test limit. At the deadline the parent sends SIGKILL itself and the result says `hung: true`. The parent's own kill is never counted as the child's (`killed` is false for a hung child), so a stuck child fails its boundary with "the child hung, it did not reach its boundary and was killed by the parent" instead of the test timing out with the process still alive (see the review below for where the per-test limit still comes first). The timer is cleared when the child exits. No fixed pause: the deadline only fires when something is wrong.
  - **One shared kill check, used by every kill file.** New `killProblem(child, labels, crashAt, label)` in `g04-fixture.ts`: the child must not have hung, must have died by its own SIGKILL without finishing, and must have reported (on stderr, just before the kill) exactly the uncrashed run's label for that boundary (the review below makes it every label up to and including that boundary). `g04-kill.ts` (main path) and `g04-wait-suite.ts` (the real kills around the second wait) now use it; before, they checked only "killed and not finished". `g04-tool.ts` uses the same function in place of its own copy.
  - **Harness probes.** `g04-child.ts` has two scenarios that open no database: `probe-hang` (never reaches a boundary) and `probe-kill` (passes boundaries `probe 0`, `probe 1`, ... and dies at the given one through the same `Chaos` kill as the real scenarios).
  - **Tests.** New `packages/integration/src/g04-harness.test.ts` (4 tests): a real child killed at boundary 2 counts, and the same death read against a shifted label list, the boundary before, or a boundary past the end counts as "died elsewhere"; a hanging child with a 1 s deadline comes back hung, not killed, and is gone; the deadline stays between 60 s and 150 s; `killProblem` on a finished child, a child that exited by itself, a child that printed no label, a label that is a prefix of the reported one ("probe 1" against "probe 10"), and a hung child that also printed a label. No database is touched, so there is no per-backend split; the kill and wait files that now use the check run on SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread and PostgreSQL (the G04 engines).
  - **Every existing kill already lands where it is meant to.** With the label check on, all G04 files pass (below), so the main path and wait children die on the uncrashed run's labels at every sampled boundary.
- **Mutation checks** (on a copy of the built package, `packages/integration/mut`, removed afterwards; `dist` untouched; each failed as stated):
  1. The parent's deadline kill read as the child's (`killed: died`): the hang test fails ("the parent's SIGKILL is not the child's own").
  2. The label check removed from `killProblem`: two harness tests fail.
  3. The `hung` check removed: two harness tests fail.
  4. No deadline (timer set to the maximum): the hang test runs into the file's time limit (60 s for this check), which is how a hung child behaved before this slice.
  5. The expected label taken one boundary later (`labels[crashAt + 1]`): two harness tests fail ("died elsewhere").
  6. An extra step in the main path child (`chaos.hit("extra step")` before `runPath`): `g04-kill-sqlite` (part 1, 19 boundaries) fails, all 18 misplaced kills named "died elsewhere" (the 19th boundary comes before the extra step and is unaffected). With the old check (killed and not finished only) the same breakage was caught at 6 of the 18, and under a wrong reason ("started before the kill but is not stored"); the other 12 misplaced kills passed.
  7. The same extra step in the wait child: `g04-wait-sqlite` fails its real-kill test ("died elsewhere").
- **NOT done.**
  - Items (3) to (7) above.
  - The deadline is per child; a hang in the parent's own restart and verification (after the kill) is still ended only by the file's time limit, as before.
  - The `WorkerHost` worker-process files (`g04-process-*`) are not changed: their kills are sent by the parent, not reached at a boundary.
  - macOS and Windows were not run (Linux only). Nothing here depends on the platform: the deadline uses `ChildProcess.kill("SIGKILL")`, which ends the process on Windows too, and "hung" is recorded by the parent before it kills, so the Windows exit-code reading of a kill cannot turn a hang into a kill.
- **Verified** (Linux, Node 22, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, after `npx tsc --build --force`, no stale compiled tests): all 24 G04 files with `NIMBLENEWT_G04_HEAVY=1` (kill, wait, tool, faults, process, connection, share and the new harness file, on SQLite, SQLite on a worker thread and PostgreSQL) 50 of 50; the whole integration package 243 tests, 230 passed, 13 skipped (the heavy G04 files without the variable), 0 failed; `scripts/*.test.mjs` 237 passed, 1 skipped. `check:deps`, `licenses:check` and `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` regenerated with no change.
- **Review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, first review with fixes, 2026-11-21; merged main `61b8434c`). (1) **Fixed: the result was taken at the child's "exit".** Node does not order "exit" against the end of the child's stdout and stderr, so on a slow machine the label the child writes just before its kill could still be unread, and a correct kill would fail as "died elsewhere" (a false failure, never a false pass, but exactly the Windows and macOS risk). `runChild` now takes the result at "close", once both pipes are read to the end; if something else held the pipes after the child is gone, it is taken 10 s after the exit with what was read (a label not read by then fails the boundary). Output is decoded as UTF-8 by the stream, not chunk by chunk. A new harness test kills `probe-kill` three times right after it writes 1 MiB to stderr and requires the whole output and the label; on Linux the old "exit" reading also passed it (the order did not differ there in any run), so it guards the slower platforms rather than proving the fix on Linux. (2) **Fixed: `probe-kill` past its last boundary went on to open the database** at the spec's path `unused` in the current folder; it now says "finished" and exits, with a test (no kill point: not killed, "finished"). The probe comment named a file that does not exist (`g04-child.test.ts`). (3) The problem text now shows the end of stderr (where the label, an error and the exit code are), not its first 300 characters. (4) **Deadline on slow machines, checked, not changed.** 120 s per child against 7 to 10 s on the hosted Windows runner is a margin of more than ten times, so it does not fire on a slow runner. It is not scaled to the limit: the 300 s limit is per test, not per file, and one kill test runs about 20 children (165 to 225 s on Windows), so a hang late in such a test still meets the test's limit first, as before this slice; under the QA job's 50-minute per-test limit the deadline is what ends a hung child. The comment and notes said "well under the 300 s file limit" and are corrected. (5) **Windows, checked.** Windows has no signals: a process ended by `process.kill`, its own or the parent's, exits with code 1, as an uncaught error does, so `runChild` counts any non-zero code as died there and the label written just before the kill is what tells a kill from a crash; a hung child is marked before the parent's kill, so the parent's kill never reads as the child's on any platform. No POSIX path: the probes use `os.tmpdir()` folders and the spec is never read. (6) No child is left behind: the hang test's child is reaped before the result ("close" follows the exit). (7) **Fixed: only the last label was compared.** Labels repeat (every claim, delivery and timer has the same "before" and "after" label), so a child that took one step more or fewer earlier in its path could die on an equal label at the same index and pass. The child now writes every label it passed, as one JSON list, and `killProblem` requires exactly the uncrashed run's labels up to and including the boundary. All kill, wait and tool files pass with it on the three engines, so the real children follow the uncrashed run step for step. Harness tests: an equal label reached after a different earlier step is "died elsewhere"; no boundary before the first. (8) **Fixed: the label write could fail on a full pipe.** Once Node has opened stderr as a stream, a POSIX pipe is non-blocking, so the synchronous label write just before the kill could get EAGAIN (or write only part) when the pipe is full, and the child would crash instead of dying at its boundary (a false failure). The child's `writeAll` now sends the rest in pieces, waiting 1 ms while the parent reads; the probe's 1 MiB filler uses it too. **Mutations** (on a copy of the built package, removed after): the parent's kill read as the child's, the hung check removed, only the last label compared, the child's first label left out, and the past-the-end check removed each fail named harness tests; taking the result at "exit" (synchronously) is not caught on Linux, see (1), and ignoring "close" only delays the result by the 10 s fallback. **Runs** (Linux, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, after `npx tsc --build --force`): all 24 G04 files with `NIMBLENEWT_G04_HEAVY=1`, 52 of 52 (the harness file 6 of 6, with no child process left after); `scripts/*.test.mjs` 237 passed, 1 skipped; `check:deps` and `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` regenerated with no change.

## B01 (first slice): production and improvement (P/PC) work in admission (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-21)

ASSUMPTION: the first slice of B01 is the admission side of the P/PC balance, built on what already exists (the contract's `workClass`, S10; the owner's `workClass.pcFloor` and `workClass.pcCeiling` installation settings, U10/M03g; the stand-up's slot-time review, M03h). It needs no model server, makes no provider call and spends nothing: places and records only. Spend-based P/PC accounting, emergency borrowing and campaign spend limits are later slices (below). Reversible: with no allocation set admission behaves exactly as before.

ASSUMPTION: the percentages become places of the productive limit (H03/H10). The ceiling is rounded down but a ceiling above 0% is at least one place (rounding an allowed share down to none would make it "never", which the owner says with 0%), and with two places or more it always leaves production at least one place; a floor above 0 keeps at least one place (rounded up) and never more than the ceiling. With a single productive place the two kinds take turns by the existing patience rule. Only the installation layer counts (admission is installation-wide); a project-layer allocation is read by the stand-up review but not by admission.

**What is done (plain words).**
- **The class goes with the work.** When the dispatcher first asks for a place for an attempt it now reads the task's P or PC class from the contract along with the priority, keeps it on the attempt (`ask.workClass`) and puts it on the admission request (`workClass`). A replay after a crash asks for the same thing. Relabeling the task later changes nothing already asked for: the place, and the stand-up review's count of the attempt's slot time, stay with the class it was admitted under (the review now reads `ask.workClass` first; attempts from before this slice still count by the task's class now). Inquiries and reviews are never P or PC (a class on them is refused): a production review stays in the control lane.
- **Reserved places and a ceiling.** Admission reads the owner's allocation at every decision (`AdmissionService` reads the installation settings on its own storage, so the dispatcher's, the API's and every controller's admission read the same figures). Improvement work over its ceiling waits ("... improvement (PC) attempts are already running, the most the owner's P/PC allocation allows ..."). Production cannot take a free place the reserve still owes to improvement work that is waiting and could run ("the free place is kept for improvement (PC) work that is waiting ..."). A continuous backlog of either kind cannot starve the other: the reserve serves improvement work, the ceiling leaves production its places.
- **Lending and reclaim.** When no waiting improvement work could use a reserved place, production is admitted into it and the request is marked `lent` with the reason. Nothing running is ever stopped to reclaim: the place comes back when that attempt ends (the safe boundary), and then goes to waiting improvement work before any production, whatever production's priority. Ownership never changes.
- **Allocation changes are revisions for pending work only.** A changed allocation counts from the next admission decision; a lower ceiling stops nothing running. Changing it in chat is the existing setting edit (policy edit of `workClass.pcFloor` / `workClass.pcCeiling`, shown first and applied on the owner's yes), tested through the composed controller.
- **The owner can ask.** The `capacity` status view (chat: "is improvement work getting starved?") has a fourth group, the P/PC work balance: the allocation and the places it keeps and caps, production and improvement attempts running and waiting, lent places (at most 20 listed, with the total), and, when improvement work waits short of its reserve, how many places and why (every place taken and which are lent, or what else holds the waiting work). The interpreter's list of status kinds and `status.ask` describe it (a few dozen characters of the chat prompt; the worker's fixed part is untouched). `AdmissionService.balance` is owner only.
- **Damage and errors.** A floor above the ceiling or a figure that is not a whole percentage is damage, never a guess. An allocation that cannot be read admits nothing new (a request is refused `integrity` with a fixed text; the reader's own message is never passed on, and an `integrity` text from a reader is passed through the credential scan and cut to 200 characters); release and stop still work and free places. Restart-safe: the allocation is a setting and the class and `lent` marks are in the admission record, so a restarted controller decides the same. Two controllers deciding at once meet the admission record's revision check (tested with two services on one storage, all four backends, PostgreSQL included).

**Tests.** `admission/balance.test.ts` (2 pure tests + 10 per backend x4 = 42), one dispatcher-suite test (x4 backend files), one stand-up test (x4), `api/start-work-balance.test.ts` (1, composed controller, chat). **Deliberate breakages** on the built files, each caught: the reserved place not kept (12 failures), no protected production place (8), lent not marked (16), single place never turning (4), the reader's text passed unscanned (4), an agent reading the balance (4), release depending on the allocation (4), the class not passed to admission (dispatcher test), relabeling moving slot time (stand-up test, 4).

**First review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-21).** Found and fixed, each with a test: (1) a ceiling under one place (20% of 4) rounded to none, so improvement work never ran even with a floor above 0 promising it a place; a ceiling above 0% is now at least one place and the wait reason says it was rounded up. (2) An allocation change let waiting work in only at the next request or release, so in a quiet controller (say, only improvement work waiting behind a 0% ceiling) a raised ceiling admitted nothing until some other work came or went; `ConfigurationService` now takes an `onChanged` hook (after an apply or change puts keys in force, not on a repeat; a failure of the hook is not the change's), and the composed controller runs an admission sweep when an installation P/PC key changes (tested through chat: the raised ceiling admits the waiting work with nothing else happening). (3) A free place could stand empty: production was kept out of a reserved place for improvement work that `promote` itself would pass by (held behind an older request that had waited the patience number of times for the same host); "could use" now leaves out work such a request holds back, so production is lent the place. (4) Production waiting while no place was free was also given the "the free place is kept for improvement work" reason; the reserve now holds only when a place is free. (5) The status line on lent places said "the oldest 20 are counted here" though none are listed; dropped. Noted, not changed: a production attempt admitted into a lent place keeps its `lent` mark after the reserve is met by another place freeing (the mark records how it was admitted); an attempt's stand-up slot time is counted under the class of its latest request, so a relabel between two requests of one attempt moves the earlier slots too; a damaged installation configuration layer now stops new admission even with no allocation set (as a damaged caps record does). Breakages on the built files, each caught: the sweep hook not run, the configuration hook not called on a change, the ceiling rounded to none, "could use" ignoring held-back work, the reserve holding with no place free.

**Second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, with a fix, 2026-11-21; merged main `45933339`, notes conflict kept both sections).** (1) **Fixed: a repeat of an allocation change did not let waiting work in.** `ConfigurationService.onChanged` was told only on the first run of an apply or change, so a stop between the write and the admission sweep (or a caller that lost the answer and sent the same command again, as the chat's yes does with its fixed command ID) left the raised ceiling or new floor in force with waiting work still waiting until some other request or release. A repeat now tells the hook again with the keys and revision its history entry recorded (the caps' `onChanged` is already told on a repeat); the sweep's command ID `pc-sweep:<revision>` makes the second telling a replay when the first sweep ran. A stop with no repeat still leaves the sweep to the next decision, as for the caps. Test added in `configuration.test.ts` (four backends): told on a change and an apply with only the changed keys, told again on each repeat with the same keys and revision, never on a refused change, a refused apply or its repeat, or a change to a value already in force; a failing listener neither fails nor undoes the change; another layer is told with its own scope. Checked and left: the hook runs after the command has returned (no storage lock or transaction held, no re-entry into the configuration service), and for keys other than the installation P/PC keys it returns at once, so no other configuration path changes; two controllers sweeping meet the admission record's revision check and `#retrying`, and each sweep re-reads the record and the allocation, so a sweep racing a request or release cannot admit twice or past a cap; a failed sweep is ignored and the next decision admits. The admission policy against floor and ceiling, a single place, everything lent, a floor above the places, a 0% ceiling, an allocation changed while work waits, a held-back older request and hosts of different capacity: no further problem found (the `reserved` hold requires a free place and an improvement request `promote` would admit, so it never leaves a place empty). **Deliberate breakages** on built files (each alone, restored byte-identical by SHA-256), each failed the one file that should catch it: no hook on a repeated change and a failing hook passed on (`configuration.test`, 4 of 4 each); the ceiling compared with `>` (balance, 12 failures); the reserve holding only when fewer places are free than owed (12); held-back older work ignored when deciding whether improvement work could use a place (4); the lent mark missing when the free places equal the reserve owed (16); the sweep bound to the project layer (`start-work-balance`). **Runs** (Linux, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, short `TMPDIR`, after `npm run clean` and `npx tsc --build --force`), by the owner's rule only the changed files and three neighbours: `admission/balance`, `api/start-work-balance`, `standups/standups` and `configuration/configuration` 331 of 331 before the fix, `configuration` and `start-work-balance` 93 of 93 after it; the B01 dispatcher test on the four backend files 4 of 4; neighbours `chat/model-budget` and `chat/capacity` 69 of 69, integration `fixed-part-budget` 5 of 5. Not run: whole directories, the other dispatch, chat and integration files and `scripts/*.test.mjs` (CI is the net). `check:deps`, `licenses:check` and `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` unchanged by `api:docs:write`.

**What is NOT done (later B01 slices).**
- Spend-based accounting: P/PC share of provider spend (`costMicros`) and of slot time over a period as an admission input (this slice balances places at once, not time used over a window), and "no catch-up debt" beyond places (nothing is owed across time today, by construction).
- A wait bound for approved improvement work: reclaim waits for a lent attempt to end, which is as long as that attempt runs.
- Emergency borrowing of the reserve by explicit owner direction (reason, scope, expiry, review) and the expiring override that survives restart; repeated urgency not removing the floor.
- Explicit "approved PC work" (today any PC-labelled task counts) and charging reflection, experiments and monitoring runs that are not tasks.
- An attempt's class is not re-read for a waiting request (priority is, by `#reprioritize`); a relabel counts from the attempt's next request.
- Campaign spend limits, delegation interplay with R05 budgets, and a chat answer for "what was delivered" per kind beyond the stand-up review's existing lines.
- Paused or suspended work is not woken by this slice (admission only admits requests that are waiting); no separate test of it here.

**Runs** (Linux, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, short `TMPDIR`, after `npm run clean` and `npx tsc --build --force`): admission, status, standups, planning and configuration with the capacity, stand-up allocation and work-balance start tests 741 of 741; all 60 dispatch files 1,597 of 1,597; all chat and web files with `start-docs` 1,470 of 1,470; `scripts/*.test.mjs` 252 passed, 1 skipped. `check:deps`, `licenses:check` and `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` regenerated (the `status.ask` summary names the fourth capacity group). Not run here: the full exhaustive suite (CI is the net) and Windows/macOS (no fixed pauses, paths, signals or time zones are involved: the new code is pure decisions over stored records and fixed clock values in tests).

## B02 (first slice): observations, deduplicated by where they come from (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-21)

ASSUMPTION: the first slice of B02 is the observation record itself, its storm limits, two controller sources that already have a hook (a failed review and a denied request), the agents' own friction reports through the state API, and the owner's view and settling by chat. It needs no model server and no credentials. Approval stalls and redundant prompts as sources, and a worker bridge tool, are left for the next slice (below). Nothing here touches B01's budget admission.

`packages/controller/src/observations/` (`ObservationService`), four state API operations (`observation.submit`, `observation.get`, `observation.list`, `observation.dispose`; `api-v1.md` regenerated), the status kind `observations`, the chat operation `observation.dispose` (revision filled in) and one sentence in the interpreter prompt. Wired in `api/start.ts`. Record kinds: `observation`, `observation-index` (one per project, the open ones), `observation-rate` (one per project, the current hour). New ID prefix `obs`.

**Done:**
- **What an observation is.** A record of something in a project's work: `correction`, `failure`, `recovery`, `friction`, `approval-stall`, `redundant-prompt` or `failed-review`; who first told it (`origin` controller or agent), one line of summary, optional detail, the records it comes from (`sources`, 1 to 10: task, artifact, desk-record, submission, review, observation), the task it is about, every reporter (20 listed) and how many reports joined it, first and last seen, owner and disposition. It changes no work, grants nothing and makes no task.
- **Duplicate retellings count once (provenance, not wording).** Sources that are an event (a submission, a review request) decide sameness: any later report of the same event, by the controller or by any agent, in any words and of any kind, joins the first observation (`reports` goes up, the reporter is listed), and a report that cites an observation joins it. The record's ID is derived from that key, so two controllers telling the same event at once make one record (tested on PostgreSQL with two service instances). A report that cites only context (a task, an artifact, a desk record) has no shared event, so it is the same only when the same reporter tells the same words (case and spacing ignored) about the same records. A retelling of a settled observation is counted and does not reopen it.
- **Controller sources wired.** A review submission with verdict `changes` or `reject` becomes a `failed-review` observation (source: the review submission), and a request a reviewer or the owner denies becomes a `correction` (source: the review request, the reason as detail). Both are made in the existing best-effort hooks with stable command IDs (`obs-review:<submission>`, `obs-deny:<request>`), so a hook run again after a restart answers with what was recorded; a failure to record is reported to `onInternalError` and never touches the review.
- **Cross-scope data stays restricted.** Every source must be of the observation's project; an agent may cite only records it can read now (task: `task.read`; artifact: `artifact.read`; desk record: the desk rule; submission: its own or `task.read` on the task; review: its own request or `task.read`; observation: one it may read). Missing, foreign and unreadable sources are refused with the same words. The controller's sources must all be of one project. Reads: the owner and holders of `meeting.read` or `meeting.manage` in the project; a reporter may read what it reported but sees only itself as a reporter (and no other agent as owner or in the history; see the first review). Anyone else gets "not found".
- **Rate limits prevent storms.** Per project and clock hour (UTC, from the record's ISO time, so no time zone or locale is involved): 60 new observations; per agent and hour: 10 reports (new or joined); 500 open per project. An agent over a limit is refused (`unavailable`, saying until when). The controller is never refused, because its event must not fail: the observation is not made and is counted as `suppressed` on the project's rate record (with the hour's count, the running total and the last one's kind and reason), which the list and the status view show. The controller's retellings always count. The limits are checked in the same write as the record, so they hold across two controllers (tested: eight concurrent records from two instances against a limit of four).
- **Owner and disposition.** Agent friction is owned by its reporter; a manager (`meeting.manage`) or the owner settles: `promoted` (names the improvement proposal of this project it became), `dismissed` or `resolved` (with a reason), or `open` again, optionally with a new owner; ten history entries. Settled ones leave the open list.
- **Agent-submitted friction.** `observation.submit` for agents with `meeting.agenda` (as `improvement.propose`): own words, credential-shaped text refused (the controller's text is redacted instead). Improvement proposals themselves stay with M03's `ImprovementService`; an observation is linked to one by promotion.
- **Owner by chat, in any words.** The status kind `observations` (project in focus; `observationKind` keeps one kind) lists the open ones with reports, owner, ID and revision, and the hour's storm count; `observation.dispose` settles one, with the revision filled in. The prompt sentence gives free-word examples. The worker's fixed part is unchanged (no bridge tool was added).
- **Tests.** `observations/observations.test.ts` (6 tests on each of the four backends: retellings, context-only sameness, cross-scope and readability, storm limits and the next hour, disposition, two controllers), `chat/observations-chat.test.ts` (the prompt, and the owner asking and settling by chat on each backend), `api/start-observations.test.ts` (the composed controller: a failed review and a denied request observed by themselves, an agent's retelling joining, a stranger refused, the status view, a restart). Mutation-checked on the built files: nine deliberate breakages (the provenance key per reporter, other projects' sources accepted, the hour limit off by one, the per-agent limit dropped, reads without a meeting right, any submission readable, a settled observation kept on the open list, a controller storm refused instead of counted, the failed-review hook firing on approvals) each fail a named test.
- **Runs** (Linux, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, after `npx tsc --build --force`, stale dist tests removed): `observations` + `status` + `chat` 1,662 of 1,662; `scripts/*.test.mjs` + `api` + `review` + `submissions` 1,311 of 1,313 with 1 skipped and one failure (the `status.ask` summary must name every status kind: `observations` added to it, then `api.test.js` and the B02 files 276 of 276); after that fix `scripts` + `chat` + `observations` 1,695 passed, 1 skipped. `check:deps`, `licenses:check` and `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` regenerated.

**NOT done (next slice):**
- Approval stalls and redundant prompts as sources: no hook exists yet. A stall is a review or needs-you item waiting past a time (the attention view or the review's deadline could feed it, from a dispatcher loop); a redundant prompt needs the chat or the approval load to recognise the same question asked again (the approval-load view counts asks, but nothing links two asks of the same thing).
- Other controller sources: attempt failures, recoveries (V02's stall concerns and recovery steps) and owner corrections in chat are not wired; `ObservationService.record` takes them when a later slice adds the hooks (each needs an event record to cite, or the source kinds list to grow).
- No worker bridge tool: an agent reports friction through the state API only; adding a tool would grow the worker's fixed part, which has almost no room left.
- No semantic matching: two agents describing the same friction in different words with no shared event record are two observations; a manager can promote both to one improvement proposal (or M03's grouping applies there).
- Nothing turns observations into lessons or triage (B03), and nothing removes old settled observations (retention has no rule for these kinds yet).
- The per-agent limit counts agents per hour in one list of at most 200; a 201st agent in the same project and hour is refused until the next hour.
- **First review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, with fixes, 2026-11-21; merged main `82207a3d` and later, interpreter prompt and notes conflicts kept both sides). (1) **Fixed: the storm counts started again at zero when the clock went back.** The rate record's hour was replaced whenever it differed from the current hour, so a controller whose clock is behind another's (or a clock set back) reset the hour's counts and both limits could be passed by alternating between two controllers. The hour now never goes back: a time before the recorded hour counts against the recorded hour (ISO UTC strings compared as text, no time zone involved), and the list shows that hour's counts. Test (four backends, clocks moved by the test only): a second service two minutes behind across 11:00, and the whole clock set back an hour, are both held at the recorded counts; the next hour starts new. (2) **Fixed: a reporter's own view showed other agents.** A reporter without the project's meeting rights saw only itself among the reporters, but the record's `owner`, every `history` entry's `by`, the first reporter's `detail` and the context records another reporter named were shown as stored. Now another principal is shown as "someone else", the detail only to the first reporter, and to later reporters only the event sources (which they could read to join). Readers and managers of the project's meetings, and the owner, see the whole record. `reports` (how many reports joined) is still shown. (3) The refusal texts said "try again after HH:59 UTC"; they now name the next hour ("after 12:00 UTC"), and an agent refused because 200 agents already reported this hour is told that instead of "you have reported 0". Checked and left: who may submit (meeting.agenda or meeting.manage, a task credential only for its own project, the owner), read and settle; missing, foreign and unreadable sources and observations refused with the same words; the hooks' stable command IDs after a restart; the two-controller race for one event (the loser's create conflict is retried and joins) and for the counters (one write with the rate record's revision); bounds (sources 10, reporters 20, history 10, page 100, open 500, rate list 200); chat `observation.dispose` is applied directly (it changes no work and is undone by reopening), the prompt sentence needs no fixed phrase; the new tests use no timers, paths or signals. A reporter beyond the 20 listed cannot read the observation (left; it still counts). **Mutation checks** (built files, each alone, restored byte-identical by SHA-256), each failed a named test: the hour allowed to go back; the reporter view showing the owner; showing another reporter's context sources; the event key made per reporter; the per-agent limit off by one; the failed-review hook only on rejections. **Runs** (Linux, `/tmp/nn-slot.sh`, `NIMBLENEWT_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=1`, offline guard, after `npx tsc --build --force`): `observations/observations.test`, `chat/observations-chat.test`, `api/start-observations.test` 34/34; neighbours integration `fixed-part-budget` and `t2-chat-budget-launcher` 6/6. Not run, by the reduced test-load rule (CI is the net): the rest of `chat/*`, `status/*`, `api/*`, `review`, `submissions` and `scripts/*.test.mjs`. `check:deps`, `licenses:check`, `roadmap:check` pass; `api-v1.md` unchanged by `api:docs:write`.
- **Second review** (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, clean context, with fixes, 2026-11-21; merged main `1e77a3ef`, `api/start.ts` status line and notes conflicts kept both sides). (1) **Fixed: a controller with a far-future clock held everyone's counts in its hour.** The hour-never-goes-back rule trusted any later recorded hour, so one controller whose clock was days ahead moved the rate record there and every other controller then counted against that hour until it came, never starting new counts (after 60, everything suppressed). A recorded hour more than a day ahead of a controller's own hour is no longer trusted: that controller's own hour is used and its counts start again; up to a day ahead still holds. Test: a controller three days ahead does not hold the others; one 23 hours ahead still does. (2) **Fixed: an agent that told an event first decided the controller's record of it.** An agent can cite its own review request before the decision (it is the requester); the owner's denial then joined the agent's friction, so the observation stayed kind `friction`, in the agent's words, without the denial's reason, owned by that agent, and was missing from the `correction` list. When the controller tells an event an agent told first, the controller's kind, summary, detail, sources and task become the record, `origin` and `reportedBy` become the controller's, and an owner the agent had only by reporting is dropped (a manager's choice is kept); the agent stays a reporter and its report counted, as when it tells the event after the controller. (3) **Fixed: agents could crowd out the controller.** Agents' new observations share the project's 60 an hour and 500 open with the controller, so a few agents reporting at their own limit made the controller's observations suppressed. Agents may now add at most three quarters of the hour's limit (45) and nine tenths of the open list (450); the rest is kept for the controller (joins are unchanged). (4) **Fixed: a later reporter saw the first agent's words.** The reporter's own view hid the first reporter's detail but showed its summary and the task its context records named; a later reporter of an agent-first observation now sees a placeholder summary and no task (the first reporter, readers and managers see everything; a controller summary comes from the event records and stays).
