- ASSUMPTION: a backup sealed for everything counts as a verified checkpoint on its manifest alone (said in the record), rather than failing every window of an encrypted installation or reading the owner's passcode.
- Still open after the review: a window whose release was activated stays quiet (paused) until the controller restarts into it and the launcher confirms it; nothing ends that wait on its own (the health deadline is still recorded only), though the owner can resume the installation by chat. A Suspend of an attempt cancels its local calls in flight (the dispatcher's own Suspend; ledger calls are never cut). Each held sweep still waits up to 10 seconds per attempt that will not go quiet. Two controllers on one PostgreSQL store are kept apart by the epoch and revision-guarded writes; a doubled checkpoint backup is possible if both reach that step in the same instant.
- **Second review (clean-context Claude agent, 2026-11-23).** Merged origin/main `db7757ca`. Problems found and fixed, each with a test:
    - An activated window keeps its pause and its suspended attempts until NimbleNewt next starts on the new release, and nothing restarts it in this slice; the owner was not told, so a switch at night with no restart left the installation paused with no notice. The window now files one needs-you notice ("A maintenance window waits for a restart": the release, that new work stays paused and how many attempts stay suspended, restart NimbleNewt to finish) at the first sweep after the switch whose outcome is still open, and records `heldToldAt` so it is said once; nothing is said when the start was already confirmed (4 backends).
    - The checkpoint used `backUpNow`, which hands back a backup already running: a scheduled backup that began before the installation went quiet would have been recorded as the window's checkpoint. `BackupService.backUpFresh` waits while any backup runs and then starts its own; the controller's checkpoint uses it.

It now carries the note "only its secrets are sealed: its files were checked, its secrets and the manifest's seal were not".

    - Mutation checks on built files, each restored byte-identical by SHA-256, all caught: restart notice repeated each sweep (4 failing), `backUpFresh` reusing the running backup (1), secrets-only note dropped (1), restore ignoring a Stop's takeover (4), restore lifting any freeze (4), sealed manifest not compared (1).

    - Checked and left: a window loop with stubborn attempts or a large backup can run past the dispatcher's 60-second loop bound; the tick then goes on and the loop is not started again until it ends (the scheduled backup loop behaves the same). The checkpoint is a `manual` backup, so the owner's backup scope (old scratch, transcripts and delivered-message logs left out) applies to it; state, configuration and artifacts are whole. While the window holds the installation pause, an owner who asks to pause is told it is already paused, and that pause is lifted when the window ends (the one-pause gate does not say whose pause it is); the owner can pause again afterwards. A freeze the owner lifts by hand before the window is quiet is set again by the next sweep.

## P09 owner view of the landing checks (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-23)

Plain words first. The owner can now ask, in any words, why a task's landing did or did not go ahead ("why did the importer work not land?", "what did the checks say?") and is shown, for the newest landing attempts, each required check and what it said, the tree and patch it was judged on, and whether the last look at the records right before the landing (the final re-read) changed or refused anything. Card P09 stays planned (see "Not done").

- **The view (`status.ask`, kind `landing_checks`).** Owner only (an agent, a task credential or a viewer gets nothing; the chat of an agent is refused before it is read). Asked as `{ kind: "landing_checks", taskId }` (in chat the task by its title, like the other task views) or, with no task, `{ kind: "landing_checks", projectId }` (the project in focus in chat); `after` is a count (how many attempts were already shown, never an ID or a name the model cannot know); five attempts per page, newest first, and the last line says what `after` to ask for next. For each attempt: its request record (ID, when it was made and finished, what became of it), the submission judged (the queue's head, or the one the request named), the checks required then, the integrated tree, base and patch and the test-command contract version, the overall verdict, then one line per check (`tests`, `review`, `qa`, `docs`, `director`, `defects`, and any check the policy names) with its result in words, the gate's own sentence, each test command with its state and exit code (never its output), a note where the author's own evidence disagreed with the gate, and a check judged on another tree than the integrated one. Then the re-read line, whether the owner was asked to set test commands, and which author was sent the results. A landing refused before any check says so and gives the request's own refusal sentence. Every line cites its `workspace-request` record.
- **What the final re-read found is now recorded (`WorkspaceRecordBody.rechecked`).** Before this slice the record kept the re-read's result only inside the results of a changed check and the refusal sentence; "found everything still passing" and "a check was newly required" left nothing. Now `rechecked` is `{ outcome: "unchanged" | "changed" | "added" | "unreadable", checks? }`, written in the same write as the request's outcome. Absent when the landing never reached the re-read (refused earlier, no check required, no re-read wired); the view says so in words. Records made before this slice have no `rechecked` and are shown as "was not made for this attempt", which is not claimed to be true of them; the view cannot tell the cases apart.
- **A per-task and a per-project index of landing requests (`workspace-landings`, `workspace-landings-project`).** The workspace service had no way to list a task's requests (only the open one and a refresh counter). The request's ID now goes to the front of both lists (once, cut to 20 for a task and 40 for a project) in the same write that finishes the request (`#settle`, with the existing retry on a lost race), so an index never names a request that is unrecorded. `WorkspaceOpService.landings(scope, after, limit)` reads it without a caller (the status view allows only the owner); an entry whose record is gone or belongs to another task or project is left out. A request that never finished (no outcome written) is not listed.
- **Safe output.** Texts the gate wrote go through the same `shown` cleaning the other views use (credential shapes cut, control and invisible characters escaped, bounded), and, new for this view, absolute host paths (POSIX folders of two or more parts, `~/` paths, drive paths and network paths) are replaced by `[a path]`, since a check's sentence can quote the path of the machine that ran the tests. Test output is never shown; neither are the lease, the host or any credential.
- **Chat reach (no magic phrase).** The interpreter prompt gained one sentence (`"Why did that not land?" or "what did the checks say?" reads landing_checks (the task by title, else the project)`) and the status list's own entry for the kind. Prompt size grew by 334 characters (153,455 to 153,789, within the 350 allowed); `prompt-room.test.ts` is pinned to 153,789. The chat resolves `taskTitle` as for the other task views (one exact match decides, several ask which, none refuses) and a request with no task takes the project in focus. `status.ask`'s summary and `api-v1.md` (regenerated) name the kind; the guide has a "Landing checks" paragraph and a status-kinds line asked through the real launcher and chat by `d01-user-guide.test.ts`.
- **Tests.** `workspace-ops-p09-view.test.ts` (real gate, workspace service, submissions and status service; controlled host): a passing landing, a re-read that changed a check, one that found a newly required check, one that could not read, a landing refused before any check, a failed run with a path, a credential and output planted (none shown), paging by count over seven attempts, bad requests refused, owner only, and a controller without the reader; each on all four backends (20 cases). `landing-checks-chat.test.ts`: the prompt sentence, then through the real chat and the real `ModelInterpreter` with a stand-in model on all four backends: by title, by the project in focus, the older page by count, an unknown title refused, an agent refused (5 cases).
- **Mutation checks (8, each applied, seen failing, restored).** (1) the owner-only test dropped (4 cases fail); (2) paths not hidden (4); (3) "unchanged" not recorded after the re-read (4); (4) the index written oldest first (8); (5) `after` ignored (4); (6) the chat not resolving a task title for the kind (4); (7) the project in focus not taken when no task is named (4); (8) "added" not recorded (4).
- ASSUMPTION (shape): one kind for a task or a project (exactly one of `taskId` and `projectId`; a request naming both or neither is refused) rather than two kinds, so the prompt grows by one entry only. Reversible: split the kind.
- ASSUMPTION (page size): five attempts per page. Each attempt prints about five to ten lines; five keeps one answer inside the chat's reading size. The indexes keep 20 (task) and 40 (project), which bounds the work of one read.
- ASSUMPTION (no backfill): landings made before this slice are not in the indexes and the view says "a landing made before this view existed is not listed" rather than scanning every request record ever made. A one-time backfill would need a full scan of the request store; left out. Reversible by adding that scan to a maintenance step.
- ASSUMPTION (test output): never shown, even redacted: the gate keeps only the end of each command's output, and that is what is most likely to hold a path or a secret. The command name, state, exit code and time-out are enough to tell what failed; the output stays on the request record for `workspace.get`.
- **Not done.** (1) A landing's refusal that happened before the gate (no host, the lease, the queue) shows only the request's own sentence, not a structured reason. (2) The view does not link an attempt to the task's later landing or say "the next attempt passed"; the owner reads the next line up. (3) `recheck` still cannot see a change that lands after the host was asked (unchanged; the first slices' limit). (4) A remote host answers no `landingChecks`, so its landings are refused before any check (unchanged). (5) No view over a specific request by ID (`workspace.get` already returns the whole record). (6) The prompt sentence was checked by a stand-in model only; no real model was asked (Radiance is off limits here).

### P09 owner view of the landing checks: first review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5 reviewing, 2026-11-23)

Plain words first. The view was sound in its access rule and in how its index is written (in the same write as the outcome, retried with the rest of that write when another landing of the project finishes at the same moment), but it could leave out or misdescribe some attempts and let some host paths through. Fixed:

- **Landings that ended with an unknown result were missing.** A landing left running by a controller that stopped is recorded as `uncertain` by the recovery sweep (`#markUncertain`), which did not add it to the indexes, so the view left out exactly the attempt the owner most needs to check. That write now carries the index change too (deduplicated, so the real outcome arriving later lists it once). Such an attempt has no check results recorded; the view had said "the project required none, or the landing was refused before the checks were asked", which is untrue for it. It now says no check result is recorded because the attempt ended before its outcome could be recorded.
- **Host paths that were shown.** `file:///...` and `file:/...` URLs, paths after a colon (`path:/srv/...`), relative paths leading out of the checkout (`../../x`, `..\..\x`), paths with mixed separators (`/home/rob\q/w`, the tail was shown) and paths with control characters in them passed through; `\\?\C:\x` came out as "[a path] path]". The rules now run file URLs, network and `\\?\` paths, drive paths, then absolute, `~` and `..`-led paths with either separator; `https://host/a/b` addresses and ordinary text (`pass/fail`, `1/2/3`) are left as they are. Linear on a 1.2 MB value (7 ms).
- **Paging and numbering when an index entry cannot be read.** The service skipped such entries, and the view then numbered attempts and computed the next `after` from the items it got, so the next page repeated attempts and "showing 1 to N" was wrong. `WorkspaceOpService.landings` now returns each item's position, the next `after` (past every entry covered, read or not) and how many entries were left out, and the view says how many were left out.
- **Truncation was not told.** With more than 20 (task) or 40 (project) landings the view said "20 landing attempt(s) on record". It now says only the newest 20 (or 40) are kept for this view, so older attempts are not listed.
- **The re-read line for an attempt without `rechecked`.** "was not made for this attempt" is now "No final re-read ... is recorded for this attempt", with the reason (the checks had already refused it) only when the record shows that.
- **Chat.** An interpreter that named a project beside a task title made the view refuse "not both"; the task now decides (the project gives way). The owner test also refuses a task-scoped principal explicitly (task credentials are agents, so this changes nothing today). A stray doc comment of `landingSettingsLines` was moved back to it.
- **Checked and left:** the index write is in the same command as the outcome, so a failure to write it fails the outcome write as any of that write's parts would (a lost race on it is retried with the outcome, up to the existing 20 attempts; the landing itself, the gate and the host call are unchanged and ordered as before). Two controllers on PostgreSQL: the same retry. The own-words guard for a task title is the one every task-titled view uses (the title is looked up in the focus project; nothing is read on no match or several).
- **Tests added** (`workspace-ops-p09-view.test.ts`, four backends): a landing recorded `uncertain` by another controller's recovery is listed with the right wording and listed once after its real outcome; two landings of one project that settle at the same moment (forced together at the host) are both listed; 41 landings show the 20 and 40 caps, the told truncation and the last page; seven path forms, each in its own short command name (one combined name had let a leak hide behind the 60-character cut), plus a web address that stays; index entries that cannot be read keep numbering and paging. Chat: a project named beside a task title reads the task.
- **Mutation checks on built files (10, each restored byte-identical by SHA-256, all caught):** no index on the uncertain path (4 failing), no index on settle (32), task cap 21 (4), no deduplication (4), file URLs not hidden (4), network paths not hidden (4, first missed; the test was then rewritten), next page from items read (4), truncation not told (4), uncertain wording dropped (4), chat keeping the project (4).

### P09 owner view of the landing checks: second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5 reviewing, 2026-11-23)

Plain words first. A landing could in principle go unrecorded because of the view's own bookkeeping: the project's landing index is one record that every landing of the project rewrites, and it was written in the same write as the landing's outcome, so a busy project used up the tries that record a landing. The outcome now wins: past its first tries it is written without the index, and the index entry follows on its own. Some host path forms were still shown (URL-encoded, look-alike slashes, home and environment names); they are now hidden.

- **Write path.** `#settle` keeps the index in the outcome's write for its first 12 of 20 tries; from the 13th the outcome (with the queue, commit and open-index records it is written with) goes without it, and `#indexAlone` then writes the entries in a command of their own (`workspace.landing-index`, command ID `<outcome's>:index`, five tries with a short jittered wait, never an error). `#markUncertain` does the same after its second try (it has five, with no wait). Kept as before: no orphan entries (an entry is only written with or after an outcome, never for a request that never finished), one entry per request (a later real outcome moves the `uncertain` entry to the front), and the landing order, queue and outcome are not changed by the index. What can now happen: a controller that stops between the outcome and its separate index write, or five more lost races, leaves that attempt out of the view; the landing itself is recorded. Before, the same contention could make `#settle` throw "could not be recorded" after the host had landed the work.
- **Paths.** `%2F`/`%5C` are read as separators and division, fraction and full-width slashes (U+2044, U+2215, U+29F8, U+FF0F, and the reverse forms U+29F5, U+29F9, U+FE68, U+FF3C) as plain ones before the path rules; paths led by `~`, `~user`, `$HOME`, `${HOME}` or `%USERPROFILE%` are marked even with a single part. Credentials are cut (`redactText`) before the paths are read, so reading `%2F` cannot split a credential the redaction would have found; `shown` cuts again after. Checked and left: drive-relative `C:Users\x` (no separator after the colon) is shown; a JSON-escaped `C:\\Users\\x` shows as `C:[a path]`. Each rule is linear on 400,000-character single tokens (about 10 ms).
- **Checked and found sound:** owner only, no existence answer to anyone else (a non-owner or task-scoped principal gets nothing before any read; an owner asking for a task or project that does not exist gets nothing); one view call reads the index, the task or project and at most five request records (no scan); passing is the gate's `passed`/`result`, never the author's evidence (shown only as a disagreement); states are named from the record (`done`, `refused`, `failed`, `uncertain`), and "required then" is the list judged at that attempt. Secrets in a command (`KEY=value cmd`, `--token sk-...`, a URL password) are already cut when the gate writes the record and again in the view.
- **Merge.** origin/main d29e4870 (chat gaps 2) merged: `start.ts` status wiring combined by hand (main's `disputes` and this card's `landingChecks`); prompt measured with a copy of the built prompt-room test at 154,471 characters (154,137 + 334), SIZE pinned there.
- **Tests added** (`workspace-ops-p09-view.test.ts`, four backends): a landing whose project index is refused on every try is still recorded `done` (a repeat answers it; the view lists nothing rather than something false), and one refused only on the tries that carry the index is recorded and listed through the separate write; the new path forms; a credential in a command name; and the view's own cleaning of raw text from a stand-in record. Leak checks use names that cannot occur in the random IDs on the same line.
- **Mutation checks on built files (7, each restored byte-identical by SHA-256, all caught):** index always in the outcome's write (1 failing); no separate index write after the fallback (1); `%2F` not decoded (1); look-alike slashes not mapped (1); home/environment-led rule removed (1); the view's redaction removed (1, caught after the stand-in record test was added); project cap 40 changed to 400 (1).
- **Re-check (clean context, 2026-11-23).** The write path traced again against main: the outcome record is the same with and without the index, the 20 and 5 tries are unchanged, a lost race, a thrown error, two controllers or a stop between the two writes either records the outcome once or fails as before, and the separate index write cannot throw into the landing or name a request without an outcome. Changed: `hidePaths` no longer decodes the text it shows. `%2F`/`%5C` and the look-alike slashes count as separators where they stand, so `50%2Fmonth` or `1∕2` outside a path reads as written (the first version showed `50/month`); a JSON-escaped `C:\\Users\\x` now goes whole with its drive letter. Tests added: the uncertain path under a busy project index (recorded `uncertain` when every index write is refused; listed through the separate write when only the first two are), and the wording outside a path kept. Six more mutation checks on built files, each restored byte-identical (uncertain index always joined; no separate index write on the uncertain path; settle index always joined; settle separate write dropped; separate write throwing; decoding put back): all caught. Still shown, as before this card: a path after a leading `//` (`//home/x`, `%2F%2Fhome%2Fx`), read as a protocol-relative URL.
## Q02 leftovers: vote cannot override an owner decision, required verdict citations, carry-over only by unchanged patch ID (Claude agent, Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-23)

Card Q02 stays planned (not flipped). Branch `card-q02-leftovers` off origin/main `dfcebde1`. Plain words first: three clauses of Q02 that a clean-context audit found open. (1) A test now proves, through the real review path, that a majority of reviewers and an adopted meeting vote cannot make a review pass over an owner decision. (2) The owner can switch on a project rule that every verdict must cite the criteria version (and a rejection must name the unmet requirement). (3) QA evidence and a reviewer verdict now carry over to a later submission only when the patch ID is unchanged.

- **(1) Vote versus owner decision.** The behaviour already existed (decisions are owner-only; approvals are refused while the task relies on a superseded or disputed decision). New: `submissions/qa-leftovers.test.ts` on four backends. All three reviewers of a project (a majority, in fact all) approve work bound to a superseded decision, cited and uncited: each is refused; a meeting-decision record "adopted, 3 yes" is planted and changes nothing; a request for changes is still recorded; only the owner's settled decision (the reliance made current again) lets a later approval stand, and a decision superseded again takes the next approval away again. ASSUMPTION: the meeting vote is a planted `meeting-decision` record, not a run of the whole meeting service (the point is that no reader of such a record exists in the review path; a real vote cannot write a decision, which `decisions/decisions.ts` states and tests).
- **(2) Required citations.** New project-policy field `requireVerdictCitations` (on the `qa-review-policy` record; absent in old records means off). Owner only (`qa.review.policy.set`, agents forbidden), read by `qa.review.policy.get`, shown on the `qa_policy` status line ("A reviewer's verdict must cite the criteria version it judged against" or "need not"). Scope as the rest of the policy (a task outside the scope is not asked). Enforced in `SubmissionService.record` for reviews through the new option `citationRequired` (wired in `api/start.ts` to `QaReviewService.requiresCitation`), after the repeat check: an uncited review of a task in scope is refused with `criteriaRevision` named; once cited, the existing rules apply (stale version, decisions in force, approval names every relied-on decision, a rejection names the unmet requirement). Chat: reachable in free words (the interpreter prompt names it in one clause, +89 characters in all, SIZE 153,455 to 153,544); the own-words guard `reviewPolicyForeign` refuses a model-supplied `requireVerdictCitations` unless the owner's message speaks of citing, criteria, decisions, requirements, versions, verdicts or rejections, and then asks which was meant; shown first, applied on the owner's yes.
- **(3) Carry-over by patch ID.** Until now evidence and verdicts were bound to one submission; P09 already bound approvals to the patch at landing, but a re-submitted rebase started with nothing. New: each code submission is added, in the same write, to a small `patch-lineage` record (task and patch ID; at most 20 IDs). `SubmissionService.carriedFrom(id)` answers the earlier submissions of the same task with the same patch ID (each re-read; never a later one). `approvalOf` answers with the newest verdict of such an earlier submission when the submission has no verdict of its own (`carriedFrom` says where it came from; a verdict of its own decides there). The QA gate (`QaEvidenceService`, new port `carriedFrom`) counts current independent evidence on such earlier submissions (`gate.carriedFrom` lists them); evidence that no longer holds (changed criteria, superseded decision) does not carry. Any change to the patch changes the patch ID, so nothing carries; a submission recorded before this slice has no lineage and nothing carries from it (fails closed).
  - ASSUMPTION (corrected by the reviews below): the patch ID is the submitter's word at record time. Recomputing the LATER submission's own patch at landing is not enough; a carried approval or carried QA evidence counts only where the landing gate's `review` / `qa` check has the host compute the EARLIER submission's own patch too (first review), and the landing queue takes a carried approval only where the gate checks the review (second review). Elsewhere (a release, the chat's approved-code lookup, a queue of a project that lands without the `review` check) a carried approval is not an approval.
  - ASSUMPTION: only current, still-valid evidence carries; stale evidence of the earlier submission is not shown on the later one.
  - ASSUMPTION: a carried approval is judged as the newest verdict list of the NEAREST earlier same-patch submission that has any review (no merging of lists).
- **Not done (said plainly).** The review request scheduler does not treat a carried verdict as settling a request; evidence carried over is not shown in the project QA view; a lineage older than 20 same-patch submissions drops its oldest; the composed controller wiring of `carriedFrom` is covered by the unit composition in the test, not by a separate end-to-end test; a real meeting vote run is not part of the vote test; the user guide has no sentence for the new option (the interpreter prompt and operation docs name it).
- **Tests.** `submissions/qa-leftovers.test.ts` (4 backends x 3 tests = 12); `api/start-qa-review-policy.test.ts` extended (chat proposal then yes, view line, enforcement through the composed controller); `chat/prompt-room.test.ts` pin 153,544. API docs regenerated.
- **First review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-23).** Plain words: the carry-over could let code nobody reviewed land, because the landing gate checked only the later submission's own patch claim, never the patch of the code the reviewer actually saw. Fixed, with five smaller rules.
  - **Problem (fixed): a carried approval was not tied to the reviewed code.** The ASSUMPTION above ("the landing gate recomputes it, so a false claim can inherit only until landing") did not hold. The gate computed the patch ID from the base and tree of the LANDED submission only. So an author could submit harmless code under the patch ID of a different change, have it approved, then submit the different change honestly under that ID: its own claim matched, and it inherited the approval. Now the landing gate asks the host (new `carried` on the host call, answered as `carriedPatchIds`, at most 20) for the real patch ID of each earlier submission of the same claimed patch (new dep `samePatch`, wired to `SubmissionService.carriedSources`). A carried approval, and each piece of carried QA evidence, passes only when that earlier submission's own base and tree make the same patch as the landed one; otherwise, or when it cannot be computed, the check fails. The read-again before the write uses the same answers, so a verdict that starts to carry from a submission the host did not check is refused. Test: `landing/landing-gate-carry.test.ts`, worker `landing-checks.test.ts`.
  - **Problem (fixed): a release took a carried approval as a review-gate permit.** A release recomputes no patch ID, so a carried approval would have made a permit commit of a tree nobody reviewed. `workspace.request release` now refuses an approval that is carried (`review_invalid`, "no review of its own"); the automatic release does nothing for one; the chat's approved-code lookup does not offer it. Such a submission lands through the landing checks or after a review of its own. The `submissions` view says the approval was carried and how it is checked. Test: `workspace-ops-h12o-permit.test.ts`.
  - **Problem (fixed): a reviewer could carry its own approval onto its own submission.** A reviewer that approved an earlier copy and then submitted the same patch itself was shown as approved by itself. A carried approval given by the later submission's own submitter is now not an approval ("another reviewer has to approve it"), and carried QA evidence recorded by that submitter does not count (it is a self-check there).
  - **Problem (fixed): an older rejection could be hidden.** The verdict carried was the one on the nearest earlier submission with any review, so a rejection given later on an older copy of the same patch was ignored. Now the newest verdict given on any earlier copy of the patch carries (by its time).
  - **Problem (fixed): same-millisecond submissions.** "Earlier" was decided by `submittedAt`, so two submissions recorded in the same millisecond each counted the other as earlier. Now the lineage order (the order the writes were made in) decides; a submission dropped from the 20-entry lineage has nothing to inherit.
  - Checked and left: the lineage write is in the submission's own write with a revision check, so two controllers on PostgreSQL serialize on it; carried verdicts and evidence are re-read every time, so an approval taken back or evidence invalidated later stops carrying; director sign-offs and document checks never carry; nothing crosses tasks (the lineage key and every entry name the task). The later submission's author now sees the carried verdict of an earlier copy of the same task (it was shown to the owner and the earlier author only); left, as it is the same task and the same code. The own-words guard for `requireVerdictCitations` accepts broad words ("requirement", "decision", "version"); left, since the proposal is always shown for the owner's yes.
- **Second review (Claude agent, Opus 5.5, 2026-11-23).** Plain words: one more way for unreviewed code to land on a carried approval was found and closed; the patch ID itself was checked and holds.
  - **Problem (fixed): the landing queue took a carried approval at its word.** A project with a landing branch lands only queued, approved work, and the queue asked only `approvalOf(...).approved`. Where the project's landing does not require the `review` check (the `autonomous` profile requires only `tests`; an owner can drop `review` too), nothing ever compared the earlier, reviewed submission's code with the queued one, so a false patch-ID claim could still queue and land code nobody reviewed. Now `LandingQueueOps` counts a carried approval only when the new `reviewChecked(projectId, taskId)` says the landing gate requires `review` for the task (wired in `api/start.ts` to the gate's own required-checks function, now shared as `landingRequiredChecks`); absent, false or throwing, the carried approval is "not approved" in the queue (adding, the controller's own queueing, the landing, the bounds round). It is read at every use, so an owner who drops the check after the work was queued gets a refused landing. An approval of the submission's own is unchanged. Tests: `landing/landing-queue-carry.test.ts` (4 backends, plus the option absent) and `api/start-q02-queue-carry.test.ts` (the composed controller: `integration.set` to `tests` alone refuses the carried approval in the queue, with `review` it is queued). `landing/landing-gate-carry.test.ts` now also covers a host that answers fewer patch IDs than asked (the unanswered submission fails, never borrows another's answer).
  - Checked and held: `git patch-id --verbatim` over a `--binary --full-index --no-renames` diff changes with whitespace, a file mode, a symlink made from a file with the same bytes, and binary content (tried by hand on git 2.53), so an unchanged patch ID means an unchanged change (context-only differences are the intended rebase). A host that answers fewer, no or malformed `carriedPatchIds` fails the carried check (matched by the controller's own list position; extra answers are ignored); remote hosts have no `landingChecks`, so nothing carried passes there; both sides stop at 20. Evicting the oldest lineage entries only removes what can carry (a rejection on an older copy can drop out only together with, or after, every approval older than it on an older copy; an approval on a newer copy is that copy's own and landed the same before this slice).
  - Checked and left: a document's landing check treats code whose QA gate passes as tested, and that gate counts carried evidence; the `qa` check proves carried evidence at landing, but a project that requires `docs` without `qa` takes the QA gate's word there (it decides only whether a document is pending, not whether code is tested at landing).

## W05 follow-up: the checkout is looked at again after the checks ran (2026-11-24)

W05 was already built and reviewed twice, and later slices closed its other open items (the host's attribute neutralizing, a remote host's done check, PLAN.md). One item was still open: the host looked at the checkout once, before it ran the contract's checks, while the checks run in that same checkout and a parallel tool call can write to it too. So a check (agent-written test code) or a parallel call could remove the evidence file or the change after the look, and the done would still pass on the old picture.

- **What changed (`worker/src/host/local.ts`, `doneVerifier`).** When a done carries checks, the host looks at the checkout a second time after they ran. The done never gains from the second look: an evidence file that is gone is not present, the count of changed paths and of commits ahead is the smaller of the two looks. A second look that fails turns every passed check into not-run and every evidence item into not present, so the controller refuses the done with the list and counts it toward the W03 go-on limit as before. No new field in the protocol; a remote host runs the same function.
- **Tests.** `worker/host/done-check.test.ts` (+1): unchanged, evidence and change removed, build output added, second look failing, no checks (one look only). Six mutants (smaller changed, smaller ahead, evidence loss ignored, passed checks kept on a failed look, failed look keeps evidence, second look skipped): each failed the test; restored byte for byte. Run: worker `host/done-check`, `workspace/local-host`, integration `w05-done-verify`, controller `dispatch/done-verify`: 68 of 68; `npx tsc --build --force` clean.
- **Owner controls:** none. This card adds no owner-facing setting, so nothing is added to the chat interpreter prompt and the prompt size pin is unchanged.
- ASSUMPTION: files a check only adds (build output, a dirty tree) are not read as a failure, because many ordinary test commands write untracked files and a strict "unchanged" rule would block every such task; the done is judged on the smaller counts and on evidence present at both looks. A parallel call that only adds dirt on a host where the agent commits is not caught by this.
- **Not done / only the real-model run (W09) can prove:** that real agents' checks and tool calls do not run into this in practice, and the rate of dones refused by it. Still open from before: a check can change the checkout without being seen by a count (rename of a file with the same count); the agent controls the code a check runs (review reads the change).
- **First review (2026-11-24).** Problem (fixed): a second look that failed reported every evidence file as not present, so the agent was told the file "is not a plain, non-empty file of your checkout ... Write it there and name it again", which was untrue and sent it to rewrite a file that may well be there. Now an evidence file the first look found is left out of the report when the second look fails, and the controller says it could not be looked at (a "could not be checked" item, still refused and counted toward the W03 go-on limit as before); one the first look did not find stays not present. Hardened: the two looks' evidence is matched by path, not by place in the list, and a path the second look does not name is left out (not known to be there) instead of keeping the first look's "present". New end-to-end test in `integration/w05-done-verify.test.ts`: in the real sandbox, a check that deletes the evidence file (the whole change) and exits 0 gets the done refused for no change and the missing evidence, with no host path in the refusal. Eight mutants on the built `local.js` (second look skipped, either count not the smaller, max instead of min, evidence loss ignored, passed checks kept on a failed look, present evidence kept on a failed look, a missing second-look entry kept): each failed a test; the skipped look and ignored loss also failed the end-to-end test; restored byte for byte by sha256.
  - Checked and held: remote hosts run the same `doneVerifier` through the responder, and the controller's `reportOf` already accepts a shorter evidence list (no protocol change). Removal, emptying, or replacing the evidence with a link or folder by a check is seen; a check that creates evidence missing at the first look does not help the done. The local layout's git directory is outside the sandbox, so a check cannot commit there; on a host where the agent commits, `ahead` takes the smaller count. The look uses the same bounded `GitBridge.doneState` (each git step capped at 120 s, at most 30 evidence paths); a second look doubles that cost, and a host slower than the controller's 60 s margin past the check times ends in a refusal ("could not check"), never a pass.
  - Left as before: a parallel tool call can still change the checkout after the second look (the submission is staged from the checkout as it then stands and reviewed); a check that only adds files, or rewrites tracked files (a formatter), is not refused, by the ASSUMPTION above; a rename that keeps the count is not seen; evidence that only a check writes is not present at the first look and the done is refused (unchanged from W05).
- **Second review (2026-11-24).** Problem (fixed): when the second look failed, a passed check was reported not-run with the reason "the checkout could not be looked at again after the checks ran", and the controller prints that after "could not be run by the host:", so the agent read that its check never ran. The reason now says the check ran and passed, that its pass is not taken because the checkout could not be looked at again, and that calling work.end again checks again. Test gap (fixed): no test covered checks without required evidence (the most common contract), so skipping the second look there went unseen; `done-check.test.ts` now covers it, and also that a failed check stays failed (not turned into not-run) when the second look fails. Seven mutants on the built `local.js` (failed checks also turned not-run, old reason wording, path match ignored, the second look's dirt count taken, second look only with evidence, first-look-missing evidence dropped on a failed look, the second look's reason for a missing file dropped): all seven fail a test now (the fifth survived until the new test); restored byte for byte by sha256.
  - Checked and held: evidence names are checked by the controller before the host sees them (`work-end.ts` `EVIDENCE_PATH`: relative, `/` only, no drive letter, no empty, `.` or `..` part, at most 30 entries, each item once; the controller also asks each path once), so absolute, `..` and Windows-separator paths and over-long lists never reach `doneState`. Evidence is read from the tree `git add -A` makes, so a link (also a parent folder swapped for a link), a folder, a nested repository (a gitlink), an empty file and a file an added ignore rule now hides are all not present at the second look; a check that writes and then deletes the evidence is refused. Contract check names are unique (at most 10), so the controller's lookup by name cannot read one check's pass for another's failure. On a case-insensitive disk a different letter case of the evidence name is not the same path (refused, fail closed, unchanged from W05). A worker without the second look sends the same report shape and still works. One look over this repository takes about 0.4 s, so the second look is small against the controller's 60 s margin (local and remote).
  - Left as before: a "could not check" verdict (for example a second look that failed) counts toward the W03 go-on limit like any refused done; that is W05's existing rule for a host that cannot check, it bounds the retries (the attempt ends blocked with the list for the owner), and changing it is a controller policy change outside this slice. The count of changed paths is compared, not the paths themselves: a check that removes the agent's change but writes the same number of non-ignored files (or more) keeps the "has a change" item passing; required evidence still catches the removed files, and the checks themselves ran against that checkout.

## W04 follow-up: variant C nudge fix (2026-11-24, branch `card-w04-nudgefix`, off main `da42e304`)

**Why.** In the real variant C batch 20261124T052216 the nudge said "end with nimblenewt__work-end as your last call", but the bench agent (Pi command line; tools bash, read, write, edit) has no such tool (B's prompt says so). In 5 of 12 contaminated runs the agent hunted for it right after a nudge: `env | grep PI_` found `PI_EVAL_CONTINUATION_FILE` and `PI_EVAL_CONTINUATION_CONFIG` (which `pi-agent.mjs` put in its environment), then it read `continuation.json`, `continuation-config.json` and its own `prompt.md` in the run's results folder, or searched `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json`; one run wrote `work-end-report.txt` into the results folder, so the folder was writable from inside the sandbox.

**Done (offline, no model calls).**
- Wording: where the extension is loaded (`pi-agent.mjs`), the nudge is the bench's command-line wording: the two work-end sentences ask for a final report whose first line states the result (done, partial or blocked) / blocked or partial, and the last sentence says a reply that is not a final report does not end the work. Bound, mark, cut-off lead and everything else are the worker's, read from the built pi-adapter; `packages/pi-adapter` is untouched and its wording test still passes. A worker text that no longer has the replaced phrases stops the agent before the first request (never a silent pass-through); a result still naming the tool is refused. `continuation-used.json` holds the exact words that ran; the record's `continuation` carries `wording` and digests.
- Environment: the settings reach the extension on a descriptor (an unlinked file as Pi's descriptor 3, taken only if it is a regular file of the bench's kind, then closed). `pi-agent.mjs` removes `PI_EVAL_CONTINUATION_*` from Pi's environment (Windows keeps them: no descriptor can be passed there).
- Results folder: the agent writes into a per-run output folder (`iso.out` in its own fresh folder) and the runner copies it out; its prompt is given from there too. In the sandbox the results folder is hidden (whole, or this run's artifacts alone when something the agent keeps is inside it). Verified offline with the real Pi and the stand-in server: its shell sees no `PI_EVAL_CONTINUATION` or `continuation` in its environment, no open bench file among its descriptors, `ls`/`cat` of the run folders fail, and a write into the results folder never reaches the host.
- Classifier: `~/` and `$HOME` in a call are the run's fresh home (`ownHomeText`; `foreignPaths` too), so reading its own `~/.pi/agent` no longer flags the run as owner credentials. The owner's real paths (`/home/rob/.ssh`, `~rob/...`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, the team's key folder) are still flagged, and without a sandbox home the old reading stands.

**Not done / what only a real run shows.** Whether the agent now ends with a report after a nudge, and how often, needs the real model (card W09). The agent can still read what any same-user process can (for instance the parent's `/proc` entries) if it hunts for it; this fix removes what it found by ordinary means, it does not make the bench unreadable to its own agent. The results of the first batch stay as recorded (C rows before this fix carry no `wording`).

**Not done: near-copy checkout paths.** A run's own checkout path mistyped by one character is still read as another checkout. I found no rule that is safe: a one-character difference between two real checkouts (`eval-work/…-r1` and `…-r2`) is the normal case, so any tolerance would hide real contamination. ASSUMPTION: leave it; such a run stays flagged and is read by hand.

- ASSUMPTION: the sentence "A reply without a tool call does not end the work" is replaced in the command-line wording, since for this agent a final report is a reply without a tool call and ends the work; keeping it would contradict the new ending.
- ASSUMPTION: the output folder is copied out whole (except the runner's own files) so test agents' own report files keep working.

**Review (2026-11-24, before the real C run).** Compared every path of `da42e304` with the branch; the real Pi was checked through the bench's sandbox, key proxy and bridge against the stand-in server (no model calls). Fixed: (1) the runner's `continuation-config.json` (the worker's words, naming `nimblenewt__work-end`) sat in the agent's output folder, which the agent can list as `~/../out` and find through `PI_EVAL_ARG_CLEAN_FILE` in its environment: `pi-agent.mjs` now removes it once read (the run's artifacts keep the runner's copy); (2) a text that sets HOME (`HOME=/home/rob cat ~/.pi/agent/auth.json`, `env HOME=`, `export HOME=`) or runs as another user (sudo, su, runuser, doas, pkexec, machinectl) had its `~`/`$HOME` read as the sandbox home and was not flagged: such a text is now read as the owner's; (3) the output folder is copied after leftover processes are stopped, and also when a bench error ends the run after the agent started; `setup.log` and `agent-stderr.log` are runner-owned like `prompt.md`. Tests for each; 11 mutation checks, all caught. Left as they were: variant B's (and so C's) prompt names the tool on purpose, to say it is absent; the bench's own scripts (readable to the agent, as before) name it; `ln -s /home/u/.pi x` and `/proc/self/environ` were not flagged before this card either.
## wsb-repair: every `wsb` command through a one-shot scheduled task; the runner's own group in the G05 base check (2026-11-24, Claude agent; separately scoped authorization from Rob)

Why: in the own-hardware job (run 45097817234) `wsb list` ended after about 30 s with a gRPC timeout to localhost:80 in every launch that stays under the job's own process, but a one-shot scheduled task run in the signed-in session (variant 5) answered in one second. Consequence: no sandbox capacity, the real Sandbox tests failed, G05 did not run, Y02 passed 7 of 8, and the cleanup said "G05 BASE LEFT ALONE".

**Done (all proven offline with injected launchers; Windows cannot be run here).**
- **The launch (`worker/src/sandbox/windows-task-launch.ts`, `windows-task-child.ts`, `windows-real.ts` `runWsb`).** Every `wsb` command the product runs (list, start, exec, stop) now goes through `runWsbCommand(host, ...)`, which uses the host's `runWsb` when it has one and its plain `run` otherwise (so every test that injects a launcher or simulated host keeps its direct path). The real host's `runWsb` makes a private folder for the call (checked with the same access-list rule as the records folder: not a link, changeable by no other account), writes the request there as data (program, argument list, working folder, limit), and runs a fixed PowerShell helper that registers and starts a one-shot task for the same user (interactive; the run level was Highest when written and is Limited since 2026-11-24, see "Run level: Limited, from a measured result"). The task runs this program's own `windows-task-child.js` with the folder as its only argument; the child runs the command with an argument list (no shell, so no quoting of the Sandbox configuration text) and writes `started.txt` first, then `out.txt`, `err.txt` and, last and by rename, `code.txt` with the whole unsigned exit code. The helper waits for `code.txt`, the task's end, or the limit (the command's limit; a task that has not begun within 20 s is stopped), always removes the task (in `finally`, and the caller checks and deletes it again), and the folder is removed in `finally`. The helper's own limit is the command's plus 30 s.
- **When each launch is chosen (`launchWsb`).** `NIMBLENEWT_WSB_LAUNCH`: `auto` (default; also any unknown value) tries the task and falls back to the direct call ONLY when the command provably did not start (the task could not be registered or started, never began within 20 s, the helper could not run, the private folder was not believed private, or no folder is configured) and `started.txt` is absent; `direct` never uses the task; `task` never uses the direct call. Off Windows the direct call is always used. Once the child has begun, there is never a second launch and never a direct call: start, exec and stop are not retried (only `wsb list` is called again, by `listSandboxes`, as before: up to three calls, each through the strategy). A helper that hung with no answer is reported as "cannot be said whether the command ran", also with no direct call.
- **What the owner sees.** Plain sentences without a path, folder or account, for example "the Windows Sandbox command was run through a one-shot scheduled task in the signed-in session but did not end within 30 s and was stopped", or, when the task is switched to only: "the Windows Sandbox command was not run: the scheduled-task launch is not available (the task could not be registered (error 0x80070002)) and the direct call is switched off". The way each call was launched (and why the direct call was used) is kept in the result's `via` and shown in the `wsb list` record (`call 1: ok after 1204 ms (through a one-shot scheduled task ...)`).
- **The variants script answers unambiguously (`scripts/wsb-launch-variants.mjs`).** Its scheduled-task variant now runs a batch file that writes wsb's own exit code to a file; the line ends with a fixed verdict: SUCCESS only for exit code 0 read from that file (and then says whether a list was printed or the empty list, which is the right answer when no sandbox is running), FAILED with the code otherwise, "NOT an answer" when the task ended but wrote no exit code. In run 45097817234 the variant's 1-second "answer" was read from the task's own last result only, so whether it was a success with an empty list could not be told from a silent failure; this removes that doubt for the next run.
- **One line for a failing `wsb list` (`scripts/wsb-list-line.mjs`, workflow step `wsblist`).** After the context step the workflow prints one line built from the product's own path: each `wsb` call it made (how launched, how it ended, how long) and the outcome (`OK: the list answered ...` or `FAILED: no list could be had`). Fixed words and numbers only, through the credential scanner and the log redaction; it always exits 0 and the outcome step does not read it. The evidence job's limit went from 420 to 480 minutes (the new step has 25).
- **The G05 base-folder check (`windows-records.ts`, `windows-cleanup.ts`, `scripts/wsb-cleanup.mjs`).** `recordDirProblem` now notes, in a redacted form, who could change the folder (well-known system accounts and the runner's group by name, every other account as `account 1`, `account 2`, the running account as "the account running the cleanup"), and does not count the runner's own built-in group as "another account" when ALL of: its bare name matches `GITHUB_ActionsRunner_<letters and digits>`, it belongs to THIS machine (the part before the backslash equals the machine name), and Windows reports its members (`Get-LocalGroupMember`, read-only, name only) as only the running account or none. The cleanup prints `G05 base access evidence: ...` lines, so the next run shows the evidence whether or not the base is trusted.
- ASSUMPTION: the group name pattern alone is not believed, because the group could also hold another account that could then change the base folder. A group whose members cannot be read, or whose members include any other account (a service account, for example), stays "another account" and the base stays left alone, now with the evidence printed to show which. This is the safest reading of "by prefix AND membership evidence"; if the next run shows the group holds the runner's service account only, the answer is a one-time fix of the runner's folder (the paragraph in own-hardware-runners.md), not a looser rule.
- ASSUMPTION: the private folder for each call lives under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\NimbleNewt\wsb-task` (or `NIMBLENEWT_WSB_TASK_DIR`), where the account's own access list applies; it is a fresh folder per call, removed afterwards. A task that begins after the launcher gave up and removed the folder runs nothing (the child needs `in.json`).
- ASSUMPTION: a task that does not begin within 20 s is counted as never started (nobody signed in, or the Task Scheduler service not answering), so a direct call is allowed; a small race remains if the child starts in the instant between the helper's last look and its stop (then the helper's answer says "not begun" but `started.txt` appears: that case is tested and is treated as begun, with no direct call).

**Tests.** `worker/sandbox/windows-task-launch.test.ts` (23: the real child on a request, exit codes above 2^31, arguments with quotes, percent signs and XML kept as data, every unavailable and begun case, no direct call once begun, no retry, cleanup of folder and task, the helper text pins, mode choice, `wsb list` called up to three times through the strategy, the child's request validation, the G05 group rules and the redacted evidence); `worker/sandbox/windows.test.ts` (+3: start, exec, stop launched through the strategy once each, a failed start never launched twice, a host without a strategy still works through `run`); `scripts/wsb-launch-variants.test.mjs` (+1, others adjusted), `scripts/wsb-list-line.test.mjs` (2), `scripts/evidence-workflows.test.mjs` (+1, limits adjusted).
**Mutation checks (10 on built dist files, each restored byte for byte and checked by sha256; all caught).** Start launched by the plain run (3 tests fail); the "began" proof ignored (2); the direct fallback allowed after an answer (4); the machine-name check of the group removed (2); the member check removed (2); the task's removal removed from the helper (2); an exit code written for a command with no code (2); the via note dropped from the list record (2); the "no exit code is not an answer" verdict removed (1); the `task` mode made unreachable (2). Two first attempts were not caught (the began-proof mutation left other evidence in place, and a child mutation that was equivalent); a test (the marker appearing after the helper gave up) and a stronger mutation closed both.

**NOT done / only a real Windows run proves it.** That the task registered by the helper actually starts in the runner's interactive session and that the child (node) there reaches `wsb` the same way the batch file of variant 5 did; that `Get-LocalGroupMember` answers for the runner's group and what its members are; that the private folder passes the access-list rule under the runner account (when it does not, the launch falls back to the direct call and says why in the `wsb list` line); what the G05 base's access list really contains (the next run prints it). Nothing about the machine, the runner, installs or secrets was changed. The next own-hardware dispatch decides: read the "wsb list (product launcher)" line, the scheduled-task verdict of the variants record and the "G05 base access evidence" lines.

**First review (2026-11-24, Claude agent).** Problems found and fixed, with tests:
- `wsb exec` could never run through the task: the backend gives exec a 24-hour limit, but the child refused any request over one hour, so it ended before `started.txt` and `auto` quietly used the direct call (and `task` mode always failed). The child now accepts up to 48 hours; a test sends an exec-length request through the child.
- "Never started" is now a proof, not a timing judgement: the child claims the request by renaming `in.json` to `claimed.json` before anything else, and the launcher withdraws it (`in.json` to `withdrawn.json`) before it counts the command as not started. Only one rename can succeed, so a task that begins after the 20 s grace time (or after a helper error or a stop that did not take) runs nothing, and a claimed request with no `started.txt` yet is reported as "cannot be said whether it ran", with no direct call. This replaces the small race the earlier ASSUMPTION described. Because the withdrawal proves it, a helper that hung before anything began now allows the direct call (it used to report "cannot be said").
- The task's trigger ended ten minutes after registration, and Task Scheduler deletes expired tasks, which could come before a long exec ends. It now ends ten minutes after the command's own limit. A failed look at the task while waiting (Get-ScheduledTaskInfo) no longer ends the wait, which would have left a running command unwatched with no exit code. The wait looks once a second after the child began (200 ms before).
- A task still registered after the helper is now ended (`schtasks /End`) before it is deleted, because deleting a task does not stop its running program.
- The call folder must be new: a folder that already exists is not used (the real host makes the last level without `recursive`), so a folder prepared in advance cannot be adopted.
- `Everyone` and `CREATOR OWNER` are shown by name in the redacted evidence (they are not accounts of a person).
- Considered and kept: the helper is fixed text, and all names reach it through the environment; the task action takes only the node path, child path and folder, which are checked to hold no `"`, `%`, line breaks or NUL; the command, arguments and working folder travel only in `in.json` and are run with an argument list. [Superseded 2026-11-24, see "Run level: Limited, from a measured result": this said Highest gives the task the same rights as the elevated runner's direct call and that the minimum level was unproven; a measured run then showed Highest failing and Limited answering. Kept as history.] The runner-group rule relaxes only for a group of this machine whose members Windows reports as only the running account or none. Nested groups, unreadable members, other machines' or domain groups and different letter case all keep the old refusal. Adding a member later needs an administrator, who is already trusted.
- Mutation checks (9 on built dist files, each restored byte for byte and checked by sha256; all caught): the withdrawal failure ignored; the child's limit back to one hour; a pre-existing folder accepted; no `/End` before `/Delete`; the trigger end back to ten minutes; the look at the task without its catch; the child not claiming the request; a hung helper counted as done; `Everyone` not well known.

**Second review (2026-11-24, Claude agent, clean context).** Problems found and fixed, with tests:
- The helper could never register the task on a real Windows machine: it built the task's time limit with `New-TimeSpan -Milliseconds`, a parameter Windows PowerShell 5.1 (`powershell.exe`, which the launcher runs) does not have (only -Days/-Hours/-Minutes/-Seconds; -Milliseconds came with PowerShell 6). With `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` the helper stopped before `Register-ScheduledTask`, so every call was "unavailable" and `auto` silently used the direct call (the repair would have changed nothing; `task` mode always failed). It now uses `[TimeSpan]::FromMilliseconds(...)`. A test pins the full list of cmdlets the helper uses, so a new one is looked at on purpose.
- At the command's limit the helper stopped the task at the same moment the child's own limit fell (the child counts from its own, later start), so the task was normally stopped first. Stopping a task ends only its program (the child), not what the child started, so `wsb` could keep running unwatched and the partial output was lost. The helper now waits a margin (`CHILD_MARGIN_MS`, the start grace plus 10 s, so also a child that began late reaches its own limit first) past the command's limit before stopping the task; the child stops the whole tree itself (taskkill /T) and writes the partial output. The helper's own limit is the command's plus 75 s (was 30 s) to hold registration, the margin, stopping and removal. Worst case for the cleanup's `wsb list` (three calls, each possibly followed by the direct call) stays near 14 minutes, under the step's 25.
- Only the call folder was checked to be private, not the folder it is made in. An account allowed to delete or rename entries of the base folder (with no inherited write on the call folder) could swap the call folder for its own after the check. The base folder is now checked as well (after it is made on the first call).
- A shared folder of a job could include the scheduled-task launch's base folder (for example a home or work folder at or above `%LOCALAPPDATA%\NimbleNewt`), which would let the guest change a request before the task runs it. `admit` now refuses such a share like one reaching the supervisor's files; the base is found the same way in both places (`wsbTaskBase`: `NIMBLENEWT_WSB_TASK_DIR` when set and not empty, else under LOCALAPPDATA).
- A request with a limit over the child's 48-hour maximum would be claimed and then refused by the child, which reads as "cannot be said whether it ran"; it is now turned away before anything is made (one constant shared by launcher and child). A task that ended without claiming the request is reported as "the task ended before the command began" instead of the start-grace text.
- Considered and kept: renames of `in.json` within one folder are atomic on NTFS (MoveFileEx); when either rename fails for a sharing violation (antivirus holding the file), the child runs nothing and the launcher, if its own withdrawal fails, says "cannot be said" and makes no direct call, so both failures are safe. Task Scheduler expands `%` in action arguments, which `PLAIN` refuses; `& ^ '` and non-ASCII are not special there (no shell). The child runs the verified absolute `wsb.exe` path with an argument list (no PATH search, no shell), with the same UTF-8 decoding and 16 MiB cap as the direct call. A short (8.3) or linked base path counts as a link and makes the task unavailable (direct call in `auto`). A controller crash leaves at most one folder and one task per call: the task's only trigger lies in the past (it does not fire again) and Task Scheduler deletes it ten minutes after the command's limit; the folder stays, harmless, in the private base.
- Mutation checks (8 on built dist files, each restored byte for byte and checked by sha256; all caught): `New-TimeSpan -Milliseconds` back; the helper waiting only to the limit; the base folder not checked; no upfront limit check; the ended-before-began reason dropped; `admit` ignoring the task base; the margin not passed to the helper; the margin not above the start grace.
- The own-hardware cleanup step gets 40 minutes (was 30): each failing `wsb list` is now a little longer through the task; the job limit (480) stays above the sum of the step limits (425) plus 30.
- Only a real Windows run shows: that the helper now registers and starts the task under 5.1; whether stopping the task leaves `wsb` running (the margin makes it moot in the normal case); that `Get-LocalGroupMember` answers for the runner's group.

**Second review re-check (2026-11-24, Claude agent, clean context).** One fix, with tests: `wsbTaskBase` returned `NIMBLENEWT_WSB_TASK_DIR` (or the `%LOCALAPPDATA%` path) as written, while the shared folders it is compared with in `admit` are normalised, so `D:/nn/task` or `D:\nn\.\task` missed the overlap check although the call folders are made there. The base is now `win32.normalize`d with trailing separators dropped, and only a folder below a drive's root or below a UNC share is taken (not a root, a relative or rooted-without-drive path, or a `\\?\` / `\\.\` device path); anything else gives no base, so the task launch is not used and `admit` has nothing to guard (consistent: both use the same function). Checked and kept: every cmdlet, parameter and .NET call of the helper exists in Windows PowerShell 5.1 with the ScheduledTasks module, with no PowerShell 7 syntax; `-RunLevel Highest` needed an elevated runner and a non-elevated one failed at registration (the safe "nothing ran" path); [superseded: the helper now registers at Limited, which needs no elevation, see "Run level: Limited, from a measured result"]; the trigger's boundaries are local time without an offset on both ends; every limit passed is whole seconds, so ExecutionTimeLimit has no fraction; the base folder is made by `mkdirp` before its one check. Mutation checks on built dist files (each restored, sha256 checked; all caught): no normalisation; the base folder's privacy result ignored; the task base left out of `admit`'s guarded list.

### Run level: Limited, from a measured result (2026-11-24, card wsb-limited)

**What was measured.** An agent on the owner's Windows PC measured this today (its brief was `docs/nimblenewt/windows-box-agent-instructions.md`):
- `wsb list` from a NON-elevated Git Bash answered in under 1 s; from an elevated Git Bash (high integrity) it answered in 0.4 s.
- From an elevated PowerShell (direct, and through cmd, powershell, node and `start /wait` children) it FAILED after about 30 s (a gRPC timeout to localhost:80, exit 0x80131500), 5 of 5.
- A one-shot scheduled task registered at run level **Limited** (same user, interactive logon) ANSWERED in 1.3 s with task result 0 and cleaned up. The same task at run level **Highest** FAILED after about 31 s, also with this repository's own `wsb-launch-variants.mjs` task variant, from both elevated shells, every time.
- Registering at Highest from a non-elevated shell fails at registration (0x80131500). A Limited task needs no elevation.

**What changed.** The fixed PowerShell helper (`windows-task-launch.ts`) registers the task with `-RunLevel Limited`, the minimum, and never Highest; a test pins the run level to Limited, counts exactly one `-RunLevel`, and fails if "Highest" appears anywhere in the helper. The rest of the protocol is unchanged (claim and withdraw, `started.txt` and `code.txt`, margins, cleanup, the fall-back rules). In `scripts/wsb-launch-variants.mjs` the scheduled-task variant (5) now registers at Limited and is the verdict-bearing one; a sixth variant, `scheduledTaskHighest`, records the Highest task for comparison only, with the same exit-code-file verdict and clean-up, so the next run shows both side by side. The script builds both helpers from one text that differs in the run level word only (a test pins that). Time: the whole run's limit is now 460 s (worst case 4 x (45 + 15) for the plain variants plus 2 x (45 + 64) for the two tasks = 458 s, so all six can be tried even when each runs to its limit); the workflow step "Record the job's process context before wsb" has 15 minutes (240 s context script + 460 s + a minute for starting node = 760 s of 900 s), the sum of step limits rises by 5 minutes (430) and the job's 480 minutes still exceeds it by more than 30 (a test checks this).

**Not known (no cause is claimed).** Why an elevated PowerShell and a Highest task fail while an elevated Git Bash and a Limited task answer. The measurements show the pattern only.

**ASSUMPTION:** Limited is enough for `wsb list`. `wsb start`, `exec` and `stop` at Limited are unproven; a Windows run shows it (the product's own one-line record and the Sandbox tests of the own-hardware job). A failed Limited registration (or a task that provably did not start) falls back to the direct call exactly as before in `auto` mode; `task` mode still fails. The direct call from an elevated runner may time out as measured; nothing here changes that.

**Review (2026-11-24, Claude agent, clean context).** One fix, with a test: both task variants of `scripts/wsb-launch-variants.mjs` wrote their helper answer to the same `task.json`, so if the Highest helper wrote nothing (stopped at its limit, or powershell not started) variant 6 would have reported variant 5's registered/started state. Each task variant now has its own answer file (`<variant>.task.json`); a test has the Limited helper answer and the Highest helper stay silent and checks that line 6 says "no answer from the helper" and that the two helpers get different answer paths (it fails with the shared file). Checked and kept: no product code, workflow or doc still registers at Highest or assumes an elevated task; a failed Limited registration still gives the unchanged "nothing ran" fall-back. The private-folder check (`recordDirProblem`) reads who can change the folder, not its owner, so a call folder owned by Administrators (made by an elevated job) or by the user (made by a non-elevated job) passes alike when no other account can change it, and the Limited child writes there through the user's own inherited entry; if it could not, the claim and withdraw renames keep the fall-back safe (no claim: withdrawn, direct call; claimed but `started.txt` not written: "cannot be said whether it ran", no second run). `schtasks /Query`, `/End` and `/Delete` run from the job's own process on a task the same user registered. The limits recomputed from the code: plain variants 4 x (45 + 15) = 240 s, task variants 2 x (45 + 25 + 15 + 3 x 8) = 218 s, 458 s within 460 s; context 240 s + 460 s + 60 s = 760 s within the step's 15 minutes; the job's step limits sum to 430 minutes against 480. Variant 6 runs after variant 5 and with its own task name and files, so it cannot change variant 5's verdict; its helper is bounded by its limit plus 25 s and the same removal checks and expiry. PowerShell 5.1: only the `-RunLevel` value changed (`Limited` is a TaskRunLevel value). Mutation checks on built dist files (each restored, sha256 checked; all caught): the helper back to Highest; the "claimed but not started" guard removed; the private-folder check ignoring other writers.
- **X09b watch tests, date dependence fixed (2026-11-24).** Three X09b watch tests (long host name, restart, escaped host name) failed on the exhaustive run of main 37ec6de7 on every operating system, and passed on the run before. Cause: the tests set the controller's dispatch clock to a fixed date (2026-11-17) but left the notification service on the real clock. The notice retention (7 days, `#expireNotices`) is counted on the notification service's clock, so once the real date was a week past the fixed one, the sweep closed the new notice as old and the owner's inbox did not show it; no product code was wrong (in a running controller both clocks are the real one). Found by running the file with the fixed date moved to 2026-11-24 (all pass) and by dumping the inbox (the notice was settled, only an unrelated stall notice remained). Fix: the test rig passes the same fake clock to `notifications`, and a new test runs with a clock 30 days behind the real date so a stale date cannot bring this back. ASSUMPTION: a test-only change is right, because the dispatcher and the notification service sharing one clock in production is already the case; no product behaviour changed. Other tests with fixed past dates were not found failing: all 240 `api` test files plus notifications and release tests pass (1,546 of 1,546). Breakages of my own on built files (restored, checksums equal): the rig's notification clock removed (4 tests fail, including the new one), the timed-out notice label emptied so it is refused (3 fail).

- **Tests that go red only because real time passes: sweep and fixes (2026-11-24).** After the X09b watch failure (a fixed past date next to a part that reads the real clock), every compiled test file was run with the machine's clock moved forward (a preload outside the repository that offsets `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, file times and child processes by +30 days and by +400 days). Covered: all 1,030 compiled test files of `config`, `contracts`, `registry`, `ui`, `worker`, `pi-adapter`, `integration` and `controller` (203 in the small packages, 827 in `controller` in twelve batches of 70) at +30 days and again at +400 days, the 29 `scripts/*.test.mjs` files at both shifts, and the 27 test files that name a date from 2027 on at +2200 days (2032). There is no `apps` folder. What failed with a moved clock but passes today, and is a real defect: (1) `security/access.ts`: `allows`, `allowsExactly` and `requireAction` judged a grant's end time by the machine's clock when the caller gave no time, although the principal carries the time its rights were loaded as of (`asOf`, from the controller's own clock). The toolbox-maintainer list therefore dropped an agent whose grant ended on 2026-12-01 as soon as the real date passed it, however the rig's clock was set (`catalog/toolbox-maintainers.test.ts` would have gone red on 2026-12-01). Product fix: the default time is now `principal.asOf` (in a running controller that is the same moment, to the millisecond; an explicit `now` still wins; a principal with no `asOf` is still refused). New `security/access-clock.test.ts` (3 tests, both dates far in the past of any real run); the maintainer test's grant now ends a day after the rig's clock and before any real run, so it holds only if the rig's clock is used. (2) `api/start-qa-evidence.test.ts` asserted that an observation dated 2027-01-01 is "in the future": red from 2027-01-01; it now uses two days after the real clock the controller runs on. (3) `api/start-chat.test.ts` used 2030 as the end of owner-confirmed rights, which are refused once past: red from 2030-01-01; it now uses 2099. Moved-clock failures that are NOT defects (the rig of the sweep, not the code): the six files that start a TLS server with a certificate made from `new Date()` (`transport/http`, `remote/transport`, `mcp/http-client`, `dependencies/resource-read`, `integration/h12k-composed-host`; OpenSSL reads the real clock, so the certificate looked "not yet valid"); file times and child processes needed the preload to follow the moved clock, after which `thinking-purge`, `workspace` and `sandbox/containment` passed. All of them pass with no shift. Not covered: PostgreSQL's own clock (no SQL `now()` is used in product code), and real expiry of an operating-system certificate. ASSUMPTION: defaulting to `asOf` is right rather than keeping the machine clock as the default, because `asOf` is by definition the time the rights were judged as of, and the machine clock disagrees with it only in rigs. Mutation checks (each restored, build repeated): the access default put back to the machine clock: `access-clock` 1 test fails and the maintainer test 4 fail with no shift at all; the QA literal put back: 1 fails at +400 days; the chat 2030 dates put back: 1 fails at +2200 days. Runs after the fix: the four changed files 41/41 with no shift, at +400 and at +2200 days; the 293 test files of `controller` `security`, `catalog`, `policy`, `projects`, `api`, `lifecycle`, `dependencies` pass with no shift.

  **Review (2026-11-24, Claude agent, clean context).** The default of `asOf` was not safe for a principal kept longer than one request, and is replaced. Where principals come from: every request (state API, web door, conversation adapter, task credentials, `PrincipalService.current`) takes a new one through `effectiveOf`, whose `asOf` is always the controller's clock (never a caller's value), so for those the change made no difference. But the dispatcher's own service principal is authenticated once in `composeDispatch` and passed to every dispatcher loop tick for the life of the controller (`loop.run(this.#deps.principal)`; only the stall scan and the automatic recovery step read it again), and a few service principals are built by hand with a fixed past `asOf` (meeting floor 2026-01-01, maintenance 2026-11-11). With `asOf` as the default, a grant with an end that was in such a snapshot would have held until the next restart (loaded 10:00, grant ends 10:30, still allowed at 12:00); with the machine's clock it ended on time. No current check was found that reaches an expiring grant through the kept dispatcher object (its `recovery.*` checks use a principal read again each tick), so this was a latent gap, not a live one. Fix: `allows`, `allowsExactly` and `requireAction`, given no time, judge expiry by `expiryTime`: the controller's clock at the moment of the check, read from the loader that took the snapshot (`effectiveOf` registers `runner.now` beside the object in a `WeakMap`, so the principal stays plain data and a rig's fake clock is still respected), and never earlier than `asOf`. A principal with no registered clock (built by hand, or a spread copy) is judged at the later of `asOf` and the machine's clock, which is the old behaviour or stricter. Later is always the stricter answer here: a snapshot's grants carry only an end; a grant record's `notBefore` is applied when the snapshot is taken, so a grant not yet valid then is not in it, before or after this change. An explicit `now` still wins; a principal with no `asOf` is still refused. Not changed (as before this card): a kept snapshot does not see a revocation, a new restriction, an idle lapse or a parent grant ending after it was taken; that is the documented contract of `GrantService.effective` ("call it again"). `security/access-clock.test.ts` rewritten: 5 unit tests (a kept principal loses the grant when its loader's clock passes the end; a clock set behind `asOf` does not revive it; hand-built and spread-copy principals use the machine's clock; explicit time wins; no `asOf` refused) and, on all four storage backends, a principal authenticated once and kept while the rig's clock moves past its grant record's end (refused, as are a new one and `current`). Breakages on built files (each restored, sha256 equal): the default back to `asOf` alone (6 of the 37 tests in `access-clock` and the maintainer file fail, among them the kept principal on every backend), the loader clock ignored in favour of the machine's (11 fail), the floor at `asOf` removed (2 fail), `effectiveOf` no longer registering its clock (8 fail: the backend tests and the maintainer test). Runs after the fix (no clock shift): controller `security`, `catalog`, `policy`, `projects`, `lifecycle`, `dependencies`, `health`, `agents` 2,360/2,360; `api` 729/729; `dispatch` 1,601/1,601; 19 other folders whose tests make grants 2,701/2,701; `chat` and `meetings` 2,723/2,723.
